raw_record.support_text: A prospective analysis of 1,033 adult patients enrolled in the United States Acute Liver Failure Study Group through July 2007 demonstrates that acetaminophen overdose accounts for 46% of acute liver failure cases, followed by indeterminate ALF (15%) and idiosyncratic drug reactions (12%). Acetaminophen overdose is also described in the paper as the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States and Western countries.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (deliberate or excessive exposure); injury reported as acute liver failure (ALF), the leading US cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose accounts for 46% of 1,033 consecutive adult ALF cases in the ALFSG (through July 2007). Spontaneous recovery was highest (~58-64%) among acetaminophen overdose, HAV, and pregnancy cases; overall survival was 67% at 3 weeks (46% spontaneous improvement, 25% emergency transplantation). Early N-acetylcysteine therapy and supportive care improve recovery; regulatory actions were recommended to prevent future cases. Incidence appears to be increasing. Reported clinical phenotype: acute liver failure (fulminant hepatic injury with coagulopathy and encephalopathy).

raw_record.support_text: The ALFSG showed that nearly 50% of acetaminophen-related acute liver failure occurs without overt suicide intent (non-intentional acetaminophen overdose). Most of these patients ingested more than the maximal daily recommended dose of 4 grams/day, about half reported ingesting only 4 to 10 grams/day, and 38% ingested a multitude of products. 95% received NAC, and spontaneous survival was similar to patients with intentional overdose (64% vs 66%). Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is described as the leading cause of acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Non-intentional (unintentional) acetaminophen overdose; amounts generally exceeded the 4 g/day maximal recommended dose, with roughly half of patients ingesting 4-10 g/day and 38% ingesting multiple acetaminophen-containing products.
raw_record.extra_details: Nearly 50% of acetaminophen-related acute liver failure in the ALFSG occurred without suicide intent; these patients had more advanced encephalopathy at presentation, presumably due to frequent narcotic administration; spontaneous survival was 64% vs 66% compared with intentional overdose patients; 95% received NAC. In the UK, blister packaging and restricted dispensation reduced intentional overdoses and liver transplantation referrals; the FDA proposed labeling changes for OTC acetaminophen- and NSAID-containing products.

raw_record.support_text: The AKRENDO1 trial assessed the dose–response relationship of five oral doses of the AKR1C3 inhibitor BAY1128688 relative to placebo for endometriosis-related pain. The trial was prematurely terminated after hepatocellular drug-induced liver injury was detected in two participants, one of whom fulfilled Hy's law criteria, indicating a safety profile that precludes further clinical development of BAY1128688.
raw_record.extra_details: Trial prematurely terminated after detection of hepatocellular DILI in two participants, one fulfilling Hy's law criteria. ALT increase >3xULN seen in 8 of 90 BAY1128688-treated participants, with increases observed relative to cessation of treatment in seven of these eight; no hepatotoxicity observed until after 8 weeks of exposure across dose groups, consistent with the preceding 4-week multiple-dose phase I trial. A separate, dose-related early elevation in total, direct, and indirect serum bilirubin (up to ~2xULN, peaking weeks 1-8, not associated with aminotransferase elevations) was described as 'isolated' and was not classified as DILI; the limited number of completers prevented inferential statistics, so no efficacy conclusions were drawn.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone was reported to cause severe drug-induced liver injury in two patients treated for hyperuricaemia. A 58-y-old male treated for hyperuricaemia developed fever, jaundice and hepatic encephalopathy after 7 months of benzbromarone (unstated dose), with AST 736, ALT 1168, AP 792 and γGT 1102 IU/L; hepatic encephalopathy and increased PT ensued and liver biopsy at recovery showed fibrosis and bile-duct-like structures. A 53-y-old female took benzbromarone 100 mg/day with allopurinol for 2 months and developed fulminant hepatic failure (AST 3090, ALT 1140 U/L, PT 26.5 s); a positive lymphocyte stimulation test for benzbromarone was reported, she underwent living-related liver transplantation after failed haemodiafiltration/plasma exchange and died of sepsis 3 months later, with liver biopsy showing massive centrilobular necrosis consistent with fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were treated for hyperuricaemia/gout; one case (female) co-administered allopurinol with benzbromarone, and benzbromarone was used for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia in three of the four patients in the paper's case series.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (58-y-old male): onset after 7 mo, unstated dose; mild fever, malaise, anorexia, dark urine, pruritus, jaundice; total bilirubin 135 mg/L, AST 736, ALT 1168, AP 792, γGT 1102 IU/L; HBsAb positive but other hepatitis virus markers negative; LST for benzbromarone negative; co-medications allopurinol, tocopherol, niacin, alprazolam, theophylline, azelastine, nilvadipine; condition deteriorated despite stopping benzbromarone, with hepatic encephalopathy and prolonged PT; treated with prednisolone 30 mg/day, plasma exchange and haemodiafiltration; recovery biopsy showed fibrosis, bile duct-like structure, lymphocyte aggregation, nuclear enlargement. Case 2 (53-y-old female): benzbromarone 100 mg/day plus allopurinol for 2 mo; diarrhoea, nausea, anorexia, fatigue, jaundice; albumin 2.5 g/dL, AST 3090, ALT 1140 U/L, LDH 945 U/L, AP 123 U/L, total bilirubin 233 mg/L, NH3 160.6 µg/dL, PT 26.5 s; HAV/HCV/EBV/CMV negative, autoantibodies negative; LST positive for benzbromarone; massive centrilobular necrosis on biopsy; death from sepsis 3 mo after transplant. Paper also estimated incidence of benzbromarone-induced hepatotoxicity in Europe at approximately 1 in 17,000 treated patients (based on ~5 fulminant hepatitis cases over 1995-2000 among ~84,000 treated patients), possibly higher in Japan.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone has caused published cases of hepatotoxicity (four published cases of hepatitis), and the drug was removed by Sanofi-Synthélabo because of hepatotoxicity. Risk factors for hepatotoxicity are difficult to determine because only a few cases are available for examination, and the four published cases do not indicate the rate at which the hepatitis developed.
raw_record.extra_details: Four published cases of hepatotoxicity/hepatitis attribute injury to benzbromarone at therapeutic urate-lowering doses; the drug was removed by Sanofi-Synthélabo because of hepatotoxicity; risk factors are hard to determine from the few available cases; using the drug only for recurrent gout (not asymptomatic hyperuricaemia) would have prevented three of the four published cases of hepatotoxicity; monitoring of liver function tests was recommended because the cases do not indicate the rate at which hepatitis developed.

raw_record.support_text: Iproniazid, initially developed for tuberculosis and approved by the FDA for depression in 1958, was reported in several published cases of hepatic injury. In 1959, Zimmerman et al reported 86 patients who developed jaundice while receiving iproniazid; most had hepatocellular injury with a mortality rate of about 20%, and in most cases ALT or AST levels were above 7x ULN while ALP was not higher than 2x ULN in nearly 60%. Iproniazid was withdrawn from the market in 1961 due to hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from the US market in 1961 due to hepatotoxicity; initial indication tuberculosis and subsequently depression; 86 jaundiced patients reported by Zimmerman et al in 1959; most cases had ALT/AST >7x ULN and ALP not higher than 2x ULN in ~60%; mortality rate ~20%.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first thiazolidinedione approved in the US for type 2 diabetes in January 1997, was followed by numerous reports of severe liver injury and several published reports of acute liver failure. Clinically significant liver injury was estimated to occur in ~1:10,000 recipients, and the drug was withdrawn from the US market in March 2000. In combined North American clinical trials, ALT elevation >3x ULN occurred in 1.9% of troglitazone-treated patients versus 0.6% of placebo recipients, and two troglitazone-treated patients had ALT >3x ULN plus total bilirubin >2x ULN consistent with Hy's law.
raw_record.extra_details: First thiazolidinedione approved in the US, licensed for type 2 diabetes January 1997; numerous reports of severe liver injury and published reports of acute liver failure; clinically significant liver injury estimated ~1:10,000 recipients; withdrawn from US market March 2000. Retrospective analysis of combined North American clinical trials: ALT>3x ULN in 1.9% (48/2510) vs 0.6% (3/475) placebo; ALT>10x ULN in 0.5% (none in placebo); ALT>20x ULN in 5 patients (0 placebo); peak ALT typically delayed to 3rd-7th months; treatment discontinued for abnormal liver tests in 20 patients (0.8%); 2 patients met Hy's law criteria; placebo group had higher incidence of any ALT elevation, possibly due to beneficial effect on steatosis.

raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor developed for prevention and treatment of thromboembolic conditions, had its pending FDA and EMA marketing applications withdrawn in February 2006 due to reports of abnormal liver tests and DILI during clinical trials. In trial data, 7.9% of treated patients had ALT >3x ULN versus 1.2% of the comparator group; combined ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN occurred in 37 patients (0.5%), 11 of whom had no alternative cause, and one of these patients sustained severe liver damage with liver failure and eventually died.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral direct thrombin inhibitor for prevention/treatment of thromboembolic conditions; pending FDA and EMA applications withdrawn February 2006 due to abnormal liver tests and DILI in clinical trials; ALT>3x ULN in 7.9% vs 1.2% comparator; combined ALT>3x ULN plus TBL>2x ULN in 37 patients (0.5%), 11 with no alternative cause, one of whom had severe liver damage with liver failure and died; already approved in several European and South American countries at time of FDA withdrawal; animal studies and primary human hepatocyte cultures showed no hepatotoxic effects even at concentrations considerably above therapeutic plasma levels; cellular mechanism unknown.

raw_record.support_text: Over 6 years, 2533 children with acute liver disease were identified, 48 of whom had toxic hepatitis and 40 exhibited DILI, including 22 paracetamol-related and 14 albendazole-related cases. Type of injury was hepatocellular in 70% of patients (mostly paracetamol toxicity), cholestatic in 11%, and mixed in 19% (albendazole-related). Coagulopathy was identified only in the acetaminophen group. Applying the DILI severity index, 81% were mild and 19% moderate-severe/severe, with no deaths reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric cohort; overdose of acetaminophen leading to dose-dependent/intrinsic injury; coagulopathy confined to the acetaminophen group.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 of 40 pediatric DILI cases were paracetamol-related; mean time from drug ingestion to diagnosis 25.4 h; hepatocellular injury pattern; mean initial ALT 1020 U/L for all DILIs; median hospitalization 6.9 days; no deaths. Mechanism described: CYP2E1-mediated NAPQI formation, GSH depletion, mitochondrial oxidative stress, hepatocyte necrosis and acute liver injury, potentially life-threatening.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that albendazole administration commonly causes elevation of liver enzymes that normalize after drug discontinuation, with few reported cases of obstructive jaundice and rare cases of acute liver failure and fulminant hepatitis. The mechanism is not well established and is considered an idiosyncratic reaction involving immunological processes. In the authors' cohort, patients who developed DILI secondary to albendazole ingestion had received the correct medication dose for an appropriate time with one exception (10 days of administration), so individual immunological specifics are considered responsible. Coagulopathy was identified in 21% of these patients. Paragraph 48 adds that RUCAM scores for the albendazole-related group ranged from 10 to 13 points for all patients, confirming a high likelihood of medicine-associated liver disorder; per the R ratio, injury was hepatocellular in 70% of cases, cholestatic in 11%, and mixed in 19%.

raw_record.extra_details: Liver enzyme elevations return to normal after drug discontinuation without complications. RUCAM scores ranged from 10 to 13 points for all patients. R-ratio-derived injury pattern: hepatocellular 70%, cholestatic 11%, mixed 19%. Pediatric posology 15 mg/kg/day up to a maximum daily dose of 800 mg; adverse reactions usually occur with prolonged therapy (>7 days) and high doses and are mostly mild and transient. Coagulopathy in 21% of affected patients. Mechanism considered idiosyncratic, involving immunological processes. Literature: few reported cases of obstructive jaundice, rare acute liver failure and fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that, similar to phenytoin, carbamazepine is associated with idiosyncratic DILI and that adverse liver reactions are well recognized in carbamazepine users, unrelated to serum concentration and indication. The type of injury is approximately as often cholestatic as hepatocellular, and reported pathology includes ductopenia, hepatic necrosis, granulomatous hepatitis, and immunoallergic hepatitis. Analysis of published case reports of carbamazepine-associated liver injury shows that all fatal or transplant cases were hepatocellular type with hepatic necrosis, and that children and longer therapy duration were associated with poor outcome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Serious hepatotoxicity described in children; deaths most common in children under 5 years of age; longer duration of therapy (median 30 weeks in fatal cases vs 4 weeks in recoverers) was associated with poor outcome.
raw_record.extra_details: Analysis of 60 published case reports (reference 20): 10 death/transplantation versus 50 recovery; all death/transplant cases were hepatocellular type (8/8) with hepatic necrosis 100%, versus hepatocellular in only 12/30 recoverers (P=0.0005). ~5-10% of carbamazepine users have asymptomatic liver test elevations; ~60% GGT elevation and 10-15% ALP elevation (unusually high values should raise suspicion of ductopenia). Swedish pharmacovigilance in the 1970s-1980s reported 10% of adverse effects were liver reactions; SADRAC review 1970-2007 found 15% involved the liver. Median 5 weeks from treatment start to hepatotoxicity diagnosis. Two major manifestations: immunoallergic reactions with generally good outcome and metabolically induced injury that can lead to irreversible damage; the 10,11-carbamazepine epoxide metabolite and reactive arene oxide implicated.

raw_record.support_text: From 1998 to 2003, the ALF Study Group prospectively collected 610 detailed patient histories, including 262 cases of acute liver failure caused by acetaminophen (APAP, N-acetyl-para-aminophenol), an over-the-counter (OTC) drug product. These APAP patients had a median age of 36, median recorded peak ALT of 4310 IU/L, peak serum total bilirubin of 4.3 mg/dL, and 67% survival without transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: Between 1/06 and 9/09, 6 of the 7 cases of DILI attributed to duloxetine in the DILIN Prospective Study were assessed as definite or very likely. Median patient age was 49 years, 6 (86%) were women, median latency from drug initiation to DILI onset was 50 days, 6 patients developed jaundice, and the median peak ALT in the 5 patients with acute hepatocellular injury was 1633 IU/L. Ascites developed in 1 patient and acute renal dysfunction in 2 others. All patients recovered without liver transplantation even though 3 had pre-existing chronic liver disease, and liver histology in 4 cases demonstrated varying patterns of liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Seven subjects (~1% of ~600 sequential cases) in the DILIN database had suspected hepatotoxicity from duloxetine. In six cases duloxetine was the only implicated agent with causality rated either definite (n=2) or very likely (n=4); all patients showed improvement in liver test abnormalities during follow up, none required liver transplantation, and no deaths were reported. Five patients had a hepatocellular pattern, two a cholestatic pattern, and three had underlying chronic liver disease (hepatitis C, alcoholic liver disease, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Three of the seven patients had underlying chronic liver disease (hepatitis C, alcoholic liver disease, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis), and one patient admitted significant alcohol consumption; one additional series case had multiple suspect drugs (causality scored 'possible').
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 7 patients (median age 49 years, 86% women) enrolled 2006-2008 at three DILIN sites; six cases attributed to duloxetine alone were scored definite (n=2) or highly likely (n=4), while one case with multiple suspect drugs scored 'possible'. Median time to onset of symptoms or laboratory abnormalities was 50 days (about 6-7 weeks). Hepatotoxicity appeared more common at 60 mg daily than 30 mg (5 vs 2). Three patterns: three patients had severe acute hepatic necrosis with precipitous aminotransferase rises and extrahepatic organ damage (bone marrow or kidney) with rapid recovery; two had cholestatic hepatitis; two had ALT/AST elevations with no or minimal jaundice. Two patients with acute hepatic necrosis developed concurrent acute renal injury, one requiring hemodialysis; one patient had bone marrow suppression (thrombocytopenia and mild leucopenia). Four of seven cases considered severe with evidence of hepatic failure or accompanying bone marrow/renal failure; all recovered, no liver transplantation and no deaths. Skin rash, fever, eosinophilia and immunoallergic/autoimmune features were uncommon. One patient with underlying liver disease developed new onset ascites. A prior published case report of duloxetine hepatotoxicity (reference 9) was less compelling because the patient also received concomitant mirtazapine.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine was developed as antiviral therapy for hepatitis B infection. In a phase II study, fialuridine caused severe toxicity: irreversible acute hepatic failure in 7 out of 15 patients, myopathy, myoglobinuria, severe lactic acidosis, and neuropathy after 9–13 weeks of treatment. Five out of 7 participants with severe hepatotoxicity died and two survived after liver transplantation. Preclinical toxicology studies in mice, rats, dogs, and primates gave no indication that FIAU would be hepatotoxic in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II study in hepatitis B patients; irreversible acute hepatic failure in 7/15 patients, with myopathy, myoglobinuria, severe lactic acidosis, and neuropathy after 9–13 weeks of treatment; 5 of 7 patients with severe hepatotoxicity died, 2 survived after liver transplantation. Histology showed prominent microvesicular fat with chronic active hepatitis and variable macrovesicular steatosis, little hepatocellular necrosis, without substantial serum aminotransferase elevations; electron microscopy showed markedly swollen mitochondria with loss of cristae, matrix dissolution, and vesicular inclusions. Mechanism (mechanism 1, mitochondrial impairment): inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma by the triphosphate metabolite leading to mtDNA depletion. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, dogs, and primates showed no hepatotoxicity signal.

raw_record.extra_details: HLA-B*57:01 carriers have ~80-fold higher risk (odds ratio = 80.6; Daly et al. 2009). Reactions driven by drug-specific activation of CD8+ T lymphocytes; flucloxacillin-responsive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from DILI patients characterized, and naive CD8+ T cells from volunteers expressing HLA-B*57:01 are activated by flucloxacillin (Monshi et al. 2013). Covalent modification of flucloxacillin is thought to be a prerequisite for injury and modifies specific lysine residues on human serum albumin; the relationship between adduct formation, immune activation, and liver injury is not yet defined.

raw_record.support_text: During the Berlin Case-control Surveillance Study, eight cases of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) associated with flupirtine were identified, all leading to hospitalisation. Based on the RUCAM scale, two cases were classified as highly probable, five as probable, and one as possible; only the seven cases judged at least probable were examined. The liver damage was hepatocellular in all cases (based on ratio R and liver biopsies showing liver cell necroses without cholestasis), three patients developed acute liver failure, and two developed hepatic encephalopathy. Discontinuation of flupirtine was followed by ALT normalisation in five patients within the first two months.

raw_record.support_text: The study analyzed 57 cases of nimesulide-induced liver injury (nimesulide-DILI) from the Spanish and LATIN DILI registries, with causality assessed by the RUCAM scale. Mean age was 59 years (86% women), median time to onset 40 days, 46 patients (81%) were jaundiced, and the injury pattern was hepatocellular in 38 (67%), mixed in 12 (21%), and cholestatic in 7 (12%). Twelve patients (21%) developed acute liver failure, five (8.8%) died, and three underwent liver transplantation; mean transaminases were ~20x ULN, and the authors concluded nimesulide-DILI is associated with ALF and death in a high proportion of patients, making its risk/benefit ratio unfavorable.

Median time to recovery 60 days. 12/57 (21%) developed acute liver failure; 5 (8.8%) died, 3 underwent liver transplantation, 4 resolved. It highlights the severity of this reaction, which frequently results in acute liver failure and death, and that a shorter duration of therapy is not associated with a less serious outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Twelve cases of liver injury due to olanzapine have been described in the literature, affecting both males and females with a mean age of 48 years (range 17-78) and a mostly hepatocellular pattern of liver injury, although cholestatic cases have also been reported. Most cases were asymptomatic, but some involved jaundice and hypersensitivity features (rash, fever, eosinophilia). Time to onset varied from a few weeks to up to 3 years after therapy initiation; most cases resolved rapidly (within a few days to up to 4 weeks) after drug discontinuation, and no cases of acute liver failure were described. Rechallenge of olanzapine 2 months after a cholestatic hepatic injury led to recurrence with aminotransferase elevation more than two times the ULN, prompting discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: 12 published cases (mean age 48 yr, range 17-78, both sexes); mostly hepatocellular pattern although cholestatic cases reported; some cases had jaundice and hypersensitivity features (rash, fever, eosinophilia); time to onset from a few weeks to up to 3 years after initiation; most resolved within a few days to up to 4 weeks after discontinuation; no acute liver failure cases described; rechallenge after 2 months elicited recurrence with ALT >2x ULN prompting discontinuation. Pharmacokinetics: extensively metabolized by CYP1A2, CYP2D6 and flavin-containing mono-oxygenase system; lower doses recommended in renal/hepatic impairment and elderly. Separate finding: asymptomatic transient aminotransferase elevations in up to 10% of olanzapine-treated patients in trials (label, especially early in treatment), 26.9-30% of patients in retrospective chart reviews (up to 60% in 17 children), and elevations >2-3x ULN in 1.8-7.6% of patients.

raw_record.support_text: Flupirtine is described as the first in-class selective neuronal potassium channel opener used for pain, and the paper states that its use can be associated with severe drug-induced liver injury (sFILI). The injury is framed as severe idiosyncratic flupirtine-induced liver injury; the paper also notes that since its 1984 approval in Germany over 12 million patients were exposed, that increased reports prompted a 2013 EMA safety re-evaluation examining nearly 600 case reports including 49 cases of liver failure with 15 resulting in liver transplantation or fatal outcome, and that in the reported cohort a case with fatal outcome occurred despite NAC treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Approved in Germany in 1984 with reportedly >12 million patients exposed. EMA/PRAC/310015/2013 safety re-evaluation in 2013 examined nearly 600 case reports including 49 cases of liver failure with 15 resulting in liver transplantation or fatal outcome. Reported management with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and prednisolone; two patients with late NAC/prednisolone start developed hepatic encephalopathy and required liver transplantation, while remaining patients recovered without long-term sequelae; sFILI cases resolved more rapidly (p<0.01) compared with untreated sFILI patients, and one treated case had fatal outcome. Presented mechanism invokes reactive quinine diamine metabolites detoxified via glutathione conjugation.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine (Aza) is described as a well-known cause of drug-induced liver injury with at least four patterns: transient, usually asymptomatic serum ALT/AST elevations in 5-15% of treated subjects; an idiosyncratic cholestatic hepatitis typically occurring after 1-3 months; sinusoidal obstruction syndrome when given in high doses as with cancer chemotherapy; and nodular regenerative hyperplasia with long-term use. In the DILIN prospective cohort (paragraph 30), Aza- and 6-MP-associated liver injury accounted for 1-2% of DILI cases, with jaundice and a cholestatic pattern in the majority, latency generally a few weeks to 3 months, and a course that improved rapidly on stopping treatment, though one patient with pre-existing autoimmune hepatitis and cirrhosis developed acute-on-chronic liver failure and required liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: One patient had pre-existing autoimmune hepatitis and cirrhosis and developed acute-on-chronic liver failure requiring liver transplantation; apart from that, no acute liver failure deaths occurred in the absence of pre-existing liver disease. Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome was associated with high-dose use (as in cancer chemotherapy), and nodular regenerative hyperplasia with long-term use, particularly in organ transplantation or acute leukemia settings.
raw_record.extra_details: In the DILIN prospective study (22 patients in this series), Aza ranked in the top 20 causes of DILI; presenting symptoms included fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice; itching was uncommon and immunoallergic features rare. Of 22 patients, 1 had chronic liver injury marked by persistent asymptomatic Alk P elevations after severe cholestatic hepatitis. 6 of 22 patients had asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations without jaundice; 16 presented with jaundice, most with a cholestatic pattern. Latency to onset after starting therapy or dose increase generally a few weeks to 3 months, rarely exceeding 6 months; some received the thiopurine for years. Features include cholestatic hepatitis (whether or not superimposed on chronic liver disease) and anicteric hepatitis with hepatocellular enzyme elevations.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is metabolized in part to the toxic intermediate N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NADPQI); with insufficient glutathione stores, NADPQI covalently binds proteins leading to hepatocyte cell death and fulminant hepatitis, and is described as mainly responsible for acute liver disease due to acetaminophen. Several cases of acetaminophen-related liver failure have been reported in newborns and infants, and reported severe fulminant disease is linked to inadvertent overdose; histology of acetaminophen-related fulminant hepatitis shows diffuse apoptosis (confluent coagulative cell death), less severe reactions show zonal perivenular hepatocyte death, and combined hepatocellular and cholestatic injury has been reported following acetaminophen intoxication.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Fulminant (acute) liver disease attributed to inadvertent overdose; several reported cases in newborns and infants; metabolite formation and detoxification vary in neonates (reduced glucuronidation, greater glutathione synthesis, low CYP isoforms) affecting toxic-metabolite production.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: ~5-15% metabolized by CYP 2E1, 1A2, 3A4 to toxic N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NADPQI); 20-40% undergoes sulfation/glucuronidation; GSH normally inactivates NADPQI to mercapturic acid; with GSH depletion NADPQI covalently binds proteins causing hepatocyte death and fulminant hepatitis. Histology: diffuse apoptosis/confluent coagulative cell death in fulminant hepatitis; zonal perivenular (zone 3) hepatocyte death with epithelioid noncaseating granulomas (sarcoidosis-like) in less severe cases; combined hepatocellular and cholestatic injury reported following acetaminophen intoxication. Mode of cell death (apoptosis vs necrosis) controversial.

raw_record.support_text: Among 73 cases included in the final causality-assessed analysis of statin-induced DILI, the vast majority were due to atorvastatin (n = 30) and simvastatin (n = 28). The biochemical types among the whole cohort were hepatocellular (59%), cholestatic (30%) and mixed (11%).

Causality grades across cohort: 52 possible, 14 probable, 7 highly probable. Median time to abnormal liver tests 3 months; ~35% jaundice at presentation; median ALT 10 x ULN. Rechallenge cases had negative viral (HAV/HBV/HCV/CMV/EBV) markers and no suspicion of alcoholic liver disease or hypotension.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is described as a leading cause of hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure. In a study from the US DILI Network (DILIN), isoniazid was the second most frequently reported hepatotoxic agent in the registry, with cases likely under-reported. Investigators found a significant delay in discontinuing isoniazid after hepatitis-related symptoms developed: over 50% of patients who met criteria that would warrant immediate drug cessation continued isoniazid for more than 7 days, and 24 patients (40%) continued for more than 14 days; 9 of 13 patients who continued for more than 7 days were listed as having died or needing a liver transplant.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin, a semi-synthetic beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin, has a higher potential to cause hepatotoxicity. Its incidence is estimated at 1 case per 10,000-15,000 prescriptions, and in large case series it is the most frequent cause of DILI. Hepatic damage is characteristically cholestatic, can persist for months or years after discontinuation, and can be fatal; ductopenia and vanishing bile duct syndrome can result in cases with protracted cholestasis. The dose and route are not predictive of toxicity, and age >55 years and treatment >14 days are recognized risk factors.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Recognized risk factors are age >55 years and treatment periods >14 days; injury can persist for months or years after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence estimated as 1 case per 10,000-15,000 prescriptions. Cholestasis can be fatal; ductopenia and vanishing bile duct syndrome occur with protracted cholestasis. Dose and route not predictive of toxicity. Reported as the most frequent cause of DILI in large case series from countries where it is marketed. A GWAS (866,399 markers, 51 cases, 282 controls) showed an association peak in the MHC region (strongest P=8.7x10-33 for rs2395029[G]) on the extended MHC 57.1 haplotype (HLA-B*5701), present in <4% of Europeans.

raw_record.support_text: In the reported case, the RUCAM score was 9, which made the diagnosis of acute pirfenidone-induced liver injury highly probable (Table 1), while the RECAM score was 3, making the diagnosis possible. The R-factor was calculated as 15.16, indicating a hepatocellular pattern, with ALT ⩾5x ULN. Pirfenidone was used therapeutically for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Present case: DILI occurred 6 months after pirfenidone introduction; R-factor 15.16 (hepatocellular); RUCAM score 9 (highly probable); RECAM score 3 (possible, losing points for unprocessed HCV PCR and ANA titer >1/80); ALT ⩾5x ULN; fully recovered after discontinuation. Liver biopsy showed lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate consistent with an immunogenic reaction; ANA titer 1/320 left an autoimmune-like reaction not excluded. Large RCTs: ALT >3x ULN in 4% of pirfenidone patients, mostly asymptomatic with rapid normalization, drug withdrawn in ~1%; monthly ALT monitoring recommended for first 6 months. A 2018 published case of idiosyncratic pirfenidone DILI occurred 1 month after exposure and led to acute liver failure and death on day 4 of hospitalization. In 2020 the EMA warned of several severe cases of DILI associated with pirfenidone and recommended close monitoring. Pirfenidone is metabolized by CYP1A2 and, to a lesser extent, CYP2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 2E1, with 5-carboxy-pirfenidone as main minimally active metabolite; concurrent simvastatin (CYP3A4) with no known interaction.

raw_record.support_text: The study analyzed 20 cases of halothane hepatitis notified in institutional pharmacovigilance between 2012-2016, involving 18 women and 2 men aged 35-65 years. The injury was cholestatic in 12 cases and cytolytic in 8 cases; three cases turned out to be fulminant, resulting in death of the patient. Free radicals produced by liver metabolism of halothane can modify cellular proteins and introduce neo-antigens to the immune system; sensitization to these neo-antigens induces a more severe response after multiple exposures, with most type 2 hepatitis cases occurring after repeated contact.
raw_record.extra_details: 20 halothane hepatitis cases notified in institutional pharmacovigilance 2012-2016; 18 women and 2 men aged 35-65 years; cholestatic pattern in 12 cases and cytolytic in 8; 3 fulminant cases resulted in death. Paper notes newer halogenated anesthetics (enflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane) are less metabolized in the liver and cause few cases of sensitization.

raw_record.support_text: Chlorpromazine is the most studied phenothiazine regarding hepatotoxicity and is associated with hypersensitivity reactions. With modern pharmaceutical modification, cholestatic chlorpromazine-induced jaundice is rare but still occurs in 0.16% of cases, and this increases to 0.3% in persons over the age of 70 years. A dose-dependent acute cholestasis is documented in animals.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rate of cholestatic chlorpromazine-induced jaundice increases to 0.3% in persons over the age of 70 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Associated with hypersensitivity reactions. Historically, due to impurities in the initial formulation, jaundice was noted in up to 2% of cases, rising to 42% when mild abnormalities were included. Cross-reactivity between phenothiazines is rare. Dose-dependent acute cholestasis documented in animals. Phenothiazines in general cause isolated liver enzyme increases in up to 20% of patients and overt hepatotoxicity at a 0.1%-1% rate.

raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old female with metastatic HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer developed liver enzyme elevation under ribociclib treatment. Ribociclib was withdrawn 8 weeks after initiation due to enzyme elevation. A liver biopsy performed after further enzyme increase (peak ALT 2836 U/l), jaundice (peak bilirubin 353 µmol/l) and coagulopathy (INR 1.8) revealed acute hepatitis with 30% parenchymal necrosis; the RUCAM score was 7 points (probable).

raw_record.support_text: A patient on ribociclib therapy developed acute DILI with a hepatocellular biochemical pattern; the RUCAM score was 7, supporting a probable causal association of liver injury due to ribociclib. Despite discontinuing ribociclib, transaminases continued to rise, and liver biopsy showed extensive lobular necrosis accentuated in zone III (30% of liver parenchyma) with lymphohistiocytic inflammation, later accompanied by endothelialitis, mild cholestasis, jaundice (peak bilirubin 353 µmol/l) and coagulopathy (peak INR 1.8). Liver enzymes and bilirubin normalized within 10 weeks after ribociclib discontinuation, without encephalopathy. The authors report this as the first case of acute, extensive liver necrosis due to ribociclib intake.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report of endocrine-resistant HR+ breast cancer treated with ribociclib (600 mg/day) for cancer therapy; co-medication letrozole was explicitly excluded as the cause. Peak ALT 2896 U/l, peak AST 875 U/l, peak bilirubin 353 µmol/l, peak INR 1.8, nadir serum albumin 28 g/l. Biopsy twice showed 30% lobular necrosis (zone III) with ceroid-containing macrophages, apoptosis, moderate inflammation, mild cholestasis, endothelialitis and slight siderosis without fibrosis. Treated with prednisone 60 mg OD and N-acetylcysteine; the authors noted steroids did not immediately lower transaminases. Case reported to Swissmedic. No acute liver failure or encephalopathy occurred; enzymes normalized within 10 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is one of the most commonly used drugs in the United States and is also an important cause of serious liver injury. Taking more than the recommended amount can cause liver damage ranging from abnormalities in liver function blood tests, to acute liver failure, and even death, with many cases caused by patients inadvertently exceeding the recommended dose of 4 g/d or taking more than one acetaminophen-containing product.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury attributed to supratherapeutic exposure: taking more than the recommended dose (4 g/d) of one product or taking more than one acetaminophen-containing product; includes both unintentional overdose and intentional self-poisoning.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism is via a toxic metabolite (not named) that binds to liver proteins and causes cellular injury; extent of injury depends on the liver's ability to remove the metabolite. In a study combining data from 22 US specialty medical centers, acetaminophen-related liver injury was the leading cause of acute liver failure during 1998-2003; almost half the cases were unintentional overdoses. The high share of unintentional-overdose liver-failure cases was also observed in a 2007 study. Injury spectrum includes abnormalities in liver function blood tests, acute liver failure, and death.

A complete work-up failed to reveal another cause, liver biopsy showed subacute injury, and the clinical course was consistent with drug-induced liver injury. Despite aggressive measures the condition deteriorated and care was withdrawn; the authors conclude this is a case of fulminant hepatic failure and death involving duloxetine.

raw_record.support_text: The patient's clinical course and the temporal relationship between her duloxetine dose increase and symptom onset argue in favor of severe drug-induced liver injury. Jaundice developed within 6 weeks of dose escalation, and evaluation with the Naranjo nomogram, CIOMS scale, and Maria and Victorino clinical scale indicated a probable association between the duloxetine dose increase and the patient's hepatic injury. The patient was maintained on a lower duloxetine dose for almost a year without difficulty, developing clinically significant hepatotoxicity only after the dose was doubled.

Clinical course continued to worsen after drug discontinuation; causality assessed with Naranjo et al nomogram, CIOMS scale, and Maria and Victorino scale, all indicating probable association.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of 39 amiodarone-induced liver injury case reports published between 1984 and 2007 found that 19 (49%) developed cirrhosis attributed to amiodarone, with low ALT, AST and TB values observed in these patients but no statistically significant differences versus non-cirrhotic patients; the cumulative amiodarone dose was significantly higher in patients who developed cirrhosis (p = 0.01). raw_record.extra_details: 39 published amiodarone-induced liver injury case reports (1984-2007); 19 (49%) developed cirrhosis, 15 patients died (20 did not, 4 not registered). Likelihood-ratio model compared published cases with LFT abnormalities of any other cause in a general population; LRs >1 for AST 1-3×ULN (1.98), ALT 1-3×ULN (1.70), age >65 y (2.27), and AP >8×ULN (4.42) categories.

raw_record.extra_details: Epidemiologic study; 10 cases of cholestatic hepatitis diagnosed within 45 days of flucloxacillin and 1 case 46-90 days after prescription. Flucloxacillin is a semi-synthetic penicillinase-resistant penicillin indicated for suspected staphylococcal infections.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 1, a 39-year-old woman, was prescribed flucloxacillin 500 mg four times a day for five days for a boil. She presented four weeks later with pruritus and jaundice (bilirubin 68 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 565 IU/L; normal 60-230). A liver biopsy was interpreted as cholestatic hepatitis, and intrahepatic cholestasis was recorded. Flucloxacillin was prescribed again with subsequent exacerbation of jaundice; no other apparent cause was present, and the attending clinician ultimately considered flucloxacillin liver toxicity the likely cause of the cholestatic jaundice, which resolved by November 1989.

raw_record.support_text: Among 132,087 persons who received flucloxacillin, six patients were judged to have a characteristic history of cholestatic hepatitis within 45 days: onset began one to four weeks after drug therapy stopped, all had laboratory evidence of cholestatic jaundice, and elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase with no evident non-drug cause. All six eventually recovered; five were hospitalized, five were women, and in one case erythromycin was also received before the onset of jaundice.

raw_record.extra_details: Case-history review study; 6 of 132,087 flucloxacillin recipients identified with characteristic cholestatic hepatitis within 45 days. Cholestatic disease manifesting one to five weeks after treatment stopped; flucloxacillin-associated jaundice is cholestatic and tends to appear one to five weeks after treatment stops. Five cases used daily dose 2000 mg or less and five had treatment for 10 days or less; four used for minor skin infections; recovery period at least two months in all cases; little evidence of generalized systemic reaction. raw_record.support_text: In the current case of DILI attributed to ribociclib, ALT/AST peaked at 1,967/1,621 U/L and liver biopsy demonstrated significant parenchymal confluent necrosis, representing one of very few reports of submassive hepatocyte necrosis secondary to ribociclib. This pattern was compared with the Schaeffer et al case (41-year-old female with 30% zone III parenchymal necrosis, ALT 2,896 U/L, AST 875 U/L, bilirubin 353 µmol/L) and with a retrospective analysis of 22 DILI cases secondary to CDK4/6 inhibitors (ribociclib and abemaciclib) by Meunier et al, in which 12 liver biopsies showed centrilobular hepatitis with some foci of necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Current case ALT/AST peak 1,967/1,621 U/L with significant parenchymal confluent/submassive hepatocyte necrosis; causality supported by RUCAM, R-factor, and Naranjo in conjunction with histopathologic correlation, all strengthening ribociclib as the offending agent. Schaeffer et al case: 41-yo female, 30% zone III necrosis, ALT 2,896 U/L, AST 875 U/L, bilirubin 353 µmol/L. Meunier et al retrospective: 22 DILI cases secondary to CDK4/6 inhibitors (ribociclib and abemaciclib), 12 liver biopsies showing centrilobular hepatitis with some foci of necrosis (necrosis extent not quantified). Proposed mechanisms: reactive-metabolite formation and piperazine hydroxylation generating iminium ions (oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis), bile salt export pump (BSEP) inhibition causing cholestatic features with jaundice and elevated bilirubin, CYP3A4 metabolism with drug-drug interactions (azole antifungals, macrolides) exacerbating hepatotoxicity, and immune-mediated injury (ANA and anti-mitochondrial antibodies, lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration, response to glucocorticoids). Some patients showed marked LFT improvement following NAC supplementation.

raw_record.support_text: The compiled case series (Table 1) reports numerous patients who developed drug-induced liver injury during therapeutic rivaroxaban treatment at doses of 10-30 mg/day for indications including knee replacement surgery, atrial fibrillation, and venous thromboembolism prevention. Latencies ranged from about 2 to 180 days, with symptoms of jaundice, nausea, pruritus, and fatigue; hepatocellular (H), cholestatic (C), and mixed (M) biochemical patterns were documented, and most cases recovered after rivaroxaban discontinuation, while one 89-year-old patient died of acute liver failure. RUCAM causality scores ranged from 3 to 9 across cases. The two new cases presented in this article (an 79-year-old man and an 84-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation) showed hepatocellular injury with ALT >35× ULN and >9× ULN respectively, negative viral and autoimmune serology, and recovery within 1-4 weeks after rivaroxaban withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Doses 10-30 mg/day; latencies approximately 2-180 days across cases; symptoms included jaundice, nausea, pruritus, fatigue, vomiting, and right hypochondrial pain. Most patients recovered after discontinuation (within 1-4 weeks in the two new cases), one 89-year-old female died of acute liver failure (RUCAM 6), and one elderly male died of paralytic ileus. Liver histology in some cases showed cholestasis with portal inflammation and eosinophilic infiltration, centrilobular cholestasis with mixed portal inflammation, or severe lobular hepatitis with perivenular confluent necrosis. RUCAM scores 3-9. Naranjo score 7 (probable) for case 1 and 4 (possible) for case 2. No rechallenge performed. The discussion notes a meta-analysis of 29 phase III trials (152,116 patients) with DOACs including rivaroxaban found no increased risk of hepatotoxicity, but argues trial populations are too small and short-term to capture rare idiosyncratic DILI. Case 2's concurrent drugs (lansoprazole, amlodipine, carvedilol, furosemide) were continued and considered unlikely alternative causes.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old patient with Behcet's disease, previously on cyclosporine for uveitis (switched to azathioprine because of cyclosporine hepatotoxicity 1.5 months earlier), developed weakness, nausea, vomiting and jaundice. Labs showed Total Bilirubin 18 mg/dl rising to 25 mg/dl, Direct Bilirubin 13 mg/dl, AST 57 IU/L, ALT 57 IU/L, ALP 95 IU/L, GGT 39 IU/L, INR 1.62, PT 17.6 s. Viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune markers were negative. Liver biopsy findings were consistent with drug toxicity. Azathioprine was stopped, after which bilirubin and transaminases normalized by the end of the second month. The authors conclude that, although rare, azathioprine can cause severe cholestatic hepatitis and the drug must be stopped immediately.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with Behcet's disease treated for uveitis; azathioprine started 1.5 months after switching from cyclosporine, which had itself been stopped for hepatotoxicity (potential pre-existing drug-related hepatotoxicity and underlying disease as competing context).
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (Absno 2251, Topic 18). Liver biopsy histopathology consistent with drug toxicity. Dechallenge: on stopping azathioprine, bilirubin decreased slowly but steadily and normalized together with transaminases by the end of the second month. Laboratory values at admission: Total Bilirubin 18 mg/dl, Direct Bilirubin 13 mg/dl, AST 57 IU/L, ALT 57 IU/L, ALP 95 IU/L, GGT 39 IU/L, INR 1.62, PT 17.6 s, albumin 3.8 g/dL; total bilirubin increased to 25 mg/dl during hospital stay.

raw_record.support_text: Usnic acid derived from lichens is described as a well-documented agent of liver injury, with the first reported cases dating to 2000 in relation to the dietary supplement LipoKinetix. Approximately 21 cases of LipoKinetix-induced liver toxicity were reported, leading to one death and one liver transplant, and the supplement has since been removed from the market. The known mechanism of liver injury is dose- and time-dependent, through decoupling of oxidative phosphorylation and induction of oxidative stress via glutathione depletion.

raw_record.extra_details: ~21 cases of LipoKinetix-induced liver toxicity, 1 death and 1 liver transplant; first reported in 2000; mechanism described as dose- and time-dependent via decoupling of oxidative phosphorylation and oxidative stress from glutathione depletion.

raw_record.support_text: The authors characterize terbinafine-induced DILI as a rare but serious, idiosyncratic and rapidly evolving event that clusters in the first 6 weeks of treatment, occurring in patients treated for a mean of 30 days (range 5-84 days). They identified 69 patients with clinical presentation, all symptomatic, none detected through monitoring, including one with symptom onset after drug discontinuation. In the same systematic review, three patients developed fulminant liver failure attributed to terbinafine and required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Literature-based critical appraisal topic (CAT) assessing usefulness of laboratory monitoring for early DILI detection; 69 patients (65 of 69 clinically obviously sick by 6 weeks), symptomatic only and none found on monitoring; mean 30 days treatment, onset 5-84 days; symptoms included jaundice (most common per FDA), nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, anorexia, dark urine, with pruritus added as a potentially isolated symptom (in >20%, n=16). Three case reports of fulminant liver failure requiring successful liver transplant (48-year-old female symptomatic within 5 days; 50-year-old male with jaundice, dark urine, acholic stools followed by weight loss, anorexia, myalgias, pruritus, deteriorated after discontinuation; 41-year-old female no further details). Three reports of death associated with terbinafine-induced hepatic dysfunction occurred but in complex patients with multiple medications or disease and without clear attribution to terbinafine. Authors conclude routine blood monitoring is not helpful for detecting this DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A publication described 14 patients with rivaroxaban-associated liver injury reported to a Swiss regional Pharmacovigilance Center. Patients had a median age of 71 years (9 female, 5 male), treated for atrial fibrillation (n=4) or after knee/leg surgery (n=10); median dose was 10 mg/day, and median latency was 15.5 days. All but one were symptomatic and 11 were jaundiced; ALT exceeded 2x ULN in all (median 7.8x ULN). Eight had hepatocellular, four cholestatic and one mixed liver injury; median bilirubin was 6.6x ULN. RUCAM causality was highly probable in 4, probable in 7 and possible in 3 patients; one patient died, all others recovered. Author database searches found rivaroxaban as a suspected DILI cause in WHO (179 reports), EMA (375) and FDA FAERS (87) databases. A second Swiss case report described two further patients (10 mg rivaroxaban after surgery) presenting with jaundice 1-2 months later; one had hepatocellular and one mixed injury, causality probable/possible, with full recovery 2 weeks after stopping.
raw_record.extra_details: First series of 14 patients: median age 71 y (range 41-91), 9 female/5 male; indications AF (n=4) and knee replacement/leg surgery (n=10); median dose 10 mg/day (range 10-20); latency 15.5 d (range 3-62); 13/14 symptomatic, 11 jaundiced; ALT >2x ULN in all (median 7.8x, range 2.5-53.7); ALP <2x ULN in 5 and >2x ULN in 9 (median 2.5x); 8 hepatocellular, 4 cholestatic, 1 mixed; bilirubin in 10 patients median 6.6x ULN (range 1-21.6); RUCAM: highly probable 4, probable 7, possible 3; one death, others recovered. Two patients biopsied showed cholestatic injury with centroacinar cholestasis, focal hepatocyte ballooning, portal lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltration and biliary epithelial alterations. Pharmacovigilance database searches: WHO VigiBase 179 DILI-compatible reports, EMA EudraVigilance 375 events, FDA FAERS 87 cases with rivaroxaban as suspected cause. Second case series (2 patients, 52 y man and 73 y woman, 10 mg after surgery): jaundice 1-2 months later, massively raised transaminases with slight ALP rise; 1 hepatocellular and 1 mixed injury; causality probable/possible; full recovery ~2 weeks after stopping; biopsy in the hepatocellular case showed confluent centroacinar hepatocyte necrosis with macrophage infiltration and minimal portal lymphocytic infiltrate.

raw_record.support_text: In the case of fialuridine (FIAU), a thymidine analog, the potential for hepatotoxicity was not appreciated during preclinical evaluation. Subjects treated with FIAU for 9–13 weeks developed severe and sometimes fatal hepatotoxicity associated with lactic acidosis, occurring in the intended population with Hepatitis B. The hepatotoxic syndrome (hepatic steatosis, increased bilirubinemia, increased prothrombin time, and lactic acidosis) was attributed to mitochondrial DNA damage in hepatocytes involving thymidine kinase 2.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Fialuridine was administered to subjects with chronic Hepatitis B (the intended treatment population) for 9-13 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Preclinical evaluation in healthy rodent, dog, and nonhuman primates did not reveal hepatotoxicity; the syndrome of delayed toxicity (hepatic steatosis, increased bilirubinemia, increased prothrombin time, lactic acidosis) was reproduced in woodchucks infected with hepatitis. Mechanism attributed to mitochondrial DNA in hepatocytes with high affinity for thymidine kinase 2, leading to mitochondrial enzyme mutations, defective oxidative phosphorylation, electron leakage, superoxide anion production, and increased oxidative stress. Injury was severe and sometimes fatal.

raw_record.support_text: In controlled clinical trials, 1.3% of subjects given troglitazone developed ALT values >3× the ULN and 1% developed ALT >8× ULN, representing a mild reversible hepatotoxicity that appeared in <2% of subjects. After drug approval, several cases of severe and sometimes fatal liver failure were reported, in subjects showing elevated serum enzymes and bilirubin and signs of hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis; histologically troglitazone elicits hepatocellular necrosis with bridging necrosis and fibrosis and/or collapse.
raw_record.extra_details: Life-threatening idiosyncratic reactions in man; reactive quinone/quinone epoxide/quinone methide and reactive isocyanate/thiazolidine sulfoxide intermediates implicated; induces CYP3A4 which bioactivates it. ALT >3× ULN in 1.3% and >8× ULN in 1% of trial subjects; post-marketing severe and sometimes fatal liver failure; acute liver failure incidence ~1:20,000; signs appeared at inconsistent times with no consistent dose relationship; monthly monitoring insufficient; histology shows hepatocellular necrosis with bridging necrosis, fibrosis and/or collapse.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical use, bromfenac at recommended therapeutic doses of 25–100 mg/d for at least 90 days (labeled recommended duration >10 days) was associated with severe symptomatic hepatocellular disease with associated hypoprothrombinemia. There was no evidence of a hypersensitivity reaction. Extensive confluent parenchymal necrosis originating in central zones was associated with lymphocytic infiltrate with nodular regeneration in 2 subjects with more prolonged disease prior to transplantation. Histologic lesions included acute lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis and fibrous expansion of portal tracts, and fulminant liver failure requiring liver transplant has been recorded after inadvertent rechallenge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic doses of 25–100 mg/d for at least 90 days, exceeding the labeled recommended duration of >10 days; delayed idiosyncratic onset.
raw_record.extra_details: During clinical trials bromfenac caused only reversible minor AST elevations. In clinical use it produced severe symptomatic hepatocellular disease with hypoprothrombinemia and no hypersensitivity reaction; extensive confluent parenchymal necrosis originating in central zones with lymphocytic infiltrate and nodular regeneration in 2 subjects with prolonged disease prior to transplant. Histology showed acute lobular hepatitis with bridging necrosis and fibrous expansion of portal tracts. Prognosis is usually good with resolution, but fulminant liver failure requiring liver transplant occurred after inadvertent rechallenge. Risk-benefit: continued use was not justified once delayed idiosyncratic severe hepatotoxicity was identified given the availability of alternatives.

raw_record.support_text: Ten days after starting diclofenac, the patient developed hepatotoxicity with ALAT rising to 13.5x ULN and ALP to 2.2x ULN; an ALAT/ALP ratio of 6.1 classified the injury as hepatocellular. Non-drug causes of the liver damage were largely excluded, and the good temporal correlation with reversibility after discontinuing diclofenac led the authors to grade the causal relationship between the hepatocellular liver injury with jaundice and diclofenac as probable. NSAIDs are among the most common causes of drug-induced liver injury, with diclofenac the most frequently involved NSAID; transaminase elevations are common, hyperbilirubinemia with icterus rarer, and hepatitis including fulminant hepatitis up to liver failure is very rare.

raw_record.support_text: A 78-year-old Taiwanese man developed yellowing of the skin and generalized pruritus one month after beginning fosinopril therapy. Other drugs taken by the patient were excluded as probable causes of the jaundice. According to the CIOMS scale fosinopril scored 10 points, placing it in the 'highly probable' category; liver biopsy showed cholestasis without bile duct damage. The diagnosis was that fosinopril with high probability induced cholestatic jaundice. During hospitalization the patient developed severe jaundice and liver failure despite conservative treatment and fosinopril withdrawal, then a 5-day plasma exchange cycle reduced serum bilirubin and his liver function returned to normal after 2 months.
raw_record.extra_details: ACE inhibitor reported to be rarely associated with hepatotoxicity. Latency about 1 month after starting fosinopril; CIOMS causality score 10; liver biopsy showed cholestasis without bile duct damage; abdominal ultrasound, CT and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography excluded biliary obstruction or intra-abdominal tumor; condition progressed to severe jaundice and liver failure despite drug withdrawal and conservative care; 5-day plasma exchange reduced serum bilirubin; liver function normalized 2 months later.

raw_record.support_text: Based on the CIOMS scale result and the pathological characteristics of the liver, the authors concluded it was highly probable that fosinopril had induced cholestatic jaundice in the patient. The liver failure progressed, with serum bilirubin peaking at 25 mg/dL on hospital day 14 despite conservative treatment and withdrawal of fosinopril. The patient ultimately required plasma exchange and liver function returned to normal 2 months after discharge.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of cholestatic jaundice attributed to fosinopril 10 mg once daily, an antihypertensive switched from prior therapy one month before presentation. CIOMS scale scored fosinopril as highly probable cause. Admission labs: total bilirubin 21.4 mg/dL (60% direct), ALT 41 IU/L, AST 47 IU/L, ALP 242 IU/L, GGT 136 IU/L, LDH 152 IU/L, albumin 3.3 g/dL; viral/metabolic/autoimmune markers negative. Liver biopsy on hospital day 10 showed marked cholestasis with hepatocyte swelling/damage and portal lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration, no piecemeal necrosis or portal fibrosis, interpreted as drug-related cholestasis. Bilirubin peaked at 25 mg/dL on day 14; treated with plasma exchange (20 units/day x 5 days), ursodeoxycholic acid 600 mg/day, cholestyramine 8 g/day, cyproheptadine 4 mg 4 times/day; hypertension switched to amlodipine; glyburide discontinued and insulin used for diabetes. Liver function returned to normal 2 months after discharge.

One patient died from liver failure and all others recovered without liver transplantation. 66% of cases had mixed intoxication with other drugs and 43% used alcohol concomitantly.

raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of paracetamol toxicity 25 per 100,000 inhabitants/year; hospitalized rate 14 per 100,000/year. 177/194 (91%) cases intentional (93% females). Abnormal liver tests in 40/194 (21%), more frequent in unintentional than intentional cases (71% vs 16%, p<0.001). Severe hepatotoxicity (ALT>1000) in 14/182 (8%), higher in patients over 50 years (27% vs 3%, p<0.001). Acute liver failure in 9/197 (4.6%), more common among males (10% vs 3%, p=0.056). One death from liver failure; no liver transplantation during the study period. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) used in 146/188 (78%) of cases.

raw_record.support_text: Fifteen well characterized patients with liver injury attributed to terbinafine who were enrolled into the ongoing DILIN Prospective registry study are presented. Most patients were symptomatic with pruritus and jaundice, 2 were hospitalized and 1 required eventual liver transplantation, and most had either a cholestatic or mixed liver injury pattern at onset with a generally favorable prognosis. raw_record.support_text: A case series by Dijmarescu et al. reported 14 child cases of albendazole-related idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (iDILI), representing 38% of all their DILI cases, with a mean time to onset of 21 days. The paper additionally notes that albendazole is frequently linked to elevations in liver enzymes, with only a few cases of clinical significance developing iDILI, typically as an immune-mediated idiosyncratic injury accompanied by short latency and possible hypersensitivity with autoantibody production; recurrent albendazole-induced injury in pediatric patients carries a high rechallenge risk, so the drug should not be recommended again after one iDILI episode.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; supporting human evidence is a child case series.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 child cases of albendazole-related iDILI reported (38% of all DILI cases in the series); mean time to onset 21 days; most common pattern hepatocellular with cholestatic and mixed types also seen; mechanism described as immune-mediated idiosyncratic liver injury with possible hypersensitivity and autoantibody production; short latency (within a couple of months), earlier after repeated treatment regimens; high risk of rechallenge with recurrent injury, so drug should not be re-administered after one iDILI episode. Most cases of liver-enzyme elevation are not clinically significant.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac, the most widely prescribed NSAID, is the prototypical example of NSAID hepatotoxicity and ranks second among DILI cases in Iceland, with a DILI risk of 1 per 9,148 exposed subjects. Asymptomatic transaminase rise is more common, and in a prospective study of 17,289 patients transaminases rose over 3x ULN in 3.1%, primarily in the first 4 to 6 months. Diclofenac liver injury seems more common in the elderly and women, jaundice is associated with a mortality of 8%, and hepatocellular followed by mixed pattern hepatitis is typical.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver injury more common in the elderly and in women; topical diclofenac does not seem to produce significant DILI (with a small proportion showing asymptomatic transaminase elevations).
raw_record.extra_details: Ranks second in the Icelandic DILI cohort with risk of 1 per 9,148 exposed subjects; prospective study of 17,289 patients showed transaminases >3x ULN in 3.1%, primarily in the first 4-6 months; jaundice associated with 8% mortality; hepatocellular followed by mixed pattern hepatitis is typical; two drug-induced ALF cases in ALFSG; hepatotoxicity linked to UGT2B7 and ABCC2 gene polymorphisms (8-fold and 5-fold risk respectively) and IL10 and IL4 polymorphisms (5-fold risk); topical diclofenac produced asymptomatic transaminase elevations in 6.4-7.3% of older patients in one study.

raw_record.support_text: In a multi-centre prospective observational study of 240 patients presenting with acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose (median ingested dose 20 g, IQR 10-40), 36 (15%) developed hepatotoxicity defined as ALT>1000 U/L. Patients who developed hepatotoxicity had higher initial acetaminophen-protein adduct concentrations than those who did not (1.63 vs 0.26 nmol/mL, p<0.0001). The paper characterises acetaminophen overdose as causing acute liver toxicity manifesting as elevated ALT (hepatotoxicity), with toxic metabolite (NAPQI) binding to cellular proteins.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; patients aged >=14 years; 228/240 (95%) received intravenous acetylcysteine at a median 6 h (IQR 3.5-10.5) post-ingestion, with hepatotoxicity occurring despite treatment in 36 patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Median ingested dose 20 g (IQR 10-40); 240 participants, 1009 samples; 204 (85%) acute ingestions; 36 (15%) hepatotoxicity cases, 22 of whom had ALT<=1000 U/L at initial adduct measurement. Acetaminophen-protein adducts are a specific biomarker of toxic acetaminophen metabolite (NAPQI) exposure; an adduct threshold of 0.58 nmol/mL was 100% sensitive and 91% specific for predicting hepatotoxicity among those presenting with ALT<=1000 U/L. ROC-AUC for adducts 0.98 (95%CI 0.96-1.00) vs ALT 0.89 (95%CI 0.82-0.96) for predicting hepatotoxicity. Mechanism involves NAPQI binding to cellular proteins with release of acetaminophen-protein adducts.

raw_record.support_text: In this study of 240 patients presenting after acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion, 36 (15%) developed hepatotoxicity, of whom 25 developed a peak INR ≥ 2.0 and eight had severe coagulopathy (INR ≥ 5.0). There were no deaths, but one patient who ingested 50 g of acetaminophen required liver transplantation. The cohort comprised acute ingestions of immediate-release and modified-release acetaminophen and repeated supratherapeutic ingestions (RSTI), establishing human hepatotoxicity associated with acetaminophen exposure.

Cohort included acute IR (n=158), MR (n=35), combined, and RSTI (n=36; 24 therapeutic purpose, 8 codeine abusers, 4 staggered acute). raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose causes hepatotoxicity and acute liver injury. In a study of 240 patients with acetaminophen overdose, six patients developed hepatotoxicity despite an ALT ≤ 50 U/L on presentation; Patient B required a liver transplant despite antidote treatment at 2.5 h, and Patient E developed acute liver failure after ingesting 10 g of acetaminophen with a serum acetaminophen concentration below the nomogram line. The paper links this injury to hepatic metabolism, noting that APAP-protein adducts reflect hepatic glutathione depletion and the metabolic activation of acetaminophen through cytochrome P450 oxidation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (acute supratherapeutic ingestion) exposure; includes a case of acute liver failure after 10 g ingestion and a case requiring liver transplant despite antidote treatment at 2.5 h.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP-protein adducts at presentation predicted later hepatotoxicity and were superior to ALT, AST, and acetaminophen-multiplication products; initial adduct value moderately correlated with maximum ALT (Spearman r=0.54, 95% CI 0.44–0.63, n=240) and INR (Spearman r=0.49, 95% CI 0.37–0.59, n=205). Patients who developed hepatotoxicity had higher median maximum adduct concentrations (9.20 nmol/mL, IQR 2.67–17.75, n=36) than those who did not (0.35 nmol/mL, IQR 0.22–0.57, n=204). Injury attributed to NAPQI production and hepatic glutathione depletion via cytochrome P450 metabolic activation.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old male patient presented with acute onset jaundice and highly elevated liver enzymes (>20-fold ALT increase). Viral or autoimmune hepatitis and biliary etiology were ruled out. Withdrawal of several medications including ramipril resulted in an immediate decrease in liver enzymes, whereas subsequent re-exposure with ramipril resulted in a striking increase (>35-fold ALT increase). After definitely discontinuing ramipril, a rapid decline was observed, suggesting a certain causal relationship between drug intake and hepatic damage. The authors describe this as the first case of ramipril-induced liver injury proven by positive rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: In a 40-year-old man with a history of chronic pancreatitis due to alcohol abuse treated for hypertension, ramipril therapy (10 mg/d) was reinitiated after initial withdrawal of all medications. After re-exposure, liver enzymes rose sharply (ALT 1555 U/L; ALP 523 U/L; bilirubin only marginally increased at 23.1 µmol/L on hospital day 6), and ramipril was definitively discontinued, after which values declined rapidly (hospital day 11: ALT 322 U/L, ALP 276 U/L, bilirubin 11.8 µmol/L). The paper describes this as the first report of a ramipril-induced liver injury proven by positive rechallenge, fulfilling all requirements for certain drug causality according to WHO criteria.

raw_record.extra_details: Positive rechallenge proving causality; certain causality per WHO criteria; Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment (RUCAM) applied. Liver biopsy demonstrated DILI with no typical features of alcohol-induced injury (no hepatic steatosis). Patient discharged in good condition on hospital day 11 with insulin as only medication.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old male, treated with trandolapril, alfuzosine, and finasteride since 2006, developed deep calf venous thrombosis and started acenocoumarol in January 2008. Five months later he experienced marked jaundice requiring hospitalization, with ALT 349 U/L, AST 65 U/L, AIP 267 IU/L, Gamma-GT 276 U/L, and total bilirubin 182 µmol/L. A presumptive diagnosis of hepatotoxicity related to acenocoumarol was made and the drug stopped; viral, autoimmune, tumoral, and metabolic causes were excluded, and lithiasis was excluded by biliopancreatic imaging. Liver biopsy showed cholestasis without bile duct or hepatocyte damage, and bilirubin reached 427.5 µmol/L 15 days later, requiring one cycle of albumin dialysis for refractory cholestatic pruritus. The authors concluded on a probable acenocoumarol-related acute cholestasis based on the temporal relationship and absence of other causative factors.

raw_record.support_text: Levofloxacin was determined to be the most likely culprit of this patient's DILI as she had not started any other new medications prior to the development of DILI. She had completed a 10-week course of levofloxacin (2 weeks IV followed by 2 months oral) immediately preceding the diagnosis of abnormal liver tests and jaundice. After cessation of levofloxacin her liver tests remained elevated but improved, with ALT decreasing over fivefold within 9 months and ALP and bilirubin slowly improving.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: No other new medications before the DILI developed; no competing causes identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosed as DILI consistent with a vanishing bile duct pattern along with predominant cholestatic injury; liver biopsy showed hepatocellular cholestasis, dilated bile canaliculi, lobular necroinflammation and apoptotic bodies, mild fibrosis with bile duct loss, and CK7 immunostain confirming bile duct absence. Course consisted of 2 weeks IV followed by 2 months oral levofloxacin (10 weeks total). Following drug cessation, ALT decreased over fivefold within 9 months while ALP and bilirubin remained elevated with slow improvement. Reported as the first case of levofloxacin-induced vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS); only a few prior reports describe prolonged cholestasis associated with levofloxacin.

raw_record.support_text: The study prospectively identified and adjudicated 18 cases of clinically apparent liver injury as probably, highly likely, or definitely owing to azithromycin. Hepatocellular injury outnumbered cholestatic injury, latency to onset was 1 to 3 weeks (recognized 2 weeks after stopping azithromycin in 16 patients), typical symptoms were fatigue, nausea and abdominal pain followed by itching and jaundice, and recovery usually was prompt (2 to 5 weeks) with complete resolution.
raw_record.extra_details: 18 prospectively identified, adjudicated cases of clinically apparent DILI (probable, highly likely, or definite). Latency 1-3 weeks after azithromycin; onset typically after completing the course (only 2 of 18 developed jaundice while taking it). Typical regimen 250-500 mg once daily for 4-7 days. At 6-month follow-up for 14 patients, 8 recovered, 4 had chronic injury, 1 died of multi-organ failure, 1 underwent liver transplantation. Four patients (1, 3, 6, 11) met chronic DILI definition; 3 had initial hepatocellular injury with jaundice and later mild-moderate ALT/Alk P increases. Histology showed ductopenic portal areas, zone 3 cholestasis with hepatocellular and canalicular bile accumulation, chronic hepatitis with perivenular inflammation and hemorrhage, and mild veno-occlusive changes. Recovery usually prompt, resolving in 2-5 weeks; median time to 50% reduction of peak bilirubin 12 days (8-27 d) and to normalization 35 days (25-46 d).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of severe high-dose methylprednisolone-induced acute hepatitis in a 16-year-old girl with a new diagnosis of multiple sclerosis. Hepatic insufficiency with grossly elevated liver enzymes; liver biopsy showed focal centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis with interface hepatitis. Clinical, laboratory and histological data followed for 2 years. Authors note the causal relation between methylprednisolone therapy and hepatotoxicity has been proven in the literature.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents ticlopidine as a recognized cause of drug-induced hepatotoxicity, analyzing 49 reports of ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity patients (47 previously published cases described in table I plus two new cases described in this paper). A Bayesian causal-assessment method based on analytical and demographic traits was applied to attribute abnormal liver function to ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine was given at 250 mg twice daily. Case 2 (76-year-old man) had abnormal liver function emerging after 21 weeks and severe enzyme elevations (AST 91 IU/L, ALT 134 IU/L, GGT 1029 IU/L, ALP 754 IU/L) with total bilirubin rising to 11.5 mg/dl by week 28; enzymes and bilirubin improved after ticlopidine discontinuation at week 64. The Danan causality assessment gave a suggestive relationship, and the Bayesian method assigned ticlopidine a posterior probability (PsP) of 87.30% at week 21 and 81.89% at week 64. The analytical profile emphasized alkaline phosphatase (ALP >720 IU/L had a likelihood ratio of 109.50); alcohol, viral hepatitis, mononucleosis, and drug-associated/uncertain etiologies had statistically different PsP from ticlopidine. Published ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity cases (47 in table I plus the 2 new cases) were used to build the model.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 71 tuberculosis patients on a conventional antituberculosis regimen, 11 (15.4%) patients developed isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity (IIH), diagnosed according to Benichou et al. A high isoniazid serum concentration (C3, measured 3 h after the morning dose) was a risk factor for IIH (AUC 0.74, P=0.007, 95% CI 0.56–0.93), with a cutoff at 3.69 mg/L (OR 13.2, P=0.0007, 95% CI 2.9–59). A combined CYP2E1 Dral(C/D)/slow-acetylator NAT2 genotype also increased IIH risk (OR 8.41, P=0.01, 95% CI 1.54–45.76).
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity reported as 11/71 (15.4%) in Tunisian tuberculosis patients on a conventional antituberculosis regimen; diagnosed per Benichou et al. Risk factor analysis: isoniazid serum concentration C3 > 3.69 mg/L (AUC 0.74, P=0.007, 95% CI 0.56–0.93; OR 13.2, P=0.0007, 95% CI 2.9–59) was the only independent multivariate risk factor; combined CYP2E1 Dral C/D plus slow-acetylator NAT2 genotype increased risk (OR 8.41, P=0.01, 95% CI 1.54–45.76) vs other combined profiles, while NAT2 and CYP2E1 variants analyzed separately did not increase risk. Demographic factors (age, weight, gender) were not associated with hepatotoxicity. Introduction notes INH causes a range of 1–36% incidence of hepatotoxicity depending on study criteria.

raw_record.support_text: In the presented case report, DILI due to varenicline was judged the most likely etiology of the patient's acute liver injury. Extensive testing for other causes of acute liver injury was negative, and the patient had no evidence of outflow obstruction, hepatic ischemia, or biliary obstruction. Although the patient was HCV antibody positive with detectable HCV RNA and stage 2 fibrosis on biopsy, acute HCV infection was deemed very unlikely given the lack of recent risk factors. The patient demonstrated a predominantly hepatocellular injury with a substantially elevated total bilirubin and a mild INR elevation, consistent with a moderately severe liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis is described as a rare serious but reversible adverse effect of the drug, with more than 40 cases reported in the literature plus 2 additional cases reported in this paper. The latent period, severity, and duration after discontinuation are highly variable, but cholestasis resolved after the drug was discontinued in all cases. In vitro T-cell stimulation studies at therapeutic ticlopidine concentrations support a possible T-cell-mediated mechanism, and the authors recommend monitoring liver function tests in patients receiving ticlopidine.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis (cholestasis with jaundice) attributed to ticlopidine used as part of pharmacological management of percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA). More than 40 published cases plus 2 new reported cases; latent period from drug introduction to hepatotoxicity, its severity, and duration after discontinuation are highly variable, and remission was complete in all cases. In vitro T-cell stimulation assay showed therapeutic ticlopidine concentrations stimulated T cells from the two cholestatic patients but not from healthy individuals, supporting a possible immune/T-cell-mediated mechanism; underlying mechanism otherwise unknown. Recommendation to include liver function tests in routine blood monitoring for ticlopidine recipients.
