raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 154 DILI cases admitted to a tertiary care centre in Hamburg (2008-2017), metamizole was the second most frequent putative agent causing DILI, accounting for 23 of 154 cases (14.9%, after phenprocoumon). The biochemical pattern on admission was hepatocellular, with median ALT 779 U/L (64-3532 U/L) far exceeding median ALP 131 U/L (42-578 U/L). Liver biopsy in 17/23 cases showed moderate-to-severe inflammatory activity and severe centrilobular necrosis (>30%) in 76.5% and 35.3%, respectively. Metamizole was involved in 2 DILI cases progressing to acute liver failure that received liver transplantation and were alive at assessment; re-exposure supported causality in 4 patients. A search of the EMA database identified about 300 reports of suspected metamizole-induced DILI in Europe.
raw_record.extra_details: Analgesic frequently prescribed in Germany, Russia and South America; off-market in the UK, USA and Scandinavia due to side effects including agranulocytosis. Liver side effects are not mentioned in the German drug label. Second most frequent putative DILI agent after phenprocoumon in the series (23/154, 14.9%). Infiltration of immune cells on liver histology; 2 cases progressed to acute liver failure and received liver transplantation, alive at assessment; causality supported by re-exposure in 4 patients. EMA (European Medicines Agency) database search identified about 300 reports of suspected metamizole-induced DILI in Europe.

raw_record.support_text: Metamizole was the second most frequent putative agent causing idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury at the center, accounting for 23 of 154 (14.9%) non-paracetamol DILI cases from 2008 to 2017. Median RUCAM score was 7 (probable), including 4 cases rated highly probable; the prevailing biochemical pattern was hepatocellular (14/23, 61%), followed by mixed (22%) and cholestatic (17%). Median latency from first metamizole administration to elevated liver enzymes or jaundice was about 4 weeks, and 4 of 23 patients (17.4%) were accidentally re-exposed, resulting in another episode of acute icteric hepatitis. Two of 23 (8.7%) cases progressed to acute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy; both received liver transplantation and survived, and there was no mortality in the follow-up of all 23 cases.

raw_record.extra_details: 23 idiosyncratic non-paracetamol DILI cases (2008-2017) at a single center; median age 40 yr (26-79), ~65% female; median RUCAM 7 (possible 4-5, probable 6-8, highly probable >8), 4 cases highly probable. Latency ~4 weeks; accidental rechallenge in 4/23 (17.4%) caused further acute icteric hepatitis episodes. 48% fulfilled Hy's law (ALT>3xULN, TB>2xULN), 39% jaundiced at presentation; ANA positive ~50% (median titre 1:160, peak 1:5120); 2 anti-smooth muscle Ab positive, 3 anti-mitochondrial Ab positive (regarded as nonspecific, not PBC); all negative for anti-LKM and anti-SLA/LP. Histology (17/23 biopsied): moderate-severe lymphocytic inflammation 76%, centrilobular necrosis >30% in 35%, steatosis/cholestasis 12% each, low-grade fibrosis (stage 1-2) in 29%. Steroids (prednisolone ~1 mg/kg) used in ~70% for acute hepatitis; no infectious complications. EVDAS/BfArM pharmacovigilance search identified 143 liver-related metamizole reports in Germany and 296 in the EEA; top categories hepatic failure, DILI, jaundice, hepatitis; hepatitis cholestatic 11% in EEA vs 3% in Germany. Peak enzymes for 2 ALF cases: ALT 3502/3574 U/L, AST 1998/4172 U/L, peak TB 24.5/30.5 mg/dL, peak MELD 23/33.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical course and laboratory data in this case are consistent with the diagnosis of cholestatic hepatitis probably due to thioctic acid. The report states this is the first report of probable liver toxicity due to thioctic acid, a proposed 'hepatoprotectant'. raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient who developed cholestatic hepatitis attributed to thioctic acid (alpha-lipoic acid), taken for worsening neuropathic symptoms (proposed hepatoprotectant). Symptoms included fever, nausea, pruritus, and asthenia. Increased serum liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT) and bilirubin appeared less than 2 months after initiation, resolved on discontinuation, and recurred on rechallenge (positive rechallenge), with resolution again after stopping. RUCAM causality score = highly probable; Maria and Victorino scale = probable. Liver biopsy showed zone 3 parenchymal bilirubinostasis with an isolated necrotic hepatocyte focus surrounded by minimal lymphocytic infiltrate; no bile duct damage, ductopenia, ductular proliferation, portal inflammation, or portal fibrosis. Viral, autoimmune, iron, copper, thyroid, and imaging workup negative. First reported case of probable liver toxicity due to thioctic acid.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane had been widely used as an anesthetic and causes two forms of liver damage: a mild increase in serum aminotransferase seen in up to 20% of patients, probably from direct toxicity by drug metabolites, and a more severe form characterized by massive hepatocyte necrosis and acute liver failure. Susceptibility to the severe form was enhanced in adults, females, and obese persons, and increased with frequency of exposure. Severe halothane hepatitis was uncommon after first exposure (1 in 35,000 patients) but its incidence rose to 1 in 3700 after the second exposure.

Incidence of severe halothane hepatitis was 1/35,000 after first exposure and 1/3700 after second exposure. Mechanism: halothane is oxidatively metabolized by CYP2E1 with release of bromide to form trifluoroacetyl chloride, which covalently binds to proteins as trifluoroacetylated (TFA) adducts presented on hepatocyte membranes; anti-P450 2E1 autoantibodies detected by ELISA in 14 of 20 sera from patients with halothane hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Six cases of hepatotoxicity secondary to trazodone have been well described, one confirmed by inadvertent drug rechallenge. Liver injury self-limited on discontinuation. p49: main psychoactive metabolite is mCPP via CYP3A3/4 hydroxylation, further metabolized by polymorphic CYP2D6; poor metabolizers have higher mCPP steady-state concentrations; thioridazine (CYP2D6 inhibitor) increased mCPP plasma concentrations ~50%; the only fatal liver failure case involved combined trazodone and trifluoperazine (neuroleptic) treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Nefazodone, a phenylpiperazine derivative structurally similar to trazodone, was reported in 1999 in a total of four cases of severe hepatic injury that led to subfulminant hepatic necrosis with hepatic encephalopathy and liver failure despite drug withdrawal, with histopathology showing prominent hepatocellular necrosis in centrolobular areas. A 2000 report described a woman with severe hepatocellular jaundice 20 weeks after initiation of nefazodone who fully recovered after discontinuation. The mechanism appears to be metabolic idiosyncrasy given the absence of hypersensitivity features and long latency. All reported cases were women, and its use is contraindicated in patients with liver disease or elevated baseline aminotransferase levels.

Mechanism metabolic idiosyncrasy (no hypersensitivity features, long latency). Withdrawn from European market by Bristol Myers Squibb due to excess severe hepatic risk without relevant advantages.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) causes human drug-induced liver injury with a delayed onset; anti-INH and/or anti-P450 antibodies were found in 15 of 19 patients with INH-induced liver failure, and covalent INH binding was identified in a human liver biopsy from a patient with INH-induced liver failure. raw_record.support_text: Ximelagatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, developed for long-term and short-term use, caused serious hepatotoxicity in long-term clinical trials. Among 6,948 treated patients, 7.6% and 1.1% developed ALT increases >3x and >10x ULN respectively, and 0.5% had concurrent total bilirubin >2x ULN versus 0.08% for warfarin. Among the 37 ximelagatran-associated cases (13 with no alternative etiology) there were three deaths linked to liver injury, and a comprehensive review judged ximelagatran-induced serious hepatotoxicity 'highly likely' a cause in one death. The initial NDA was not approved in 2004 and the drug was withdrawn from all markets in 2006 after a severe hepatotoxicity case in an orthopedic surgery trial.

raw_record.support_text: Propylthiouracil is widely used in the treatment of hyperthyroidism, and isolated hepatotoxicity due to propylthiouracil has been reported only rarely, with 13 adult and 5 pediatric cases reported in the English-language literature. Almost all patients with propylthiouracil-induced hepatitis had jaundice with nausea, vomiting, malaise, hepatic tenderness, or hepatomegaly; histology in 9 of 18 patients showed massive/submassive hepatic necrosis, chronic active hepatitis, or portal inflammation. In the patient of this report, propylthiouracil therapy was stopped and she developed propylthiouracil-induced hepatitis with dense portal inflammation and confluent zone 3 necrosis, later progressing clinically to cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of propylthiouracil-induced hepatotoxicity in a hyperthyroid woman treated for Graves disease; hepatic necrosis primarily involving zone 3 with dense portal inflammatory infiltration, bridging between lobules, and subsequent progression to cirrhosis (ascites and splenomegaly at 48 weeks, no follow-up biopsy due to prolonged prothrombin time). Course complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation and prolonged prothrombin time; hepatitis A/B/C serology negative. Discontinuation of propylthiouracil was followed by clinical deterioration eventually; lab values included AST up to 549 units/L, ALT up to 475 units/L, total bilirubin up to 3.2 mg/dL. Literature summary: 18 reported cases (13 adult, 5 pediatric, 16 female), onset 1 day to 15 months after starting therapy; histology in 9 cases: 5 massive/submassive hepatic necrosis (1 survived), 3 chronic active hepatitis, 1 portal inflammation with cholestasis.

raw_record.extra_details: Patient treated for hot flushes; lab course: ALT 372 U/L (ref 0-20), AST 99 U/L (ref 0-31), alkaline phosphatase 483 U/L (ref 35-104), GGT 962 U/L (ref 5-36) at peak; symptoms and enzyme elevations recurred on rechallenge (2/26/04), resolving after final discontinuation. Characterized as highly probable on the Naranjo probability scale. Venlafaxine is a bicyclic antidepressant inhibiting serotonin, norepinephrine, and, to some extent, dopamine uptake; metabolized by CYP2D6 to active metabolite O-desmethylvenlafaxine (longer half-life ~11 h; venlafaxine ~5 h). Product information lists hepatitis as a rare adverse effect (<1/1000 patients); voluntary postmarketing reports identified hepatic events including GGT and other enzyme elevations, liver damage, necrosis, liver failure, and fatty liver. An analysis of >3000 venlafaxine clinical-trial patients found 0.4% had AST >3x ULN (vs 0.2% placebo, 0.9% active control) with no clinical evidence of hepatic disease; no adverse hepatic effects in 14 acute-overdose patients; WHO adverse-drug-reaction database analysis found no difference in hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, hepatic failure, or pancreatitis incidence vs SSRIs. A MEDLINE search (1966-July 2005) found 5 case reports of venlafaxine-associated hepatitis, 3 in patients on 150 mg/day without other causative factors and 2 with competing factors (hepatitis B; sertraline overdose).

raw_record.support_text: Flupirtine, a non-opioid analgesic, has been reported to cause liver injury of idiosyncratic type in rare instances. In a study of six cases (five liver biopsies of patients with severe liver injury and one explanted liver of a patient with flupirtine-induced acute liver failure that required transplantation), extensive perivenular necrosis with ceroid pigment-laden macrophages and a mild to moderate lymphocytic infiltrate was common to all cases; necrosis extent corresponded to serum aminotransferase levels, and accidental reexposure of one patient produced a plasma cell rich hepatitis with perivenular necrosis. The study provides evidence that flupirtine can cause substantial liver injury of hepatocellular type.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Idiosyncratic injury in rare instances, occurring at therapeutic analgesic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Six cases total: five patients with severe liver injury (liver biopsies) and one patient with flupirtine-induced acute liver failure requiring transplantation (explanted liver). Histology: extensive perivenular necrosis with ceroid pigment-laden macrophages and mild to moderate lymphocytic infiltrate; histological extent of necrosis corresponded to serum aminotransferase levels. Accidental reexposure in one patient resulted in a plasma cell rich hepatitis with perivenular necrosis. Clinical and histological features raise the possibility of immune-mediated toxicity. Flupirtine is licensed in several European countries, Russia and China for treatment of acute and chronic musculoskeletal pain, tension-type headache, pain in metastatic malignancies, dysmenorrhea, and postoperative pain; its analgesic effect is believed to be mediated through activation of G-protein-regulated inwardly rectifying potassium channels.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of six patients with flupirtine-associated liver injury, flupirtine was the only common drug, and all five patients who recovered shared characteristic histological features and identical clinical courses after discontinuation of flupirtine. Using the international consensus score (RUCAM), flupirtine causality was rated 'probable' in four cases and 'highly probable' in two cases, with ultimate proof of causality provided by accidental reexposure in one case; the authors concluded flupirtine has to be regarded as the causative drug. One patient (patient 6) required liver transplantation.

raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 6 patients. Median latency (time to admission after drug initiation) 4 months (range 3 weeks to 24 months). Histology showed centrolobular/zone 3 necrosis with prominent ceroid-laden macrophages, lobular and portal inflammation, plasma cells, eosinophils, interface hepatitis, ductular reaction, acidophil bodies; some canalicular cholestasis and fibrosis in individual patients. No evidence of autoimmune hepatitis. Mean follow-up 16 months (range 5-55; median 9). Patient 6 underwent liver transplantation and is alive without transplant dysfunction; other patients recovered. RUCAM: probable in 4, highly probable in 2; one case had accidental reexposure providing proof of causality. Author notes up to Sept 2007, 151 cases of flupirtine-associated liver injury including 70 cases of hepatitis reported, and a clinical trial of 100 patients receiving flupirtine 5-7 days showed elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin in 3 patients. Flupirtine should be included in the list of drugs capable of causing severe liver injury; monitoring of liver function is warranted. Mechanism remaining unclear; authors classify injury as idiosyncratic/type B, dose-dependent mechanism unlikely.

The patient had jaundice with ALT 1826 U/L, ALP 741 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 897 U/L, total bilirubin 242 µmol/L and elevated serum bile acids (279 µmol/L); a liver biopsy showed mild hepatocellular necrosis, moderate interface hepatitis and isolated eosinophils without evident cholestasis or fibrosis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report being confident that a causal relationship exists between rofecoxib therapy and liver dysfunction in two described cases, both rated highly probable of drug-induced liver injury on the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) causality scale. The temporal association was appropriate (symptoms within two to six weeks of drug initiation) and clinical and biochemical improvements occurred rapidly upon rofecoxib discontinuation. Other causes including viral hepatitis, other toxins, and autoimmune hepatitis were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of severe hepatotoxicity attributed to rofecoxib. In the presented case, ALT 995 U/L, ALP 243 U/L, GGT 99 U/L, total bilirubin 207 µmol/L, INR 1.1, positive ANA (1:320 speckled), slightly elevated IgG; histology showed mild macrovesicular steatosis with established portal and perivenular fibrosis and mononuclear portal/lobular infiltrate, interpreted as acute drug-induced hepatotoxicity superimposed on previously subclinical liver injury. Symptoms resolved within a week of discontinuation and liver biochemistry normalized over the following month. The first patient had previously received rofecoxib on brief occasions without hepatotoxicity; the authors speculate sensitization by repeated use with toxicity on prolonged exposure. Authors cite 4 additional reported rofecoxib cases of severe hepatic injury in the English literature.

raw_record.support_text: The two cases described in this report illustrate the variability in presentation of rofecoxib-induced hepatic injury. Both patients had cholestatic symptoms but differed in biochemistry and histology: the first had a mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic injury (cholestatic hepatitis) with predominantly zone 1 injury, while the second had significant ALT elevation with minimal ALP rise and mild zone 1 and zone 3 injury. Previously reported cases of rofecoxib-induced hepatotoxicity were primarily cholestatic.

raw_record.extra_details: Two new patients plus four previously reported literature cases (six total severe rofecoxib-induced hepatotoxicity cases). Doses 12.5 or 25 mg/day for 10 days to 22 months. All had jaundice/cholestatic symptoms; liver biochemistry showed elevated ALT (31-1826 U/L), ALP (243-2968 U/L), and bilirubin (95-420 µmol/L). Histology showed hepatocellular/canalicular cholestasis, portal/perivenular inflammation with lymphocytes and eosinophils, bile duct destruction, and focal hepatocyte necrosis. No patient developed acute liver failure. Complete biochemical normalization took from 1 month to more than 2 years (one case with persistently cholestatic enzymes and suspected but unproven vanishing bile duct syndrome); UDCA, prednisone, and MARS were used. No hypersensitivity reaction attributable to rofecoxib was seen.

raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old man worked as an anaesthetist for 3½ months during which he was exposed daily to small amounts of halothane (Fluothane, I.C.I.), with no known exposure to hepatitis. He fell ill at the end of July 1965 with fatigue and nausea, and early in August noticed dark urine and jaundice. Peak laboratory findings included serum-bilirubin (direct) 4.6 mg/100 ml, S.G.P.T. 1590 units, S.G.O.T. 555 units, S.L.D.H. 505 units, and 7% eosinophilia. On October 12, 1965 the patient was anaesthetised with halothane for a few minutes as a provocation test and within hours developed chills, nausea, headache, myalgia and fever (39.4°C); without jaundice but with significantly increased transaminases, slightly increased bilirubin, eosinophilia up to 1238 per c. mm. and abnormal B.S.P. retention, consistent with halothane-induced hepatitis. A second similar case was reported by Klatskin and Kimberg in 1969.

A second similar case was reported by Klatskin and Kimberg in 1969. Alias: Fluothane.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac, the most widely used NSAID in the world, is discussed as a cause of human hepatotoxicity. Banks and co-workers analyzed 180 cases referred to the FDA (1988-1991), finding liver disease in 85% of patients within the first 6 months, jaundice in 90 of 120 patients, and 7 jaundiced patients who died from liver disease; LFTs showed a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern in 66% of cases and cholestatic in 8%. In the prospective, randomized, double-blind MEDAL program (17,289 patients), hypertransaminasemia >3xULN occurred in over 3% of arthritis patients on diclofenac 150 mg daily, ALT >10xULN in 0.5%, liver-related hospitalizations at 16 per 100,000 patient-years (0.023%), and Hy's cases at 0.012%. The authors conclude diclofenac bears a low liver toxicity rate while still causing hepatic reactions.
raw_record.extra_details: NSAID; Banks 1995 analysis of 180 FDA-referred cases (1988-1991): liver disease in 85% within 6 mo, higher latency >6 mo in 12%; jaundice in 90 of 120 patients, 7 jaundiced deaths; LFTs mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic in 66%, cholestatic in 8%, indeterminate remainder. MEDAL program: prospective randomized double-blind, 17,289 osteoarthritis/rheumatoid arthritis patients >50 y on diclofenac 150 mg daily vs etoricoxib (60/90 mg); excluded prior liver disease and >14 weekly alcoholic drinks; hypertransaminasemia >3xULN in >3%; ALT >10xULN in 0.5%; liver-related hospitalizations 16/100,000 patient-years (0.023%); Hy's cases 0.012%. Authors concluded diclofenac has a low liver toxicity rate. Mechanistic context: metabolic idiosyncrasy or immunologic injury via drug adduct formation, reactive metabolite formation and clearance.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that in 2009 the authors' series included 43 well documented cases of nimesulide-induced liver damage associated with a wide clinical and histological spectrum of hepatotoxicity, the largest series of nimesulide hepatotoxicity ever reported. Main presenting symptoms were jaundice (70%), malaise (65%), and pruritus (50%); two thirds of patients started liver toxicity 15 to 90 days after drug intake, with only 11% having a latency shorter than 15 days, and normalization exceeded 90 days in 27% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Largest reported series of nimesulide hepatotoxicity (43 well documented cases). In the authors' institution, 5 of 30 cases (17%) had severe liver injury. Nine patients developed severe liver disease and fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) occurred in 6 cases, predominantly females older than 50 years (per Walker et al); 2 patients died before liver transplant due to multiorgan failure, and a 9-year-old girl successfully underwent orthotopic liver transplantation. ALT/aspartate transaminase: a wide range of variations; per Bjarnason, 33 case reports showed ALT elevation of at least 2-fold in 100% and 5-fold in 89% of patients. Liver damage spectrum included acute hepatitis, cholestasis, mixed forms, and massive and submassive hepatic necrosis: hepatocellular necrosis in 64%, cholestatic hepatitis in 27%, pure cholestasis in 9%. Symptoms: jaundice, malaise, pruritus; latency 15-90 days in two-thirds, only 11% shorter than 15 days; normalization exceeded 90 days in 27%; in cholestatic injury, alkaline phosphatase normalization can exceed 1 year. Proposed mechanism (unconfirmed): reactive metabolite formation and genetic variation in drug metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: In a study population of 1044 patients, the incidence of hepatic adverse reaction to dantrolene sodium, reflected by elevation of serum transaminase levels with or without jaundice, was 1.8%, and the incidence of overt hepatitis manifested by jaundice and biochemical evidence of hepatic injury was 0.6%. Fourteen patients died of drug-related hepatic injury, with 8 of the fatal cases exposed for at least 6 months; no hepatic injury was observed with exposure under 1 month, and no fatalities occurred with exposure under 2 months. Hepatic injury was more frequent (P < 0.05) at daily doses of 300 mg or more, and fatal cases were almost restricted to this dose, with none below 200 mg/day. The mechanism remained obscure; hypersensitivity hallmarks were absent and the long exposure before damage weighed against drug allergy, with injury possibly attributable to an idiosyncratic metabolic reaction, and the pattern was consistent with chronic active hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In this series of 82 patients with suspected disulfiram adverse liver reactions, four patients died during the initial hospitalisation and four underwent successful liver transplantation. Deceased or transplanted patients had higher serum bilirubin, AST, AST/ALT ratio and INR values than those who recovered, with no difference in age, sex, or duration of treatment. The study frames these as drug-induced liver injury cases attributed to disulfiram.
raw_record.extra_details: 82 patients with disulfiram suspected adverse liver reactions (1979-2004 reports); median ALT 46xULN and bilirubin 6.0xULN across the cohort. 49 patients fulfilled Hy's rule (ALT>=3xULN + bilirubin>=2xULN), with a 16% (8/49) mortality/transplantation rate. 4 patients died, 4 underwent liver transplantation. Liver biopsy in one patient who used alcohol showed eosinophilic infiltration and no evidence of alcohol-induced injury. In a multivariate analysis, bilirubin (P=0.0005, OR 1.214, CI 1.088-1.355) was the only independent predictor of death or liver transplantation. Median treatment duration 42 days (IQR 35-60). Two patients had documented alcohol use during treatment.

In a case series of patients with disulfiram-induced liver injury undergoing liver biopsy, eosinophilic leucocyte infiltration was associated with a better outcome whereas hepatocyte drop-out was associated with a poor outcome, and bilirubin, but not age, duration of therapy, or abnormal baseline liver tests, predicted death or liver transplantation.

Mechanism described as incompletely understood, with both immunoallergy/hypersensitivity and toxic-metabolite hypotheses; autoantibodies against specific cytochrome P450 enzymes were identified in serum of a patient with disulfiram-induced hepatitis. Bilirubin, but not age, therapy duration, or baseline abnormal liver tests, predicted death or liver transplantation. The paper notes no evidence that baseline abnormal liver tests increase susceptibility to DILI, though pre-existing cirrhosis is associated with worse outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Following post-marketing exposure, two cases of reversible hepatocellular liver injury were reported by different healthcare professionals, suggesting drug-related liver injury had occurred. In both patients, hepatic biochemical test abnormalities resolved when atomoxetine was stopped, and one case of hepatitis recurred following rechallenge with atomoxetine, supporting a causal relationship. These cases were deemed sufficient evidence of an increased risk of liver toxicity to warrant a 2004 label change for atomoxetine. Considering the now extensive exposure (>4 million patients after 4 years), these reactions are very rare and fit the pattern of an idiosyncratic drug reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases of liver injury probably related to atomoxetine are known to Eli Lilly and Company; case 4 was reclassified as only possibly related because of a second hepatitis episode after atomoxetine was discontinued, while cases 2 and 3 were deemed probably related. Estimated global exposure was about 2.2 million patients when the initial cases arose, and >4 million patients after 4 years. Spontaneous adverse event reporting rate of liver injury, regardless of aetiology, was <0.01% (351 cases among 4,328,000 exposed patients); reporting rate was 23.7 per 100,000 person-years, within the range of background liver injury rates (0.7–164.9 per 100,000 person-years). A 2004 US package insert label change included a warning with a Dear healthcare professional letter. Preclinical testing in rats, mice and dogs showed no liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: At therapeutic doses acetaminophen (APAP) is mostly conjugated via glucuronidation and sulphation, with a minor fraction oxidized to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which is responsible for APAP hepatotoxicity and detoxified via glutathione. On acetaminophen overdose, the glucuronidation/sulphation pathways saturate and excess NAPQI depletes glutathione, causing liver injury; NAC is the only approved antidote and is most effective when started within 8 hours. In this systematic review, all APAP cases treated with NAC (oral or intravenous) recovered with no adverse effects except one infant who died, possibly due to delayed NAC administration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paediatric population; unintentional higher-than-therapeutic (overdose) administration; one infant death possibly due to delayed NAC administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity intrinsically related to unintentional higher-dose exposure above the recommended threshold; NAPQI is the reactive metabolite responsible for the hepatotoxicity, detoxified through the glutathione pathway; NAPQI excess depletes glutathione and causes liver injury; NAC (oral or intravenous) replenishes hepatic glutathione and was given to all APAP cases; one recovered infant death possibly due to delayed NAC.

raw_record.support_text: An ad hoc group adjudicated 42 spontaneous reports of liver injury associated with telithromycin reported to the FDA as of April 2006. Five cases had severe outcomes (4 deaths, 1 liver transplantation); more than half were considered highly likely or probable in causal association with telithromycin. Typical clinical features were short latency (median 10 days) with abrupt onset of fever, abdominal pain, and jaundice, sometimes with ascites. The paper concludes that telithromycin is a rare cause of drug-induced liver injury with a distinctive clinical signature and associated high mortality rate.
raw_record.extra_details: Ketolide antibiotic approved by the FDA in 2004 for upper and lower respiratory infections, dosed 800 mg once daily. 42 cases comprehensively reviewed and adjudicated by an expert group; 5 severe outcomes (4 deaths, 1 liver transplantation); >half considered highly likely or probable. Pre-marketing development included one case of significant hepatocellular injury with eosinophilia and high aminotransferases 10 days after a 10-day course, and mild cholestatic liver injury in European/Latin American post-marketing reports. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports clinical features of 42 spontaneously reported cases (MedWatch) of telithromycin-associated liver toxicity. Median age was 50 years (range 22-90), including 29 women (69%) and 13 men (31%); leading indications were sinusitis (52%) and bronchitis (17%). Median latency from treatment initiation to symptom/biochemical onset was 10 days (range 2-43). Initial symptoms included abdominal pain (45%) and fever (29%); 7 patients (17%) presented with or developed ascites (transudate in the 3 examined). Four of the 42 patients died of liver failure and one underwent emergency liver transplantation. Causality was assigned by five independent reviewers using possible/probable/very likely categories and DILIN severity grades.

Cases mostly serious: 60% had clinical jaundice or hyperbilirubinemia (bilirubin ≥2.5 mg/dL) plus ALT elevation, consistent with Hy's law. DILIN severity grade distribution: grade 1 (serum enzyme elevations only) 8 cases (19%), grade 2 (jaundice no hospitalization) 4 (10%), grade 3 (jaundice + hospitalization) 16 (38%), grade 4 (jaundice + hepatic failure) 9 (21%), grade 5 (death of liver failure or transplant) 5 (12%). Four patients died of liver failure; one underwent emergency liver transplantation. Eight cases reported eosinophilia. Four cases had prior telithromycin exposure with re-onset after 2-6 days. Highest reported values: total bilirubin median 4.5 mg/dL (range 0.5-29.0); ALT median 934 IU/L (range 189-25,098); alkaline phosphatase median 200 IU/L (range 33-598). raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of liver failure attributable to nafcillin use in a 68-year-old male treated for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus osteomyelitis. After 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy he presented with painless jaundice, required drug discontinuation, and a liver biopsy showed findings consistent with drug-induced liver injury; liver function tests trended toward normal with cessation of nafcillin, and he was discharged with a diagnosis of nafcillin-induced acute liver injury. The abstract frames nafcillin-induced acute liver injury as a rare and potentially fatal complication known since the 1960s.
raw_record.extra_details: Intravenous nafcillin 2 g every 4 h, on therapy for 4 weeks at presentation; presenting labs bilirubin/direct bilirubin 9.4/8.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 311 IU/L, aspartate transaminase/alanine transaminase 109/127 IU/L; painless jaundice, dark urine, grey stools, 20-lb weight loss; imaging showed no hepatobiliary/pancreaticobiliary obstruction; serology negative for viral, autoimmune, Wilson disease, and hemochromatosis; liver biopsy consistent with DILI; positive dechallenge with LFTs peaking at day 7 of admission and trending normal after nafcillin cessation; recovered and discharged. Intro labels cholestatic hepatitis as a rare complication of nafcillin; first cohort study (Viehman et al., 224 patients on antibiotics >1 month) reported acute hepatic toxicity in 4% of nafcillin users, no significant difference vs oxacillin (3%).

raw_record.support_text: The case report highlights early recognition of nafcillin-induced acute liver injury. Complete withdrawal of nafcillin resulted in complete recovery of liver function and the drug effects were proven reversible, adding to the literature supporting the finding of DILI. The current opinion is that nafcillin is generally well tolerated, with the most common side effects being mild to moderate gastrointestinal and hematological toxicities.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case. Due to the acute nature of presentation, the cholestatic pattern of the liver injury, and eosinophilia, there was high suspicion for DILI; pathology further confirmed the diagnosis. Patient presented with painless jaundice, marked transaminitis, and hyperbilirubinemia. Thorough workup found no underlying etiology, no prior hepatic or renal disease, and no other hepatotoxic drugs at the time. Following discontinuation, symptomatology dramatically improved and liver function normalized. The case concerned prolonged use of nafcillin (long-term treatment); authors recommend serial liver function testing in patients on long-term nafcillin and class-equivalent narrow-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotics.

raw_record.support_text: A 47-year-old woman developed weakness, fatigue, pruritus, and scleral icterus 10 days after completing a self-prescribed 7-day course of oral methylprednisolone; she was also taking topiramate. Admission liver tests were ALT 2478 U/L, AST 1600 U/L, total bilirubin 10 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 138 U/L, and GGT 242 U/L; no other causes of liver dysfunction were identified. The final diagnosis was mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury caused by methylprednisolone, with enzyme levels returning to normal within 45 days after drug discontinuation. An objective Naranjo-scale causality assessment indicated hepatotoxicity was probably related to methylprednisolone, making this the third published case of methylprednisolone-induced toxic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin causes rare RUCAM-based idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury, described for a cohort of 197 patients (gender F/M 133/64, mean age 62±13 years, mean time to onset 24±18 days, total days on drug 10±6 days). The liver injury pattern was hepatocellular in 20%, mixed in 43%, and cholestatic in 38% of cases, and RUCAM scoring was probable or higher in most cases. The paper describes flucloxacillin iDILI as presenting as both cholestatic and hepatocellular injury, with cholestatic injury explained metabolically (via CYP3A4/3A7-mediated toxification to 5′-hydroxymethylflucloxacillin) and hepatocellular injury requiring both metabolic and HLA B*57:01-restricted immune activation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatocellular injury specifically occurs in HLA B*57:01-positive patients; cholestatic injury is explained via metabolic toxification by CYP3A4/3A7.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 197 patients with RUCAM-verified iDILI; gender F/M 133/64, mean age 62±13 years, mean time to onset 24±18 days, total days on drug 10±6 days; injury pattern hepatocellular 20%, mixed 43%, cholestatic 38%; RUCAM scoring probable or higher in most cases. Incidence estimated around 0.01%. Mechanism: CYP3A4/3A7-mediated toxification to 5′-hydroxymethylflucloxacillin (cytotoxic to human biliary epithelial cells in culture, simulating cholestatic injury) for cholestatic injury; covalent binding of flucloxacillin to albumin as hapten with HLA B*57:01-restricted activation of drug-specific T-cells (CCR4/CCR9, CCL17/CCL25, interferon-γ, cytokines) for hepatocellular injury.

RUCAM drug causality scale scored the likelihood. Three cases evolved into chronic hepatitis and one followed a typical acute hepatitis with slow resolution. All cases occurred with modern volatile anaesthetics, predominantly sevoflurane, and were proven with specific antibody tests, liver histology and a causality scale. This is the first report of chronic liver injury due to volatile anaesthetic exposure.

raw_record.support_text: The text states there is little doubt that, rarely, halothane causes hepatitis. Convincing evidence comes from challenge experiments, such as an anaesthetist who developed clinical, biochemical, and hepatic histological deterioration on rechallenge with halothane. Two controlled prospective clinical trials (Oxford and Southampton) reported an increased incidence of raised transaminase values in those receiving halothane; in the Oxford trial four of 18 halothane-treated patients showed serum transaminase values exceeding 100, compared with none of the 21 controls. Liver biopsies showed definite and sometimes severe acute hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Challenge/rechallenge cases (e.g., an anaesthetist with clinical, biochemical and histological deterioration on rechallenge, ref 40). Oxford trial: 4/18 halothane-treated patients with serum transaminases >100 vs 0/21 controls; Southampton trial also showed increased raised transaminases. Delay between anaesthesia and hepatic reaction (usually pyrexia) at least seven days after first exposure; jaundice appears two to three days later. Mortality high if deep jaundice develops; recovered patients show no late chronic effects despite marked bridging necrosis. Histology shows centrilobular necrosis, sometimes with fat. Metabolism to trifluoroacetic acid, bromide and chloride; reductive metabolites proposed as toxic and potentially covalently binding (direct injury); possible immunological mediation (fever, eosinophilia, skin rash, smooth muscle antibodies, liver-kidney microsomal antibody, leucocyte migration tests).

raw_record.support_text: A healthy 28-year-old male from rural United States was taking doxycycline for Lyme disease. After five days of therapy he developed nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and significant transaminitis consistent with a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury. After a thorough workup ruled out infection, autoimmune diseases, liver malignancy, and vascular, structural, and metabolic disorders, his liver injury was attributed to doxycycline, supported by a consistent temporal association between doxycycline intake and the injury and complete recovery upon cessation. The authors note doxycycline versus minocycline has a short latency period and that recognition of doxycycline as a cause of DILI should be considered. The patient was prescribed doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for two weeks for early localized Lyme disease and discontinued it on day 5 due to nausea.

raw_record.support_text: The FDA received 11 reports (three fatal) of hepatocellular damage associated with labetalol in the United States. Temporal circumstances strongly implicate labetalol: nine patients improved after cessation of labetalol therapy and one had a recurrence after therapy was restarted. Follow-up with each reporting physician found no historic or laboratory evidence for other viral, toxic, or drug-induced causes, and the series lacked demographic/historic risk factors expected for non-A, non-B hepatitis. Microscopic examinations (5 cases) showed changes consistent with hepatocellular necrosis in four instances and chronic active hepatitis in one. The clinical presentation was most compatible with a metabolic idiosyncrasy mechanism.

Case 1 was a 49-year-old black woman on labetalol (stabilized at 300 mg/day) who developed jaundice after ~60 days, with marked AST/ALT elevation, alkaline phosphatase ~2x normal, total bilirubin 308 µmol/L (18.0 mg/dL); negative for hepatitis A IgM, HBsAg, and anti-HBc (anti-HBs positive); no blood transfusion or alcohol history; referred for liver transplant on 20 Dec 1986 and died 4 days post-transplant. raw_record.support_text: The 11 aggregate cases are far more consistent with labetalol producing severe hepatocellular damage: normal baseline liver function before exposure, development of hepatitis after drug exposure, and marked clinical improvement after discontinuation in 9 of 11 cases (the other two had already evolved to hepatic failure). A documented recurrence after re-exposure in case 2 makes labetalol-induced hepatocellular necrosis the best explanation. The subacute time course (median time to onset ~2 months) and absence of hypersensitivity hallmarks support metabolic idiosyncrasy as the likely mechanism, although pathogenesis is not definitively resolved.
raw_record.extra_details: Eleven cases of labetalol-induced hepatotoxicity reported to the U.S. FDA Adverse Drug Reaction Reporting System, 1985-1989. Average patient age 56 y; predominantly women (9/11, 82%); estimated average daily dose 285 mg; median time to onset 60 d; case fatality rate 3/11 (27%), with 3 deaths (cases 1-3) and 8 hospitalizations (all recovered). Recurrence after re-exposure documented in case 2 (previously described by Douglas et al.). Pathogenesis ascribed to metabolic idiosyncrasy, possibly due to genetically determined cytochrome P-450 isozyme differences; eosinophils were present in two of five pathology reports but fever, eosinophilia, and rash were almost entirely absent (rash 1/11, peripheral eosinophilia 1/7, elevated temperature 0/8). Non-A, non-B hepatitis was considered and largely excluded as an alternative explanation. Laboratory values used were those obtained soonest after clinical diagnosis, expressed as multiples of the upper limit of normal.

raw_record.support_text: Clopidogrel (Plavix) is reported to cause a rare severe cholestatic hepatitis. The authors describe a 34-year-old male on aspirin and clopidogrel for coronary artery disease who developed jaundice 4 months after re-starting clopidogrel, with AST peaking at 2,107 U/L, ALT at 1,562 U/L, total bilirubin 5.7 mg/dL, and prothrombin time 19.8; other etiologies (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, immune panel) were negative. Liver biopsy showed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate mainly of neutrophils with plasma cells and proliferation of bile ducts. After clopidogrel discontinuation, progressive cholestasis led to a trial of steroids plus ursodiol, followed by rapid normalization of liver tests. The discussion states the patient had severe cholestatic hepatitis due to clopidogrel, with onset in reports ranging from 4-180 days and a possible idiosyncratic toxic-metabolic mechanism with a superimposed immune-mediated component.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 34-year-old male with coronary artery disease (and remote coronary stent) treated with aspirin and clopidogrel; prior 2-month clopidogrel course 12 years earlier without adverse effect. Latency approximately 4 months after re-starting. Peak AST 2,107 U/L, ALT 1,562 U/L, total bilirubin 5.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 19.8; no peripheral eosinophilia. Imaging (ultrasound, CT, ERCP) negative for obstruction. Biopsy showed mixed inflammatory infiltrate predominantly neutrophils with plasma cells and bile duct proliferation. Co-medications aspirin and metoprolol had been used for years with normal liver tests (aspirin, metoprolol and other etiologies excluded). Received empiric vitamin K; progressive cholestasis and rising INR led to steroids plus ursodiol with rapid normalization of LFTs. Literature-reported onset 4-180 days; one prior case associated with rash, fever, and leukopenia. Mechanism proposed as idiosyncratic toxic-metabolic with possible superimposed immune-mediated component.

Acute injury has presented as both hepatocellular and cholestatic disease, while chronic disease has consisted of granulomatous changes and the development of chronic active hepatitis. raw_record.extra_details: In the 20 cases: elevated bilirubin in 14, increased AST in all 20, hypoalbuminemia in 87%, hyperglobulinemia in 28%, positive ANA in 71%, positive SMA in 91%; CAH histology in 17 of 20 biopsied, cirrhosis in 4; 5 of 14 had simultaneous pulmonary disease. raw_record.extra_details: Approximately 10% of recipients develop mild aminotransferase abnormalities associated histologically with focal hepatocellular necrosis; more severe damage occurs in about 1%. raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old female with latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection receiving oral isoniazid 300 mg daily was admitted for epigastric and right-sided flank pain of one-week duration; laboratory results and imaging confirmed hepatitis. After ruling out all other possible causes, she was diagnosed with isoniazid-induced acute hepatitis, rated a probable association by the Naranjo scale. She was readmitted with severe coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, hepatic encephalopathy, and cardiorespiratory arrest and, despite maximal hemodynamic support, did not survive. The paper also reviews literature from European countries and the USA reporting a low incidence of mortality due to isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity when isoniazid is used as a single agent for latent tuberculosis infection, and notes that withdrawal of isoniazid is the first management step and rechallenge is usually discouraged.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral dose 300 mg daily for latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection; presented with epigastric and right-sided flank pain for one week; hepatitis confirmed by labs and imaging; later severe coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, hepatic encephalopathy, and cardiorespiratory arrest requiring two rounds of CPR; patient died despite maximal hemodynamic support. Naranjo scale rated probable. Patient was 65 years old (age is a well-confirmed risk factor per the paper's discussion). Literature review (European countries and USA) indicates a low incidence of mortality when isoniazid is used as single-agent therapy for latent TB; management is withdrawal of isoniazid and rechallenge is usually discouraged. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncratic reactions; CYP2E1 c1/c1 homozygous slow acetylators at increased risk. Historical context: 1970 Capitol Hill TB outbreak, 19 prophylaxis workers developed signs/symptoms of liver damage and 2 died.

Rodman et al.: 6 patients, 2 deaths from massive/submassive necrosis, one 72-year-old female rechallenged twice with recurrence of symptoms and transaminase elevation. raw_record.support_text: Detectable titres of serum autoantibodies, mostly antinuclear antibodies, were present in 3 cases of lumiracoxib-induced hepatotoxicity, suggesting an immune-mediated mechanism in the pathogenesis of coxib-induced DILI. A genome-wide association study in 41 cases of lumiracoxib-induced DILI and 176 drug-tolerant lumiracoxib-exposed controls found a strong association with HLA class II markers, with HLA-DQA1*0102 being the most sensitive (73.6%) in predicting risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Three reported cases of lumiracoxib-induced hepatotoxicity had detectable antinuclear antibodies, suggesting an immune-mediated/immune mechanism in the pathogenesis. Genetic susceptibility is supported by a GWAS of 41 lumiracoxib-induced DILI cases versus 176 drug-tolerant lumiracoxib-exposed controls, with strong association to HLA class II region markers; HLA-DQA1*0102 was the most sensitive (73.6%) in predicting risk. Proposed mechanisms include reactive metabolites generating antigenic drug-protein adducts presented by HLA complexes triggering a T-cell-mediated immune response, or direct interaction of lumiracoxib with the HLA complex.

Laboratory values showed total bilirubin 4.4 mg/dL, ALT 55 U/L, AST 209 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 374 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 627 U/L and prothrombin time 70%. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis were excluded, and liver biopsy showed oedema and inflammation of the portal tract with intracanalicular cholestasis and moderate macrovesicular steatosis. The authors concluded the patient had cholestatic hepatitis secondary to methimazole treatment; methimazole was withdrawn. The CIOMS/RUCAM scale gave a score of 6 points, indicating a probable relationship between methimazole and hepatotoxicity, and the authors stated that the drug history, absence of viral hepatitis markers, and liver biopsy results indicated methimazole was the cause of the cholestatic hepatitis.

Acute viral and autoimmune serologies and toxicology were negative; liver biopsy showed necrotic hepatic parenchyma likely due to drug toxicity. Based on the clinical presentation, time course, biopsy pattern and lack of an alternative explanation, her liver failure was most likely associated with orlistat use, and she ultimately underwent orthotopic liver transplantation. raw_record.support_text: Flucloxacillin, used for treatment of staphylococcal infection, is associated with a characteristic cholestatic hepatitis that is more common in females, the elderly, and with prolonged treatment courses; in the UK the incidence of flucloxacillin-induced DILI was estimated at 8.5 per 100,000 new users in days 1-45 after starting treatment. The paper's genome-wide study of 51 flucloxacillin DILI cases (86% classified as cholestatic injury, 92% with ICC causality scores of probably or highly probably attributable to flucloxacillin) confirmed the causal relationship and identified HLA-B*5701 (and ST6GAL1 rs10937275) as susceptibility loci.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis phenotype; 51 eligible DILIGEN study cases, average age at onset 63 years, higher proportion of females; 86% classified cholestatic flucloxacillin-induced injury; 92% of ICC causality scores probably or highly probably due to flucloxacillin; UK incidence 8.5 per 100,000 new users in days 1-45; more common in females, the elderly, and with prolonged treatment courses; genome-wide association peak in MHC region (rs2395029[G], P=8.7x10^-33), in complete LD with HLA-B*5701 (OR=80.6, P=9.0x10^-19), replicated in 23 additional cases; rs10937275 in ST6GAL1 genome-wide significant (OR=4.1, P=1.4x10^-8); in vitro CYP3A4-generated 5'-hydroxymethylflucloxacillin metabolite toxic to biliary epithelial cells but not hepatocytes.

raw_record.support_text: Seven individuals with DILI exposed to co-amoxiclav in addition to flucloxacillin and 16 recently recruited individuals with flucloxacillin DILI were genotyped for HLA-B*5701 for replication; 20 of these 23 additional subjects (87%) were HLA-B*5701 positive (P = 6.62 × 10^-13). The paper is a genome-wide association study of a human DILI cohort that treats flucloxacillin-induced liver injury as an established clinical entity, additionally reporting that HLA-B*5701 did not correlate with pattern of injury and that four subjects with low ICC causality scores were all HLA-B*5701 positive.
raw_record.extra_details: Genome-wide association study of flucloxacillin DILI. Causality supported by Hill causality/HLA cohort with ICC causality scores (four subjects had low ICC scores). HLA-B*5701 genotype did not correlate with pattern of injury. Only 1 in every 500-1000 HLA-B*5701 carriers develops DILI when treated with flucloxacillin; population attributable fraction (PAF) of HLA-B*5701 estimated at 0.64. Additional genetic factors suspected; a chromosome 3 SNP (rs10937275) reached P = 1.4 × 10^-8 (allelic OR = 4.1, minor allele frequency 0.29 vs 0.09) in 48 risk-allele-carrying cases. Most subjects (65%) had at least one extrahepatic manifestation; no common CNV associated with DILI. Co-amoxiclav exposure was present in some subjects as a co-medication.

raw_record.support_text: The study included cases with suspected liver injury due to flucloxacillin, defined by clinically apparent jaundice or bilirubin >40 µmol/l (after excluding hemolysis), ALT >5× ULN, or ALP >2× ULN plus any raised bilirubin. The causal relationship of liver injury to flucloxacillin was assessed using international consensus criteria (ICC). Cases were identified by searching histological databases and discharge records at UK Regional Liver Units for DILI or cholestasis/hepatitis of unknown etiology.
raw_record.extra_details: Case inclusion required clinically apparent jaundice, bilirubin >40 µmol/l (post-hemolysis exclusion), ALT >5× ULN, or ALP >2× ULN plus raised bilirubin; case finding covered DILI or cholestasis/hepatitis of unknown etiology. 51 retrospective and prospective cases were collected October 2004–December 2007, with a further 16 recruited after December 2007 (including one from a UK MHRA ADR report); a separate group of 7 cases also received concomitant co-amoxiclav. Causality was assessed by international consensus criteria (ICC). For candidate gene analyses, 64 UK controls had been prescribed flucloxacillin within the last 5 years without DILI symptoms.

raw_record.support_text: Methimazole (MMI) is used to treat Graves' Disease and its treatment has been reported to be associated with hepatotoxicity. A well-characterized phenotypic cohort of 40 MMI-DILI cases (57.5% women, 50% cholestatic liver damage, occurring days to months after MMI dosing) and 118 MMI-tolerant controls was studied. The paper states that individuals carrying the HLA-C*03:02 allele are at increased risk of developing MMI-induced DILI, and HLA-A*02:01 was also associated with MMI-induced cholestatic/mixed liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: DILI in Chinese patients with Graves' Disease receiving MMI as anti-thyroid therapy; risk is increased in carriers of HLA-C*03:02 (OR 15.4) and HLA-A*02:01 (associated with cholestatic/mixed injury).
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-thyroid drug (thiourea) used for Graves' Disease; estimated DILI incidence 0.1-0.2%, typically developing in the first few weeks of drug consumption. Pattern mainly classified as cholestatic; 50% of the 40 cases were cholestatic. Proposed mechanisms include reactive metabolite formation, oxidative stress, intracellular target dysfunction, and immune-mediated toxicity. HLA-C*03:02 frequency 6.7% in cases vs 0.4% in tolerant controls (OR 15.4, 95% CI 1.77-133.9); HLA-A*02:01 OR 3.13 (95% CI 1.45-6.91) for cholestatic/mixed injury.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report of gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity, the responsibility of gefitinib was retained with an intrinsic imputability score of I3 (très vraisemblable / very likely). The absence of elevation of bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase along with elevated transaminases favored a hepatocellular injury, with no signs of immunologic toxicity (no fever, rash, or hypereosinophilia). An immunoallergic mechanism remained suspected because hepatotoxicity reappeared after rechallenge, with a shorter cytolysis recurrence delay (1 week) and rapid favorable evolution upon drug discontinuation. Doxycycline causality was not retained due to a non-consistent chronology. Gefitinib was stopped because of the occurrence of severe hepatotoxicity, and the authors note that EGFR-TK inhibitor hepatotoxicity is rare but that hepatic monitoring is recommended after treatment initiation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Immunoallergic mechanism suspected based on recurrence after rechallenge; rechallenge positive with shorter cytolysis recurrence delay (1 week) and rapid favorable evolution on discontinuation; doxycycline co-suspect explicitly not retained.
raw_record.extra_details: Intrinsic imputability score I3 (très vraisemblable/very likely), chronology C3, absence of other etiologies (viral, biliary, carcinomatous) scored S2. Transaminase elevation without bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase elevation and without fever/rash/hypereosinophilia. Gefitinib is an EGFR-TK inhibitor; hepatotoxicity noted as rare but hepatic monitoring recommended after treatment initiation and regularly thereafter due to long half-life. Erlotinib reported as an effective and well-tolerated option in patients for whom gefitinib was stopped due to severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI) of paracetamol remains one of the most common calls to Poisons Information Centres and emergency-department presentations worldwide, and that the commonest reason for acute liver failure in the developed world is paracetamol overdose. raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 88 patients with RSTI; 9 (10%) had initial ALT ≥50 IU/L and developed or had established hepatotoxicity (defined as ALT >1000 IU/L), median ALT 3383 IU/L (IQR 1445–4634) at 8 h post-acetylcysteine, peak INR 4.5; lowest initial ALT in those developing hepatotoxicity was 104 IU/L; of 16 patients with presentation ALT 50–100 IU/L, one developed ALT >1000 (peak 304 IU/L) needing 20 h acetylcysteine; median acetylcysteine duration 20 h (IQR 20–25) non-abbreviated vs 10.4 h (IQR 4.8–12.0) abbreviated, associated with shorter length of stay (0.6 vs 1.8 days). Paracetamol overdose is described as the commonest cause of acute liver failure in the developed world.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of nafcillin-induced liver injury in a patient treated with nafcillin 12 g/day for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus infection, with onset of liver injury on day 27. The patient's liver panel showed a cholestatic pattern (ALK and bilirubin elevated out of proportion to ALT/AST), evidence of immune-mediated idiosyncratic liver injury supported by peripheral eosinophilia (11.7%, absolute eosinophil count 1100), a liver biopsy showing lobular necrosis, portal inflammation and mild bile stasis without steatosis, no encephalopathy, and normal INR/PT. LFTs declined with supportive treatment and the patient was discharged on day 42.
raw_record.extra_details: Nafcillin 12 g/day IV for MSSA bacteremia; onset of liver injury day 27; peak labs on day 30-40: total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dl (7.0 direct), ALK 865 IU/L, AST 206 U/L, ALT 415 U/L; eosinophilia 11.7% (absolute 1100); biopsy showed lobular necrosis, severe portal tract inflammation with mixed infiltrate, mild bile stasis, mild periportal fibrosis, no steatosis; no encephalopathy, INR/PT normal; recovered with supportive care after ERCP (day 33) for biliary sludge; discharged day 42. Authors describe the cholestatic pattern as drug-induced liver injury and direct causality to nafcillin.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic injury was judged "probable" isoniazid-related when the patient had biochemical abnormalities characteristic of acute hepatocellular injury (an SGOT value above 250 Karmen units, or an SGPT value equal to or above SGOT) and improved when the drug was withdrawn; 114 patients fell into this "probable" category, all with overt clinical hepatic disease occurring during isoniazid chemoprophylaxis. Elsewhere in the same reports (paragraphs 24-25), the U.S. Public Health Service surveillance program of 13,838 new recipients of isoniazid (300 mg daily) was described as identifying the risk of isoniazid-induced hepatic injury, and Dr. Zimmerman stated that isoniazid can cause serious hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: U.S. Public Health Service special surveillance program (July 1971-November 1972) of 13,838 patients receiving isoniazid 300 mg daily as a single dose for tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis at 26 clinics; 18% <20 y, 23.2% 20-34 y, 30.2% 35-49 y, 28.6% >=50 y; only 48% completed 12 months. Causality: "probable" = acute hepatocellular injury biochemical abnormalities (SGOT >250 Karmen units, or SGPT >= SGOT in 14 patients) with improvement on drug withdrawal; "possible" = lesser biochemical abnormalities or other possible causes (12 patients). 114 patients in the "probable" category (66 hospitalized, 48 outpatient). Clinical features among 66 hospitalized: 55% gastrointestinal symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distress), ~35% attributed symptoms to "viral" illness, 10% presented with jaundice, hepatomegaly with abdominal tenderness in 33%, fever >100 F in 4, joint pains in 3, rash in 4, evidence of chronic liver disease in 2, splenomegaly in 2. Table shows isoniazid serum concentration (6 h post-dose) distributions in 147 patients by race and in 19 of 23 patients with at least one SGOT value >=60.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid was associated with hepatic injury in this series of 114 patients. Two patients had previously received isoniazid; one, who had completed a first course uneventfully, developed hepatic injury 7 months after starting a second course of the drug, and the other, who had stopped isoniazid after 1 month because of nausea and malaise, developed severe hepatitis 3 months after isoniazid was readministered, supporting a causal rechallenge relationship. Thirteen of the 114 patients (12.3%) died, 11 with a fulminant course within 4 to 14 days and 2 in hepatic failure 3 to 4 weeks after exploratory laparotomy.

raw_record.extra_details: 114 patients with isoniazid-related hepatic injury. Duration to onset varied: 46% developed evidence of hepatic disease within 2 months (peak in the 2nd month, 31%), while 54% became symptomatic after >2 months, some as late as 11 months. Peak SGOT exceeded SGPT in 51 patients, SGPT exceeded SGOT in 43, equal in 2. Marked hyperbilirubinemia (>20 mg/dl) in 29 (25%), generally with poor prognosis. Alkaline phosphatase above normal in 92% but >4x normal in only 11 patients (10%). Eosinophil counts >300/mm3 in 10%. Prothrombin times abnormal in 20/54 (35%); 12 died. raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that 'hepatic disease in most of these patients undoubtedly was induced by isoniazid.' They argue the uniformly negative HbAg results in 57% of patients tested early in the illness weigh against viral hepatitis as the cause, and that isoniazid liver injury is primarily a disease of the middle-aged and elderly, unlike sporadic viral hepatitis. Alcoholic liver disease was largely excluded because the study required an SGOT above 250 Karmen units or comparable SGPT elevation, and liver biopsy in 33 patients confirmed the absence of alcoholic liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of 114 patients with isoniazid hepatotoxicity; 13 deaths. Most patients who became ill within the first 8 weeks of therapy had milder and usually nonfatal disease, with only 2 deaths in that subgroup versus 11 deaths among those ill after >8 weeks. Race/sex/age distribution: White 55, black 36, Oriental 23; female 60, male 54; most patients aged 41-60. Deaths among black women were disproportionately prevalent (9 of 13). Mean age did not differ between fatal and nonfatal groups. Peak bilirubin exceeded 20 mg/dl in 11 of 13 fatal but only 19 of 101 surviving patients. After stopping isoniazid, transaminase values fell an average of 63% within 1 week and 87% by the third week (30 patients); peak bilirubin fell 44% by week 1 and 72% by week 3 (22 patients). Viral hepatitis and alcohol-related liver injury were considered and largely excluded as competing causes.

raw_record.support_text: The paper asserts a risk of isoniazid hepatic injury during its use for tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis, reporting high mortality (12.3% of patients with overt liver damage), increased mortality in patients developing hepatitis late in the course of isoniazid therapy, and liver biopsies from some patients showing chronic irreversible liver damage progressing to chronic active hepatitis or cirrhosis. Moderate SGOT abnormalities occur in many isoniazid recipients but usually subside despite continuation of therapy. The authors conclude it is essential for all physicians to recognize the risk of isoniazid hepatic injury and recommend that isoniazid chemoprophylaxis be stopped in patients over 35 years of age who develop any biochemical evidence of liver injury unless critically ill with suspected tuberculosis.

raw_record.extra_details: Mortality 12.3% among patients with overt liver damage; increased mortality in patients developing hepatitis late in the isoniazid course; liver biopsies in some patients showed chronic irreversible liver damage with development of chronic active hepatitis or cirrhosis. Moderate SGOT abnormalities occur in many recipients but usually subside despite continued therapy, undermining routine transaminase monitoring; clinical monitoring is likewise considered ineffectual in predicting serious hepatic injury. A pathogenetic mechanism is alluded to but not resolved.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity due to niacin therapy can be seen at low dosages but most commonly occurs at dosages of ≥3 grams per day. Niacin hepatotoxicity represents a spectrum ranging from mild elevation of liver enzymes and bilirubin with some degree of hepatic dysfunction to fulminant hepatic failure. Fatty infiltration of the liver, focal or diffuse, is one described form of niacin hepatotoxicity, and it usually resolves within 1–2 months of discontinuation with no long-term effects on liver function and no association with increased risk of hepatobiliary neoplasm. The patient's jaundice and liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin returned to normal within 2 months of stopping the sustained-release niacin.

In the patient case, jaundice and liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin returned to normal within 2 months of discontinuing sustained-release niacin; follow-up MRI at 1 month showed no liver mass; hypertriglyceridemia treatment continued with Gemfibrozil 600 mg bid.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 14 patients (10 males, 4 females) with tiopronin (mercaptopropionyl-glycine)-induced liver injury, most of whom manifested intrahepatic cholestasis on liver biopsy. Mean duration of tiopronin administration was 26 days and mean duration of jaundice was 4.5 months. The authors conclude that long-lasting tiopronin-induced intrahepatic cholestasis is highly linked to HLA-A33, -B44 and -DR6, indicating an immunogenetic predisposition.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 patients with tiopronin-induced liver injury (10 M, 4 F); mean duration of drug administration 26 days, mean jaundice duration 4.5 months; elevation of biliary enzymes lasted 2 months to 10 years. Histology showed intrahepatic cholestasis with hepatitic change (IHC-C), pure intrahepatic cholestasis (IHC-P), acute cholestatic hepatitis (ACH), and chronic aggressive hepatitis (CAH), with bile ductular degeneration in most patients. Lymphocyte transformation test with tiopronin positive in 6/8 (75%) tested. HLA linkage: A33 in 13 (92.9%), B44 in 10 (71.4%), DR6 in 9 (64.3%), haplotype A33/B44 in 71.4% and A33/B44/DR6 in 57.1%. One patient (case 13, M/72) died from heart failure associated with hepatorenal syndrome. Patients required hospitalization and frequently plasmapheresis. Tiopronin is 2-mercaptopropionyl-glycine, a thiol-containing chelating agent clinically used for liver disease, dermatitis/PSS, cataracts in Japan and rheumatoid arthritis in Europe.

raw_record.support_text: After a first course of sertraline therapy was associated with symptomatic hepatitis and an elevated serum ALT, the patient resumed sertraline for worsening depression; three weeks later her serum ALT rose significantly. Sertraline was discontinued again and her ALT fell to the normal range over 89 days, and was later shown to have dropped near normal within four weeks of the first discontinuation. Inadvertent rechallenge with sertraline was followed by a prompt rise in ALT, a rechallenge phenomenon the authors consider diagnostic of drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (Persky and Reinus). Rechallenge (inadvertent) after resumption of sertraline produced a prompt rise in serum ALT, described as diagnostic of DILI. Liver biopsy during second admission showed lobular disarray with lymphocytic infiltrate, scattered neutrophils and eosinophils, spotty hepatocyte necrosis, and Councilman bodies, consistent with drug-induced or autoimmune hepatitis. Diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis was made initially and treated with oral prednisone 20 mg daily; ALT did not permanently normalize on corticosteroids, and hepatitis was later presumed sertraline-induced rather than autoimmune. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic etiologies negative (anti-HAV, HBsAg, anti-HCV, ANA, ceruloplasmin, ferritin, CMV). Prior acetaminophen use was only at therapeutic doses with serum level <10 µg/ml at presentation. ALT normalized within 89 days after permanent sertraline discontinuation; depression subsequently treated with amitriptyline.

raw_record.support_text: The causality of fluconazole inducing hepatotoxicity was established by the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM)/CIOMS score. Components included a hepatocellular pattern, second exposure, onset <5 days (+1), satisfactory dechallenge (+1), alcohol as a risk factor (+1), age <55 (0), >50% improvement within 8 days (+3), no concomitant therapy (0), nondrug-related causes ruled out (+2), and positive response to re-administration (+3), giving a total score of 11, interpreted as 'Highly Probable' (>8).
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report; RUCAM/CIOMS score 11 ('Highly Probable', >8) with hepatocellular pattern, positive rechallenge, and satisfactory dechallenge. The conclusion states fluconazole is a known cause of elevated liver function tests but is rarely reported in the literature as an agent associated with acute liver failure (ALF); it is generally linked to dose-dependent hepatotoxicity and concurrent risks such as chronic liver disease, renal impairment, and HIV. This patient developed ALF with none of these apparent risk factors, and further investigation was warranted specifically for IV administration.

raw_record.support_text: Prolonged and acute ingestion of arsenic leads to toxicity of many organs including the liver. Increased liver tests (ALT, AST, ALP) were best documented in two patients under a herbal, arsenic-containing therapy with arsenical medication, with liver-test values meeting the criteria for liver injury required for HILI (Table 1) and RUCAM-based causality gradings of at least probable. The first patient (68 y, male) was on the arsenic-containing remedy for 32 days with ALT 473 U/L, AST 498 U/L, ALP 188 U/L; the second (48 y, female) was on it for 10 days with ALT 1122 U/L, AST 898 U/L, ALP 364 U/L. Histology from prolonged arsenic uptake in patients shows liver fibrosis and non-cirrhotic portal hypertension.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurred during use of a herbal arsenic-containing therapy (arsenical medication); two patients who met HILI liver-injury criteria and RUCAM causality of at least probable.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1 (68 y male, 32 days on remedy): ALT 473 U/L, AST 498 U/L, ALP 188 U/L. Patient 2 (48 y female, 10 days on remedy): ALT 1122 U/L, AST 898 U/L, ALP 364 U/L. Chronic prolonged arsenic uptake in patients is histologically associated with portal tract fibrosis, non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, and mild fatty change. In a patient with fatal arsenic intoxication, the liver showed the highest total arsenic concentration, with arsenite (As3+) predominant and MMA higher than DMA. Mechanism involves arsenic binding to sulfhydryl groups of enzymes and membrane proteins, oxidative DNA changes, and ROS.

raw_record.support_text: In the intention-to-treat analysis of this randomized clinical trial in Japanese tuberculosis patients, isoniazid-related liver injury (INH-DILI) occurred in 78% of the slow acetylators receiving the conventional standard treatment (~5 mg/kg isoniazid), while none of the slow acetylators on the NAT2 genotype-guided treatment (2.5 mg/kg isoniazid) experienced INH-DILI or early treatment failure. The trial treats INH-DILI as drug-induced liver injury caused by isoniazid and shows that NAT2 genotype-guided dosing stratification significantly reduces its incidence.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized trial comparing NAT2 genotype-guided (PGx) with conventional standard (STD) dosing of isoniazid (INH) for drug-sensitive tuberculosis, isoniazid-related liver injury (INH-DILI) occurred in 7 of 9 slow acetylators receiving STD INH (5 mg/kg) within the first 4 weeks, versus 0 of 7 slow acetylators in the PGx group during the first 8 weeks (attributable risk difference 77.8%, p=0.003). Multivariable analysis showed the NAT2 slow acetylator genotype was associated with INH-DILI in the STD treatment. Few rapid acetylators had INH-DILI (4.2% STD, 4.6% high-dose PGx), equivalent to intermediate acetylators (4.7%). Standard-dose INH was concluded to be too much for slow acetylators. One slow acetylator required INH withdrawal after standard treatment was interrupted due to INH-DILI.

raw_record.extra_details: Randomized controlled trial (n=155 evaluable patients) comparing NAT2 genotype-guided (PGx) vs conventional standard (STD) INH dosing for drug-sensitive tuberculosis. INH-DILI incidence: 77.8% (7/9) in slow acetylators on STD vs 0% (0/7) on PGx (p=0.003); 4.2% (2/48) rapid acetylators STD, 4.6% (2/44) rapid acetylators high-dose PGx, 4.7% (3/64) intermediate acetylators. INH doses: STD 5.5 mg/kg, PGx slow acetylators 2.6 mg/kg, PGx rapid acetylators 8.8 mg/kg. One rapid acetylator with INH-DILI showed no clinical improvement by week 8; 2 of 9 slow acetylators with INH-DILI on STD showed no improvement and INH was withdrawn in one. Derived from prior study assumptions of INH-DILI incidence 65% (control) vs 15% (test) in slow acetylators; combined unfavorable-event endpoint (INH-DILI or early treatment failure) reduced with PGx dosing (RR 0.354, 95% CI 0.177-0.707).

raw_record.support_text: Among the 11 patients with abnormal liver tests, 2 met the clinical chemistry criteria for drug-induced liver injury. The liver injury was considered probably caused by isavuconazole in two patients who experienced ALP elevations of 3.3- and 3.6-fold ULN with accompanying GGT elevations after 25 and 20 days of treatment. Severity was mild (bilirubin below 2-fold ULN), and liver tests returned to normal 48 and 26 days after isavuconazole discontinuation. Causality was qualified as 'probable' because the ALP and GGT abnormalities had a reasonable time relationship to isavuconazole intake, were unlikely attributed to disease or other drugs, and resolved after discontinuation. Both patients received oral isavuconazole 200 mg/day over 127 days for invasive aspergillosis and IV 200 mg/day over 21 days for mucormycosis, respectively, and both received concomitant potentially hepatotoxic medication (cyclosporin and tacrolimus) continued throughout the study.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 44-year-old female developed anorexia, nausea, and jaundice after six months of isoniazid (INH) monotherapy for latent tuberculosis. Other causes of liver injury were ruled out, and liver biopsy showed submassive necrosis, hepatocellular dropout, and lobular inflammation with no fibrosis; she also had acute portal hypertension. She was diagnosed with drug-induced liver injury (DILI), treated with NAC, ursodiol, and vitamin K, and recovered without liver transplantation. The paper notes severe hepatitis occurs in up to 1% of INH patients and supports monitoring of liver tests during INH therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case of a 44-year-old female also taking pantoprazole for gastroesophageal reflux disease; latent TB prophylaxis monotherapy setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Six months of INH monotherapy for latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis before symptom onset (~2 weeks of anorexia, right-sided abdominal pain, jaundice). Labs on day 1: ALT 651 U/L, AST 1134 U/L, ALP 186 U/L, total bilirubin 14.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.7 mg/dL, INR 1.75, MELD-Na 24; subacute liver failure with concurrent acute portal hypertension; biopsy showed submassive necrosis, hepatocellular dropout, lobular inflammation, no fibrosis; treated with N-acetyl cysteine, ursodiol, and vitamin K; recovered without liver transplant. Paper also cites up to 20% asymptomatic aminotransferase increases and severe hepatitis in up to 1% of INH patients.

raw_record.support_text: INH (isoniazid)-induced liver injury has a myriad of presentations, from mild subclinical liver injury (aminotransferases < 100 U/L, up to 20% of patients) to severe hepatitis (up to 1% of exposed patients). The paper describes known INH hepatotoxicity and the idiosyncratic nature of isoniazid DILI, with the featured patient developing acute liver failure with concurrent portal hypertension attributed to isoniazid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case is a patient with liver injury during isoniazid treatment of latent tuberculosis; was treated medically without orthotopic liver transplant, which is reported in some acute liver failure cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Mild subclinical liver injury (aminotransferases < 100 U/L) in up to 20% of patients; severe hepatitis in up to 1% of exposed patients. Common presentations: fatigue, malaise, nausea; jaundice presenting symptom in 10% of cases. Most cases occur 2-3 months into therapy, range 1 week to 14 months. Susceptibility factors: alcoholism, viral hepatitis, advanced age, Asian racial background, slow acetylator status, female sex. Featured patient had acute liver failure with concurrent portal hypertension; liver enzymes still elevated one month later, possible progression to chronic liver injury (>6 months). Known INH hepatotoxicity; guidelines (CDC/ATS) recommend stopping isoniazid if ALT >3x ULN with jaundice/symptoms or >5x ULN without symptoms; no standard monitoring guidelines exist.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin is described as a well known cause of drug-induced liver injury with autoimmune features; in this Prospective DILIN cohort, 70% of nitrofurantoin injury cases displayed autoimmune features. Nitrofurantoin-associated liver injury tended to be more severe and more likely to persist than the other three agents, and all but one of the fatalities in the cohort were attributed to nitrofurantoin, with available fatal-case histology showing massive necrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Focused on autoimmune-like DILI phenotype. 70% of nitrofurantoin cases had autoimmune features. Injury tended to be more severe and persistent; one case displayed a chronic hepatitic pattern with mild aminotransferase elevation, no jaundice, presenting >1 year after starting the drug; one fatal case showed massive necrosis histology. Authors note nitrofurantoin fits the 'Hy's Law' pattern of hepatocellular injury with jaundice and high fatality rate. Latencies of 1-6 months were common (n=26 overall, 30%) and short latency (<1 month) was infrequent (10, 11%, across the four drugs). Autoimmune markers were more frequent with severe hepatic injury and prolonged latency.
