raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses the aetiology of halothane hepatitis, a form of drug-induced liver injury following anaesthesia with halothane. Previous exposure to halothane is described as crucial: Inman and Mushin (1978) found 82% of cases had been exposed to halothane on at least one prior occasion (80% within 28 days), Moult and Sherlock (1975) reported 70% of patients received at least 2 halothane exposures within 28 days, and the shorter the interval between exposures the shorter the period between the last anaesthetic and onset of jaundice. Halothane hepatitis is characterised by liver cell necrosis, postoperative pyrexia, peripheral eosinophilia, the anti-LKM1 autoantibody, and eosinophilic infiltration/granulomas on liver biopsy, and is described in the context of immune-mediated, idiosyncratic drug hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury is typically associated with repeated or recent prior halothane exposure (e.g., 82% with prior exposure, 70% with at least 2 exposures within 28 days); a history of drug allergy and obesity have been suggested as risk factors but their roles are not clearly substantiated.
raw_record.extra_details: Analysis of over 600 cases in the literature shows an overall history of drug allergy in 15%, similar to a general anaesthesia population. Features include liver cell necrosis, postoperative pyrexia (noted as non-specific), peripheral eosinophilia, serum autoantibodies, anti-liver kidney microsomal (LKM1) antibody directed against a cytochrome P450 isoenzyme, and eosinophilic infiltration with granulomas on liver biopsy in isolated cases. Earlier/interval dependence: the shorter the interval between halothane exposures, the shorter the period to onset of jaundice.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurred in 228/466 patients (49%), 141 male/87 female, mean age 36±12 years, 77 living-related and 151 cadaveric donor grafts. Severe hepatotoxicity required serum bilirubin >3 mg/dl with SGOT/SGPT >500 IU/L plus LDH and AP elevations; isolated LDH or AP elevations were not considered hepatotoxicity. Managed by CsA dose reduction to trough ≤100 ng/ml. Biliary evaluation used ultrasound, CT, radionuclide biliary imaging, ERCP, and liver biopsy. CsA serum levels measured by radioimmunoassay (Sandoz kit); serum trough target 50-200 ng/ml.

raw_record.extra_details: 228 patients affected (male:female 141:87, mean age 36±12 yr); compared with 212 previously reported patients. raw_record.support_text: A GWAS on 41 cases of DILI resulting from the NSAID lumiracoxib found a highly significant association (p=6.8×10^-25; allelic OR 5.0; 95% CI 3.6–7.0) with an HLA class II haplotype that includes DRB1*1501, and the association was replicated in a further 98 lumiracoxib DILI cases. RUCAM score was 10 (highly probable) and the ALT-ULN/ALP-ULN ratio (2.11) classified the injury as mixed.

All clinical and biologic manifestations of liver toxicity rapidly disappeared upon discontinuation of flutamide alone, with no sequelae at follow-up (18, 22, 31, and 62 months).

raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of flutamide-related liver toxicity studied prospectively in 1,091 consecutive patients with liver function tests at 4, 8, 12 weeks and every 3 months. Four patients (0.36%) had AST/ALT at ≥4x upper normal limit; 2 (0.18%) developed clinical manifestations. Rechallenge positive in 2 patients (causal link assessed by temporal relationship and rechallenge). One biopsy showed mixed cytotoxic and cholestatic histopathologic changes. Peak lab values in patient 1: ALT 209, AST 106, gamma-GT 355, total bilirubin 126 mmol/L. All manifestations resolved on flutamide discontinuation; no sequelae at long-term follow-up (18, 22, 31, 62 months). Authors recommend serial aminotransferase monitoring at 2 and 4 weeks to detect early possible flutamide-induced hepatic injury.; confidence_note: None

raw_record.support_text: Biochemical abnormalities returned to normal within 8 weeks after discontinuing flutamide (at 2, 4, 8, and 8 weeks for Patients 2, 4, 1, and 3). Two patients were rechallenged with half the flutamide dose (125 mg every 8 hours) and their serum aminotransferases more than doubled within 3 days, confirming flutamide as the cause of the observed liver injury in these four patients with 'flutamide-induced liver injury.' All four patients continued the LHRH agonist alone with no further signs of liver toxicity.

Four of 1,091 total patients developed the injury; no concomitant drugs were taken during therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice was present on admission in one patient (Patient with visible jaundice) who showed histologic signs of acute cholestatic hepatitis. Histology showed mixed cytotoxic and cholestatic drug-induced lesions with spotty necrosis, acidophilic (Councilman) bodies with nuclear remnants, bile pigments within hepatocytes with feathery degeneration, bile plugs in cholangioles, and lymphocytic portal inflammation; no portal fibrosis, steatosis, or zonal necrosis. Coombs' tests were negative; abdominal ultrasound showed no gallstones or biliary duct dilatation. Recovery of liver tests occurred within 8 weeks (at 2, 4, 8, and 8 weeks for Patients 2, 4, 1, and 3); rechallenge (125 mg every 8 h) more than doubled serum AST and ALT within 3 days in two patients. All four patients remain alive after 18, 22, 31, and 62 months of follow-up. In the other 1,087 patients no major liver function test abnormality was observed, though minor transient ALT/AST changes occurred during the first 6 months and normalized (flutamide-associated hepatotoxicity). Authors recommend monitoring serum AST and ALT to detect possible flutamide-induced liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 1,091 prostate cancer patients all treated with the antiandrogen combination of flutamide and an LHRH agonist with serial liver-function monitoring, only 4 patients (0.36%) developed liver toxicity: 2 with clinical signs of liver toxicity and 2 with hepatic enzyme levels at least fourfold above upper normal limits without symptoms. All four displayed abnormal findings within 4 weeks of treatment onset, and the authors concluded that the clinical and biochemical sequence indicates cases of flutamide-induced liver toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prostate cancer indication; flutamide administered in a fixed combination regimen with an LHRH agonist. All four affected patients had pretreatment serum liver values within 20% of normal.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence 0.36% (4/1,091) of flutamide-related liver toxicity; 2 patients with clinical signs and 2 with asymptomatic enzyme elevations (transaminases up to 60-fold above pretreatment, one ~2-fold alkaline phosphatase rise, normal bilirubin in those three). One patient had a mainly cholestatic pattern with overt jaundice, fatigue, nausea, no pruritus; peak bilirubin >120 µmol/L, 6-fold alkaline phosphatase, 16-fold ALT, 5-fold AST; biopsy showed acute cholestatic hepatitis with mixed cytotoxic (spotty necrosis, acidophilic bodies) and cholestatic (bile plugs, bile pigment, feathery degeneration, periportal inflammation) findings, no zonal necrosis or portal fibrosis. The other three showed a 'pure' hepatocellular-type pattern. All patients recovered rapidly and completely within 2 to 8 weeks after flutamide discontinuation. Classified as an idiosyncratic response without signs of hypersensitivity, assumed toxic-metabolite dependent. Liver function tests remained within normal limits in almost all 1,091 patients during the 36-month observation. Upper normal values: ALT/AST 24 IU/L, γ-GT 28 IU/L, bilirubin 20.5 µmol/L.

raw_record.support_text: Using the UNOS liver transplant database from 1990 to 2002, 270 liver transplant recipients with drug-induced acute liver failure were identified. raw_record.support_text: Two patients treated with capmatinib 400 mg twice daily for MET-amplified NSCLC developed hepatocellular drug-induced liver injury (DILI) within 6 to 8 weeks, with markedly elevated transaminases and total bilirubin and signs of early acute liver failure leading to treatment discontinuation and hospitalization. Viral, vascular, and autoimmune causes were ruled out, and with a Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score of 11 (>8, high probable) in both, a diagnosis of DILI associated with portal fibrosis (Ishak 3 and Metavir 3) was made; both patients recovered with hepatoprotective treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: Latency from capmatinib initiation to DILI was 8.86 weeks (patient 1) and 5.71 weeks (patient 2); max ALT 1689 U/L (<50) and 955 U/L (<35); max AST 512 and 543 U/L; max total bilirubin 9.12 and 4.64 mg/dL; MELD 22 and 17; RUCAM 11 in both; liver biopsy in patient 1 showed drug-induced liver damage with portal fibrosis (Ishak 3 Metavir 3) and in patient 2 lobular and periportal necrosis with portal fibrosis (Ishak 3 Metavir 3); PD-L1 expressed in 10% and 30% of hepatocytes; elastography at resolution showed severe hepatic fibrosis (12.3 kPa and 10.9 kPa); treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine, adenomethionine, and oral ursodeoxycholic acid with progressive normalization of liver tests; both patients later discontinued therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old white male with underlying alcoholic liver disease and a history of hepatitis C virus infection experienced elevated aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase levels consistent with acute hepatic injury after initiation of varenicline for smoking cessation. The hepatic injury manifested 4 weeks after starting varenicline (0.5 mg once daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily); after discontinuation aminotransferases rose for 2 days before declining to baseline over ~4 months, and alkaline phosphatase rose for 8 days before returning to baseline within 1 month. Rechallenge was not attempted.

raw_record.extra_details: Smoking-cessation indication. Dosing: 0.5 mg once daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily. Latency ~4 weeks after initiation. Dechallenge: aminotransferases continued to rise for 2 days then declined to baseline over ~4 months; alkaline phosphatase rose for 8 days after discontinuation then returned to baseline within 1 month. Naranjo probability scale and CIOMS/RUCAM algorithm rated varenicline as the probable cause; the Maria and Victorino algorithm rated it a possible cause. Reported as the first case of acute hepatic injury associated with varenicline.

raw_record.support_text: The patient's presentation is consistent with acute hepatic injury from drug toxicity, including AST and ALT levels greater than 300 U/L, AST:ALT ratio greater than 1, peak bilirubin less than 5 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase less than 3 times the upper limit of normal. Other potential drug causes were excluded because the drug regimen remained consistent before and after the event, except for varenicline, which was the only drug with a temporal relationship to the event. raw_record.extra_details: Case report of acute hepatic injury attributed to varenicline. Naranjo probability scale scored a probable adverse drug event related to varenicline; CIOMS/RUCAM determined varenicline was the probable cause of hepatotoxicity; the Maria and Victorino method rated it a possible cause. Rechallenge was not performed due to an unacceptable risk-benefit ratio. Laboratory findings: AST and ALT >300 U/L (aminotransferases over 15x the upper limit of normal), AST:ALT ratio >1, peak bilirubin <5 mg/dL, ALP <3x the upper limit of normal. Acute hepatitis C was ruled out by persistently negative HCV RNA; hepatitis A, hepatitis B, CMV, herpesvirus, and EBV ruled out by serology; alcoholic and ischemic hepatitis excluded. The paper discusses DILI types including predictable and idiosyncratic reactions but does not explicitly classify this injury.

raw_record.support_text: Trabectedin is described as a drug with predictable hepatotoxic effects in animals and humans. Even with dexamethasone prophylaxis and careful dosing, monotherapy shows significant hepatic injury potential; in soft tissue sarcoma patients the incidence of grade 3/4 ALT elevations was 47%, and 1.2% of patients met Hy's Law criteria. An irreversible liver failure case was attributed to a multihit process involving ABCC2 genetic variants and concomitant medication, showing chronic hepatobiliary toxicity with portal fibrosis and cholangiolitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported in selected soft tissue sarcoma patients with dexamethasone prophylaxis (20 mg IV) and detailed dose adjustment criteria; an irreversible liver failure case involved ABCC2 genetic variants and concomitant medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Grade 3/4 ALT elevations 47%; grade 1/2 hyperbilirubinemia 21%; median time to peak ALT 5 days, most elevations decreasing to grade 1 or normal by day 14, recovery longer than 25 days in 2% of cycles; Hy's Law 1.2% in 19 single-agent phase II studies. Mechanism: covalent DNA minor-groove guanine adducts; hepatotoxic metabolites formed by CYP3A cleared by transporters ABCB1, ABCC2, ABCC3. Liver failure case showed portal fibrosis, cholangiolitis damage, chronic hepatopathy.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old female patient developed toxic hepatitis due to levofloxacin after receiving a single 750 mg dose of levofloxacin tablets for a pulmonary infection 10 days earlier. She experienced itching, redness, and rash, followed on day 5 by abdominal pain, vomiting, and jaundice. She was deemed a liver transplant candidate but suffered cardiopulmonary arrest and died before transfer; multiple organ failure was secondary to the toxic hepatitis. The authors emphasize that hepatotoxicity and death due to levofloxacin are uncommon.
raw_record.extra_details: Single 750 mg oral levofloxacin dose for pulmonary (lower respiratory tract) infection; began with pruritus, redness, and rash that regressed over 3 days with whole-body desquamation; from day 5 onward abdominal pain, vomiting, and jaundice (icterus). Presented at emergency department 10 days post-dose with confusion (GCS 12), acute hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia (53 mg/dL), and multiple organ failure. Toxic hepatitis resulted in fatal outcome: patient was a liver transplant candidate but had cardiopulmonary arrest and died before transfer to a transplant center. Hepatic necrosis described in the general context of drug-induced hepatotoxicity. No other co-suspect drug is reported.

raw_record.support_text: Three participants in the tolvaptan pivotal trials TEMPO 3:4 (NCT00428948) and its extension TEMPO 4:4 met criteria for severe drug-induced liver toxicity known as Hy's law (serum ALT or AST ≥3x ULN plus total bilirubin >2x ULN, in the absence of cholestasis and without any other reason to explain the elevations), a condition carrying a high risk (~10%) of acute liver failure or orthotopic liver transplant. The trials also showed a higher proportion of tolvaptan-treated participants with ALT >3x ULN (4.4% tolvaptan vs 1.0% placebo).
raw_record.extra_details: DILI identified in ADPKD patients (tolvaptan's indicated use). In TEMPO 3:4, 4.4% of tolvaptan vs 1.0% of placebo had ALT >3x ULN; three participants (TEMPO 3:4/4:4) met Hy's law criteria (severe drug-induced liver toxicity), which carries ~10% risk of acute liver failure or orthotopic liver transplant. In REPRISE (NCT02160145), ALT >3x ULN occurred in 5.6% tolvaptan vs 1.2% placebo with no Hy's law cases; the long-term safety extension (NCT02251275) also reported no Hy's law cases. Clinical development data indicate the first 18 months of therapy carry the greatest likelihood of liver enzyme elevations. EU labelling requires monthly liver monitoring for the first 18 months then every 3 months; US REMS mandates liver chemistry monitoring before start, at 2 and 4 weeks, then monthly for the first 18 months, then every 3 months. Post-marketing pharmacovigilance from a US REMS setting and an interim analysis of the EU-required post-authorization safety study (PASS) further characterize liver safety. Liver chemistry monitoring frequency increased over the development program from every 4-6 months to monthly.

raw_record.support_text: A single-patient case report attributes cholestatic DILI to methimazole. The patient presented with signs and symptoms of cholestatic disease with concern for obstructive biliary pathology; malignancy, autoimmune, and infectious etiologies were ruled out, and choledochoscopy showed normal bile duct mucosa. The R-value at symptom onset was 0.64 (cholestatic pattern), the RUCAM score was 8 points, and the temporal relationship between methimazole initiation and symptom onset, together with improvement in symptoms and a downward trend in liver function tests after methimazole discontinuation, argued in favor of DILI. Six months after discontinuation the LFTs remained normal and the patient was symptom-free.

Dechallenge: symptoms and LFTs improved after methimazole discontinuation, CBD stent later removed; LFTs remained normal and patient symptom-free 6 months later. Phenotype is cholestatic liver injury mimicking obstructive biliary pathology.

raw_record.support_text: Gatifloxacin was implicated as the cause of a fatal case of acute hepatitis progressing to fulminant hepatic failure. The patient had markedly elevated liver function tests with a normal alkaline phosphatase, consistent with hepatocellular injury, and jaundice appeared only a few days after initiation of gatifloxacin; the discussion states the onset corresponded with the time frame expected for fluoroquinolone hepatotoxicity. The patient died 25 days after completing the course of gatifloxacin due to multiple organ failure. An additional gatifloxacin case (hepatocellular pattern) with improvement at 5 weeks, plus a meta-analysis of 15 clinical trials finding liver-test alterations (>5xULN) in <0.1% (AST, ALT, ALP) and <0.4% (bilirubin) and 1 hepatitis case in >16,000 treated patients, was also reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: 76-year-old, onset ~10 days (jaundice few days after gatifloxacin initiation); peak ALT 787 U/L, AST 743 U/L, ALP 150 U/L, total bilirubin 34.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 28.7 mg/dL; hepatocellular injury with normal alkaline phosphatase; progression to fulminant hepatic failure, INR peaked 7.04, hepatic encephalopathy with elevated ammonia (peak 274 microg/dL), renal impairment (creatinine peak 5.5 mg/dL), multiple organ failure; died 25 days after completing gatifloxacin. Additional reported case: 44-year-old, onset 5 days, peak ALT 669 U/L, ALP 297 U/L, bilirubin 9.4 mg/dL, hepatocellular, improvement at 5 weeks. Meta-analysis (Breen et al., 15 clinical trials): ALT/AST/ALP >5xULN in <0.1%, bilirubin in <0.4%; 1 hepatitis case linked to gatifloxacin in >16,000 postmarketing-treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: The FDA issued a nonapprovable letter for lumiracoxib in 2007, and postmarketing surveillance identified serious instances of DILI not foreseen in clinical trials. In the large TARGET trial, 2.6% had aminotransferase elevations >3× ULN, with six cases of probable or possible clinical hepatitis that all resolved on drug cessation and no reports of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: FDA nonapprovable letter (2007); postmarketing surveillance identified serious DILI not foreseen in trials. TARGET trial: 2.6% AT >3× ULN; six cases of probable/possible clinical hepatitis all resolved; no liver failure. Pharmacogenetic GWAS (Affymetrix 6.0, >900,000 SNPs) in 41 cases (ALT/AST >5× ULN) vs 176 matched controls, validated in 98 cases vs 405 lumiracoxib-exposed controls (ALT/AST >3× ULN), associated lumiracoxib DILI with MHC class II SNPs on chromosome 6 (leading rs9270986, P = 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) and extended haplotype HLA-DRB1*1501-HLA-DQB1*0602-HLA-DRB5*0101-HLA-DQA1*0102 (most significant allele P = 6.8 × 10⁻²⁵, OR 5.0; 95% CI 3.6-7.0). No similar relationship seen in ibuprofen (n=18) or naproxen (n=9) DILI control cases. All patients with ALT >20× ULN and all three Hy's law (ALT/AST >3× ULN, bilirubin >2 ULN) cases carried the implicated haplotype. HLA-DQA1*0102 had best negative predictive value (99%) and sensitivity (73.6%). Curated table lists HLA-DQA1*0102 OR 6.3 (4.1-9.6) for lumiracoxib DILI.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis developed drug-induced liver injury (DILI) after initiating maintenance therapy with the multimatrix system 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA). She presented with grade 4 liver enzyme elevation on day 98, mixed liver injury on blood tests, and liver biopsy showing acute lobular hepatitis with interfacial activity. The DDW-J 2004 scale gave a total score of six, indicating a high probability of DILI; 5-ASA was discontinued and she was treated with ursodeoxycholic acid and neominophagen C, with gradual improvement without steroids. The authors definitively diagnosed DILI based on pathological findings and the clinical course after discontinuation of 5-ASA.

raw_record.extra_details: Multimatrix system formulation at 2,400 mg/body; latency day 98 after initiation; grade 4 liver enzyme elevation; imaging unremarkable except mild lymph node enlargement; liver biopsy showed acute lobular hepatitis with interfacial activity; DDW-J 2004 scale total score 6 indicating high probability of DILI; treated with ursodeoxycholic acid and neominophagen C without steroids, with gradual liver function improvement; definitive DILI diagnosis based on pathology and clinical course after 5-ASA discontinuation. The authors note 5-ASA (mesalazine) liver injury is usually mild and reversible but can sometimes cause severe disease.

raw_record.support_text: The authors performed a PubMed literature review (January 2023) for case reports of liver dysfunction, hepatotoxicity, or liver injury caused by 5-ASA (mesalazine), excluded cases not associated with 5-ASA-induced liver injury, and identified 7 published case reports plus their own case (8 total). All events occurred after initiation of 5-ASA, with onset ranging from 1 week to 8 months; one case was classified as idiosyncratic DILI (allergic type) and the others as idiosyncratic DILI (metabolic type). The paper concludes that although mesalamine is generally safe, serious 5-ASA-related liver injury can occur and regular monitoring of liver function is needed.

One case classified as idiosyncratic DILI (allergic type; Hautekeete et al., CTCAE grade 4), the rest as idiosyncratic DILI (metabolic type). CTCAE grades ranged 3-4. Patients had ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease; treatment included withdrawal of 5-ASA, PSL, UDCA, and SNMC. Literature search limited by small number of reports suggesting possible publication bias; pathogenesis and timing not well understood. Authors note 5-ASA-related DILI is typically classified as a blood-test abnormality with a median onset of about 55 days (~2 months), but can present in various ways including mimicking IBD exacerbations or lupus-like symptoms.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes nifedipine-induced hepatitis as a rare type of drug-induced liver injury that presents in an idiosyncratic manner, acutely within days or subacutely within 4-8 weeks after medication start, with chronic/latent cases diagnosed up to 3 years later. Symptoms include jaundice, nausea, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, fatigue, and abdominal pain; laboratory investigations show profound elevations in AST, ALT, GGT, and conjugated bilirubin, with possible eosinophilia, and liver biopsy typically shows immune cell infiltration, cholestasis, and a steatohepatitis picture. Treatment is drug discontinuation with supportive care; all published instances were self-limiting without mortality due to fulminant liver failure but can take months to resolve.
raw_record.extra_details: Known but very rare clinically-apparent hepatitis that can take months to resolve; a case is presented in a 78-year-old Caucasian female with no prior liver or autoimmune disease. Latency: acute (within days) or subacute (4-8 weeks); chronic/latent cases up to 3 years after drug start. Symptoms: jaundice, nausea, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, fatigue, abdominal pain. Labs: profound elevations in AST, ALT, GGT, conjugated (and total) bilirubin; peripheral eosinophilia possible. Histology: immune-cell infiltration, cholestasis, steatohepatitis. Treatment: immediate drug discontinuation and supportive care; no randomized evidence for corticosteroids. All published cases self-limiting, no mortality from fulminant liver failure. Listed among idiosyncratic antihypertensive causes of DILI.

In the absence of immunoallergic manifestations, an idiosyncratic type of drug-induced liver disease was judged probable, especially since rechallenge at only 2.5% of the usual therapeutic dose (10 mg/day) again produced an increase in aminotransferase activities.

raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients had ≥ grade 3 DILI (three upfront therapy, three pre-docetaxel therapy, one post-docetaxel). There were four hepatocellular-type and three cholestatic-type DILI cases. Liver injury developed in all cases between the fourth and eighth weeks after drug administration; abiraterone acetate was immediately discontinued in all affected patients. The incidence of DILI was significantly higher in the upfront therapy group. Liver metastases (OR = 6.667, p = 0.043, 95% CI 1.063-41.773) and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase levels (OR = 7.556, p = 0.013, 95% CI 1.534-37.214) were significantly associated with grade ≥ 3 DILI in single logistic regression. The paper concludes severe DILI is a potential complication of abiraterone acetate therapy and recommends close monitoring for liver injury, especially in the first few months.

DILI developed within eight weeks; liver function monitoring recommended at least every two weeks for the first 12 weeks of treatment and every four weeks thereafter. Incidence of DILI was significantly higher in the upfront therapy group; liver metastasis and abnormal gamma-GTP (γ-GTP) levels were identified as risk factors for DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Methimazole (MMI) has been used in the therapy of Grave's Disease (GD) since 1954, and drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is one of its most deleterious side effects. A case-control genetic study included 44 GD patients with MMI-DILI and 118 GD patients without MMI-DILI, genotyping 33 SNPs in 20 candidate genes. Associations with SLCO2B1 rs12422149, ABCB1 rs2032582_AT, SLCO1B1 rs2306283, and UGT1A1 rs4148323 were seen but were not significant after Bonferroni correction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Grave's disease (hyperthyroidism) patient population; genetic susceptibility case-control cohort (44 MMI-DILI cases vs 118 controls).
raw_record.extra_details: Possible mechanisms of MMI-DILI proposed include reactive metabolite formation, oxidative stress induction, intracellular target dysfunction, and immunological reaction, though the specific mechanism is not clarified and diagnosis relies on exclusion. Haplotype analysis found SLCO1B1*1a (388A521T) significantly more frequent in MMI-DILI cases (OR=2.21, 95%CI 1.11-4.39, P=0.023) and SLCO1B1*1b (388G521T) more frequent in controls (OR=0.52, 95%CI 0.29-0.93, P=0.028), suggesting SLCO1B1 polymorphisms are predisposing factors for MMI-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Acarbose-related liver injury has been reported in humans. Early trials reported increases in transaminases or rarely jaundice in 3.8% of acarbose users versus 1.1% on placebo. The first case report was a 65-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes taking acarbose 300 mg/day for 2 months, presenting with malaise and anorexia and a hepatocellular damage laboratory pattern, with spontaneous recovery after discontinuation. Subsequent case series indicated that acarbose-related liver toxicity reports mostly came from Japan and Spain, had an average latency of 2–6 months after therapy initiation, frequently recurred after rechallenge, and were predominantly hepatocellular injuries.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus on therapeutic acarbose; general treatment population, not restricted to renal impairment. Post-marketing reports predominantly from Japan and Spain.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: 65-year-old woman, type 2 DM, acarbose 300 mg/day for 2 months, malaise and anorexia, hepatocellular damage pattern, spontaneous recovery after discontinuation. Early trials: transaminase elevations or rarely jaundice in 3.8% of users vs 1.1% placebo. Case series: average latency 2–6 months, frequent recurrence after rechallenge. Indication: type 2 diabetes mellitus (alpha-glucosidase inhibitor). Putative mechanisms (unproven): CYP2E1 induction, increased reactive oxygen species production, and influence of sex hormones; acarbose hepatotoxicity likely not via metabolites given low and unpredictable incidence.

His symptoms and transaminases normalized on withdrawal of oxycodone, which the authors took as confirming that oxycodone was the probable cause of the hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old patient with pemphigus foliaceus, previously on corticosteroids, was started on azathioprine 100 mg daily (2 mg/kg per day). Three weeks after initiation he developed jaundice, dark urine and pruritus; laboratory investigations revealed severe hepatitis and cholestasis, with other hepatitis aetiologies negative. After azathioprine was withdrawn the jaundice regressed and hepatic tests normalised slowly; a low thiopurine methyltransferase activity (0.48 IU/mL red blood cells; normal 9.3–17.6) was found. The paper frames this as a severe case of azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity; concurrent chronic corticosteroid treatment for pemphigus foliaceus.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg daily (2 mg/kg/day); latency 3 weeks after therapy onset; jaundice, dark urine and pruritus; severe hepatitis and cholestasis on laboratory tests; other viral/aetiologic causes of hepatitis negative; dechallenge led to regression of jaundice and slow normalization of hepatic tests; TPMT activity 0.48 IU/mL red blood cells (normal 9.3-17.6). Discussion attributes toxicity to drug accumulation related to low TPMT activity.

raw_record.support_text: Sulfasalazine was prescribed for ulcerative colitis in a 35-year-old woman and for Crohn's disease in a 17-year-old man. Signs of the hypersensitivity (DRESS) syndrome appeared 20 and 31 days after administration. Both presented skin rash, fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis with an imputation score of 'very likely (13)' for sulfasalazine; the drug was stopped and patients improved only after glucocorticoid treatment. The sulfapyridine portion of sulphasalazine is noted as the metabolite most frequently implicated in the hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients treated for ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease; hepatitis occurred within a systemic DRESS/hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS/drug hypersensitivity syndrome presenting as skin rash, fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis; two cases (ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease); latency 20 and 31 days after administration; imputation score 'very likely (13)'; improved only after glucocorticoids; sulfapyridine metabolite implicated in the hypersensitivity reaction (mechanistic, not separately identified as the hepatic injuring entity).

raw_record.support_text: In 60 EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer patients with blood samples taken before gefitinib treatment, severe hepatotoxicity was detected in 19 (32%). Multivariate logistic regression showed the rate of severe hepatotoxicity was significantly higher in CYP3A5 poor metabolizers than non-PM (48.4% vs 13.8%, P=0.0069) and in CYP2D6 PM vs non-PM (80.0% vs 27.3%, P=0.0364). Of 9 patients switched from gefitinib to erlotinib due to severe hepatotoxicity, 8 had a PM phenotype; all were managed without exacerbation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer cohort; severe hepatotoxicity most frequent in CYP3A5/CYP2D6 poor metabolizer phenotypes.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity in 19/60 patients (32%). Risk significantly elevated in poor metabolizers (CYP3A5 PM vs non-PM 48.4% vs 13.8%, P=0.0069; CYP2D6 PM vs non-PM 80.0% vs 27.3%, P=0.0364). 9 patients switched from gefitinib to erlotinib due to severe hepatotoxicity, of whom 8 had a PM phenotype for CYP2D6 or CYP3A5; all managed without exacerbation. Conclusion: SNP evaluation in CYP3A5 and CYP2D6 can predict gefitinib-induced severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 239 NSCLC patients harboring EGFR mutations who were treated with gefitinib, severe hepatotoxicity was graded per CTCAE v4.0 and defined as grade 3+ transaminase elevation (ALT >=210 U/L or AST >=165 U/L) with any total-bilirubin elevation (>=1.2 mg/dL), or grade 2+ transaminase elevation with grade 2+ total-bilirubin elevation (>=1.8 mg/dL), based on the FDA Guidance for Industry on DILI. The study endpoint was the severe hepatotoxicity rate, defined as the proportion who experienced gefitinib-induced severe hepatotoxicity during treatment, which is the cause of gefitinib withdrawal; the study examined associations between this gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity and SNPs in metabolic enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of 239 NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations treated with gefitinib at a single institution (Jan 2009-Dec 2012); endpoint was severe hepatotoxicity rate per CTCAE v4.0 and the FDA DILI Premarketing Clinical Evaluation guidance (grade 3+ ALT>=210 U/L or AST>=165 U/L with any total-bilirubin elevation, or grade 2+ transaminases with grade 2+ bilirubin); severe hepatotoxicity is the cause of gefitinib withdrawal. Study examined SNPs in CYP1A2, CYP2A6, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A5, NAT2 and UGT1A1 as potential determinants (these gene/HLA associations themselves are not extracted as DILI causes). Blood samples were available for 60 of 239 patients from the National Cancer Center Biobank.

raw_record.support_text: In this integrative analysis of metabolic enzyme SNPs in Japanese NSCLC patients treated with gefitinib, poor metabolizer (PM) phenotypes for CYP2D6 and CYP3A5 were associated with an increased risk of severe hepatotoxicity induced by gefitinib. Patients with PM phenotypes for both CYP2D6 and CYP3A5 were more likely to experience severe hepatotoxicity than those with a PM phenotype for either enzyme alone or with non-PM phenotypes for both.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study restricted to Japanese non-small cell lung carcinoma patients; severe hepatotoxicity risk was increased in poor metabolizer phenotypes for CYP2D6 and CYP3A5 (genotype-restricted susceptibility).
raw_record.extra_details: Of 60 gefitinib-treated patients, 19 experienced severe hepatotoxicity. Re-administration of gefitinib (16 patients) led to re-exacerbation of severe hepatotoxicity in 9 (56%); the nine switched to erlotinib were managed without re-exacerbation (one showed grade 3 T-bilirubin elevation). Multivariate analysis: CYP2D6 PM OR 14.50 (95% CI 1.56-346.50, p=0.04); CYP3A5 PM OR 6.84 (95% CI 1.87-33.15, p=0.0069). Patients PM for both CYP3A5 and CYP2D6 had 100% severe hepatotoxicity rate (p=0.0011). Mechanism proposed: reduced CYP2D6/CYP3A5 activity raising gefitinib plasma levels. Gefitinib oral bioavailability ~60% at 250 mg; Cmax varies up to 15-fold.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old man with metastatic carcinoma of the prostate took flutamide (750 mg/day) for 7 months and suddenly developed jaundice and general weakness. Blood chemistries were compatible with cholestatic hepatitis; ultrasonography, viral markers and auto-antibody studies revealed no attributable causes, and a liver biopsy showed centrilobular cholestasis, nuclear glycogenosis and mild sinusoidal lymphocytic infiltration. Discontinuation of flutamide resulted in almost full recovery of liver function in 2 months, and the authors report a case of flutamide-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 75-year-old male with metastatic carcinoma of the prostate undergoing combined therapy including flutamide and an LH-RH analogue (zoladex); concurrent co-exposure to zoladex present.
raw_record.extra_details: Flutamide 750 mg/day for 7 months; jaundice and general weakness; blood chemistries compatible with cholestatic hepatitis; ultrasound, viral markers and auto-antibodies negative; liver biopsy disclosed centrilobular cholestasis, nuclear glycogenosis and mild sinusoidal lymphocytic infiltration; discontinuation led to almost full recovery in 2 months. Case is described as acute cholestatic hepatitis. Literature review notes flutamide hepatotoxicity including toxic hepatitis, cholestatic hepatitis, hepatic failure, and even death (e.g., Gomez 1992: 4 hepatitis cases in 1,091 patients; Prattichizzo 1994: 1 hepatitis case in 200 patients; mortality reported by Corkery 1991 and Wysowski 1993); patients usually fully recover once flutamide is discontinued. The active metabolite 2-hydroxyflutamide is discussed only as a mechanistic mediator, not as an independently causal injuring entity.

raw_record.support_text: Flutamide is reported to cause hepatotoxicity and hepatitis in humans. In 1989 Hart and Stricker reported a detailed study of flutamide and hepatotoxicity; after US FDA approval of flutamide for prostate cancer in February 1989, Wysowski et al. (1993) reported 19 cases of flutamide-induced hepatitis reported to the FDA over two years. The incidence of flutamide-induced hepatitis is estimated at about 1%, possibly as high as 5%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Indication-restricted to prostate cancer; flutamide commonly used together with the LHRH analogue zoladex, which is described as non-hepatotoxic and showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity alone after recovery from flutamide-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset of hepatitis reported from 30 to 210 days (Gomez et al. 4 weeks; Wysowski et al. 80 days; the reported case at 210 days). Manifestations include asymptomatic elevation of serum aminotransferase, toxic hepatitis with jaundice, ascites, hypoalbuminemia, and hepatic encephalopathy, and cholestatic hepatitis with marked elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase and r-GTP; mortality from hepatic failure and hepatic encephalopathy reported. Histology showed severe diffuse hepatocyte necrosis in hepatic failure, with cholestasis and focal necrosis common, and portal inflammation/zonal necrosis in a few cases; the reported case showed centrilobular cholestasis and mild sinusoidal lymphocytosis without necrosis. Patients usually recover several weeks to months after discontinuation; Gomez et al. described a rechallenge attack in recovered patients. Mechanism unknown; proposed possibilities include idiosyncratic immunologic hypersensitivity/association with eosinophilia and accumulation of flutamide or toxic metabolites directly damaging hepatocytes.

raw_record.support_text: The study enrolled acetaminophen (APAP) overdose patients at two medical centers; the diagnosis of APAP overdose was made by a physician based on standard clinical criteria (reported history of APAP overdose, detectable serum APAP, and/or aminotransferase level of ≥1500 IU/l), and patients with liver injury from other causes (e.g., viral hepatitis) were excluded. Plasma samples were collected to assess the time course of circulating bile acids after APAP overdose. The authors frame the cohort as acetaminophen-induced acute liver injury (AALI) and acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (AALF) patients, confirming that total and individual serum bile acid levels are substantially elevated in APAP-induced ALF patients.

Cohorts described: acetaminophen-induced acute liver injury (AALI) patients and acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (AALF) patients; AALF samples from the Acute Liver Failure Study Group network included both survivors and non-survivors, with only samples showing evidence of tissue necrosis (peak ALT ≥1000 U/l) used. Reference to serum bile acid elevations in mice and rats given toxic doses of APAP is preclinical and not part of this human claim.

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid (Ticrynafen), a uricosuric diuretic used in hypertension, was associated with drug-associated hepatotoxicity characterized by fever, abdominal pain, jaundice, raised serum transaminases, and a histological picture resembling viral hepatitis. Until its withdrawal from sale in the US in 1980, there were 340 instances of hepatic injury considered likely drug related in an estimated exposed population of 265,000 (frequency ~1 in 800 in the USA versus about 1 in 10,000 in France).
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic used for hypertension; withdrawn from US sale in 1980. 340 reported instances of hepatic injury likely drug related in ~265,000 exposed (US frequency ~1 in 800 vs France ~1 in 10,000; difference attributed in part to a slightly greater amount of tienilic acid isomer in the US preparation). Features: fever, jaundice, elevated serum transaminases (max rise 2013 IU/l), histology resembling viral hepatitis, prompt recurrence on rechallenge, eosinophils on liver histology, and anti-LKM2 autoantibodies (ceasing within 3-9 months of stopping drug). Patients in the antibody study: 40 with presumed tienilic acid hepatotoxicity (17 men, ages 32-84, median 69; median dose 250 mg/day, range 125-500; abnormal LFTs first noted 30 days to 4 years after start, median 3 months; 24 had jaundice; 25 had anti-LKM2). Sera from 16/36 tested induced significant ADCC against hepatocytes from rabbits pretreated with BNF then tienilic acid, suggesting sensitization to drug-altered liver cell determinants.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 26-year-old woman with hirsutism treated with flutamide 250 mg/day who developed liver toxicity during therapy; other causes of liver toxicity were ruled out, and the CIOMS and Maria & Vitorino (M&V) causality scales both indicated a highly probable relationship between the liver toxicity and flutamide therapy. Severe liver dysfunction has rarely been documented in hirsute women treated with flutamide, though fulminant liver failure cases have been described, and the mechanism is unknown but mitochondrial dysfunction seems implicated.

raw_record.support_text: Among 93 reviewed patients with refractory mCRC treated with regorafenib at the authors' institution, 3 presented severe and icteric toxic hepatitis caused by the treatment, which was fatal for 1 patient. Histological liver lesions differed by onset: acinar zone 3 necrosis in acute symptoms versus portal tract inflammation with porto-central bridging and fibrosis in the delayed presentation. None of the patients had CYP3A4 gene mutations, while similar UGT1A9 promoter region polymorphisms (variant -118T9>10, rs3832043) were found in both patients who developed acute hepatitis, both of whom had also previously experienced significant toxicity on irinotecan-based chemotherapy.

raw_record.extra_details: Severe and icteric toxic hepatitis in 3 of 93 reviewed patients, fatal in 1. No CYP3A4 gene mutations; UGT1A9 promoter polymorphism -118T9>10 (rs3832043) found in both patients with acute hepatitis. Described as first report of severe hepatotoxicity with liver histology and genetic assessment of enzymes involved in regorafenib metabolism; authors emphasize close liver test monitoring during regorafenib treatment.

raw_record.support_text: This report describes a clinical case of acute, toxic imatinib-induced hepatitis in a 56-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia and concomitant sulfa allergy and rheumatoid arthritis. The patient developed acute imatinib-induced hepatitis after three months of imatinib treatment and three days after increasing the dose from 400 mg/day to 600 mg/day, resolving within three months after imatinib discontinuation and prednisolone administration. The paper notes the drug can cause hepatic failure and death in rare cases, and that approximately 25 clinical case reports of imatinib-induced hepatitis have been published.

Baseline ALT 12 U/L, AST 18 U/L, total bilirubin 0.33 mg/dL. Nausea after dose increase; fever of unknown cause during first two months of therapy. Paper states approximately 25 case reports of imatinib-induced hepatitis published and that imatinib can cause hepatic failure, acute liver failure, and death in rare cases; predisposing factors not identified.

The International Organization of Medical Sciences Diagnostic Scale and the Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale both graded the association between atomoxetine and hepatitis as 'probable,' with a positive rechallenge needed to make it 'definitive.' raw_record.support_text: The paper presents clinical and laboratory data for nine patients with methyl dopa (α-methyl dopa) associated liver disease, spanning acute hepatitis (cases 1-3, AST up to 952 IU/l), chronic active hepatitis (case 4), and fulminant hepatic failure (cases 5-9, AST up to 3630 IU/l). Daily doses ranged 750-2000 mg and therapy duration before symptoms ranged from 7 weeks to 3 years. Five patients (the fulminant hepatic failure group) had a short history of nausea, anorexia, and jaundice with rapid deterioration to grade IV hepatic encephalopathy and death two to six weeks after the first symptom; necropsy showed massive hepatic necrosis, most marked centrilobularly, with cholestasis and, in three cases, early portal tract fibrosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine patients with methyl dopa associated liver disease: three acute hepatitis (AST 81, 59, 952 IU/l), one chronic active hepatitis (AST 140 IU/l), five fulminant hepatic failure (AST 400-3630 IU/l, PT prolonged). Doses 750-2000 mg daily; duration before symptoms 7 weeks to 3 yr. Autoantibodies (ANA/SMA/parietal cell) present in six of nine; case 1 had coexisting Coomb's-positive haemolytic anaemia. None took other known hepatotoxic agents; daily ethanol <60 g; seronegative for hepatitis A/B, CMV, EBV, toxoplasmosis. Five deaths with grade IV encephalopathy 2-6 weeks after first symptom; histology massive centrilobular necrosis with cholestasis, early portal fibrosis in three.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from five of nine patients with methyl dopa associated hepatotoxicity induced significant antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity to hepatocytes isolated from rabbits pretreated with Arachlor and methyl dopa. None of the sera from patients with other forms of liver disease or from patients taking methyl dopa without liver damage induced significant cytotoxicity. The methyl dopa related antibody was present in one patient with methyl dopa associated chronic active hepatitis and in two of three patients with an acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine patients with methyl dopa associated hepatotoxicity were studied. A circulating IgG antibody reacting with a methyl dopa-related hapten/neo-antigen on rabbit hepatocytes was detected in five of nine patients; antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity dropped from 44±15% to 8±8% with F(ab)2 to human Fc of IgG and to 6±4% after absorption. Immunofluorescence on patient liver sections showed peripheral hepatocyte staining. Clinical spectrum included acute hepatitis and chronic active hepatitis. Evidence supports an immune-mediated mechanism; methyl dopa is metabolized by hepatic cytochrome P450 to a reactive quinone/semi-quinone that covalently binds macromolecules, with lymphocytes from patients sensitized to the quinone derivative. Arachlor (enzyme inducer) and phenobarbitone were used only in the rabbit target-cell preparation, not implicated as human DILI causes.

raw_record.support_text: In 1975, Mitchell et al. prospectively followed psychiatric hospital patients treated with isoniazid (INH) during a tuberculosis outbreak, collecting blood before starting INH and up to 1 week after study termination. INH (isoniazid) resulted in elevated liver enzymes in 38% of patients, which subsided in the majority despite continued INH treatment, including several who developed concomitant hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law cases). The text notes that although INH toxicity can result in severe liver injury and even liver failure, no cases of liver failure were reported in this study.
raw_record.extra_details: Classic example of adaptation: 38% of patients developed elevated liver enzymes, resolving in the majority despite continued INH; several developed concomitant hyperbilirubinemia (Hy's Law). Though INH toxicity can cause severe liver injury and even liver failure, no liver failure cases occurred in this study. Patients were psychiatric hospital patients treated during a tuberculosis outbreak; liver enzymes followed every 4 weeks. Figure 1 shows AST and bilirubin trends (AST >60 and bilirubin >1.2 mg/dl, with three Hy's Law cases having bilirubin >2x ULN) plotted by Dr John Senior (FDA).

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old male on Terbinafine 250 mg once daily for onychomycosis for 1 month developed progressive jaundice and pruritus. LFTs showed a mixed cholestatic hepatitis picture (bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL, AST 119 U/L, ALT 216 U/L, GGT 205 U/L, ALP 202 U/L, R ratio 3) with negative viral serologies, autoimmune markers, and negative biliary obstruction workup. A liver biopsy showed extensive intraductal and canalicular cholestasis, minimal lobular inflammation, and portal tract expansion with mixed infiltrate and Kupffer cell hyperplasia, with no autoimmune hepatitis or granuloma. A diagnosis of Terbinafine-induced liver injury was made (RUCAM score 9, highly probable); he was given ursodeoxycholic acid for 3 months and recovered.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg once daily for onychomycosis; jaundice latency ~1 month after start. Bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL (direct 11.7), AST 119 U/L, ALT 216 U/L, GGT 205 U/L, ALP 202 U/L, R ratio 3 (mixed). RUCAM score 9 (highly probable). Biopsy showed maintained lobular architecture, extensive intraductal and canalicular cholestasis, minimal lobular inflammation, portal tract expansion with mixed infiltrate, Kupffer cell hyperplasia; no autoimmune hepatitis or granuloma. Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid 300 mg three times daily until LFT normalization (~3 months), with a prolonged recovery phase of 3 months after drug discontinuation. Discussion notes Terbinafine DILI incidence 0.5-3/100,000 exposed; reported phenotypes include acute hepatitis, cholestasis or mixed picture, acute liver failure, and vanishing bile duct syndrome; latency to jaundice generally 2-6 weeks, bilirubin peaks 3-5 weeks after discontinuation, normalization 2-12 months; rarely acute/subacute liver failure requiring liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The study reports two patients with itraconazole (ITZ)-induced cholestatic liver injury who had markedly high serum ITZ concentrations. The paper then characterizes the mechanism using ITZ-treated rats and MDR3-expressing LLC-PK1 cells, showing that ITZ inhibited MDR3-mediated biliary phospholipid secretion, which the authors conclude is involved in ITZ-induced cholestasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients presented with itraconazole-induced cholestatic liver injury with markedly high serum ITZ concentrations; the specific clinical phenotype is cholestatic liver injury/cholestasis. Mechanistic work in ITZ-treated rats and MDR3 (ABCB4)-expressing LLC-PK1 cells showed drastically reduced biliary phospholipids (rather than bile acids) and significantly reduced MDR3-mediated efflux of [14C]phosphatidylcholine at clinically relevant ITZ concentrations, whereas BSEP-mediated [3H]taurocholate transport was not significantly affected. The authors conclude MDR3 inhibition is involved in ITZ-induced cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen liver injury is characterized by a hyperacute biochemical pattern with markedly high ALT (median 4,149 U/L, up to 26,600 U/L) and modest bilirubin elevation (median 4.5 mg/dL). Among a prospective consecutive series of 275 cases of acute liver failure due to acetaminophen overdose, women predominated (74%), median age was 36, and despite better survival acetaminophen-related cases made up the largest number of deaths. Intentional (n=122) and unintentional (n=131) overdose cases showed similar total doses, severity, spontaneous survival (66% vs 64%), transplantation (7% vs 9%), and death without transplantation (27% each).
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose exposure; prospective consecutive series of 275 ALF cases due to acetaminophen overdose. ALT median 4,149 U/L (max 26,600), bilirubin median 4.5 mg/dL, women 74%, median age 36 years. Intentional n=122 vs unintentional n=131; total dose medians 25 g vs 20 g, dose/day 25 g vs 7.5 g; spontaneous survival 66% vs 64%, transplantation 7% vs 9%, death without transplantation 27% vs 27% (all NS). Unintentional cases more often used narcotic compounds (63%) and multiple acetaminophen preparations (38%); alcohol use more common in unintentional cases though its role is unclear. Injury involves the reactive intermediate NAPQI, detoxified by NAC (mercapturic acid path); NAC given within 24 h decreases risk of liver injury.

Forty-seven children were identified from published cases, cases reported to the FDA, and cases from Children's Hospital Medical Center, Cincinnati. Mean peak aspartate aminotransferase was 10,225 IU/L and alanine aminotransferase 7355 IU/L; 24 of 43 patients (55%) died, with an additional three surviving after orthotopic liver transplantation. Parents were advised about the potential hepatotoxicity of acetaminophen when given to ill children in doses exceeding weight-based recommendations.

raw_record.support_text: In a compiled case series of children with repeated accidental overdosage of acetaminophen (dosages estimated at 60–420 mg/kg/day for up to 6 weeks), hepatotoxicity was severe: only 20 of 43 (46.5%) survived, four additional patients survived only because of orthotopic liver transplantation, and 21 of 47 cases had histologic evidence of zone 3 (centrilobular) necrosis on biopsy or autopsy. This indicates that acetaminophen causes dose-related intrinsic hepatotoxicity in the supratherapeutic-exposure setting.

Of 30 cases with timing, 22 had serum levels above the Rumack-Matthews nomogram line associated with hepatotoxicity. 21/47 had zone 3 centrilobular necrosis histology. 9 patients received N-acetylcysteine (44% survived). This is described as the largest collection of liver injury from long-term acetaminophen administration in children; the number likely underrepresents true hepatotoxicity cases.

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' public health clinic treating latent tuberculosis infection, the incidence of liver injury was 0.3% among patients starting isoniazid, with no deaths or hospitalizations among the patients with liver injury. The difference in incidence versus the Seattle clinic (0.1%) was attributed to differing criteria; using the Seattle definition, which excluded asymptomatic transaminase elevation, only six patients (incidence under 0.2%) would have met hepatotoxicity criteria. The authors included asymptomatic transaminase elevation as compatible with ATS/CDC guidelines, which recommend withholding isoniazid when transaminase exceeds 3x ULN with symptoms or 5x ULN when asymptomatic.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that the high PRR, plausible temporal relationship, consistency and specificity of the association, positive dechallenge in several cases and rechallenge in one case, positive dose-response relationship, plausible biological mechanism, and lack of alternative explanations support a causal association between IPT (isoniazid preventive therapy with INH) and hepatotoxicity. The cases were spontaneously reported by healthcare professionals and were voluntarily reported hepatotoxicity cases among Eritrean HIV patients enrolled in IPT, with several severe or very severe cases including four fatal outcomes. Older age greater than 35 years, inappropriate laboratory monitoring, and overdose were identified as possible risk factors.

raw_record.extra_details: From 2014 to June 2016, 4919 patients in Eritrea were enrolled in IPT; 4398 completed 6-month therapy and 188 interrupted treatment due to adverse drug reactions; fatalities included four cases; causality supported by PRR, positive dechallenge (several cases) and rechallenge (one case), dose-response relationship, and absence of alternative explanations; >35 years, inadequate laboratory monitoring, and overdose were identified risk factors; INH-induced hepatotoxicity follows a theophylline-avoidance style recommendation to stop INH and provide symptomatic treatment; a deferred diagnosis of >=5x transaminase elevation or >=3x elevation with symptoms is associated with >50% mortality risk mainly from hepatic failure unless liver transplantation is performed; routine monitoring not recommended by WHO due to rarity.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen causes hepatotoxicity through its transformation into the reactive intermediate NAPQI via the cytochrome P450 2E1 pathway and depletion of protective glutathione. Increased acetaminophen concentration and delayed NAC therapy are risk factors for hepatotoxicity due to a higher NAPQI load and more prolonged glutathione scarcity. In the study of acute acetaminophen overdose patients, hepatotoxicity cases were identified, and elevated aminotransferases and prolonged INR (≥ 2) were used as markers of acute acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity results from transformation into the reactive intermediate NAPQI via cytochrome P450 2E1 and glutathione depletion. Increased acetaminophen concentration and delayed NAC therapy increase risk. Study evaluated Psi (Rumack-Matthew nomogram-based) and APAP x AT (acetaminophen x aminotransferase multiplication product) as risk-assessment tools for predicting hepatotoxicity in 255 acute overdose patients; a presenting APAP x AT above 1500 mg*IU/L^2 was associated with hepatotoxicity despite NAC therapy. Prolonged INR (>= 2) used as hepatotoxicity endpoint.

APAP group was disproportionately female (79%) and Caucasian (67% vs 47% in indeterminate group); ALF due to APAP occurred more commonly in cooler months (not significant, p=0.2240). raw_record.support_text: A patient with metastatic NSCLC on crizotinib presented with scleral icterus, right upper quadrant tenderness, and markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 4093, ALT 3653 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, INR 10, MELD 39). Serologic, autoimmune, and metabolic work-ups were negative. The history and labs were suggestive of crizotinib-associated hepatotoxicity, and the updated RUCAM score was 8, consistent with probable drug-induced liver injury. The case was reported as crizotinib-induced fulminant hepatitis with recovery; crizotinib was discontinued and liver tests returned to normal 26 days after presentation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Indication: metastatic NSCLC (ALK/ROS1-positive); competing causes (viral hepatitis, hepatic metastasis, alcoholic liver disease, other DILI) were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM (Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method) score of 8; admission labs AST 4093 U/L, ALT 3653 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, conjugated bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 358 U/L, INR 10, MELD 39; treated with IV N-acetylcysteine (100 mg/kg continuous infusion for 7 days) and vitamin K 10 mg/day for 3 days; no liver biopsy due to improvement; full recovery with normalization of liver tests 26 days after presentation. Crizotinib is a multitarget tyrosine kinase inhibitor of ALK, MET, and ROS1; metabolized by CYP3A4; usually causes mild LFT elevations, mechanism poorly understood (toxic metabolite accumulation or immune-related).

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old man with stage IV NSCLC was prescribed dacomitinib (45 mg daily, oral); 37 days after administration he was admitted with jaundice and elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin. After dacomitinib discontinuation liver enzymes decreased but bilirubin continued to rise, peaking at 18-fold on day 26 after termination and normalizing on day 146. A 'probable' cause of DILI by dacomitinib was determined by the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method, and the DILI severity was assessed as acute liver failure. The paper reports this as the first case of DILI caused by dacomitinib monotherapy in a real-world setting.

Total bilirubin peaked at 18-fold on day 26 after dacomitinib termination and normalized on day 146 after discontinuation. Causality assessed as 'probable' by the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method. Severity assessed as acute liver failure. Reported as the first case of DILI caused by dacomitinib monotherapy in a real-world setting. Patient also received a single dose of cisplatin (40 mg, intrapleural perfusion) but injury attributed to dacomitinib monotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: Among 3,377 adults (aged ≥25 years) started on isoniazid (INH) therapy for latent tuberculosis infection in a public health TB clinic over a 7-year period, 19 patients developed isoniazid hepatotoxicity defined as aspartate aminotransferase (AST) >5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), a rate of 5.6 per 1,000 patients. Only 1 of 19 patients had prodromal symptoms. Age >49 years (p<0.02) and baseline AST >ULN (p<0.0003) were identified as risk factors for INH hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study restricted to adults aged ≥25 years; exclusion criteria included pregnancy, INH initiation within 3 months postpartum, baseline AST >3 times ULN, and history of INH allergy.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as AST >5 times ULN; 19 events among 3,377 patients (5.6/1000). Events per 1000 patients were 2.75 at 1 month, 7.20 at 3 months, and 4.10 at 6 months of therapy. Age-specific events per 1000: 4.40 (25-34 y), 8.54 (35-49 y), 20.83 (≥50 y). Risk factors: age >49 years (p<0.02) and baseline AST >ULN (p<0.0003). Moderate-to-severe hepatotoxicity frequently occurred without symptoms, supporting value of AST monitoring. Authors note INH is well documented to cause liver adverse effects ranging from mild transient aminotransferase elevations (approximately 10-20% of patients) to overt hepatitis; risk factors include age >35 years, female gender, and concurrent ethanol use, with some data suggesting African-American and Hispanic women at greater risk. Consistent with earlier trials, INH hepatotoxicity is age related.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 3,377 patients treated with isoniazid (INH) for latent tuberculosis, 19 patients developed hepatotoxicity, defined as serum AST >5 times the upper limit of normal; INH was immediately discontinued. The incidence was 5.63 hepatotoxic events per 1,000 patients started on therapy. The events were attributed to INH therapy, with peak AST elevations peaking 1 to 6 months after treatment start, and some affected patients were icteric with elevated total bilirubin.
raw_record.extra_details: 19/3,377 patients (0.56%) had hepatotoxicity (AST >5x ULN), 5.63 events per 1,000 patients started. Only 1 of 19 had prodromal symptoms; two icteric patients had total bilirubin 5.8 and 6.4 mg/dL with malaise/nausea. Peak AST ranged 212-1602 U/L, 1-6 months after starting INH. raw_record.support_text: Serial changes in circulating monocyte populations were characterised in consecutive patients with paracetamol overdose complicated by significant liver injury (POD-ALF, paracetamol overdose acute liver failure), including patients who subsequently died or required emergency liver transplantation. Circulating CD3+ lymphocytes and CD56+ natural killer cells were significantly reduced and related to outcome, and immune cell changes were most pronounced in POD patients with poor outcomes (death or transplantation).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: paracetamol overdose complicated by significant liver injury; the study cohort comprised 35 POD patients, 20 of whom developed acute liver failure (hepatic encephalopathy) and 10 of whom died or required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of circulating immune cells (monocytes, neutrophils, CD3+ lymphocytes, CD56+ NK cells) in paracetamol overdose acute liver failure (POD-ALF). Clinical phenotype is acute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy (ALF), not a specific histologic syndrome. Monocytopenia with reduced classical (CD14+CD16-) monocytes and expansion of intermediate (CD14+CD16+) monocytes in patients who died or required transplantation; CD3+ and CD56+ cell reductions related to outcome. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) identified as the inducing agent via overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Single-centre prospective study of consecutive patients with paracetamol overdose-induced acute liver failure (POD-ALF). No liver histology available; findings extrapolated from other data. Study focus was on monocyte phenotype, gene expression (microarray, qPCR), and peripheral cytokine protein expression as predictors of adverse patient outcome; paracetamol-induced acute liver failure did not show the same monocyte reduction pattern as non-paracetamol ALF.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic injury mimicked acute viral hepatitis with sharp serum aminotransferase elevation, jaundice (recurrent toxic hepatitis), elevated bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time/aPTT; treated with IV fluids and monitored over 6 days, followed 1 month, with liver enzymes and bilirubin returning to normal within 2 weeks. Naranjo score 11 corresponded to 'definite' causality. The paper notes ecstasy-induced hepatic injury ranges from benign viral-hepatitis-like forms to liver failure from massive hepatic necrosis, and cites Andreu et al who found ecstasy was the second most common cause of liver injury in patients under 25 years, with 5 of 10 such cases ecstasy-related. Mechanism thought to involve a reactive metabolite (glutathione depletion, calcium influx, oxidative cell-membrane lipid changes) partly via CYP2D6 metabolism; mortality described in MDMA- and 3,4-methylenedioxy-N-ethyl-amphetamine postmortem series. One reported case of fulminant hepatitis and two of acute hepatitis after a single ecstasy tablet.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity was defined as hepatic dysfunction in the presence of a history consistent with excessive (overdose) paracetamol ingestion when alternative causes of acute hepatic dysfunction were less likely. Hepatocellular injury was defined as an ALT > 3 times the upper normal limit, severe hepatotoxicity as a peak aspartate aminotransferase > 1,000 IU/L, and acute liver failure (ALF) as severe hepatotoxicity plus coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5) plus any degree of encephalopathy. In the study cohort of 177 adults admitted with paracetamol overdose, this overdose-related hepatocellular injury and ALF were attributed to paracetamol.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: supratherapeutic ingestion for therapeutic intent without deliberate self-harm or intentional (deliberate) overdose; injury assessed in adults (excluding patients <18 years of age, n=54).
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective single-center study (NUH) over three years; 237 patients with matching ICD codes screened, 177 adult overdose visits included. Overdose risk categories predicted from plasma paracetamol levels using the Rumack-Matthew nomogram at ≥4h and <24h post-ingestion: above 200-line = probable risk; below 150-line = no risk; between 150- and 200-line = possible risk. Hepatotoxicity required ALT >3x ULN (hepatocellular injury); severe hepatotoxicity peak AST >1,000 IU/L; ALF = severe hepatotoxicity + INR ≥1.5 + any encephalopathy. Median age 25 (range 18-75) years; 50.3% aged 18-25; female predominance (75.0% of intentional overdose).

Ten (5.6%) developed severe hepatotoxicity (AST > 1,000 IU/L), among whom two fulfilled criteria for acute liver failure and two had concomitant acute renal impairment. raw_record.extra_details: Hepatocellular injury defined as ALT > 3 x ULN; severe hepatotoxicity as AST > 1,000 IU/L. Dose of paracetamol ingested was predictive of hepatocellular injury and severe hepatotoxicity (OR 1.07, p < 0.05); increasing time delay to NAC administration was associated with higher rates of hepatocellular injury (OR 1.17, p < 0.01) and severe hepatotoxicity (OR 1.12, p = 0.04). Hepatocellular injury occurred in half of patients receiving NAC > 24 h post-ingestion vs none among those treated within 8 h. Median hospitalisation 3 (1–28) days; no liver transplantation, no deaths.

raw_record.support_text: A 79-year-old woman treated with intravenous (IV) amiodarone for atrial flutter abruptly developed coagulopathy, altered mental status and liver enzyme derangement, and was diagnosed with acute liver failure (ALF) secondary to an amiodarone adverse drug reaction, with a Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 7. Amiodarone was withheld and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was initiated; clinical improvement was seen within 48 hours of holding the drug and complete recovery was reported at follow-up.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intravenous amiodarone administration (IV push then infusion) for atrial flutter in a 79-year-old woman; N-acetylcysteine co-administered as treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Received 150 mg amiodarone IV push followed by an IV infusion totalling 930 mg over 24 hours, then transitioned to oral amiodarone 200 mg twice daily. Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 7 supports a probable causal relationship. Clinical improvement within 48 hours of holding the drug and within 24 hours of initiating NAC; complete recovery at post-hospital follow-up, making this the only reported survivor among seven total cases of amiodarone-induced ALF (the prior six reported cases were all fatal). Chronic oral amiodarone is noted to be associated with asymptomatic hepatotoxicity.

Case 1: in the absence of other etiologies for ALF, a strong history of etodolac intake before illness and a RUCAM causality instrument score of 7 (consistent with probable DILI) supported the diagnosis of etodolac-induced DILI leading to ALF. The authors made a diagnosis of liver failure due to taking ibuprofen-sustained release capsules. After 9 days of hepatoprotective and nutritional therapy the symptoms improved, liver function returned to near normal, and follow-up at 2 weeks showed normal liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old man; single ibuprofen-sustained release capsule taken the day before symptom onset for headache. Presenting features: 4-day history of tea-colored urine, oil avoidance, jaundiced skin, anorexia, impaired liver function. Diagnosis of liver failure attributed to ibuprofen; hepatotoxic drugs discontinued, then hepatoprotective agents, nutritional support, correction of acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities. Marked improvement after 9 days (no discomfort, subsided jaundice, clear urine, near-normal liver tests), discharged, normal liver function at 2-week follow-up. No formal causality instrument reported.

raw_record.support_text: The patient had taken ampicillin (500 mg every 6 hours orally) for 5-7 days before each of three episodes of recurrent cholestatic hepatitis, with the onset of cholestatic symptoms gradually shortening with each attack and resolving within 10-12 days following drug cessation. The first episode began 5 days after 7 days of ampicillin 500 mg q6h, with subsequent episodes occurring during renewed ampicillin treatment, indicating positive dechallenge and rechallenge. No other etiology (viral hepatitis markers, autoantibodies, ultrasonography) was found, and the patient did not use acetaminophen or naproxen sodium for 2 months preceding.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis with jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools; alkaline phosphatase 455 U/L, ALT 250 U/L, AST 150 U/L, direct and indirect bilirubin 2.1 and 1.2 mg/dL. Hepatobiliary ultrasonography and viral/autoimmune workups were negative. Ampicillin 500 mg every 6 hours orally.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that ampicillin, one of the most commonly used antibiotics, can cause recurrent cholestatic hepatitis, and recommend considering this adverse effect during diagnostic evaluation of patients with hepatic lesions. A case summary describes a 23-year-old patient hospitalized for recurrent, limited cholestasis symptoms; on three occasions ampicillin use led to cholestasis symptoms, with clinical and biochemical recovery on discontinuation of the antibiotic, negative workup otherwise, and no recurrence one year after stopping ampicillin, with the causal relationship deemed probable on the Naranjo scale. The discussion notes that ampicillin-related hepatotoxicity is very rare and usually causes hepatocellular injury, and that this appears to be the only reported case of cholestatic toxicity secondary to ampicillin.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a 23-year-old patient; recurrent cholestasis symptoms on three separate ampicillin exposures, with clinical and biochemical recovery on drug withdrawal and no recurrence one year later; causality assessed as probable on the Naranjo scale. raw_record.support_text: Using the Hanson conditions and CIOMS criteria, the authors concluded that their two cases matched the parameters for propylthiouracil to be causative of fulminating hepatitis. Viral hepatitis was ruled out via negative hepatitis A, B, and C markers, autoimmunity tests were largely negative, and neither patient had congestive heart failure or other extrathyroidal risk factors; fulminating hepatitis was diagnosed based on jaundice, severe clinical evolution like viral hepatitis, encephalopathy, terminal multiple organ failure, and autopsy-confirmed histologic hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients (case series). Case 1: varying intermittent dose of propylthiouracil over 4 months, jaundice onset 92 days after start, death 30 days after icterus onset. Case 2: propylthiouracil 200 mg/day for 5 months plus constant 150 mg/day for 15 days, jaundice onset at 162 days, death 50 days after icterus. Hepatitis A/B/C ruled out; CMV and EBV not tested (optional per CIOMS). Autoantibody testing largely negative except low-titer antinuclear antibodies. Histology: extensive areas of necrosis with hemorrhagic infiltration, widened portal triads with edema and incipient fibrosis, perilobular cholestasis, slight ductal proliferation, lymphoplasmocytic portal infiltrate, centrolobular hepatocyte lysis, moderate cholestasis. No laboratory tests before propylthiouracil intake. Indication: thyrotoxicosis (mild to moderate).

raw_record.support_text: Two cases of fatal fulminant hepatic failure associated with propylthiouracil (PTU) used to treat Graves disease are reported. Both cases were considered probable on the Naranjo scale and met all requirements for hepatotoxicity according to the Hanson criteria and the CIOMS International Committee. The literature review found only 8 deaths associated with PTU use up to 1999, to which these 2 cases are added.
raw_record.extra_details: Two adult women (age 30, Case 1; age 32, Case 2) with Graves disease, no prior hepatic disorder; PTU doses 450 mg/d for 4 months and 200 mg/d for 5 months; jaundice appeared after 4-5 months of treatment; symptoms resembled viral hepatitis progressing to severe hepatic dysfunction with death despite extensive therapy. One patient was pregnant and miscarried during her liver illness. No history of alcoholism, drug abuse, blood transfusion, or hepatitis A/B/C exposure; abdominal ultrasound excluded extrahepatic obstruction; serologic and immunologic studies negative. Autopsy histology showed massive liver necrosis in both cases. Causality graded probable by Naranjo and meeting Hanson/CIOMS hepatotoxicity criteria.

raw_record.support_text: Case 3: A 60-year-old woman with prior steatohepatitis had undergone modified mastectomy for breast carcinoma and started tamoxifen citrate (20 mg daily) two months before admission. She developed hepatomegaly with elevated liver enzymes (ALT 377, AST 284, GGT 342, ALP 290 U/L, Bil 1.5 mg/dL), and a liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis compatible with drug-induced hepatitis after excluding metastases, obstruction, and viral causes. Tamoxifen was withdrawn and corticosteroids were given; ALP/GGT normalized within five weeks. Final diagnosis: acute cholestatic hepatitis caused by tamoxifen citrate.

raw_record.support_text: Among 430 patients treated for active TB between 1990 and 1999, side effects resulting in modification/discontinuation of therapy or hospitalization were attributed based on resolution after withdrawal and/or recurrence with rechallenge. The incidence of all major adverse effects was 1.48 per 100 person-months (95% CI, 1.31-1.61) for pyrazinamide. The paper concludes that the incidence of pyrazinamide-induced hepatotoxicity and rash during treatment for active TB was substantially higher than with other first-line anti-TB drugs and higher than previously recognized.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective observational study (Anand 1997), 31 patients with paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure and arterial pH < 7.30 received supportive care, with mortality as the outcome. Throughout this Cochrane review, paracetamol overdose is consistently attributed as the cause of hepatotoxicity (defined as aspartate aminotransferase > 1000 IU/L) and fulminant hepatic failure; for example, the additional table on liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure aggregates patients with paracetamol-induced liver failure who either received transplantation or supportive treatment, with many deaths.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Attribution is for paracetamol overdose (supratherapeutic ingestion); several patients had severe overdose with fulminant hepatic failure and encephalopathy and some required liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was defined in this review as aspartate aminotransferase > 1000 IU/L. Multiple observational studies report paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure (e.g., Anand 1997, 31 patients pH<7.3; Bernal 1998, 124 patients eligible for transplantation; Harrison 1990, 98 patients; Keays 1991, 50 patients with paracetamol-induced FHF; Schiodt 1996, Shakil 2000, Chung 2003, Brandsaeter 2002). Pooled transplant-table data: transplanted groups had mortality 19/67 (28%) versus supportive 121/180 (67%) under Kings College criteria. In supportive-treatment-only cohorts mortality reached 50-88%. Patients were treated with antidotes (N-acetylcysteine, methionine, cysteamine, dimercaprol) and interventions (charcoal haemoperfusion, gastric lavage); outcomes included mortality, hepatotoxicity, liver transplantation, and severe liver injury.

The paper states that although rare, clinically significant and potentially life-threatening liver injury can result from hydralazine use.

raw_record.extra_details: Hydralazine 100 mg three times daily orally for treatment of hypertension, started 10 weeks before presentation. CIOMS/DILI causality assessment score 9 ('high probable'). Presented with painless jaundice and scleral icterus; elevated ALT 242 U/L, AST 439 U/L, total bilirubin 22.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 15.7 mg/dL, ALP 166 U/L, INR 1.23. Paper recommends monitoring of liver function during hydralazine treatment.
