raw_record.support_text: The study found that indeterminate acute liver failure (ALF) accounts for ~14% of all ALF referred to tertiary centers, and that this group includes ~18% suffering from unrecognized acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity, demonstrated by high levels of APAP-cysteine adducts in serum and clinical and biochemical profiles virtually identical to known APAP overdose cases. Patients presenting with hyperacute ALF of undetermined cause were considered potential APAP cases and treated as APAP toxicity, and clinically defined APAP-adduct-positive overdose cases (n=188) confirmed acetaminophen as the hepatotoxic agent.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (suicidal, accidental/unintentional, or unknown); includes unrecognized APAP toxicity detected only by serum APAP-cysteine adduct assay rather than reported history.
raw_record.extra_details: Unrecognized APAP toxicity accounted for ~18% of indeterminate acute liver failure cases. Detection used serum APAP-cysteine adducts with assay-positive defined as ≥1.0 nmol/mL; unrecognized APAP group (Group 2, n=20) had median ALT 5156 IU/L, AST 8126 IU/L, bilirubin 5.05 mg/dL, median adduct 9.2 nmol/mL, 55% spontaneous survival, 10% transplantation. Clinically defined APAP overdose (Group 3, n=188) had median adduct 11.1 nmol/mL, 63.8% spontaneous survival, 8% transplantation. Clinicians were advised to consider the hyperacute pattern (short duration illness, high aminotransferases, low bilirubin) as indicating APAP toxicity and to use N-acetylcysteine (NAC) promptly because of its low toxicity and established value in acetaminophen toxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Diagnostic accuracy study of the AcetaSTAT rapid assay versus central HPLC-EC for serum acetaminophen-protein (APAP-cys) adducts. Consensus with causality review diagnosis in 77/81 subjects (95.1%); sensitivity 100%, specificity 86.2%, PPV 89.2%, NPV 100% vs diagnosis. Agreement with HPLC-EC adduct threshold of >=1.0 nmol APAP-cys/mL in 76/81 (93.8%). In 4 non-acetaminophen-diagnosed cases AcetaSTAT was positive; 3 had HPLC-EC adducts near/above the toxicity threshold suggesting toxic APAP exposure, and 1 (autoimmune hepatitis diagnosis) was negative by HPLC-EC. AcetaSTAT completed in median 27 min (range 25-45).

raw_record.support_text: In the current study, detection of threshold levels of the acetaminophen protein-adduct, either by AcetaSTAT or HPLC-EC, reliably identified acetaminophen as the etiology of acute liver failure (ALF) or acute liver injury (ALI) based on a single determination in 77 of 81 cases (95.1%), whereas serum acetaminophen, transaminases, and INR cut-points were not reliable. The paper reports acetaminophen as the cause of ALF/ALI in these patients, including cases in which the site investigator did not diagnose acetaminophen overdose; post-hoc analysis determined three disparate cases to be highly likely/definite acetaminophen toxicity supported by positive adduct assays.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings concern acetaminophen overdose/toxicity presenting as acute liver failure or acute liver injury; some cases had competing/uncertain etiologies (denied or minimized ingestion, or possible ischemia) resolved by post-hoc analysis as acetaminophen toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen protein-adduct is a unique product of acetaminophen metabolism and elevated adduct levels occur only as a consequence of acetaminophen toxicity, remaining elevated after the parent drug is metabolized. Classic biochemical profile of very high aminotransferases (ALT, AST) and low bilirubin was compatible with acetaminophen-induced liver injury. Adduct detection (AcetaSTAT or HPLC-EC) identified acetaminophen as ALF/ALI etiology in 77/81 cases (95.1%); serum acetaminophen was detected in only 17 of 33 bona fide acetaminophen cases and in 3 of 29 non-acetaminophen cases. NAC treatment is most effective when given early.

raw_record.support_text: Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, has been very rarely associated with drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The report presents a case of an elderly male who developed severe but asymptomatic DILI associated with acetazolamide use, with severity established by markedly elevated serum transaminases. Rechallenge of acetazolamide at a higher dose resulted in increased severity of the elevations, suggesting a causative effect, and liver function tests improved after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: 66-year-old man with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with lumbar spinal metastases and a postoperative CSF leak treated with acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily for five days to reduce CSF production. Three days post-treatment, ALT rose from 12 to 426 U/L (35-fold), AST from 16 to 251 U/L (16-fold), ALP from 51 to 278 U/L, while total bilirubin remained stable at 0.34 mg/dL, consistent with a hepatocellular injury pattern. Rechallenge at a higher dose increased severity of the elevations; liver function tests improved after acetazolamide discontinuation. Only two prior documented cases of acetazolamide-induced DILI exist in the literature.

raw_record.support_text: After worldwide release with 60,000 patients exposed (40,000 patient-years), tolcapone was reported in 1998 to induce liver toxicity. Four patients experienced serious liver dysfunction, and three of them died of acute liver failure; at examination they were jaundiced with significant serum ALT elevation. The hepatic dysfunction was attributed to tolcapone, and the single autopsy showed centrolobular necrosis consistent with drug-induced toxicity from tolcapone. These patients had been on tolcapone for 2-4 months and none had been monitored as recommended, after which tolcapone was withdrawn from European and Canadian markets and the US FDA revised the label to require strict liver enzyme monitoring.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Used in Parkinson disease in conjunction with levodopa; none of the reported patients had been monitored with liver enzymes as recommended at the time of injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Four patients with serious liver dysfunction after 2-4 months of tolcapone; three died of acute liver failure; patients were jaundiced with significant serum ALT elevation; one autopsy showed centrolobular necrosis. Follow-up expert panel consensus noted that all clinical and enzymatic liver dysfunction occurred within 6 months of initiating treatment and recommended routine liver enzyme monitoring. Tolcapone was withdrawn from European and Canadian markets; the US FDA implemented a revised label requiring strict liver enzyme monitoring (e.g., every 2 weeks in the first year).

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is described as progressing to irreversible liver failure and as a leading cause of drug-induced acute liver failure and liver transplantation. In one study, 20% of the center's liver transplantation cases were due to APAP overdose (the most common cause of acute liver failure prompting transplantation), while only 12% of patients presenting with acute liver failure from APAP overdose actually received a transplant. A multicenter US Acute Liver Failure Study Group study reported 54% of liver failure cases were APAP-related; those APAP-associated cases fared better in 2-year survivorship if not transplanted.

raw_record.extra_details: APAP is also written as acetaminophen; reactive metabolite NAPQI and NAC antidote discussed elsewhere in the paper. raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure caused by acetaminophen overdose in a multicenter cohort of 308 patients (120 acetaminophen cases). Acetaminophen group had shorter disease duration, higher ALT (mean 4310 U/L, range 136-17670) and AST (mean 4333 U/L), higher creatinine, and lower bilirubin (mean 74 µmol/L) and arterial pH than other causes. Mean INR 2.8; coma grade at admission I-IV distributed across the group. Survival without transplant 68%; overall survival 73%; transplantation received by 6% (7 patients); 56/120 (47%) fulfilled transplant criteria but only 32 (57%) were listed, the rest excluded for psychosocial or medical reasons such as sepsis or cerebral edema.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is the most widely used nonprescription analgesic in the U.S. The paper states there is very little evidence of liver injury when acetaminophen is used according to package recommendations, but that it is a common putative cause of severe liver injury because of its recognized dose-related hepatotoxicity, easy availability, and possible cofactors such as alcohol use and starvation. Most patients with presumed acetaminophen overdose had overdosed accidentally, 83% exceeded the daily maximum recommended dose, and the median dose in the series was more than three times that value; only the most severely ill patients (usually taking the largest overdoses or with a long delay before antidote treatment) developed acetaminophen-related liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury attributed to overdose/supratherapeutic exposure; 83% of patients exceeded the daily maximum recommended dose and median dose exceeded the daily maximum by more than threefold; possible cofactors such as alcohol use and starvation; overdoses were largely accidental rather than suicide attempts.
raw_record.extra_details: 76% of Americans reported using a nonprescription product in the previous month and 36% specified acetaminophen. Of patients with acetaminophen-related acute liver failure, 73% survived, only 6% received liver transplants, and 33 patients died (28% of the acetaminophen group and 11% of all patients admitted to the study); 43% were not considered for transplantation because of medical contraindications or psychosocial reasons. 11% of all cases in this acute liver failure registry were attributed to acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 65 patients with prostate cancer receiving a total androgen suppression (TAS) regimen, flutamide was discontinued because of liver function test (LFT) elevations in 14 patients (22%), and hepatotoxicity contributed to discontinuation in others. ALT elevation was the most sensitive finding (37/60 evaluable patients had ALT ≥41 U/L), and grade 3-4 toxicity with ALT >5 times normal occurred in 4/60 patients. AST and ALT were significantly elevated relative to baseline during flutamide therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: 65 prostate cancer patients on a TAS regimen; flutamide discontinued for LFT elevation in 14 (22%); median time to discontinuation 8 weeks (range 1-16). ALT elevation most sensitive: 37/60 (62%) ≥41 U/L; grade 3-4 toxicity (ALT >5x normal) in 4 (7%) of 60. AST: 24/61 (39%) ≥41 U/L. Median AST/ALT rose from 21/25 to 35/50 U/L; no rise in alkaline phosphatase. Baseline only 4/65 had AST/ALT ≥41. P<.02 for AST, P<.005 for ALT. In 12/14 discontinued patients transaminase elevation noted; one isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation; one patient had pruritus with bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL and GGT 112 U/L with normal transaminases.

raw_record.support_text: The case report describes fulminant hepatic failure in a 53-year-old female caused by inadvertent rechallenging with diclofenac, treated by orthotopic liver transplantation. The first episode (diclofenac 50 mg three times daily for one month) produced jaundice with raised serum transaminases and biopsy showing active hepatitis suggestive of drug-induced liver damage, which resolved on withdrawal; a later inadvertent rechallenge with generic diclofenac produced abdominal pain, vomiting, jaundice and fulminant liver failure. Diclofenac is described as previously shown to be hepatotoxic.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose 50 mg three times daily (both episodes), oral. First episode: one month of use leading to jaundice, raised serum transaminases; negative hepatitis A/B/C serology and auto-antibody screen; liver biopsy showed active hepatitis with peri-central venous degeneration, suggestive of drug-induced liver damage; symptoms settled and transaminases returned to normal on withdrawal (positive dechallenge/recovery). Rechallenge: within 48 h abdominal pain and vomiting, then jaundice, progressing to fulminant liver failure; no other risk factors for liver disease; treated with orthotopic liver transplantation. Abstract states diclofenac is the most frequently prescribed NSAID and reviews the literature on NSAID hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac, the most frequently prescribed NSAID, causes minimal serum transaminase elevations in about 15% of patients; severe hepatic dysfunction is rare but 27 case reports of severe diclofenac-induced hepatitis have been described worldwide, including four fatalities. This report describes the second case of diclofenac-induced liver failure successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Diclofenac produces a type II idiosyncratic liver injury; most cases are thought to occur by a metabolic mechanism, though hypersensitivity cases occur. In this case the mechanism was probably a hypersensitivity reaction, evidenced by short exposure duration, dramatic response to rechallenge, and eosinophils in the liver biopsy. Repeated hepatotoxicity on rechallenging with diclofenac has been described, while challenge with a different NSAID was not hepatotoxic, indicating an idiosyncratic rather than class effect. About 15% of patients show minimal transaminase elevations; 27 reported cases of severe hepatitis include 4 fatalities; this is only the second liver-failure case successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: Indicine N-oxide, a pyrrolizidine alkaloid investigational anticancer agent, caused severe human hepatotoxicity in clinical trials. In a trial by Letendre et al. in acute leukemia patients, 5 of 11 patients experienced severe hepatotoxicity and 4 died of liver failure. A 5-year-old boy with acute myelocytic leukemia given 7.5 g/m² indicine N-oxide developed acute hepatic failure 3 days later and died 9 days later with hepatic necrosis. A phase I trial by Whitehead et al. in children with leukemia or solid tumors found hepatotoxicity limited the dose in leukemia patients, and a phase II trial by Miser et al. in children with relapsed acute leukemia associated indicine N-oxide with severe and irreversible hepatotoxicity, ending clinical investigation despite some anti-leukemic activity.

raw_record.extra_details: Letendre et al. trial in acute leukemia: 5/11 patients experienced severe hepatotoxicity, 4 died due to liver failure. Whitehead et al. phase I trial in children: myelosuppression limited dose in solid tumors, hepatotoxicity limited dose in leukemia; no clinically significant objective responses. Miser et al. phase II trial in children with relapsed acute leukemia: showed some anti-leukemic activity but severe and irreversible hepatotoxicity. Severe hepatotoxicity ended scientific investigation of the compound.

raw_record.support_text: An adult developed acute hepatitis after initiation of atomoxetine therapy, with jaundice and high serum aminotransferase levels. Upon discontinuation, jaundice resolved and laboratory levels began to normalize. The report notes only four other similar cases of atomoxetine-induced hepatitis in the literature, mostly in children, and that while most hepatic abnormalities from atomoxetine are transient, this case demonstrates a serious potential to lead to acute liver failure.

Label modified to include severe liver injury among adverse events; the authors note a serious potential to lead to acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes acetaminophen (APAP) as causing hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure, noting that prompt empiric NAC therapy should be considered in any patient with acute AST/ALT elevations and significant APAP ingestion (>4 g), and that the Rumack-Matthew nomogram predicts hepatotoxicity risk after acute overdose. Acetaminophen-induced ALF is treated as an established entity throughout the text, with the US ALF Study Group (n=386) data showing APAP-related severe acute liver injury (ALT ≥10x ULN and INR ≥2.0 without encephalopathy) more likely to progress to ALF, liver transplantation, or death.

raw_record.extra_details: Rumack-Matthew nomogram used to predict hepatotoxicity risk after single acute overdose; supratherapeutic APAP >20 µg/mL (or >10 µg/mL with risk factors) predict hepatotoxicity. >90% of established APAP hepatotoxicity cases resolve spontaneously; more than two-thirds of APAP-induced ALF cases are spontaneous survivors, better than non-APAP etiologies. US ALF Study Group (n=386) data. APAP-protein adducts serum half-life median 42.0 (22.6-61.2) h vs parent APAP 5.4 (0.8-119.7) h; a rapidding APAP-protein adducts immunoassay showed 100% concordance with HPLC-EC (100% sensitivity, 100% negative predictive value). raw_record.support_text: In 1993, 15 participants in a phase II trial received the nucleoside analogue fialuridine to treat hepatitis B virus infection. Seven participants developed liver failure and lactic acidosis; analysis of liver tissue revealed steatosis (fatty degeneration), intracellular fat droplets, and swollen mitochondria. Five participants subsequently died, and two required liver transplantation. The paper states that human-specific mitochondrial toxicity underlies fialuridine's human hepatotoxicity, which was not predicted by preclinical animal testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Two hepatotoxins: 7 of 15 phase II participants (treated for hepatitis B virus infection) developed liver failure and lactic acidosis; histology showed steatosis with intracellular fat droplets and swollen mitochondria; 5 died and 2 required liver transplantation. Toxicity attributed to human-specific mitochondrial toxicity of the nucleoside analogue. Preclinical testing in mice, rats, dogs, and primates gave no indication of hepatotoxicity, and a 1,600-fold dose over 4 days produced liver failure and lactic acidosis only in chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers (toxicity in human-hepatocyte regions).

raw_record.support_text: In a case report of a single patient, the diagnosis of trazodone-induced hepatotoxicity was supported by a liver biopsy showing no significant inflammation or fat and, more importantly, by the biochemical response to inadvertent rechallenge with trazodone (given on 8/10/98 and 8/11/98). Viral and serological markers were negative, there was no biliary radiographic abnormality, and the liver tests essentially normalized approximately 2 weeks after discontinuation of trazodone and again after stopping the inadvertent challenge. The atypical rapid rise in AST on rechallenge was considered consistent with (but not diagnostic of) an idiosyncratic mechanism, described as an idiosyncratic, possible immune reaction. The reaction occurred almost 18 months after drug initiation.

Trazodone bears structural similarity to fluorobutyrophenone antipsychotics; major metabolite is m-chloro-4-phenylpiperazine.

raw_record.support_text: Case 1: a 29-year-old woman with Graves' disease previously treated unsuccessfully with methimazole was prescribed propylthiouracil (PTU) 50 mg PO every 8 hours. Aminotransferases were normal before therapy; mild elevations appeared by week four and increased progressively, and by week ten she developed jaundice and other symptoms. On admission, PTU was attributed as the cause of acute hepatic failure (INR 3.9, total bilirubin 19.3 mg/dL, AST 503, ALT 443, alkaline phosphatase 509 U/L); PTU was discontinued but coagulopathy worsened with hepatic encephalopathy, and she underwent orthotopic liver transplantation eight days after admission. The explanted liver showed submassive confluent necrosis with parenchymal hemorrhage, cholestasis, bile plugging, and lymphoplasmacytic/eosinophilic infiltrates with positive IgG4 immunostain; she recovered with normal liver function 6 months post-transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Both patients were being treated for Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism) and had no antecedent liver disease; hepatitis (A, B, C) and autoimmune markers were negative. Alternative therapeutic options are discussed.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports of PTU-induced acute hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation. Case 1: PTU 50 mg PO every 8 h; transaminase elevations from week 4, jaundice by week 10; underwent OLT 8 days after admission; explant showed submassive confluent necrosis, cholestasis, eosinophilic/lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, positive IgG4; recovered. Case 2: PTU 150 mg PO twice daily; malaise at 6 weeks, progressive jaundice; INR 4.3, total bilirubin 22.8 mg/dL, AST 1081, ALT 1227 U/L; transjugular biopsy showed extensive parenchymal necrosis, lobular collapse, bile duct proliferation, periportal inflammation; required a first transplant 3 days after listing and a second transplant 6 days later due to severe graft rejection, with delayed recovery and discharge ~5 months later. PTU-induced liver injury ranges from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to fulminant hepatic failure and death; frequent monitoring advised.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient with severe hepatitis with jaundice following flutamide use (with improvement after flutamide withdrawal and UDCA treatment) and reviews attributable literature cases: Dourakis et al described a fatal massive hepatic necrosis and a severe hepatitis with predominant hepatic necrosis; Møller et al reported two cases of flutamide-associated hepatotoxicity, one hepatocellular-type jaundice and one hepatitis with cholestasis. raw_record.extra_details: Reported liver-injury incidence from less than 1% to about 5%. Reported phenotypes include severe hepatitis with jaundice (own case, cholestatic features present), fatal massive hepatic necrosis, severe hepatitis with predominant hepatic necrosis, hepatocellular-type jaundice (biochemical recovery 20 weeks after withdrawal), and hepatitis with cholestasis (resolved two months after withdrawal). UDCA treatment was started on admission contemporaneously with flutamide withdrawal in the index case, with progressive clinical and biochemical improvement and discharge six weeks after admission. Serial serum liver enzyme monitoring during flutamide administration is advocated because fatal flutamide-related hepatitis has been reported.

raw_record.support_text: The study demonstrated a clear relationship between methotrexate (MTX) therapy and chemically and histologically defined liver damage. The rapidity of onset and severity of abnormal liver function tests correlated with the intensity of therapy, with more hepatotoxicity observed in the group showing hematologic and gastrointestinal chemotherapy side effects. LFT abnormalities following intermittent MTX resolved completely within one month after cessation, and continued moderate-dose MTX therapy was associated with normal or near-normal liver function without progressive hepatic damage, including in patients with eye disease.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity included abnormal SGOT/SGPT and BSP retention, with histologic findings of portal fibrosis, fatty metamorphosis, mild toxic degeneration of hepatic parenchymal cells, and slight bile stasis. LFT abnormalities correlated with intensity of therapy and resolved within one month after cessation of intermittent MTX. Five patients received maintenance MTX 10-25 mg/m² IV once weekly for 3 months to 1.5 years; liver function returned to normal in 4 of 5, while one had persistent abnormalities (SGOT 30-60, SGPT 60-130, BSP 7-11%). Four intensive-therapy patients died of infectious complications of leukemia 4-6 months post-study with hepatic disease not involved; all showed leukemic portal infiltration, one with moderate fatty metamorphosis, one with slight portal fibrosis and moderate fatty metamorphosis.

raw_record.support_text: A patient on bupropion SR presented six months after starting the drug with markedly elevated serum aminotransferases and bilirubin, showing a severe acute hepatocellular injury with autoimmune features. Enrolled in the DILIN prospective protocol with all other competing causes of liver injury excluded, the case scored 8 on RUCAM, categorized as a 'highly probable' case of DILI, and also scored 'probable' on a drug-induced hepatitis validation scale. The authors concluded the patient presumably developed fulminant hepatitis with autoimmune features due to bupropion given the temporal course, exclusion of competing etiologies, and compatible histology.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: bupropion SR 150 mg BID for 180 days, peak ALT 20x ULN, peak bilirubin 37 mg/dl, positive ANA, liver biopsy showing acute hepatocellular injury with autoimmune features; progressed to fulminant liver failure and death with disseminated aspergillosis despite cessation and corticosteroids. RUCAM score 8 (highly probable DILI); scored probable on a drug-induced hepatitis validation scale and probable autoimmune hepatitis on the International autoimmune hepatitis consensus scale. Table 1 lists prior published cases of bupropion hepatotoxicity (Oslin '93: 300-400 mg QD, 54 days, ALT 5.4x ULN, resolution; Hu '00: 200 mg QD, 42 days, ALT 6660 IU/L, bilirubin 3.8, resolution; D. Alvaro '01: 150 mg BID, 20 days, ALT 49x ULN, bilirubin 38, resolution; Humayun '07: 150 mg BID, 180 days, ALT 20x ULN, bilirubin 37, death), all occurring within the first 6 months of use with a hepatocellular injury pattern; this is described as the first reported fatal bupropion hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Multiple reports demonstrate that MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine) causes hepatotoxicity, producing a spectrum of liver damage ranging from asymptomatic liver injury with mild transient liver function test elevations to acute and fulminant liver failure with multiorgan failure and death. The liver is described as the organ most vulnerable and sensitive to the toxic effects of MDMA. Reported cases of acute liver failure due to MDMA intoxication from 1992-2015 include outcomes ranging from full recovery to orthotopic liver transplantation and death.

raw_record.extra_details: Multiple case series and published reports, including a compiled table of acute liver failure cases from the medical literature 1992-2015 (Henry, Ellis, Milroy, Brauer, Andreu, Garbino, Caballero, Lange-Brock, Guneysel, Payancé, Nadkarni, Atayan). Liver biopsy histology resembles severe viral hepatitis with centrilobular mononuclear infiltration, plus steatosis/fatty infiltration, ballooning degeneration, cytoplasmic vacuolation, cholestasis, and focal or massive necrosis with acute inflammatory response. Presenting features include jaundice, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deranged coagulation, elevated liver enzymes, hepatic encephalopathy, and coma; some patients are asymptomatic. Interventions included conservative medical management and orthotopic/auxiliary liver transplantation, with deaths due to sepsis after transplant in some cases. The first UK hepatotoxicity cases reported in 1992 (Shearman: 27-year-old woman with jaundice, palmar erythema, elevated bilirubin/AST/ALP and acute hepatitis on biopsy; Gorard: 20-year-old student after 20 tablets over 3 months). Exact pathophysiologic mechanisms, including accumulation of toxic MDMA metabolites, remain under investigation.

raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism attributed to toxic acetaminophen metabolites: covalent binding to mitochondrial proteins, depressed mitochondrial respiration and ATP synthesis, mitochondrial oxidant stress with peroxynitrite production, collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential, release of mitochondrial proteins, and oncotic necrosis of hepatocytes; innate immunity (Kupffer cells, NK cells, neutrophils) exacerbates hepatic injury. Epidemiology: 26,000 hospitalizations and >450 deaths annually in the US; acetaminophen identified as cause of ALF in 20% (late 1990s) then 39% to 42% of cases, with suicidal intent in 27% to 44% and unintentional overdose in 48% to 61%; incidence rose from 28% in 1998 to 52% in 2003; pediatric multicenter study attributed 14% of ALF to acetaminophen overdose. raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen is the most widely used analgesic-antipyretic, present in more than 600 products. Toxicity involves excessive formation of the reactive intermediate N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) via cytochrome P450 (CYP2E1), which covalently binds cell proteins via cysteine residues when glutathione detoxification is exceeded, forming acetaminophen-protein adducts. In a prospective study of 66 ALF patients from 24 US tertiary centers, serum acetaminophen-protein adducts (measured by HPLC with electrochemical detection) were detected in 100% of known acetaminophen ALF cases and none of the other defined-cause ALF cases (sensitivity/specificity 100%); 7/36 (19%) indeterminate cases had detectable adducts suggesting acetaminophen contributed to their ALF, and low adduct levels were present in 2/15 overdose patients without significant liver injury. Adducts decreased in parallel with aminotransferases on serial sampling. Markedly elevated aminotransferases and undetectable plasma acetaminophen levels are characteristic but non-diagnostic; N-acetylcysteine is the antidote. Intentional (single large-dose) overdose is typically easy to diagnose when a history or elevated blood level is present, whereas unintentional cases are often unrecognized.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty patients with definite acetaminophen toxicity causing acute liver failure were studied in the U.S. ALF Study Group cohort, each confirmed to have had rapid-onset disease typical of acetaminophen-induced injury. The site criteria required history of ingestion exceeding package labeling (>4 g/24 hours, in most cases greatly exceeded) within 7 days, detection of acetaminophen in plasma, and/or ALT ≥3500 IU/L. The paper describes acetaminophen-protein (NAPQI-derived) adduct formation as the initial irreversible step in development of hepatic toxicity.

In 20 acetaminophen-related ALF cases: 85% had history of excessive ingestion, 15 ingested >10 g (median ingestion 21 g; group median 24 g), 75% had detectable plasma acetaminophen, 85% had ALT >3500 IU/L; median ALT 5640 IU/L, AST 4404 IU/L, bilirubin 5.0 mg/dl, INR 3.2, adduct concentration 1.17 nmol acetaminophen-CYS/mg protein; 10% transplanted, 85% alive. 15 patients with intentional overdose but minimal liver injury (median peak ALT 26 IU/L) recovered; 8 judged at toxicity risk by Rumack nomogram, median APAP 108 mg/dL at presentation.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, an antidiabetic drug, caused life-threatening idiosyncratic reactions in patients. Mild, reversible hepatotoxicity appeared in pre-marketing clinical trials in <2% of patients; after marketing in early 1997 several cases of severe, even fatal, liver failure emerged, forcing market withdrawal in 2000. Affected patients had elevated serum enzymes and bilirubin and signs of hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis; livers showed necrosis and inflammatory infiltrates including neutrophils. Injury was idiosyncratic with no obvious dose relationship.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that most first-line anti-tuberculosis drugs have potential side effects such as hepatotoxicity, and among these isoniazid (INH) is the most effective but also the drug that can most easily induce hepatotoxicity. The major INH metabolism pathway is acetylation by NAT2 to acetylisoniazid followed by hydrolysis to isonicotinic acid and acetylhydrazine; in NAT2 slow metabolizers the accumulation of hepatotoxic precursors such as hydrazine and acetylhydrazine in the liver underlies the injury. The study also found that carriers of the rs1495741 AA genotype (lower NAT2 activity) required lower INH doses to develop antituberculosis drug-induced hepatotoxicity (ATDIH).

raw_record.extra_details: INH is a first-line antituberculosis drug. NAT2 slow metabolizers acetylate INH, hydrazine and acetylhydrazine more slowly, causing accumulation of hepatotoxic precursors hydrazine and acetylhydrazine in the liver. Study endpoints included ATDIH (antituberculosis drug-induced hepatotoxicity) and ALFTs (abnormal liver-function tests); the rs1495741 AA genotype associated with lower NAT2 enzyme activity, a higher hepatotoxicity risk, and lower cumulative INH doses required to develop ATDIH (P<0.05 for ATDIH, P<0.01 for ALFTs). rs1495741 also significantly affected INH plasma concentration-time profile, clearance, and metabolic ratio in 23 healthy individuals (P<0.001).

The study used this assay on sera from children enrolled in the multicenter Pediatric Acute Liver Failure (PALF) Study to determine the role of APAP toxicity in ALF of indeterminate cause.

raw_record.extra_details: At toxic APAP doses, increased amounts of the CYP2E1-generated metabolite N-acetylbenzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) are produced, forming cysteine adducts (APAP-CYS) concurrently with glutathione depletion; APAP-CYS adducts form in hepatocytes that subsequently undergo APAP-mediated necrosis, and serum APAP-CYS levels reflect hepatic adduct formation. APAP-CYS remained detectable in sera up to 7 days after presentation, enabling identification of APAP-related ALF cases with delayed presentation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews the clinical features of halothane hepatitis in humans, describing fever as characteristically the first sign: among 42 cases reviewed by Klion et al., 37 had fever, and in 94 cases reported by Bottiger et al. the average delay in fever onset was 7 days after first exposure and 4 days after multiple exposures. Across many series some patients lacked fever (Walton et al. reported 21% never experienced postoperative fever). The paper further describes jaundice latency (jaundice appearing 10-28 days after single exposure, 3-17 days after multiple exposures), lab findings typical of parenchymal damage (transaminases 500-1500 IU or greater, bilirubin 5-15 mg/dl or greater), and prognosis, with 60% mortality in patients with bilirubin >10 mg/dl and 100% mortality when prothrombin time exceeded 20 seconds.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane administered as an inhaled anesthetic; liver injury termed halothane hepatitis. Fever present in 75% of cases, chills 30%, rash 10%, myalgia 20%, anorexia/nausea 50%. Jaundice never in the first 2 postoperative days unless prior halothane anesthesia within the prior 2 weeks; delayed jaundice distinguishes halothane hepatitis from benign postoperative cholestasis. Latency to first symptom/jaundice: 6/11 days (single exposure) and 3/6 days (multiple exposure); Klion series 10-28 days to icterus after single and 3-17 days after multiple exposures; Bottiger average jaundice at 8 and 7 days. Transaminases 500-1500 IU or greater, bilirubin 5-15 mg/dl or greater; SGOT and alk phos not predictive. 60% mortality with bilirubin >10 mg/dl vs none below 5 mg/dl; 100% mortality with prothrombin time >20 seconds. Eosinophilia in 32% (Walton, 76 patients); liver-kidney microsomal antibodies in 28%. Mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly.

raw_record.support_text: Prospective data on 662 consecutive patients meeting standard ALF criteria (coagulopathy and encephalopathy) at 22 US tertiary centers identified 275 (42%) cases attributable to acetaminophen liver injury. Median ingested dose was 24 g (48 extra-strength tablets); 131 (48%) were unintentional overdose, 122 (44%) intentional suicide attempts, and 22 (8%) unknown intent. Outcomes were: 178 (65%) survived, 74 (27%) died without transplantation, and 23 (8%) underwent liver transplantation; 71% were alive at 3 weeks. Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity far exceeded other causes of ALF in the US, with the annual proportion rising from 28% in 1998 to 51% in 2003.

In the unintentional group, 38% took ≥2 acetaminophen preparations simultaneously and 63% used narcotic-containing compounds; 81% took acetaminophen and/or other analgesics for acute or chronic pain. Susceptible patients had concomitant depression, chronic pain, and alcohol or narcotic use. Outcomes: 65% survived, 27% died without transplantation, 8% transplanted, 71% alive at 3 weeks. Annual percentage of acetaminophen-related ALF rose from 28% (1998) to 51% (2003). Paper notes acetaminophen causes severe hepatic necrosis leading to ALF after suicidal overdoses and after unintentional daily doses exceeding 4 g/day recommendations; N-acetylcysteine can prevent hepatic injury if given within 12 hours of a single ingestion.

Susceptible patients include those with chronic pain, depression, and substance abuse, including alcohol. The paper frames acetaminophen as a preventable cause of ALF.

Unintentional overdose is the leading form of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity, with suicidal ingestions also relevant. Overall transplant-free survival among acetaminophen subjects was 65%; King's college criteria at admission were inaccurate in predicting outcome and APACHE II was more accurate. UK legislative restrictions on acetaminophen sales reduced deaths and transplants from acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed features of hepatocellular toxicity and hepatic encephalopathy one week after the last dose of azithromycin, with markedly elevated ALT, AST, ALP and serum ammonia, elevated conjugated bilirubin and prolonged prothrombin time suggestive of subfulminant or fulminant necrosis. The diagnosis of azithromycin-induced hepatotoxicity was based on the temporal relationship between drug intake and symptom onset and the absence of other causes of liver disease; the Naranjo probability scale (score 6) and WHO causality assessment scale indicated azithromycin as the probable/likely cause of the drug-associated hepatocellular toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo probability scale score 6 and WHO causality assessment indicated probable/likely causation. Hepatocellular toxicity with hepatic encephalopathy one week after the last dose; markedly elevated ALT, AST, ALP and serum ammonia, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged PT, suggestive of subfulminant/fulminant necrosis; normal serum LDH and no other organ dysfunction; ischemic hepatitis deemed unlikely. The discussion additionally notes (review assertion) that azithromycin has a long half-life with liver concentrations exceeding serum levels ~50-fold, with early injury possibly hypersensitivity-mediated and rare reported cases of cholestatic hepatitis and severe iatrogenic hepatitis requiring hepatic transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient who became jaundiced and febrile during malaria chemoprophylaxis, chloroguanide (proguanil) was stopped; a toxic reaction to chloroguanide was considered the most likely cause of the clinical presentation. Because liver enzymes and bilirubin remained elevated, a liver biopsy was performed 3 weeks after admission and showed hepatitis with periportal infiltrates consisting mainly of lymphocytes and eosinophils, indicative of drug-induced hepatitis. Other causes (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, leptospirosis, malaria, Salmonella, parasites) were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient presenting with fever to 39.0 °C, chills, vomiting, mild abdominal cramp, anorexia and jaundice (total bilirubin 4.4 mg/dL, conjugated 3.1 mg/dL; ALT 58 rising to 183 U/L, AST 33 to 45 U/L, GGT 96 U/L, ALP 158 U/L). Differential diagnosis initially considered either a toxic reaction to chloroguanide or a bile-duct infection (e.g., Salmonella); infection was excluded by negative blood/stool cultures, parasite examination, and serology (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, leptospirosis, malaria). Chloroguanide was stopped and ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily given for 6 days; patient became afebrile within 3 days, bilirubin normalized after 2 months and aminotransferases after 4 months. Liver biopsy (3 weeks after admission) showed hepatitis with periportal lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates indicative of drug-induced hepatitis. Reported as an adverse effect not previously described. Systemic involvement (fever, chills, eosinophilic infiltrate) fits the idiosyncratic pattern discussed in the paper. Patient had a history of hepatitis in 1980 probably due to ketoconazole and consumed 2-4 glasses of beer/wine weekly.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient with Graves' disease treated with carbimazole, both the minor effects and the major adverse effects (agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity) were reported to be probably related to the carbimazole therapy by the Naranjo probability scale. The patient developed cholestatic jaundice with hepatocellular damage that resolved and liver enzymes normalized after carbimazole was withdrawn.
raw_record.extra_details: Graves' disease/hyperthyroidism; carbimazole 30 mg/day started at day -21 and stopped at day 0. Hepatic injury presented as cholestatic jaundice (total bilirubin up to 28.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin up to 23.8 mg/dL) complicated by hepatocellular damage (ALT up to 164 U/L, AST up to 225 U/L); referred to as severe hepatotoxicity with significant cholestatic enzyme elevations and moderate aminotransferase elevations. Naranjo probability scale = probable. Other causes excluded (normal hepatobiliary ultrasound; negative IgM for EBV, CMV, VZV, HSV). No liver biopsy performed; clinical evolution favorable with normalization of liver enzymes. Co-managed for coexisting agranulocytosis (WBC 0 granulocytes) with G-CSF; propranolol 160 mg/day and 131I ablation started day 8 with enzyme/granulocyte recovery despite continued propranolol, argued against interaction. The authors concluded cholestatic jaundice and secondary hepatocellular damage were attributable to carbimazole.

raw_record.support_text: Our patient developed agranulocytosis and severe mixed hepatotoxicity following the administration of the thionamide drug carbimazole, which had been administered for the treatment of Graves' disease. Following withdrawal of the drug, ablation of the thyroid with ¹³¹I, and treatment with G-CSF followed by standard care, a favorable outcome was achieved, and clinicians need awareness of these potentially fatal adverse effects. The possibility that carbimazole induced these undesirable effects was considered 'probable' based on the Naranjo probability scale.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: 37-year-old woman with severe hyperthyroidism due to Graves' disease; developed severe mixed hepatotoxicity with cholestatic jaundice that reversed after drug withdrawal, alongside agranulocytosis and minor side effects (pruritus, skin rash, urticaria, fever, arthralgia). Causality rated 'probable' on the Naranjo probability scale. Treated with thyroid ablation using ¹³¹I and G-CSF; agranulocytosis treated with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor following bone marrow biopsy. Authors note these are rare side effects often related to patient age and administered dose, and describe them as potentially fatal.

The symptoms appeared to resolve after carbimazole was discontinued, and thyroid ablation with I-131 was successfully performed since continued antithyroid drug medical therapy was not possible. The agranulocytosis confirmed by bone marrow biopsy was treated with granulocyte growth factor.

raw_record.support_text: In January 2006, three reported cases of severe telithromycin hepatotoxicity prompted an FDA label revision warning of potential severe liver injury. The cases developed jaundice and elevated liver enzymes within 2-7 days of starting telithromycin; one had enzymes >10x ULN that normalized within 8 weeks, a second required orthotopic liver transplantation, and a third died. Three additional cases were reported to FDA Medwatch. An editorial compared the reported acute liver failure rate with telithromycin as greater than trovafloxacin and troglitazone and similar to bromfenac. FDA removed bronchitis and sinusitis indications in February 2007.

Rechallenge: 6 of 12 subjects developed recurrent transaminitis within 1-4 days of re-exposure; 4 of 5 rechallenged off steroids recurred (grade 2,1; grade 3,2; grade 4,1) vs 2 of 7 rechallenged on steroids. 16 subjects (67%) received steroids for transaminitis. Higher day-28 CCL-3 and CCL-4 were associated with hepatotoxicity; lower Treg percentages were associated with on-drug toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib, an oral small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting ALK, ROS1 and MET, is the FDA-approved first-line treatment for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer. Nearly 0.1% of crizotinib-treated patients experienced fatal hepatotoxicity across clinical trials. Per FDA adverse events, 11.2% and 5.7% of patients had ALT and AST elevations >5x ULN, respectively, after crizotinib treatment, and 1.0% required permanent discontinuation due to elevated transaminases, generally within the first 2 months. A reported case involved a 62-year-old patient who presented with acute liver failure after 24 days of crizotinib therapy and died after 40 days despite crizotinib discontinuation and intensive supportive therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: In ALK-positive NSCLC therapeutic use. Nearly 0.1% fatal hepatotoxicity across clinical trials; FDA adverse events showed 11.2% ALT and 5.7% AST elevations >5x ULN; 1.0% permanent discontinuation due to elevated transaminases, generally within the first 2 months of treatment. Case: 62-year-old patient with acute liver failure after 24 days of crizotinib therapy, died after 40 days despite discontinuation and intensive supportive therapy (van Geel et al., 2016). Cell-based mechanistic work in HL-7702 and human primary hepatocytes showed crizotinib-induced hepatocyte apoptosis independent of ALK/ROS1/MET involving MMP decrease, DNA damage and ROS generation, stated as consistent with clinical cases.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib received FDA accelerated approval for ALK-positive NSCLC in August 2011. A meta-analysis of clinical trials showed the dose had to be reduced or treatment discontinued in 6.5% of patients because of toxicity, and the most clinically significant toxicities of crizotinib included hepatotoxicity. One case of fatal drug-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in a crizotinib-treated patient following closure of the FDA safety database, prompting investigation of the mechanism of crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity. The paper presents this as established human hepatotoxicity and studies its mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: ALK-positive NSCLC. A meta-analysis of clinical trials reported crizotinib dose reduction or treatment discontinuation in 6.5% of patients because of toxicity. Severe hepatotoxicity is observed with most receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors in clinical applications. One case of fatal drug-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in a crizotinib-treated patient after the FDA safety database closed. The paper's mechanistic work (HL-7702 cells and human primary hepatocytes) indicates ALK, ROS1 and MET are not targets of crizotinib-induced hepatocyte death/apoptosis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case of severe Isoniazid (INH)-induced drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis in a 62-year-old man, characterized by markedly elevated transaminases and profound hyperbilirubinemia, with liver biopsy showing severe acute hepatitis with interface hepatitis, lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, and multiple foci of lobular confluent necrosis. INH discontinuation alone proved insufficient, but prednisone therapy led to rapid clinical improvement and normalization of liver biochemistries over 3 months. The authors also note that liver injury from INH occurs in up to 20% of patients, about 1% develop severe injury, and INH ranks among leading causes of DILI-related acute liver failure in the United States.

Response to prednisone with normalization over 3 months. Background: INH liver injury occurs in up to 20% of patients (80% asymptomatic/minor transaminase elevations resolving on drug removal), severe injury in ~1%, and INH ranks among leading causes of DILI-related acute liver failure in the US.

raw_record.support_text: In a patient on isoniazid (INH), a liver biopsy revealed severe acute hepatitis with features suggestive of drug-induced immune-mediated injury, including prominent interface hepatitis, a lymphoplasmacytic portal infiltrate, and multiple foci of lobular confluent necrosis. Given the severity and progressive course despite INH discontinuation and a low TB reactivation risk, the patient was started on prednisone for presumed INH-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis. Two months after starting INH he had developed jaundice, markedly elevated transaminases (AST 2126 U/L, ALT 2617 U/L), hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 15.7 mg/dL) and mild coagulopathy (INR 1.4), and his liver tests met DILI Network grade 3 severity criteria; he improved on prednisone and had normalized liver enzymes at 6-month follow-up.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper frames this as drug-induced autoimmune-like hepatitis (DI-ALH), a subgroup of DILI recognized by AASLD Practice Guidance and an expert group report ('liver injury with laboratory or/and histological evidence of autoimmunity'). Latency was 2 months after starting INH; presentation included jaundice, RUQ pain, fatigue, ALT 2617 U/L, AST 2126 U/L, total bilirubin 15.7 mg/dL, INR 1.4; on readmission liver injury met DILI Network grade 3 severity criteria. Biopsy showed interface hepatitis, lymphoplasmacytic portal infiltrate, lobular confluent necrosis, and no fibrosis on trichrome. Viral hepatitis, CMV, EBV and autoimmune (ANA, ASMA) markers were negative. Patient was treated with prednisone 40 mg daily with tapering over 1 month, with no recurrence and normal enzymes at 6-month follow-up. INH was discontinued (dechallenge) with worsening before steroid therapy. Indication was latent TB treatment/prophylaxis; no TB reactivation occurred.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old male patient developed elevated transaminases in 1999 during phenprocoumon treatment for deep vein thrombosis; the elevation fully resolved after phenprocoumon was stopped, and non-phenprocoumon causes were excluded. After re-prescription in 2003 following a new thrombosis, phenprocoumon again caused a transaminase rise that progressed to cholestatic hepatitis and fulminant liver failure, requiring liver transplantation, with subsequent good graft function under immunosuppression. Enoxaparin (LMWH) was then chosen for ongoing anticoagulation.

raw_record.support_text: This discussion of anticoagulation options states that hepatotoxicity is a very rare complication of coumarin therapy and documents liver toxicity reported for Warfarin, Phenprocoumon, and Acenocoumarol. Coumarin-induced liver damage frequently resembles viral hepatitis and can present with cholestasis, chronic aggressive hepatitis, subacute parenchymal inflammation, cirrhotic transformation, and cytolytic or necrotizing reactions; liver explants showed massive hepatocellular necrosis or complete fine-nodular cirrhosis with cholestasis and diffuse pericholangitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Cumarin-induced hepatotoxicity reported since the 1960s-70s; in a systematic evaluation of 10 coumarin-induced hepatotoxic reactions 4 patients had abnormal transaminases 2-7 days after therapy start while 6 required inpatient care with latencies from 10 days, 10 weeks, up to 6 years. Schimanski et al. reported 8 phenprocoumon patients with liver insufficiency, 3 with (sub)acute liver failure, the rest recovering after switch to another coumarin/heparin. Phenotypes attributed include cholestasis, chronic aggressive hepatitis, subacute inflammation with parenchymal destruction, cirrhotic remodeling, cytolytic and necrotizing reactions, and cholestasis with diffuse pericholangitis in explants; improvement after drug withdrawal is typical. A described case: rapid recurrence of hepatitis after phenprocoumon re-exposure (positive antinuclear and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies, lacking hypergammaglobulinemia) and a 56-year-old woman with hepatitis after 8 months of phenprocoumon.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of a 60-year-old male with MET exon 14-mutated non-small cell lung cancer who developed grade 4 liver injury after starting the oral MET-kinase inhibitor capmatinib. The injury did not respond to capmatinib discontinuation, but eventually responded to N-acetyl cysteine plus ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol) therapy, and the paper frames the case as capmatinib-induced hepatotoxicity with scarce published data on its management.
raw_record.extra_details: Grade 4 hepatotoxicity in a 60-year-old male NSCLC patient with MET exon 14 skipping mutation. Supportive trial data from the GEOMETRY mono-1 study (373 patients, 400 mg twice daily) reported ALT/AST elevation in 14% of patients, about half (7%) grade 3 or 4 (defined as >5x and >20x ULN), with median time to onset of grade 3+ ALT/AST elevation of 1.8 months (range 0.5-46.4 months). FDA label (Tabrecta) instructs holding or permanently discontinuing capmatinib for grade 3 or 4 ALT/AST elevation with or without bilirubin elevation. Injury did not improve with drug discontinuation but showed significant improvement one day after N-acetyl cysteine plus ursodeoxycholic acid, near-resolution in two months. Mechanism relevant to MET/HGFR pathway.

raw_record.support_text: Applying the Karch-Lasagna algorithm and Paris Consensus criteria, the causal relationship between the liver injury in this 56-year-old woman and treatment with tamoxifen is classified as probable, based on a compatible chronological relationship between drug administration and altered liver enzymes, absence of other potential causes of liver disease (alcohol, prior chronic hepatopathy, hepatotropic viruses), and persistence of the liver changes when all other medications except tamoxifen were withdrawn. The probability was not upgraded to 'definite' because there are no data on enzyme changes after tamoxifen discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: 56-year-old woman treated with oral tamoxifen 10 mg/12 h since 1996 after right mastectomy for intracystic papillary carcinoma. Presented with right hypochondrial pain, vomiting, coluria and slight mucosal jaundice; liver biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis with marked portal inflammation and moderate macrovesicular steatosis. Lab values: total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl, AST 199 U/l, ALT 184 U/l; later GGT 331 U/l and alkaline phosphatase 483 U/l. No alcohol intake or blood transfusions; hepatitis B surface antigen, HCV, ANA, AMA, anti-smooth muscle and ANCA all negative. Other potential hepatotoxic drugs (fluvastatin, lansoprazole, ofloxacin, omeprazole, metamizole) were withdrawn and re-introduced without any change in liver values, supporting tamoxifen as the cause. Biopsy findings concordant with a chronic hepatitis resembling a previously published case of tamoxifen hepatotoxicity; steatosis component and active chronic hepatitis pattern imply a mixed mechanism of metabolic idiosyncrasy and autoimmune phenomena. Discussion notes that published tamoxifen hepatotoxicity cases show two predominant injury patterns: cholestasis with or without cytolysis and steatohepatitis, including cholestatic jaundice without cytolysis, cholestasis with cytolysis, a case of hepatic peliosis, a case of fatty liver with liver failure and death, and several cases of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis; additional cases collected by pharmacovigilance systems with little detail.

raw_record.support_text: Azathioprine, an immunosuppressant used for myasthenia gravis, can cause hepatotoxicity. The paper presents a 47-year-old man on azathioprine for 1 year who developed painless jaundice; azathioprine was discontinued due to potential acute liver failure secondary to azathioprine toxicity, and a liver biopsy showing drug-induced liver injury with high serum 6-methylmercaptopurine nucleotide confirmed azathioprine-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The case report describes a patient hospitalized with cholestatic jaundice and acute liver failure taking azathioprine; azathioprine was not restarted and AST/ALT improved to 86/83 U/L with total bilirubin 14.2 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 10.2 mg/dL. Measurement of azathioprine metabolites confirmed the diagnosis of azathioprine-induced liver toxicity: serum 6-MMPN was 20 202 pmole/8×10^8 RBC (normal <5700), while 6-TGN was within normal range. The discussion attributes the patient's acute liver failure to azathioprine-induced toxicity based on improvement after drug cessation, biopsy findings suggestive of drug-induced injury, and markedly elevated 6-MMPN.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: abrupt onset of cholestatic jaundice 1 year after azathioprine initiation; four-day hospitalization; on admission and during stay AST/ALT improved to 86/83 U/L, total bilirubin 14.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 10.2 mg/dL; liver biopsy showed cholestasis with bile plugging plus portal pericholangitis and hepatocellular injury; 6-MMPN 20 202 pmole/8x10^8 RBC (normal <5700) confirmed diagnosis, 6-TGN within normal range; complete recovery of all laboratory values at 1-, 2- and 3-month follow-up. Discussion context: azathioprine used as immunosuppressant for organ rejection and autoimmune disease; mean annual azathioprine-induced liver injury rate ~1.4%; hepatotoxicity attributed to glutathione depletion, mitochondrial injury, ATP depletion and hepatocyte necrosis; three latency syndromes described (hypersensitivity, idiosyncratic cholestatic reaction, endothelial cell injury causing portal hypertension/veno-occlusive disease); Pol et al reported 21 patients with azathioprine-induced hepatitis, mean time to presentation 41 months (range 4-143 months); 6-MMPN is the metabolite implicated in hepatotoxicity, 6-TGN the metabolite for therapeutic efficacy.

raw_record.support_text: The first reports that acetaminophen (APAP) is hepatotoxic were published in 1966. Boyd and Bereczky found that acute doses of APAP in rats produced hepatotoxicity, while Davidson and Eastham reported two individuals who developed hepatotoxicity following APAP overdose; both died on the third day after overdose, with microscopic examination revealing acute fulminating centrilobular hepatic necrosis extending through midzonal to periportal areas, with hepatocyte eosinophilic degeneration, nuclear pyknosis, vacuolization, and mild polymorphonuclear leukocytic infiltration. Additional overdose reports followed (Thomson and Prescott 1966; Rose 1969; Proudfoot and Wright 1970; Boyer and Rouff 1971; Prescott et al. 1971), describing nausea/vomiting, right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain, dramatic rises in circulating ALT, AST and LDH, mild hyperbilirubinemia, increased prothrombin time, and APAP half-life greater than four hours, with hepatic coma when half-life exceeded 12 hours.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatotoxicity occurred following acute acetaminophen overdose, and the two initially reported patients died on the third day after overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: First human overdose reports date from 1966 (Boyd and Bereczky 1966; Davidson and Eastham 1966). Necrosis was centrilobular extending through midzonal to periportal areas, with eosinophilic degeneration, pyknosis, vacuolization, and mild polymorphonuclear leukocytic infiltration. Clinical features (Boyer and Rouff 1971): nausea/vomiting within 2-3 h, upper-right-quadrant abdominal pain, liver dysfunction within ~24 h peaking at 4 days. Biochemistry (Prescott et al. 1971): dramatic ALT, AST, LDH increases; mild hyperbilirubinemia; increased prothrombin time; APAP half-life >4 h, with hepatic coma when half-life >12 h. Subsequent overdose reports: Thomson and Prescott 1966; Rose 1969; Proudfoot and Wright 1970; Boyer and Rouff 1971; Prescott et al. 1971. The 1966 Boyd and Bereczky finding of acute APAP hepatotoxicity in rats is supportive animal evidence.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews that acetaminophen (APAP) overdose causes hepatotoxicity in humans. Biomarkers GLDH and mtDNA were elevated in APAP overdose patients with liver injury (peak ALT ≥ 1000 U/L), nuclear DNA fragments were reported in plasma after APAP overdose, and these serum values are at least modestly predictive of death in APAP-induced acute liver failure patients. The authors conclude the mechanisms of APAP-induced liver injury are similar in humans and mice.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose in humans causes mitochondrial damage and DNA fragmentation. Elevated biomarkers GLDH and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) seen in overdose patients with liver injury (peak ALT ≥ 1000 U/L); nuclear DNA fragments reported in plasma after overdose; long-chain acylcarnitine values higher in blood from patients with delayed NAC treatment; GLDH, mtDNA, and nuclear DNA fragment serum values are at least modestly predictive of death in APAP-induced acute liver failure patients; apoptosis (caspase 3) not a major cell-death mechanism in humans. In cultured human hepatocytes (HepaRG, fresh PHH), APAP toxicity involves GSH depletion, protein binding, mitochondrial depolarization and oxidative stress preceding cell death, with JNK activation in PHH; these cellular findings support the human mechanism but are not independent evidence.

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer was started on fulvestrant and ribociclib (600 mg daily); liver enzymes and function were normal with no hepatic metastasis at initiation. After 8 weeks she developed rising liver transaminases (initially Grade 1, rapidly to Grade 4) and Grade 3 bilirubin elevations. Viral serology, autoimmune enzymes and iron overload work-up were negative; MRI showed acute hepatitis without metastases. Ribociclib was discontinued with no improvement, and a liver biopsy was 'compatible with drug-induced acute fulminant toxic hepatitis'. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale score was 7, and the patient recovered fully with 1 mg/kg prednisolone. The authors report this as a first case of ribociclib-induced acute fulminant hepatitis diagnosed by liver biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: Between 1992 and 2008, 663 patients were admitted with paracetamol-induced severe liver injury, of whom 161 (24.3%) had taken a staggered overdose. Staggered overdose patients were more likely to be encephalopathic on admission and had higher mortality than single time point overdoses (37.3% vs. 27.8%, P=0.025), though the overdose pattern did not independently predict death. The King's College poor prognostic criteria had reduced sensitivity (77.6, 95% CI 70.8-81.5) for this overdose pattern; delayed presentation beyond 24 h post overdose was independently associated with death/liver transplantation (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.23-4.12, P=0.009).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; staggered repeat supratherapeutic ingestion pattern (frequently for pain relief) compared with single time point overdose; delayed hospital presentation beyond 24 h independently associated with death/liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning described as the major cause of severe acute hepatotoxicity and the commonest cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the UK. Cohort of 663 patients admitted with paracetamol-induced severe liver injury (1992-2008); 161 (24.3%) staggered overdose. Staggered overdose patients were older and more likely to abuse alcohol, had lower total ingested doses and lower admission serum ALT, but more encephalopathy, renal replacement therapy or mechanical ventilation. Mortality 37.3% (staggered) vs 27.8% (single time point), P=0.025; stagger pattern did not independently predict death. King's College poor prognostic criteria sensitivity 77.6 (95% CI 70.8-81.5) for staggered pattern. Of 396/450 single time point overdoses, 178 (44.9%) presented >24 h; delayed presentation independently associated with death/liver transplantation (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.23-4.12, P=0.009). The paper studies a cohort of 663 paracetamol overdose patients (161 staggered, 450 single time point, plus others) who developed acute severe liver injury, and reports outcomes including development of hepatic encephalopathy, need for renal replacement therapy/mechanical ventilation, King's College criteria fulfillment, spontaneous survival, and death/OLT.

raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 663 paracetamol overdose patients (n=450 single time point, n=161 staggering, remainder other patterns). Outcomes compared by pattern: spontaneous survival 62.7% in staggered vs 72.4% in single time point (P=0.025); encephalopathy developed in 55.9% (staggered) vs 46.9% (single time point); death or liver transplantation (OLT considered equivalent to death) analyzed; 47.2% of those presenting >24 h required mechanical ventilation and 39.9% required renal replacement therapy; 33.7% of >24 h presenters met King's College criteria; transplanted counts range 5.1-10.7%. Independent predictors of death/OLT included encephalopathy on admission, increased prothrombin time, leukocytosis, renal impairment, and hypoalbuminaemia (staggered cohort) and older age (single time point cohort). Admission ALT concentrations ~8000 IU/L in all groups.

raw_record.support_text: Although disopyramide has fewer gastrointestinal side effects, cases of hepatotoxicity have been reported, as well as hepatic ischemia secondary to cardiac failure by passive congestion. Rarely, disopyramide can cause cholestatic jaundice that in most cases appears within the first week of taking the medication and generally resolves promptly on discontinuation. A case of severe hepatocellular toxicity with disseminated intravascular coagulation was reported, which improved after discontinuation of disopyramide.
raw_record.extra_details: Comparison of disopyramide-induced hepatotoxicity cases (Scheinman et al. two cases: hepatic necrosis with congestion on biopsy, elevated AST/ALT/LDH, improved on day six after discontinuation, recurrence of symptoms on rechallenge with the drug switched to procainamide; second case improved with diuresis, liver enzymes normalized, and recurred on rechallenge). Doody case: severe hepatocellular toxicity with disseminated intravascular coagulation (prolonged PT, elevated fibrin split products), liver enzymes and functions improved 14 days after discontinuation. Barkins et al. case: jaundice and abnormal liver enzymes after one week, prompt clinical resolution on discontinuation. Also noted hepatic ischemia secondary to cardiac failure/passive congestion (indirect mechanism) and negative inotropic effect worsening heart failure. Generally cholestatic jaundice appears within first week.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman undergoing aftercare for chronic alcoholism (liver function tests normal at baseline) was started on disulfiram 250 mg daily; she took no medication except vitamin B1. Jaundice appeared 13 days after treatment onset, and acute liver failure was diagnosed on day 18 after a total disulfiram dose of 4.5 g (Quick value <10%, bilirubin 460 µmol/l, GPT 5099 U/l, GOT 4142 U/l) together with early renal failure (creatinine 300 µmol/l). Viral infection, autoimmune hepatitis and metabolic liver disease were excluded, and toxicology tests were negative. The patient died 25 days after starting disulfiram in hepatic coma from fulminant hepatitis with hepatorenal syndrome; biopsy and autopsy showed acute hepatic dystrophy without cirrhosis. The temporal relationship, exclusion of other causes, and histology compatible with chemical-toxic hepatitis indicated a disulfiram-induced fulminant hepatitis. The authors state that disulfiram hepatotoxicity is a very rare idiosyncratic reaction that is often fatal.

raw_record.support_text: Ein 49-jährige Frau starb an den Folgen einer fulminanten Hepatitis, die mit größter Wahrscheinlichkeit durch Disulfiram induziert worden war. Nach einjähriger stationärer Alkoholentziehungskur und normalen Leberwerten wurde eine Disulfiramtherapie in einer Dosierung von 250 mg/d eingeleitet; nach 13 Tagen trat ein Ikterus auf und nach 18 Tagen (Gesamtdosis 4,5 g) wurde ein akutes Leberversagen diagnostiziert. Die Patientin starb 25 Tage nach Therapiebeginn im Coma hepaticum mit hepatorenalem Syndrom. Die Autopsie ergab eine akute Leberdystrophie ohne Zirrhose mit Totalnekrose der Leber und dicht gelagerten entzündlichen Infiltraten mit zahlreichen eosinophilen Granulozyten, die als Hinweis auf eine medikamentös induzierte Hepatitis gewertet wurden. Der zeitliche Zusammenhang, der Ausschluss anderer Ursachen und die Leberhistologie sprechen für eine Disulfiram-induzierte fulminante Hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP), an over-the-counter drug sold in billions of units annually in North America, is a powerful dose-related toxin. Over the past 40 years APAP toxicity has accounted for 46% of all acute liver failure (ALF) in the United States and between 40% and 70% of all cases in Great Britain and Europe. APAP toxicity dwarfs the number of ALF cases resulting from all prescription drugs combined.

raw_record.extra_details: APAP toxicity accounted for 46% of ALF cases in the US (registry data 1998-2019, total 2614 enrolled patients) and 40-70% of ALF cases in Great Britain/Europe; described features include very high aminotransferases, mild hyperbilirubinemia, hypoglycemia, centrilobular necrosis, and rapid-onset illness. Spontaneous/transplant-free survival from APAP ALF is approximately 70%, and deaths from this etiology are almost double those from other xenobiotics. Historical: first case reports associating paracetamol with severe liver injury and fatal outcomes appeared in 1966; by 1970 paracetamol was the most frequently used suicidal agent in the UK (report of 41 cases); first North American case reported by Boyer and Rouff in 1971.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes 3 patients who developed signs of liver disease shortly after starting cimetidine, plus 4 previously published cases of cimetidine-induced liver injury. In the 3 new patients the link between cimetidine and liver injury was rated 'probable' according to the diagnostic criteria of Orlandi, in view of the absence of rechallenge confirmation. Because hepatic injury caused by cimetidine is very rare, it is designated as an idiosyncratic response to the drug, involving both metabolic idiosyncrasy from production of toxic metabolites and hypersensitivity in different patients.

raw_record.extra_details: 7 patients total (3 new cases plus 4 published cases of Villeneuve and Warner, Züchner, Lorenzini et al., and Ruiz del Arbol et al.). Latency period ranged from 2 to 120 days (7-20 days in the new cases). Histology included centrilobular/centrolobular (zone 3) confluent necrosis, cholangiolitis, cholestasis, steatosis, siderosis, and mononuclear portal inflammation. Case 2 progressed to acute liver failure. Biochemical abnormalities resolved within the first month after withdrawal in all except the Ruiz del Arbol patient (nearly 3 months). Rechallenge reproduced liver dysfunction in the 4 previously described patients. Recurrence of the rash with progressively shorter intervals on rechallenge and rash with musculoskeletal pain in Lorenzini's patient are suggestive of hypersensitivity-related injury; the centrilobular necrosis pattern is suggestive of toxic-metabolite-dependent injury via cytochrome P450 metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with Fingolimod developed acute liver failure. Hepatic encephalopathy developed on the 7th day of follow-up, and a cadaveric liver transplant was performed on the 9th day, 44 days after initiation of Fingolimod treatment. Massive necrosis was detected in the pathological examination of the explanted liver.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of fingolimod (Gilenya)-treated MS patient. Duration of treatment 15 days; onset of symptoms on 12th day; laboratory abnormalities on 14th day; R ratio 11.4 (hepatocellular pattern) at first application; modified RUCAM +8 (Probable); severity grade 5+ (Fatal). Initial labs: ALT 517 U/L, AST 646 U/L, total bilirubin 36.7 mg/dL, INR 3.7, creatinine 0.66 mg/dL. Hepatic encephalopathy developed on day 7; cadaveric liver transplant on day 9 (44 days after therapy initiation); explant pathology showed massive necrosis with bile duct proliferation and perivascular connective tissue. Patient survived and complies with liver transplant outpatient follow-up. Therapeutic plasmapheresis was performed; patient had not received steroids before transplant.

raw_record.support_text: In troglitazone-induced liver damage cases, the review describes a liver biopsy showing diffuse necrosis of hepatocytes with bridging necrosis and regenerating hepatocytes, with therapeutic help the patient improved over 3 months, whereas a liver failure case autopsy showed extensive hepatocyte necrosis in the centrilobular region and a lack of regenerative activity, resulting in death. The paper attributes these outcomes to troglitazone-mediated idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity in diabetic patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Diabetic patients; discussion framed around idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity in diabetes.
raw_record.extra_details: Marketing and clinical use of troglitazone were discontinued due to hepatotoxicity. Includes a recovering subfulminant-liver-injury case with hepatocyte regrowth (Gitlin et al., 1998) and a fatal case with centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis and absent regenerative activity (Fukano et al., 2000). No association found between age and susceptibility to troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity (Watkins and Whitcomb, 1998).

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old previously healthy man who took sildenafil 50 mg 1 month before symptom onset was diagnosed, on the basis of criteria for drug-induced liver disorders and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, with probable sildenafil-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity. He used no other medications, and his laboratory values improved without treatment, returning to normal 4 months after onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Presenting with jaundice, pruritus, and malaise. Labs: AST 42 IU/l, ALT 64 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 476 IU/l, total bilirubin 8.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 6.3 mg/dl, albumin 3.6 g/dl, eosinophils 2.8%. Liver biopsy showed marked intrahepatic cholestasis with bile stasis in canaliculi around the peripheral area and minimal portal necroinflammation. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune, and obstructive etiologies excluded. Symptom onset about 1 month after a single 50 mg dose; recovered without treatment by 4 months.

raw_record.support_text: A series of 67 excessive-drinker patients who developed hepatitis after taking paracetamol at therapeutic doses was compared with 94 previously reported cases; 60% of patients had taken less than 6 g/day. Excessive drinkers showed severe cytolysis with peak transaminases above 3000 UI/L and ASAT/ALAT ratio greater than 1, moderate hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged Quick time and hypoglycemia; histology, when available, showed typical zone 3 acinar necrosis. Prognosis was poor with 20% mortality, supporting the hypothesis of exacerbated paracetamol toxicity at therapeutic doses in excessive drinkers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Excessive-drinker (chronic alcohol) population; therapeutic dosing; background of heavy alcohol consumption. Acute alcohol consumption can transiently be protective, whereas chronic alcoholism exacerbates paracetamol hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: 60% of the 67 patients took <6 g/day paracetamol; peak transaminase >3000 UI/L with ASAT/ALAT >1, moderate hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged prothrombin time, hypoglycemia; histology showed zone 3 acinar necrosis (CYP-rich zone with highest reactive metabolite concentrations); mortality 20%, close to that of suicidal massive paracetamol ingestion. A separate analysis of two studies including 854 paracetamol-hepatitis patients showed more severe injury in excessive drinkers: lower prothrombin nadir (13% vs 28%), higher transaminases (6717 vs 3818 UI/L), creatinine (248 vs 86 µmol/L) and bilirubin (118 vs 30 µmol/L), hepatic encephalopathy in 46% vs 9.6%, and death or emergency transplantation in 26% vs 5.3%.

raw_record.support_text: Pillans et al. report three women who developed severe hepatotoxicity with lumiracoxib, a recently introduced COX-2 inhibitor, all with histologic evidence of significant hepatocellular necrosis. One patient died from acute liver failure, another needed a liver transplant. Five further cases have been reported to the Australian TGA, of which two patients died and two underwent liver transplantation. Drug dose or duration of use was not predictive of liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Three reported index cases, all with significant histologic hepatocellular necrosis; one died from acute liver failure, one required liver transplant. Five additional cases reported to the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration, with two deaths and two liver transplants. Anti-nuclear antibodies noted in all three cases. GWAS of 41 lumiracoxib-induced liver injury cases vs 176 exposed controls found association with HLA class II markers; HLA-DQA1*0102 had highest sensitivity (73.6%). Health regulators called for withdrawal of lumiracoxib from clinical use. Structurally similar to diclofenac, sharing proclivity for forming reactive hepatotoxic metabolites and glutathione adducts.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed acute liver injury a day following initiation of IV levofloxacin therapy. Laboratory values included ALT of 4525 (ULN 49) and ALP of 52 (ULN 107), yielding an R-factor of 190, indicating a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury. The paper concludes this is a case of quinolone-induced acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: IV levofloxacin started on Day 3 and discontinued immediately upon recognition of acute liver failure on Day 4. Peak labs on Day 4: AST 9334 U/L, ALT 4525 U/L, PT 24.6 s, INR 2.22, ammonia 157 umol/L, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL; ALP remained near normal (52 U/L on Day 4). R-factor of 190 calculated from ALT/ULN vs ALP/ULN. Patient presented with Grade III hepatic encephalopathy and coagulopathy. Notable improvement in liver function testing in the days following discontinuation with supportive care, supporting quinolone-induced ALF. Short latency (injury one day after initiation), consistent with fluoroquinolone hepatic injury. Mechanism described as not clear; severity ranges from transient mild LFT elevation to ALF.
