raw_record.support_text: A review compilation of case reports attributes drug-induced liver injury to ciprofloxacin in a range of presentations, including hepatocellular injury, mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular injury, cholestatic injury, acute hepatitis, delayed and prolonged cholestatic hepatitis with ductopenia, and acute hepatitis with multisystem failure. Diagnoses were expressed as 'hepatocellular injury associated with ciprofloxacin', 'mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular injury probably associated with ciprofloxacin', and 'acute hepatitis induced by ciprofloxacin'. Outcomes ranged up to acute liver failure with one patient dying of liver failure and one patient being transplanted.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: General therapeutic use in adults; in one case causality was attributed to ciprofloxacin and/or amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (unresolved co-suspect), and some cases involved co-treatment (e.g., cloxacillin and ceftriaxone, or levofloxacin) or pre-existing conditions (chronic hepatitis B, hemodialysis, Crohn's disease).
raw_record.extra_details: Reported latencies and patterns: hepatocellular injury with ALT 1684 IU/L and bilirubin 21.1 mg/dL after 13.3 days; probable mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular injury (ALT 420, ALP 275, bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL after 4.8 days) and probable mixed injury in another case; hepatocellular injury (ALT 1632, ALP 771, bilirubin 17.1 mg/dL after 5.2 days with rash/fever); cholestatic injury (ALT 413, ALP 891, bilirubin 1.2 after 1.6 days, HSR pneumonitis); cholestatic injury with rash/fever/eosinophilia; acute hepatitis induced by ciprofloxacin in two Turkish cases with ALT up to 500 IU/L after 2 days; cholestatic hepatitis with ductopenia after 6 months (ALT 740, ALP 642, gamma-GTP 3005, bilirubin 5.8); cholestatic jaundice associated with ciprofloxacin; acute hepatitis with multisystem failure (AST 1782, ALT 2144, LDH 3631) with one death from liver failure; vanishing-bile-duct-like severe injury and liver transplantation in another case. Some diagnoses were biopsy-confirmed.

Biochemistry showed total bilirubin 17.2 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 13.1 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 460 IU, AST 120 IU, and ALT 100 IU with negative hepatitis B and C serology. raw_record.support_text: Methyldopa, a centrally acting antihypertensive, was associated with rare but serious hepatotoxic effects. A 31-year-old woman with hypertension developed acute hepatitis with fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes about six weeks after starting methyldopa; viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes were excluded, and liver function normalized after discontinuation with full recovery, supporting DILI. RUCAM scoring gave a score of 9, indicating a 'highly probable' link between methyldopa and the hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used for hypertension, including in pregnancy. Case: 31-year-old woman (class III obesity, asthma). Onset ~6 weeks after start; symptoms fatigue, jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, RUQ pain, malaise, nausea. RUCAM score 9 ('highly probable'). Diagnosed as DILI mimicking autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) clinically and histologically. Viral, autoimmune, metabolic causes excluded; full recovery after dechallenge. Estimated incidence of methyldopa-induced hepatitis 0.1%-0.5%. Mechanism discussed as immune-mediated (reactive metabolites creating neoantigens driving T-cell autoimmune response, autoantibodies, AIH-like histology) and less prominent direct toxic injury via oxidative stress/mitochondrial dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid, a major antitubercular agent introduced in 1952, has been given alone as a prophylactic agent, permitting a precise assessment of its intrinsic hepatotoxicity. The paper establishes that about 10% of patients receiving isoniazid monotherapy develop serum transaminase increases, about 1% develop symptomatic hepatitis (with jaundice, marked transaminase rises possibly exceeding 10x ULN and bilirubin possibly exceeding 200 µmol/L), and a fulminant, encephalopathic course is observed in 5-10% of symptomatic patients (0.05-0.1% of treated patients). Histology shows liver cell necrosis and hepatocellular ballooning with portal inflammatory infiltrates and occasional cholestasis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic isoniazid monotherapy or prophylactic use in general adults; age above 50 years, female gender, delayed onset (≥2 months), continued isoniazid administration after symptom onset, and serum bilirubin above 350 µmol/L associated with higher mortality; daily doses of 10 mg/kg or more (markedly above the usual 5 mg/kg/day) possibly at higher risk of fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: About 10% of treated patients develop serum transaminase increases, mainly within the first 10 weeks, usually resolving spontaneously even with continued therapy. About 1% develop symptomatic hepatitis, typically within the first 3 months but occasionally from 1 week to 12 months; jaundice is the main sign with anorexia, nausea and vomiting, fever/arthralgia/rash usually absent. Fulminant course in 5-10% of symptomatic hepatitis (0.05-0.1% of treated patients) heralded by prolonged prothrombin time and encephalopathy. Histology: liver cell necrosis and hepatocellular degeneration (ballooning), portal inflammatory infiltrates, occasional cholestasis. In large series injury was independent of isoniazid dosage; in 2 series of multidrug-regimen patients with probable isoniazid-induced fulminant liver failure the mean daily dose was markedly above recommended.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of the overt hepatic disease that developed in 114 patients while taking isoniazid for chemoprophylaxis of tuberculosis showed it to be mainly hepatocellular. Severity was manifested by 13 fatalities (12.3%) and by histologic demonstration of submassive necrosis in 9 and massive necrosis in 4 patients; among 20 others, 16 had moderately severe acute hepatocellular injury (4 with a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic pattern) and 4 had chronic hepatic diseases (1 with cirrhosis). The study concluded that the observations offer no support for the view that isoniazid-induced hepatic disease results from hypersensitivity, while considering data supporting hepatotoxic metabolites of isoniazid as responsible for the injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Ischemic/isoniazid-induced hepatic injury assessed in 114 patients from the US Public Health Service surveillance program (13,838 patients enrolled July 1971-Nov 1972, receiving isoniazid 300 mg/day) plus additional reported patients. Hepatotoxicity manifested as submassive necrosis (9) and massive necrosis (4); 16 moderate acute hepatocellular injury (4 mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic), 4 chronic liver disease (1 cirrhosis). Hepatic injury recognized in 15% during month 1 and an additional 31% during month 2; in 54% after 2-11 months. Fatal outcome more likely when injury presented after 2 months, especially with bilirubin >20 mg/100 ml. Case fatality rate significantly higher in black females than in black males or whites of either sex. Premonitory complaints: vague digestive complaints (55%), 'viral'-like complaints (35%); jaundice presenting in 10%; fever and rash in <4%; modest eosinophilia in ~10%. Fever/rash/eosinophilia present in few, offering no support for hypersensitivity mechanism; hepatotoxic metabolites implicated instead.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatitis attributable to rifampicin was defined by either a rise in AST or ALT to both ≥5 × pre-rifampicin baseline and ≥5 × ULN, or a rise in ALT/AST to both ≥3 × baseline and ≥3 × ULN with a concurrent rise in serum bilirubin to both ≥2 × baseline and ≥2 × ULN, together with a RUCAM score of ≥6 ('Probable' or 'Highly probable') for rifampicin hepatitis. In a cohort of 105 patients with chronic liver disease prescribed rifampicin (without concurrent isoniazid, mostly at 300 mg/day) for pruritus by the liver medicine department between 2012 and 2016, five (4.8%) developed this defined hepatitis (Table 1).

raw_record.support_text: Of the 105 patients followed up for a median of 131 days taking rifampicin for pruritus in cholestatic liver disease, 5 (4.8%) patients were diagnosed with hepatitis consistent with rifampicin-induced hepatitis with a RUCAM score ≥ 6. The median time to diagnosis of rifampicin-induced hepatitis was 70 days (range 27-130). Table 2 (supporting paragraphs 25-26) documents RUCAM scores of 6-11 for these patients and notes that one patient (patient 3) received a rechallenge with rifampicin after resolution of initial hepatitis which again provoked significant serum transaminase elevations.

raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 105 (4.8%) patients developed rifampicin-induced hepatitis; RUCAM scores 6, 7, 8, 8, 11 (≥6 = probable); median time to diagnosis 70 days (range 27-130); starting rifampicin dose was 300 mg/day in all 5 affected patients. Three other patients with biochemical DILI criteria were scored as not related to rifampicin (RUCAM -2, -2, -1; alcohol excess, deteriorating PSC, and undiagnosed febrile illness respectively), and one additional patient had rifampicin-associated acute kidney injury without hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: In this real-world cohort of patients treated with rifampicin for pruritus in liver disease, 95% had no concern for hepatotoxicity, but in 5% a rifampicin-induced hepatitis was diagnosed. The observed hepatitis rate of 4.8% is higher than the median 1.1% reported for tuberculosis treatment regimens not containing isoniazid, within the range reported for TB patients treated with both isoniazid and rifampicin, and less than reported rates of 10%-20% for any increase in serum transaminase activity with rifampicin therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients treated for pruritus in the setting of underlying liver disease (primary biliary cholangitis and mixed etiologies); pre-existing liver disease and its effect on biochemistries were accounted for via a variation on the original RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 of 105 patients (4.8%) developed rifampicin-induced hepatitis; causality assessed with a RUCAM variant adjusted for deranged baseline liver biochemistry. Liver biochemistry resolved to baseline after cessation in 4/5 (80%); one patient with primary biliary cholangitis was admitted and biopsy showed bridging fibrosis, patchy predominantly mononuclear infiltrate (lymphocytes and plasma cells), interface hepatitis, and marked confluent parenchymal hepatocellular necrosis, and she was treated with corticosteroids with subsequent resolution to baseline. One patient with acute kidney injury recovered to baseline after cessation. 21 (20.0%) patients received rifampicin dosage uptitration; 2 of the 5 hepatitis patients had uptitration before developing hepatitis. No statistically significant features predicted hepatitis. Findings contrast with controlled trials of rifampicin for pruritus reporting no hepatitis cases, but are consistent with isolated case reports and tuberculosis-therapy literature.

raw_record.support_text: An 80-year-old woman developed drug-induced liver disease with a hepatocellular pattern 30 days after starting clopidogrel following angioplasty and stent placement. Liver failure developed (INR 1.6, low factor V at 4%), and clopidogrel was considered the most probable causative drug given the close temporal relationship, exclusion of alternative causes, and normalization of liver biochemical tests 29 days after discontinuation. The Clinical Diagnostic Scale for Drug Induced Hepatotoxicity gave a high probability diagnosis (score 16). The paper identifies this as the second reported case of clopidogrel-associated hepatitis with acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patient (80-year-old woman); liver injury attributed to clopidogrel monotherapy as the only imputable drug during therapeutic use, with congestive heart failure treated concurrently.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report; second reported case of clopidogrel-associated hepatitis with acute liver failure. Liver tests at diagnosis: AST 388 U/L, ALT 540 U/L, total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL, GGT 209 U/L, ALP 139 U/L, LDH 1412 U/L; liver failure shown by INR 1.6 and factor V 4%. Clinical Diagnostic Scale for Drug Induced Hepatotoxicity score 16 (high probability). Latency 30 days after clopidogrel initiation; normalization 29 days after discontinuation. No rechallenge performed. Biopsy not performed. Alternative causes excluded (negative viral hepatitis serology, negative autoimmune antibodies, normal ultrasound and ERCP); other co-medications (glibenclamide, furosemide, isosorbide dinitrate, acetylsalicylic acid, simvastatin) taken for years without adverse effects. Indication: acute coronary syndrome after angioplasty/stent. Mechanism considered likely non-dose-dependent, via hypersensitivity immune mechanism or metabolic idiosyncratic process.

raw_record.support_text: Only 12 cases of clopidogrel hepatotoxicity are described in the literature, in eight men and four women aged 56-89 who developed liver injury 4 days to 6 months after clopidogrel intake. The liver injury pattern was mainly mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic, though hepatocellular injury and systemic inflammatory response syndrome with hepatic injury also occurred. The reported index case exhibited liver failure documented by factor V and prothrombin time alterations, and a separate recent published case of clopidogrel liver injury had a fatal outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 70-year-old woman with cholestatic hepatitis attributed to chronic vitamin A intake. Following chemotherapy for prior breast and ovarian cancer, supportive therapy included weekly vitamin A (retinol) injections of 100,000 IU. Liver biopsy showed an acute toxic liver injury with focal parenchymal necrosis, sinusoidal lesions, inflammatory infiltrate (round cells, macrophages), and activation/proliferation of stellate cells; hepatic vitamin A concentration was significantly elevated, with no intrahepatic metastasis or cirrhosis. Supporting facts include onset of symptoms only after vitamin A application with worsening despite omission of all other medication except weekly vitamin A injections, absence of prior cholestasis or hepatitis history, other clinical signs of chronic hypervitaminosis A, exclusion of other liver/bile-duct causes, histology and electron microscopy supporting excess vitamin A, and elevated hepatic vitamin A concentrations.

raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis with liver cell necrosis, microvesicular steatosis and inflammatory infiltrates on histology; electron microscopy showed sinusoidal structures with hepatic stellate cells packed with lipid vacuoles and adjacent hepatocyte cytoplasmic lipid vacuoles. Peak bilirubin 20 mg/dl and AST/ALT >3000 U/L; the patient responded to ursodeoxycholic acid (250 mg thrice daily) with normalization of transaminases and bilirubin over about three weeks. The authors note liver diseases induced by vitamin A are well known, mostly fibrosis or cirrhosis, while cholestatic hepatitis is a rare form of chronic hypervitaminosis A. The paper also states daily intake of 25,000 IU for more than 6 years or 100,000 IU for more than 6 months is considered toxic, with wide interindividual variability.

raw_record.support_text: The study of massive acetaminophen (APAP) overdose patients treated with standard intravenous NAC found that standard dosing prevented hepatotoxicity in 91% (n=40) of patients who received NAC within 8 h, with no deaths or hepatic transplants in this cohort. The authors conclude that hepatotoxicity due to massive APAP overdose is more likely secondary to delayed NAC treatment than to insufficient NAC dosing, while noting APAP overdose is the most common cause of acute liver failure in the Western world.

raw_record.extra_details: Poison center chart review cohort of 104 massive APAP overdose cases; hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 U/L (some studies used ALT doubling or >150 U/L as acute liver injury); dose-response risk for hepatotoxicity related to the plotted serum APAP concentration above the 300 mcg/mL and 500 mcg/mL nomogram lines; 91% (n=40) of patients receiving NAC within 8 h were protected; no deaths or hepatic transplants; delay in NAC treatment was the main driver (13.9 vs 6 h in comparison studies); prior data: 2-5% hepatotoxicity with NAC within 8 h (Smilkstein oral protocol), ~3% in Chiew study with one liver transplant.

raw_record.extra_details: Most common form of acute liver failure in the US, unknown prior to 1980. Cases presented with jaundice within about 1 day, ALT 4310 IU/L, bilirubin 4.3 mg/dL, 6% transplanted, 68% spontaneous survival and 73% overall survival. Among acetaminophen ALF cases, suicidal (n=45) and accidental (n=67) groups were similar once ALF was reached; accidental group had mean dose 21 g and ALT 3280 IU/L, suicidal group 28 g and ALT 5867 IU/L. Alcohol abuse was less important than in earlier studies; the association of alcohol abuse with acetaminophen overdose is described as controversial.

raw_record.support_text: The use of flucloxacillin has been associated with characteristic cholestatic hepatitis, which appears more common in females than males and to increase in frequency with patient age and duration of treatment, with an estimated DILI incidence of 8.5 per 100,000 new users in the first 1-45 days after starting treatment. The adverse event can be severe, with a mortality rate of around 1 in 20 and transplantation required in some cases, and reports from Europe and Australia have confirmed that flucloxacillin contributes significantly to the burden of DILI. The paper frames flucloxacillin DILI as a rare but serious complication in the context of idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury more common in females and increases in frequency with patient age and duration of treatment; 51 confirmed flucloxacillin DILI cases genotyped.
raw_record.extra_details: Characteristic cholestatic hepatitis phenotype; estimated incidence 8.5 per 100,000 new users in first 1-45 days after starting treatment; mortality rate around 1 in 20 with transplantation required in some cases. Flucloxacillin is a human PXR agonist at pharmacologically relevant concentrations; the CYP3A4-generated 5'-hydroxymethyl metabolite was toxic to biliary epithelial cells but not hepatocytes in vitro, while the parent compound was nontoxic to either cell type. Genetic risk factors: CC genotype of PXR polymorphism rs3814055 (C-25385T) associated with increased risk (OR 3.37, 95% CI 1.55-7.30, P = 0.0023), and association with HLA allele B*5701; positive T cell reactivity reported in a single case.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol overdose is the main cause of acute liver failure in both the United Kingdom (60.9%) and the United States (46%), and is becoming a common cause of ALF in other European countries. Intentional overdose-related ALF predominates in the UK, whereas in the US paracetamol hepatotoxicity is usually secondary to accidental overdose (multiple doses for pain relief without suicidal intent). A comparison of 122 subjects with intentional and 131 with unintentional overdose showed that unintentional overdose patients were older (median 38 vs 32 years, P=0.002), more frequently used multiple paracetamol-containing preparations (38% vs 5%), were less likely to report depression (24% vs 45%), had lower serum paracetamol (16 vs 84 µg/dL), and were more likely to have severe (grade 3 and 4) hepatic encephalopathy on admission.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose accounted for 46% of ALF in a US survey (1998-2008, 1147 patients; paracetamol also implicated in 11% drug-related ALF and as a contributing factor in an acute hepatitis A series), 60.9% of fulminant hepatic failure in the UK, 20% of the French series (1986-2006, 500 patients), and 8% of transplanted fulminant hepatic failure in the European Liver Transplantation Registry (1972-2007). Comparison of 122 intentional vs 131 unintentional overdose subjects detailed: age, multiple preparation use, depression history, serum paracetamol, and encephalopathy grades.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical safety evaluation of CP-724,714 in patients with advanced malignant solid tumors overexpressing HER2, the drug displayed dose-limiting toxicities including reversible cholestatic liver dysfunction with elevated ALT, AST, GGT, and hyperbilirubinemia. The incidence and severity were generally dose-dependent: grade 3 hepatotoxicity (>3- to 10-fold increase of total bilirubin and/or >5- to 20-fold increase of transaminases) was reported in 25% of patients at 250 mg QD and 40% at 400 mg BID, with a median onset of 15 days. Elevation of liver function tests significantly correlated with steady-state systemic exposures of CP-724,714, and the parent compound remained the main plasma peak with no remarkable metabolites identified, indicating the parent molecule played a key role in the toxicity. CP-724,714 was discontinued from clinical development due to this unexpected hepatotoxicity, likely exerted via both hepatocellular injury and hepatobiliary cholestatic mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: Clozapine is associated with a spectrum of human drug-induced liver injury in therapeutic use. The most common abnormality is an isolated asymptomatic increase in aminotransferase levels (ALT increased in 53% and AST in 39% of 164 clozapine-treated patients; an increase in one enzyme in 61% of 125 patients). Icteric hepatitis has been reported twice, with biopsy-confirmed zone 3 (piecemeal) necrosis in one case and normalization of bilirubin and aminotransferases within 4 weeks. Cholestatic or mixed hepatitis has been reported in two cases, with jaundice within 8 weeks and confirmed cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy. Fulminant hepatitis with encephalopathy and coagulopathy is very rare, with only 2 cases (0.001%) among 136,000 patients in the manufacturers' database over 6 years. The mechanism is unclear, but the drug is hepatically metabolized via cytochrome P450 and reactive metabolites are presumed to mediate the damage, with insufficient evidence to distinguish toxic from immunoallergic hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Common isolated asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation: ALT increased in 53% and AST in 39% of 164 patients; in 125 patients an increase in one of AST, ALT, GGT, alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase in 61%, with ≥2-fold increase in 31%; no jaundice reported in that cohort; regulatory data reported aminotransferase increase in 30%. Icteric hepatitis reported twice, associated nausea within 4 weeks, biopsy-confirmed zone 3 necrosis in one case, bilirubin/aminotransferase normalized in 4 weeks; manufacturers reported icteric hepatitis in 84/136,000 (0.06%). Two cases of cholestatic or mixed hepatitis with jaundice within 8 weeks and biopsy-confirmed cholestatic hepatitis; liver tests normalized upon discontinuation. Fulminant hepatitis with encephalopathy and coagulopathy: 2 cases (0.001%) among 136,000 patients over 6 years, including the present case. Mechanism unclear; predominantly hepatic cytochrome P450-dependent metabolism; reactive metabolites presumed, insufficient evidence to distinguish toxic vs immunoallergic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: This case report is described as the fifth known case of ramipril-induced hepatotoxicity. Following discontinuation of ramipril, the patient's alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin began declining promptly, though biochemical markers had not yet returned to baseline at one month post-discharge. The biopsy revealed bland cholestasis with no ductular changes.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of ramipril-induced hepatotoxicity, the fifth known case. Current case: bland cholestasis with no ductular changes on biopsy; onset 8 weeks after beginning ramipril (latency range 5 weeks to 10 months across cases); ALP and bilirubin declined after discontinuation but not returned to baseline at one month; prior cholestatic cases (biopsies showing cholestasis and bile duct necrosis) returned to near baseline at 6 and 14 months. Two other prior cases: one mixed pattern (markedly elevated ALT and ALP, minimal bilirubin increase, parenchymal inflammation on biopsy, unintended positive rechallenge confirming diagnosis) and one unclassifiable (mild liver enzyme increases, no biopsy). Symptomatic presentation varied from incidental blood-work findings to jaundice and severe pruritus. Cholestasis described as the most common liver injury pattern in ACEI-induced hepatotoxicity. First described cross reactivity between ramipril and methimazole in recurrent DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is well tolerated by patients with chronic liver disease. In a double-blind, two-period, cross-over study comparing acetaminophen, 4 g daily for two weeks, with placebo in 20 patients with stable chronic liver disease, laboratory tests and clinical evaluations revealed no evidence of hepatotoxicity and no adverse nonspecific effect on laboratory abnormalities associated with liver disease, no significant drug accumulation despite modestly impaired metabolism, no enhanced formation of the toxic metabolite as reflected in conjugate excretion, and no glutathione depletion. raw_record.support_text: The present report describes a case of acute cholestatic hepatitis occurring in a 39-year-old woman after administration of venlafaxine. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis predominantly involving zone 3 of the hepatic lobule with portal inflammation and abundant eosinophils. The clinical course rapidly improved after cessation of venlafaxine and administration of corticosteroid; liver toxicity recurred with a medium dose upon initiation of therapy and with increase of dosage after reinitiation of low-dose venlafaxine. The positive rechallenge clearly supports the association between venlafaxine and liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old woman; liver biopsy (Nov 17, 2011) showed cholestatic hepatitis predominantly involving zone 3, perivenular feathery degenerated hepatocytes with cytoplasmic bile pigment, intrasinusoidal lymphocytes, activated Kupffer cells, occasional apoptotic bodies and single liver cell necrosis, portal lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils; no bile duct lesions or bile plugs. Diagnosed as venlafaxine-associated cholestatic hepatitis. Positive rechallenge: toxicity recurred with reinitiation of low-dose venlafaxine and dose increase; improved after cessation with methylprednisolone 50 mg/day tapering. Elevated AST 734 U/L, ALT 805 U/L, AP 167 U/L, γGT 102 U/L, bilirubin 11.2 mg/dL on readmission.

raw_record.support_text: In a descriptive study of 662 patients enrolled by the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group, 275 (41.5%) had acetaminophen (APAP) overdoses meeting ALF criteria of coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy. Both unintentional (staggered) and intentional suicidal overdoses produced nearly equally high aminotransferases, and the paper attributes acute liver failure to APAP overdose, with toxicity enhanced by glutathione depletion from alcohol or starvation. The text also notes paracetamol was understood in the UK as responsible for a rising number of deaths as a suicide agent, and a 1975 Lancet editorial urged replacing paracetamol because it 'cannot cause liver damage.'
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (both intentional self-harm and unintentional/staggered overdoses); not therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: US ALF Study Group cohort of 662 patients, 275 (41.5%) APAP overdose meeting ALF criteria (coagulopathy INR ≥1.5 and encephalopathy); 7% reported less than 4 g, suggesting possible enhanced sensitivity, possibly via alcohol or starvation depleting glutathione; APAP half-life about 2-3 h; both phenotypes with nearly equally high aminotransferases and similar antidepressant/other substance use; ~2/3 of unintentional patients habituated/adicted to high-dose hydrocodone/APAP products; Dangers recognized in UK case reports from 1970; paracetamol used as a suicide agent with rising UK deaths; 1975 Lancet editorial ('cannot cause liver damage'); UK 1998 legislation limiting package size (16 convenience stores, 32 pharmacies) and requiring blister packing.

raw_record.support_text: In the ALFSG experience, patients with acetaminophen (APAP) acute liver failure progress to death, transplant, or recovery in a short time interval; virtually all APAP patients reached an endpoint by 4 days after admission, and overall 36% of ALF patients were listed for transplantation, but only 22% of those with APAP ALF vs 56% of the non-APAP group; only 36% of listed APAP patients received a graft, and the very sick APAP patients often die because a liver cannot be found in time.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose (both intentional and unintentional phenotypes) causes acute liver failure (ALF); spontaneous resolution occurs with or without N-acetylcysteine in nearly 2/3 of cases. In the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) experience, virtually all APAP patients reached their endpoint by 4 days following admission, whereas DILI patients continued to die or receive liver grafts over 7-10 days. 36% of ALF patients were listed for transplantation, only 22% with APAP ALF vs 56% non-APAP; only 36% of those listed received a graft vs 74% of non-APAP group. The listed APAP patients were sicker in clinical/biochemical features.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that acetaminophen (APAP) is the leading cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the USA Adult Registry data (n=2,436), with 1,115 APAP cases; among these, 8.6% required transplantation and overall survival was 71.5%. A separate Parkland Hospital study of APAP overdoses identified 71 qualifying acetaminophen-toxicity cases (50 suicidal, 21 unintentional); in the unintentional group 8 developed ALF and 6 (29%) died, whereas the suicidal group had 1 ALF/death in 50 (2%). The paper treats acetaminophen toxicity/overdose as a direct cause of acute liver failure and death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional or unintentional (therapeutic-misuse) overdose as the exposure setting for the attributed acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: USA Adult Liver Failure registry (ALFSG) data, Jan 1998–Dec 2016, n=2,436 overall: APAP n=1,115, Tx 8.6%, spontaneous survival 64.4%, overall survival 71.5%; APAP group younger (median 37 y), 76% female, higher ALT (median 3798.5 IU) and lower bilirubin (median 4.3). Parkland Hospital study (F.V. Schiødt, NEJM 1997;337:1112-17): 71 cases over 40 months; suicidal n=50 (1 ALF/death, 2%), unintentional n=21 (8 ALF, 6 died, 29%); unintentional cases had later presentation and higher ALT. APAP phenotypes table (n=606): intentional vs unintentional differences in sex, age, coma grade ≥3 (39 vs 55%), ALT (6053 vs 4207 IU/L), opioid compound use (18 vs 63%), multiple preparations (5 vs 38%). Mechanism: NAPQI formed when glucuronidation/sulfation capacity is exceeded; glutathione detoxifies to mercapturic acid; when glutathione is exhausted NAPQI binds cell proteins disrupting function. Figure 3 Sankey plot shows APAP deaths/transplants concentrated in first 48–72 h after registry enrollment. FDA Advisory Committee meeting 2009 discussed APAP toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The study addresses shortened N-acetylcysteine courses in patients with acetaminophen poisoning at low risk for toxicity, and aimed to determine which clinical findings best identified patients at lowest risk for acetaminophen-related hepatotoxicity after an acute overdose. This frames acetaminophen overdose as a cause of hepatotoxicity in the human population studied.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single acute overdose setting (acute acetaminophen poisoning with concentration above the possible toxicity nomogram line); patients presenting within 24 hours of ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective 10-year analysis of hospital admissions for acute acetaminophen poisoning; 41 of 95 identified charts met inclusion criteria (PT, AST, and ALT measured within 24 hours of ingestion); 16 patients had hepatotoxicity. PT, AST, and ALT within the first 24 hours postingestion did not identify all patients with hepatotoxicity; normal PT, AST, or ALT within 48 hours of ingestion best predicted low risk of toxicity. Early N-acetylcysteine treatment after single acute ingestions reduces the incidence of severe hepatotoxicity to <=10%.

The best predictor of low risk of hepatotoxicity was normal PT, AST, or ALT values within 48 hours of ingestion, whereas abnormal values were highly sensitive indicators of pending hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In combined North American clinical trials, ALT elevations more than three times the upper limit of normal were seen in 48 of 2,510 patients (1.9%) treated with troglitazone versus 0.6% on placebo, and two patients were confirmed to have suffered serious hepatocellular injury from an idiosyncratic drug reaction. Troglitazone was associated with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, with some patients showing severe or fatal liver damage, leading to its withdrawal from the US and Japanese markets in March 2000. The recommended therapeutic dose was 200-600 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: ALT >3x ULN in 1.9% (48/2,510) troglitazone-treated patients vs 0.6% placebo; two patients confirmed to have serious hepatocellular injury from an idiosyncratic reaction; some patients showed severe or fatal liver damage; withdrawn from US and Japanese markets March 2000; recommended dose 200-600 mg/day; hepatotoxicity was not predicted in conventional animals or cynomolgus monkeys (300-1200 mg/kg/day for 52 weeks).

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old woman developed acute hepatitis and acute liver failure (jaundice, impaired synthetic function with INR 2.7, low-grade encephalopathy) after taking norfloxacin 2 g (400 mg twice daily) for 3 days for suspected bacterial gastroenteritis. Liver biopsy demonstrated acute hepatitis with centrilobular hepatocyte drop-out, ceroid-laden macrophages, pericholangitis/cholangitis, and parenchymal and portal inflammation with eosinophilia. Using the Council for International Organisation of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) scale for DILI causality, norfloxacin-induced hepatotoxicity was deemed 'highly probable'. Liver enzymes and INR normalised after N-acetylcysteine infusion, though it was 3 months before liver tests fully normalised.

raw_record.extra_details: Norfloxacin dose 2 g (400 mg twice daily) taken starting 3 days before admission. CIOMS DILI causality scale gave 'highly probable'. ALF resolved after N-acetylcysteine 18 g/24 h infusion over 2 days, with complete normalisation of liver tests at 3 months.

Three months after discontinuing propafenone, the patient was asymptomatic and all liver tests normalised, supporting propafenone as the cause after exclusion of other causes of elevated liver enzymes.

Propafenone is a class Ic antiarrhythmic mainly metabolised by the liver; hepatotoxicity is rare with only a few reported cases.

raw_record.support_text: Our patient developed cholestatic liver injury approximately 2 weeks after starting propafenone, with development of jaundice and pruritus within 3 to 4 weeks thereafter. Three months after withdrawal, the patient was asymptomatic and all liver tests had normalised. The paper frames propafenone as a very rare cause of hepatotoxicity (DILI) and recommends discontinuing the drug when cholestatic and/or hepatocellular injury is suspected.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic liver injury with jaundice and pruritus, latency approximately 2 weeks from drug initiation; jaundice/pruritus developed 3-4 weeks after start; complete resolution ~3 months after withdrawal; RUCAM causality assessment performed (criteria tabulated: onset 5-90 days +2, ALT decrease >=50% within 8 days of withdrawal +3, age >=55 +1, all-cause exclusion +2); positive dechallenge; concurrent C. freundii gastroenteritis with sepsis/hypotension and meropenem use were evaluated and excluded as causes. Prior case reports show cholestatic injury with jaundice, latency generally 2-8 weeks; liver biopsies described portal tract enlargement with lymphocytic/monocyte/macrophage/granulocyte infiltrates, bile duct proliferation, hepatocyte ballooning, and macrovesicular steatosis; proposed mechanism includes hepatic toxic metabolite accumulation (p-quinone intermediates) and enterohepatic recirculation.

raw_record.support_text: Seven of 23 previously unexplained cases of fulminant hepatic failure at the authors' hospital had been under ecarazine hydrochloride (a hydralazine derivative) therapy for hypertension when they developed the condition. The authors concluded these cases were caused by ecarazine, characterized by rapid decrease in serum ALT after drug discontinuation, prolonged jaundice, high incidence of ANA (57%), and histology of extensive hepatocellular necrosis ranging from bridging to massive necrosis. Four of the seven patients died of fulminant hepatic failure; these four had received high doses of ecarazine hydrochloride for prolonged periods. The cases lacked typical drug-induced-signs including skin rash and a positive lymphocyte stimulation test.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with hypertension taking ecarazine long-term for chronic hypertensive disease; in all cases fulminant hepatic failure developed more than 10 days after clinical recognition of hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 23 reviewed cases of previously unknown-cause fulminant hepatic failure attributed to ecarazine. Cases lacked skin rash and positive lymphocyte stimulation test with the drug, which the authors cite as reasons the cause was not previously identified. Clinical features included rapid serum ALT decrease after discontinuation, prolonged jaundice despite discontinuation, ANA positivity in 57%, and histology of extensive hepatocellular necrosis (bridging to massive necrosis). Four of seven patients died; the fatal cases had received high doses for prolonged periods. Cases were in the context of long-term drug therapy for hypertension.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the clinical course of seven patients who developed fulminant hepatic failure caused by ecarazine hydrochloride, an antihypertensive agent. Course details include massive hepatic cell necrosis (Case 1, fatal), zonal hepatic cell necrosis with a positive rechallenge and positivity for ANA (Case 2), a fatal case with jaundice, hemorrhage and renal failure (Case 3), and Case 4 with elevated ALT/AST to 1,090 IU/L and 1,205 IU/L after being prescribed ecarazine with warfarin and dilazep.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients developed fulminant hepatic failure attributed to ecarazine hydrochloride given as an antihypertensive agent. Case 1 (69-year-old man) died after hepatic encephalopathy and renal failure; necropsy showed massive hepatic cell necrosis. Case 2 demonstrated zonal hepatic cell necrosis on biopsy, ANA converted to positive (1:80), and rechallenge 2 weeks later produced fatigue with AST 1,305 IU/L, ALT 1,197 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL that normalized after discontinuation; anti-HCV antibody and HCV RNA were negative. Case 3 (74-year-old man) died from exacerbated jaundice, hemorrhagic tendency and renal failure. Case 4 (postpartum woman) had ALT 1,090 IU/L and AST 1,205 IU/L with concurrent warfarin and dilazep co-medication. Cases treated with plasma filtration, plasma exchange and prednisolone.

raw_record.support_text: Table 1 summarizes the clinical features of seven patients who developed fulminant hepatic failure caused by ecarazine (an antihypertensive drug). There were three men and four women, ages 22 to 74 years (mean 58.7); four of the seven died of hepatic failure. Daily ecarazine dosage was 60 mg in three cases and 90 mg in four cases, and the interval from start of therapy to onset of hepatic failure ranged from 11 days to more than 1 year. Case reports show ANA and other autoantibodies, jaundice, hepatic cell necrosis on biopsy (including submassive centrilobular necrosis), and hepatic encephalopathy; two patients improved on prednisolone, while cases 5 and 6 died.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Used to treat hypertension; all seven cases had concomitant drugs in use when hepatic failure developed, with no particular tendency in type; liver biopsy showed hepatic cell necrosis in some cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven patients (3 men, 4 women; ages 22-74, mean 58.7); four died of hepatic failure. Daily dose 60 mg (n=3) or 90 mg (n=4); cumulative dose 10.0 +/- 7.4 g (range 0.7-21.9 g); latency from start to onset 11 days to >1 year (longer than 4 weeks in six cases, 11 days in one). Presentation included jaundice, general fatigue, anorexia, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and positive ANA/anti-DNA/antithyroglobulin/antimicrosome autoantibodies; liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic cell necrosis around the centrilobular area (Cases 5, 6, 7) and bridging necrosis (Case 5). Two patients recovered gradually after prednisolone therapy; others died. Lymphocyte stimulation test with ecarazine was performed in four cases with no positive results. High cumulative doses tended toward poorer prognosis.

Daily dose 60-90 mg/d; onset 11 to >365 days after first dose; cumulative dose 0.7-21.9 g; time from onset to encephalopathy 12-62 days. Peak ALT 1,906±1,079 IU/L, total bilirubin 35.8±7.5 mg/dL, prothrombin time 29.0±7.0 s. HAV, HBV, anti-HCV and HCV RNA negative in all; WBC >9,000/mm3 in 2; mild eosinophilia (3-5%) in some; ANA positive in all 4 female patients (max titer 1:10,240); ANA titers rose with symptom exacerbation in cases 5 and 7. Histology: severe centrilobular necrosis with mild inflammatory infiltration. Case 2 later developed acute hepatitis upon ecarazine resumption 7 years after improvement. Chemical name: N1-ethoxycarbonyl-N2-hydrazinophthalazine hydrochloride, a hydralazine derivative used as antihypertensive.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study, 22 patients with prostate cancer were treated with the combination of flutamide (250 mg three times daily) and goserelin or orchiectomy. Severe hepatotoxicity appeared in two of 22 (9%) patients. Following discontinuation of flutamide, one patient died due to acute liver failure, and the other improved after cessation of flutamide. The authors concluded that patients treated with flutamide who have symptomatic or asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations should be taken off therapy as soon as possible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prostate cancer patients; flutamide given as combination therapy with goserelin (LHRH analogue) or orchiectomy.
raw_record.extra_details: 22 patients, ages 47-79, treated 1995-1997 at Erciyes University Hospital. Severe hepatotoxicity in 2/22 (9%); one died of acute liver failure after flutamide discontinuation, the other improved after cessation. Abnormal LFTs (ALT, AST, gamma-GT, bilirubin) appeared within 4-8 weeks of treatment in the two affected cases. Hepatotoxicity assessed per WHO criteria. Literature incidence reported as low (not exceeding 0.36%; FDA received 20 flutamide-hepatotoxicity death reports 1989-1994, ~0.03%). LFTs obtained at 4, 8 and 12 weeks and every 2 months.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer was started on the TAS regimen (flutamide 250 mg three times daily plus goserelin 3.6 mg subcutaneously monthly). After an initially normal month, liver function tests rose during week 5, flutamide was discontinued, and by week 7 AST was 840 U/L, ALT 380 U/L, bilirubin 16.7 mg/dl (direct 10.4), ALP 2761, and γ-GT 684, with negative viral serology and elevated prothrombin time. Hepatic encephalopathy and acute renal failure developed and the patient died of acute cholestatic hepatitis on 29 October 1997.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prostate cancer patient; flutamide was part of the TAS regimen with concomitant goserelin (3.6 mg monthly), though causality was attributed to flutamide.
raw_record.extra_details: Flutamide 250 mg three times daily began 2 September 1997 and was discontinued 7 October 1997; liver test abnormalities began during the fifth week. Peak values AST 840, ALT 380, bilirubin 16.7 (direct 10.4), γ-GT 684, ALP 2761 U/L; viral hepatitis serologies negative. Prothrombin time rose to 28 s and partial thromboplastin time to 126 s. Development of hepatic encephalopathy and acute renal failure, progressing to deep coma; cause of death recorded as acute cholestatic hepatitis.

condition_text: Injury occurred at therapeutic doses in chronic alcoholics, framed as a therapeutic misadventure (enhanced susceptibility of the alcoholic) rather than deliberate overdose; several patients had fever, and in two patients hepatitis screening results were not reported, with viral hepatitis not absolutely excluded.

raw_record.support_text: This response letter argues that the thrust of the authors' paper is that the alcoholic is at increased risk for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity as a therapeutic misadventure rather than as a consequence of deliberate overdose. They defined a syndrome in alcoholics who take acetaminophen for symptom relief, characterized by towering aminotransferase levels, often with renal injury, a high fatality rate, and histologic changes consistent with a toxic cause. The paper explicitly refers to acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis and recommends measuring plasma acetaminophen levels as a diagnostic aid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurred at therapeutic doses in chronic alcoholics, framed as a therapeutic misadventure (enhanced susceptibility of the alcoholic) rather than deliberate overdose; several patients had fever, and in two patients hepatitis screening results were not reported, with viral hepatitis not absolutely excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Reports a dramatic syndrome with towering aminotransferase levels and often renal injury, high fatality rate, and histologic changes consistent with a toxic cause. Refers to 19 patients in literature cases; doses were 1.86 g thrice daily in one report, and in 12 of 19 literature patients total daily dose did not exceed 7.5 g/day, the mean being 6.4 g/day (1.6 times manufacturer's recommended daily dosage). Authors recommend measuring plasma acetaminophen levels and taking a history of acetaminophen intake in alcoholics with this syndrome. Fever was absent in four patients, mild in the fifth, and associated with alcohol withdrawal in the sixth.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old Caucasian male with relapsed lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, on zanubrutinib for 30 months in a clinical trial, presented with jaundice, choluria, and pruritus and showed severe hepatocellular injury with jaundice (ALT 2474 IU/L, total bilirubin 141 umol/L, mild coagulopathy). No alternative explanation was found after extensive virology, autoimmune, and metabolic work-up plus abdominal ultrasound. Zanubrutinib-induced liver injury was suspected and the updated RUCAM score indicated a probable causal relationship; liver histology was consistent with drug-induced liver injury, and liver biochemistry improved after stopping zanubrutinib and normalized after 8 weeks. The paper reports this as the first case of severe liver injury secondary to zanubrutinib.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of severe liver injury due to zanubrutinib (Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor licensed in refractory mantle cell lymphoma, under phase 3 trials). Patient had relapsed lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Onset after 30 months of treatment; jaundice, choluria, pruritus for 10 days. ALT 2474 IU/L, total bilirubin 141 umol/L, mild coagulopathy. Extensive work-up (virology, autoimmune, metabolic) and abdominal ultrasound found no alternative cause. Histology consistent with DILI. RUCAM probable. Liver biochemistry improved after cessation and normalized after 8 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: The liver injury in a 56-year-old man on zanubrutinib 160 mg twice daily for relapsing Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia was hepatocellular with an R-value of 63.2, and the updated RUCAM causality assessment score for zanubrutinib was 7, indicating 'probable drug-induced liver injury'. A liver biopsy showed patchy necrosis, cholestasis and moderate to severe lobular and portal inflammation suggestive of DILI with no evidence of alcohol-related liver disease. His liver enzymes improved after drug cessation and normalised 28 days after discharge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 56-year-old Caucasian man with Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia randomised to the zanubrutinib arm of a phase 3 BeiGene trial comparing zanubrutinib with ibrutinib; took zanubrutinib 160 mg twice daily with aciclovir and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. After 28 months of treatment he developed an asymptomatic transaminase and total bilirubin rise, followed 8 weeks later by pale stools, dark urine, pruritus and jaundice; admission labs ALT 2474 (ULN 45 IU/L), AST 1257, ALP 114, TB 141 (ULN 21 umol/L), PT 14 sec, R-value 63.2. Full liver screen negative excluding other causes; ultrasound showed echo-bright texture in keeping with fatty changes. Biopsy showed patchy necrosis, cholestasis and moderate/severe lobular and portal inflammation; immunohistochemistry showed reactive CD3-positive T-cell-predominant infiltrate with no light chain restriction. Zanubrutinib was withheld as suspected cause and permanently stopped; discharge after 9-day admission, liver profile normalised 28 days later. No clinical signs of liver failure at admission.

raw_record.support_text: Four published case reports describe ibrutinib-induced DILI; the pattern of injury was hepatocellular in all cases, with time of onset ranging from 2 weeks to 9 months and the course resolving after drug cessation. RUCAM (or updated RUCAM calculated from published data) graded the cases as 'probable' [16], 'possible' [17], and 'unlikely' [14] because of an unexplained recurrent enzyme rise and missing hepatitis A serology. These cases highlight ibrutinib's potential risk of severe liver injury and acute liver failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Indications were refractory WM in 3 of 4 cases and relapsed/refractory CLL in one; ages 48-77; onset 2 weeks to 9 months; reported RUCAM 7 'probable' [15] and calculated 8 'probable' [16] and 6 'possible' [17]; histology included centrilobular cholestasis, acute hepatitis with mixed inflammation, and hepatocellular cholestasis/necrosis; all patients stopped ibrutinib, one also received prednisolone; enzymes normalized in 5-8 weeks in three patients, while one patient died from the original illness with enzymes improved but not normalized.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty patients in clinical trials of lapatinib (for adjuvant/metastatic breast cancer and one head and neck cancer case) were adjudicated as potentially susceptible to lapatinib-associated Hy's Law events, characterized as 'probable' DILI (n=13), 'possible' DILI (n=6), or 'inadequate information' (n=1). The cases exhibited hepatocellular and mixed liver-injury patterns; 14 (70%) carried the HLA-DQA1*02:01/DRB1*07:01 alleles, and Gilbert's syndrome UGT1A1*28/*28 genotypes were also represented. All cases fell within the Hy's Law quadrant by concurrent ALT/TBL and alkaline phosphatase values, and the farthest excursions (grade 3 ALT >5xULN) were all in HLA-positive carriers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HER2-positive breast cancer patients (adjuvant and metastatic settings) and one head and neck cancer patient; some cases received lapatinib in combination with trastuzumab, letrozole, capecitabine, bevacizumab, or paclitaxel.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious grade 3 ALT elevations (>=5xULN) reported in 1.6% and serious liver injury with hyperbilirubinemia in 0.2% of treated patients, leading to lapatinib discontinuation. Adjudication: probable DILI n=13, possible DILI n=6, inadequate information n=1. 14/20 (70%) were carriers of HLA-DQA1*02:01/DRB1*07:01; 1 homozygous, 13 heterozygous. HLA-positive carriers had higher mean/median maximum ALT (13.4x/8.0xULN, n=14) vs HLA-negative (4.2x/4.2xULN, n=6), P=0.02. HLA-positive subjects generally showed hepatocellular injury; HLA-negative predominantly mixed. Liver injury type classified by R ratio (max ALT/max ALP during concurrent elevation): hepatocellular, mixed, or cholestatic. One case (subject 11) had biopsy consistent with moderate autoimmune hepatitis. All cases occupied the Hy's Law quadrant (concurrent ALT >3x and TBL >2xULN); grade 3 ALT >5xULN cases (n=11) were all HLA-positive. Subjects with lapatinib-associated serious liver injury analyzed; six cases adjudicated 'unlikely' or 'weakly possible' DILI excluded.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen/paracetamol (APAP) is generally considered safe, but at higher doses APAP can cause severe acute liver injury, and describes the mechanism of APAP toxicity as a target of intensive research.
raw_record.extra_details: Paper reports immunohistochemistry on liver samples from 5 individuals with severe APAP intoxication that required liver transplantation (demographic/biochemical data previously reported), where SIRT1 immunostaining was absent in areas of severe liver damage. The overdose/liver-failure claim is part of a mechanistic study of SIRT1 modulation via the IL1beta/NFkB pathway; supporting in vivo mouse data used APAP 300 mg/kg. Alias: paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: Among reported cases, 26 met inclusion criteria where diclofenac was the sole suspected drug, the patient recovered after drug withdrawal, no other treatment or probable cause of hepatic dysfunction was found, and serial liver function tests were available including a recovery-phase value. Serology for hepatitis A and B was negative in 15 tested, and imaging ruled out biliary obstruction in 7 cases; one liver biopsy favored drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 cases analyzed; average age 64 years (range 37-84), 70% female. Main features included jaundice (total bilirubin deviate ratio >2) in half, hepatomegaly (sometimes painful), anorexia, nausea; itch, malaise, or vomiting less common; 25% asymptomatic; mild thrombocytopenia in 2 reports; no extrahepatic hypersensitivity phenomena reported. Onset within first 6 months in 18/21 reports; median duration of exposure 76 days (range 6-417 days); median cumulative dose 8.7 g (1.4-63.5 g). Dominant biochemical feature was raised transaminases with lesser rises in alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase, and bilirubin; severity ranged to fortyfold transaminase elevations. Significant log dose vs log peak AST (r²=0.68, slope 0.91, p=0.0001) and ALT (r²=0.71, slope 1.04, p=0.001) relations. Transaminases fell exponentially after withdrawal with post-peak half-lives of 13.7 days (AST) and 13.2 days (ALT).

raw_record.support_text: Among all drug toxicity cases of ALF, acetaminophen overdosing was identified as the most predominant etiology. Sixteen patients (72.7% of these cases or 11.9% of all patients) ingested a median amount of 22 g acetaminophen with suicidal intent, while six patients (27.3%) accidentally intoxicated themselves by ingesting 3-5 g of acetaminophen on a given day. Patients with acetaminophen-induced liver failure were significantly younger than ALF patients of other etiologies (30 vs 43 years) and showed a shorter disease duration, higher serum AST than ALT, and lower bilirubin levels.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: suicidal (22 g median) and accidental (3-5 g/day) ingestion; acetaminophen-induced ALF patients were significantly younger (30 vs 43 years) than those with other etiologies.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdosing caused 22 of the 53 drug-toxicity ALF cases (16 suicidal with median 22 g; 6 accidental with 3-5 g/day). Associated with shorter disease duration, higher serum AST than ALT, and lower bilirubin compared to other etiologies. Patients with acetaminophen- or HAV-related ALF had a four-week survival of 82% under conservative therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Phenylbutazone is described as a toxic agent recognised to cause toxic hepatitis with several fatalities and the formation of hepatic granulomas. In a series of 800 patients, 2 developed toxic hepatitis (incidence 0.25%); the first detailed report described 5 patients with jaundice 6 to 40 days after starting therapy, and there have subsequently been many reports of toxic hepatitis, including 8 fatalities. Hepatic granulomas were recorded in 11 patients, with fever, pruritus, jaundice, and occasionally eosinophilia.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis with several fatalities; incidence 0.25% (2/800); first report of 5 patients with jaundice appearing 6-40 days after start of therapy; 8 fatalities subsequently; hepatic granulomas in 11 patients accompanied by fever, pruritus, jaundice, occasionally eosinophilia.

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based study of 1543 patients hospitalized for acetaminophen overdose between 1995 and 2004 identified from administrative data, 70 patients (4.5%) developed hepatotoxicity. Unintentional overdose (OR 5.18), alcohol abuse (OR 2.21), underlying liver disease (OR 3.50), and N-acetylcysteine treatment (OR 6.75) were independently associated with hepatotoxicity. raw_record.support_text: A patient prescribed minocycline for the treatment of rosacea discontinued the medication after 30 days and went into liver failure 4 days later. The diagnosis of minocycline-induced hepatic failure was made after exclusion of the most common causes of hepatopathies including viral, metabolic, and autoimmune liver disease, supported by eosinophilia, marked IgE overproduction, positive autoantibodies, and a liver biopsy pointing to an allergic/hypersensitive drug-induced injury of hepatic parenchyma.

raw_record.extra_details: Patient discontinued minocycline after 30 days and developed liver failure 4 days later; recovered following high-dose intravenous prednisolone. Liver biopsy showed liver cell necrosis with marked inflammatory activity, noted as the most common pattern in idiosyncratic adverse drug reactions. The paper classified the case as an allergic/hypersensitive drug-induced injury with a DRESS/DIHS-type hypersensitivity pattern. WHO (1997) reported 425 adverse-reaction cases associated with minocycline involving the liver (hepatitis, jaundice, fatty liver, abnormal liver function), CNS, and skin. Seaman et al. case-control study reported an incidence of liver dysfunction of 1.04 per 10,000 exposed person-months and a weak association between minocycline use and liver dysfunction. Lawrenson et al. divided 45 reported cases of hepatic involvement into a hypersensitivity-type reaction (eosinophilia, exfoliative dermatitis, worse prognosis, within weeks of starting therapy) and an autoimmune-hepatitis type with lupus-like symptoms (after a year or more, better outcome); among these reported cases 58% were female and 94% were under 40 years. Patient's cultured PBMCs showed several-fold higher percentages of IFN-gamma- and TNF-alpha-producing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells after minocycline stimulation, indicating both type I and type II immune responses.

After ruling out other etiologies, they concluded the most likely diagnosis was idiosyncratic levocetirizine-induced liver injury, supported by timing of drug administration, improvement of clinical and laboratory parameters after drug discontinuation, and histological findings similar to another reported case.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver disease accounts for about 50% of acute or subacute liver failure in the United States. The authors report a case of terbinafine-induced severe liver failure requiring liver transplantation. A variety of antifungal medications are known to cause a range of liver injury from mild hepatocellular-cholestatic injury to acute/subacute liver failure, and terbinafine (Lamisil), a widely prescribed antifungal for onychomycosis, is one antifungal associated with such liver injuries.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old African American male with onychomycosis treated with terbinafine for approximately 3 months. At the 3-month outpatient visit he was jaundiced with dark urine, acholic stools, weight loss, anorexia, myalgias, and pruritus; labs showed AST 95 IU/L, ALT 149 IU/L, total bilirubin 29 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. After 33 days, at outside hospital admission: AST 228 IU/L, ALT 144 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 497 IU/L, albumin 2.2 mg/dL, bilirubin 68.6 mg/dL, BUN 114 mg/dL, creatinine 14.2 mg/dL. Negative serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, ANA, ASMA, AMA, HIV; undetectable serum acetaminophen; normal ceruloplasmin. His condition deteriorated, requiring hemodialysis and orthotropic liver transplantation. Explant pathology showed portal areas lacking corresponding bile ducts (cholestatic liver disease). The report notes terbinafine usually produces mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic injury that is reversible after discontinuation, with previous reports of prolonged cholestasis and disappearance of interlobular bile ducts. Brand: Lamisil (Novartis).

raw_record.support_text: A 77-year-old white male with pneumonia was treated with levofloxacin 500 mg once daily. On the seventh day of treatment he developed elevation of transaminases, and an acute hepatitis was diagnosed. The temporal relation, exclusion of other causes of hepatitis, and a compatible liver biopsy were consistent with levofloxacin-associated hepatotoxicity. Levofloxacin was stopped and the patient made a full recovery. Naranjo score was 'probable' (7) and Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score was 'highly probable' (9).

raw_record.extra_details: Levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for pneumonia. Onset of elevated transaminases on the 7th day of treatment. Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale 'probable' (score 7); Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method 'highly probable' (score 9). Liver biopsy performed 14 days after identification of hepatitis was compatible; drug withheld and full recovery. Slight aggravation of anemia noted at 3-day follow-up. Authors note 5 reported levofloxacin hepatitis cases in the literature, of which this is the only one with a biopsy during the course and survival.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol predictably produces acute liver injury when taken in suicidal overdose. After an initial two to three days of irritability, jaundice and other signs of acute liver failure appear; by the fourth day the liver is tender and histologically shows uniformly distributed centrilobular coagulative necrosis with vacuolation of adjacent surviving hepatocytes. Of 200 patients admitted to the Liver Unit at King's College Hospital with signs of liver damage after an overdose of between 10 and 100 g of paracetamol, 29 died in fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Centrilobular coagulative necrosis with vacuolation of adjacent surviving hepatocytes in early stages; two to three day initial period of irritability followed by jaundice and signs of acute liver failure by the fourth day; 29 of 200 overdose cases died in fulminant hepatic failure (Portmann et al., 1975).

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose is reported as the main cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the UK (60.9%) and USA (46%), and has recently become a common cause in other European countries. In the UK, ALF/fulminant hepatic failure is more often due to intentional paracetamol overdose, whereas in the USA paracetamol hepatotoxicity is usually due to accidental overdose (multiple doses for pain relief without suicidal intent).
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose is the main cause of ALF in the UK (60.9%) and USA (46%). Comparison of 122 intentional vs 131 unintentional overdose subjects: unintentional subjects were older (median 38 vs 32 years, p=0.002), more often used multiple paracetamol-containing preparations (38% vs 5%, p<0.0001), less often reported depression (24% vs 45%, p<0.0001), and had severe (grade 3 and 4) hepatic encephalopathy on admission more often than intentional overdose subjects (55% vs 39%, p=0.002). Median paracetamol dose was lower in accidental (12 g) than suicidal-intent (20 g) overdose (p=0.009). Chronic alcohol consumption and malnutrition likely contributed to liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: A MEDLINE review (1966–April 1996) of 27 published cases of propylthiouracil (PTU) hepatotoxicity plus two institutional cases showed that although most patients recovered once PTU was stopped, seven patients died. Survivors were more likely to have received ¹³¹I during the illness than those who died (P < 0.03). The paper also reports the first pediatric patient with PTU hepatotoxicity to undergo liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients treated for hyperthyroidism/thyroid disease; includes a pediatric (14-yr-old) patient who underwent liver transplantation and an adult case in hepatic failure who died of multisystem organ failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Twenty-seven published English-language cases from a MEDLINE search (1966–April 1996) plus cross-referenced cases, of which 85% met the management-information selection criterion; two additional institutional cases of hepatic failure presented. Seven patients overall died. Survivors were significantly more likely to have received ¹³¹I during the illness (P<0.03, Fisher's exact test). In the two institutional patients, hyperbilirubinemia was linearly associated with decreasing T4 levels (r=0.91, P<0.001) despite clinical thyrotoxicosis in one patient. One institution case was successfully treated with liver transplantation; the other died of multisystem organ failure. First reported pediatric liver transplant for PTU hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A literature review identified 28 cases of propylthiouracil (PTU)-associated hepatotoxicity, and including the 2 cases presented in this paper there were 30 total cases. The paper attributes the hepatic disease to PTU therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Combined analysis of 28 literature cases plus 2 new cases (n=30). Female:male ratio 8.3:1; PTU dose at presentation with hepatotoxicity 426±199 mg/day; months of continuous PTU therapy before hepatotoxicity 3.6±3.5; 7 fatalities and 21 survivors; age 27.9±17.1 yr. One additional case via transplacental passage (symptomatic at 5 days of age) was excluded from analysis, and the initial case report of hepatocellular jaundice was excluded because jaundice was not noted until after PTU discontinuation. PTU was discontinued in all reported cases once hepatotoxicity was recognized. 131I treatment of hyperthyroidism after presentation was associated with survival (P=0.024). Four cases received oral iodide; propranolol alone or methimazole was used without complication in seven cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case of a young East Asian male with gout who developed acute immunoallergical hepatitis, complicated by DRESS syndrome with a severe cutaneous reaction, as a result of allopurinol intake. The patient was positive for the HLA-B58*01 gene, a risk factor for allopurinol-induced liver injury, and his liver injury and skin reaction improved with IV methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone. Allopurinol was given at 100 mg daily for about six weeks before the rash appeared.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Young (21-year-old) East Asian/Vietnamese male, positive for HLA-B*58:01, treated for gout with brief concurrent colchicine use; no prior liver disease, no IV drug use, no alcohol history.
raw_record.extra_details: Allopurinol 100 mg daily for long-term gout; hepatocellular injury mediated through a hypersensitivity reaction (acute immunoallergical hepatitis) characterized by fever, rash, facial edema, myalgias, arthralgias, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy. Complicated by DRESS syndrome with desquamating diffuse rash of face, back, arms, hands; fevers and tachycardia; ~6-week latency. Injury resolved with IV methylprednisolone and a course of oral prednisone. Background: chronic allopurinol therapy for gout associated with transient liver enzyme abnormalities in 2-6% of patients that typically resolve spontaneously; in one DILI study 67% of allopurinol-induced DILI cases were associated with DRESS; DRESS carries up to 10% mortality.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes an allopurinol-induced immunoallergic reaction involving fever, acute hepatitis, and DRESS in a patient treated with allopurinol for gout. Transjugular liver biopsy showed a hepatocellular pattern of injury, scattered acidophil bodies, extensive lobular and mixed inflammatory infiltrate, and focal intracellular cholestasis, consistent with medication-induced liver injury from allopurinol. RUCAM scoring gave allopurinol a grade of 7, indicating it is a 'probable' contributor to the liver injury. The patient's liver enzymes and bilirubin returned to normal after 50 days, and the paper notes that in rare cases the sequelae of allopurinol-induced hypersensitivity proved lethal, ranging from cardiac arrest due to DRESS syndrome to fatal liver necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient also took colchicine for the first three days of allopurinol therapy (RUCAM 3, possible contributor, considered less likely cause of the liver injury).

raw_record.support_text: A single 28-year-old woman developed severe liver injury and jaundice after treatment with zileuton 400 mg four times daily for approximately 6 weeks. At discontinuation she was jaundiced with AST 19×ULN, ALT 33×ULN, alkaline phosphatase 1.3×ULN and total bilirubin 6.6×ULN; all viral hepatitis serology was negative and no alternative aetiology was identified. Total bilirubin reached 12.8×ULN 8 days after stopping zileuton; within 35 days ALT and AST returned to normal and bilirubin fell to 2.6×ULN, and the patient fully recovered with normal bilirubin after 70 days. This case was the basis for a long-term liver surveillance study.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult female (28 years old); no pre-existing liver disease noted; no alternative aetiology identified.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency approximately 6 weeks; dose 400 mg four times daily; symptoms fatigue, nausea, itching, influenza-like symptoms; AST 19×ULN, ALT 33×ULN, ALP 1.3×ULN, total bilirubin 6.6×ULN at discontinuation, rising to 12.8×ULN 8 days after stopping; ALT/AST normalized within 35 days, bilirubin normal after 70 days; full recovery; viral hepatitis serology negative; no alternative aetiology identified; motivated a 12-month surveillance study of zileuton liver safety.

raw_record.support_text: A single patient developed hepatocellular jaundice among 2517 patients treated with zileuton in phase II/III clinical trials; in a long-term study of 2458 zileuton-treated patients there were no cases of jaundice, but one patient met a conservative definition of Hy's law. For the total zileuton experience in over 6000 patients, these two cases were used to predict a risk of liver failure of approximately 1 in 30,000 treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Zileuton-associated liver injury signature defined as a hepatocellular injury generally occurring within 3 months of starting therapy and resolving within 1 month of discontinuing therapy; generally asymptomatic, with treatment often continued under monitoring in asymptomatic patients with enzyme elevations between 3 and 5 × ULN. A single treatment-arm patient developed hepatocellular jaundice (total bilirubin >3 mg/dL). Predicted risk of liver failure ~1:30,000 over 6000 treated patients per Hy's law, but true risk is uncertain because incidence as a function of treatment duration is unknown. Paper notes monitoring (stopping when ALT >5 × ULN) likely prevented progression to clinically important liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Drug-induced liver injury from phenylbutazone has been described in at least 75 patients, less common than its myelotoxicity. Susceptibility increases with age and females are more commonly affected. About 65% of cases occurred within a month of starting therapy, while 10% developed after 12 months. Hepatotoxicity occurs in a generalized systemic illness (jaundice, abdominal complaints, rash, fever, arthralgia), and varying hepatic injury types include cholestasis, hepatocellular injury, mixed-hepatocellular injury, and granulomas; hepatocellular injury tends to occur with a generalized reaction whereas cholestasis tends to occur without systemic features.

raw_record.extra_details: DILI described in at least 75 patients; ~65% of cases within one month of therapy onset and 10% after 12 months; hepatotoxicity usually accompanied by systemic illness (jaundice, abdominal complaints, rash, fever, arthralgia), though a minority have liver disease without systemic illness; injury types include cholestasis, hepatocellular injury, mixed-hepatocellular injury, and granulomas; hepatocellular pattern associates with generalized reaction while cholestasis occurs without systemic features.

raw_record.support_text: In 60 patients receiving chronic tramadol treatment at Zagazig University Hospitals, tramadol caused hepatotoxicity: 42 patients with CYP2D6*1 allele developed mild to moderate hepatotoxicity (grade 1-2) within 13-16 months, and 7 patients with the duplicated CYP2D6*DUP allele developed moderate to severe hepatotoxicity (grade 2-3) within 10-11 months. Tramadol-treated patients showed significant increases in serum hepatic damage markers including alpha-glutathione transferase (α-GST) and liver function enzyme activities, especially in carriers of the enhanced or normal-function CYP2D6 alleles, suggesting oxidative stress via accumulation of the active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol (M1).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic tramadol treatment over about 10-16 months; vulnerability attributable to enhanced or normal-function CYP2D6 alleles (CYP2D6*1 and CYP2D6*DUP).
raw_record.extra_details: 60 chronic tramadol-treated patients compared with controls; 42 patients with CYP2D6*1 had mild-to-moderate hepatotoxicity (grade 1-2) within 13-16 months; 7 patients with CYP2D6*DUP had moderate-to-severe hepatotoxicity (grade 2-3) within 10-11 months; higher urinary active metabolite M1 (O-desmethyltramadol), serum lipid peroxidation, and lower total antioxidants in *DUP then *1 carriers; elevated α-GST and liver function enzymes. Authors recommend CYP2D6 genotyping and dose adjustment to avoid hepatotoxicity. The M1 metabolite is discussed as a mechanistic contributor, not independently causal.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that in their patient imatinib mesylate was a probable cause of acute severe hepatitis because other causes were excluded. They note hepatotoxicity has been observed in about 2-5% of patients receiving imatinib, mostly mild elevation of liver enzymes resolving after dose reduction or discontinuation, while imatinib-induced acute severe hepatotoxicity and death from hepatic failure were rarely reported (deaths due to imatinib-induced hepatic failure had been reported in four patients).
raw_record.extra_details: Attribution for the reported patient is 'probable cause' by exclusion of viral, autoimmune, and other causes. Imatinib hepatotoxicity reported in about 2-5% of treated patients, usually mild enzyme elevation resolving after dose reduction or discontinuation; acute severe hepatotoxicity and hepatic-failure deaths rarely reported (four deaths documented). Latency to hepatic dysfunction ranged from 11 days to 18 months across 12 histologically studied cases (Table 2: diagnoses CML, GIST, PV), with histology spanning focal necrosis with lymphocytic infiltration, periportal/massive necrosis, cytolytic acute hepatitis, cholestasis, and autoimmune-hepatitis-like changes (positive anti-liver cytosol 1 and antinuclear antibodies in some cases). Case 6 required liver transplantation and died; case 10 (PV patient) died of extensive hepatic necrosis with microthrombi. Our patient (53, F, GIST) developed acute hepatitis 10 weeks after starting imatinib; after discontinuation she developed grade 2 encephalopathy and acute hepatic failure, which resolved upon prednisolone 0.8 mg/kg/day; biopsy showed sinusoidal congestion, perivenular hepatocyte necrosis, dropout and central hemorrhagic necrosis consistent with drug toxicity. Study reports 12 published cases with histology plus the index case, and cites corticosteroid (prednisone 25-37 mg/day or methylprednisolone 40 mg/day or prednisolone 40 mg/day) reversal of severe imatinib-induced hepatotoxicity in five patients.

raw_record.support_text: Between April 1996 and January 1997 six patients with apparent nimesulide-induced liver injury were admitted and analyzed with a causality scoring system developed by the French and International consensus meeting group. Four women developed centrilobular (three) or panlobular (one) bridging necrosis, whereas two men showed bland intrahepatic cholestasis; jaundice was the presenting symptom in five of six cases, and two cases had eosinophilia/hypersensitivity features. Causality was rated highly probable in one patient, probable in four, and possible in one; one patient died from an unrelated pancreatic tumor, and the others recovered fully within 6 to 17 months.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of severe phenytoin hepatitis in a patient with seizures who initially presented with fever, pharyngitis, rash, and atypical lymphocytosis resembling infectious mononucleosis. After phenytoin was stopped she was inadvertently rechallenged with 1 g of intravenous phenytoin, which was followed by nausea, abdominal pain, edema, exfoliative dermatitis, markedly elevated transaminases (peak SGOT 2900 U, SGPT 1530 U), rising bilirubin (peak 16.0 g/liter), prolonged prothrombin time, and hepatic coma, before recovery. Negative viral serologies and the response to rechallenge supported phenytoin reaction as the etiology. The authors also reviewed 44 additional adequately documented cases of phenytoin hepatitis, in which rash, eosinophilia, and jaundice were typical.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: initial presentation mimicked infectious mononucleosis (fever, pharyngitis, malaise, mild hepatitis, atypical lymphocytosis). Inadvertent rechallenge with 1 g IV phenytoin produced nausea, abdominal pain, facial/oral edema, and severe hepatic necrosis; laboratory findings on day 3 post-rechallenge: total bilirubin 5.6 g/liter, SGOT 2355 U, SGPT 1530 U, alkaline phosphatase 267 IU; peak SGOT 2900 U and SGPT 1530 U on Jan 18; total bilirubin reached 16.0 g/liter with prothrombin time 20.4/11.8 sec and arterial NH3 144 mg; lapsed into hepatic coma, then recovered with resolution of liver tests. Viral serologies and cultures (CSF, blood, urine, cervix) negative, including monospot, EBV titers, ANA, HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HAV-IgM, toxoplasmosis, Brucella, tularemia, and CMV. Authors reviewed 44 additional adequately documented phenytoin hepatitis cases plus this one (45 total); in that series morbiliform rash 90%, exfoliative rash 44%, eosinophilia 56%, jaundice 88%, leukocytosis 70%, lymphadenopathy 70%. Phenytoin was stopped on admission; discharged on valproic acid for seizure disorder.

Mean time from onset to drug discontinuation was 6 days in mild and 14 days in severe hepatitis, suggesting early withdrawal decreases mortality.
