Histology across cases included massive necrosis, focal necrosis, portal inflammation, cholestasis, and granulomas; several patients died of liver failure. No liver biopsy was performed. Hypothyroidism later treated with triiodothyronine 35 μg/day with no recurrence.

raw_record.support_text: The authors attributed the patient's liver injury to levothyroxine because drug exposure preceded onset, underlying liver disease was excluded, cessation led to improvement in liver enzymes, and symptoms recurred rapidly upon rechallenge. A Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale total score of 8 supported a causal effect, and a Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method score of 11 indicated that an adverse drug reaction was highly probable. The improvement on drug cessation argued against transaminitis due to hypothyroidism itself.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of levothyroxine-induced liver injury; Naranjo score 8 and RUCAM score 11 (highly probable). Disproportionate elevation of serum aminotransferases versus alkaline phosphatase, with elevated bilirubin and reduced albumin (albumin reduction attributed to negative acute-phase response). Liver enzymes normalized after drug cessation and recurred on rechallenge. No liver biopsy performed. DIAIH considered but argued against by negative autoimmune antibodies and no need for immunosuppression. One prior report (Kang et al.) observed DILI with levothyroxine tablet but not powder form, suggesting a possible causal role of additives, leaving the mechanism unclear. Treating hypothyroidism with triiodothyronine was effective without liver enzyme derangement.

raw_record.extra_details: Rifampin hepatotoxicity first reported in 1971 with an incidence rate of 5 to 12.5%. Injury classified as hepatocellular (R>=5), cholestatic (R<=2), or mixed (2<R<5) by International Consensus Meeting Criteria. Study: 273 unrelated rifampin-treated patients in Chongqing, China (118 with DILI, 155 without); DILI defined as serum ALT >=3x ULN and/or bilirubin >=2x ULN after rifampin treatment >3 months. Proposed mechanisms include competitive inhibition of hepatocyte bilirubin transport and inhibition of hepatic uptake of bile acid via OATP1B1; functional studies showed markedly reduced bile acid uptake activity for the *15 haplotype.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Exposure was via barium-enema (diagnostic use); affected patients were children in the three deaths and in one of the five Canadian cases halothane anesthesia was also administered (unresolved co-suspect).
raw_record.extra_details: 0.75% tannic acid enemata; deaths of three children (McAlister, 1963); five Canadian cases of fulminating liver failure; vomiting and abdominal pain late same day or next morning after enema, then irritability and drowsiness progressing to jaundice and coma; survival 1-5 days; autopsies in four cases showed generalized haemorrhages and marked centrilobular degeneration and necrosis with survival of peripheral cells and minimal cellular reaction; picture did not resemble acute viral hepatitis; positive Nessler reaction obtained in one case.

A retrospective cohort study of 185 consecutively hospitalized adult patients with paracetamol overdose found 25 who developed severe hepatotoxicity (plasma aminotransferase >1000 IU/L) and 31 with mild to moderate liver injury (aminotransferases above upper normal but below 1000 IU/L); the conclusion attributes this to paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity.

Paper also notes paracetamol poisoning is the most common cause of acute liver failure in developed countries.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine, a pyrimidine nucleoside analogue developed for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B virus infection, is presented as an exemplar of drug hepatotoxicity that caused severe human injury. A subsequent phase II trial was terminated in the 13th week of treatment due to sudden onset of multi-system mitochondrial toxicity involving liver, muscle, nerve, and pancreas. Progressive lactic acidosis and severe hepatotoxicity resulted in five deaths and two emergency liver transplants; liver biopsies revealed hepatocellular lipid accumulation, cholestasis, and mitochondrial abnormalities presumed to result from mitochondrial toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial terminated in the 13th week of treatment for multi-system mitochondrial toxicity involving liver, muscle, nerve, and pancreas; progressive lactic acidosis and severe hepatotoxicity resulted in five deaths and two emergency liver transplants. Liver biopsies revealed hepatocellular lipid accumulation, cholestasis, and mitochondrial abnormalities. Mechanism attributed to mitochondrial toxicity via human ENT1-mediated mitochondrial transport and inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma; retrospective rodent studies (10 weeks at doses 1000 times higher) showed no toxicity, while chimeric mice with humanized livers detected the hepatotoxicity. Fialuridine is 1-(2-deoxy-2-fluoro-1-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouracil, developed for chronic hepatitis B virus infection.

raw_record.support_text: A liver biopsy was taken from a patient suffering ibuprofen (IBU)-induced DILI. An extensive work-up (hepatitis screen, ultrasonography, MRI, ERCP) was normal, and liver biopsy showed severe cholestasis and mild portal inflammation. After metformin was discontinued the liver enzymes normalized except for a persistently increased alkaline phosphatase, attributed to a prolonged cholestatic effect of metformin.

raw_record.support_text: The study aims to present life-threatening paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning and the treatment of acute liver failure occurring after excessive (overdose) drug ingestion. In 2002–2014, 35 patients were hospitalized due to acute paracetamol poisoning and referred from Toxicology Centres across Poland as potential liver transplant candidates, with signs of severe liver failure including elevated transaminases, coagulation deficiency, and impaired consciousness. Paracetamol-induced acute liver failure was assessed according to the King's College Criteria.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury arises after deliberate excessive (supratherapeutic) ingestion of paracetamol in a hospitalized cohort of severe poisonings referred as potential liver transplant candidates.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 35 patients (17 women, 18 men), aged 17–59 years (mean 32.3 years), hospitalized 2002–2014 for acute paracetamol poisoning (PP). Managed in a surgical intensive care unit; candidate selection for urgent LTx used the King's College Criteria (arterial pH <7.3, or INR >6.5, creatinine >3.3 mg/dl, and HE grade 3–4). Median admission labs in the cohort: INR 3.8, AST ~2400 U/l, ALT ~2300 U/l, creatinine 2.2 mg/dl, pH 7.3. Patients received N-acetylcysteine per poisoning guidelines, albumin dialysis (Prometheus/FPSA), and support for hepatic encephalopathy graded by West Haven Scale. The phenotype is overtly acute liver failure rather than a listed canonical histopathologic syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: This paper describes 35 patients with acetaminophen (paracetamol)-induced acute liver failure who were referred to a transplant department as potential liver transplant candidates following toxic poisoning in Poland; all had been treated with N-acetylcysteine without success and their liver function had worsened. Of these, 9 underwent liver transplantation, and 31 of 35 (88.8%) survived, with 4 deaths overall, including one patient who died on the 5th post-operative day from central nervous system brain-stem hemorrhage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute (toxic) overdose/poisoning with paracetamol; a subset had concomitant alcoholic cirrhosis after ingesting a significant quantity of paracetamol; all had failed standard N-acetylcysteine treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 35 patients with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (median ALT 2300 U/l, AST 2400 U/l, INR 3.8). 9 patients underwent liver transplantation (7 with prior albumin dialysis/Prometheus), 4 patients died overall; 31/35 (88.8%) survived. One patient died on post-operative day 5 from brain-stem hemorrhage; 3 non-transplanted patients died due to severe condition/neurological symptoms from coagulation disorders and ventricular hemorrhage. Severe coagulopathy and anemia were managed with pFFP and pRBC transfusions; mean 6 units pFFP and 4 units pRBC per patient.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective randomized trial of LTBI contacts in Taiwan, clinically relevant hepatotoxicity was more common in the 9H (9-month daily isoniazid) group than in the 3 HP (weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid) group (5.3% vs 1.5%; p = 0.103). raw_record.support_text: In an unmatched case-control study of 22 Japanese patients with ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity versus 85 ticlopidine-tolerant Japanese patients, ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity correlated significantly with five HLA alleles (HLA-A*3303, -B*4403, -Cw*1403, -DRB1*1302, -DQB1*0604; Pc<0.01). HLA-A*3303 was present in 68% of cases vs 14% of controls (OR 13.04; 95% CI 4.40–38.59; Pc=1.24×10⁻⁵) and in 86% of the 14 patients with ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity (OR 36.50; 95% CI 7.25–183.82). Severe cholestatic hepatotoxicity occurred more frequently in subjects with HLA-A*3303 and its haplotype, supporting an immune-mediated mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Japanese population; hepatotoxicity believed immune-mediated via ticlopidine-reactive metabolite(s); both cholestatic-type and hepatocellular-type damage observed across cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Anti-platelet agent used for secondary prevention of atherothrombosis. Hepatotoxicity mainly of cholestatic type; increased rate of hepatic adverse reactions reported in Japanese vs Caucasian patients. HLA-A*3303 in 15/22 (68%) all-hepatotoxicity cases vs 12/85 (14%) tolerant controls (OR 13.04; 95% CI 4.40–38.59; Pc=1.24×10⁻⁵) and in 12/14 (86%) cholestatic cases (OR 36.50; 95% CI 7.25–183.82; Pc=7.32×10⁻⁷). Haplotype HLA-A*3303/-B*4403/-Cw*1403/-DRB1*1302/-DQB1*0604 in 12/22 (55%) cases (10 cholestatic) vs 9/85 (11%) controls. Hepatocellular-type-damage patients lacked these alleles. Mechanism proposed via reactive metabolite of the thiophene ring, analogous to tienilic acid (CYP2C9).

raw_record.support_text: The study identified 22 Japanese patients with ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity (cases) and 85 ticlopidine-treated patients with no adverse reactions (controls). The diagnosis of ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity was based on clinical history and laboratory findings (serum bilirubin >1.5 mg/dL or serum AST/ALT at least twice the upper limit of normal), and cases were divided into cholestatic (n=14), mixed (n=5), and hepatocellular (n=3) damage categories per Danan's criteria. There were no differences in age, gender, or ticlopidine dosage between groups; all subjects were Hondo Japanese.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a patient who developed nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fatigue 2 weeks after starting rosiglitazone therapy, and state that they believe the most likely cause of his symptoms and elevated liver enzyme levels was rosiglitazone-associated hepatotoxicity. Rosiglitazone was discontinued on admission, symptoms immediately improved, and liver enzyme levels returned to normal over ensuing weeks. Because the patient had no fever, rash, or eosinophilia, the authors concluded the liver injury caused by rosiglitazone seemed to be idiosyncratic rather than a classic immune mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: patient was an icteric, obese male with prior acetaminophen use (up to 4 g/d for 2 years, 3-4 tablets daily 3 months before admission) and prior brief exposures to troglitazone (discontinued after 1 week for nausea) and repaglinide (discontinued for nausea/dizziness); acetaminophen level on admission was 3.2 µg/mL (normal 10-30). Symptoms appeared ~2 weeks after starting rosiglitazone; rosiglitazone was discontinued on admission; symptoms resolved and liver enzymes returned to normal 7 weeks after discontinuation. No signs of hepatic failure at any time; aspartate aminotransferase fell rapidly while ALT remained elevated during 8 days of hospitalization. No fever, rash, or eosinophilia (peripheral eosinophil count 90 x 10^6/L). Abdominal CT consistent with fatty liver.

After cyclophosphamide and glatiramer acetate were suspended and IVIG added (with methylprednisolone maintained), she had further episodes of acute hepatitis and liver enzyme elevation, including three episodes while medicated only with high doses of methylprednisolone, with liver biopsy showing focal centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis with minimal interface hepatitis. raw_record.support_text: A patient admitted with markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 1,581 IU/L, ALT 2,540 IU/L, ALP 734 IU/L, γ-GTP 553 IU/L, T-Bil 7.82 mg/dL), prolonged prothrombin time, and slight liver atrophy on CT had negative viral and autoimmune markers. A drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test (DLST) for isoniazid (INH) was positive [249 S.I. (>180%)], and the patient was diagnosed with INH-induced hepatitis. Despite discontinuing INH and starting ursodeoxycholic acid, the injury progressed to acute liver failure with Grade II hepatic encephalopathy; the patient rejected proposed liver transplantation and died of liver failure four months after admission.

raw_record.support_text: Eleven cases of hepatic injury were attributed to the intake of flucloxacillin and reported to the Netherlands Center for Monitoring of Adverse Reactions to Drugs between 1982 and 1992. The biochemical pattern was compatible with cholestatic hepatitis in seven cases, mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular injury in one, hepatocellular pattern in two, and mild liver enzyme elevations in one. Two patients died, one from fatal bleeding from the liver after biopsy and one from combined hepatic and cardiac failure; the rest recovered. In paragraph 9, the causal relationship was assessed as 'probable' in eight cases and 'possible' in three.
raw_record.extra_details: Eleven patients (4 men, 7 women; mean age 57 years) treated for staphylococcal infection; oral flucloxacillin 1500-4000 mg/day for 2-28 days; symptoms appeared about 10-30 days after start. Causal relationship 'probable' in 8 cases (no. 1-8) and 'possible' in 3 (no. 9-11) using temporal-relationship plus exclusion-of-other-causes criteria. Biochemical patterns: cholestatic hepatitis in 7, mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular in 1, hepatocellular in 2, mild liver enzyme elevations in 1; peripheral eosinophilia in 3; autoantibodies absent; hepatitis A/B (and some C), CMV, and infectious mononucleosis serologically excluded; extrahepatic cholestasis excluded by ultrasonography. Histology in 7 cases showed cholestatic hepatitis in 5 (with cholangitis/cholangiolitis in 4), centrilobular cholestasis with bridging fibrosis, and portal-central bridging necrosis in the others. Two deaths: fatal liver bleeding after biopsy, and combined hepatic and cardiac failure; survivors recovered on average 72 days (range 17-180) after peak aminotransferases. Case 4 developed injury on three occasions after flucloxacillin; her second-biopsy hepatocellular damage had initially been attributed to ranitidine and diclofenac before flucloxacillin causality was recognized. Nine patients used other drugs concurrently but, except case 11, continued them without recurrent injury.

raw_record.support_text: After ingestion of acetaminophen overdoses, abnormally large amounts of the toxic metabolite intermediate are formed; the toxic metabolite binds covalently to vital hepatocellular protein macromolecules, thereby causing hepatic necrosis (Fig. 1 and Table 1 quantify the relationship among plasma acetaminophen concentration, time after ingestion, and percent probability of occurrence of hepatotoxicity in man).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury described specifically after acetaminophen overdosage ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen is primarily cleared through hepatic microsomal biotransformation; a toxic reactive metabolite binds covalently to hepatocellular proteins, injuring the hepatic endoplasmic reticulum and causing hepatic necrosis. Elimination half-life increases after overdosage in patients with hepatotoxicity; a half-life exceeding 4 h makes hepatic necrosis likely, and over 12 h hepatic coma must be expected. A computer-derived nomogram (Rumack-Matthew, based on Prescott data) relates plasma acetaminophen concentration and time after ingestion to percent probability of hepatotoxicity; patients with 4-h levels >300 µg/ml all incurred liver damage while those <120 µg/ml had no evidence of liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) is commonly taken in overdose and can cause acute liver injury via its toxic metabolite NAPQI formed by the cytochrome P450 pathway. In this Australian prospective observational (ATOM) study of 200 patients following acute APAP ingestion, 26 developed hepatotoxicity (peak ALT > 1,000 U/L) defined as the primary outcome; those who developed hepatotoxicity had higher CYP-metabolite concentrations on presentation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute APAP overdose (deliberate self-poisoning or accidental overdose); the paper notes APAP is safe at recommended doses in healthy individuals.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury occurs via the toxic metabolite NAPQI formed by CYP P450 2E1 and 3A4; in overdose glutathione becomes depleted and NAPQI binds to cellular sulfhydryl proteins, causing oxidative stress, mitochondrial injury, hepatocyte necrosis, and acute liver failure. APAP toxicity is described as a leading cause of acute liver failure in North America, Europe and Australia. Study details: median ingested dose 20 g; 191/200 patients received acetylcysteine at median 5.8 h post-ingestion; 26 patients developed hepatotoxicity. Hepatotoxicity patients had higher total CYP metabolite concentrations (36.8 vs 10.8 μmol/L), higher CYP-metabolite proportion (5.4% vs 1.7%, P<0.001), lower APAP-Sul concentration (49.1 vs 78.7 μmol/L) and lower APAP-Sul percentage (6.3% vs 13.1%). APAP-Cys and APAP-Mer (NAPQI conjugates) were measured as metabolites; NAPQI protein adducts quantified as APAP-Cys. Metabolites proposed for early identification of high-risk patients for possible adjunct therapy (e.g., fomepizole).

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute single-ingestion overdose in adults (median ingested dose 20 g, IQR 10-41 g); patients with repeated supratherapeutic ingestion and those presenting >24 h post-ingestion were excluded; 20% co-ingested ethanol.
raw_record.extra_details: Of the 200 included patients, 140 (70%) were female, median age 25 years, median weight 65 kg; 152 immediate-release, 48 modified-release/combo ingestions. 26 (13%) developed hepatotoxicity; 15 had INR > 2.0 (5 with INR > 5.0); 4 developed severe acute kidney injury (AKIN stage 3). One liver transplant and one death (respiratory failure secondary to aspiration 30 h post-ingestion). 42 patients developed peak ALT > 100 U/L. 191 (96%) received acetylcysteine. Cohorts compared immediate-release vs modified-release ingestions.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is presented as the well-established clinical example of drug-induced liver injury in humans, for which NAC is the only approved antidote. In plasma of APAP overdose patients, APAP protein adducts correlated with the severity of liver injury, and markers of mitochondrial injury (glutamate dehydrogenase activity; mitochondrial DNA) were detected in APAP overdose patients with substantial liver injury. Clinical findings support that necrosis is the dominant form of cell death, with massive release of cell contents including liver enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: NAC is the only approved treatment for APAP hepatotoxicity. Formation of a reactive metabolite with GSH depletion and protein binding originally shown in mice; APAP protein adducts in plasma of overdose patients correlated with severity of liver injury and support reactive-metabolite formation and protein binding in humans. Mitochondrial injury markers (glutamate dehydrogenase activity, mitochondrial DNA) were raised in overdose patients with substantial liver injury, correlating with mitochondrial damage. Low/variable levels of a caspase-dependent cleavage product of cytokeratin-18 have been detected, but necrosis is considered the dominant cell death mode; mechanisms in mice and primary mouse hepatocytes are also observed in human hepatocyte cell lines and patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with type 2 diabetes developed liver injury 49 days after starting ipragliflozin (50 mg/day) to replace sulfonylurea: AST rose from 13 to 622 U/L, ALT from 9 to 266 U/L, ALP from 239 to 752 U/L, and γ-GTP from 19 to 176 U/L, with total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV serologies were negative, while a lymphocyte transformation test for ipragliflozin was positive. CT showed mild fatty liver. After discontinuing ipragliflozin with liver supportive therapy, he was discharged 18 days later with AST and ALT reduced to 20 and 13 U/L. The authors describe this as a case of ipragliflozin-induced liver injury, emphasizing the need to monitor liver function during SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.

raw_record.extra_details: Ipragliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor) 50 mg/day; liver injury developed 49 days after start. Peak AST 622 U/L, ALT 266 U/L, ALP 752 U/L, γ-GTP 176 U/L; total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL (no jaundice), ZTT 3.5 U, TTT 0.4 U. Negative IgM hepatitis A antibody, hepatitis B antigen, hepatitis C virus antibody, IgM CMV antibody, and IgM EB VCA antibody; positive lymphocyte transformation test for ipragliflozin. Abdominal CT showed mild fatty liver with no nodular lesions. Patient was admitted for liver supportive therapy and discharged 18 days later with AST 20 U/L and ALT 13 U/L after discontinuation. Report recommends monitoring liver function during SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective review (1992-2002) of children admitted with paracetamol overdose induced significant hepatotoxicity was performed at the national liver unit, Birmingham Children's Hospital. Significant hepatotoxicity was defined as serum ALT or AST >1000 IU/l (normal 10-40 IU/l), and severe hepatocellular injury was defined as hepatic failure with ALT/AST >1000 IU/l, altered mental status, and/or coagulopathy (prothrombin time increased >50% above the upper limit of normal). Of 51 patients, group II (n=11) developed fulminant liver failure and required listing for orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT); all received the antidote N-acetylcysteine except 4 patients referred in 1992-93.

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective case series of 51 children (median age ~13-14 years; group I n=40 recovered conservatively, group II n=11 required OLT listing). Significant hepatotoxicity defined as peak ALT/AST >1000 IU/l; severe hepatocellular injury required hepatic failure with ALT/AST >1000 IU/l, altered mental status, and/or coagulopathy. Reported paracetamol doses ~285-348 mg/kg (range 91-645 mg/kg); doses >150 mg/kg considered hepatotoxic; delayed presentation (up to 96 h) increased risk of clinically significant hepatocellular injury. All patients received standard acute-liver-failure protocol management with N-acetylcysteine except 4/51 referred 1992-93. A grade ≥III encephalopathy was present in all group II patients; the King's College Hospital criteria (PT >100 s, creatinine >300 µmol/l, pH <7.30, encephalopathy ≥grade III) predicting <10% survival without transplant were assessed but not validated in children.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical characteristics of 51 children (6 males) with paracetamol induced significant hepatotoxicity are described. The median age was 14.7 years, with a bimodal distribution; 6/51 children were less than 7 years. In adolescent patients overdose was usually an impulsive act with female predominance (43/45). The median dose for single paracetamol ingestion was 345 mg/kg (range 91-645). Two patients who took supratherapeutic doses (97 and 127 mg/kg) showed significant hepatotoxicity without encephalopathy and survived. 27% with significant hepatotoxicity received N-acetylcysteine treatment despite paracetamol level being less than the nomogram treatment line.

raw_record.support_text: In children with paracetamol overdose, encephalopathy grade II resolved spontaneously, whereas those with grade ≥III died or required orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT); in this study all children with grade III were listed for OLT but only 18% survived. The main cause of death was progressive irreversible cerebral oedema following extensive hepatic necrosis and fulminant liver failure, indicating severe hepatocellular injury after paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic transaminase levels were markedly elevated in both study groups. Jaundice was not an apparent clinical feature although serum bilirubin was significantly elevated. Poor-prognosis risk factors included severe coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy grade, raised serum creatinine, and metabolic acidosis; PT >100 s had 88% sensitivity and 61% positive predictive value for death. Predictors of listing for transplantation: PT >50 s considered for listing, PT >100 s worse prognosis; encephalopathy grade ≥III was the single best prognostic indicator. In children, development of hepatic encephalopathy grade III or higher was the best predictor of outcome and listing for transplant.

raw_record.support_text: In a mixed USA and UK patient cohort of paracetamol overdose patients, paracetamol-induced liver injury was confirmed by established liver injury markers, with serum total HMGB1 and miR-122 substantially elevated and correlating with ALT activity. Necrosis (85%) and apoptosis (15%) of hepatocytes were identified as features of paracetamol-induced liver injury in humans, and paracetamol overdose patients who died, required a liver transplant, or met the King's College Criteria for liver transplantation had elevated immune-derived (acetylated) HMGB1. The paper frames therapeutic paracetamol doses as producing only transient ALT rises without clinically significant liver injury.

A 129-patient UK cohort study showed biomarkers (miR-122, HMGB1, necrosis K18) were elevated at first admission before ALT and predicted subsequent liver injury in 15/99 patients with initially normal liver tests. A case report described paracetamol-induced acute liver injury missed by standard biomarkers at first presentation where miR-122 was elevated 50-fold. Antidote NAC treatment discussed; therapeutic doses (7 days) in healthy volunteers produced transient ALT increases and proportionally more apoptotic cell death without clinically significant injury.

raw_record.support_text: In this single-centre study of paracetamol overdose, 21 of 118 patients (18%) developed hepatotoxicity, defined as a peak ALT >1000 U/L. Those who developed hepatotoxicity had a significantly longer median time to acetylcysteine treatment (16.5 h; IQR 6.8–22.4) versus those who did not (4.5 h; IQR 3–7.8, p < .0001). In multivariable analysis, larger ingested paracetamol dose, higher paracetamol ratio, and longer time to acetylcysteine were independently associated with increased risk of hepatotoxicity, with adjusted ORs of 1.46 (95% CI 1.15–1.86) per 100 mg/kg dose increment and 2.13 (95% CI 1.32–3.45) per increase in paracetamol ratio.

No hepatotoxicity patient required liver transplant or developed hepatic encephalopathy. One death in the study (87-year-old male) was from respiratory failure secondary to aspiration 30 h post-ingestion, unrelated to liver failure. Two patients developed AKIN stage 3 acute renal injury (peak creatinine 500 and 600 umol/L). raw_record.support_text: In this case, the likely cause of liver failure was chronic use of nitrofurantoin, supported by liver histology corroborating a drug-induced cause. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Score was 6 out of 13, indicating a probable adverse drug reaction to nitrofurantoin. The patient, who had taken nitrofurantoin at 100 mg twice daily for 12 months, developed jaundice with transaminitis, direct hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated INR; liver biopsy on day 4 showed active hepatitis with prominent parenchymal necrosis and accompanying cholestatic elements compatible with drug-induced (nitrofurantoin) liver injury. She developed refractory hepatic encephalopathy and ascites, was deemed unsuitable for transplant, and died on day 24.

Presenting labs: ALT 1219 U/L, AST 1497 U/L, ALP 361 U/L, GGT 511 U/L, total bilirubin 203 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 161 µmol/L, INR 2.1. raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman with ER-positive/PR-negative/HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer experienced Grade 3 hepatotoxicity following initiation of a clinical trial of fulvestrant, palbociclib, and erdafitinib. Fulvestrant was determined to be the drug most likely responsible for this hepatotoxic effect. The case report details the timing and nature of this drug-induced liver injury.

raw_record.extra_details: 49-year-old woman; Grade 3 hepatotoxicity. The paper notes this adds support to an area with little published work on the detailed course/timing of fulvestrant-induced liver injury; fulvestrant is associated with asymptomatic, transient, non-dose-limiting serum liver enzyme elevations in up to 15% of patients, exceeding 5x upper limit of normal in only 1-2%; one prior case report described clinically apparent hepatotoxicity following fulvestrant that resolved within 2 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: This case report of fulvestrant-associated hepatotoxicity in a breast cancer patient documents that nausea and fatigue occurred 2 days after fulvestrant injection, worsening right upper quadrant pain continued over the next 2 days and largely resolved by Day 7, and AST and ALT elevations reached Grade 3 by Day 8 (peaking on Day 9-10 and resolving by/partially by Day 15). The authors state the data add support to prior suggestions that fulvestrant, although rarely, can cause severe elevations in liver enzymes, showing this hepatotoxicity can be severe and symptomatic and is reversible with discontinuation of the drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Breast cancer patient receiving fulvestrant as endocrine therapy; single-agent attribution based on a case report.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset 2 days after injection, nausea/fatigue and worsening RUQ pain resolving by Day 7; AST Grade 3 within 8 days, peaked Day 9, normal by Day 15; ALT Grade 3 by Day 8, peaked Day 10, Grade 2 by Day 15; alkaline phosphatase Grade 1 by Day 8, peaked Day 10, remained Grade 1 by Day 15. Injury reversible with drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Fulvestrant is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4; toxic or immunogenic metabolic products proposed as possible mechanism, exact mechanism uncertain.

raw_record.support_text: Two hundred intentional paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose cases were identified (median dose ingested 50 g, IQR 45–60 g, median time to presentation 3.5 h). Twenty-eight (14%) patients developed hepatotoxicity, with a further 9 (5%) having a peak ALT between 150 and <1000 U/L. Those who developed hepatotoxicity had a significantly longer time to treatment (13.9 h) than those who did not (6 h, p<0.001). One patient required a liver transplant despite acetylcysteine being commenced 2.5 h post-ingestion; there was one death unrelated to paracetamol ingestion. The 200 patients were identified across four sites with comparable data.

raw_record.extra_details: 28/200 (14%) developed hepatotoxicity and 9/200 (5%) had peak ALT 150–1000 U/L. Median time to treatment 13.9 h in hepatotoxic patients vs 6 h in non-hepatotoxic (p<0.001). Six patients who developed hepatotoxicity had treatment within 8 h (paracetamol ratios 2.7, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.5, 5.8); one patient required liver transplant despite acetylcysteine started 2.5 h post-ingestion; one death unrelated to paracetamol. Median paracetamol ratio 1.9; 79 (40%) had initial concentration more than double the 150 mg/L 4-h nomogram line. Activated charcoal within 4 h associated with 45% decrease in paracetamol ratio (adjusted RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.43–0.69).

raw_record.support_text: This study of 'massive' paracetamol overdose highlights prolonged absorption and persistently high concentrations in these patients, with some showing delayed paracetamol peak concentrations out to 60 h suggesting pharmacobezoar formation. Acetylcysteine within hours of the overdose did not prevent severe liver injury in several patients. The paper confirms that very high early paracetamol concentrations are an independent risk factor for hepatotoxicity even when acetylcysteine is given, with hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 U/L in this high-dose cohort.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as ALT >1000 U/L despite IV acetylcysteine given within 8 h of ingestion; high early paracetamol ratio (above the 300 mg/L at 4 h nomogram line) was an independent risk factor for hepatotoxicity even when adjusted for time to acetylcysteine and ratio. In patients presenting within 16 h of ingesting ≥40 g receiving 'standard' treatment (no activated charcoal, standard acetylcysteine dose), hepatotoxicity rate was 11% (n=10/87), vs 5% (n=4/87) with activated charcoal or increased acetylcysteine. Toxic intermediate NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) discussed as the metabolite acetylcysteine detoxifies; NAPQI not independently blamed as separate causal entity. Activated charcoal within 4 h associated with reduced paracetamol concentrations and reduced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In a 1993 Phase II clinical trial of fialuridine (FIAU), a nucleoside analogue for treatment of hepatitis B, 7 of 15 subjects unexpectedly developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis and pancreatic failure and subsequently died by week 13. Liver histology revealed steatosis and cholestasis, and electron microscopy showed hepatocytes with cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria with a reduced number of cristae.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial conducted in 1993 in 15 subjects with HBV infection; trial terminated by week 13. 7 subjects developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis and pancreatic failure and died. Histology: steatosis and cholestasis; electron microscopy: cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria with reduced cristae. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, dogs, and monkeys provided no indication of such toxicity; rats tolerated 510 mg/kg-day (2,000-fold the maximum human dose) for 10 weeks. The paper concludes FIAU has a direct toxic effect on human hepatocytes that does not require a comorbidity (e.g., viral infection) and is not immune mediated.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of 94 reports to the Swedish Adverse Drug Reaction Committee of patients with liver injury after surgery and halothane anaesthesia (including 13 fatal cases) revealed no other factors responsible for the liver injury than the halothane administration. Eighty-two percent of the total material and 12 of 13 fatal cases had multiple exposures, and the liver injury appeared more severe after repeated exposures, with higher maximum serum bilirubin and SGOT values after an increasing number of halothane exposures.

It states that malnutrition, starvation, chronic alcohol misuse, and concomitant use of cytochrome P450-inducing drugs increase the risk of paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity, and argues for considering dose reduction in those with low body weight and/or other risk factors.

raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 (43-year-old man): AST 12,769 IU/l, INR 9.1, severe lactic acidosis, paracetamol concentration 92 mg/l despite supervised standard maximum adult dose; no other cause identified (never hypotensive, negative viral serology); treated with N-acetylcysteine but died 12 days later of multiorgan failure. Case 2 (32-year-old woman with chronic alcoholism): peak AST 7,116 IU/l, INR 3.2, paracetamol concentration 105 mg/l; recovered with supportive care including N-acetylcysteine and discharged after 15 days. Mechanism: paracetamol is metabolized by glucuronidation/sulfation; 5-10% is converted by cytochrome P450 to reactive NAPQI, which overwhelms glutathione and binds hepatocyte macromolecules causing necrotic cell death. Prescribing information considers total 4 g daily safe in adults; paracetamol is described as the commonest cause of acute liver failure in western Europe.

raw_record.support_text: A 47-yr-old male presented with fever, chills, myalgia, nausea, vomiting and skin rash about 6 hr after antiparasitic (albendazole) ingestion 2 days before. Labs showed AST 5,402 IU/L, ALT 4,622 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 40 IU/L and total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL; viral, autoimmune, alcoholic and metabolic hepatitis were ruled out. Liver biopsy showed periportal invasion of inflammatory cells, cytotoxic necrosis and steatosis. He had a prior history of albendazole-associated hepatitis 3 yr earlier. The patient was diagnosed with toxic acute hepatitis due to a CIOMS (RUCAM) score of 9 and improved with conservative treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM/CIOMS causality score of 9 (compatible with drug-induced hepatitis). Liver biopsy showed periportal steatosis and periportal necrosis with inflammatory cell invasion. Symptoms (fever, chill, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, skin rash) developed within 6-12 hr of ingestion; mild eosinophilia (8.2%). AST 5,402 IU/L, ALT 4,622 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 40 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL, r-GTP 101 IU/L. Rapid improvement by day 8 (AST 35, ALT 301). Previous history of albendazole ingestion in 2002 with rise in liver tests, and repeat episode in 2005. No prior literature found on albendazole-induced hepatitis requiring admission; in clinical trials mild-moderate hepatic enzyme elevations in approximately 16% of patients, generally returning to normal on discontinuation.

ALT was increased to 4,622 IU/L with ALP within normal limits, classified as hepatocellular-type injury, and liver biopsy showed features of acute hepatocellular hepatitis. raw_record.support_text: In a post-marketing case series of 14 cases of clinically significant DILI associated with dimethyl fumarate (DMF), causality was assessed as probable for 11 cases. No cases resulted in transplant or death, but 10 cases resulted in hospitalization; severity was moderate/moderate-severe in eight and mild in six. The pattern of liver injury was categorized as hepatocellular for 12/14 cases based on an R value ≥5.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality assessed as probable for 11 of 14 clinically significant DILI cases. Severity moderate to moderate-severe in eight and mild in six; 10 cases resulted in hospitalization; no transplant or death. Mean time to event onset 101 days (median 83.5, range 4 to 302 days); seven cases occurred within 1 month of DMF initiation. DMF discontinued in all cases; ALT/bilirubin returned to normal within days to weeks. Two cases had liver biopsies consistent with DILI; hepatocellular pattern in 12/14 cases (R value ≥5), two cases lacked AP so R value not calculated but ALT exceeded 20x ULN. Seven cases met ATs >3x ULN with TBili >2x ULN; five fulfilled Hy's law criteria. Reported DILI mechanisms include hypersensitivity, autoimmune hepatitis, or infection; four cases had eosinophil elevations including one probable DRESS. Demographics: 12 female, 2 male, ages 25-56, mean/median age 42.

raw_record.support_text: Between 1980 and 2010, 162 in-hospital deaths were associated with an acetaminophen (APAP) ingestion, with 93 adjudicated as APAP deaths by Roussel Uclaf Causality Factor (RCF) levels 'Undoubtedly responsible', 'Probably responsible', or 'Contributory'. APAP deaths typically presented with supratherapeutic APAP concentrations and hepatotoxicity (median AST or ALT 4000 IU/L), acidaemia (arterial pH 7.22), coagulopathy (INR 3.8) and/or encephalopathy; the median time from hospital presentation to death was 53 hours for APAP deaths, and four cases who underwent liver transplant died nonetheless.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of 162 in-hospital deaths associated with APAP ingestion, 1980-2010. RCF causality levels: Undoubtedly responsible n=26, Probably responsible n=40, Contributory n=27 (deemed APAP deaths, n=93); Probably/Clearly not responsible n=39 non-APAP deaths; Unknown n=30. APAP deaths showed supratherapeutic APAP concentrations, hepatotoxicity with median AST/ALT 4000 IU/L, arterial pH 7.22, INR 3.8, encephalopathy; cerebral oedema in records of 55/63 patients deemed APAP deaths. Four liver-transplanted cases died, all adjudicated 'Undoubtedly' due to APAP. Median time from presentation to death 53 h (APAP deaths) vs 103 h (non-APAP). 12% had documented acute single APAP ingestion at known time. Acetylcysteine started median 12 h from end of ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: The study examined a cohort of acetaminophen-related fatalities to evaluate established prognostic criteria (King's College Hospital, MELD, lactate, phosphate) for identifying patients who die from APAP. APAP-induced fulminant liver failure (fulminant hepatic failure) is explicitly attributed as the cause of death in the 93 adjudicated APAP deaths, confirming acetaminophen overdose as a cause of fatal human hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning setting in a fatalities-only cohort; attribution to APAP adjudicated as responsible for or contributory to death.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 162 acetaminophen poisoning fatalities, of which 93 were adjudicated as APAP deaths and 39 as non-APAP deaths (30 unknown). Presenting features included hepatic encephalopathy (grades 0-4), elevated aminotransferases, INR, lactate and phosphate. Prognostic criteria assessed included KCH criteria (sensitivity 0.85), MELD ≥33 (0.55), lactate ≥3.5 mmol/L (0.86), phosphate ≥1.2 mmol/L at 48+ h (0.83), and KCH or lactate (0.94). raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the development of the acetaminophen (paracetamol, APAP) nomogram using 30 previously published untreated cases from the Edinburgh Poisons Unit plus 34 additional unpublished untreated cases, plotting initial plasma APAP levels against time to discriminate patients who subsequently developed hepatotoxicity (defined as serum AST > 1000 IU) from those who did not. All 64 cases were untreated with antidotes (NAC, methionine, or cysteamine). The 1971 publication had stated that plasma levels greater than 300 µg/mL at 4 hours and 50 µg/mL at 12 hours were associated with toxicity, and the additional untreated cases led to lowering the 4-hour level to 200 µg/mL, so the nomogram line was drawn from 200 µg/mL at 4 hours to 50 µg/mL at 12 hours (a 4-hour half-life slope). The nomogram was intended to predict whether patients would develop hepatic toxicity after a single acute APAP overdose, based on an initial plasma level obtained 4 or more hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single acute oral overdose with a measured initial plasma level obtained 4 or more hours after ingestion; nomogram not intended for chronic ingestions.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as serum SGOT/AST greater than 1000 IU at any time during the hospital course. Based on 30 published plus 34 unpublished untreated cases (all untreated with N-acetylcysteine, methionine, or cysteamine). The 1971 publication correlated levels >300 µg/mL at 4 h and >50 µg/mL at 12 h with toxicity, and a half-life >4 h with likely toxicity and >12 h with likely hepatic coma; the revised nomogram threshold was 200 µg/mL at 4 h to 50 µg/mL at 12 h (4-hour half-life slope). Therapeutic oral absorption of APAP is 70-90% with peak plasma values at 20-90 min. Co-ingested propoxyphene was noted to delay gastric emptying, favoring sampling at 4 h or later.

Mechanism discussion (paragraph 21) indicates the present case was attributed to hypersensitivity to captopril because the patient, despite renal failure, received a low dose and underwent haemodialysis three times a week without captopril supplementation.

raw_record.extra_details: Jaundice and elevated liver biochemistry appeared around the time of captopril treatment; within three days of withdrawal the jaundice almost disappeared and the biochemical pattern progressively returned to normal, supporting dechallenge. A previously described captopril case resulted in death due to hepatic failure secondary to hepatic necrosis. Mechanism speculated to be hypersensitivity (the authors' view for this case) or a direct toxic effect via kinase II inhibition increasing prostaglandins and leukotrienes; the low dose was argued to weigh against dose-related direct toxicity. No cross-reaction between captopril and ACE inhibitors lacking a proline has been reported (reference [10]).

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that methyldopa is undoubtedly hepatotoxic, based on a strong temporal relation between drug administration and the development of jaundice, and in four patients the reappearance of liver damage after a second exposure (rechallenge) provided ultimate proof. They acknowledge that coincidental viral hepatitis cannot always be excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: The resulting hepatic reaction to methyldopa spanned a wide spectrum clinically and histologically. Case 9 showed typical features of chronic aggressive hepatitis with lobular distortion, irregular septa, bridging, and plasma cells in the infiltrate. Case 13, examined at necropsy, showed massive hepatic necrosis with a 540 g liver and surviving islands indicating attempted regeneration with nodule formation. Two patients in the series had predominantly cholestatic hepatitis, described as unusual. Rechallenge reproduced liver damage in four patients. A mixed inflammatory portal infiltrate with eosinophils was noted to help distinguish methyldopa liver damage from viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Non-dose-related or idiosyncratic valproate hepatotoxicity occurs rarely (about 1 case in 20,000) and is characterized by fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy, impaired coagulation, high serum transaminase levels (100-8,000 IU/dl), and cholestasis. Onset typically occurs about 2 months after starting valproate therapy and nearly always within 6-12 months; most or nearly all cases are fatal, and typical histopathology is microvesicular steatosis and necrosis.

Liver function declined on day 4; dose reduction and tacrolimus resumption did not reverse deterioration. A liver biopsy showed cytotoxic injury, and the updated RUCAM scale evaluation gave 7 points, indicating 'probable' causality between tigecycline and liver injury. raw_record.support_text: In a series of 30 patients with clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH), initial liver biopsies mostly showed acute hepatitis, with 17 cases (68%) being acute cytolytic hepatitis (centrolobular clarified and balloonized hepatocytes, two with multinucleated giant hepatocytes and two with moderate eosinophilic infiltration). Seven patients (28%) showed stigmas of chronic active hepatitis, and one case showed micronodular cirrhosis. A repeat biopsy after rechallenge with clometacin in one patient showed severe acute hepatitis with aggravation of hepatic lobule lesions. Mortality related to the first hepatitis was 13% (4/30), with three patients dying in the acute phase of hepatocellular insufficiency with hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: 30-patient case series of clometacin-induced hepatitis with autoimmune features. Histology: 68% acute cytolytic hepatitis, 28% chronic active hepatitis, 1 case micronodular cirrhosis; rechallenge in one patient aggravated lesions. First-hepatitis mortality 13% (4/30): 3 died rapidly of hepatocellular insufficiency with hepatic encephalopathy, 1 in the 4th month after downhill progression. The 26 survivors clinically and biochemically recovered within ~2 months of drug withdrawal, with anti-tissue antibodies (anti-actin cable, anti-N, anti-M2) becoming undetectable 3-9 months after clometacin withdrawal. Autoimmune markers: anti-smooth muscle (anti-actin cable) antibody present in 70% (21/30); anti-actin cable positivity in 19; anti-N in 16 (14 in common with anti-SM); transient drug-induced anti-M2 in 2; anti-LKM absent. Mean serum gammaglobulin 23 g/l, >18 g/l in 73%.

raw_record.support_text: From our 30 cases and several other reports it appears that clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH) is idiosyncratic in nature: absence of dose dependence (dose was 4 times less than the pharmacological dose in 25% of patients), low incidence of toxicity under therapy (about 60 cases of hepatotoxicity reported per about 1 million people treated), and prompt recurrence following rechallenge, which also occurred in 7 of our patients. Some features of CIH resemble autoimmune chronic active hepatitis (lupoid hepatitis).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Marked female predominance (97%) in the series; autoimmune/lupoid-like features; rechallenge setting described separately.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 cases of clometacin-induced hepatitis (CIH). Low incidence: ~60 hepatotoxicity cases per ~1 million treated. Dose was 4 times below the pharmacological dose in 25% of patients. Rechallenge in 7 patients reproduced chills, fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and jaundice with transaminase elevations; incubation periods shortened with each exposure (1-120 days, median 22 days for the second episode; 1 day for the third). No death from rechallenge; transaminases normalized within days to 2 months. Hypergammaglobulinemia and anti-tissue antibodies (anti-SM of anti-actin type and anti-N) present.

INH-induced hepatitis (INH-H) or elevated liver enzymes including hepatitis (INH-ELE) was diagnosed using the clinical diagnostic scale (CDS). CYP2E1 *1A/*1A genotype was significantly associated with INH-ELE (OR 3.4; 95% CI 1.1-12; p=0.02) and showed a nonsignificant trend for INH-H (OR 5.9; 95% CI 0.69-270; p=0.13); PPV 39% (95% CI 26-54%) and NPV 84% (95% CI 69-94%). raw_record.support_text: Several cases of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) secondary to imatinib use have been reported in the literature; among individuals taking imatinib for GIST, only six cases of DILI have been reported. The pattern is usually hepatocellular, although cholestatic patterns have been reported as well. The development of imatinib-induced severe acute hepatitis, as in the presented patient, ranges from within one week of starting the medication to several years out, and discontinuation proved effective.

raw_record.extra_details: Index case: liver biopsy showed moderate steatosis, portal inflammation, ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes (hepatocellular injury), mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes and occasional eosinophils), loss of liver cell plate cohesion, and mild fibrosis. Transaminases decreased after imatinib discontinuation (AST 483 U/L, ALT 544 U/L) and returned to normal within two months. Latency of imatinib-induced severe acute hepatitis reported from within one week up to several years. Discontinuation of the medication proved effective in reported cases; some case reports demonstrated a role for immunosuppression with prednisone. The paper also notes the usual pattern is hepatocellular with cholestatic patterns reported as well, and that reactivation of chronic hepatitis B during imatinib therapy for GIST can present like an acute hepatitis and be misidentified as DILI.

Time to liver injury development at recommended dosage was 1–23 months. In the present cohort, rs4946935 AA (in FOXO3) was associated with higher hepatotoxicity risk (OR = 18.020, 95%CI = 2.473 to 459.1784, P = 0.018) in a gefitinib-concentration dependent pattern. raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with elevated transaminases while on rivaroxaban for 13 days. After ruling out thyrotoxicosis, hepatitis B reactivation, and transient hypotension-related ischemia, a calculated RUCAM score of 8 indicated rivaroxaban as the 'probable' cause of DILI. A preliminary diagnosis of DILI due to rivaroxaban was made; rivaroxaban was switched to apixaban on the sixth day of admission, and liver enzymes trended downward, further supporting the diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM causality assessment score of 8 (probable). Hepatocellular pattern with calculated R-factor of 18.8. Patient on rivaroxaban for 13 days at presentation; median time to liver injury reported as 15 days. Elevated AST/ALT peaked around day 7 (ALT 1702 U/L, AST 810 U/L) then downtrended after discontinuation, normalizing by 2 months. Patient had malaise but no jaundice or vomiting. Competing causes (thyrotoxicosis, hepatitis B reactivation, ischemia) ruled out. Tenofovir already being taken for hepatitis B. Mechanism likely idiosyncratic and possibly immunologic; no CYP3A4 inhibitor co-medication present. Rivaroxaban has dual elimination (one-third renal, two-thirds hepatic, CYP3A4-dependent). Rarely reported to cause acute liver failure and, very rarely, death.

raw_record.support_text: Minocycline, a tetracycline widely used in acne vulgaris in adolescent teenagers, has immense potential for hepatotoxicity. The DILIN prospective study observed minocycline to be the single most commonly implicated antimicrobial in children, and case reports describe minocycline-induced liver dysfunction ranging from acute hepatitis, DRESS, autoimmune hepatitis to acute liver failure resulting in death/transplantation. Minocycline can result in two types of hepatotoxicity - hypersensitivity hepatitis (days to weeks, 1-3 months of use, with fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, peripheral eosinophilia and exfoliative dermatitis) and drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (months to years after use). A Cochrane review found an increased risk of liver dysfunction with minocycline (1.04/10,000 exposed person-months, OR 2.1), and HLA-B*35:02 carriers are at increased risk of minocycline-related liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adolescent acne vulgaris treatment; increased liver-injury risk in HLA-B*35:02 carriers; overall incidence rare (1.04/10,000 exposed person-months).
raw_record.extra_details: Used for acne vulgaris in teenagers. Two attributed hepatotoxicity types: hypersensitivity hepatitis (1-3 months latency, fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, peripheral eosinophilia, exfoliative dermatitis) and drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (months to years latency, sometimes after stopping). Reported spectrum: acute hepatitis, DRESS, autoimmune hepatitis, acute liver failure leading to death/transplantation. DILIN prospective study identified it as the most common antimicrobial cause in children. Cochrane review: OR 2.1 for liver dysfunction. HLA-B*35:02 carrier risk (Urban et al.). Re-exposure discouraged, especially with transaminases >5x ULN or jaundice.

Analyses used Cox proportional hazards regression (hazard ratio) adjusted for gender, calendar year, alcohol abuse, other substance abuse, schizophrenia, affective disorder, borderline personality disorder, eating disorder, cancer, COPD, diabetes, arterial hypertension, and ischemic heart disease; age-specific mortality rate ratios plotted with natural splines. raw_record.support_text: Although acetaminophen is a dose-dependent hepatotoxin, elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels were measured in some healthy adults following 7–14 days of the maximum daily dose of 4 g/day, and rare case studies have reported development of acute liver injury (ALI) even at therapeutic doses. These findings confirm that some healthy individuals experience mild to severe liver injury in response to therapeutic doses of acetaminophen.

The paper proposes genetic polymorphisms in acetaminophen-metabolizing enzymes explain ethnic and interindividual differences in degradation and hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In 20 patients with refractory inflammatory bowel disease treated with methotrexate (mean cumulative dose 2633 mg, mean weekly dose 20 mg, mean duration 131.7 weeks), liver biopsies showed methotrexate-related hepatotoxicity: 17/20 biopsies (85%) fulfilled Roenigk's grade I histological change, 2 patients had grade II changes, and 1 patient (patient 4, after 1650 mg) developed grade IIIB changes with bridging fibrosis, prompting methotrexate discontinuation. Roenigk grade I in 17 biopsies (3 entirely normal), grade II in 2 (cumulative dose <2000 mg), grade IIIB in 1; no cirrhosis (grade IV). One biopsy performed for 2-fold transaminase rise (still within normal). Discussion notes liver biopsy as gold standard, unreliable LCTs in psoriasis, and lower hepatotoxicity prevalence in rheumatoid arthritis than psoriasis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a probable case of escitalopram-induced liver injury. A 56-year-old Chinese lady presented with fever and cholestatic liver injury two weeks after initiation of escitalopram for the treatment of psychotic depression. Investigations for stones, viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver disease were unyielding, and upon stopping escitalopram repeat liver function tests showed downtrending liver enzymes with eventual normalization of serum aminotransferase levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case: 56-year-old Chinese lady with psychotic depression; cholestatic liver injury with fever developed two weeks after escitalopram initiation; CT abdomen/pelvis and hepatitis A, B, C and autoimmune liver disease workup were unyielding; after drug cessation, AST and ALT downtrended and normalized by one week post-discharge. Probable causality per case report. Clinical phenotype: cholestatic liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of alcoholic patients who took acetaminophen, 17 of 53 patients died (mortality rate 32%). For patients with a contributing cause of death the acetaminophen dose ranged from 1.3 g/day to 10 g/day, and for those without a contributing cause the dose ranged from 5 to 14 g/day; autopsy findings of severe centrilobular necrosis were consistent with acetaminophen toxicity. The report also notes that as few as 5.8 g of acetaminophen can cause significant hepatotoxicity and 15 g is potentially lethal, describing dose-related formation of NAPQI causing hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Study subjects were alcoholics; alcohol use lowers glutathione and induces cytochromes P450IIE1 and P450IA2, enhancing toxicity at relatively modest doses; 9 patients received N-acetylcysteine; 1 death involved concurrent barbiturate use.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 53 patients; 17 deaths (32% mortality); 7 had contributing causes (bleeding esophageal varices, rhinocerebral mucormycosis, acute cholecystitis, urosepsis and renal failure, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, psittacosis, barbiturate co-use) with doses 1.3-10 g/day; 10 without contributing cause with doses 5-14 g/day. Liver histology showed severe centrilobular necrosis (and one case with bridging fibrosis, steatosis, cholestasis consistent with acetaminophen-induced necrosis on alcohol-induced fibrosis). Serologic and biopsy criteria excluded other hepatotoxic causes; mean peak AST >800 U/L criterion. Mechanism: ~95% metabolized to glucuronide/sulfate conjugates; ~5% converted to reactive NAPQI detoxified by glutathione; dose-related saturation causes hepatic necrosis over ~12 h. N-acetylcysteine given in 9 cases, 6 of whom died.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews 53 cases of unintentional acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in alcoholic patients. These consequences were not due to deliberate ingestion of excessive doses with suicidal intent; rather, acetaminophen was prescribed or taken for painful conditions or cold symptoms, and excessive doses were sometimes taken due to unwitting ingestion of acetaminophen in more than one preparation. Acetaminophen-alcohol liver toxicity affected relatively young individuals with an average age of 42 years.

raw_record.extra_details: The paper frames 'acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity' explicitly (paragraph 23: mechanism via glutathione depletion, N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is beneficial within 8 h, up to 24-36 h). The 53-case review in alcoholics showed extraordinary AST elevations (contrasted with median AST ~650 U/L in viral hepatitis and ~120 U/L in alcoholic hepatitis), diagnosis initially missed 36% of the time, no patient received a liver transplant, multiple deaths, and mortality possibly inflated by selective reporting. Treatment was supportive; only one non-hospitalized patient presented within N-acetylcysteine effectiveness window and did not receive the drug. N-acetylcysteine is reported as a treatment, not a cause.

raw_record.support_text: The paper's literature review concludes that the acetaminophen-alcohol syndrome causes hepatotoxicity in relatively young, frequently healthy alcoholic patients taking acetaminophen for relief of pain rather than with suicidal intent. A typical laboratory picture of a very high AST level was defined, and the mortality rate was 32%. The syndrome arises from the ubiquitous combined use of acetaminophen and alcohol, with acetaminophen present in many over-the-counter and prescription drugs.

raw_record.extra_details: 2 newly reported fatal cases plus 51 reviewed cases (mean mortality 32%). Peak AST was required to exceed 800 U/L; typical picture is an extraordinarily high AST level. Mean ingested amounts ranged roughly 1.3-20 g/day over ~1-30 days. N-acetylcysteine treatment was generally not effective because of delayed presentation/diagnosis. History of alcohol use, use of multiple acetaminophen-containing products (Tylenol, Extra Strength Tylenol, Nyquil, Darvocet N-100, Tylenol with codeine, Exedrin) was common; increased toxicity potential in the setting of alcohol use. Four prior series of acetaminophen-alcohol syndrome are summarized (Zimmerman & Maddrey registry, McClain et al., Denison et al., Whitcomb & Block).

raw_record.support_text: The signs and symptoms of hepatic failure in the patient appeared approximately 14 days after beginning sulfadiazine therapy. The Naranjo probability scale gave a probable causality link between sulfadiazine and the patient's hepatorenal syndrome (score = 5), and the CIOMS and Maria and Victorino clinical scales also indicated a probable link. The patient's hepatitis seemed hepatocellular in nature, since ALT and AST were significantly increased, mixed to some extent with a cholestatic pattern due to hyperbilirubinemia and approximately normal alkaline phosphatase. The patient required five hemodialysis sessions, recovered, and was discharged on hospital day 20.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the first case of severe hepatotoxicity and probable hepatorenal syndrome associated with sulfadiazine. Patient also received leucovorin and pyrimethamine; leucovorin is not hepatotoxic and pyrimethamine alone has no published reports of hepatic failure, so toxicity was attributed to sulfadiazine. Onset ~14 days after starting therapy. Naranjo score = 5 (probable); CIOMS and Maria-Victorino scales also indicated probable. Peak ALT 5340 U/L and AST 5825 U/L with hepatocellular pattern mixed to some extent with cholestasis (hyperbilirubinemia, approximately normal ALP). Patient required five hemodialysis sessions and recovered fully.

raw_record.support_text: Instances of jaundice were reported as associated with clinical and functional indications of hepatocellular injury following the intake of iproniazid (1-isonicotinyl-2-isopropylhydrazine, or Marsilid), an amine oxidase inhibitor used in the treatment of tuberculosis and various mental disorders. Biopsy and autopsy liver specimens from these patients showed histological manifestations usually considered characteristic of viral hepatitis, with no relationship observed between the dose of iproniazid and the extent of the lesion.
raw_record.extra_details: Material comprised 16 autopsy and 22 biopsy specimens from a total of 34 patients who developed jaundice while receiving iproniazid or up to 20 days after cessation of treatment; iproniazid was prescribed for depression in almost every instance. Histological findings were characteristic of viral hepatitis; no dose-relationship to extent of lesion was observed. Fourteen patients showed a severe spotty necrotic hepatitis on biopsy; of the fatal cases, 11 presented acute hepatitis with massive, submassive, or zonal necrosis and subsequent collapse, 7 showed subacute hepatitis and 1 chronic hepatitis of the same type with varying nodular regeneration; 2 showed almost complete histological recovery.

raw_record.support_text: The patient presented with icteric sclera, generalized jaundice, mild right upper quadrant tenderness and a palpable liver edge; LFTs on arrival showed AST 1,400, ALT 2,253 and TB 9.9. The RUCAM/CIOMS causality scale, a validated tool for assessing causality in suspected DILI, gave a score of 9, suggestive of a highly probable adverse drug reaction. The patient was only taking rosuvastatin and admitted no other drugs, supplements, or herbal products.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of rosuvastatin-associated DILI. RUCAM score 9 (highly probable). LFTs on presentation: AST 1,400, ALT 2,253, TB 9.9, normal CBC and electrolytes; later AST 942, ALT 1,312, ALP 167, TB 17.2. Liver biopsy showed acute severe hepatitis with portal and lobular mixed inflammatory infiltrate (neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils) with interface activity and bile duct damage, interpreted as a likely immune-mediated drug reaction. Workup for chronic liver disease, autoimmune antibodies (ASMA, ANA, anti-LKM), hepatotropic viruses, HSV/CMV/EBV, and copper/iron/trichrome stains was unrevealing. Treated with IV N-acetylcysteine for 5 days and Ursodiol without enzyme improvement; evaluated for possible liver transplantation; patient remained stable without hepatic encephalopathy. Abdominal ultrasound showed nonspecific hepatitis findings and CT showed mild periportal edema. Patient denied alcohol and other co-medications.

raw_record.support_text: The Homberg et al. series of 157 cases of drug-induced hepatitis identified the major culprit drugs causing hepatotoxicity as clometacin (29 cases), α-methyldopa (12 cases), troleandromycin (11 cases), ajmaline (8 cases), halothane (6 cases) and perhexiline (6 cases), with the drugs most often associated with autoimmune serologic reactions being clometacin (17/29), fenofibrate (4/4), papaverine (4/5) and tienilic acid (3/3).
raw_record.extra_details: Most common culprit in Homberg series of 157 drug-induced hepatitis cases (29 cases); 17/29 also had autoimmune serologic reactions characterized by antismooth muscle antibody (ASMA) and antinuclear antibody (ANA).

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid (ticrynofen), 2,3-dichloro-4-(2-thenoyl)phenoxy acetic acid, is a uricosuric diuretic whose association with severe liver damage was analyzed in 340 cases by Zimmerman et al. The high frequency of hepatotoxicity led to withdrawal of the drug in the United States and other countries. Homberg and colleagues reported as many as 67 cases, with death in the acute phase in 11; histology in 36 biopsies did not correspond with chronic active hepatitis, and anti-LKM2 antiorganelle response occurred in about 50% of cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic; 340 cases analyzed by Zimmerman et al.; 67 cases reported by Homberg with 11 acute-phase deaths; histologic changes in 36 biopsies not consistent with chronic active hepatitis; delayed recovery in 14 cases responded to prednisolone and azathioprine; anti-LKM2 antiorganelle response in ~50% of cases; high hepatotoxicity frequency led to drug withdrawal in the US and other countries.

A total of 20/26 (76.9%) paracetamol patients and 6/7 (85.7%) non-paracetamol patients developed hepatic encephalopathy and thus acute liver failure during the study, and eight patients (five paracetamol, three non-paracetamol) subsequently underwent emergency orthotopic liver transplantation. Paracetamol patients had significantly higher admission INRs and ALT levels than non-paracetamol patients, with a median time from overdose to sampling of 56 (44-68) hours.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report an increase in plasma syndecan-1 concentrations in patients with APAP-induced acute liver failure (ALF). In these APAP-ALF patients, shed syndecan-1 concentrations were ~200-fold higher than in APAP overdose mice, and HMGB1 and ALT were also higher in patients with APAP-ALF than in the healthy control group, consistent with a previous report. APAP (acetaminophen) is thereby explicitly attributed as the cause of ALF in these human patients.

raw_record.support_text: Most reported instances of hepatotoxicity from ingestion of acetaminophen within or only slightly above the usual therapeutic dose range have been in alcoholic patients. Two alcoholics (a 31-year-old woman and a 52-year-old man) consumed 10 and 14 g per day of acetaminophen respectively, developed evidence of severe hepatic toxicity and died. The first American patient with hepatotoxicity from moderate acetaminophen doses was a 59-year-old alcoholic man who took about 30 g over 4 days (7.5 g/day); he was severely ill but survived despite hepatic encephalopathy and marked prolongation of the prothrombin time.

raw_record.extra_details: Reported acetaminophen doses ranged from 10-14 g/day (2 fatal cases) down to approximately 7.5 g/day (30 g over 4 days) in the first reported American case. Manifestations included severe hepatic toxicity, hepatic encephalopathy, and marked prolongation of the prothrombin time; two patients died and one survived. First association report was published in 1977.

All 25 had evidence of severe acute hepatocellular necrosis with jaundice, coagulation defects, and often extraordinary aminotransferase elevations. The reported acetaminophen dosage ranged from 2.6-16.5 g/24 h; 15 of 25 ingested <8 g/24 h and 11 did not exceed 6 g/24 h.

raw_record.extra_details: 25-patient series (19 from literature + 6 new). All had severe acute hepatocellular necrosis with jaundice and coagulation defects. AST was more elevated than ALT in all patients; AST >3,000 IU/L in 22 (88%) and >10,000 IU/L in 6 (24%); some had hypoglycemia; bilirubin 1.3-23.9 mg/dl (median 7.3). Initial symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, then right-upper-quadrant pain, jaundice, coagulation abnormalities, hepatic encephalopathy. Biopsies in 7 patients showed centrilobular (perivenular) necrosis in 5; one alcoholic with pancreatitis had repeated toxic hepatitis after 6 g/day with perivenular fibrosis. Hepatic encephalopathy frequent, severe coagulopathy in several; aminotransferases highest on admission then fell over 24-48 h; 5 of 25 patients died.

Hepatotoxicity, defined as aminotransferase >1,000 IU/L, developed in 7 (15%) of 47 patients presenting with aspartate aminotransferase 50-1,000 IU/L (1 death) and in 6 (16%) of 37 patients presenting with aspartate aminotransferase above 1,000 IU/L (who died or received liver transplants). The conclusion states that the injury caused by acetaminophen repeated supratherapeutic ingestion is apparent at presentation and related to dose magnitude and duration.

raw_record.extra_details: Prospective case series, 249 of 277 eligible patients enrolled. Hepatotoxicity defined as aminotransferase >1,000 IU/L. At presentation AST <50 IU/L in 126 patients (none developed hepatotoxicity), AST 50-1,000 IU/L in 47 patients (7 developed hepatotoxicity, 1 died), AST >1,000 IU/L in 37 patients (6 died or received liver transplants); AST data missing for 39 patients. No patient with AST <50 IU/L at presentation developed hepatotoxicity. Acetylcysteine recommended if serum acetaminophen >10 mg/L or AST >50 IU/L. Minimum follow-up 72 hours. raw_record.support_text: In pediatric patients, acetaminophen overdose (intentional, dosing-error, and therapeutic-misadventure) is associated with hepatocellular injury, hepatic failure, and death. Across several pediatric case series, hepatocellular injury developed, hepatic failure occurred (e.g., in 4 of 322 patients with one death from multisystem organ failure), and factors such as age 10-17 years, presentation >24 hours after ingestion, intentional overdose, an ingested dose >150 mg/kg, and white race were associated with hepatocellular injury.

Concomitant P450-inducing medications, non-pediatric formulations, label-reading failure, and delays in N-acetylcysteine contributed to hepatotoxicity.

Labs showed AST 1,899 IU/L (normal 8-48) and ALT 533 IU/L (normal 7-56), indicating severe liver damage; the paper presents this as a case of acute liver failure (ALF) caused by repeated supratherapeutic ingestions of acetaminophen, with the patient achieving full recovery.

Severe liver toxicity defined as peak AST or ALT >1,000 IU/L; toxicity mediated by the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) formed via CYP2E1, with genetic variants affecting production.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes that prolonged and excessive use of acetaminophen adversely affects the liver, disrupting normal function. In cases of excessive intake, CYP2E1 metabolizes about 20% of the drug (80% detoxified by sulfation and glucuronidation), and excessive consumption depletes hepatic glutathione reserves; the resulting free radical increase underlies the injury. The FDA advises adults not to exceed 4,000 mg of acetaminophen daily and to avoid prolonged use beyond ten days. This is presented as a case of acetaminophen overdose leading to acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose (supratherapeutic/excessive intake); the case also had a positive urine drug screen for cocaine and a serum acetaminophen level of 29 mcg/mL on admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient presenting with acute liver failure (ALF) with jaundice and severe hepatic transaminase elevation >10,000 U/L; INR peaked at 3.08 and total bilirubin at 22.5 mg/dL on hospital day 4. Normal iron studies, negative autoimmune panel, negative viral hepatitis and HSV serology, and no portal or hepatic vein thrombosis on Doppler ultrasound. Managed with continuous N-acetylcysteine infusion (15 mg/kg/hour for seven days) and supportive fluids, with eventual recovery of liver function. Mechanistically attributed to CYP2E1-mediated metabolism and NAPQI-mediated glutathione depletion.

raw_record.support_text: In population-based surveillance for acute liver failure (ALF) across 8 counties of Metropolitan Atlanta (Nov 2000-Oct 2004, 65 enrolled cases), acetaminophen (APAP)-related ALF was the most common etiology (41%) in adults, and was also 25% of pediatric cases. Unintentional APAP overdose was the most common type (61%) of APAP-related cause. Per the methods, the diagnosis of APAP toxicity required a toxic serum APAP level based on the APAP toxicity nomogram or a history of ingestion in excess of therapeutic dose, and intentional APAP overdose was based on stated intent and/or inpatient psychiatric evaluation.

APAP attribute criteria: toxic serum APAP level per nomogram or history of ingestion in excess of therapeutic dose; intentional overdose based on stated intent/psychiatric evaluation; unintentional overdose 61% of APAP-related causes. Clinical phenotype is acute liver failure (fulminant hepatitis).

raw_record.extra_details: Incidence 12.6% (101/802). ALT was the critical index for evaluating hepatotoxicity. In a prospective observational cohort of 117 acetaminophen-poisoned patients requiring N-acetylcysteine (median self-ingested dose 16 g, 9-30), liver injury (ALT >100 IU/L) occurred in 38 patients (32%) with a median peak ALT of 2020 IU/L (577-4248); the poisoning was treated as an overdose exposure.

Admission procalcitonin (PCT) was higher in liver-injury patients (21.5 ng/ml vs 0.1 ng/ml, p<0.01), preceded ALT rise by 33 h (10-74), and PCT>1 ng/ml was associated with liver injury (HR 7.2, 95%CI 2.3-22.6, p<0.001; AUROC 0.91). raw_record.support_text: The paper opens by stating established knowledge that a nomogram has been used for decades to predict acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, noting that this nomogram has not been validated in common scenarios such as chronic overdose or when the time from ingestion is unknown. In a prospective cohort of 117 acetaminophen-poisoned patients receiving N-acetylcysteine, plasma procalcitonin on admission was associated with liver injury and its rise preceded alanine aminotransferase elevation, highlighting the need for better biomarkers to identify patients at higher or lower risk of acetaminophen-related acute liver injury.

raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury labeled LI, with acute liver injury (ALI) as outcome; 117 prospective patients in a toxicological ICU cohort (2012-2017). Plasma procalcitonin (PCT) on admission predicted liver injury with excellent accuracy and negative predictive value, and its rise preceded alanine aminotransferase rise by a median of 33 h. Other candidate biomarkers mentioned: acetaminophen protein adducts, miR-122, HMGB1, keratin 18, GLDH. Predictive nomogram covers time-from-ingestion and dose scenarios.

Median procalcitonin was 21.6 ng/ml in LI patients with acute liver failure versus 9.2 ng/ml in LI alone, and 11 of 38 developed LI during follow-up despite NAC treatment. raw_record.extra_details: Observational cohort of 117 acetaminophen-poisoned patients treated with NAC, 38 cases of LI. Admission procalcitonin (PCT) >1 ng/ml independently predicted onset of LI (HR 7.2 [95%CI 2.3-22.6], p<0.001); delay to NAC administration HR 1.03 (95%CI 1.0-1.1, p=0.04). In 11/38 patients developing LI despite NAC, PCT increase preceded ALT rise by 33 h (10-74). Median PCT 21.6 (4.5-42.5) ng/ml in LI+ALF vs 9.2 (0.4-50.4) ng/ml in LI alone (p=0.49). Admission PCT correlated with peak ALT (rs=0.58, p<0.001) and delay to NAC (rs=0.54, p<0.001). Example: 90-year-old woman, unknown paracetamol dose, acetaminophen plasma 136 mg/ml, PCT 27 ng/ml, normal liver tests on admission. Some cases progressed to acute liver failure (ALF). Consistent with reports of high PCT in acetaminophen-induced ALF (Jackson ~9.4 ng/ml; Mallet 10.6 vs 0.8 ng/ml). Discussed direct inhibitory toxic effect of acetaminophen on mitochondrial cellular respiration; no baseline lactate >3 mmol/L patients progressed to LI or ALF.

The paper frames patients at high risk of liver injury (LI) as potentially benefiting from earlier recognition of acute liver failure (ALF) and appropriate listing for liver transplantation, while its study uses high plasma procalcitonin on admission as an early predictor of LI in the setting of acetaminophen poisoning. The limitations section also cites a large US cohort of 1162 patients with acetaminophen-induced liver injury, and a threshold of serum ALT > 100 IU/L as indicating substantial liver injury in acetaminophen-poisoned patients.
