raw_record.support_text: The authors present a patient who developed drug-induced cholestatic liver injury attributed to ticlopidine. Histopathology showed mild periportal inflammation with neutrophils and eosinophils, foci of piecemeal necrosis, and mild collagen deposition, and MRP2 immunoreactivity was reduced and cytosolic. Ticlopidine therapy was stopped and liver biochemistry normalized 6 weeks after drug withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Ticlopidine is an anti-platelet drug described as inducing idiosyncratic DILI, typically cholestatic hepatitis occurring 2-12 weeks after therapy initiation. In this case the calculated R value was 0.85, confirming a cholestatic injury. Histology showed periportal inflammation (neutrophils and eosinophils), piecemeal necrosis with inflammatory infiltrate, and mild collagen deposition, with no iron or copper accumulation. MRP2 immunoreactivity was weaker and mainly cytosolic. Liver biochemistry normalized 6 weeks after stopping ticlopidine. This is noted as the first human evidence of abnormal hepatic MRP2 immunoreactivity in drug-induced cholestasis, consistent with pre-clinical DILI models.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP), although considered safe at therapeutic doses up to 4000 mg/day, can at higher doses induce centrilobular necrosis generally leading to a fatal outcome. APAP intoxication is responsible for about one-half of all cases of acute liver failure in the United States and the United Kingdom, and in a Thai study of 184 patients with APAP overdose, 15.6% had mild hepatotoxicity, 6.4% severe hepatotoxicity, and 3 (1.6%) developed acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury attributed to high-dose/supra-therapeutic exposure (APAP overdose above therapeutic 4000 mg/day); safe at therapeutic doses per the paper.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP intoxication estimated responsible for about half of all cases of acute liver failure in the US and UK. Thai study of 184 APAP-overdose patients: 15.6% mild hepatotoxicity, 6.4% severe hepatotoxicity, 3 patients (1.6%) acute liver failure. At higher doses induces centrilobular necrosis which generally leads to fatal outcome. Mechanism described: N-acetyl-p-quinone-imine (NAPQI), a reactive metabolite generated by cytochrome P450 enzymes at high doses, depletes glutathione and binds cellular proteins, especially mitochondrial proteins, driving mitochondrial oxidant stress and cell death; immune system (Kupffer cells, neutrophils, macrophages) contributes to progression.

raw_record.support_text: In a pooled analysis of TGCT patients (ENLIVEN trial plus longer follow-up), 130 patients were exposed to pexidartinib for a median treatment duration of 19 months; 4 had serious hepatic adverse reactions, all starting within the first 8 weeks of treatment. Although reversible in the TGCT population, the duration of liver injury was prolonged in some cases, and in the overall clinical program there were 2 irreversible cases of cholestatic liver injury: 1 patient died with advanced cancer and ongoing liver toxicity, and 1 patient required a liver transplant. The analysis reported no new mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity beyond the first 8 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: TGCT (tenosynovial giant cell tumor) patient population treated for this indication; 1 fatal case occurred in a patient with advanced cancer and ongoing liver toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: 130 patients, median 19 months exposure; 4 serious hepatic adverse reactions all within first 8 weeks of treatment; events reversible in the TGCT population but liver injury duration prolonged in some; overall clinical program had 2 irreversible cholestatic liver injury cases (1 death, 1 liver transplant); no new mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity beyond first 8 weeks; because of hepatotoxicity risk pexidartinib is available only through the Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) program in the United States with frequent liver function monitoring and dose modification.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe three multiple sclerosis patients who developed severe acute hepatotoxicity after methylprednisolone (IVMP) infusion, after discarding other etiological agents. All three cases were classified in the 'probable adverse drug reaction' category of the Naranjo scale and the WHO causality assessment criteria, leading to the hypothesis that IVMP was the possible cause of the hepatotoxicity. The paper notes that pharmacological hepatotoxicity is usually idiosyncratic and based on individual and genetic susceptibility.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Relapsing-remitting or progressive MS patients treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone for relapses; patients had no prior hepatopathy history and excluded viral/autoimmune hepatitis, alcohol, alternatives, and supplements.
raw_record.extra_details: Three cases: (1) 28-year-old woman developed jaundice, choluria, acholia, nausea, vomiting ~7 weeks after last IVMP bolus; hepatic biopsy showed mild architectural damage; subsequent relapse treated again with IVMP led to another severe acute hepatitis episode (~1 month later) with biopsy showing lymphocyte-edematous background and fibrotic mild chronic hepatitis. (2) 37-year-old man with IVMP for transverse myelitis; ~6 weeks later liver enzymes increased 18x with prolonged INR and no clinical manifestations; biopsy after resolution showed no inflammatory findings. (3) 35-year-old woman; 3 days after IVMP, 42-fold increase in liver enzymes, clinically asymptomatic. Falls in 'probable' category of Naranjo scale and WHO causality criteria. Methylprednisolone given at 1000 mg for 3-5 days (± 500 mg courses); glatiramer acetate subsequently initiated given its low hepatotoxicity rate.

raw_record.support_text: Abnormal liver function studies developed in 29 of 93 (31.2%) evaluable patients treated with BCNU (carmustine). Ten patients (10.8%) had severe, delayed hepatotoxicity (median onset day +40, range +19 to +76) that was fatal in eight patients (8.6%). Clinically this was painless cholestatic jaundice with ascites and progressive hepatic insufficiency; two patients slowly improved. Pathology in eight of nine patients showed massive centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis, while one melanoma patient with prior dacarbazine exposure had veno-occlusive disease at necropsy.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity was significantly dose-related: 6/17 (35.3%; 95% CI 14.2-61.7%) patients at BCNU 1500-2850 mg/m2 vs 4/76 (5.3%; 95% CI 1.5-13.0%) at 600-1200 mg/m2 (P<0.01). At 1200 mg/m2 the incidence of severe was 6.1% and fatal hepatic necrosis 3.0%. CNS tumor diagnosis was also associated (9/44, 20.5% vs 1/49, 2.0%; P<0.01). A transient asymptomatic liver enzyme elevation pattern was seen in 19 patients. Fatal in 8/10 (8.6%); 2 recovered. Pathology: massive centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis (8/9); veno-occlusive disease in one patient with prior dacarbazine exposure (co-suspect). No correlation with mannitol, anticonvulsants, or corticosteroids. BCNU hepatic toxicity grading scale defined (grades 0-4).

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe BCNU (carmustine) hepatotoxicity observed with intensive BCNU therapy with marrow transplantation: early reversible hepatotoxicity, delayed liver toxicity in three of seven patients at BCNU 800-1200 mg/m², and fatal hepatic necrosis in 3.0% of patients at BCNU 1200 mg/m². Severe hepatotoxicity was frequent at higher doses, especially BCNU 1800 mg/m² and above, and was noted in only one of six evaluable patients at 1500 mg/m². The paper concludes that BCNU doses above 1200 to 1500 mg/m² are associated with a high incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Early, reversible hepatotoxicity at BCNU 600-1400 mg/m² (Hochberg et al.) and in the authors' study; delayed liver toxicity in three of seven patients at BCNU 800-1200 mg/m² including one fatal case at 1200 mg/m² (Hochberg et al.); hepatotoxicity not noted in Spitzer et al. series at 600-750 mg/m² possibly due to short survival. Pathologic finding of centrilobular necrosis in all cases except one (veno-occlusive disease found in one patient who had prior exposure to decarbazine); veno-occlusive disease also reported after BCNU 1500 mg/m² by McIntyre et al. Fatal hepatic necrosis also encountered during dose deescalation at BCNU 1800, 1500, and 1200 mg/m²; CNS malignancy was an unexplained predisposing risk factor.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a special case of acute severe hepatocellular injury 'highly likely induced by fenofibrate' after a short period of therapy in a patient without primary or secondary liver disease. Fenofibrate, a fibric acid derivative used to treat hypertriglyceridemia and dyslipidemia, is noted to cause DILI very rarely (only 0.6% of patients).

The rapidly-recovering sudden-onset presentation is described as different from those in the LiverTox database. Fenofibrate is a fibric acid derivative widely used for hypertriglyceridemia and dyslipidemia; DILI associated with fenofibrate occurs very rarely (0.6% of patients).

They note this setting should prompt physicians to seek a history of acetaminophen intake and propose measurement of acetaminophen blood levels as a diagnostic adjunct.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes halothane hepatitis, a form of drug-induced hepatitis with an immunological basis. Sera from patients with halothane hepatitis recognized a number of heterologous CF3CO-proteins present in liver microsomal membranes of halothane-exposed rats; in patients biopsied 6-7 days after halothane exposure, CF3CO-proteins were no longer detectable. The CF3CO-protein adducts arise through covalent interaction of the trifluoroacetyl chloride intermediate (formed from halothane) with lysine residues in target proteins.
raw_record.extra_details: Immune-mediated mechanism; sera from patients with halothane hepatitis contain autoantibodies recognizing CF3CO-proteins (trifluoroacetylated proteins) formed in liver microsomes via covalent binding of the trifluoroacetyl chloride intermediate to lysine residues. CF3CO-proteins no longer detectable in liver biopsies taken 6-7 days after halothane exposure, and 10 days after exposure in rats. Recognized CF3CO-proteins include trifluoroacetylated protein disulfide isomerase, microsomal carboxylesterase, ERp99/GRP94, ERp72, BiP/GRP78, and calreticulin.

raw_record.support_text: The study examined 35 sera from patients with a clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis. 17 of these sera recognized the trifluoroacetylated protein CF₃CO-RSA on immunoblots in a manner sensitive to competition by CF₃CO-Lys and lipoic acid, and these sera were further analyzed for reactivity against the lipoylated autoantigens (E2 subunits of the PDC, OGDC, and BCOADC, and protein X). The authors also analyzed liver biopsies of seven patients with halothane hepatitis and observed unusually low amounts of immunorecognizable 52 kDa proteins and the E2 subunit of the PDC in 5 of 7 patients, suggesting a possible association between low aberrant expression of these hepatic proteins and susceptibility to halothane hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis (drug-induced hepatitis) with an apparent autoimmune component: sera from patients reacted with CF₃CO-RSA and with the lipoylated E2 subunits of the PDC (15/17 reactive sera), OGDC (13/17), BCOADC (9/17), and protein X (13/17). Two autoantibody populations were distinguished by competition with CF₃CO-Lys/lipoic acid. Liver immunoblots showed low immunodetectable amounts of 52 kDa proteins and PDC-E2 in 5 of 7 halothane hepatitis patients, suggesting HLA-like or expression-related susceptibility, mechanistically linked to lipoic-acid-containing autoantigens also involved in primary biliary cirrhosis. 35 patients with clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis studied.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of acute cholestatic liver injury attributed to ciprofloxacin in a 32-year-old female who developed pruritus, jaundice, and abdominal pain three days after completing a 10-day ciprofloxacin course for a urinary tract infection. Hepatic enzymes showed a cholestatic pattern, an extensive workup excluded other cholestasis causes, and liver biopsy was consistent with drug-induced cholestasis. A diagnosis of ciprofloxacin-induced cholestatic liver injury was made based on symptom onset after ciprofloxacin use, biochemical and clinical improvement after cessation, and biopsy findings; the patient recovered with liver enzymes returning to baseline six weeks after admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 32-year-old female; a 10-day ciprofloxacin course for urinary tract infection; symptoms (pruritus, jaundice, abdominal pain) began three days after completing the course; hepatic enzymes showed a cholestatic pattern; liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced cholestasis; workup excluded viral, autoimmune, and imaging-based cholestasis causes; supportive treatment; liver enzymes returned to baseline six weeks after admission; patient advised to avoid ciprofloxacin and other quinolones. The paper notes 25 previously reported cases of ciprofloxacin-induced severe liver injury in the literature and that ciprofloxacin usually causes mild transient liver enzyme elevation in 2-3% of patients. Prior courses of fosfomycin and cefixime were taken three months before symptom onset and not implicated.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of ciprofloxacin-induced DILI that improved and recovered after cessation; it notes that apart from three reported cases of fulminant hepatitis and death, the remainder of ciprofloxacin-induced liver injury cases improved rapidly after drug cessation. The conclusion states that although ciprofloxacin has a good safety profile, it has the propensity to cause severe drug-induced liver injury and, in very rare cases, acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report of ciprofloxacin-induced DILI with liver biopsy performed; patient improved two weeks after cessation and achieved complete recovery six weeks after admission. The paper additionally cites three reported cases of ciprofloxacin-induced fulminant hepatitis with death, while the remaining reported cases improved after cessation, and notes acute liver failure occurs in very rare cases. Ciprofloxacin belongs to the quinolone group, so patients with ciprofloxacin-induced DILI are advised to avoid ciprofloxacin and other quinolones due to cross-sensitivity.

No child developed hepatic failure; one death was unrelated, and all surviving children subsequently tolerated IPT.

raw_record.support_text: Thirty-two of the 33 patients (97%) survived their hepatic injury, and after ketoconazole was discontinued, jaundice cleared and biochemical abnormalities returned to normal in an average of 7 weeks (range, 1-16 weeks) in 13 patients with follow-up. No instances of chronic hepatic injury have been reported to the FDA-DDE or are known by the authors. One patient (FDA case #6) died of hepatic failure with massive necrosis noted at autopsy, and ketoconazole was continued in this individual despite clinical symptoms and laboratory data that prompted withdrawal in all other patients. Liver histology in biopsied cases showed zonal necrosis, cholestasis, portal inflammation, ballooning degeneration, and steatosis in occasional cells.

Memantine was discontinued and symptoms and liver enzymes resolved (normal after 20 days). raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of severe acute liver injury from axitinib with cholestatic hepatitis; grade 4 liver enzyme elevation (AST and ALT >10x ULN). raw_record.support_text: In six patients (18%, all nontransplant) a definite overall diagnosis of medication-induced hepatitis was made, based on liver injury occurring after use of a specific medication, improvement upon discontinuation, and exclusion of other etiologies. raw_record.support_text: Liver toxicity is an emerging issue in the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, and pazopanib is emphasized as having a higher incidence of high-grade liver toxicity than other VEGFR inhibitors. A recent phase III trial (COMPAZ) directly compared pazopanib to sunitinib in 1002 RCC patients, finding ALT elevation significantly higher with pazopanib (31% vs. 18%).
raw_record.extra_details: Severe and fatal hepatotoxicity listed as an FDA black box warning. COMPAZ phase III trial (1002 RCC patients) showed ALT elevation 31% with pazopanib vs 18% with sunitinib. High-grade AST incidence 6.9% (95% CI 5.5-8.6) and high-grade ALT incidence 9.4% (95% CI 7.8-11.4) from this meta-analysis. Package insert notes two fatal outcomes from initial studies attributed to disease progression and hepatic failure; four pazopanib-arm treatment-related fatal adverse events including two with abnormal hepatic function. Meta-analysis found low risk of fatal hepatotoxicity, not a significant increase in fatal hepatic AEs (incidence 0.7%, 95% CI 0.2-2.7%; RR 2.51, 95% CI 0.12-51.91, p=0.552). Pazopanib primarily hepatically metabolized (<4% renal clearance); contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment with dose adjustment for baseline moderate impairment. Metabolized by liver, eliminated in feces.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH), introduced in 1952, was recognized as hepatotoxic when hepatitis was reported in 19 individuals receiving prophylactic INH in Baltimore, USA, with jaundice developing in 13 and 2 deaths; these events led to reassessment of INH's hepatotoxicity. Early case reports documented liver damage and jaundice associated with INH use and overdosage, and studies of patient series receiving INH revealed increases in AST, ALT and other LFT disorders, establishing INH as a cause of antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Baltimore series: 19 hepatitis cases (13 jaundiced, 2 died); a concurrent increase in liver cirrhosis deaths during that period in Baltimore initially gave an excessively negative picture of INH hepatotoxicity. Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled INH chemoprophylaxis trial: 20,838 INH recipients vs 6,991 placebo; 95 hepatitis cases in INH group vs 7 in placebo (highly significant) and 75 vs 5 jaundiced. Chennai trials (20 years): hepatitis with jaundice incidence 1.9% among 1,757 slow acetylators vs 1.2% among 1,238 rapid acetylators (not significant). Early case reports also linked INH use and overdosage to liver damage and jaundice; patient series showed increases in AST, ALT and other LFT. Early INH animal studies demonstrated liver damage (supporting, non-human).

raw_record.support_text: After ruling out other etiologies (sepsis, ischemic hepatitis, low cardiac output), the case was attributed to pharmacological hepatotoxicity. Since no changes were made to the patient's treatment except for the introduction of metformin (metformina) 2 weeks earlier, metformin was considered the causal agent, supported by concurrent renal insufficiency and lactic acidosis, a known complication of metformin. The paper also noted 7 previously published cases of metformin hepatotoxicity (references 5-11), mostly cholestatic or mixed-pattern hepatitis appearing 2-6 weeks after starting metformin for diabetes, described as idiosyncratic reactions not associated with other drugs or triggering factors. Causality assessment gave Naranjo and María-Victorino scores of 10 points (definitive hepatotoxicity) and a CIOMS/RUCAM score of 9 points (very probable or defined pharmacological hepatotoxicity).
raw_record.extra_details: Diabetes treatment with metformin; reaction was early (within 2 weeks in this patient; 2-6 weeks in the 7 literature cases). Elevated aminotransferases (hyperaminotransferasemia) normalized fully within less than a month, with improvement starting one week after drug withdrawal; complete recovery in all described cases; no liver biopsy performed. Causality: Naranjo 10 (definitive), María-Victorino 10 (definitive), CIOMS/RUCAM 9 (muy probable or definido). Concurrent renal insufficiency and lactic acidosis present. Differential diagnoses excluded: septic shock (negative cultures), ischemic hepatitis/hepatic shock from heart failure, hepatic venous congestion. Patient had cardiac failure decompensation and hypotension at admission but these were excluded as the cause. Literature cases mostly cholestatic or mixed-pattern hepatitis (refs 5-11).

raw_record.support_text: Labetalol is reported to cause transaminitis and rarely significant hepatotoxicity, hepatocellular injury, hepatocellular necrosis, liver failure, and death. The hepatotoxicity is most often considered an idiosyncratic response presenting at therapeutic doses with an indolent and variable latency period ranging from 5 to 90 days. In a multicenter open-label trial, labetalol caused reversible asymptomatic transaminase elevations in 8% of patients, and some patients rechallenged with the drug again showed transaminase elevation; the hepatotoxicity of labetalol has been documented in multiple reports since the 1980s.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurred in pregnancy; labetalol used as first-line treatment for hypertension in pregnancy. Case attributed to therapeutic-dose exposure with idiosyncratic response.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury made with prompt improvement in liver enzymes after discontinuation of labetalol; delivery at term 9 weeks later with near-normal AST (42 U/L) and ALT (83 U/L). Liver biopsy showed normal architecture without fibrosis, steatosis, or cholestasis, sparse inflammatory cells and no eosinophils, no viral inclusions; consistent with idiosyncratic toxicity. Latency range 5 to 90 days. Multicenter open-label trial reported reversible asymptomatic transaminase elevations in 8% of patients, with re-elevation on rechallenge. Rare progression to hepatic failure in pregnancy possible. Mechanisms discussed: mitochondrial cytochrome P450 pathway, autoimmune and inflammatory response; allergic reaction argued against due to lack of eosinophils and indolent time course. Idiosyncratic reactions account for ~20% of liver injury severe enough for hospitalization and occur more commonly in women.

raw_record.extra_details: Nimesulide (Nexen) 200 mg/day for 3 days for arthralgias, with onset of symptoms about 8 weeks later and one month of asthenia, epigastralgia, conjunctival subicterus and dark urine before diagnosis. Laboratory: aspartate aminotransferase 1239 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 1435 IU/L, cytolysis with cholestasis, prothrombin time 24% not corrected by vitamin K. Reasonably defined fulminant hepatitis (hepatitis with hepatic insufficiency and encephalopathy). MARS temporary hepatic support and orthotopic liver transplantation 12 hours after admission (reported: 12 heures après l'admission); ICU discharge 4 days post-transplant. Viral (A/B/C/E, HIV, CMV, EBV, VZV, HTLV1) and autoimmune (ANA, smooth-muscle, LKM1, antimitochondrial) workups negative; no Budd-Chiari thrombosis. Nimesulide is a preferential COX-2 inhibitor NSAID available in several European countries, marketed in France since 1 March 1998.

Sodium valproate is described as having serious idiosyncratic side effects, particularly hepatotoxicity, and is noted as the most common drug to induce liver injury among antiepileptic drugs.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatal acute liver failure (ALF) with thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). Presenting signs included extreme fatigue, severe jaundice with oliguria, soy sauce-colored urine, and ecchymosis; rapid decrease in platelet count and hemoglobin, severe liver and kidney dysfunction, and coagulation disturbance. raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of 46 pediatric acute promyelocytic leukemia patients treated with arsenic trioxide (As₂O₃) by IV drip at a therapeutic dose during remission induction, liver impairment occurred in 24.4% of patients, mostly mild to moderate in severity, and manifested primarily as increases in alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and gamma-glutamyl transferase. The increases mostly appeared within 1 to 3 weeks and returned to normal after 4 weeks. Liver impairment improved after suspension of As₂O₃ and liver protection treatment, and no patient died of liver failure. Changes in short-term cumulative dose of As₂O₃ did not correlate with hepatotoxicity, but patients with differentiation syndrome were at higher risk. The authors conclude that hepatotoxicity induced by As₂O₃ at a therapeutic dose for pediatric APL is mild and temporary.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old Taiwanese male with chronic hepatitis B began oral terbinafine 250 mg once daily for dermatophyte toenail onychomycosis with normal baseline liver enzymes. Near the end of the 12-week course he developed anorexia, malaise, ascites and jaundice; diagnosis of acute autoimmune drug injury was supported by transient autoantibodies and a liver biopsy consistent with acute autoimmune hepatitis, with no other medications, herbal supplements, or alcohol, and no evident HBV flare. Three weeks after discontinuing terbinafine, peak AST was 1282 IU/L, ALT 1044 IU/L, bilirubin 5.9 mg/dL, and platelets had fallen to 77 × 10³/mm³; liver function normalized 6 weeks after discontinuation.

raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo probability scale and Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) both supported a probable relationship between the hepatitis and terbinafine. Peak AST 1282 IU/L, ALT 1044 IU/L, bilirubin 5.9 mg/dL, platelet nadir 77 × 10³/mm³, treated with vitamin K for coagulopathy, diuretics for ascites, and adefovir to prevent hepatitis B exacerbation; liver studies normalized 6 weeks after discontinuation. Terbinafine-induced hepatobiliary dysfunction due to hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, or mixed form has been reported. raw_record.support_text: The review describes halothane-associated hepatitis, a recognized clinical syndrome in humans. In Brisbane, 6 of 300 patients receiving multiple halothane exposures for uterine carcinoma developed severe hepatocellular jaundice and 2 died; in Sheffield, 3 of 57 patients receiving multiple halothane exposures developed severe hepatocellular disease, and no further cases occurred after this anesthesia was stopped. The association, also supported by direct rechallenge cases (Belfrage; Klatskin & Kimberg) and registry data, implicates a sensitization mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury predominantly reported after repeated (multiple) halothane anesthetic exposures, typically in surgical patients; mechanism is sensitization rather than dose-related direct toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane-associated hepatitis characterized by postoperative unexplained fever, eosinophilia, granuloma formation in liver, and mitochondrial antibodies, suggesting sensitization rather than direct hepatotoxicity. Direct rechallenge reproduced acute hepatitis with liver biopsy confirmation (Belfrage 1966; Klatskin & Kimberg). Incidence: ~1 death from halothane-associated liver necrosis per 8000 uneventful anesthetics (Montreal); National Halothane Study found 7 of 9 unexplained fatal massive hepatic necroses had received halothane; Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Study reported halothane-associated hepatitis in 20% of first 150 patients and 18% of 600 stage IV coma patients, with worse survival than viral/drug-induced etiologies. Not dose-related; viral etiologies considered as competing causes. Liver necrosis, hepatocellular jaundice and hepatocellular disease reported.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients developed acute cholestatic hepatitis during treatment with propafenone. Viral infections, alcohol abuse, hepatotoxicity by other drugs, and biliary obstruction were excluded as causes. In one patient, liver biopsy showed changes consistent with a drug-associated injury, and another had serum autoimmune antibodies (ANA). Following propafenone withdrawal, the clinical and biochemical profiles of both patients improved. The authors describe hepatic toxicity from the antiarrhythmic drug propafenone as highly uncommon, noting that most cases reported had acute cholestatic hepatitis after a latency of two to four weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Two new cases added to seven previously published, for a total of nine (none fatal). Acute cholestatic hepatitis usually after a latency of two to four weeks; one new case had an extremely long latency period and circulating antinuclear antibodies (ANA). One patient's liver biopsy showed changes consistent with drug-associated injury. Both patients improved after propafenone withdrawal. Case 1: 67-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus type II and hypertension, on glibenclamide 5 mg/day and enalapril 20 mg/day for 5 years, started propafenone 450 mg/day 6 weeks before hepatitis symptoms for atrial fibrillation; other hepatotoxic drugs, viral infection, alcohol, and biliary obstruction excluded as causes. Mechanism unknown, proposed as either hypersensitivity reaction or idiosyncratic toxic reaction due to a propafenone metabolite; hepatic metabolism influenced by cytochrome P-450 2D6 activity with 5-hydroxy and N-desalkyl active metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old woman who underwent cholecystectomy under halothane anesthesia in 1967 developed postoperative vomiting, dark urine, jaundice and a tender enlarged liver, with marked eosinophilia and elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and SGOT; liver biopsy was interpreted as subacute hepatitis and the diagnosis was halothane-induced hepatitis. She recovered and a later cataract extraction under halothane-free anesthesia was uneventful.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane given in 1967 for cholecystectomy; symptoms began by postoperative day 13 (indigestion, chills, vomiting), dark urine day 18, jaundice day 22. Liver biopsy at day 38 showed subacute hepatitis; the patient recovered without specific treatment. Other drugs received during that episode included meperidine, atropine, thiopental, succinylcholine, gallamine, neostigmine, nitrous oxide, aspirin, codeine, propoxyphene, carbromal and barbiturates. raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) is a widely used analgesic and antipyretic that is a dose-related toxin and can produce severe hepatotoxicity if used in excess. In the United States and many European countries, nearly half of all drug-related liver injuries are caused by APAP, and there has been an increase in drug-induced acute liver failure due to AILI (acetaminophen-induced liver injury).
raw_record.extra_details: APAP is described as a dose-related toxin causing severe hepatotoxicity when used in excess, and is the leading cause of drug-induced acute liver failure (AILI). In the US and many European countries nearly half of all drug-related liver injuries are attributed to APAP. Pathogenic mechanism: excess APAP is metabolized by CYP2E1 and CYP1A2 to the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which depletes glutathione (GSH), forms APAP protein adducts (APAP-AD), and leads to mitochondrial damage and hepatocyte necrosis; oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, ER stress, microcirculatory disorders are implicated. Human serum samples were collected from 40 AILI patients and 20 healthy controls; 3 transplant recipients met APASL AILI diagnostic criteria.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-yr-old woman developed subacute hepatitis and liver failure after a 1-month course of treatment with the NSAID bromfenac. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C were negative, as were antinuclear antibodies and ceruloplasmin, and a transjugular liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis. The course was complicated by encephalopathy, fluid retention, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, prompting consideration for liver transplantation. The authors conclude that prolonged bromfenac use was the etiological agent and that this drug can cause severe hepatotoxicity resulting in liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 40-yr-old woman; bromfenac sodium 25 mg t.i.d.; prior short courses (10 days and ~3 wk) with pain recurrence after discontinuation and reinstitution; jaundice and nausea/vomiting/fever developed, jaundice and biochemical hepatitis followed. Initial labs: total bilirubin 5.2 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 223 IU/L, ALT 2001 IU/L; admission labs total bilirubin 15.0 mg/dl, ALT 1966 U/L, AST 2144 U/L, INR 1.7. Transjugular biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis; subacute hepatic failure with consideration for liver transplant; supportive management led to resolution of jaundice and fluid retention over ~3 months. Negative hepatitis A/B/C serologies, ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody; normal ceruloplasmin; no acetaminophen, ethanol, prior liver disease, or other co-medications at the time. Prior agents tramadol and cyclobenzaprine were discontinued and ibuprofen stopped 7 days before reinstating bromfenac and are not attributed as causes.

raw_record.support_text: A literature review identified 72 cases of dapsone-induced hepatitis (DIH) published 1949-2015 that fulfilled DILI-defining criteria (females>males). Liver was the commonest extra-dermatologic organ involved in dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS), with DHS present in 64/72 patients (88.8%). Mean latency was 31.8 days (range 7-150). Dapsone rechallenge in a third of patients resulted in DHS/DIH with shortened latency and severe disease including death. Mean bilirubin was 8.4 mg/dl, mean AST 379 IU/L, mean ALT 562 IU/L, mean ALP 815.5 IU/L; overall mortality was 19.4% (14/72) and one patient required liver transplantation.

raw_record.extra_details: Latency 31.8 days mean (range 7-150); 72 published cases (females>males) fulfilling DILI criteria. Mean bilirubin 8.4 mg/dl, AST 379 IU/L, ALT 562 IU/L, ALP 815.5 IU/L. Severity indices: jaundice 62%, encephalopathy 16.7%, ascites 12%, raised INR (>1.5) 24%. Overall mortality 19.4% (14/72); one patient required liver transplantation. Steroid treatment (n=28) led to faster recovery and less mortality. Mixed hepatitis described as commonest hepatitis pattern; liver injury ranges from mild (resolving on drug discontinuation) to ALF and death, most occurring within first 4-6 weeks of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A 54-year-old woman prescribed acarbose (50 mg three times daily) for NIDDM presented 5 months later with fatigue, dark urine, and jaundice; AST 2436 U/l, ALT 2556 U/l, total bilirubin 4.67 mg/dl, GGT 601 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 174 U/l. Viral hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV were ruled out, no autoantibodies, normal ultrasound. Acarbose was stopped and liver tests normalized within 5 months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had NIDDM and was not taking other medications or herbal remedies.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2 of the report: acarbose 50 mg three times daily for NIDDM; onset of fatigue/dark urine 5 months after starting; jaundice; AST 2436 U/l, ALT 2556 U/l, total bilirubin 4.67 mg/dl (direct 3.19), GGT 601 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 174 U/l; ultrasonography normal; liver tests normalized within 5 months after stopping. Causality supported by temporal relation, resolution on dechallenge, and absence of alternative explanations. Mechanism attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy rather than hypersensitivity (no fever, rash, or eosinophilia), involving the original compound or its metabolites, mainly 4-methylpyrogallol derivatives. Hepatotoxicity described as a very rare but potentially severe adverse event of acarbose therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a patient who developed two episodes of methyldopa-associated hepatitis; the second, after rechallenge following discontinuation, progressed to fatal submassive hepatic necrosis. The authors state that liver cell damage during methyldopa therapy is well documented and that it seems likely the submassive hepatic necrosis was the ultimate result of use of that drug. The hepatic lesion resembled viral hepatitis but the autopsy specimen contained abundant lipid, effectively excluding viral hepatitis, and no other drugs (beyond long-tolerated reserpine, hydralazine, chlorothiazide, and chlorthalidone) were taken.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was nonalcoholic with no viral-source exposure (viral hepatitis excluded by abundant lipid in the autopsy specimen); had long tolerated concomitant reserpine, hydralazine, chlorothiazide, and chlorthalidone; injury followed rechallenge after prior recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Methyldopa (trade name Aldomet). Initial episode of jaundice occurred 12 weeks after methyldopa was begun, and liver tests returned to normal within 6 weeks after withdrawal; no hepatic dysfunction for the following 18 weeks. After reinstitution, 9 weeks later abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and liver-function aberrations appeared, and liver failure progressed inexorably despite discontinuation. Necropsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis with lipid demonstrated by oil red O (original magnification x100). Authors note methyldopa-induced liver disease is chemically and clinically indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, and the usual histologic pattern is a nonspecific hepatitis without cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: In an adjudicated IDILI patient cohort, 4 single drugs caused IDILI in at least 3 patients each, and only INH (isoniazid)-induced liver injury showed significant DEGs compared to IDILI not due to INH. All three patients with INH-induced IDILI were in the 'fatal' IDILI group: two died because of their injury and one required a liver transplant. Of 25 DEGs associated with INH-induced hepatotoxicity, 80% were elevated in the INH patients, and 40% overlapped with the DEGs related to IDILI severity.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients with INH-induced IDILI were in the fatal IDILI group: two died from their injury and one required liver transplant. Of 25 DEGs associated with INH-induced hepatotoxicity, 80% were elevated in INH patients, 40% overlapped with general IDILI-severity DEGs; TRBV7-2, encoding a TCR subunit, was reduced in INH patients. No canonical pathways were significant. No differences in circulating T-cell percentages or concentration were observed between INH-related and other severe/all IDILI patients. Study note: patients frequently take multiple medications/supplements concurrently, complicating culprit identification; INH-induced injury was the drug-attributable subgroup analyzed.

raw_record.support_text: After a multidisciplinary consultation and a Naranjo score of 13 indicating a definite reaction, the authors diagnosed sub-acute liver injury from paclitaxel-induced hepatotoxicity in a patient with ovarian cancer. Elevated serum aminotransferases up to 12 times ULN with normal total bilirubin and ALP appeared 14 days after IV paclitaxel plus carboplatin, and alternative causes were excluded, leading to attribution of the liver injury to paclitaxel.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver injury occurred in a patient with ovarian cancer receiving IV paclitaxel in combination with carboplatin; later rechallenged at a reduced dose after recovery.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale total score of 13, classified as a definite reaction. Elevated ALT/AST up to 12 times ULN with normal total bilirubin and ALP ~14 days after the first IV paclitaxel plus carboplatin dose. Treated with glutathione 1.2 g and magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate 0.2 g IV for 14 days; LFTs improved and were stable within 2-3 times ULN across subsequent cycles. Rechallenged with paclitaxel at a reduced dose of 180 mg (135 mg/m2 instead of 175 mg/m2) per package-insert recommendations. LiverTox likelihood score D (possible cause of acute hepatic necrosis associated with a hypersensitivity reaction to initial infusions); hypersensitivity reaction was excluded in this case (no chest tightness or facial flushing). Hypersensitivity and acute liver failure were ruled out.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 95 patients with active tuberculosis treated with isoniazid (INH) 10 mg/kg, rifampicin (RMP) 10 mg/kg, and ethambutol (EMB) 25 mg/kg, the authors investigated the influence of acetylator phenotype on isoniazid hepatotoxicity. They found a 12.6% incidence of isoniazid hepatitis (SGOT, SGPT >200 U/l) and a significantly higher risk of isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity in slow acetylators (p <0.01): 26/56 slow acetylators (≈46.4%) vs 4/30 rapid acetylators (≈13.3%) had transaminases >50 U/l, and all 12 patients with the most severe hepatotoxic side effects (SGOT/SGPT >200 U/l) were slow acetylators. Women developed severe hepatic injury more often than men (p <0.05). In isoniazid hepatitis cases therapy was stopped or reduced to RMP+EMB; transaminases normalized within 2-4 weeks and no new elevation occurred upon resuming full therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Confirmed active pulmonary tuberculosis; triple therapy with rifampicin and ethambutol as co-medication; slow acetylator phenotype carries higher risk; women affected more often than men.
raw_record.extra_details: Doses: isoniazid 10 mg/kg, rifampicin 10 mg/kg, ethambutol 25 mg/kg (INH 10 mg/kg mentioned). Isoniazid hepatitis defined as SGOT/SGPT >200 U/l, incidence 12.6% of treated. Transaminase elevations >50 U/l in 46.4% of slow vs 13.3% of rapid acetylators. Onset constant in the 2nd-4th week (19 +/- 7 days); transaminases normalized within 2-4 weeks; no new transaminase elevation on rechallenge with full triple therapy. Authors propose an interaction between rifampicin and isoniazid metabolism limited to the early phase of chemotherapy.

Nineteen had SGPT/SGOT rises of 50-200 U/l with a de Ritis ratio near 0.5 that normalized spontaneously despite continued therapy, while 12 developed a clinically manifest severe hepatotoxic reaction ('INH-Hepatitis') with transaminases of 200-900 U/l, bilirubin elevations to 10 mg%, and marked secondary coproporphyrinuria. The injury was attributed to isoniazid, since usually only INH was withdrawn; transaminases and bilirubin normalized within 2-4 weeks, and re-exposure to the full combination did not produce notable enzyme rises.

raw_record.extra_details: 31/95 (32.6%) showed liver damage; 19 had SGPT/SGOT 50-200 U/l that normalized despite continued treatment, and 12 had severe clinically manifest INH-hepatitis with transaminases 200-900 U/l, some with jaundice and bilirubin 2-10 mg%, and 4-6-fold elevated urinary coproporphyrins. raw_record.support_text: A 12-year-old patient treated for tuberculosis with isoniazid (11 mg/kg daily, 200 mg/d) and vitamin B6 for 5 months presented with jaundice, markedly elevated AST (3576 U/L), ALT (2546 U/L), conjugated bilirubin (147 µmol/L) and INR 1.7. Ultrasound findings were consistent with acute hepatitis, and a transjugular liver biopsy showed subacute necrosis with micronodular cirrhosis. Toxicology screening was negative, acetaminophen was not detected, and serologic and PCR testing for hepatitis A/B/C, HIV, EBV, CMV, HSV, VZV and parvovirus were negative; no other prescription, over-the-counter or herbal medications were taken, and pharmacy errors and inadvertent overdosing were ruled out. The most likely diagnosis was drug-induced hepatitis (hepatotoxicity). The patient subsequently developed hepatic encephalopathy and was placed on a liver transplant waiting list when INR peaked at 2.3, but spontaneously improved and was removed from the transplant list 13 days after discontinuing isoniazid, recovering overall.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient treated for tuberculosis; isoniazid was continued by the family for at least 10 days after symptom onset before being withheld. Co-medication with vitamin B6. Competing causes largely ruled out via serology, toxicology and history.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid dosed 11 mg/kg daily (200 mg/d); hepatotoxicity developed at the 5-month visit (characteristically late in treatment). Peak AST 4066 U/L (3 days after discontinuation), peak ALT 2895 U/L (5 days after), peak INR 2.3 (9 days after); hepatic encephalopathy developed; placed on transplant waiting list and removed 13 days after isoniazid stopped; discharged 3 weeks after admission with improving liver function. Histology: subacute necrosis with micronodular cirrhosis. Key points note hepatotoxicity is the most common complication of isoniazid and can occur at any point during treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac appears to be the inciting agent for the liver disease in the three reported patients. Alcohol, viral, and other genetic causes of liver disease were excluded, and transaminases returned to and remained normal after discontinuation of therapy; the biochemical abnormalities reappeared on reintroduction of diclofenac (or another anthranilic acid derivative). Two hepatic reactions were observed: patients 1 and 2 had serologic and histologic features of autoimmune chronic active hepatitis (ACAH) that were initially misdiagnosed, and patient 3 presented with features of acute hepatitis with elevated transaminases, jaundice, low-grade fever, nausea, marked peripheral eosinophilia, and low-titer ANA. The paper states it is likely that diclofenac can induce several types of hepatotoxicity and classifies the reactions as idiosyncratic (type II), with patients 1 and 2 falling into the metabolic-aberration category and patient 3 showing a hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Three new patients (Scully, this study) treated for osteoarthritis or back pain. Causality supported by dechallenge with normalization of transaminases and rechallenge with reappearance of biochemical abnormalities. Patients 1 and 2: autoimmune chronic active hepatitis features, elevated ANA (1/640, 1/40), negative ASMA, normal IgG, no fibrosis on biopsy, initially treated with corticosteroids without relapse after withdrawal; patient 1 also had presumed isoniazid hepatotoxicity and vitiligo, patient 2 had high-titer antithyroglobulin antibodies; none developed SLE. Patient 3: acute hepatitis with jaundice, low-grade fever, nausea, marked peripheral eosinophilia, low-titer ANA, background multiple sclerosis. Type II idiosyncratic classification: patients 1-2 metabolic aberration, patient 3 hypersensitivity. Review table of 26 published diclofenac-induced liver disease cases (22F/4M, age 58 ± 11 yr, treatment duration 12.6 ± 10.6 weeks): 4 died, 20 improved, 2 steroid-treated; 13 jaundiced; phenotypes included periportal/lobular inflammation, hepatic necrosis, mixed hepatitis with cholestasis, fatty change with centrilobular hepatocyte loss, multilobular necrosis, bridging fibrosis; maximum reported severity includes fatal cases.

raw_record.support_text: The patient developed biochemical evidence of hepatocellular injury without any related clinical symptoms. Differential diagnosis included metformin-induced drug hepatitis, NASH, and autoimmune hepatitis; autoimmune hepatitis was deemed unlikely given absence of musculoskeletal symptoms, lower ESR compared to her rheumatism flare ups, and normalization of ALT despite subsequent flare ups. After metformin was stopped, the ALT fell from a peak of 738 U/l to 273 at 5 days and normalized to 16 U/l at 1 month, remaining normal over 2 years follow-up; a rechallenge test was declined.

raw_record.extra_details: Current case: ALT rose from 31 U/l at 2 weeks to 738 U/l at ~20 weeks poststarting metformin; GGT peaked at 42 IU/l (5 months); ALP normal throughout; negative viral hepatitis serology (A, B, C) and negative ANA, AMA, ASMA; abdominal ultrasound showed diffuse fatty infiltration, no biliary obstruction. raw_record.support_text: Although all patients had taken other medications, flucloxacillin almost certainly was the cause of their jaundice. Jaundice developed two to five weeks after the initial dose, similar to the usual time for idiosyncratic drug reactions. ERCP was normal in four cases, there was no serological evidence of viral hepatitis, and liver biopsy in all patients was consistent with drug-induced cholestasis without evidence of large-duct obstruction.

raw_record.extra_details: Five cases. Jaundice developed 2-5 weeks after the initial flucloxacillin dose. ERCP normal in four cases; imaging of liver and common bile duct normal in all cases; no serological evidence of viral hepatitis; liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced cholestasis without large-duct obstruction. Marked cholestasis with consistently raised serum alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase, which remained elevated after jaundice disappearance in three of five cases; AST and ALT raised up to 10 times normal in the first month. All patients had prolonged deep jaundice lasting at least two months; two patients still icteric and pruritic after six and nine months; Patients 4 and 5 had continuing pruritus and elevated liver enzymes 13 and 16 months after drug ingestion. Patient 4 had severe pruritus, jaundice and hypercholesterolaemia with some response to plasmapheresis, and a second biopsy showed advanced fibrosis and features of chronic biliary disease; one patient with bile-duct loss (Case 4). Pruritus unresponsive to cholestyramine, phenobarbitone, prednisone and antihistamines; rifampicin gave some relief in Patients 4 and 5.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year old patient with carbamazepine-induced hepatotoxicity, associated with hypersensitivity manifestations of fever, rash and eosinophilia, is described. Mononuclear leucocytes from the patient were more sensitive to oxidative metabolites of carbamazepine than control cells, and serum from the patient recognised a single 94 kDa protein band on human liver microsomes, which none of 25 control sera recognised. The paper presents this as a human case of carbamazepine hepatotoxicity with an immunoallergic/autoantibody basis.

Subsequent studies showed that a carboxylic acid metabolite of panadiplon caused redistribution of cellular coenzyme A stores and inhibition of β-oxidation, rendering hepatocytes sensitive to secondary stress (e.g., hypoxia), which subsequently produced apoptosis and hepatocellular necrosis.

Hepatic toxicity was not predicted by rat, dog, or monkey preclinical studies. In vitro, co-treatment with pyruvate reduced the level of LDH leakage caused by panadiplon under hypoxic conditions (Bacon et al. 1996). This ximelagatran-related review is anchored to prior mechanistic data on panadiplon.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP, N-acetyl-p-aminophenol) is safe at therapeutic doses but in overdose produces potentially fatal fulminating centrilobular hepatic necrosis that can bridge to periportal regions of the liver lobule. Acetaminophen toxicity results annually in more than 50,000 US emergency room visits, several thousand hospitalizations, and between 400 and 500 deaths. In the adult acute liver failure (ALF) Study Group (Jan 1998 to Jul 2007, 1147 patients at 23 US sites), acetaminophen overdose accounted for 46% of cases, making it the most frequent cause of adult ALF.

raw_record.support_text: TAK-875 was discontinued due to liver toxicity, and Marcinak et al. published post hoc results of a Liver Safety Evaluation Committee pooling 15 double-blind phase II/III trials totaling 9,139 patients with type 2 diabetes. Patients treated with TAK-875 had an increased incidence of serum ALT elevations above 3-, 5-, and 10-fold ULN versus placebo or comparators (ALT >3x ULN was 2.7% in the TAK-875 group vs 0.8% comparator and 0.5% placebo), with no dose response seen at 25 and 50 mg/day, and the elevated ALT resolved upon discontinuation. Shavadia et al., analyzing 7,595 patients across 8 trials before program termination, reported a greater frequency of possible Hy's law cases and a 3–7-fold higher risk of ALT/AST increase in the TAK-875 group, with an overall probability of drug-induced liver injury of 0.64% versus 0.06% in placebo/comparator.
raw_record.extra_details: GPR40 (FFAR1) partial agonist (fasiglifam). Terminated at phase III due to liver toxicity. Post hoc pooled analysis of 15 phase II/III trials (9,139 T2D patients): ALT >3x ULN 2.7% vs 0.8% comparator and 0.5% placebo; no dose response at 25 vs 50 mg daily; ALT resolved after discontinuation. Second analysis (7,595 patients, 8 trials): possible Hy's law cases more frequent, 3-to-7-fold higher ALT/AST increase risk, overall DILI probability 0.64% vs 0.06% placebo/comparator. Proposed mechanisms (preclinical): acyl glucuronidation (TAK-875AG reactive metabolite), inhibition of mitochondrial respiration, bile acid transporter inhibition, ROS generation, increased bile acid biosynthesis.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective observational study of 500 adults with suspected APAP (acetaminophen) overdose, 318 subjects met inclusion criteria and APAP was confirmed as the cause of liver injury. Hepatotoxicity (defined as peak ALT > 1000 IU/L) occurred in 10 of 160 subjects with initial ALT ≤ 50 IU/L and in subjects with higher initial ALT values; among 127 subjects with initial ALT > 100 IU/L, 29 developed hepatic encephalopathy (HE) and 12 died from APAP. These outcomes are explicitly attributed to acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose setting; patients received N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment initiated at enrollment; hepatotoxicity defined as peak ALT > 1000 IU/L.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective observational study (500 subjects ≥18 y, suspected APAP overdose; 318 included; Banner Health IRB approved). Initial ALT assessed ±4 h of starting NAC. Among 160 subjects with initial ALT ≤50 IU/L: 10 developed hepatotoxicity (PPV 0.06; 95% CI 0.03-0.11), 1 developed hepatic encephalopathy (PPV <0.01; 95% CI 0-0.03), none died. Among 191 with initial ALT ≤100 IU/L: 1 HE (NPV 0.99; 95% CI 0.97-0.99), no APAP deaths (NPV 1.0; 95% CI 0.98-1.0). raw_record.extra_details: In the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group report (1998-2016), 45.8% of ALF cases were attributed to APAP. Mechanism described: most APAP metabolized by UGT/SULT to non-toxic compounds; ~5-9% oxidized by cytochrome P450 to the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzo-quinoneimine (NAPQI), whose accumulation with glutathione depletion promotes reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial dysfunction leading to hepatocellular necrosis/apoptosis.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old woman with aspirin-sensitive asthma and allergic rhinitis began montelukast therapy after baseline liver function tests were normal. After 3 weeks of montelukast, she developed jaundice, severe pruritus, and nausea, with elevated total bilirubin (181.3 µmol/L), alkaline phosphatase (231 IU/L), AST (123 IU/L), ALT (174 IU/L), and γ-glutamyltransferase (224 IU/L); serologic testing for hepatitis A, B, and C was negative. Therapy was stopped and jaundice and pruritus resolved, with most liver test results normalizing over 5 months though aminotransferases remained elevated; a liver biopsy 14 months after starting montelukast showed mild chronic portal inflammation without lobular inflammation or fibrosis. They underwent intensive serial clinical, laboratory, and serial needle aspiration biopsy studies, documenting chlorpromazine-induced cholestatic liver injury with associated liver cell degeneration.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine psychiatric inpatients with chlorpromazine jaundice; 26 percutaneous needle aspiration biopsies. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that clinical hepatitis caused by nevirapine was an uncommon effect in the authors' HIV-1-infected cohort, with possible contributions from underlying factors such as HCV infection and other hepatotoxic agents (e.g., alcohol or antituberculous drugs). It cites anecdotal cases of fulminant hepatitis with nevirapine-containing regimens and a randomized placebo-controlled trial (FTC-302) reporting 9.4% nevirapine-associated hepatotoxicity, with two patients dying due to hepatotoxicity. The paper concludes that although fulminant hepatitis risk must be considered when prescribing nevirapine, it seems extremely low and cannot currently be anticipated.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP; N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide) overdose has been identified as a major cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the United States. Diagnosis of APAP overdose relies on history of a large dose (defined as 7.5 g of APAP in adults) supported by elevated blood APAP; many patients develop ALF rapidly, characterized by encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5).
raw_record.extra_details: APAP-protein adducts (3-(cystein-S-yl)-APAP) formed by hepatic metabolism to the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine serve as specific biomarkers of APAP toxicity; peak APAP adduct concentrations correlated with peak aminotransferase concentrations (r=0.779) in 53 adults with APAP-related ALF. APAP overdose diagnosis required use >4 g/day within 7 days or detection of APAP on admission or ALT >1000 IU/l with APAP history. Patients had acute liver failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5); excluded other etiologies. Acute liver failure is the clinical phenotype (characterized by encephalopathy and coagulopathy), recorded here as other_specific_phenotype. Adducts disappeared with first-order kinetics after N-acetylcysteine therapy (mean t1/2 1.72 ± 0.34 days) and were detected up to 12 days postingestion. Single acute suicidal ingestion; 230 samples from 53 subjects.

Eight deaths from isoniazid hepatitis were reported including three in the authors' series. Mechanism presumed hypersensitivity.

Liver histology included focal necrosis of hepatocytes, hepatic necrosis, acute severe cytolytic hepatitis with necrosis and mild cholestasis, acute cytolytic hepatitis with spotty and piecemeal necrosis, portal and lobular inflammation with bridging and multifocal lobular necrosis, and severe necrosis with multilobular confluent cell dropout, reticulin collapse and multinodular regeneration. Outcomes ranged from resolution after stopping the drug to fatal acute hepatic necrosis and death 10 days after liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Reported cases were imatinib-treated patients with chronic myeloid leukemia or polycythemia vera (hematological malignancy indication); one case involved a prior diagnosis of polycythemia vera.
raw_record.extra_details: Time to hepatic dysfunction ranged from 12 days to 2 years. Referenced cases: Ohyashiki et al (2002) focal hepatocyte necrosis, resolved; Lin et al (2003) hepatic necrosis, fatal acute hepatic necrosis; James et al (2003) 49 wk acute severe cytolytic hepatitis with necrosis and mild cholestasis, resolved, and 22 wk acute cytolytic hepatitis with spotty/piecemeal necrosis, resolved; Kikuchi et al (2004) 36 wk hepatic necrosis, resolved; Ayoub et al (2005) 2 yr portal/lobular inflammation with bridging and multifocal lobular necrosis, resolved; Cross et al (2007) 77 wk severe necrosis with multilobular confluent cell dropout, reticulin collapse and multinodular regeneration, patient died 10 d after liver transplantation; Ridruejo et al (2007) 22 wk, fatal acute hepatic necrosis. Manufacturer package insert recommends monitoring of liver function tests before initiation and monthly.

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluates ADH1B as a biomarker to monitor acetaminophen-induced acute liver injury (ALI) progression, using longitudinal serum samples from patients with acetaminophen overdose. Acetaminophen is treated throughout as a known human cause of acute liver injury and acute liver failure, manifesting as hepatocyte cytolysis and necrosis with massive hepatocyte loss, and in this cohort some patients (e.g., patients 11 and 16) developed ALF requiring liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurred following acetaminophen overdose; study cohort of patients with acetaminophen-induced ALI/ALF, including two patients (patients 11 and 16) who developed acute liver failure and underwent liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Longitudinal human cohort (n=14 with acetaminophen-induced ALI and 5 with non-acetaminophen ALI). Injury reflects massive hepatocyte cytolysis/necrosis causing depletion of the intracellular ADH1B pool; standard biological parameters (INR, bilirubin, creatinine) indicated severe liver failure. ADH1B is proposed as a biomarker of hepatocellular injury leaked into blood following cytolysis. Excessive ADH1B leakage appears specifically correlated with acetaminophen-induced ALI/ALF; serum ADH1B rapidly returned to baseline during liver regeneration, and its drop preceded INR decrease (10-48 h interval) in 5/14 spontaneously recovering cases.

raw_record.support_text: Rumack et al (retrospective observational study, Class II) analyzed 662 acetaminophen overdose patients using a modified Rumack-Matthew nomogram that added a possible hepatotoxic zone placed 25% below the original line. Patients at possible or probable risk for hepatotoxicity were treated with NAC, and the incidence of severe hepatotoxicity varied by nomogram risk group, with fatal outcomes reported in related studies (11 of 2,540 risk patients [0.54%] died in the Smilkstein prospective study of 11,195 suspected acetaminophen poisonings). The paper frames acetaminophen overdose as causing severe hepatotoxicity and mortality that is reduced by early NAC treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute acetaminophen overdose/supratherapeutic exposure; risk stratified by the Rumack-Matthew nomogram; most treated patients received NAC, which reduced severe hepatotoxicity and mortality when given early.
raw_record.extra_details: Nomogram-based risk classification (possible/probable/no risk). Rumack 1981 (n=662): severe hepatotoxicity in 0.34% (1/297) of no-risk, 5% of possible-risk, and 7%/29%/62% of probable-risk patients depending on NAC timing (<10h, 10-16h, 16-24h); no deaths among those treated within 24h. Smilkstein 1988 (n=11,195; 2,540 at risk): severe hepatotoxicity 2.9% (<8h NAC delay), 6.1% (<10h), 26.4% (>10h delay); 11 deaths (0.54%), 9 with high presenting concentration and >16h delay. Level C recommendations support NAC for possible/probable risk to reduce severe hepatotoxicity and mortality.

A retrospective analysis of 97 children with acute liver failure attributed to acetaminophen poisoning at Barnesville Junction Teaching Hospital in Monrovia, Liberia between August 2016 and June 2017 was performed; the mean age was 14.6 months and 52% died during hospitalization.

raw_record.extra_details: 97 children with acute liver failure attributed to acetaminophen poisoning admitted August 2016-June 2017; 52% died during hospitalization; 84 (87%) received NAC. raw_record.support_text: Among patients at probable risk of hepatotoxicity after acetaminophen overdose, hepatotoxicity developed in 6.1 percent of those treated with N-acetylcysteine within 10 hours and in 26.4 percent of those treated 10 to 24 hours after ingestion; in the high-risk subgroup the rates were 8.3 percent (within 10 hours) and 34.4 percent (10 to 24 hours). raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as AST or ALT >1000 IU/L. raw_record.support_text: Lumiracoxib, a selective COX-2 inhibitor registered in Australia in 2004 at 200 mg daily for osteoarthritis, was associated with severe liver injury: in March 2007 the first Australian patient with fulminant liver failure was admitted and died within a week, followed by two further cases of serious liver injury at the same hospital, one requiring liver transplant. Two cases were reported to the Australian TGA and contributed to eight reports of severe liver injury leading to lumiracoxib's withdrawal from the Australian market in August 2007.

Case 2 (53F, 200-400 mg x 6 months): AST 2150, ALT 1180, AP 393, bilirubin 300 U/L, PT 29 s, ANA 1:2560 nucleolar; severe hepatic necrosis; liver transplant. Case 3 (49F, 200 mg x 6 months): AST 817, ALT 652, AP 344, bilirubin 82 U/L, PT 15 s, ANA 1:640 speckled, IgG anti-cardiolipin 24 U/mL; hepatocellular necrosis; post-necrotic cirrhosis. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports three cases of hepatitis following methyldopa administration. Eight to ten weeks after starting methyldopa therapy the patients presented with features similar to acute viral hepatitis, but Australia antigen was not detected; instead immunologic disturbances were noted. The first patient went into hepatic coma and died from massive hepatic necrosis, the second had a protracted course but gradually improved, and the third recovered fully.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for moderate or severe hypertension. Three cases described; Case 1 (50-year-old woman) received methyldopa 250 mg twice daily added to chlorothiazide, diazepam and spironolactone taken for years without untoward effects; jaundice appeared 8-9 weeks later, and she died from massive hepatic necrosis after hepatic coma. Methyldopa hepatotoxicity described as a rare, not generally known side effect among the drug's 'allergic' reactions (e.g., fever, hemolytic anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, positive lupus and rheumatoid factor tests).

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old woman on reserpine, chlorothiazide, guanethedine, digitalis, and chlordiazepoxide for hypertension had methyldopa 250 mg twice daily substituted for reserpine on November 10, 1970. About 10 weeks later she developed loss of appetite, fatigability, dark urine, and later palpitations and orthopnea; on hospitalization she was mildly icteric. A liver biopsy on February 6, 1971 revealed necrosis, mononuclear-cell infiltration, and portal exudate with a histologic diagnosis of acute viral hepatitis. Methyldopa was continued despite jaundice; the drug was briefly suspended February 8-12 but resumed on February 13. She became more severely jaundiced and was rehospitalized on March 25 with the liver extending 4 cm below the costal margin, a positive direct Coombs test, and diffuse antinuclear antibodies (1:10). After discontinuation she improved over 4 weeks, and a June 8, 1971 biopsy showed a chronic active hepatitis-like lesion.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2 (E.M., female, age 55). Methyldopa 250 mg twice daily started Nov 10, 1970; jaundice appeared ~10 weeks later (late Jan 1971). Drug continued despite jaundice; suspended Feb 8-12 but resumed Feb 13 on histologic diagnosis of 'viral hepatitis', followed by progressive worsening jaundice and rehospitalization March 25. Serology: direct Coombs negative initially then positive on rechallenge; no Australia antigen; antinuclear antibodies 1:10; negative LE cells, latex fixation, antithyroid antibodies. Histology: initial biopsy acute viral hepatitis-like (necrosis, acidophilic bodies, portal exudate); follow-up biopsy chronic active hepatitis-like (parenchymal collapse, cicatization, chronic inflammatory exudate, condensation of portal tracts). Improvement within 4 weeks of drug discontinuation; LFTs returned to normal in clinic.

raw_record.support_text: Voriconazole has the potential for its metabolism to be affected by and affect the metabolism of other drugs and cause hepatitis. There is a near-linear dose-response relationship between serum bilirubin concentration and voriconazole concentrations; the higher the concentration of voriconazole, the higher the risk for cholestatic hepatitis (Tan et al., 2006). Cholestatic hepatitis is not an uncommon finding in patients treated with voriconazole. The reported case describes recurrent cholestatic hepatitis in a patient taking voriconazole, induced initially by concomitant lansoprazole and later by simvastatin.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes acetaminophen as one of the most commonly used analgesics whose well-known major adverse effect is massive hepatic necrosis with potentially fatal consequences, noting that such complications can occur from intentional overdose or in the presence of certain predisposing factors, and frames the condition as acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. The presented patient, after an acetaminophen overdose, declined into multiorgan failure and died after support was withdrawn (p:23).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose case culminating in massive hepatic necrosis, multiorgan failure and death; the patient had ongoing alcohol use and was declined for liver transplantation. Background discussion: ~5% of a dose is metabolized by CYP (primarily CYP2E1, CYP1A2, CYP3A4) to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, considered likely involved in hepatotoxicity; NAPQI is normally conjugated with glutathione but its formation exceeds conjugation capacity at increased doses. Most authorities regard doses <6 g/d as non-toxic with recommended daily cumulative doses not exceeding 4 g/d, and 2 g/d for those with long-term excessive alcohol exposure or other hepatic dysfunction. Whether therapeutic doses increase the risk of massive hepatic necrosis in patients with long-term excessive alcohol exposure is controversial; a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of repeated 4 g/d dosing in chronic alcoholics reported no evidence of liver injury.

The resulting acute hepatic failure is characterized by hepatic encephalopathy, cerebral edema, and central nervous system depression.

The paper describes death as almost certain under these conditions; acute liver failure is the reported liver-injury outcome.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman taking citalopram (Cipramil) at 20 mg/d for 3 weeks presented with weakness, asthenia, weight loss and jaundice, with elevated bilirubin (11 mg/dL), AST, ALT and GGT. Biopsy showed subacute liver dystrophy and liver cell necrosis consistent with drug-induced liver injury; all other causes (alcohol, other drugs, metabolic, viral, hereditary, bile duct obstruction) were excluded. Stopping citalopram led to complete normalization of liver tests within 3 months. The authors establish a causal association for this acute hepatic injury based on temporal relationship, histology and improvement after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Female, 56 years old; citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/d for 3 weeks. Symptoms: weakness, asthenia, weight loss, jaundice, mild hepatomegaly; abdominal ultrasound compatible with acute hepatitis. Labs: bilirubin 11 mg/dL (<1), AST 5.7 µmol/s per L (0.1-0.60), ALT 14.2 µmol/s per L (0.17-0.60), GGT 6.9 µmol/s per L (<1.10). Histology: subacute liver dystrophy with complete necrosis of hepatocytes of zones 2 and 3, indistinguishable from acute virus hepatitis; lymphocytes and macrophages infiltrate zone 1 at the necrosis border. No alcohol, no other drugs, no transfusion, no pre-existing liver disease; metabolic, viral, hereditary and autoimmune causes and bile duct obstruction excluded. Complete normalization of liver tests within 3 months after drug discontinuation; no rechallenge. The paper notes a prior report (Lopez-Torres et al) of possibly citalopram-related hepatotoxicity in a patient receiving two other drugs. Authors do not recommend routine liver function monitoring due to long cohorted clinical experience without previously described hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 30-year-old Latino male newly diagnosed with HIV started efavirenz-based HAART (tenofovir 300 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, efavirenz 600 mg once daily). Eleven days after beginning therapy he developed a hypersensitivity reaction with rash and fever preceding severe drug-induced hepatitis, with peak liver enzymes of AST 3410 U/L and ALT 2132 U/L. Hepatitis resolved with HAART discontinuation. Rechallenge with tenofovir and emtricitabine one year later produced no adverse reactions. The Naranjo probability scale demonstrated a probable relationship between this adverse reaction and efavirenz, and the authors concluded efavirenz is the most probable cause of the rash and acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report: 30-year-old Latino male, newly diagnosed HIV, efavirenz 600 mg once daily with tenofovir 300 mg and emtricitabine 200 mg. Onset 11 days after starting therapy; hypersensitivity with erythematous maculopapular rash and fever preceding hepatitis; peak AST 3410 U/L and ALT 2132 U/L; resolved on discontinuation; rechallenge with tenofovir+emtricitabine one year later caused no adverse reaction. Naranjo score = probable. MEDLINE search (2004–Sept 2007) found 2 prior cases of rash preceding hepatitis with efavirenz, both in women. Mechanism speculated to involve efavirenz half-life/auto-induction and CYP2B6-mediated clearance (CYP2B6 responsible for ~90% of efavirenz clearance); higher efavirenz concentrations reported in black and Latino patients.

Discussion notes efavirenz autoinduction (t1/2) and CYP2B6-mediated metabolism (~90%), with higher efavirenz concentrations reported in black and Latino patients. Clinicians recommended withholding efavirenz and monitoring liver enzymes when rash, fever, and enzyme elevations >3x ULN occur.

raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo adverse-reaction imputability scale indicated a probable link between the adverse effect and EFV. Latency 11 days after HAART introduction. Rash and fever preceded hepatitis. AST/ALT peaked at 3410/2132 U/L. Hepatitis resolved upon stopping the HAART. MEDLINE search found 2 prior cases of rash preceding hepatitis with EFV introduction in women; no prior male hypersensitivity case. CYP2B6 mediates about 90% of EFV clearance; recent pharmacokinetic data show higher EFV concentrations in Black and Latino patients; the paper notes possible liver impairment at peak transaminase elevation reducing EFV clearance. In conclusion, EFV was deemed the most probable cause of the hypersensitivity reaction manifesting as maculopapular erythema and acute hepatitis; liver function monitoring recommended for patients developing rash after starting EFV-based HAART.

raw_record.support_text: This prospective multicenter study evaluated acetaminophen-protein adducts as biomarkers of acetaminophen-induced hepatic injury in 51 children and adolescents with acute or chronic acetaminophen overdose. Six subjects developed 'severe' hepatotoxicity (transaminase elevation >1000 IU/L) and 6 had transaminase elevation of 100–1000 IU/L. Acetaminophen-protein adducts were detected in serum of only 1 subject, who had marked transaminase elevation (>6000 IU/L) and high risk of hepatotoxicity per the Rumack nomogram.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen-protein adducts (3-Cys-A) are highly specific for acetaminophen-induced hepatic injury and correlate with transaminase elevation; their presence in centrilobular liver in laboratory animals follows toxic doses. In humans the reactive metabolite NAPQI covalently binds hepatic protein after overdose. Serum adducts were detected in only 1 of 51 study subjects. Six subjects had 'severe' hepatotoxicity (transaminase >1000 IU/L), 6 had transaminase 100–1000 IU/L; the adduct-positive subject had transaminase >6000 IU/L and high risk per the Rumack nomogram. Acetaminophen-protein adducts have previously been detected in the serum of several adults with large overdoses presenting late and in 2 children with chronic overdoses. Detection with current methodology requires significant biochemical evidence of hepatocellular injury.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old woman ingested 66 g of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA, aspirin) in a suicide attempt. Nine days after ingestion she developed hepatic encephalopathy and was diagnosed with acute liver failure with hepatic coma, accompanied by acute pancreatitis and acute renal failure, attributed to the ASA overdose. She was treated with emergency living donor liver transplantation using a left lobe graft and subsequently recovered. ASA-induced hepatic injury is described as a well-known adverse effect, with ALF from ASA overdose being rare.

ASA also known as aspirin.

The authors note that ASA-induced hepatic injury is a well-known dose-related phenomenon tied to the intrinsic hepatotoxicity of salicylate, whereas ASA-induced ALF is rare. The patient developed ALF with hepatic coma and received emergency living donor liver transplantation.

Histopathology showed swelling and microvesicular steatosis consistent with Reye's syndrome, but presence of cholestasis and periportal neutrophil infiltration contraindicated Reye's; loss of hepatocytes and cholestasis were also noted. Patient received emergency LDLT; ALF score at transplantation was 4.

raw_record.support_text: Acute intoxications with iron commonly occur through ingestion, by intention or unintentionally. There are reports on fatal iron toxicity in adults causing fulminant hepatic failure, with normal serum iron levels at 36 h after ingestion due to redistribution of iron to the intracellular compartment. In one detailed patient, plasma iron was high on day 3 and ferritin high, plasma activities increased on day 2 with ALT and AST > 15,000 U/L followed by rapid decline; despite repeated lavages, chelating therapy, and plasma exchange, the patient died of fulminant hepatic failure, and autopsy liver histology showed complete disappearance of hepatocytes.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute iron intoxication by intentional or unintentional ingestion; fatal cases in adults caused fulminant hepatic failure with redistribution of iron to the intracellular compartment (normal serum iron at 36 h). One patient had high plasma iron and ferritin on day 3, ALT and AST > 15,000 U/L on day 2 followed by rapid decline; despite repeated gastric and intestinal lavages, chelating therapy, and plasma exchange the patient died of fulminant hepatic failure, with autopsy histology showing complete disappearance of hepatocytes. No evidence-based treatment guidelines exist.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a probable case of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) with cholestasis and cholangiopathy in a patient receiving Lutetium-177 vipivotide tetraxetan (LuPSMA) therapy, and advise clinicians to remain vigilant for potential hepatotoxicity in such patients. Proposed mechanisms (Table 2) included hepatic canalicular insult via canalicular PSMA expression, cholangiocyte radiosensitivity, microvascular ischemic injury of the peribiliary vascular plexus, a bile duct necrosis and fibroinflammatory stricture cascade, and immune-inflammatory amplification; the authors also noted that prior LuPSMA liver-injury reports had competing causes such as ischemia, biliary obstruction, or mass effect from peritumoral edema.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as a probable case of DILI with cholestasis and cholangiopathy during LuPSMA therapy for cancer; known as Lutetium-177 vipivotide tetraxetan (LuPSMA). Proposed DILI mechanisms: hepatic canalicular insult from canalicular PSMA expression impairing bile secretion and bile acid transporter integrity; radiosensitivity of cholangiocytes; microvascular ischemic injury of the peribiliary vascular plexus; bile duct necrosis with fibroinflammatory stricture cascade and multifocal stricturing; and immune-inflammatory amplification from repeated cycles. Prior LuPSMA reports of liver injury had competing causes (ischemia, biliary obstruction, mass effect from peripancreatic/porta hepatis nodal edema). Compared against a prior single-dose case with AST 2,105 U/L and ALT 2,307 U/L, sinusoidal dilatation and severe zone 3 injury.
