raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with imatinib mesylate developed hepatotoxicity including an increase in total bilirubin to a maximum of 513.4 µmol/l on hospital day 7, with normalization after 6 weeks following discontinuation of imatinib and short steroid therapy. After resuming imatinib mesylate at a reduced dose of 400 mg daily, the patient experienced no further hepatotoxicity. The authors attribute the liver abnormalities to imatinib mesylate.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of imatinib mesylate-induced hepatotoxicity in a patient with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia. Transaminase activity and bilirubin increased after 10 days of imatinib use; levels normalized after interruption for 6 weeks with minimal corticosteroid use. Bilirubin level and ALP activity reached grade 4 toxicity, aminotransferase and γ-glutamyltransferase activities grade 3. Liver biopsy (day 4) showed portal tract inflammation with cholestasis, acute hepatocyte injury, scattered acidophilic bodies, occasional ballooning degeneration, canalicular cholestasis, moderate inflammatory infiltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils and many eosinophils, and eosinophil infiltration of interlobular bile ducts with ductal epithelial damage. Associated skin rash and hypereosinophilia (max 2.47 x 10^9/l, ~40% WBC) resolved after stopping imatinib. Rechallenge at reduced dose 400 mg daily produced no further hepatotoxicity and patient continued imatinib for 18 months. Authors concluded the single dose of a Korean ginseng herbal remedy did not cause the hepatic function abnormalities.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as serum AST or ALT >1,000 IU/L. In excluded patients on the standard 72-h regimen, incidence was 12.5% (1/8) with NAC initiated within 10 h and 54.5% (6/11) after 10 h; slower elimination of acetaminophen (median 54 h; range 30-80 h) and earlier aminotransferase elevations were noted. No study-group patient died. Among the 6 deaths, case 2 (42-year-old man) died within 24 h comatose with elevated prothrombin times but no focal or centrilobular necrosis at autopsy, and other deaths involved alcohol-related disease or acute GI bleeding. Mechanism noted: NAC prevents liver injury as a glutathione substitute and by increasing glutathione production; toxic intermediate is scavenged by glutathione or binds hepatic macromolecules.

raw_record.support_text: The case is presented as isoflurane-induced hepatitis with centrilobular hepatic necrosis involving zones 2 and 3 and macro- and micro-vesicular fatty change. The authors support a diagnosis of isoflurane-induced hepatitis based on a timescale of 5 days from exposure to jaundice, prominent pyrexia, an initial mild rise in aspartate aminotransferase followed by a delayed grossly elevated level of aminotransferases with elevated bilirubin and prolongation of the prothrombin time (a pattern associated with halothane hepatitis), and prior exposure with possible sensitization to isoflurane. Other causes of hepatic injury, including ciprofloxacin, ranitidine, and amiodarone, were excluded.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case report; patient had been previously exposed and possibly sensitized to isoflurane.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic necrosis was widespread centrilobular involving zones 2 and 3 with macro- and micro-vesicular fatty change; timescale of 5 days from exposure to jaundice; pyrexia was prominent; initial mild rise in aspartate aminotransferase followed by delayed grossly elevated aminotransferases, elevated bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time; pattern associated with halothane hepatitis. Prior convincing cases (refs 3, 6, 7) showed similar centrilobular necrosis with lack of surrounding inflammation and were of milder degree. Injury is very rare; the authors conclude isoflurane is not free of the hepatotoxic effects of halothane, occurring much less frequently.

raw_record.support_text: The paper characterizes erythromycin-induced liver injury in humans, noting that thirteen liver biopsy reports are recorded in the literature and findings are comparable to those in the authors' nine patients: mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular injury with minimal to moderate portal and periportal inflammation including eosinophils. These pathological findings help differentiate erythromycin-induced liver injury from extrahepatic biliary tree obstruction.
raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis-like injury that can mimic extrahepatic biliary tree obstruction, viral hepatitis, and other conditions; distinguished histologically by absence of interlobular bile duct cholestasis, bile lakes, acute cholangitis, and periductal fibrosis, minimal cholangiolar proliferation, increased hepatocyte mitotic activity, and acidophilic/ballooning degeneration with focal necrosis. Phenotype includes marked mostly centrilobular cholestasis, mixed portal infiltrates with eosinophils, and eosinophils within sinusoids. Nine patients in the present series plus reported cases (31 recorded); 13 liver biopsy reports in the literature. Four reported patients underwent laparotomy with no extrahepatic biliary disease found. Prognosis always good with recovery within a few weeks after drug withdrawal; one reported case of jaundice lasting 10 weeks that led to laparotomy. One patient with prior gallstones had normal endoscopic retrograde cannulation of pancreatic and biliary ducts.

raw_record.support_text: The study identified patterns of urinary metabolites that distinguished healthy subjects susceptible to mild acetaminophen-induced liver injury from subjects who were not susceptible, during therapeutic acetaminophen dosing. The distinction appeared only after the start of acetaminophen treatment and not before it, and this robustness argument was extended in the discussion, where NAPQI metabolites tended to be higher in responders.
raw_record.extra_details: Metabolomics study comparing responders (susceptible to mild acetaminophen-induced liver injury) vs nonresponders under therapeutic dosing. Pretreatment metabolome was not predictive; post-treatment endogenous metabolome distinguished groups. NAPQI metabolites tended to be higher in responders, providing biological plausibility. Glycine was elevated in responders on days 5-6 and 9-10, with a smaller fall in glycine excretion in responders than nonresponders (2.2% vs 17% from days 3 to 6; 1.5% vs 11% from days 3 to 10), though not statistically significant; creatine was generally higher in nonresponders. Endogenous-metabolite OPLS-DA models excluding acetaminophen metabolites retained predictive capacity (71.4% for days 5-6, P=0.01; 77.1% for days 9-10, P=0.001).; confidence: 0.9; needs_more_context: False

raw_record.support_text: The study included nine patients with previous history of amineptine-induced hepatitis, with no prior liver or biliary disease, no alcohol abuse, and no other evident cause of hepatitis. Hepatitis occurred 8 days to 11 months after starting amineptine 100 or 200 mg daily, with clinical manifestations mimicking acute biliary obstruction; withdrawal of amineptine was followed by prompt improvement and complete recovery within 5 months. The diagnosis of amineptine hepatitis was considered definite or probable based on these criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Nine patients diagnosed with amineptine hepatitis (considered definite or probable). Latency 8 days to 11 months from start of amineptine 100 or 200 mg daily. Clinical manifestations mimicked acute biliary obstruction; serologic testing excluded hepatitis A, B, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus infection; no drug addiction, transfusion, or surgery within 6 months; ultrasonography of liver and biliary tract normal in eight tested patients. Amineptine withdrawal led to prompt improvement with complete recovery within 5 months.

raw_record.support_text: Nine patients with amineptine hepatitis were studied after therapeutic amineptine administration (daily doses 100-200 mg for 7 days to 11 months). They presented with asthenia, abdominal pain, fever, pruritus, jaundice, and, in one case, skin rash. Maximal serum bilirubin reached up to 256 µmoles/liter, maximal ALT up to 16x upper limit of normal, and maximal alkaline phosphatase up to 5.0x upper limit of normal; liver histology in three cases showed acute mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic hepatitis (AMH) or acute cholestatic hepatitis with microvesicular steatosis (ACH + MVS).
raw_record.extra_details: Daily doses 100-200 mg; latency 7 days to 11 months; duration of liver dysfunction 1-4.5 months. Maximal bilirubin up to 256 µmoles/liter, ALT up to 16x ULN, AP up to 5.0x ULN. Histology: AMH (acute mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic hepatitis) and ACH + MVS (acute cholestatic hepatitis with microvesicular steatosis). Several patients received co-medications (ascorbic acid, glucuronamide, mephenesin, bromazepam, nifedipine, metapramine, fenofibrate, norethisterone, ethinylestradiol, levonorgestrel). Paper also describes an in-vitro lymphocyte cytotoxicity assay to assess susceptibility to amineptine reactive metabolites generated by a phenobarbital-preinduced mouse microsomal oxidation system, comparing patients versus healthy controls.

raw_record.support_text: The study subjects are patients with amineptine hepatitis, i.e., humans who developed hepatitis from therapeutic use of amineptine. The paper further discusses 'amineptine hepatotoxicity' throughout, and reports that this susceptibility was constitutional and inherited based on in vitro lymphocyte testing of 9 patients (8 tested after complete recovery) and their relatives.
raw_record.extra_details: About 9 patients with amineptine hepatitis; hepatotoxicity attributed to a reactive amineptine metabolite (cytochrome P-450/NADPH dependent, detoxified by glutathione/epoxide hydrolase). Susceptibility was constitutional and inherited, not related to debrisoquine/dextromethorphan (CYP2D6) poor-metabolizer phenotype, and not due to impaired glutathione synthesis (basal lymphocyte glutathione and acetaminophen-metabolite cytotoxicity were similar to controls). In vitro lymphocyte cytotoxicity test (amineptine 1-2.5 mM) positive in first-degree relatives, some never exposed to amineptine. Phenotype reported as hepatitis (acute/chronic not specified).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of severe sirolimus-induced acute hepatitis confirmed by liver biopsy in a renal transplant recipient. Hepatotoxicity is described as a side effect of m-Tor inhibitors, generally causing a transitory and small increase in transaminase levels, but this case was severe and completely cured within a few weeks after sirolimus withdrawal.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 54-year-old man following first renal transplantation; hepatotoxicity with sirolimus typically a transitory, small transaminase increase considered benign, but this case was exceptional for its severity; complete recovery within a few weeks after sirolimus withdrawal (dechallenge).

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluates whether being overweight or obese (BMI ≥ 25) is associated with increased development of hepatotoxicity and acute liver injury (ALI) in patients with acute acetaminophen overdose, noting increased incidences of hepatotoxicity observed in obese patients with acute acetaminophen overdose. In the retrospective cohort at Siriraj Hospital (2004-2012), all patients were treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurs in acute acetaminophen overdose; patients were treated with intravenous N-acetylcysteine. Being overweight or obese (BMI ≥ 25) was an independent risk factor for acute liver injury in this overdose setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort study, January 2004 to June 2012, Siriraj Hospital. 197 patients analyzed: 35 (17.8%) obese, 24 (12.2%) overweight, 138 (70%) normal BMI. Hepatotoxicity developed in 25 (12.7%) and ALI in 40 (20.3%) cases. Multinomial logistic regression: overweight-obesity status and log10(psi value) were significant risk factors for ALI, OR (95% CI) 2.68 (1.21-5.95) and 1.74 (1.27-2.38), respectively; only log10(psi) was significant for hepatotoxicity, OR (95% CI) 378.51 (39.49-3627.99). Stratified overweight-obesity had significant OR for ALI in strata with low acetaminophen concentration, early N-acetylcysteine initiation, and low psi. High psi defined as ≥ 5.0 mM-hour.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is described as the most common pharmaceutical product involved in acute overdoses worldwide, able to result in life-threatening hepatotoxicity through conversion of acetaminophen to the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzo-quinoneimine, with the resulting hepatitis preventable by N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment. High acetaminophen concentrations at presentation and a delay in NAC therapy of more than 8 hours post-ingestion are associated with hepatotoxicity risk as high as 45%, and a larger psi parameter is associated with increased incidence of hepatotoxicity after acute acetaminophen overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose setting; study population limited to patients with acute acetaminophen ingestion of 150 mg/kg or more and NAC started when timed acetaminophen concentration was above the 150 line of the Rumack-Matthew Nomogram, aged 12 years or older, at Siriraj Hospital (Thailand).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity occurs through conversion of acetaminophen to the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzo-quinoneimine (NAPQI) via CYP2E1. Risk determinants include timed serum acetaminophen concentrations and delayed NAC onset (>8 h giving up to 45% hepatotoxicity risk); the psi parameter predicts hepatotoxicity risk. Retrospective cohort study (Siriraj Acute Acetaminophen Hepatotoxicity Project) evaluating whether being overweight/obese increases hepatotoxicity and acute liver injury (ALI) risk. NAPQI itself was only described as a mechanism, not independently attributed as the injuring agent.

raw_record.support_text: The patient presented with cholestasis complicating hyperthyroidism. Because the RUCAM scale score for methimazole (MMI) was 7, he was diagnosed as having MMI-induced liver injury. The R-value (ALT/ULN divided by ALP/ULN) was 0.667, indicating cholestatic hepatitis. MMI was stopped at admission; over 10 days serum total bilirubin rose from 410.5 to 519.9 µmol/L and prothrombin time activity fell from 81.0% to 52.2%, requiring three plasma exchanges.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis as the treated indication; cholestasis in hyperthyroidism is a competing consideration, and radioactive iodine was later added to control hyperthyroidism.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 7 for methimazole. R-value 0.667 indicated cholestatic hepatitis. Serum TBil rose from 410.5 to 519.9 µmol/L then to 669.8 µmol/L and peaked at 776.8 µmol/L after radioactive iodine; PTA fell to 52.2%. Three plasma exchanges and dexamethasone (10 mg IV) with 2000–2500 mL frozen plasma were given; oral prednisone 30 mg/day was added ~3 weeks after admission and tapered, with liver function near-normalized after 3 months. No hepatic encephalopathy. MMI discontinued at admission.

raw_record.support_text: A percutaneous liver biopsy performed on day 54 after the first Ticlopidine intake showed preserved liver architecture with edema of the portal fields and mild lymphocytic/granulocytic infiltrates containing eosinophils, an excessive cholestasis with dilated canaliculi filled with bile thrombi, vacuolar cytoplasmic transformation of hepatocytes, and small focal parenchymal necroses. The overall pattern of severe intrahepatic cholestasis with mild parenchymatous hepatitis was interpreted as drug-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report. Cholestatic hepatitis: severe intrahepatic cholestasis with bile thrombi and mild parenchymatous hepatitis on biopsy. Clinically presented with icterus and pruritus (controlled by antihistamines). Transaminases normalized rapidly after discontinuation, while cholestasis parameters returned to normal only 79 days after stopping Ticlopidine. No rechallenge was performed. Biopsy also showed vacuolar hepatocyte transformation, small focal parenchymal necroses, mild parenchymal siderosis.

raw_record.support_text: Clometacin is described as a cause of drug-induced hepatitis (DIH), classified with drugs such as oxyphenisatin that produce antiorganelle antibodies similar to those in autoimmune hepatitis I. The paper reports a series of clometacin-induced hepatitis with 29 females and 1 male (30:1 female:male ratio), 68 females and 2 males accumulated from several pharmacovigilance centers, hypergammaglobulinemia of 23 g/L, and antiorganelle antibodies (anti-N 28%, anti-M2 10%, anti-SM 59%). Acute forms showed centrilobular necrosis on biopsy, unknown in autoimmune hepatitis I.
raw_record.extra_details: Clometacin-induced hepatitis shows female predominance (29 females/1 male in this series; 68 females/2 males in pharmacovigilance accumulation), female consumers represent 73% so ratio only partially explained by differential consumption; hypergammaglobulinemia 23 g/L ±10; antiorganelle antibodies (anti-N 28%, anti-M2 10%, anti-SM 59%); acute form showed centrilobular necrosis on liver biopsy; individuals treated with ~4x lower than usual dose in 20% of cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes an 18-month-old girl who developed halothane-associated liver damage and renal failure after her third halothane anaesthetic, following two earlier uneventful enflurane anaesthetics. The diagnosis was confirmed by detecting antibodies specific for halothane-associated liver failure using a recently developed enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (18-month-old girl); third halothane anaesthetic with two prior halothane anaesthetics within the preceding year; single case without rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane-associated liver damage occurred without jaundice, combined with reversible renal failure. Diagnosis confirmed by ELISA detection of antibodies specific for halothane-associated liver failure. The first two halothane anaesthetics were followed by pyrexia of 38-39°C for 1-2 days after surgery. Enflurane anaesthetics were uneventful and not implicated in liver injury. The paper also notes the combination of hepatic necrosis with reversible renal failure is very rare in halothane hepatitis.

During the initial antituberculous regimen the patient had received isoniazid 300 mg/day, rifampin 720 mg/day and pyrazinamide 1800 mg/day; approximately one month later he developed jaundice (bilirubin 12.2 mg/dL, AST 2062 IU/L, ALT 1993 IU/L) and the treatment was stopped with partial resolution of the hepatitis.

Background review (introduction) notes hepatitis, hepatic necrosis and death have been described with isoniazid and that 10-20% of patients show a slight aminotransferase increase.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first drug for improving insulin resistance, was reported to cause severe hepatotoxicity in patients shortly after its introduction in Japan and the U.S. in March 1997. Following this, the Japanese government recommended monthly liver function assessment and the U.S. FDA recommended ALT monitoring. The authors report on a patient who developed liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone treatment, highlighting uncertainty about how long liver-function tests should be continued to detect troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity reported in patients soon after market introduction in Japan and the U.S. (March 1997). Regulatory responses: the Japanese government recommended monthly liver-function assessment; the U.S. FDA recommended ALT measurement before therapy, monthly for the next 8 months, every 2 months for the remainder of the first year, and periodically thereafter. Case report: patient developed liver dysfunction after 19 months of troglitazone treatment; authors note the unknown duration of monitoring needed to detect troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: Metformin produced an exceptionally rare hepatotoxic reaction in an 83-year-old man with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes. He presented with a marked constitutional syndrome and hepatic biochemical alterations of predominantly cholestatic profile, with elevated CA 19-9. After an oncologic etiology was ruled out and complete clinical and biochemical resolution was observed upon metformin withdrawal, the hepatotoxicity reaction due to this drug was established. The reactions appear to respond to an idiosyncratic mechanism.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 83-year-old man with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes, hypertensive heart disease and chronic atrial fibrillation; hepatotoxicity attributed to metformin after an oncologic (tumoral) etiology was ruled out; habitual co-medications included acenocoumarol, digoxin, torasemide, irbesartan, atenolol and simvastatin.
raw_record.extra_details: Metformin 850 mg every 12 h, added 14 weeks before presentation. Case presented with a 3-month constitutional syndrome (asthenia, hyporexia, 10 kg weight loss, intestinal rhythm alteration), hepatic biochemical alterations of predominantly cholestatic profile, and elevated CA 19-9. Complete clinical and biochemical resolution after drug withdrawal; only a few isolated cases of metformin hepatotoxicity have been documented, appearing to reflect an idiosyncratic mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity induced by gefitinib (an EGFR TKI) was reported in the IDEAL 1 trial, with grade 1/2 ALT elevation in 10.7% of patients at 250 mg/day and 17.9% at 500 mg/day, and gefitinib was discontinued in 4% of patients due to grade 3/4 hepatic enzyme elevations. The authors' own study found elevated ALT in 6.5% (6/92) and elevated AST in 5.4% (5/92) of gefitinib-treated patients, consistent with the prior trial. In paragraph 24, the authors note gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity was generally mild to moderate and self-limiting in their 6 patients, with one grade 2 case, a case of severe liver impairment reported by Ho et al., and grade 3/4 ALT elevation in 1.9% of patients.
raw_record.extra_details: IDEAL 1 trial: grade 1/2 ALT elevation 10.7% at 250 mg/day and 17.9% at 500 mg/day; discontinuation in 4% for grade 3/4 hepatic enzyme elevations; grade 3/4 ALT elevation in 1.9% of patients. Authors' study: elevated ALT 6.5% (6/92) and AST 5.4% (5/92); transaminase elevation observed from 7 days to 6 months after starting gefitinib, returning to normal within 3-7 months; each case generally mild and self-limiting, one grade 2 (moderate) case managed by dose reduction; 250 mg every other day used in one patient with moderate hepatic impairment. Ho et al. reported a case of severe liver impairment with chronic hepatitis and active necrosis on biopsy.

raw_record.support_text: In the randomized 12-week trial of simvastatin plus rifaximin in patients with cirrhosis, one of 16 patients in the simvastatin 40 mg/day plus rifaximin 1200 mg/day group had a marked aminotransferase increase (peak ALT 696 IU/L, peak AST 1350 IU/L) described as consistent with drug-induced liver injury related to simvastatin, accompanied by an INR increase from 1.4 to 1.9; abnormal liver tests returned to baseline 2 months after stopping the study medication. The three patients with aminotransferase increases also had creatine kinase elevations.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had pre-existing cirrhosis; simvastatin administered as 40 mg/day in combination with rifaximin 1200 mg/day; elevated creatine kinase (muscle toxicity) present.
raw_record.extra_details: Peak ALT 696 IU/L and AST 1350 IU/L with INR increase from 1.4 to 1.9; no complications of cirrhosis developed; liver tests returned to baseline 2 months after stopping study medication. The fixed combination administered was simvastatin plus rifaximin, but causality for this DILI was explicitly assigned to simvastatin.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 54-year-old male treated with a 2-week course of metronidazole for Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea presented 3 months later with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Laboratory tests (total bilirubin 12.7 mg/dL, ALT 973 IU/L, AST 867 IU/L, AP 96 IU/L, INR 1.9) indicated a hepatocellular pattern of injury with mild hepatic failure, and biopsy showed severe acute to subacute hepatitis with bridging necrosis suggestive of an immunoallergic etiology. After excluding viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes, a clinical diagnosis of metronidazole-induced liver injury was made, with marked improvement following oral prednisone therapy.

raw_record.extra_details: Delayed immune-allergic hepatocellular injury masquerading as autoimmune hepatitis; onset approximately 3 months after metronidazole; symptoms included RUQ pain, jaundice, pruritus, acholic stools, dark urine; admission labs total bilirubin 12.7 mg/dL (direct 7.2), ALT 973 IU/L, AST 867 IU/L, AP 96 IU/L, INR 1.9 ('mild hepatic failure'); extensive workup (viral, autoimmune serology, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1 antitrypsin) unremarkable; liver biopsy showed severe acute to subacute predominantly portal and lobular hepatitis with confluent perivenular and bridging necrosis, suggestive of immunoallergic drug reaction or autoimmune hepatitis; treated with oral prednisone, with substantial improvement at 2-week follow-up (total bilirubin 7.2 mg/dL, ALT 420 IU/L, AST 276 IU/L, AP 183 IU/L, INR 1.5).; extra_note: None

raw_record.support_text: The diagnosis of hydrochlorothiazide-induced acute hepatitis is supported by: occurrence of hepatic injury 4 weeks after exposure to hydrochlorothiazide; clinical and biological improvement after drug discontinuation; elimination of other causes of acute hepatitis; and a liver biopsy suggestive of DILI. International causality assessment methods (DILIN Expert Opinion and RUCAM) classified the role of hydrochlorothiazide as probable/highly probable. This was a serious case of acute hepatocellular hepatitis associated with cholangitis documented by liver biopsy, of moderate severity without signs of liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Injury occurred 4 weeks after hydrochlorothiazide exposure; clinical manifestations and liver tests improved after drug discontinuation (with mild persisting ALP and GGT elevation). Liver biopsy showed portal inflammation with biliary dystrophies, lymphocytic cholangitis, and canalicular bilirubinostasis suggestive of DILI. Acute hepatocellular hepatitis was associated with cholangitis; severity was moderate without signs of liver failure per revisited international definitions. Causality assessed as probable/highly probable by both DILIN Expert Opinion and RUCAM. Liver tests: ALT 633 IU/L, AST 263 IU/L, GGT 261 IU/L, ALP 419 IU/L, total bilirubin 72 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 61 µmol/L; negative viral and autoantibody (except ANA 1/640) screens.

raw_record.support_text: Long-term amiodarone administration causes hepatotoxicity in patients on chronic oral amiodarone therapy, attributed to iodine accumulation in the liver. Three clinical cases of amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity are presented. The paper also reports that hepatotoxicity and elevated transaminase levels occur in 15% to 50% of patients with long-term amiodarone use.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term (chronic) oral amiodarone therapy at low dose for the prevention of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients underwent dual-energy computed tomography (DECT); iodine accumulation in the liver was proposed as the mechanism of hepatotoxicity. Liver enzymes were elevated in all three; abdominal DECT without contrast showed highly increased attenuation and increased hepatic iodine concentration. Case 1 showed a reversible course of liver function and decreased CT values after amiodarone discontinuation. Case 2 had increased hepatic iodine concentration and liver damage but died of multiple organ failure after rapidly progressive pneumonia (death not attributed to liver injury). Case 3 had increased hepatic iodine concentration and elevated liver enzymes, continued oral amiodarone, and required routine liver function tests every 3-6 months. The paper states hepatotoxicity/elevated transaminases occur in 15%-50% of patients on long-term use.

raw_record.support_text: In this first-in-man study of the CDK inhibitor PHA-793887, DLTs occurred in two of three patients at 66 mg/m² and in three of nine patients at 44 mg/m²; in all but one patient the DLT was hepatotoxicity, with fatal hepatorenal failure in one patient treated at 44 mg/m². The study concluded that PHA-793887 induces severe, dose-related hepatic toxicity, which was not predicted by preclinical models, and the trial terminated after enrolment of 19 patients due to the severe hepatic toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: First-in-man phase I dose-escalation study in cancer patients; PHA-793887 is an inhibitor of CDK2, CDK1 and CDK4. Dosing: 11, 22, 44 and 66 mg/m² as 1-hour intravenous infusion on days 1, 8 and 15 of a 4-week cycle. DLTs: 2/3 patients at 66 mg/m² and 3/9 at 44 mg/m²; DLT was hepatotoxicity in all but one patient. Fatal hepatorenal failure in one patient at 44 mg/m². Study terminated after 19 patients due to severe hepatic toxicity. Toxicity was not predicted by preclinical models. No objective responses; disease stabilization in five patients. Most frequent events across dose levels were gastrointestinal or nervous system events.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I trial of PHA-793887, one patient treated at 66 mg/m² experienced a drug-related grade 4 hepatic failure with pancytopenia, and one patient treated at 44 mg/m² had a fatal hepatorenal failure. There was no dose relationship in the rate of clinical adverse events, but there was a clear dose relation with regard to their severity. Biochemical abnormalities related mainly to liver biochemistry tests, with evidence of a dose relation in the frequency and severity of AST, ALT and bilirubin elevations; all grade ≥3 liver biochemistry toxicity developed during cycle 1 within 2–4 days after initial drug administration and generally improved over 3–4 weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I dose-escalation study in patients with advanced solid tumors; an investigational agent.
raw_record.extra_details: One drug-related grade 4 hepatic failure with pancytopenia at 66 mg/m²/day and one fatal hepatorenal failure at 44 mg/m²/day; two patients died during study (one from fatal hepatorenal failure, one from disease progression). Grade ≥3 AST and ALT elevations occurred in 2 of 9 patients at 44 mg/m² and 1 of 3 at 66 mg/m²; bilirubin grade ≥3 in 1 of 9 at 44 mg/m² and 2 of 3 at 66 mg/m². All grade ≥3 liver biochemistry toxicity developed during cycle 1 within 2–4 days of first dose and improved over 3–4 weeks; affected patients were not re-treated. Kinetic parameters: terminal half-life 6–13 h, Vss 1.9–2.2 L/kg, clearance 0.14–0.48 L/h/kg.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that in this first clinical trial, PHA-793887 induced a severe, unexpected dose-related hepatic toxicity. The nature and severity of this toxicity, together with difficulty identifying its underlying mechanisms, led to the decision to discontinue clinical development of PHA-793887. One patient with liver toxicity underwent liver biopsy showing microvesicular steatosis, periportal inflammation and signs of cholangitis without necrosis of hepatocytes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with advanced solid malignancies refractory to prior therapy enrolled in a two-center open-label phase I dose-escalation study; single-agent attribution without required co-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-related toxicity described as severe and unexpected. One affected patient's liver biopsy showed microvesicular steatosis, periportal inflammation and signs of cholangitis without hepatocyte necrosis. Evaluated dose range up to 44 mg/m² (toxic/unacceptable at 44 mg/m²; biomarker modulation and disease stabilization at 22 mg/m²). Clinical development of PHA-793887 was discontinued. Off-target activity on GSK3β noted; possible additional kinase inhibition hypothesized as contributing to hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity is described as the most common cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the UK, accounting for over 50% of ALF cases. The study compared 36 patients who underwent emergent liver transplantation between 1999-2004 for acetaminophen-induced ALF with patients transplanted for non-acetaminophen ALF and chronic liver disease, reporting higher pretransplant illness severity (APACHE II) in the acetaminophen group and 1-year 87% / 5-year 75% survival.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a cohort of patients transplanted at a single centre for acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (ALF, n = 36), compared with patients transplanted for non-acetaminophen ALF (n = 35) and chronic liver disease (n = 34). Acetaminophen overdose resulted in ALF requiring transplantation, with high admission INR (median 8.7), bilirubin (199 µmol/L), MELD 40, encephalopathy ≥ grade 3 in 86% and cerebral oedema in 47%. Post-transplant 1-, 3- and 5-year survival in the acetaminophen-induced ALF group was 87%, 79% and 75%, respectively, with seven deaths over follow-up.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen intoxication (overdose) led to ALF requiring transplantation. Post-transplant survival: 1-year 87%, 3-year 79%, 5-year 75%; 7 deaths over follow-up (asystolic arrest, graft failure, cerebral oedema, sepsis/multi-organ failure, suicide). 56% had a pre-morbid axis-one psychiatric diagnosis; 5 patients had previously taken an acetaminophen overdose. raw_record.support_text: Two female patients aged 69 and 61 yr developed fulminant hepatitis induced by pirprofen, a new nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug, after 7 and 9 months of treatment. Hepatitis was not preceded or accompanied by hypersensitivity manifestations. The liver lesion consisted of massive, predominantly centrilobular hepatic cell necrosis and microvesicular steatosis; one patient died of liver failure. The authors recommend measuring serum aminotransferases and interrupting pirprofen in patients treated for more than 2 months who complain of asthenia, nausea, or vomiting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concomitant medications assessed as unlikely causes (only dihydralazine in patient 1 is known hepatotoxic but had been taken continuously for 4 yr); prior acute or chronic liver disease, infection, transfusion, and excessive alcohol intake excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports: 69-yr-old and 61-yr-old women given pirprofen 400 mg b.i.d. for 7 and 9 months; no hypersensitivity manifestations. Histology showed massive predominantly centrilobular hepatic cell necrosis, microvesicular steatosis, mild mononuclear infiltration, and cholestasis without fibrosis. One patient died of liver failure; the other recovered with normalization of liver tests. Discussion concluded it is reasonable that fulminant hepatitis was the result of pirprofen (exclusion of viral hepatitis A/B/CMV/EBV/herpes, non-A non-B, chronic liver disease, and alcohol). Concurrent medications in patient 1: oxprenolol, dihydralazine, triazolam; in patient 2: amiloride, hydrochlorothiazide, metoprolol, indomethacin. Authors recommend ALT monitoring and drug interruption after >2 months of treatment for patients with asthenia, nausea, or vomiting.

raw_record.support_text: The paper characterizes flucloxacillin as a cause of drug-induced cholestatic hepatitis in humans, describing 30 individual case reports of cholestasis across twelve publications. Most patients were women (77%) with a mean age of 61, predominant symptoms being jaundice (95%) and pruritus (77%), and characteristic biochemical abnormalities of elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamyl transferase. The authors add flucloxacillin to the list of drugs responsible for the vanishing bile duct syndrome, an established cause of protracted severe cholestasis, and note fibrosis in one case and cirrhosis in another.
raw_record.extra_details: 30 individual case reports in twelve publications; predominantly women (77%), mean age 61; symptoms jaundice (95%), pruritus (77%), dark urine, pale faeces, nausea, abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, lethargy, anorexia, weight loss; pruritus refractory to prednisone, cholestyramine, antihistamines, phenobarbitone; elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma glutamyl transferase with lesser aminotransferase elevations. Onset after cessation of flucloxacillin in 68% (mean 16.6 days, range 1-42); course averaging ~11 weeks; LFTs abnormal after symptoms in 42% for ~5 more weeks; one case of severe cholestasis persisting >7 years after an 18-day course. Pathology: moderate to severe cholestatic hepatitis with centrilobular bile stasis with canalicular dilatation, portal lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils, mild to moderate fatty infiltration, interlobular bile duct damage (oedema, degenerate epithelium, duct disappearance); vanishing bile duct syndrome attribution; fibrosis in one case; cirrhosis in another. First flucloxacillin-induced hepatitis case reported 1982; data from literature, Australia spontaneous ADR reporting, and WHO Collaborative Centre for International Drug Monitoring.

Unintentional patients most often repeatedly exceeded the 4 g per 24 h package limit, either through ignorance or simultaneous use of multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations; among these, use of narcotic-acetaminophen combinations occurred in 62% and 38% had taken more than one acetaminophen-containing agent. Aminotransferase levels were similarly high in both groups, with median values between 3800 and 4500 IU/L and individual cases often exceeding 10 000 IU/L.

N-acetylcysteine (oral or intravenous Acetadote) given early (usually within 12 h) provides protection and prevents many deaths. No chronic injury pattern leading to cirrhosis was observed.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the diagnosis of acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure, confirming the diagnosis using a history of ingestion of >4 gm/day, any detectable acetaminophen level, and an aminotransferase level of >=1000 IU/L in an analysis of 275 cases. It notes that many severe cases present late when encephalopathy clouds dosing history, and that a newly described assay detecting acetaminophen-protein adducts (formed by covalent binding of NAPQI to cell proteins via cysteine residues) identified unrecognized acetaminophen cases among indeterminate acute liver failure patients.

raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis confirmed by history of >4 gm/day ingestion, any detectable acetaminophen level, and aminotransferase >=1000 IU/L; among 275 analyzed cases 56% had a positive history, 77% a detectable acetaminophen level, 91% aminotransferases above 1000 IU/L, and 44% met all three criteria (40% met two, 13% met only one), resulting in acute liver failure. The adduct assay detected known acetaminophen cases 100% of the time, and 19% of adult (and a similar percentage of pediatric) indeterminate acute liver failure cases were strongly adduct-positive, indicating unrecognized acetaminophen cases. Characteristic pattern was high aminotransferase with low bilirubin (ALT ~849-8960 IU/L, AST ~1549-18928 IU/L, bilirubin 2.2-10.9 mg/dL in the seven adduct-positive indeterminate patients). Mechanism involves the toxic intermediate NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzo-quinone imine) binding to cell proteins. Acetaminophen levels should be interpreted together with aminotransferase and bilirubin levels to confirm poisoning, with possible false positives in other liver diseases related to high bilirubin.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen has been identified as the leading cause of acute liver injury in the United States from 1998 to 2003, with unintentional overdose accounting for 48% of acute liver injury cases, and combination APAP products remain a leading cause of fatalities. In the present case series of 40 patients with APAP-attributed hepatotoxicity, 2 patients died, 1 underwent liver transplantation, and 30 survived to discharge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases were unintentional (non-recidivating) APAP overdoses taken for excessive pain; most patients consumed multiple APAP-containing products, frequently a prescription 500 mg APAP product combined with OTC APAP or with hydrocodone, oxycodone, or butalbital/caffeine, so co-exposure to coprescribed opioids/caffeine occurred.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 cases; 29 (73%) female; ages 19–90 years; APAP use duration 24 h to 4 weeks; cumulative APAP doses 10.5–49 g in 14 cases with clear histories; AST ≥1000 IU/L in 38 (95%) patients (mean 5,861 ± 5,424 IU/L, range 772–24,406 IU/L); ALT ≥1000 IU/L in 37 (93%) patients (mean 3,383 ± 2,953 IU/L, range 486–14,883 IU/L); all patients received acetylcysteine (60% oral, 33% IV, 5% both); outcomes: 30 survived, 2 died, 1 liver transplant, 6 lost to follow-up. Discussion cites APAP as leading cause of acute liver injury in the US 1998–2003 and Larson et al. finding combination APAP products account for 63% of unintentional APAP poisonings.

The clinical, biochemical, and histopathological features resemble those of sulfonamide-induced hepatic injury, and although rare, the case and previous reports indicate the serious nature of the illness. Sulfasalazine has rarely been implicated as a cause of hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 43-year-old Chinese woman who took viaminate (a derivative of retinoic acid/tretinoin, an amide of tretinoin and ethyl p-aminobenzoate) for severe acne for more than two months and died of hepatic failure, providing insight into viaminate-induced hepatotoxicity. raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman developed severe icteric liver injury with hepatic encephalopathy after eight weeks of metoprolol use for acute myocardial infarction. A transjugular liver biopsy showed extensive bridging necrosis with a mixed neutrophilic and lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate, suggestive of acute hepatitis secondary to drug insult. Based on the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score, 'probable' drug-induced liver injury was attributed to metoprolol, the drug was stopped, and therapeutic plasmapheresis produced clinical and biochemical recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with coronary heart disease/acute myocardial infarction on concurrent aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, and atorvastatin (atorvastatin stopped after 3 weeks due to myalgia); metoprolol causally attributed as 'probable' by RUCAM.
raw_record.extra_details: Metoprolol dose 25 mg twice daily, increased to 100 mg/day after atorvastatin stoppage; approximately 8 weeks of use before onset. Presented with jaundice, darkening urine, Grade 1 hepatic encephalopathy, progressive hyperbilirubinemia and elevated transaminases (peak ALT 2262 IU/L, TB 24.8 mg/dL, INR 3.82, arterial ammonia 238 microgram/dL). Histology: extensive bridging necrosis with mixed neutrophilic/lymphocytic infiltrate and early fibrosis; no autoimmune hepatitis features or bile duct damage. Weakly positive ANA (mitochondrial pattern 1:40) that turned negative after recovery. RUCAM 'probable'; plasmapheresis (5 sessions) as salvage therapy led to biochemical normalization and clinical recovery; patient discharged and improved at follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of metoprolol-induced liver injury. RUCAM causality scoring gave metoprolol a score of 7 (probable adverse drug reaction), whereas the competing statin scored 5 (possible adverse drug reaction), leading the authors to attribute the DILI to metoprolol rather than statins. The liver injury had a hepatocellular pattern, with latency to onset between two to 12 weeks consistent with beta-blocker-associated injury, and the patient showed weak antinuclear antibody positivity with a mitochondrial pattern, supporting an immune or idiosyncratic mechanism as proposed by Lennard for metoprolol-related liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly female patient; concurrent statin therapy was evaluated as a competing cause (RUCAM 5, possible) and excluded in favor of metoprolol (RUCAM 7, probable).
raw_record.extra_details: Second reported case of metoprolol-induced liver injury and first metoprolol-induced icteric liver injury leading to hepatic encephalopathy, managed with plasmapheresis. Liver biopsy showed extensive bridging necrosis, mixed neutrophilic and lymphocytic inflammation, and early fibrosis. Patient developed jaundice and progressive overt hepatic encephalopathy and weak antinuclear antibody positivity with a mitochondrial staining pattern that became negative after plasma exchange. Drug rechallenge was not attempted due to severe first-exposure injury. The first reported case (Larrey et al.) was acute non-icteric hepatitis with biopsy showing moderate steatosis and occasional ballooned hepatocytes without inflammation or fibrosis; immunologic/idiosyncratic basis proposed, linked to debrisoquine (CYP2D6) oxidation phenotype concerns.

Twenty of 896 (2.2%; CI 1.4%-3.4%) met biochemical criteria for probable niacin-induced hepatotoxicity, and 42 of 896 (4.7%; CI 3.4%-6.3%) met criteria for possible or probable niacin-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings pertain to controlled-release niacin; risk factors associated with hepatotoxicity included diabetes with receipt of oral hypoglycemic agents, preexisting liver disease (history of alcoholic or granulomatous hepatitis), excessive alcohol use, and higher mean daily niacin dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo causality rating: 1 definite, 19 probable, 22 possible, 4 doubtful (excluded). 20/896 (2.2%) probable and 42/896 (4.7%) possible-or-probable niacin-induced hepatotoxicity. Most reactions (30 of 42) were mild biochemical changes resolving after discontinuation or dose reduction; 12 patients had vague abdominal and flu-like complaints; 2 patients required hospitalization after dosage increases (2.0-3.0 g/d and 3.0-6.0 g/d) with marked hepatic enzyme increases, decreased serum albumin, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and bilateral lower extremity edema that resolved after discontinuation. Mean daily dose was higher in probable (3.1 g) versus possible (2.1 g) hepatotoxicity (P=0.0075). Dose-related but not clinically meaningful increases in liver enzymes over 1.0-3.0 g/d range. Hepatic dysfunction not associated with patient age or diet/insulin-managed diabetes; temporal sequence with concurrent phenytoin (4 patients), carbamazepine (1), and amiodarone (1).

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes acetaminophen overdose as a cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the United Kingdom: only a small proportion of patients taking an acetaminophen overdose are at risk of liver damage, with less than 10% developing severe liver damage and only 1-2% developing ALF. In 1997 more than 38,000 patients were admitted to U.K. hospitals as a result of acetaminophen poisoning, 57 underwent emergency liver transplantation, and 562 deaths were reported in which acetaminophen ingestion was thought to have played a role.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose (mostly deliberate self-poisoning) is the exposure setting; <10% of overdose patients develop severe liver damage and only 1-2% develop ALF, primarily due to small absorbed doses and early antidotal therapy. U.K. 1997 national data: >38,000 hospital admissions for acetaminophen poisoning, 57 emergency liver transplantations, 562 deaths in which acetaminophen ingestion was thought to play a role. Fatal outcomes were more common in older men and in those consuming acetaminophen/opiate combinations.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports on patients admitted with severe acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure (ALF) to the Liver Intensive Treatment Unit (LITU) at King's College Hospital and those listed for super urgent liver transplantation in the United Kingdom, drawn from the United Kingdom Transplant Database. Comparing August 1997-August 1998 with 2001-2002 showed an overall 72% reduction in admissions and a 74% fall in deaths or transplants, while a similar proportion of those admitted (32% vs 30%) died or underwent transplantation, indicating no reduction in overall severity of ALF. The injury occurred in the context of acetaminophen overdose (deliberate self-poisoning), and a before-and-after analysis concluded the data are correlational rather than proof of causation that package-size restriction caused the reduction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury arose from overdose via deliberate self-poisoning; report covers UK registry/LITU data (United Kingdom Transplant Database, King's College Hospital) and notes potentially important regional differences across the UK.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity leading to acute liver failure (ALF; UMLS:C0162557); comparison of Aug 1997-Aug 1998 with 2001-2002 showed a 72% fall in admissions and a 74% fall in deaths or transplantation; 32% of 1997-98 admitted and 30% of 2001-02 admitted died or were transplanted. The reduction followed UK acetaminophen package-size restriction (since September 1998); before-and-after methodology is correlational, not experimental, and the paper notes most UK severe hepatotoxicity results from deliberate self-poisoning rather than inadvertent poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: The study genotyped NAT2 in 224 incident tuberculosis patients treated with antituberculosis therapy, diagnosing antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis based on a positive isoniazid rechallenge test and exclusion of viral hepatitis. Thirty-three patients (14.7%) were diagnosed with antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis, and slow acetylators had a higher risk of hepatotoxicity than rapid acetylators (26.4% vs. 11.1%, P=.013). The authors conclude isoniazid is the major drug incriminated in this hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Co-administered in fixed antituberculosis regimens with rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol; causality to isoniazid was established by a positive isoniazid rechallenge test.
raw_record.extra_details: 224 incident tuberculosis patients monitored; 33 (14.7%) developed antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis. Isoniazid given orally at 300 mg daily. Diagnosis required positive isoniazid rechallenge and exclusion of viral hepatitis; isoniazid withdrawn when ALT > 2x ULN with elevated bilirubin or isolated ALT > 3x ULN. Slow acetylators showed higher risk (26.4% vs 11.1%, P=.013) and higher aminotransferase levels; slow acetylator status (OR 3.66; 95% CI 1.58-8.49; P=.003) and age (OR 1.09; 95% CI 1.04-1.14; P<.001) were independent risk factors. Background cites that mortality from antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis is not rare, and that isoniazid is mainly metabolized via N-acetyltransferase to hepatotoxic intermediates.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective cohort of 224 tuberculosis patients treated with an isoniazid-based antituberculosis regimen, 33 (14.7%) were diagnosed with drug-induced hepatitis by the International Consensus Meeting definition. During isoniazid rechallenge, 14 of these patients (6.3%) developed serum ALT >3x ULN, which the authors classified as clinically significant isoniazid-induced hepatitis, prompting replacement of isoniazid with streptomycin or ofloxacin; the other 19 had transient hepatic dysfunction. Slow acetylator NAT2 status and older age were significant risk factors for isoniazid-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with pulmonary tuberculosis on isoniazid-based antituberculosis therapy; predominantly elderly cohort; age was a significant independent risk factor.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid rechallenge confirmed causality: 14 patients (6.3%) had ALT >3x ULN during rechallenge and were classified as clinically significant hepatitis; 19 (8.5%) had ALT <=3x ULN (transient hepatic dysfunction) and continued isoniazid safely. Peak ALT 393.6 ± 353.9 U/L (range 98-1609) and peak total bilirubin 3.25 ± 3.57 mg/dL (range 0.5-20.2) in hepatitis cases. Hepatitis risk was higher in slow acetylators (26.4% vs 11.1%; OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.32-6.23), and slow acetylators had higher peak ALT/AST and were more likely to exceed 3x ULN on rechallenge (64.3% vs 26.3%; P=.040). Multivariate OR for slow acetylator 3.66 (1.58-8.49) and age OR 1.09 (1.04-1.14). Rapid acetylator was protective (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.76).

These positive withdrawal and rechallenge tests supported that isoniazid, instead of rifampicin and pyrazinamide, was the major offending agent causing the drug-induced hepatitis in this study.

raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge led to serum ALT exceeding 3 times the upper limit of normal in a higher percentage of slow acetylators. Study incidence of antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis was 14.7%; patients with chronic hepatitis B or C were excluded.

A Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score of 8 points for edoxaban corresponded to a probable associated liver injury, and both drugs were immediately stopped. Despite treatment and drug wash-out, liver failure progressed and the patient was discharged to palliative care and died three days later.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane (1,1,1-trifluoro, 2,2-chlorobromoethane), a widely accepted anesthetic agent, has been incriminated as a cause of a hepatitis-like drug reaction. Clinical records and, in all but one case, liver biopsy or autopsy specimens were collected from 42 patients in whom a hepatitic reaction occurred after halothane anesthesia; the majority developed hepatitis after repeated exposure to the anesthetic. The lesion was considered a hypersensitivity reaction differing from shock, and 27 of the 42 patients died.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Majority of patients developed hepatitis after repeated exposure to the anesthetic; lesion attributed to a hypersensitivity reaction. No patient had evidence of preexisting liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: 42 patients (20 male, 22 female; ages 21-77 yr); 27 (64-67%) died and 15 survived. Fever and jaundice temporally related to operation; peripheral eosinophilia common, splenomegaly unusual. Histology showed hallmarks of viral hepatitis with frequent steatosis, granuloma formation, and eosinophils in the inflammatory exudate. Six sera contained antimitochondrial antibodies; electron microscopy in two cases showed mitochondrial abnormalities. Reactions are not dose related and are infrequent and not produced in experimental animals. Halothane implicated in roughly one fourth of fulminant hepatic failure cases reported to the Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Center.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is described as the predominant cause of acute liver failure in the United States. Biomarkers of mitochondrial damage and nuclear DNA fragmentation were measured in plasma from APAP-overdose patients, and the authors conclude that mitochondrial damage and nuclear DNA fragmentation are likely critical events in APAP hepatotoxicity in humans, resulting in necrotic cell death.

raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose is stated to be the most common cause of acute liver failure in most Western countries and the predominant cause in the US (~56,000 ER visits, ~26,000 hospitalizations, and nearly 500 deaths per year; about half intentional). Patient cohort (n=40 overdose patients; 20 abnormal LT group with peak ALT >=1,000 U/l and peak PT >=18 s, 20 normal LT controls) plus 6 healthy volunteers. Mechanism: CYP-mediated formation of reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) after saturation of glucuronidation/sulfation, GSH depletion, mitochondrial protein binding, mitochondrial permeability transition and nuclear DNA fragmentation via AIF/EndoG, without caspase activation (necrotic, not apoptotic, cell death) leading to centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis. Plasma biomarkers GDH and mtDNA elevated in abnormal-LT patients; peak ALT up to 8,545 U/l, peak AST up to 26,000 U/l, peak PT up to 374s, peak bilirubin up to 25 mg/dl; 6/20 abnormal-LT patients had encephalopathy grade >=1 and 95% survived.

The low injury in the second group was likely due in part to early admission and treatment prior to development of toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) intoxication is described as a common cause of severe drug-induced hepatotoxicity and the leading cause of acute liver failure in Northern Europe, the UK, and the USA. The study examined 209 consecutive patients with single-dose acetaminophen overdose, of whom 44 (21.1%) developed hepatic coma and 20 (43.5%) of these patients died.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 209 consecutive patients with single-dose acetaminophen overdose analyzed by multiple/logistic regression; 57 (27.3%) had chronic alcohol intake and 45 (21.5%) had acute alcohol intake. 44 (21.1%) developed hepatic coma (hepatic encephalopathy) and 20 of these died. Chronic alcohol intake was independently associated with hepatic coma (relative risk 5.3, 95% CI 2.2-12.4) and death (RR 1.4, 95% CI 0.5-3.9), as well as lower prothrombin index, lower platelet count, higher creatinine and higher bilirubin, indicating that chronic alcohol enhances acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. Acute alcohol intake was not significantly associated with any outcome.

raw_record.support_text: In 50 patients receiving ketoconazole for onychomycosis or dermatomycosis, a causal relationship to hepatic injury was considered likely, adjudicated as 'definite' in 1, 'probable' in 26 and 'possible' in 23 cases. The biochemical pattern was hepatocellular in 67% of 'probable' (n=18) and 39% of 'possible' cases; most 'possible' cases had mild-to-moderate liver enzyme elevations (48%). The daily dose was 200 mg in 90% of cases; the mean latent period from first intake to onset was 68 days (probable) and 52 days (possible). In almost all 'probable' cases ALAT exceeded ASAT; jaundice was reported in 63% of 27 probable cases. None of the 50 cases had a fatal course, and in 13 probable cases other drugs were continued or reinstituted without aggravation or relapse.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality adjudication across 50 'likely' cases: 1 definite, 26 probable, 23 possible. Indications were onychomycosis (54%) and dermatomycosis (30%); daily dose 200 mg (90% of cases); mean latent period 68 days (probable) and 52 days (possible), onset within 6 weeks in 44% and 79% respectively. Female predominance (81.5% probable, 87% possible); mean age 48.4 and 53 years. Biochemical pattern in this study: hepatocellular 54%, cholestatic 16%, LEE/mixed 30% (Table 2); hepatocellular in 67% of probable and 39% of possible cases. Symptoms in 27 probable cases: jaundice 63%, malaise 59%, nausea/vomiting 41%, hepatomegaly 33%, fever 11%, eosinophilia 9%, rash 4%; ALAT>ASAT in 89%. Eosinophilia (>=7%) in 2/22 probable cases. Histology (n=14 this study): mostly necrosis 57%, cholestasis 43% (centrilobular cholestasis, cholangiolitis, cholangitis, bridging necrosis, beginning fibrosis). In 13 probable cases co-medications were continued/reinstituted without relapse; griseofulvin ingestion was explicitly excluded in cases with early (≤6 weeks) onset; only 2/50 had prior idiosyncratic reaction to another drug. No death in the 50-case group; literature subgroups in the comparison table reported fatal courses (19% and 3%).

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old man developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome after multi-drug therapy following aortic valve replacement and was diagnosed with drug-induced liver injury (DILI) based on significantly abnormal liver function test results. Warfarin was identified and confirmed as the culprit drug using the ALDEN score, ELISPOT assay, and RUCAM, with improvement of lesions and liver function after warfarin discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy. The authors report it as the first case of warfarin-induced SJS/TEN with DILI.

raw_record.support_text: Routine laboratory tests showed significant hepatic injury in the patient since the onset of SJS. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, E and cytomegalovirus were negative, and RUCAM was conducted to confirm drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The RUCAM score for warfarin was 9, suggesting a strong relationship between warfarin and the liver injury. Futhermore, when warfarin was restarted for anticoagulation, the patient developed a sudden increase of atypical target lesions with blisters and a concomitant rise in transaminases, then improved after warfarin was replaced with enoxaparin, supporting warfarin as the culprit.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case with concurrent Stevens-Johnson syndrome in the same patient; multiple coprescribed drugs were present but warfarin was confirmed as the culprit; positive rechallenge occurred when warfarin was re-initiated during anticoagulation therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: RUCAM score 9 (strong relationship) and MELD score 22 indicating seriously deteriorated liver function. ALDEN score for warfarin was 6 (very probable) and a drug-specific IFN-γ ELISPOT assay was positive for warfarin and negative for vancomycin. Laboratory findings showed transaminase elevations (ALT up to 1147 U/L, AST up to 417 U/L) with normal total bilirubin; serologies negative for hepatitis A/B/C/E and cytomegalovirus. The patient recovered and was discharged on postoperative day 50.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present the case of a patient with Stevens-Johnson syndrome and severe liver injury in which warfarin was confirmed as the culprit drug; they report this as the first case of warfarin-induced SJS/TEN in an adult. Using the RUCAM score they confirmed the diagnosis of warfarin-induced DILI, and the MELD score verified seriously impaired liver function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patient with concurrent SJS/TEN; reported as the first adult case of warfarin-induced SJS/TEN.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver injury with significantly elevated transaminase values. Diagnosis of warfarin-induced DILI confirmed with the RUCAM score; the MELD score was applied to evaluate the degree of liver injury and verified seriously impaired liver function. Warfarin causality for SJS/TEN was also confirmed by ALDEN score and IFN-γ ELISPOT assay, and its discontinuation was essential for patient recovery. The authors note that in a retrospective study of 748 patients with DILI, only 36 (4.8%) presented with both SJS/TEN and DILI, with a higher mortality rate of 22%, though this does not specifically attribute those cases to warfarin.

raw_record.support_text: After initial aprindine therapy had produced jaundice and elevated bilirubin, transaminases, and alkaline phosphatase (with liver histology showing a virus-hepatitis-like reaction with single-cell necrosis and Councilman bodies interpreted as toxic drug damage), the values normalized when aprindine was stopped. A rechallenge with aprindine (three times 50 mg) after patient consent led within 24 hours to recurrence of the same complaints (headache, nausea, anorexia, constipation, right upper quadrant pressure) and renewed rises in bilirubin, transaminases, and alkaline phosphatase, so the rechallenge was discontinued; a control episode with procainamide produced no symptoms and the enzymes kept falling.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Causality was confirmed for this patient by prompt recurrence of symptoms and abnormal liver chemistries on rechallenge and by normalization on dechallenge. The patient was concurrently on Digitalis and Briserin, which were continued throughout and therefore not implicated.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (German) of aprindine used as antiarrhythmic (initial dose twice 50 mg/d; rechallenge three times 50 mg). Jaundice with elevated bilirubin, GOT/GPT and alkaline phosphatase; histology showed widened portal fields with cholangioles, round cells and granulocytes, predominantly centrilobular single-cell hyaline necrosis (Councilman bodies), occasional hepatocellular necrosis with Kupffer cell proliferation, slight cell polymorphism and frequent mitoses, described as a mild virus-hepatitis-like reaction attributed to toxic (drug) damage. Prior workup negative for hepatitis B, CMV, psittacosis, virus infections; negative cholangio-sonogram; hepatomegaly noted. Liver width improved to 12 cm and patient symptom-free after stopping; after rechallenge values normalized within 14 days except slight bilirubin elevation.

raw_record.support_text: Acht Tage nach Einnahme von Aprindin in Tagesdosen von 100 mg entwickelten sich bei der Patientin einige Symptome wie bei einer akuten Virushepatitis. 14 Tage nach Therapiebeginn trat dunkler Urin auf, vier Wochen nach Therapiebeginn (6 Tage nach Absetzen des Medikamentes) erfolgte die Aufnahme in der Klinik. Der schnelle Rückgang sämtlicher Befunde nach Absetzen sowie das Wiederauftreten nach Reexposition sprachen für eine arzneimittelbedingte Hepatitis; bei der Reexposition traten Beschwerden bereits nach 24 Stunden, biochemische Veränderungen nach 48 Stunden auf. Klinisch, histologisch und klinisch-chemisch ist die nach Aprindin beobachtete Leberschädigung eher der virushepatitisähnlichen als der cholestatischen Arzneimittelhepatitis zuzurechnen, womit Aprindin zu den potentiell hepatotoxischen Medikamenten zählt.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Antiarrhythmic therapeutic use (ongoing extrasystole); single-case report with positive rechallenge; digitalis, the Briserin combination and procainamide were tolerated before, during and after the episode, leaving Aprindin as the sole suspected culprit.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg/day orally; symptoms like acute viral hepatitis after 8 days, dark urine after 14 days, hospital admission 4 weeks after therapy start (6 days after drug discontinuation); rapid regression of all findings after withdrawal and recurrence on rechallenge (symptoms after 24 h, biochemical changes after 48 h). On rechallenge a weakly positive LE factor; leucine aminopeptidase rose slightly to 24 U/l and gamma-glutamyl transferase markedly to 130 U/l. Liver biopsy showed inflammatory infiltration of portal fields, polymorphism of hepatocytes, focal Kupffer cell proliferation and a hyaline single-cell necrosis (Councilman body). Aprindin is predominantly metabolized in the liver with a serum half-life of about 24 h. The paper notes that hepatotoxic side effects had not been observed in earlier animal experiments and clinical trials.

The study itself enrolled 26 DILI cases all prescribed isoniazid 300 mg/day, with causality assessed by RUCAM, framed around the role of NAT2 genotype in isoniazid-related DILI.

The major metabolic route of panadiplon includes biotransformation to cyclopropanecarboxylic acid, both in humans and other species; it is believed that the carboxylic acid metabolite induces a mitochondrial dysfunction in the liver.

raw_record.extra_details: Describes isoniazid-induced hepatitis during both chemoprophylaxis and standard treatment with isoniazid plus one or more companion drugs. Frequency of hepatitis in MRC-coordinated controlled trials ranged from 0% to 5% (e.g., SHT 15/3563, SH 5/2394 in international trials; HT 8/150 in Hong Kong). Mechanism is not clearly one of direct drug/metabolite toxicity: no strong association with isoniazid dosage (Madras high-dose and matrix studies), with circumstantial evidence of hypersensitivity in some patients (hepatitis recurs on rechallenge, eosinophils prominent on liver biopsy), while other patients can resume isoniazid after a short interruption. Clinically resembles viral hepatitis with onset usually during the first 3 months of isoniazid administration.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports extensive evidence that disulfiram causes human DILI: acute liver injury typically develops within 2-12 weeks of treatment initiation, with a hepatocellular pattern more frequently reported than cholestatic; the risk is not dose-related and is thought to result from a hypersensitivity reaction. A Swedish DILI registry identified 82 reports of disulfiram-induced liver injury over 36 years (1 per 1.3 million average daily doses), and in Denmark disulfiram hepatitis was the second most frequent cause of referral to a liver transplant center over a 5-year period. Severe hepatitis with liver insufficiency leading to death or liver transplantation is estimated at 1 fatal case per 30,000 treated patients per year. On the causality scoring scale, the presented acute hepatitis case was determined 'probable'; a 'definite' rating was prevented only by absence of extrahepatic manifestations including eosinophilia and no rechallenge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case in a 47-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder; drug started at half the recommended dose (200 mg daily, later 200 mg every other day). Injury is idiosyncratic, not dose-related, and unrelated to underlying liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: A diagnosis of acute DILI due to disulfiram was made based on liver biopsy showing portal lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration, mild biliary tract dystrophy, scattered necrotic hepatocytes, and microgranulomas without steatosis or fibrosis. Laboratory tests 18 days after initiation showed AST 91 IU/L and ALT 127 IU/L, rising to AST 934 IU/L and ALT 1526 IU/L by day 44, with normal bilirubin. Full recovery occurred 20 days after prednisone 30 mg daily with taper. Drug stopped and rechallenge discouraged. Literature: Swedish DILI registry 82 reports over 36 years (1 per 1.3 million average daily doses); Denmark disulfiram hepatitis second most common reason for liver transplant referral over 5 years; 1 fatal case per 30,000 treated patients per year; acute liver injury typically within 2-12 weeks; hepatocellular pattern more frequent than cholestatic; positive rechallenge and causal relationship established in most historical cases; thought to be hypersensitivity reaction involving cytochrome P450 enzymes; drug is tetraethylthiuram disulfide.

raw_record.support_text: During isoniazid chemoprophylaxis for tuberculosis, chemoprophylactic agents can cause a wide range of liver side effects, from a slight increase in transaminases to diffuse necrosis of the liver; liver damage is dose related and usually of a hepatocellular type, with most cases developing in the first 4-8 weeks of treatment, and progression to irreversible liver failure is very rare.

Reduced consciousness and delirium developed on the seventh day of treatment. Treated successfully with living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) because she refused cadaveric transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: An 84-year-old nursing-home woman developed acute cholestatic jaundice while taking ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for a urinary tract infection. On the sixth day of treatment a pruritic erythematous rash appeared on the chest and abdomen and ciprofloxacin was stopped because of a suspected allergic reaction; three days later she developed yellowish discoloration of skin and conjunctivae with abnormal liver function tests, elevated plasma cholesterol but normal prothrombin time and albumin. Liver function tests normalized within one month and remained normal at three months. The discussion and conclusions state this is considered a probable hepatic injury attributable to ciprofloxacin and, reportedly, the first case of an acute cholestatic reaction caused by ciprofloxacin.
raw_record.extra_details: 84-year-old woman in a nursing home; indication urinary tract infection; ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily; erythematous pruritic rash on chest and abdomen on day 6 prompted drug cessation; jaundice appeared 3 days later with disturbed liver function tests; elevated plasma cholesterol with normal prothrombin time and albumin; supportive fluids given; liver function normalized within one month and remained normal at three months; patient asymptomatic; authors call it probable hepatic involvement (atteinte hépatique imputable) and the first reported acute cholestatic reaction caused by ciprofloxacin; causality mechanism unknown.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of ketoconazole hepatotoxicity in a human patient in whom slight elevation of serum transaminases appeared 4 weeks after starting ketoconazole treatment and progressed to severe hepatitis because medication was continued. It also cites an FDA report of three cases of fatal massive hepatic necrosis attributed to ketoconazole, which prompted a warning about its rare but potentially serious hepatic danger. In an accompanying mechanistic discussion (paragraph 32), the authors classify the hepatic injury as a form of host idiosyncrasy with metabolic abnormality, inferring that a centrilobular hepatotoxic metabolite of ketoconazole is responsible.
raw_record.extra_details: Single reported patient; slight transaminase elevation noted 4 weeks after starting therapy, progressing to severe hepatitis because the drug was continued. No fever, rash, itching, or increased peripheral/liver-parenchymal eosinophils; LST (delayed hypersensitivity test) negative, arguing against hypersensitivity. The authors categorize the injury as host idiosyncrasy with metabolic abnormality (Zimmerman classification) and infer that a hepatotoxic metabolite formed in the centrilobular zone is responsible. FDA reportedly described three cases of fatal massive hepatic necrosis and warned of the drug's rare but potentially serious danger; this is described as the first report of ketoconazole hepatotoxicity in Japan.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe four instances of reversible hepatocellular damage associated with the use of nevirapine in patients with HIV infection; two of the four patients were also coinfected with the hepatitis C virus. Evidence of malaise, skin rash, and icteric hepatitis with pruritus occurred 4–6 weeks after the beginning of nevirapine therapy, and liver test results declined to normal or near-normal levels with pruritus disappearing 4–6 weeks after drug discontinuation, with no rechallenge. The authors conclude nevirapine can be associated with icteric hepatitis that appears reversible after withdrawal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with HIV infection treated as part of highly active antiretroviral therapy; two of four patients were also coinfected with the hepatitis C virus (injury occurred in both HCV-coinfected and non-coinfected patients).
raw_record.extra_details: Four case reports. Onset of malaise, skin rash, and icteric hepatitis with pruritus 4–6 weeks after starting nevirapine therapy; no metabolic acidosis in any patient; liver tests declined to normal or near-normal and pruritus resolved 4–6 weeks after drug discontinuation (dechallenge); no patient was rechallenged. Nevirapine is an NNRTI; previous reports of 32–48% cutaneous rash and, in published trials of 245 patients, ~8% severe (grades 3–4) rashes and 1% Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: In 76 patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia treated with an arsenic trioxide (As₂O₃)-based regimen, 29 (38.2%) developed hepatotoxicity attributed to As₂O₃, with NCI-CTC grade 1, 2, 3 and 4 toxicity in 14, 7, 4 and 4 patients respectively. For the eight patients with grade 3/4 toxicity, As₂O₃ was withheld for an average of 22.6 days until liver function tests recovered; seven were successfully re-challenged without recurrence, while one patient had recurrent hepatotoxicity on rechallenge and the drug was discontinued. Elevated liver enzymes were the prominent abnormality, and there were no cases of acute hepatic failure or mortality attributable to hepatic toxicity.

Onset during induction in 19, consolidation in 3, maintenance in 6, after completion in 1. Transient (<4 weeks) in 20 (68.9%); resolved on continuing As₂O₃ in 21 (72.4%). As₂O₃ withheld average 22.6 days (range 10-28) for grade 3/4; 7/8 successfully re-challenged without recurrence; 1 recurrent, drug discontinued. Elevated liver enzymes in 28/29 (96.6%). Homozygous mutant MTHFR 1298 (C/C) polymorphism significantly associated with hepatotoxicity (RR=8.75, P=0.004); GST M1 null genotype showed a trend (RR=3.28, P=0.06). No other baseline or polymorphism factors predicted hepatotoxicity.

In the authors' IPF cohort, 42% of patients developed nintedanib-related hepatic injury, and patients with baseline plasma KL-6 levels ≥ 2.5 ng/mL had a higher risk of nintedanib-related hepatic injury, including severe and recurrent injury.

raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of hepatic injury was 42% in the study cohort; real-world hepatic impairment ranged 1.6–9.6%; East Asian data reported relatively high hepatitis incidence reaching 67.6%. Late-onset hepatotoxicity described. Baseline plasma KL-6 ≥ 2.5 ng/mL, baseline plasma SPA ≥ 600 pg/mL, and baseline DLCO < 55% were predictors of hepatic injury risk; severe and recurrent hepatic injury occurred.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case of severe voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity in a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis, associated with highly elevated (toxic) serum voriconazole levels and reversal of hepatotoxicity after voriconazole cessation, despite administration of standard drug dosages. Histopathologic examination of the explanted liver after liver transplantation showed rhomboid-shaped crystals believed to be voriconazole.

raw_record.extra_details: Serum voriconazole level was 13 μg/mL at a dose of 300 mg/d; literature states trough concentrations >3.0 mg/L are considered hepatotoxic. Histology showed intracellular and extracellular deep amber-yellow crystalline structures (voriconazole drug crystals) under polarized light with intracellular light brown pigmentation compatible with bile stasis (H&E 600×). Hepatotoxicity reversed after drug cessation; patient underwent liver transplantation. The paper notes the exact mechanism and direct cause-effect relationship remains to be established, and that toxicity predominantly occurs with higher doses and can be interrupted by prompt dose reduction.

raw_record.support_text: In this overdose-patient cohort, serum APAP-CYS concentrations in patients with hepatic injury following acetaminophen overdose were generally much higher than those observed during therapeutic dosing, with the exception of subjects who received early N-acetylcysteine treatment or were sampled late during resolution of injury. The paper attributes these ALT elevations to acetaminophen overdose injury, including both acute overdose and repeated supratherapeutic ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Includes acute acetaminophen overdose (treated within and beyond 8 hours of ingestion), repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, and indeterminate-timing cases. Case series of overdose patients with elevated peak ALT (e.g., up to 9903, 8880, 7979 IU/L) treated with N-acetylcysteine. Patient SH-04 developed marked ALT elevation and high APAP-CYS consistent with acetaminophen-induced liver injury. One acute-overdose subject (D-07) had concurrent hepatitis C, and one repeated-ingestion subject (UCH-09) had CMV hepatitis on liver biopsy. Serum APAP-CYS was undetectable in non-acetaminophen hepatotoxin patients, supporting adduct specificity for APAP. Peak APAP-CYS correlated modestly with peak ALT (Spearman rho=0.68, 95% CI 0.36-0.85).
