raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old man with ALK-positive advanced NSCLC received crizotinib 250 mg twice daily. After 39 days he developed deranged liver function (bilirubin 5.2 mg/dL, AST 96 IU/L, ALT 64 IU/L, normal alkaline phosphatase 238 IU/L, PT 28.3 s, INR 2.6; serum ammonia 271 μg/dL). Viral, autoimmune, metabolic, and biliary causes were ruled out, and a diagnosis of drug-induced acute liver failure was made according to Hy's law. The patient developed hepatic encephalopathy (grade 2 to 4) and died after 18 days of hospitalization from multiorgan dysfunction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case in a patient with metastatic (stage IV) ALK-positive NSCLC who also received concurrent palliative radiotherapy; liver transplantation was ruled out because of metastatic disease. Competing causes (viral, biliary obstruction, alcohol, autoimmune, metabolic) were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 250 mg twice daily; symptom onset and crizotinib stop on day 39. Liver test values: bilirubin 5.2 mg/dL, AST 96 IU/L, ALT 64 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 238 IU/L (normal), PT 28.3 s, INR 2.6, serum ammonia 271 μg/dL. Fulfilled Hy's law for DILI. Development of fulminant liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy (grade 2 to 4) and papilledema; patient died of multiorgan dysfunction after 18 days of hospitalization. Discussion notes crizotinib commonly causes reversible aminotransferase increases, grade 3 to 4 enzyme increases in some patients, grade 3 enzyme increases in 14%-16% of patients in two phase III trials, one fatal acute liver failure after safety data closure, and earlier reports of two fatal hepatic failure cases and one reversible hepatitis. LFT monitoring weekly for first 2 months then monthly is recommended per prescribing information.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase 2 study of idelalisib monotherapy followed by combination with ofatumumab in 24 CLL patients (Lampson et al.), the most common serious adverse event was hepatotoxicity; 79% experienced grade ≥1 transaminase elevation and 54% had grade 3 or higher transaminitis. Younger age and mutated immunoglobulin heavy chain status were significant risk factors, and liver biopsy in two patients showed lymphocytic infiltrate with elevated CCL-3 and CCL-4 levels, suggesting transaminitis was immune mediated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia; younger age and mutated immunoglobulin heavy chain status were significant risk factors for hepatotoxicity; treatment-naive patients at greater risk than relapsed/refractory; includes idelalisib monotherapy and combination with ofatumumab or rituximab.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was one of the most common adverse events leading to idelalisib dose reduction and discontinuation. In an analysis of 863 CLL patients across clinical trials, median time to transaminitis symptoms was 8 weeks. ALT/AST elevations >5x ULN usually occurred within the first 12 weeks of treatment and were reversible with dose interruption. Fatal and/or serious hepatotoxicity occurred in 18% of patients on idelalisib monotherapy and 16% on combination with rituximab or other therapies. Liver biopsy showed lymphocytic infiltrate with elevated CCL-3 and CCL-4, suggesting immune-mediated injury. Up to a quarter of patients experienced recurrent transaminase elevation on rechallenge. Recommended monitoring: ALT/AST every 2 weeks for first 3 months, every 4 weeks for next 3 months, then every 1-3 months; withhold for ALT/AST >5-20x ULN and permanently discontinue if >20x ULN.

raw_record.support_text: A 62-year-old woman developed fulminant hepatic failure after taking Arthrotec (containing diclofenac and misoprostol) 50 mg three times per day for two months for a painful left heel. Viral and autoimmune etiologies and other drugs or chemical exposures were excluded, and the paper reports this as diclofenac-induced fulminant hepatic failure, the first such case successfully treated by orthotopic liver transplantation. Four similar previously reported diclofenac-induced cases died without transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient took the fixed combination product Arthrotec (diclofenac plus misoprostol) 50 mg three times daily for two months at a therapeutic dose. Developed jaundice, dark urine and constipation after a flu-like prodrome; had five out of five poor prognostic criteria for non-paracetamol drug-induced fulminant hepatic failure and underwent successful orthotopic liver transplantation with excellent recovery. History of immune hemolytic anemia treated with prednisolone that had been discontinued six months prior. Co-medications Coproxamol and Amoxil (jaundice noted a week before Amoxil started) and no paracetamol overdose were reported and excluded as causes. Described as the first reported successful treatment of diclofenac-induced fulminant hepatic failure; four previously reported similar cases died without liver transplantation. Putative mechanisms of diclofenac toxicity reviewed.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old female with EGFR exon 19 deletion NSCLC developing T790M mutation was switched from afatinib to osimertinib 80 mg/day, and after about 9 months of treatment progressed to jaundice with elevated AST (209 U/l), ALT (143 IU/l), total bilirubin (8 mg/dl), direct bilirubin (4.3 mg/dl), alkaline phosphatase (495 U/l), and gamma-glutamyltransferase (691 U/l). Viral (hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV, herpes, HIV) and autoimmune (ANA, RF, AMA) work-ups were negative, and imaging showed fatty liver with gallbladder wall edema and sludge but no biliary obstruction; the authors call this osimertinib-related drug-induced liver injury. The report frames the case as osimertinib-related DILI that was successfully managed with osimertinib desensitization rechallenge.

AST/ALT/bilirubin/Alk-P/GGT elevations with negative viral and autoimmune serologies; fatty liver on CT/MRCP, no biliary obstruction. Managed with Osimertinib desensitization rechallenge; prior grade 1 diarrhea, vomiting, anorexia, and skin toxicities. DILI literature on osimertinib is scarce.

raw_record.support_text: Clopidogrel is a commonly prescribed antiplatelet agent that carries a rare risk of hepatotoxicity. The authors describe a case of severe clopidogrel-induced hepatitis with liver biopsy assessment, and state that prompt recognition and withdrawal of the offending agent are imperative to prevent progression and potentially fatal liver injury.

Extensive serologies (hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, EBV, ANA, ASMA, AMA, anti-LKM, ceruloplasmin) were negative. Only other medications were aspirin and metoprolol for many years with normal liver biochemistries. Liver biopsy was performed.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was diagnosed with clopidogrel-induced severe hepatitis. After discontinuing clopidogrel, AST increased to 2,107 U/L, ALT to 1,567 U/L, and bilirubin to 37 mg/dL (predominately direct), and INR rose to 2.1 despite empiric vitamin K. A brief course of prednisone and ursodiol led to normalization of liver biochemistries.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: liver biopsy showed severe acute hepatitis with mixed inflammatory portal tract infiltrates (plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils), bile ductular reaction, patchy hepatocyte ballooning degeneration, and extensive periportal hepatocyte dropout without fibrosis. Peak ALT 1,567 U/L, AST 2,107 U/L, bilirubin 37 mg/dL (predominantly direct), INR 2.1 with coagulopathy and jaundice. Naranjo and RUCAM scores both 8, indicating probable drug-induced hepatitis. Patient treated with prednisone and ursodiol and recovered with normalization of liver biochemistries. Prior reported clopidogrel-induced hepatitis cases range from reversible injury and recovery to acute hepatic failure and death, with onset between 3 and 180 days and rechallenge-confirmed injury in some cases; clopidogrel liver injury has been reported as cholestatic, hepatocellular, or mixed.

raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old woman with onychomycosis treated with itraconazole 200 mg daily for 5 weeks developed jaundice, elevated transaminases (AST 2571, ALT 3789 IU/L), and progressive hepatic failure with ascites and coagulopathy. A liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with bile plugs, hepatocellular ballooning, and patchy necrosis, and the condition was judged consistent with acute cytotoxic and cholestatic injuries caused by drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Her hepatic failure was attributed to itraconazole and improved with corticosteroid treatment.

Treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg q8h, tapered), then oral prednisolone; condition stabilized and liver chemistries returned to normal by ~2 weeks after discharge; discharged 36 days after admission.

raw_record.support_text: When pyrazinamide plus isoniazid was first used as first-line chemotherapy in the US in the 1950s, a high incidence of hepatic toxicity was reported: 4 (5%) of 81 patients given pyrazinamide 50 mg/kg plus isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily became jaundiced (McDermott and others, 1954) and 5 (8%) of 38 patients had hepatitis in another study (Phillips and Horton, 1956). There was evidence that the incidence of hepatitis was related to the pyrazinamide dosage: in a USPHS study (1959), 4 (2%) of 160 patients given isoniazid plus pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg daily and 11 (7%) of 167 given isoniazid plus pyrazinamide 40 mg/kg daily had liver toxicity, whereas only 1 (1%) of 123 on the control isoniazid plus PAS regimen had evidence of liver toxicity. Largely as a result of these studies the use of pyrazinamide as a first-line drug was abandoned.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Dose-dependent hepatic toxicity: high incidence of hepatitis occurred at large daily pyrazinamide dosages (about 40-50 mg/kg, roughly 3 g/day) given in combination with isoniazid as first-line therapy in the 1950s; at lower dosages (20-30 mg/kg) combined with streptomycin, no hepatitis occurred. Injury is reported in isoniazid- or streptomycin-combination regimens (co-treatment setting).
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence figures: 4/81 (5%) jaundiced (McDermott 1954); 5/38 (8%) hepatitis with 2 jaundiced (Phillips and Horton 1956); USPHS 1959: 4/160 (2%) liver toxicity at 25 mg/kg vs 11/167 (7%) at 40 mg/kg, all with raised serum bilirubin and increased bromsulphalein retention, jaundice in 1 and 4 respectively; control isoniazid plus PAS 1/123 (chronic alcoholic with abnormal pretreatment tests). According to the Naranjo adverse-reaction probability scale, enoxaparin was the probable cause of hepatotoxicity in this patient.

raw_record.support_text: Table 3 shows the individual data for patients with troglitazone-induced liver injury (8 patients, mean age 59.8 ± 9.6 years, 4 female and 4 male). Mean serum ALT was 282.8 ± 328.8 IU/l (median 138), overt jaundice was observed in one patient (Case 7, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl), and all patients recovered from liver injury after troglitazone was stopped. Latent periods to liver injury were 223.0 ± 204.3 days (median 133.5, range 69–677). Liver biopsies in cases 3 and 7 showed centrilobular necrosis and expanded portal areas, with cellular infiltration and cholestasis not prominent and no pruritus, skin rash, or eosinophilia suggestive of an allergic reaction. R factor < 2 favored cholestatic injury; toxicology and viral hepatitis serology were negative and imaging/ERCP showed no duct dilation. After workup, possible DILI was entertained; the patient reported recent use of Lorazepam. Liver biopsy showed moderate lymphocytic infiltration, canalicular cholestasis and macrovesicular steatosis (~20%) suggestive of drug-induced etiology. Lorazepam was considered the culprit of DILI with a RUCAM score of 7 (probable); after discontinuation, liver function improved markedly.

Most (79%) reported taking paracetamol for pain, 63% took a prescription paracetamol/opioid combination, and 38% were consuming two paracetamol-containing products concurrently. These unintentional cases had poorer outcomes than intentional overdoses, with a significantly greater percentage presenting with severe (grades 3 and 4) hepatic encephalopathy. The paper also notes that paracetamol overdose-related hospitalisations declined from 1995 to 2004 among persons under 50 but increased for those 50 and over.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 25 pediatric patients with acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC), hepatotoxicity severity was assessed. There were highly significant relationships between maximum ALT and maximum INR (p < 0.0001), maximum AST (p < 0.0001), maximum bilirubin (p < 0.0001) and maximum pH (p < 0.0001), and a significant relationship between maximum ALT and minimum phosphate (p = 0.038). The mean time from acetaminophen intake to NAC initiation was 12.4 h (range 1.5–25.5 h), and multiple prehospital vomiting episodes were proposed as an early predictor of acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity in this pediatric cohort.

raw_record.extra_details: Mean time from acetaminophen intake to NAC initiation 12.4 h (range 1.5–25.5 h). Hepatotoxicity severity indicated by maximum ALT, INR, AST, bilirubin, pH, and minimum phosphate relationships. Prehospital vomiting (≥3 episodes in 60%, 15/25) proposed as an early predictor; significant relationship of vomiting episodes with maximum INR (p=0.013), maximum AST (p≤0.0001), maximum ALT (p=0.0005), and other biochemical parameters. Maximum ALT significantly related to maximum INR (p<0.0001), maximum AST (p<0.0001), maximum bilirubin (p<0.0001), maximum pH (p<0.0001), and minimum phosphate (p=0.038). raw_record.support_text: The study shows that paediatric patients at increased risk of developing hepatotoxicity can be identified at an early stage of hospital admission. Early biochemical parameters, the number of prehospital vomiting episodes, and the latency before NAC treatment initiation were independent risk factors for developing hepatotoxicity in paediatric patients with acetaminophen poisoning, with such predictors potentially reducing the incidence of acute liver failure in children. The paper describes acetaminophen poisoning (overdose) as causing hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure in this paediatric cohort.

raw_record.extra_details: Independent risk factors for developing hepatotoxicity were number of prehospital vomiting episodes and latency time before NAC (N-acetylcysteine) treatment initiation; maximum INR and ALT levels were predicted by initial elevated INR, initial ALT and AST, initial elevated bilirubin, initial creatinine, initial phosphate, and initial blood glucose. Initial hypophosphatemia at tertiary-department referral was significantly associated with more comprehensive hepatotoxicity. Unlike several adult studies, AST, ALT and INR levels were not correlated with the degree of acetaminophen overdose in this paediatric study.

raw_record.extra_details: Cholestatic hepatitis. Doses of gemcitabine 1300 mg and carboplatin 450 mg repeated on November 27 and December 4, 2001. Labs included peak ALT 320, AST 222 U/L, elevated alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dl at presentation later rising with direct bilirubin 9.8 mg/dl, ammonia 49 umol/l, INR 1.4. Histology showed hepatocellular ballooning/hydropic change, portal fibrosis, eosinophils/mononuclear/polymorphonuclear cells, patchy lobular necrosis, fatty metamorphosis, marked cholestasis with dilated proliferated cholangioles. Patient developed hepatic coma and died; autopsy showed 770-g liver, prominent bile stasis without obstruction, 5 L ascites. Mechanism: metabolic idiosyncratic reaction, no features of hypersensitivity reaction.

raw_record.support_text: A 29-year male soldier presented after acetaminophen overdose with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. By day 2 of referral he developed acute fulminant hepatitis attributed to paracetamol poisoning; acetaminophen blood level was 6358 ng/ml. He then progressed to multisystem organ failure with ascites and neurological symptoms and was deemed a poor liver transplant candidate, with confirmed admission acetaminophen blood level of 9874 ng/ml. N-acetylcysteine was given to inactivate the toxic metabolite NAPQI.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective analysis (2007–2017) of 90 patients referred to a tertiary hospital for paracetamol-related hepatotoxicity, with ALT >1000 IU/L on admission and a delay of ≥12 h to N-acetylcysteine antidote therapy. Poisoned patients following multiple ingestion (staggered overdose) were older, more often had liver steatosis or chronic ethanol abuse, and had a greater risk of poor outcome and higher mortality than those with a single ingestion overdose; arterial lactate was a predictor of poor outcome.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol hepatotoxicity described as a well-established leading cause of acute liver failure in the developed world. 90 patients analyzed; multiple-ingestion (staggered) overdose subgroup had higher mortality and worse outcome; arterial lactate was independently associated with poor prognosis (adjusted OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.09–2.77, p<0.02). Poor-outcome patients were older with higher ALT, bilirubin, lactate and lower factor V and arterial pH. Modified King's College liver transplantation criteria used (lactate >3.5 mmol/L; pH <7.3 or lactate >3 mmol/L; creatinine >300 µmol/L with grade 3–4 encephalopathy and INR >6.5). Also referred to as acetaminophen; synonym NAC antidote.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 90 patients admitted after paracetamol overdose (single-dose suicide attempts or multiple ingestion of a supratherapeutic daily dose for pain management), liver injury led to severe outcomes: seven fatalities and five liver transplantations in the multiple-ingestion subgroup versus two fatalities and two transplantations in the single-ingestion subgroup. Twenty-two patients fulfilled the modified King's College criteria for liver transplantation; seven were listed and transplanted. All nine fatalities presented with multiple organ failure, seven had a history of chronic ethanol abuse or liver steatosis as additional risk factors for liver injury, and all fulfilled the King's College criteria.

NAC administration delay was 12 h (38%), 12-24 h (38%), 24-48 h (10%), and >48 h (14%); delay did not influence clinical or biological variables. Twenty-two patients fulfilled modified King's College criteria (positive predictive value 100%, negative predictive value 87%); seven listed and transplanted, one listed patient recovered without graft, patients who died on the list died of neurological failure, and one transplanted patient died on day 14 due to non-recovery of multiple organ failure. Transplanted patients had good one- and five-year outcomes. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is an analgesic; cause of the multiple ingestion was management of common pain.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of psoriasis patients treated with methotrexate (MTX), hepatotoxicity is described as one of the most significant methotrexate-induced adverse events, requiring continuous monitoring. Hepatotoxicity and symptomatic adverse events were the most frequently recorded AEs in the cohort, and the number of recorded hepatotoxicity cases was sufficient for logistic regression analysis of the association between MTX-related hepatotoxicity and candidate polymorphisms. A best-fit model identified the BHMT genotype as significantly associated with MTX hepatotoxicity (OR 3.17; 95% CI 1.18-8.49 for carrying the variant 742GA/742AA allele).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was the most frequently recorded MTX adverse event in the psoriasis cohort (safety group n=137, 24 with hepatotoxicity). MTX hepatotoxicity risk was significantly associated with the BHMT genotype (dominant model): patients carrying at least one variant BHMT allele (742GA or 742AA) were 3-fold more likely to experience MTX-induced hepatotoxicity than those with the 742GG genotype (OR 3.17; 95% CI 1.18-8.49); other variables in the hepatotoxicity model (MTHFR activity, DNMT3b, FPGS, ABCC2, ABCB1 genotypes) did not reach significance. Indication: psoriasis.

raw_record.support_text: Among 589 patients admitted for drug overdoses, 71 (12%) involved acetaminophen ingestion, and 10 of 25 patients (40%) with acute liver failure (hepatic coma plus coagulopathy) during the study period were acetaminophen-overdose patients. The estimated annual incidence of potential or actual acetaminophen toxicity requiring hospitalization was 53 (95% CI, 39 to 67) per million population of Dallas County.

raw_record.extra_details: Accidental-overdose patients had higher morbidity and mortality than suicidal ones, with nearly two thirds having aminotransferase levels above 1000 IU/liter and acute liver failure developing in one third; low or undetectable acetaminophen (≤10 mg/liter) in 8 of 15 accidental-overdose vs 3 of 49 suicidal patients; acetaminophen accounted for 12% (71/589) of all overdose admissions and 40% (10/25) of acute liver failure patients; estimated annual incidence 53 (95% CI 39 to 67) per million. Mechanism: metabolism by glucuronidation and sulfation with P450 2E1 oxidation to NAPQI at supratherapeutic doses, covalent binding to proteins/DNA, glutathione depletion (aggravated by starvation and chronic alcohol ingestion) causing liver injury; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is protective.

raw_record.extra_details: Most frequent cause of acute liver failure at the hospital during the study period; five deaths. Extremely high aminotransferase levels in virtually all patients distinguished the picture from alcoholic hepatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, and other forms of acute liver injury. Reasons for accidental overdose included too-frequent dosing (e.g., every two hours), overdosing (>1 g per dose) due to persistent pain, unknowing ingestion of acetaminophen-containing compounds, simultaneous use of multiple acetaminophen preparations, and clouded sensorium due to alcohol. Package warning in the US limits ingestion to more than 4 g (eight 500-mg tablets) in 24 hours by adults.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old woman with breast cancer took cephalexin 500 mg twice daily orally for 10 days after tumor resection and a repeat course at the same dose for cellulitis. About one month later she developed fatigue and syncope, with a cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme elevation (total bilirubin 10.4 mg/dL, ALT 129 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 587 U/L, R-factor 0.7). After excluding viral and autoimmune etiologies and biliary obstruction, a biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with mild portal lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltrate and marked bile-duct damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Cephalexin 500 mg twice daily orally for 10 days, repeated for cellulitis two weeks later; cholestatic pattern with R-factor 0.7, total bilirubin 10.4 mg/dL, ALT 129 U/L, ALP 587 U/L; cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy with marked bile duct damage and bile plugs in canaliculi; follow-up biopsy showed minimal ductular proliferation and resolution of bile duct damage/inflammation. Liver enzymes remained elevated, prompting budesonide initiation 142 days after onset.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose (AOD) is the leading cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the United Kingdom, and in the United States AOD ALF accounts for more than 50% of all ALF admissions to liver units, with about half of the overdoses unintentional and up to 12% of those admitted progressing to liver transplantation. Patients are listed for super-urgent transplantation only if they fulfill the King's College criteria for acetaminophen overdose.

Unit data: 715 ALF admissions Dec 1994-Apr 2005, 427 from AOD; 97 transplants for ALF, 47 from AOD; 13 AOD ALF patients (27% of AOD transplantations) received subtotal hepatectomy plus auxiliary orthotopic whole-graft liver transplantation (ALT); 9/13 ALT patients alive (69%) vs 7/13 OLT patients (54%). raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded that the cause of the patient's severe intrahepatic cholestasis was drug-toxic injury caused by amiodarone. This conclusion was supported because even after pausing the other medications for 10 days the cholestasis parameters and transaminases continued to rise, and only after amiodarone was withdrawn (as the last potentially hepatotoxic drug) did the elevated liver values regress continuously over 7 days with complete resolution of the icterus. The cholestasis parameters and transaminases remained declining despite restarting oral anticoagulation and continuing a cholesterol synthesis inhibitor. The final diagnosis was severe intrahepatic cholestasis after intake of amiodarone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was concurrently taking other medications (oral anticoagulation and a cholesterol synthesis inhibitor); amiodarone was the last potentially hepatotoxic drug withdrawn after the others were paused without improvement, and resolution followed its discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report (German). Amiodarone (2-n-butyl-3-[3,5-dijodid-4-β-diäthylaminoäthoxybenzoyl]benzofuran-hydrochloride; brand Cordarex) is a class III antiarrhythmic used in Germany since 1982 for tachycardic arrhythmias, especially atrial fibrillation; other indications include atrial flutter, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and ventricular arrhythmias. The patient was fitted with an atrioventricular defibrillator system due to risk of malignant cardiac arrhythmias. Dechallenge led to continuous regression of liver values and complete resolution of skin and scleral icterus over 7 days; clinical phenotype was severe intrahepatic cholestasis with jaundice.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic necrosis is the major manifestation of acetaminophen overdose. In these patients it became clinically evident one to five days after ingestion, with maximal SGOT elevation two to six days after ingestion. Severity varied from mild SGOT elevation to prolonged prothrombin time (four patients) and massive hepatic necrosis with encephalopathy (two patients). Liver biopsies and postmortem examination demonstrated centrilobular necrosis, characteristic of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In this paper on the etiology of acute liver failure (ALF), acetaminophen is identified as the predominant cause of ALF in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia (36-43%). In the authors' Thai cohort, non-acetaminophen drug toxicity (26.1%) was the most frequent established cause, whereas acute hepatitis B-induced ALF occurred in only 1.8%. In a later paragraph, acetaminophen overdose is described as the most common cause of ALF in comparator US/UK studies, and acetaminophen-induced ALF is reported to carry a favorable prognosis with treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen-induced injury specifically reported in the setting of overdose; favorable prognosis attributed to availability of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) antidote and prompt therapy from overdose history.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose was the most common cause of ALF in referenced US and UK single/multi-center studies (17,26). 30-day mortality rates for ALF in those cohorts were 57% without and 16% with liver transplant (US study), and 26.7% without and 13.7% with transplant (UK study). Acetaminophen was inversely associated with 30-day mortality and was associated with 60-80% short-term survival without transplantation; about 66% of patients spontaneously recovered with NAC and supportive care. Acetaminophen-induced ALF is classified with ischemic-induced ALF as having a favorable prognosis compared with hepatitis B infection, indeterminate cause, and drug-other-than-acetaminophen-related ALF (17-25% short-term survival without transplantation).

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized clinical trial of 15 patients with chronic hepatitis B treated with fialuridine (FIAU) at 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day for 24 weeks, a severe toxic reaction developed: during the 13th week one patient suddenly developed lactic acidosis and liver failure, the study was terminated on an emergency basis, and seven patients were found to have severe hepatotoxicity with progressive lactic acidosis, worsening jaundice, and deteriorating hepatic function. The authors concluded that treatment with fialuridine induced a severe toxic reaction characterized by hepatic failure, lactic acidosis, pancreatitis, neuropathy, and myopathy, probably caused by widespread mitochondrial damage.

raw_record.extra_details: Fialuridine (1-(2-deoxy-2-fluoro-beta-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouracil, FIAU), an antiviral nucleoside analogue. Dose 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day for 24 weeks. Study terminated during 13th week; 7 of 15 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity with progressive lactic acidosis, worsening jaundice, and deteriorating hepatic function. Toxic reaction included hepatic failure, lactic acidosis, pancreatitis, neuropathy, and myopathy, attributed to widespread mitochondrial damage.

raw_record.support_text: A six-month phase 2 trial of fialuridine in patients with chronic hepatitis B was terminated on an emergency basis 13 weeks after it was begun when hepatic failure and lactic acidosis suddenly occurred in one patient. Despite immediate discontinuation of the medication, the toxicity eventually led to hepatic failure, lactic acidosis, and pancreatitis in seven patients, of whom five died; the other two survived after emergency liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had pre-existing chronic hepatitis B (the trial's therapeutic indication).
raw_record.extra_details: Phase 2 trial, 24 patients with chronic hepatitis B, randomized to 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day fialuridine orally in two or three divided doses; seven patients developed severe hepatotoxicity (five died, two survived after liver transplantation); three other patients had mild hepatotoxicity; several patients also had pancreatitis, neuropathy, or myopathy; lactic acidosis also occurred. Liver histology showed marked accumulation of microvesicular and macrovesicular fat with minimal hepatocyte necrosis or architectural change; electron microscopy showed abnormal mitochondria and fat accumulation in hepatocytes. The trial was terminated on an emergency basis after 13 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: In a clinical trial of fialuridine for chronic hepatitis B, severe hepatic failure with lactic acidosis developed in 7 of 10 patients treated for at least 9 weeks, with cumulative doses of 551 to 1753 mg. The seven patients had steadily worsening jaundice, decreasing hepatic synthetic function, worsening prothrombin times, increasing serum ammonia and lactate, and frank acidosis once lactate exceeded 12 mmol/L. This toxicity was explicitly described as fialuridine-induced.

raw_record.extra_details: A nucleoside analogue (thymidine-based). Seven of 10 patients treated at least 8 weeks developed severe hepatic failure with lactic acidosis; 5 of the 7 died (4 after attempted liver transplantation; deaths due to hepatic failure/acidosis and pancreatitis), while 2 survived after successful liver transplantation with reversal of lactic acidosis and no residual fialuridine-induced toxicity except mild peripheral neuropathy. Features included jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly-associated decreasing synthetic function, worsening prothrombin times, hyperammonemia, hyperlactatemia, and acidosis (lactate >12 mmol/L). Treatment with intravenous thymidine (8 g/kg/day) and oral uridine (24 g/day) produced no obvious clinical improvement. Values reflect a clinical trial of fialuridine for hepatitis B.

raw_record.support_text: Treatment with fialuridine (FIAU) was stopped at week 11 because of paresthesias; two weeks later the patient developed nausea, vomiting, weakness, jaundice, lactic acidosis, and shock, and died two days after orthotopic liver transplantation. Seven patients in the study developed severe hepatotoxicity attributed to fialuridine, with hepatic failure and lactic acidosis that resulted in multiple deaths and liver transplantations.

raw_record.extra_details: Fialuridine was given at 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day for 9.5-13 weeks; 7 patients had severe hepatotoxicity with hepatic failure and lactic acidosis, and 5 patients died (one per patient numbers 1-7, deaths in patients 1,2,4,6,7). All seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity also had biochemical evidence of pancreatitis (progressive serum lipase increases up to 50-fold); five had gross and microscopic pancreatitis at autopsy. Five patients with severe hepatotoxicity had peripheral-nerve injury and muscle findings similar to zidovudine-induced myopathy. Three patients (patients 5,8,9) with comparable cumulative doses had mild hepatotoxicity (nausea, abdominal discomfort, aminotransferase elevations, mild hypoalbuminemia and hypofibrinogenemia) that resolved. Five patients treated less than 4 weeks (total <200 mg) had no evidence of fialuridine-induced toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity with aromatase inhibitors is rare, and specific instances of exemestane-induced hepatotoxicity have been documented in only two prior case reports, both showing signs and symptoms of cholestatic liver injury after three to eight weeks of medication exposure. Described cases include a jaundiced patient with pruritis whose bilirubin peaked at 13.8 mg/dL and a hospitalized patient with grade 4 hyperbilirubinemia and grade 3 transaminitis whose bilirubin peaked at 21.2 mg/dL; both resolved approximately four months after exemestane was discontinued. The present report documents exemestane-induced cholestasis in a patient with underlying primary biliary cholangitis. The conclusion states that although rare, liver injury due to exemestane has been reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Index patient had pre-existing primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), an underlying hepatic dysfunction proposed as a risk factor for developing cholestasis with exemestane.
raw_record.extra_details: Steroidal aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer. Mechanism of hepatotoxicity unclear; ~42% of exemestane is excreted via the biliary system and it is metabolized by CYP enzymes including CYP1A2 and CYP3A4. Two prior case reports: a 65-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer with jaundice, conjunctival and skin jaundice, and generalized pruritis after eight weeks of therapy; and a 47-year-old postmenopausal woman hospitalized with grade 4 hyperbilirubinemia, pruritis, and grade 3 transaminitis three weeks after initiation. Total bilirubin peaked at 13.8 and 21.2 mg/dL and resolved ~4 months after discontinuation; management was symptomatic (antihistamines, or cholestyramine, phenobarbital, and lorazepam). Patient tolerated the non-steroidal AIs anastrozole and letrozole; drug resources report a higher incidence of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase elevations with exemestane, though head-to-head clinical trials showed similar hepatotoxicity rates between steroidal and non-steroidal AIs.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that excessive acetaminophen can lead to severe hepatotoxicity, with a toxic dose of more than 7.5-10 g or >150 mg/kg in adults and >200 mg/kg in children. In overdose, glucuronidation and sulfation pathways are saturated and shunted metabolism by CYP2E1 produces toxic metabolites such as NAPQI, which cause irreversible liver necrosis. Three patients with acetaminophen poisoning had liver function abnormalities refractory to conventional therapy and received DPMAS artificial liver support; despite severe acetaminophen toxicity and LFT abnormalities all three recovered.

raw_record.extra_details: Three patients with acetaminophen poisoning treated with DPMAS extracorporeal liver support (BS330 filter for elevated bilirubin, HA330-II for impaired LFTs with normal bilirubin); all recovered despite severe toxicity refractory to conventional therapy. Mechanism: saturated glucuronidation/sulfation, CYP2E1 metabolism to NAPQI causing irreversible liver necrosis. Acetaminophen poisoning diagnosed by serum level; liver and coagulation profiles; potential progression to fulminant liver failure and liver transplantation candidacy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a fatal case of nafcillin-induced hepatotoxicity confirmed by liver biopsy, with total bilirubin peaking to 21.8 mg/dl and an extensive negative evaluation for other causes of hepatic injury.
raw_record.extra_details: 53-year-old woman receiving nafcillin 12 g/day IV for MSSA bacteremia/osteomyelitis; jaundice with mild disorientation appeared on day 15 with total bilirubin 9.6 mg/dL, direct 7.3 mg/dL, ALP 388 IU/L, AST 67 IU/L, ALT 24 IU/L, GGTP 878 IU/L; peak total bilirubin 21.8 mg/dL. Dechallenge produced a mild transient drop in AST/ALT/ALP/GGTP. Extensive workup negative (coombs, ANCA MPO/PR3, RF, ASMA, ANA, HLA B27, complement, LKM, AFP, anti-TPO); ultrasound and MRCP excluded obstruction. Liver biopsy showed diffuse hepatocanalicular cholestasis with focal centrizonal bile infarct, periportal hepatocellular swelling and mild nodular hyperplasia-like changes; diagnosis of cholestatic jaundice secondary to nafcillin was made and ursodiol (10 mg/kg) started. No fulminant hepatic failure, coagulopathy, or encephalopathy at that time; GGTP and ALP remained >1500 IU/L on follow-up. Prior ertapenem had been discontinued before nafcillin. Patient had pre-existing renal insufficiency (creatinine 2 mg/dL, GFR 26 mL/min).

raw_record.support_text: A patient developed hepatocellular-pattern liver injury with aminotransferase elevations reaching ~50 times the upper normal limit, disproportionate bilirubin and minimal ALP elevation, after taking losartan. Alternative causes (acute viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, autoimmune hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, Wilson disease, malignant infiltration, biliary obstruction, and sepsis) were excluded, and there was rapid clinical recovery and laboratory normalization after losartan discontinuation. The CIOMS/RUCAM causality assessment scored >8 points ('highly probable') for losartan-related drug-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS/RUCAM score >8 ('highly probable'). Aminotransferases reached ~50x upper normal limit with disproportionate bilirubin and minimally elevated ALP; extra-hepatic obstruction considered unlikely. Other causes of acute hepatitis excluded by presentation and investigations (acute viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, autoimmune hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, Wilson disease, malignant infiltration, biliary obstruction, sepsis). Rapid clinical recovery and laboratory normalization after losartan discontinuation. Reported as the 6th case of losartan-induced hepatitis and possibly the first losartan-induced ischemic liver injury in an adult population.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report the authors state that, in their patient who received piroxicam, the temporal sequence together with exclusion of viral hepatitis A and B and an initially normal autoantibody screen all point to a drug induced hepatitis. Despite withdrawing piroxicam after the onset of jaundice, the illness progressed to fatal subacute hepatic failure, and the patient died 105 days after the onset of jaundice with a biopsy showing severe confluent centrilobular necrosis with extensive bridging collapse and an inflammatory infiltrate (subacute hepatic necrosis).
raw_record.extra_details: Patient presented with severe jaundice, grade II hepatic coma and gross ascites; bilirubin 407 umol/l, aspartate transaminase 730 IU/l, alanine transaminase 258 IU/l, prothrombin time 39/13s; antinuclear antibody titre rose to 1/160 and was associated with hyperglobulinaemia; the authors propose a self-perpetuating autoimmune reaction triggered by piroxicam. Treated with corticosteroids then suffered gastrointestinal bleeding; died 105 days after onset of jaundice; post-mortem biopsy showed subacute hepatic necrosis. The report separately notes one published report of probable piroxicam-induced cholestatic jaundice and that mild transient rises in serum transaminase have been described in piroxicam clinical trials. Patient age not stated in this window.

raw_record.support_text: This is reported as the first description of sorafenib-induced hepato-renal failure and the first fatality in an otherwise systemically well individual without underlying liver disease or known metastases. The patient had been receiving adjuvant sorafenib, and paragraph 19 explicitly states this case represents an idiosyncratic reaction as opposed to a marked example of generalized hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adjuvant treatment setting in an otherwise healthy individual without underlying liver disease or metastatic disease prior to treatment or at autopsy.
raw_record.extra_details: First documented death directly attributable to sorafenib in an otherwise well individual, with sorafenib-induced hepato-renal failure and acute liver failure. Showed pronounced immune response with elevated CRP, low-grade pyrexia, complement consumption, and an immune infiltrate in the liver, with a typical delay in onset (elevated LFTs with ALT>3xULN and ALT/ULN:AlkP/ULN ratio >5 between 3-7 weeks after initial exposure). Phenotype interpreted as an immune-mediated process. Comparatively, hepatic failure incidence was similar between sorafenib and placebo in phase III trials.

raw_record.support_text: This retrospective cohort study enrolled patients prospectively in the US ALFSG registry between January 1998 and December 2018 (n=1190) with a primary diagnosis of acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver failure (APAP-ALF) as determined by the site investigator and further adjudicated by an external review committee. Inclusion criteria required evidence of ALF, age ≥18 years, and a primary diagnosis of APAP-ALF; cirrhosis and acute-on-chronic liver failure were excluded. Patients characterized APAP overdose intent as intentional (excessive ingestion with suicidal intent) or unintentional (excessive ingestion to relieve symptoms without suicidal intent).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting in adults (>=18 years) presenting as acute liver failure; cirrhosis and acute-on-chronic liver failure were excluded from the cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective cohort of 1190 APAP-ALF patients enrolled in the US ALFSG registry (January 1998-December 2018), primary diagnosis of APAP-ALF adjudicated by an external review committee. ALF defined by INR >=1.5, any grade hepatic encephalopathy, onset <26 weeks, and no existing cirrhosis. Overdose intent classified as intentional (suicidal intent) or unintentional (excessive ingestion to relieve symptoms); unknown intent excluded. Primary endpoint was 21-day transplant-free survival. APAP is a well-established cause of overdose-related acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 25-year-old woman with no history of liver disease developed liver dysfunction with severe jaundice and general malaise following prolonged minocycline therapy for acne vulgaris (100 mg daily for about 1 year). Serum ANA was detected and IgG elevated; symptoms and liver function normalized after minocycline discontinuation and corticosteroids. The diagnosis was drug-induced hepatitis with autoimmune features, since liver histology revealed acute hepatitis. The paper notes drug-induced hepatitis should be considered when liver dysfunction develops during long-term minocycline therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 25-year-old Japanese woman with acne vulgaris treated with minocycline 100 mg/day for 12 months prior to onset; presented with deranged liver function, severe jaundice (icterus), and general malaise; serum anti-nuclear antibody detected and IgG elevated; liver histology revealed acute hepatitis; symptoms resolved and liver function normalized after minocycline discontinuation and corticosteroid administration; no history of drug/food allergy, transfusion, or significant alcohol consumption; only a few reports of minocycline-induced autoimmune hepatitis in Japan. Some reports indicate minocycline can induce abnormal immune reactions resulting in hepatitis and systemic lupus erythematosus-like syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: In HIV-infected South African patients receiving a blinded regimen of lamivudine or emtricitabine, stavudine, and either nevirapine or efavirenz, early hepatotoxicity (grade 3 or greater increase in serum aminotransferases within the first 12 weeks) occurred in 17% of the nevirapine group versus 0% of the efavirenz group, and was balanced between the lamivudine and emtricitabine arms. Two subjects died of hepatic failure, and independent risk factors included BMI<18.5, female sex, serum albumin<35 g/L, MCV>85 fL, HIV-1 RNA<20,000 copies/mL, AST<75 IU/L, and LDH<164 IU/L. The paper notes that the acute hepatic toxicity of nevirapine led to a product label change in the US and EU and that enrollment in the nevirapine stratum was terminated by health authorities.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty-one ibuprofen-induced idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity cases from the Spanish DILI Registry and five cases from the LATIN DILI Network were analysed and compared with 76 idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity events due to other NSAIDs and 844 non-NSAID-induced hepatotoxicity cases. Only cases induced by conventional medications were included, and all NSAID cases were limited to those where the NSAID was judged as a single culprit drug.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: NSAID cases judged as a single culprit drug; findings from DILI registries (Spanish DILI Registry and LATIN DILI Network).
raw_record.extra_details: 26 ibuprofen DILI patients in total (21 Spanish DILI Registry + 5 LATIN DILI Network). Ibuprofen was the most frequent causative drug (29%) among the 73 NSAID DILI cases in the Spanish DILI Registry, and accounted for 17% of 29 Latin-American NSAID hepatotoxicity cases. The ibuprofen cases contained a higher (though not statistically significant) proportion of fatal/liver transplant patients (12% vs 3-5% in the other groups). Diabetes was significantly more frequent (27% vs 7-12%, p=0.04) and hypertension less prevalent (10% vs 20-29%) among ibuprofen cases. Demographics, liver injury pattern, and laboratory parameters did not differ between ibuprofen cases and other NSAID or non-NSAID cases.

raw_record.support_text: The study characterized 26 ibuprofen DILI cases from the Spanish DILI Registry, noting that ibuprofen-induced liver injury usually develops within four weeks of treatment initiation and presents as hepatocellular type liver damage, though characteristics varied considerably between patients. The paper concludes the risk of developing ibuprofen-induced liver injury is low given the drug's extensive worldwide use but can have life-threatening consequences. Registry data showed hepatocellular injury in 15 (58%) and cholestatic/mixed in 11 (42%) cases, with 2 fatal and 1 liver transplantation outcome among the ibuprofen cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 26 ibuprofen DILI cases in the Spanish DILI Registry (N=26 ibuprofen vs 76 other NSAIDs vs 844 non-NSAIDs). Median time to onset 15 days (range 3-1767), median treatment duration 16 days (1-1826). Clinical presentation: jaundice 17 (65%), hospital admission 14 (58%), eosinophilia 6 (24%), lymphopenia 4 (17%), positive autoantibody titers 6 (27%). Prior to this, ibuprofen was considered to have very limited hepatotoxicity. Higher OTC doses marketed in Spain (200 and 400 mg) vs US (200 mg only) hypothesized to explain higher ibuprofen DILI frequency in Spain; threshold dose for idiosyncratic DILI and reactive-metabolite/oxidative-stress/JNK mechanism discussed. A multicenter Italy study reported higher adjusted risk of liver damage for ibuprofen than for diclofenac. Severity: mild 9 (35%), moderate 14 (54%), severe 0, fatal 2 / liver transplant 1 (12%). Hy's law criteria met in 11 (42%). 11 of 13 (85%) resolved within 1 year. No characteristic drug signature; diabetes mellitus trend more common in ibuprofen DILI patients (7, 27%); lower hypertension prevalence (2, 10%).

raw_record.support_text: In this double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of rimegepant 75 mg oral tablet versus placebo for acute migraine treatment, the authors state: 'No signal of drug-induced liver injury due to rimegepant was identified.' The conclusion reiterates that tolerability and safety were similar to placebo with no evidence of hepatotoxicity. This is an explicit agent-specific negative conclusion about human drug-induced liver injury for rimegepant.
raw_record.extra_details: Rimegepant 75 mg oral tablet, a small molecule CGRP receptor antagonist, in acute migraine treatment. Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03235479); 1485 enrolled, 1162 randomized (rimegepant n=582; placebo n=580), mostly female (85.5%), mean age 41.6 years. Coprimary endpoints: pain freedom and most bothersome symptom freedom at 2 h postdose. No DILI signal and no evidence of hepatotoxicity reported.

raw_record.support_text: In this randomized controlled trial of a single 75 mg rimegepant oral tablet for the acute treatment of adults with migraine, the authors state that safety and tolerability with rimegepant were excellent and that liver function testing showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Transaminase elevations comparing rimegepant (serum AST or ALT >ULN in 2.0%, 11/546) versus placebo (3.6%, 20/549) showed no signal, one participant in each group had levels >3x ULN, none >5x ULN, and no bilirubin elevations >2x ULN were observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase safety assessment of rimegepant 75 mg oral tablet for acute migraine. Serum AST or ALT >ULN: 2.0% (11/546) rimegepant vs 3.6% (20/549) placebo; >3x ULN in 0.2% each group; none >5x ULN; total bilirubin >2x ULN in 0.0% both groups. Authors explicitly concluded liver function testing showed no evidence of hepatotoxicity. Most common AE was nausea (0.9% vs 1.1% placebo).

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, amiodarone was suspected as the cause of drug toxicity and the dosage was decreased to 200 mg daily; other causes of hepatitis were investigated and excluded by serology. Liver biopsy showed marked fibrosis, lobular disarray, swollen hepatocytes with foamy cytoplasm, focal hepatocellular necrosis with inflammatory infiltrates, Mallory's bodies, proliferated bile ductules, and portal inflammatory infiltrate, with lysosomal phospholipid inclusions on electron microscopy. After amiodarone was discontinued the patient's condition deteriorated, and he died on day 21 of hospitalization; a postmortem biopsy showed micronodular cirrhosis with amiodarone and metabolite tissue levels of 180 and 1060 µg/g.
raw_record.extra_details: Elderly patient with arrhythmia treated with amiodarone; serum amiodarone and N-desethylamiodarone levels on admission were 3.0 mg/L (normal 1.0-2.5 mg/L) and 2.6 mg/L, respectively (were 2.0 and 1.6 mg/L 2 months after initiation of therapy in November 1986, when hepatic enzymes were normal). Laboratory findings at admission: total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 1.6 mg/dl, AST 223 IU/L, ALT 124 IU/L, GGT 738 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 459 IU/L, prothrombin time 39 sec (control 12.1 sec). Histology: marked fibrosis, lobular disarray, swollen foamy hepatocytes, focal necrosis, Mallory bodies, proliferated bile ductules, portal inflammation, lysosomal phospholipid inclusions in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells and bile duct epithelium; postmortem micronodular cirrhosis. Hepatitis B surface/core antibodies positive with no active disease; hepatitis A IgG positive. Amiodarone discontinued on admission; patient transferred to ICCU, given encainide which was stopped for negative inotropic effects, developed congestive heart failure, and died on day 21. Discussion notes amiodarone commonly causes asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations (15-55% frequency) and rarely clinically apparent hepatic disease (symptomatic hepatotoxicity in 6/2122 patients, 0.28%, treated mean 13 months); symptoms such as hepatomegaly, jaundice, cirrhosis, or chronic hepatitis generally subside on discontinuation, with reversal time 20 days to 17 months. Six deaths have been attributed to amiodarone-induced liver toxicity (patients aged 8-76 years; dosages 400 and 600 mg/day; durations 2 months to 4 years). Case presented at ASHP 45th annual meeting.

Laboratory: bilirubin 11 mg/dL (ref <1 mg/dL), aspartate aminotransferase 5.7 µmol/s/L (ref 0.1-0.60), alanine aminotransferase 14.2 µmol/s/L (ref 0.17-0.60), γ-glutamyltransferase 6.9 µmol/s/L (ref <1.10); autoantibodies and viral hepatitis screens normal. It states that paracetamol metabolism in the liver activates the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone amine (NAPQI), which depletes glutathione and forms cysteine adducts hypothesized to cause hepatocellular toxicity. raw_record.extra_details: Called paracetamol-induced acute liver injury (APAP-ALI). Mechanism: cytochrome P450 activation of NAPQI, glutathione depletion, cysteine adducts, reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial dysfunction. UK legislation (16 Sep 1998) limited pack sizes to 32 tablets in pharmacies and 16/24 in non-pharmacy outlets to curb overdose; liver unit admissions for paracetamol hepatotoxicity reduced 30% in 4 years; overdose-dependent suicides reduced 22% in the first year; large paracetamol overdoses reduced 20% in the second and third years; 11-year follow-up in England and Wales showed >40% reduction in paracetamol-overdose mortality with no reduction in liver transplant rates. Named acute liver injury is the principal reported clinical phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old female with metastatic breast cancer (without liver metastasis) developed a severe drug-induced liver injury (DILI) with critically elevated liver enzyme levels as a reaction to Capecitabine treatment. The patient had a RUCAM score of 7 and a Naranjo score of 6, placing the association between Capecitabine and the liver injury in the 'probable' category. The patient recovered completely and was subsequently treated with other cytotoxic drugs without liver involvement.

raw_record.extra_details: ALT rose to 1,217 U/L, LDH to 376 U/L, bilirubin to 67 μmol/L, and alkaline phosphatase to 302 U/L after the first Capecitabine cycle; clinical picture of manifest acute hepatitis with nausea, increased fatigue, discolored urine/stool, and severe decline in performance status. Liver biopsy was consistent with acute DILI (toxic hepatitis). RUCAM 7 and Naranjo 6 both indicated 'probable'. Viral hepatitis, EBV and CMV tests were negative; immunoglobulins, smooth muscle antibody, and mitochondrial antibody were normal; ultrasound of bile ducts and contrast CT (ruling out hepatic/portal vein thrombosis) were unremarkable; a DPYD gene mutation was ruled out by sequencing. The patient recovered within 2-3 months and subsequently tolerated Eribulin and Paclitaxel without liver toxicity. Literature search found five studies documenting hepatic injury after Capecitabine (including hepatic steatosis and moderately elevated liver enzymes), but none reporting severe DILI with highly elevated enzymes as an immediate response.

raw_record.extra_details: Single-center ICU cohort of 125 consecutive patients with severe acetaminophen-induced ALF (52 men, 41%; mean age 38 +/- 13 years) at the Royal Free Hospital. raw_record.support_text: The paper states that at therapeutic doses most acetaminophen is conjugated to non-toxic metabolites, but in overdose the glucuronidation and sulfation pathways become saturated, increasing CYP450 (primarily CYP2E1) metabolism to NAPQI, a toxic metabolite. This metabolite is responsible for hepatocyte necrosis and, in severe cases, liver failure, with plasma acetaminophen concentration typically correlating with dose-dependent toxicity. The paper refers to 'acetaminophen-induced acute liver injury'. In the studied cohort none of the patients developed hepatic encephalopathy, were scheduled for liver transplantation, or died.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose cohort (103 patients) considered at low risk of hepatotoxicity based on the Rumack–Matthew nomogram; median serum acetaminophen at ED presentation 42 (4.5–64.8) µg/ml. Mean ingested dose 8759.71 mg (NAC-treated) vs 5617.25 mg (no NAC). None developed hepatic encephalopathy, required liver transplantation, or died. Pathogenesis: NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) formed via CYP2E1 after saturation of glucuronidation/sulfation; hepatocyte necrosis and, in severe cases, liver failure; dose-dependent toxicity. Acetylcysteine (NAC) used as treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: Over 11 years the legislation was associated with a 43% reduction in deaths, equivalent to 765 fewer suicide/open-verdict deaths or 990 fewer when accidental poisoning verdicts were included, seen in both level and slope. Deaths involving paracetamol compounds constituted a small proportion of paracetamol-related deaths and showed no major change after the 1998 legislation. raw_record.support_text: A 52-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes developed severe hepatotoxicity after 20 weeks of treatment with troglitazone 400 mg/d, presenting with progressive jaundice, lower-extremity edema, and fatigue. Laboratory values on admission included bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL, ALT 1227 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 216 U/L, and prothrombin time 15.2 s; hepatic serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, and CMV were negative. Liver biopsy showed confluent hepatocellular necrosis with central-portal bridging, portal tract inflammation, and bile duct proliferation. The hospital course was marked by progressive cholestasis with peak bilirubin 46.8 mg/dL, followed by encephalopathy and death; the family declined postmortem examination. The authors report this as a similar case to two prior communications of severe troglitazone-related hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had type 1 diabetes and was receiving lansoprazole, L-thyroxine, and simvastatin as co-medications; no known exposure to hepatitis viruses, other hepatotoxins, or alcohol.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone (Rezulin) is an oral hypoglycemic agent. Dose 400 mg/d for 20 weeks before presentation. Admission labs: bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL, ALT 1227 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 216 U/L, prothrombin time 15.2 s, albumin 2.4 g/dL; ANA titer 1:40. Biopsy: confluent hepatocellular necrosis with central-portal bridging, expanded portal tracts with acute and chronic inflammation and bile duct proliferation. Hospital course showed progressive cholestasis (peak bilirubin 46.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 324 U/L), encephalopathy at week 2, improvement at week 3 then sudden hypotension and death despite antibiotics and vasoactive support.

raw_record.support_text: On October 27th gabapentin-related hepatotoxicity was suspected, and the drug was progressively reduced until it was withdrawn on November 2nd. The dose reduction was associated with a progressive normalization of serum liver enzymes, together with a normal leukocyte count and eosinophil percentage, 11 days later.
raw_record.extra_details: Case classified as a probable gabapentin-induced adverse reaction according to the Karch and Lassagna algorithm (paragraph 16). On October 23rd the patient developed jaundice and palpable hepatomegaly with a marked increase of serum aminotransferases together with GGT and ALP, with a GGT increase of more than six times the upper normal level that began several days before ciprofloxacin and methylprednisolone were initiated and continued after their withdrawal; resolution followed gabapentin dose reduction. Leukocyte count rose to 19.4 x 10^9/L with relative eosinophilia (11.5%); no encephalopathy, and hepatitis A (IgM)/C virus antibody and hepatitis B surface antigen negative. Ciprofloxacin (500 mg p.o. b.i.d.), metamizole, methylprednisolone (80 mg i.v. daily), and dexchlorpheniramine (6 mg p.o. t.i.d.) were considered as potential but non-attributed concomitant drugs. The only other reported case of gabapentin-related hepatotoxicity (paragraph 17) occurred in a patient receiving 1500 mg p.o. every day and showed a marked increase of aminotransferases with normal ALP and GGT and a different temporal evolution.

raw_record.support_text: This paper characterizes tacrine-induced liver injury in humans. Of 636 patients developing elevated transaminases during clinical trials, 5 had jaundice; all had ALT >3x ULN, 3 had significant alkaline phosphatase elevation, and 1 significant bilirubin elevation, and 3 patients recovered on drug discontinuation. A Hammel et al. case reported acute hepatitis in a 76-year-old woman after 20 days of tacrine 75 mg/d (jaundice and fever, markedly elevated bilirubin and ALT), with a liver biopsy showing marked centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis and mild inflammatory infiltration, and LFTs normal five days after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: From NDA clinical-trial data: 636 patients developed elevated transaminases, 5 with jaundice (all ALT >3x ULN, 3 significant alkaline phosphatase elevation, 1 significant bilirubin elevation); 3 recovered on discontinuation. Manufacturer biopsy data for 7 patients with elevated transaminases showed hepatocellular necrosis in 6 and granulomatous hepatitis in 1; an Australian study of 4 patients with asymptomatic liver-enzyme increases found focal necrosis with slight fatty changes (1 with granulomatous hepatitis). Of 56 rechallenged patients in one study, 21.4% discontinued due to recurrence of elevated LFTs, with mean time to ALT elevation of 19 days (faster than initial onset). In the adverse-effects table (NDA trials), elevated transaminases occurred in 23.5% of 2706 tacrine-treated patients vs 1.5% of 342 placebo patients (difference 22.0%).; df: None

Elevated ferritin (17,535 ng/mL); acetaminophen undetectable; viral hepatitis panel negative; autoimmune antibodies negative; normal ceruloplasmin; ammonia 27 μmol/L. Treated with N-acetylcysteine, lactulose, rifaximin. Paper also notes sunitinib disrupts oxidative phosphorylation and ATP depletion, causing hepatotoxicity; elevation of liver enzymes occurs in 39% of patients and grade 3-4 hepatotoxicity in 3%.

raw_record.support_text: In a post-hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial in rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with methotrexate (MTX), hepatotoxicity leading to MTX withdrawal was associated with absence of folate supplementation and high body mass index. Severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 36/137 (26%) of the placebo (no folate) group and 11/274 (4%) of the folate-supplemented group.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was defined as ALT >3x ULN (table footnote). Severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 36/137 (26%) of the placebo group vs 11/274 (4%) of the folate group; with BMI 20-25 hepatotoxicity occurred in 16/190 (8%) and with BMI 30-35 in 10/51 (20%). Univariate OR for folate supplementation 0.12 (0.06-0.24), multivariate OR 0.10 (0.04-0.21); BMI multivariate OR 1.09 (1.01-1.17) per unit. MTX was withdrawn in 126 patients, 91 due to toxicity. Folate supplementation also reduced MTX withdrawal due to toxicity (multivariate OR 0.25, 0.14-0.42). Study population: rheumatoid arthritis patients on MTX therapy.

Acetaminophen is metabolically oxidised by cytochrome 2E1 to NAPQI, which forms covalent adducts with thiols, and acetaminophen-induced liver toxicity is characterised by apoptosis, necrosis, inflammation and oxidative stress.

Latency from the start of oral anticoagulation was 6, 18, and 6 months. The text frames coumarin treatment as a possible etiology of acute liver failure even after prolonged administration without prior problems.

Cholestasis with jaundice clinically predominant; latency 6, 18, and 6 months. The authors note cross-reactions between different coumarin preparations can occur.

raw_record.support_text: A healthy 16-year-old girl developed fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) after intentionally ingesting 54 × 325 mg iron sulfate tablets (70.2 mg/kg elemental iron) in a suicide attempt, also co-ingesting ibuprofen-diphenhydramine and omeprazole; acetaminophen was undetectable. Despite prompt IV deferoxamine, she developed coagulopathy, acidosis, and rising transaminases consistent with FHF within 24 hours, with peaks of INR >13, ALT 12,466 IU/L, AST 11,400 IU/L, and total bilirubin 6.0 mg/dL. On day 4 she reached grade 4 hepatic encephalopathy and received an emergent deceased donor liver transplant. Explant pathology showed massive acute panlobular hepatic necrosis with focal residual hepatocytes showing intracanalicular cholestasis, diffuse centrilobular congestion and hemorrhage, and a negative iron stain. The authors describe this as iron-induced FHF successfully treated with liver transplantation.

Onset of FHF within 24 h post-ingestion; peak labs on day 3: INR >13, ALT 12,466 IU/L, AST 11,400 IU/L, total bilirubin 6.0 mg/dL (103 µmol/L); creatinine normal. Progressed to grade 4 hepatic encephalopathy on day 4; treated with IV deferoxamine and emergent deceased donor liver transplant; discharged to psychiatric service day 16. Explant: massive acute panlobular hepatic necrosis with focal residual hepatocytes showing intracanalicular cholestasis, diffuse centrilobular (zone 3) congestion and hemorrhage, mild-moderate portal lymphocytic infiltrate, no lobular inflammation, negative iron stain. Author notes iron is generally considered a peri-portal (zone 1) toxin and the observed zone 3 pathology and negative iron stain (possibly due to chelation or hepatocyte necrosis/apoptosis) are unusual.

raw_record.support_text: The study states that paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose remains the main aetiological factor responsible for acute liver failure (ALF) in the developed world, and that the only effective treatment for the condition is emergency orthotopic liver transplantation. It further notes that paracetamol-induced ALF is strongly associated with development of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) and a cascade of complications including hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol-induced ALF associated with SIRS, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and multiple organ dysfunction; coexisting prognostic concerns about King's College Criteria. Cohort of 138 consecutive single-time-point intentional paracetamol overdoses (>4 g) admitted to the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit with acute liver injury (2003-2010); overdose defined by history of toxic intake (>4 g/day), serum paracetamol >10 mg/L, and/or serum ALT >1000 IU/L within 7 days. Death and orthotopic liver transplantation considered equivalent outcomes.

raw_record.support_text: The prognostic accuracy of SIRS and SOFA thresholds was examined in a prospectively collected cohort of 38 paracetamol-induced acute liver injury patients admitted to the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh. Seven patients died or underwent emergency OLT; all manifested a SIRS response, had a SOFA score >7 and a modified SOFA >5 within 96 h of overdose. Four patients were transplanted, three died without transplantation, and 18 (47.4%) were ever encephalopathic (acute liver failure), confirming that paracetamol overdose causes acute liver injury/acute liver failure with death and liver transplantation as outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: Single time point paracetamol overdose setting. All seven non-survivors (death or OLT) had SIRS, SOFA >7 and modified SOFA >5 by 96 h post-overdose.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician treated with ketoconazole (single oral daily dose of 200 mg) for fingernail onychomycosis, with no history of liver disease and no other medications, developed sudden fatigue and nausea after 81 days of therapy, followed by markedly elevated ALT that accelerated after a single 200 mg ketoconazole dose on day 86, accompanied by icterus and markedly elevated serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase. Viral hepatitis A and B were excluded, and abnormal findings subsided to normal within 2 months. The accompanying discussion notes that hepatic damage associated with ketoconazole therapy has been reported in only a few cases and is probably an idiosyncratic reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Single oral daily dose of 200 mg for 81 days for fingernail onychomycosis (following griseofulvin unresponsiveness). ALT rose to 1030-1900 U/L (baseline 13), total bilirubin up to 111 umol/L, alkaline phosphatase up to 480 U/L, lactic dehydrogenase up to 800 U/L; icterus and malaise at day 86. Viral hepatitis A and B excluded by serology; ultrasound and CT of liver/pancreas showed no abnormalities; liver biopsy refused; laboratory values returned to normal within 2 months. Re-exposure with a single 200 mg dose accelerated the rise (associated with day 86 tests). A prior communication from the same institution described biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis in a ketoconazole-treated patient, and a manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reported the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy. Incidence estimated between 0.1% and 1%, with many subclinical cases; about 300,000 prescriptions in the US since 1981 licensure. Author recommendation to do liver function tests before and monthly during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Patients (n=7,658) receiving troglitazone provided 4,020 person-years; 5 were hospitalized with acute liver injury, an incidence of 1,244 per million person-years (95% CI 404–2,900), far greater than the expected 10–22/million. Case reports documented idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity after ≥1 month of treatment, and one patient developed acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after only 4 doses with biopsy showing patchy cholestatic hepatitis, recovering after palliative treatment. Because of the high incidence of liver injury, troglitazone was withdrawn from the market.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 7,658 patients (4,020 person-years); 5 hospitalized with acute liver injury; incidence 1,244 per million person-years (95% CI 404–2,900) vs expected 10–22/million. Withdrawn from market. Proposed mechanisms: reactive intermediates, apoptosis (potentially irreversible in acute liver failure), oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, bile salt transporter inhibition, fibrosis. Injury described as idiosyncratic and not dose-related at clinically meaningful doses; low PPARγ affinity necessitates higher doses.

Forced diuresis and hemodialysis were ineffective at preventing hepatic necrosis; mepyramine/promethazine increased paracetamol toxicity in animals and were stated to have no protective effect in man (these are not themselves attributed as human DILI causes). raw_record.support_text: Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Hepatotoxicity caused by sertraline is rare, with asymptomatic ALT/AST elevations reported in approximately 0.8% of patients, generally within the first 9 weeks of therapy, which normalize shortly after discontinuation. The paper presents a case of severe drug-induced hepatitis in a patient receiving sertraline, reported as the seventh case in the medical literature associated with severe hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: A 17-year-old man had taken sertraline 25 mg/day for 6 months for depression when he developed symptomatic hepatitis with nausea, fatigue, scleral jaundice, and dark urine. Peak labs: ALT 1,880 U/l, AST 810 U/l, ALP 483 U/l, GGT 124 U/l, total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dl. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic work-up and abdominal ultrasound were negative; liver biopsy was refused. Sertraline was discontinued and transaminases declined to normal within 6 months with no relapse. Naranjo algorithm total score was 7 (Probable). Reported as the seventh case of severe sertraline-associated hepatotoxicity in the literature. Asymptomatic ALT/AST elevations occur in ~0.8% of sertraline-treated patients, usually within the first 9 weeks of therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In the setting of iron poisoning, 4 fatal case reports from the 1970s were described as iron overdose-induced hepatic failure, with periportal necrosis found at autopsy (e.g., a 17-year-old pregnant female who died with a documented serum iron of 1700 µg/dL). Gleason et al. also documented a periportal predominance of the hepatic necrosis. Additional cases across the review recorded hepatotoxicity (pathologic and/or laboratory evidence) after iron overdose, with multiple fatalities, and a 7-year-old survivor who required emergency orthotopic liver transplantation for massive hepatic necrosis after ingesting ferrous sulfate tabs.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Iron poisoning overdose, predominantly pediatric patients (ages ~1–17 years); injury is characterized in the iron overdose setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Four fatal case reports from the 1970s in iron poisoning; documented serum iron concentrations ranged 1700–21,680 µg/dL (304–3883 µmol/L) across 6 cases; histology predominantly periportal necrosis (periportal). One 17-year-old had fatal hepatic failure; a 3.5-year-old survivor (serum iron 21,680 µg/dL 4 h after ferrous sulfate ingestion) developed stage III–IV hepatic coma and underwent emergency orthotopic liver transplantation on day 5, with massive hepatic necrosis on native-liver pathology and residual iron in mitochondria. Pestaner series of 11 children (11–36 months) who died of iron poisoning: 5 had liver involvement concentrated in the periportal region.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report 81 patients (50 retrospective and 31 prospective; median age 34 years) who met criteria for efavirenz DILI. Among those biopsied (n=73), three histological injury patterns were observed: a nonspecific hepatitis associated with grade 1–2 transaminase elevation (n=17), a mixed cholestatic-hepatitis with grades 2–3 elevation of ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase and mild/moderate jaundice (n=20), and submassive necrosis with grade 4 ALT/AST elevation, severe jaundice and coagulopathy (n=36). Skin involvement was not observed, in contrast to nevirapine DILI. No patients fulfilled clinical criteria for tuberculous immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were HIV-infected adults receiving efavirenz-based antiretroviral therapy; in the prospective group 58% (n=18) were pregnant at ART initiation; 86% were Black, 73% female; 27% used or were currently using cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.
raw_record.extra_details: 81 patients total (50 retrospective, 31 prospective); median age 34 years; median CD4+ nadir 348 cells/µl (IQR 173–522); median duration on ART 20 weeks (IQR 12–24) at DILI onset. Liver-related mortality was 11% (n=9): 6% (n=3) retrospective and 19% (n=6) prospective; most deaths occurred within 1 week of presentation. Submassive necrosis was associated with an 'immuno-allergic' inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, conspicuous eosinophils), higher transaminases (ALT 679 vs 101 vs 114 U/l, P<0.0001) and bilirubin (232 vs 86 vs 8 µmol/l, P=0.003) compared with mixed cholestatic-hepatitis and nonspecific hepatitis patterns, and higher INR (1.68 vs 1.18, P=0.0002). In multivariate analysis, submassive necrosis was independently associated with CD4+ >350 cells/µl (OR 9.4, 95% CI 2.5–35.8) and female gender (OR 9.0, 95% CI 1.4–59.8); age >30 years was protective. Median hospital stay 28 days (IQR 11–60); slow median biochemical resolution >6 months. Submassive necrosis patients were treated with low-dose prednisone (0.25 mg/kg/day); protease inhibitor-based ART successfully introduced after resolution.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case series of 81 patients with efavirenz DILI in a high HIV-prevalence setting with a massive increase of efavirenz-based first-line antiretroviral therapy. Three patterns of injury were observed, the most severe being submassive necrosis. A high baseline CD4+ count seemingly predicted risk for submassive necrosis, with female sex and younger age as additional factors, and the associated morbidity and mortality were noted as a serious concern. Clinicians were advised to manage suspected efavirenz DILI with rapid cessation of efavirenz.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 81 patients with efavirenz DILI in a high HIV-prevalence setting with massive expansion of efavirenz-based first-line ART in a developing-world program. raw_record.support_text: The patient discontinued amiodarone, which was considered the most probable cause of acute hepatitis. The modified RUCAM score was 9 points, indicating that amiodarone was a highly probable cause of acute liver injury in this case. Liver tests improved by more than 50% within a week of withdrawal; a final diagnosis of DILI caused by amiodarone was made.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication was atrial fibrillation (Holter monitoring confirmed sinus conversion); amiodarone ceased on cardiology consultation and no other antiarrhythmic started. Initial liver biopsy (H&E) showed severe lobular, portal and periportal inflammation with hepatocyte necrosis, marked centrilobular necrosis, ballooned hepatocytes, Mallory bodies, and a red granule; electron microscopy showed phospholipid-laden lysosomal lamellar bodies and fatty deposition. One week after cessation liver tests decreased >50%: AST 92 U/L, ALT 120 U/L, total bilirubin 5.51 mg/dL; bilirubin, AST, ALT, ALP, and γ-GTP normalized by 3 months, and follow-up biopsy 5 months later confirmed recovery without fibrosis. Reduced RUCAM score 9. General review note: amiodarone DILI is most commonly a sole aminotransferase elevation without liver dysfunction, but rare severe liver injury, fulminant hepatitis, or progression to cirrhosis with decompensated hepatic failure can occur; large apparent volume of distribution slows total body-store decline after discontinuation.
