raw_record.support_text: A 27 year old white woman with chronic renal disease and HLA-B8 antigen who received nitrofurantoin from 1967 to December 1973 was found to have chronic hepatitis by biopsy in 1974. Recurrent elevations in transaminase levels and clinical illness were temporally related to two rechallenges with nitrofurantoin therapy in September 1974 and January 1976. After the second, experimentally controlled rechallenge (three 50 mg oral doses on the first day), the patient developed a shaking chill, myalgias, arthralgias, fever (102°F) and hepatic punch tenderness, with serum transaminase rising over the next 12 days; biopsy showed chronic active hepatitis and cirrhosis. The authors stated that nitrofurantoin hepatotoxicity was hypothesized and confirmed by the rechallenge, with the patient improving and later having normal liver tests in 1978.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Case in a 27-year-old woman with pre-existing chronic renal disease and HLA-B8 antigen; liver disease (chronic active hepatitis/cirrhosis) documented before the final controlled rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Therapy given for chronic urinary tract indications; nitrofurantoin switched to sulfisoxazole in December 1973 with lowering of transaminases. Rechallenge in September 1974 and an experimental rechallenge in January 1976 (three 50 mg oral doses) reproduced clinical illness (fatigue, anorexia, upper abdominal discomfort, shaking chill, fever to 102°F, myalgias, arthralgias, muscle/joint tenderness, moderate hepatic punch tenderness) and biochemical relapse with serum transaminase rising over 12 days and falling over two months without steroids. Biopsies (Figures 2-5) showed cirrhosis and inactive-stage chronic active hepatitis; antismooth muscle antibody titer 1:160; albumin, alkaline phosphatase, conjugated bilirubin, complement, eosinophils, hemoglobin, white cell count, and prothrombin time unchanged. Patient was treated with prednisone (initially 60 mg daily, tapered by September 1975) and recovered, with normal liver tests in 1978.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective analysis of 180 patients with possible adverse hepatic reactions to diclofenac reported to the FDA found predominantly hepatocellular or mixed hepatocellular biochemical injury (66% of cases), with only 8% cholestatic; 75% of symptomatic patients were jaundiced and 7 of 90 icteric patients died. Injury appeared by 1-6 months in most patients, and the absence of rash, fever, or eosinophilia combined with long latency led to the inference that the mechanism is probably metabolic idiosyncrasy. The authors concluded diclofenac-related liver injury is particularly likely to involve osteoarthritic females presenting with jaundice and predominantly hepatocellular injury caused by presumed metabolic idiosyncrasy.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective FDA spontaneous-report case series, Nov 1988-Jun 1991 (434 initial reports, 180 retained after excluding duplicates, foreign sources, other causes, and inadequate data). Patients: 79% female, 71% aged >=60 years, 77% had osteoarthritis (139 OA, 22 RA, 1 ankylosing spondylitis, 1 psoriatic arthritis, 15 miscellaneous, 2 unknown). 67% of cases detected by symptoms and remainder by abnormal labs; 75% of symptomatic patients (90/120) were jaundiced; 7 of 90 icteric patients died. Biochemical pattern: hepatocellular or mixed in 66%, cholestatic in 8%, remainder 'indeterminate'. Hepatocellular defined as ALT peak >=8x ULN with ALP <3x ULN; cholestatic as ALP >=3x ULN with transaminases <8x ULN; mixed as both elevated. 21 liver sections available. Latency: injury apparent by 1 month in 24%, by 3 months in 63%, by 6 months in 85%; 12% at 6-12 months, 3% >12 months. No case had rash, fever, and eosinophilia combined (hypersensitivity); mechanism presumed metabolic idiosyncrasy. Diclofenac approved in US 1988 for OA/RA/ankylosing spondylitis; available in Europe since 1974. Approximately 60 prior literature cases of diclofenac-associated hepatic injury, mostly acute hepatocellular, several chronic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Attribution to diclofenac of the etiologic role in the hepatic injury of the 180 cases among the 434 cases reported to the FDA was based on excluding cases with other recognized possible etiology; hepatitis A and B were excluded by serological tests in 96 patients and hepatitis C tests were negative in 34 patients. The paper's DISCUSSION also states that the hepatic injury induced by diclofenac, reflected by biochemical values, is mainly hepatocellular, and that the mechanism of injury appears to be idiosyncrasy rather than intrinsic toxicity, with an 8% case fatality rate for icteric cases and 7 fatal cases, all jaundiced.

The injury was mainly hepatocellular biochemically and on histology (21 cases with material): acute hepatocellular injury (9), spotty (2), zonal (6), granulomas (1), chronic hepatitis (5), cirrhosis (1), hepatocellular-cholestatic (1), cholestatic (2), nonspecific/trivial (3). Cholestatic injury was found in 8% of patients (hepatocanalicular cholestasis in 4, canalicular in 7). Median therapy duration 24 days (range 4-69). 7 fatal cases, all jaundiced (6 female, 6 older than 60, all with osteoarthritis); peak transaminases usually >1,000 IU/L; bilirubin 13-25 mg/dL; 8% case fatality among icteric cases. Mechanism inferred as metabolic rather than immunologic idiosyncrasy; delayed response to rechallenge in all but one of 19 patients; rare hypersensitivity hallmarks, though Shapiro et al reported hypersensitivity in a few cases.

raw_record.support_text: During the preclinical testing phase of troglitazone efficacy, approximately 1.9% of patients receiving troglitazone developed severe hepatic problems with elevated serum transaminase activities. In the severe cases, troglitazone caused fulminant hepatic failures, leading to multiple human deaths. Due to the severity of troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity and the availability of structural derivatives such as rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, troglitazone was removed from the market in 2000.
raw_record.extra_details: Approximately 1.9% of patients developed severe hepatic problems with elevated serum transaminase activities; fulminant hepatic failures leading to multiple human deaths; removed from the market in 2000. Proposed mechanisms include electrophilic reactive intermediates, direct PPARγ binding, mitochondrial injury, and BSEP inhibition by troglitazone (paragraphs 0 and 4); a chromane-containing glitazone predicted as an apoptotic agonist activating p53 via the intrinsic pathway, confirmed by immunoblot.

raw_record.support_text: Between January 1968 and December 1983, 48 patients were referred to King's College Hospital with fulminant hepatic failure following halothane anaesthesia (31 female, ratio 1.8:1, age range 21-76 years, median 57). The interval between halothane exposure (anaesthetic) and onset of jaundice ranged from 2 to 26 days (median 5 days), and the median interval to onset of encephalopathy was 9 days. The paper attributes this fulminant hepatic failure causally to halothane anaesthesia.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis/fulminant hepatic failure after halothane anaesthesia. In the 1968-1983 series of 48 patients: 94% had at least one documented prior halothane exposure; 33 (69%) underwent only minor surgery (lasting <45 min) with no other operative cause for liver failure; 38 died including all with grade III/IV fulminant hepatic failure; 10 survived (5 with grade I/II hepatic encephalopathy, remainder non-encephalopathic); interval from anaesthetic to death 11-73 days (median 23). A serum antibody to a hepatocyte plasma membrane antigen associated with halothane metabolism is present only in patients with clinical halothane hepatitis, detectable in about 75% of cases; absent in halothane-exposed patients with no/minor liver-function abnormality or with liver failure from other causes (e.g., hepatitis A). In a 1983-1985 series of 40 tested sera (9 King's patients, 31 referred): 21 met fulminant hepatic failure definition (hepatic encephalopathy); age range 1-75 (median 59); ALT 127-4000 IU/l (normal <40); 65% had minor surgery; non-encephalopathic patients survived while 12 of 17 encephalopathic (71%, including all grade III/IV) died.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (N-acetyl-p-aminophenol; paracetamol) is the most commonly used drug for pain and fever. Although safe at therapeutic doses, in overdose acetaminophen produces severe hepatotoxicity, attributed to metabolism to the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) by cytochrome P450, glutathione depletion, and covalent binding of the metabolite to proteins as 3-(cystein-S-yl)-acetaminophen.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; toxicity occurs via reactive metabolite NAPQI with glutathione depletion; no pre-existing liver disease or co-exposure restriction stated.
raw_record.extra_details: HPLC-ECD assay for the protein-bound acetaminophen-cysteine conjugate (APAP-CYS, 3-(cystein-S-yl)-acetaminophen) with lower limit of detection approximately 3 pmol/mg protein. Acetaminophen protein adducts detected in liver and serum as early as 15 min after hepatotoxic dosing in mice, and detected in serum of acetaminophen overdose patients. In human serum, acetaminophen-cysteine conjugate concentration correlated positively with serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) activity and time; adducts were detected even with relatively mild liver injury as judged by AST/ALT. Reactive metabolite formed by cytochrome P450; detoxified by glutathione at therapeutic doses but depletes glutathione after overdose and covalently binds proteins. Assay proposed for diagnostic evaluation of hepatotoxicity of indeterminate etiology where acetaminophen toxicity is suspected.

raw_record.support_text: In 100 patients who had taken an acute overdose of paracetamol, percutaneous liver biopsies were obtained on day 4 or when clotting recovery allowed, and a histological grading system was described. The hallmark of severe (grade III) damage is centrilobular necrosis, for which there is probably a dosage threshold; mild (grade I) and moderate (grade II) damage show less pronounced changes. Five patients died in acute hepatic failure, and 22/100 showed severe grade III changes but survived. Forty-nine patients covering all three grades were rebiopsied after 3 months; central necrotic zones were completely reconstituted except for one patient with mild nonprogressive centrilobular fibrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose exposure; some patients had also taken alcohol with the overdose, whereas known chronic alcoholics and those taking other hepatotoxic drugs were excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (4-hydroxyacetanilide, N-acetyl-p-aminophenol, acetaminophen) overdose dose range 5-50 g; 100 patients, ages 13-65 years, 79/100 female. Grade III hallmark is centrilobular necrosis with a probable dosage threshold; mild (grade I) damage shows excess centrilobular lipofuscin pigment, sparse focal necrosis and lipofuscin phagocytosis. Five patients died in acute hepatic failure; 22/100 had grade III changes and survived. Follow-up rebiopsy of 49 patients after 3 months showed complete reconstitution of necrotic zones except one case of mild nonprogressive centrilobular fibrosis and scarring. First marketed as nontoxic in therapeutic doses but a single large overdose causes fulminant liver necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Anamnestically, the only drug or toxin exposure within the last 3 weeks before admission was propofol during colonoscopy, and the authors state it is most likely that propofol was responsible for the acute hepatitis. A liver biopsy showed changes compatible with acute toxic hepatitis, and the authors add that propofol caused hepatocellular damage with signs of an immunoallergic mechanism (eosinophilic infiltrations), as also reported in other published cases [1–6].
raw_record.extra_details: Single therapeutic exposure of propofol given during colonoscopy within 3 weeks before admission. Patient hospitalized with acute hepatitis; serum ferritin 2,420 ng/ml; ultrasound showed hepatomegaly (17.5 cm MAL) with liver stiffness 18.0 kPa and normal CAP 185 dB/m. Biopsy: oedematous portal tracts with mild mixed inflammatory infiltrate, numerous macrophages and eosinophils, no interface hepatitis or significant biliary damage, bridging necrosis of acinar parenchyma with marked bilirubin phagocytosis and initial post-collapse fibrosis, compatible with acute toxic hepatitis. Viral hepatitis A–E, EBV and CMV negative; no auto-antibodies; late-onset Wilson disease excluded. Mechanism described as immunoallergic (eosinophilic infiltration); similar propofol hepatotoxicity cases reported in refs [1–6]. Authors note propofol is generally considered less liver-toxic and usable in cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of acute liver failure patients, the paper reports outcomes following acetaminophen poisoning/overdose, including patients who died without reaching the King's College poor prognostic criteria after acetaminophen over-dose, describing acetaminophen-induced ALF as the liver-injury cause. This establishes acetaminophen (paracetamol) as a human cause of drug-induced acute liver failure in the overdose setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of acute liver failure patients comparing acetaminophen vs non-acetaminophen etiologies at a transplant center. Acetaminophen group mortality without reaching King's College poor prognostic criteria (KCHPPC): 33/161 (20.5%); non-acetaminophen 17/52 (32.7%; P=0.055). In acetaminophen-poisoned patients who died without reaching KCHPPC, admission creatinine and lactate were higher, while serum ALT, albumin, and bicarbonate were lower than in survivors. ALF-related complications on the emergency LT list were common in acetaminophen-induced ALF: cerebral edema (43/66, 65.2%), inotropic support (45/66, 68.2%), renal dialysis (56/66, 84.8%), and hypoglycemia (44/66, 66.7%). Many acetaminophen patients were excluded from LT for psychiatric reasons (most commonly active and resistant alcohol dependence). KCHPPC performance (all patients): sensitivity 82.8%, specificity 95.5%, PPV 96.4%, NPV 79.5%, LR+ 18.5, LR- 0.18. Spontaneous survival with predicted poor prognosis: acetaminophen 6/99 (6.1%).

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' single-center series of acute liver failure (ALF), 104 patients underwent liver transplantation, with similar 30-day posttransplant survival in the acetaminophen cohort (69%) and the non-acetaminophen cohort (78%). Mortality on the transplant waiting list was double in the acetaminophen cohort (31.8%) versus the non-acetaminophen cohort (15.7%), and patients with acetaminophen-induced ALF listed for emergency transplantation had an increased incidence of organ failure with cerebral edema, inotropic support, and renal dialysis.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose/poisoning causes acute liver failure (acetaminophen-induced ALF), including cases requiring emergency listing for liver transplantation. King's College poor prognostic criteria were used for transplant decisions; lactate was introduced into listing criteria. 327 in-hospital deaths were attributed to acetaminophen overdose in Scotland over 1995-2003 (27-53 deaths/year); ~600 adult (ages 20-69) admissions per quarter followed acetaminophen overdose. In the current cohort (2002-2005), 4 of 81 acetaminophen ALF patients received liver transplant vs 13 of 99 in 1993-1996; transplant waiting-list mortality for the acetaminophen cohort was 31.8%. raw_record.support_text: In adults, acetaminophen poisoning after overdose (about 15 g in normal adults, or about 10 g with chronic alcohol or enzyme-inducing drug ingestion) often resulted in hepatotoxicity. Of 60 overdose cases seen in a liver-disease treatment unit, 49 progressed to liver damage; a 20% mortality rate was observed and attributed to fulminant hepatic failure, and a 2% fatal rate in another series was attributed to acute hepatic failure with severe coagulation disturbances. The pattern was described as acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis with centrilobular reticulum collapse and congestion, with cirrhosis occurring rarely.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; toxic dose lowered to about 10 g by chronic alcohol use or enzyme-inducing co-medication.
raw_record.extra_details: Estimated toxic doses: about 15 g in adults with normal liver function, reduced to about 10 g with chronic alcohol or enzyme-inducing drugs (figures are clinical estimates partly extrapolated from animal data). Of 60 overdose cases in a liver-disease treatment unit, 49 progressed to liver damage; 20% mortality attributed to fulminant hepatic failure; 2% fatal in another series attributed to acute hepatic failure with severe coagulation disturbances. Symptoms gradual: pallor, nausea, vomiting in first 12-24 h; clinical hepatotoxicity evident 4-6 days after ingestion; sharp initial rise in serum AST (SGOT) and ALT (SGPT) returning to normal within 1-2 weeks; mild acidosis, jaundice, prolonged prothrombin time; severe coagulation disorders including disseminated intravascular coagulation in acute hepatic necrosis; centrilobular reticulum collapse and congestion on liver tissue; cirrhosis rarely occurs. Mechanism: a toxic acetaminophen metabolite is probably responsible for centrilobular liver necrosis after overdose; phenobarbital pretreatment enhanced production and potentiated necrosis in rats and mice, while metabolic enzyme inhibitors (piperonyl butoxide, cobaltous chloride) protected in animals (animal data only).

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate is attributed as a cause of hepatic injury in treated patients. The main histological anomalies reported with methotrexate are macrovesicular steatosis, inflammatory infiltration of the portal spaces, hepatocellular necrosis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, with fibrosis and cirrhosis usually observed after a cumulative dose of >= 1.5 g. Aithal et al. obtained 121 liver biopsies from 66 patients treated with methotrexate for psoriasis and none revealed cirrhosis after a median of 280 weeks of treatment and a median cumulative dose of 3206 g; the estimated cumulative probability of advanced fibrosis (Ishak score >= 4) was 0%, 2.6%, 2.6%, 8.2%, and 8.2% for 1500, 3000, 4500, 5000, and 6000 mg.

raw_record.extra_details: In psoriasis, main histology: macrovesicular steatosis, portal inflammatory infiltration, hepatocellular necrosis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis; prevalence of cirrhosis during psoriasis varies 0-26% in older studies that did not account for viral hepatitis, alcohol, or metabolic syndrome risk factors. Aithal et al: 121 biopsies from 66 patients, no cirrhosis after median 280 weeks and median cumulative dose 3206 g; estimated cumulative probability of advanced fibrosis (Ishak score >= 4) 0%, 2.6%, 2.6%, 8.2%, 8.2% at 1500/3000/4500/5000/6000 mg; 2 of 24 patients with pre-methotrexate biopsy had advanced fibrosis. In IBD: transaminase elevation in 18/306 patients (6%) across nine therapeutic trials; Lemann et al reported persistently anomalous liver tests in 3 of 49 patients treated >6 months for Crohn disease; 11 liver biopsies showed no cirrhosis and at most moderate periportal fibrosis in one case. Surveillance: liver battery weekly during first month then every three months; persistent enzyme elevation correlated with histology; non-invasive fibrosis tests (Fibrotest, Fibroscan) not validated in IBD.

The authors report 220 patients admitted after a paracetamol overdose, of whom 200 showed evidence of liver damage and 29 died from fulminant hepatic failure, with the first case of acute hepatic necrosis related to the drug reported in 1966. raw_record.extra_details: 220 patients admitted to the Liver Unit, King's College Hospital up to 1 Jan. 1974 after paracetamol overdose; 200 showed evidence of liver damage and 29 died from fulminant hepatic failure. In the 104 biopsied patients (65 females, 39 males, aged 15-58 yr), liver function became abnormal in all, 38 developed fulminant hepatic failure with grade 3 or 4 encephalopathy and 27 died. Histological grades: grade 0 (swelling, minor vacuolation/inflammation, no necrosis), grade I (confluent necrosis of centrilobular hepatocytes), grade II (confluent necrosis continuous between adjacent lobules), grade III (massive necrosis leaving a rim of liver cells around portal tracts). Dose-related injury with characteristic delay in appearance of liver damage; plasma paracetamol levels and coagulation disturbance studied.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the pathogenesis of paracetamol-induced liver injury in humans following overdose, attributing hepatic necrosis to covalent binding of a reactive intermediate metabolite to liver cell macromolecules, with toxicity once glutathione stores fall below ~30% of normal. Biopsies from overdosed patients showed centrilobular hepatic necrosis and vacuolation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; patients developing fulminant hepatic failure
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: covalent binding of a reactive intermediate metabolite to vital liver cell macromolecules, inactivated by glutathione conjugation, with toxicity occurring when hepatic glutathione falls below ~30% of normal, based on animal work by Mitchell et al. (1973). Lesions predominantly centrilobular, consistent with the location of microsomal metabolizing enzymes and poorer oxygen supply. Biopsies showed confluent eosinophilic necrosis (grade III), grade I and grade II (interlobular bridging) necrosis, vacuolation adjacent to central veins, and inflammatory infiltrate with pigment-laden macrophages. Hepatocyte volume fraction (HVF) <40% in early biopsies was found only in patients who died; three patients survived with HVF <40%, while deaths of three patients with HVF >40% were attributed to poor function of counted parenchymal cells. Paracetamol plasma half-life used as a guide to subsequent liver damage (Prescott et al., 1971).

raw_record.extra_details: 104 patients with paracetamol overdose were biopsied; 38 developed fulminant hepatic failure. Histology showed confluent centrilobular necrosis with a usually mild inflammatory reaction. Survival for two patients correlated with prothrombin time prolongation and peak plasma bilirubin in the first 10 days.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), an antiviral nucleoside analogue with activity against hepatitis B virus, was given in a phase II trial of 15 patients with chronic hepatitis B at 0.10 or 0.25 mg/kg/day for 24 weeks. The trial was halted after 9-13 weeks because of sudden, unexpected severe multisystem toxicity (hepatic failure, lactic acidosis, and pancreatitis) resulting in the deaths of five patients. Following cumulative doses of 551-1753 mg, the severe hepatotoxicity was characterized by hepatomegaly with diffuse, predominantly microvesicular steatosis, hepatocellular glycogen depletion, marked bile ductular proliferation, and cholestasis, with intracytoplasmic lipid droplets and marked mitochondrial injury on ultrastructural examination; this severe human toxicity was not predicted by preclinical animal studies.

raw_record.extra_details: Antiviral nucleoside analogue (fluoroiodoarabinofuranosyluracil, FIAU) active against hepatitis B virus. Multisystem toxicity included hepatic failure, lactic acidosis, and pancreatitis, with deaths of 5 of 15 patients. Cumulative doses 551-1753 mg. Histology: hepatomegaly, diffuse predominantly microvesicular steatosis, hepatocellular glycogen depletion, bile ductular proliferation, cholestasis; ultrastructural intracytoplasmic lipid droplets and marked mitochondrial injury. Possible mechanisms: mitochondrial injury, pyruvate oxidation inhibition; hENT1 expressed/functional in mitochondrial membrane enhances mitochondrial toxicity of FIAU, explaining missed toxicity in mouse models.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that evidence that their two patients had fluoxetine-induced acute hepatitis is convincing. No other cause was identified from history, physical examination, or laboratory tests; viral, autoimmune, metabolic, and obstructive liver disease were excluded. After fluoxetine was discontinued, both patients had prompt symptomatic improvement and steady normalization of liver biochemistry test results. Liver biopsy and fluoxetine rechallenge were not performed because symptoms diminished and liver tests normalized after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients (case series). Case 2: 45-year-old woman, fluoxetine 40 mg/d for 3 months, also on levothyroxine sodium 0.122 mg/d, no acetaminophen/alcohol use; presented with 3-day RUQ pain, nausea, anorexia, weight loss, jaundice. Labs: total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.5 mg/dL, AST 168 U/L, ALT 641 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L, GGT 92 U/L; normal prothrombin time and TSH. Jaundice present, no cirrhosis/ascites. Tests excluded viral (hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV), autoimmune, metabolic, cholelithiasis, and obstructive causes. After fluoxetine discontinuation, patient 1 normalized in ~6 months, patient 2 near-normal in ~2.5 months. Liver biopsy and fluoxetine rechallenge were not performed.

raw_record.support_text: In pediatric patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) or malignant lymphoma (ML) treated with chemotherapy including methotrexate (MTX, 3 g m⁻² intravenous), treatment is often limited by severe toxicity, including hepatotoxicity and myeloid suppression. The study investigated genetic polymorphisms to predict the hepatotoxicity of methotrexate, and elsewhere in the paper a greater risk of methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity is attributed to carrying GSTM1, with RFC1 G80A genotype associated with hepatotoxicity in GSTM1-positive patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with ALL or ML receiving MTX-containing chemotherapy; hepatotoxicity grades 0-3 assessed.
raw_record.extra_details: MTX given intravenously at 3 g m⁻²; cohort of 35 patients. Hepatotoxicity associated with RFC1 G80A genotype in GSTM1-positive patients (P<0.05, Fisher's extended exact test: GG/GA 8 vs 2; AA 0 vs 3). Serum MTX concentration >1 µmol/L at 48 h significantly associated with MTHFR C677T TT genotype (P<0.05), used to guide additional leucovorin rescue. No significant association of hepatotoxicity with single-gene genotypes of GSTM1, GSTT1, GSTP1, RFC1, MTHFR, or BCRP overall.

raw_record.support_text: In a U.S. series of 295 patients with acute liver failure, acetaminophen was the most common single etiology, accounting for 60 cases (20%), with a 60% spontaneous survival rate (excluding death or transplantation). The paper frames acetaminophen as a cause of fulminant hepatic failure, and elsewhere notes that if acetaminophen overdose is suspected, levels should be obtained and intravenous N-acetylcysteine given.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure setting (acetaminophen toxicity leading to fulminant/acute liver failure).
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen was the leading single cause of acute liver failure in this 295-patient U.S. cohort (60/295, 20%), with 60% spontaneous survival excluding death or transplantation. Patients present with massive aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase elevations, elevated bilirubin, significant prothrombin time elevation, and sometimes metabolic acidosis. Management includes IV N-acetylcysteine; liver transplantation criteria for acetaminophen toxicity (King's College Criteria) include pH <7.30 (after hydration) or INR >6.5 and creatinine >3 mg/dL with encephalopathy grade III-IV.

raw_record.support_text: A 39-year-old man was diagnosed with allopurinol-induced hepatic injury. He developed severe cholestatic liver failure without hepatic encephalopathy, and because medical treatment was transiently effective and his renal function and coagulation deteriorated, a living-donor liver transplantation (LDLT) with a right lobe graft was performed four months after onset. The explanted liver was severely enlarged (2,480 g) and cholestatic, and microscopically compatible with drug-induced cholestatic liver injury. He was discharged 55 days after LDLT, with persistent renal dysfunction at 6 months. The authors note allopurinol hepatotoxicity is rare but can be severe and even fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 39-year-old man with hyperuricemia who started allopurinol 2 months before onset of jaundice; after detailed examination no cause of liver dysfunction other than allopurinol-induced hepatic injury was found (nondrinker, no hepatitis virus infection, no blood transfusion). Serum TB reached >40 mg/dL; MELD score 31 at transfer (AST 382 IU/L, ALT 238 IU/L, TB 60.9 mg/dL, creatinine 1.74 mg/dL). Histology showed severe cholestasis around the central vein, hepatic cord atrophy, sinusoidal/pericentral venous fibrosis, atypical bile ductule proliferation, and lymphocyte infiltration, compatible with drug-induced cholestatic liver injury. Bilirubin adsorption and corticosteroid therapy were ineffective. Living-donor LT performed; discharged 55 days post-LT with TB 2.8 mg/dL; renal dysfunction remained at 6 months. Authors state allopurinol hepatotoxicity is rare but can be severe and fatal; reported as first case of successful LDLT for allopurinol-induced cholestatic liver failure without DRESS syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report 3 cases of allopurinol-induced hypersensitivity syndromes admitted with fever, generalized exanthematous rash, eosinophilia and liver dysfunction shortly after starting allopurinol for non-symptomatic hyperuricemia. Case 2 (34-year-old female) presented with severe liver dysfunction and recovered only after 9 weeks of corticosteroid therapy; case 3 (66-year-old male) developed severe liver dysfunction and renal failure and ultimately died with liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Cases occurred in patients treated for non-symptomatic asymptomatic hyperuricemia; patients with liver dysfunction and renal impairment appear at greater risk for allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) is described as an infrequent but potentially lethal adverse reaction of allopurinol therapy, with features resembling EBV infection including fever, exanthematous rash, leukocytosis, eosinophilia, impaired renal function, hepatocellular injury, and severe reactions such as toxic epidermal necrolysis and acute vasculitis. Reactions are considered cell-mediated immunity directed toward allopurinol and, more importantly, to its oxypurinol metabolite, which has a markedly longer half-life. One fatal case also complicated by iatrogenic diabetes, oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis, and severe ethmoidal rhinomucormycosis, with death due to liver failure from amphotericin B therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Among 100 cases of hepatic injury attributed to the administration of pemoline, 43 had sufficient accompanying information to permit analysis. All but two patients were younger than 20 years old and 80% were younger than 12 years; males predominated. Injury appeared as early as 1 week or as late as more than 1 year of taking the drug. The injury was uniformly hepatocellular as judged by high aminotransferase values and by death in massive necrosis in one patient, and the mechanism was judged idiosyncratic, probably metabolic rather than immunologic.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings restricted to a pediatric population (all but two patients <20 years old, 80% <12 years old); exposure was therapeutic use of the drug, generally as sole agent after excluding cases with co-administered potentially hepatotoxic drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Based on 100 FDA reports of abnormal liver-enzyme levels in pemoline-treated patients from 1971 to 1985; 43 cases of exclusive pemoline intake were analyzed after exclusions (51 incomplete data, 6 with incriminable co-agents such as aspirin, erythromycin, methylphenidate). Latency ranged from 1 week to >1 year. Males predominated. One fatal case: 12-year-old boy on pemoline alone with peak bilirubin 26 mg/dL, AST 4280, GI bleeding; autopsy showed massive hepatocellular necrosis; viral hepatitis A and B excluded by serology and no other drug implicated. Mechanism judged idiosyncratic, probably metabolic rather than immunologic.

raw_record.support_text: In the PAGANINI trial, a participant receiving eliapixant 150 mg twice daily developed a suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction (SUSAR) that was considered a moderate drug-induced liver injury (DILI) of hepatocellular origin. The participant prematurely discontinued eliapixant at the 4-week visit because of the liver event, after which liver enzyme values returned to normal. Two participants receiving eliapixant (75 mg, n = 1; 150 mg, n = 1) had alanine aminotransferase exceeding three-fold the upper limit of normal, triggering close liver observation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Attribution rests on a single adjudicated case in one participant receiving the highest study dose (eliapixant 150 mg twice daily) during a therapeutic clinical trial; the event was reported as a suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction (SUSAR).
raw_record.extra_details: SUSAR classified as a moderate DILI of hepatocellular origin; participant prematurely discontinued at the 4-week visit and liver enzyme values returned to normal after discontinuation. ALT exceeded three-fold ULN in 2 eliapixant-treated participants (75 mg, n = 1; 150 mg, n = 1), triggering close liver observation per FDA Guidance. Per a standardized search, any AE relating to 'drug-related hepatic disorders – comprehensive search' occurred in 0/1/3/0 participants in the eliapixant 25 mg, 75 mg, 150 mg, and placebo groups respectively. Dose-dependent increases in mean/median alkaline phosphatase, fibrinogen, and plasma antithrombin III activity were observed overall, with no relevant mean changes in other liver enzymes at any dose. No other study drug-related SAEs (0 in 25 mg, 0 in 75 mg, 1 in 150 mg, 0 placebo); no deaths.

raw_record.support_text: The author reports a case of hypersensitivity to para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS). The reaction consisted of generalized skin eruption and fever followed by intense jaundice and severe hemolytic anemia, with lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and ascites. Liver biopsy showed a reversible type of intrahepatic cholestasis together with some degree of hepatocellular alteration; functional tests indicated both obstructive and hepatocellular elements. There was also eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytosis. The patient recovered completely. The associated complication of toxic hepatitis and hemolytic anemia due to PAS had not previously been reported in the English literature.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of drug hypersensitivity to PAS used therapeutically. Clinical features: generalized skin eruption, fever, intense jaundice (icterus), severe hemolytic anemia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis. Liver biopsy revealed reversible intrahepatic cholestasis with some hepatocellular alteration; liver function tests showed both obstructive and hepatocellular elements. Patient recovered completely. Authors note the combined complication of toxic hepatitis and hemolytic anemia due to PAS had not previously been reported in the English literature (single case report).

raw_record.support_text: The reported case had an R factor of 12, a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury, and a RUCAM score of 8, indicating a 'probable' association of the DILI with fosfomycin. A rechallenge was not performed for ethical reasons.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented case: acute liver injury with aminotransferases >1000 IU/L, R factor 12, RUCAM score 8 ('probable'). Fosfomycin is described as a rare cause of liver injury, presenting with mild aminotransferase elevations in 1%-2% of patients. Literature: Matsumori et al. reported a 30-year-old male with mixed-pattern injury three days after oral fosfomycin who developed features of liver failure (encephalopathy and coagulopathy) without need for liver transplantation, enzyme normalization four months after onset; Durupt et al. reported a 30-year-old female with cystic fibrosis who developed liver injury four days after parenteral fosfomycin with resolution one month after discontinuation and positive rechallenge twice (enzymes increased three days after administration, normalized within a week); Wang et al. reported a 50-year-old male with mixed liver injury three days after fosfomycin exposure resolving within a week; Ferreira et al. reported a 24-year-old female with hepatocellular injury one week after a single 3 g oral dose resolving three months after exposure. First-line management was discontinuation of the agent.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical course and laboratory data are compatible with a diagnosis of severe acute cholestatic hepatitis, probably due to amoxicillin. Symptoms appeared 6 days after stopping amoxicillin treatment; symptoms reappeared after the drug was discontinued and taken again, interpreted as a positive rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: patient presented 6 days after stopping amoxicillin with jaundice and malaise; laboratory showed increased direct bilirubin, ALP, and GGT. Viral hepatitis serology (HAV, HBV, HCV) and antinuclear/antismooth muscle antibodies negative; antimitochondrial antibodies positive but anti-M2 negative; abdominal ultrasound normal. Liver biopsy (4 weeks after jaundice onset) showed pronounced centrolobular cholestasis with inflammatory infiltrates and focal portal inflammatory infiltrate involving biliary epithelium, compatible with both toxic hepatitis and PBC. Bilirubin and ALP decreased after 1 month of jaundice and later normalized; patient well with no signs of liver damage at 2 years follow-up. Differential diagnosis of primary biliary cirrhosis considered but drug-mediated toxic hepatitis favored based on positive rechallenge.

Paracetamol-associated hyperamylasaemia occurred in 13% of unselected local and 36% of selected transferred patients; 33 cases (4%) had clinical acute pancreatitis, 18 of whom also had fulminant hepatic failure, with 9 deaths and 1 transplant; overall mortality was not significantly higher in those with pancreatitis (10/33, 30%) vs those with hyperamylasaemia without pancreatitis (47/199, 24%).

raw_record.support_text: Two cases of hepatotoxicity occurred after high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone treatment of a demyelinating disease. The first patient developed a histologically documented acute hepatitis and recovered after 3 weeks; the second showed a mild augmentation of liver enzymes that normalized within a few days. The causal relationship between hepatotoxicity and methylprednisolone treatment was deemed probable in both cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 33-year-old man with first episode of demyelinating encephalopathy, 4-day high-dose IV methylprednisolone (total 2.5 g); 5 weeks later AST 349 U/L and ALT 1042 U/L; liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with focal liver cell necrosis in acinar zones 2-3, monocyte/macrophage infiltration, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, acidophil bodies, and focal microvesicular steatosis; recovery within 20 days. Case 2: 27-year-old woman treated for retrobulbar optic neuritis with 6-day high-dose IV methylprednisolone (total 4.5 g); on day 6 AST 39 U/L, ALT 122 U/L, normalizing in 4 days. Both patients had no prior liver disease, denied alcohol and any drug use for the previous 6 months, and had negative hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and autoantibody markers.

raw_record.support_text: In two cases, based on the close temporal relationship between methylprednisolone treatment and onset of liver dysfunction, on the positive dechallenge, and on exclusion of other plausible causes (exotoxins, viruses, autoimmunity), the causal relationship between hepatotoxicity and methylprednisolone was deemed probable according to the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale. In case 1, steroid therapy was followed by acute hepatitis confirmed by liver biopsy (histological pattern consistent with drug-induced acute liver disease), with conspicuous AST and ALT increases about 1 month after treatment and complete recovery ~3 weeks later. In case 2, only a mild augmentation of liver enzymes occurred on the sixth day of treatment, with recovery within a few days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone pulses for demyelinating disease; two reported cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Causal grading: probable per Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale; based on close temporal association, positive dechallenge, and exclusion of exotoxins, viruses, and autoimmunity. Case 1: acute hepatitis with biopsy showing microvesicular steatosis (area of microvesicular steatosis) and central zone necrosis (acidophilic bodies) with mononuclear infiltration and Kupffer cell hyperplasia; conspicuous AST and ALT elevation ~1 month after treatment; complete recovery ~3 weeks later. Case 2: mild liver enzyme augmentation on day 6 of treatment, recovery within days. Mechanism remains elusive; in vitro neither prednisolone nor methylprednisolone showed toxicity in cultured rat hepatocytes. Prior literature: isolated reports of liver injury after high-dose methylprednisolone in demyelinating disease; hepatotoxicity better documented after IV methylprednisolone in thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy; other reports with corticosteroids in autoimmune diseases and 1 case during lymphoma chemotherapy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded that observations of disturbances in liver function during treatment with Ibufenac indicated that the drug was hepatotoxic. Raised S.G.O.T. titres occurred in fourteen of 36 patients investigated (transient in four), a concurrent elevation of lactic dehydrogenase in one patient was shown to be a hepatic isoenzyme, and two patients developed jaundice with extremely high S.G.O.T. and S.G.P.T. levels; three additional reports of jaundice among approximately 400 patients receiving Ibufenac in rheumatic clinics in Great Britain were also received.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases were rheumatoid arthritis patients on long-term Ibufenac therapy (e.g., Case 2, a 45-year-old secretary, took 285 g Ibufenac over 101 days, escalating from 2 g to 3 g daily; S.G.O.T. rose from 22 to a peak of 1160 units and S.G.P.T. to 1250 units, serum bilirubin peaked at 4.9 mg with jaundice, and liver tests returned to ~normal within a few weeks after withdrawal). Jaundice cleared within ~18 days; both jaundiced patients ran a mild course. Hepatotoxicity was judged to impose a serious limitation on long-term use in rheumatoid arthritis.

raw_record.support_text: In a second trial of Ibufenac in 45 patients treated for 1 to 16 months for rheumatoid arthritis, the only clinically important adverse effect was hepatic dysfunction, observed in 14 of the 36 patients investigated for this, with jaundice occurring in 2 of those 14. The authors state that the frequency of the hepatic toxicity observed in this series imposes considerable limitations on the use of Ibufenac and contraindicates prolonged and unrestricted treatment with the product.
raw_record.extra_details: Ibufenac = 4-isobutylphenylacetic acid, compared to calcium aspirin in the controlled first-week trial; second trial of 45 rheumatoid arthritis patients treated for 1 to 16 months. Hepatic dysfunction in 14 of 36 patients investigated (2 of whom had jaundice). Authors conclude the frequency of hepatic toxicity imposes considerable limitations on and contraindicates prolonged unrestricted use. Also reported: dyspepsia frequency reduced vs prior treatment, minimal occult fecal blood loss, frank hyperuricemia in 13 and slight hyperuricemia in 9 of 43 patients.

Jaundice with mixed hepatocellular liver-test elevations; no rash or hepatosplenomegaly; platelet/creatinine/CRP normal. Liver tests returned to normal within 5 weeks of drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: A 29-year-old female with adult-onset Still's disease developed severe acute hepatitis (ALT 1652 U/L, AST 766 U/L) after receiving corticosteroids. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltration, proliferative Kupffer cells, and occasional apoptotic bodies. After viral and autoimmune hepatitis were excluded, corticosteroid-induced liver injury was confirmed based on clinical findings and a positive prednisolone re-challenge, since hepatic enzyme elevations recurred upon rechallenge with prednisolone and remitted after its removal.

raw_record.extra_details: A 29-year-old Taiwanese female; initial elevation (ALT 150 U/L, AST 119 U/L) noted on day 10, peaking at ALT 1473 U/L and AST 722 U/L on day 15; recurrence after discharge with ALT 1652 U/L and AST 766 U/L five days after discharge on prednisolone maintenance (20 mg/day). Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with lymphocytes, neutrophils, proliferative Kupffer cells, and occasional apoptotic bodies. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis excluded. Hepatitis remitted after prednisolone removal; reported as likely the first case of corticosteroid-induced liver injury in newly diagnosed AOSD.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old Caucasian man with metastatic melanoma developed severe vemurafenib-induced granulomatous hepatitis with chronic cholestasis. Six weeks after starting vemurafenib he was hospitalized with vomiting, abdominal pain, and elevated liver enzymes that peaked at ALT 170 U/L, AST 132 U/L, ALP 663 U/L and bilirubin 6.0 mg/dL seven days after drug discontinuation. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic injury with granulomas and eosinophils, serologies for viral/autoimmune hepatitis were negative, and the Drug Induced Liver Injury Network causality score was highly likely for vemurafenib hepatotoxicity. The ALP remained elevated at 302 IU/L with normal bilirubin eight months after presentation.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis leading to chronic cholestasis in a 69-year-old Caucasian man with BRAF V600E metastatic melanoma; vemurafenib dose titrated from 240 mg twice daily to 720 mg twice daily, DILI onset 6 weeks after start. Liver enzymes peaked 7 days after discontinuation (ALT 170, AST 132, ALP 663, bilirubin 6.0 mg/dL); biopsy showed cholestatic injury with granulomas and eosinophils; no eosinophilia, INR normal; viral (hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, EBV) and autoimmune serologies negative. DILIN causality score was highly likely for vemurafenib. Patient recovered clinically but ALP remained elevated (302 IU/L) with normal bilirubin at 8 months; coexisting medications atenolol, naproxen, tadalafil started >6 months prior; no alcohol or herbal supplements.

raw_record.support_text: The mechanism of injury in vemurafenib hepatotoxicity is unknown. In 63 patients with vemurafenib hepatotoxicity, a cholestatic or mixed pattern of liver injury was more common at presentation than a hepatocellular pattern (65% vs 35%). Most patients presented within 2 months of drug initiation, and the estimated reporting rate of vemurafenib hepatotoxicity was 5.13 (95% CI, 3.8-6.4) per 1000 patient-years of exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency to liver injury onset mostly within 2 months; estimated reporting rate 5.13 (95% CI 3.8-6.4) per 1000 patient-years; 63 patients with vemurafenib hepatotoxicity; cholestatic or mixed pattern (65%) vs hepatocellular (35%); treatment by dose reduction or discontinuation (17/63 continued at a decreased dose, 25 rechallenged, 20 able to complete therapy); mechanism unknown; associated histology (Figure 1) of granulomatous hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltration of bile ducts and canalicular cholestasis in zone 3; approved for melanoma with BRAF mutations; liver test elevation 30% with 11% grade 3-4; fatal hepatic failure reported: No.

raw_record.support_text: A cohort of 41 consecutive patients with acute liver injury included 33 cases following paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose (POD). Of these, 24/33 (72.7%) developed hepatic encephalopathy and therefore acute liver failure. Some POD patients died or required liver transplantation, and neopterin and sCD163 levels were significantly elevated, reflecting macrophage activation. The paper describes paracetamol overdose as the cause of the acute liver injury in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurs specifically in the setting of paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, manifesting as acute liver injury that progressed to acute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy in 72.7% of POD cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective cohort of 41 consecutive patients (18, 43.9%, male) with acute liver injury; 33 were paracetamol overdose cases. 24/33 (72.7%) developed hepatic encephalopathy and hence acute liver failure. Some POD patients died or required emergency/orthotopic liver transplantation. Both serum neopterin and sCD163 levels were significantly higher in PODs than in chronic liver disease and healthy controls, and correlated with organ failure scores but not serum ALT. These markers were evaluated as biomarkers of macrophage activation, which is implicated in SIRS following paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.support_text: The study evaluates serial neopterin and sCD163 levels in patients with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (ALF). Analyses included paracetamol-induced ALF patients who died, those who spontaneously survived, and patients undergoing emergency orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT), with outcomes such as hepatic encephalopathy, SIRS, and the need for OLT. The discussion concludes serum neopterin is a marker of macrophage activation following paracetamol overdose and of multiorgan failure in paracetamol-induced acute liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose as the exposure setting; injury occurred in paracetamol-induced ALF patients, some of whom died or required emergency OLT.
raw_record.extra_details: This is a biomarker-focused observational study of 33 paracetamol-overdose patients. Liver injury phenotyped as acute liver failure (ALF) with outcomes including death, spontaneous survival, and emergency OLT. Of 6 patients who died vs 6 spontaneous survivors, neopterin rose in 4/6 who died and 3/6 survivors (P=0.22). In 5 patients undergoing emergency OLT, pre-OLT sCD163 2569 (2292-3583) ng/mL fell to 1154 (571-2079) post-OLT (P=0.125) in 4 survivors; one patient died 4 days post-OLT. Elevated admission neopterin was associated with development of hepatic encephalopathy (P=0.0002), SIRS (P=0.0019), and death or OLT (P=0.036); neopterin AUROC for outcome 72.9% (95% CI 54.7-91.0%). Neopterin correlated with IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, ferritin, APACHE II, SOFA, creatinine, prothrombin time (negative with platelets). Study positions serum neopterin as a marker of macrophage activation and multiorgan failure following paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Terfenadine, an H₁-receptor antagonist, was reported to be associated with two cases of severe prolonged cholestatic hepatitis. In the detailed case, a 36-year-old man took terfenadine 60 mg twice daily from Aug 1 to 21, 1989, and presented with jaundice on Aug 31, with elevated transaminases, γ-GT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin; a liver biopsy showed severe centrilobular cholestasis and bile-duct destruction with mild portal inflammation consistent with toxic or drug-induced hepatitis. He took no other medications or herbal remedies, and liver tests returned to normal within about 6 months after discontinuing terfenadine.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as two cases of severe prolonged cholestatic hepatitis associated with terfenadine use. Case 1 (36-year-old man): terfenadine 60 mg twice daily Aug 1-21, 1989, jaundice from Aug 31; AST 247 IU/L (ref 9-34), ALT 556 IU/L (4-37), γ-GT 421 IU/L (0-47), alkaline phosphatase 275 IU/L (25-97), total bilirubin 153 μmol/L (2-17); negative serology for hepatitis A/B/C and infectious mononucleosis; absent SMA, ANA, AMA; normal caeruloplasmin and α-1-antitrypsin; normal ERCP. Liver biopsy: normal architecture, severe centrilobular cholestasis and bile-duct destruction with mild portal infiltration by lymphocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils, consistent with toxic or drug-induced hepatitis. Bilirubin peaked at 552 μmol/L about 3 months after presentation and liver function tests normalized within the next 6 months; patient recovered and remained well off the drug. No alternative medications or herbal remedies were taken. Descriptive phenotype: cholestatic hepatitis with bile-duct destruction.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old man (case 2) developed jaundice, pruritus, and epigastric discomfort after taking terfenadine 60 mg twice daily for 4 weeks (he had no other medications, herbal remedies, or risk factors for hepatitis). Initial liver tests were AST 232 IU/L, ALT 665 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 146 IU/L, and total bilirubin 185 µmol/L; a liver biopsy showed centrilobular intracellular and intracanalicular cholestasis, mild portal fibrosis, and inflammation with neutrophilic and eosinophilic leucocytes, compatible with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. After terfenadine was stopped, bilirubin rose to a maximum of 909 µmol/L but liver function tests returned to normal within 3 months.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases (case 1 and case 2) of acute cholestatic hepatitis attributed to terfenadine; case 2 took 60 mg twice daily for 4 weeks. Latency of a few weeks. Initial laboratory values case 2: AST 232 IU/L, ALT 665 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 146 IU/L, total bilirubin 185 µmol/L; peak bilirubin 909 µmol/L during recovery. Liver biopsy showed preservation of architecture with centrilobular intra- and intracanalicular cholestasis, mild portal tract fibrosis, and inflammation with neutrophilic and eosinophilic leucocytes. No rechallenge performed in either case due to severity of the initial episode; causality supported by temporal relation, absence of other identifiable causes of hepatitis, and compatible histology. The paper notes the reaction is rare and 'probably idiosyncratic', that a product monograph (Seldane) reported isolated cases of jaundice, cholestatic hepatitis and hepatitis without clear causality, and that only one prior report of possible terfenadine hepatitis (without histology) was found. Recovery within 3 months.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 110 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF), the cause was acetaminophen overdose in 88 patients. The paper reports multiple clinical outcomes in this acetaminophen-induced FHF group, including nonsurvival (patients who died had lower factor V levels) and the use of liver transplantation, establishing acetaminophen overdose as the cause of FHF in these patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 88 of 110 FHF patients had acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis/FHF; median age 26 years (range 13-60). On admission grades of coma: 45 in grade IV, 7 in grade III, 9 in grade II, 27 in grade I; 23 of 36 patients in grade I/II progressed to deeper coma. Some patients underwent orthotopic liver transplantation; nonsurvivors had significantly lower factor V (median 5%) than survivors (median 10%). Admission labs for the acetaminophen group: INR 6.9 (2.0-17.5), AST 3150 IU/L (100-15000), bilirubin 73 µmol/L, creatinine 257 µmol/L, platelets 101x10^9/L. No single factor V cutoff separated survivors from nonsurvivors; King's criteria (pH, INR, renal failure, coma) were more accurate for transplant selection.

raw_record.support_text: The hepatotoxic effects of tacrine occur in nearly half the patients treated with it. Although some patients have had increases in serum ALT as high as 20 times the upper limit of normal, no deaths have been associated with tacrine hepatotoxicity. Tacrine is described as a relatively pure hepatocellular toxin, with ALT increases usually without concomitant increases in alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin, and hepatotoxicity does not seem to be dose related.

raw_record.support_text: In controlled clinical trials of tacrine for Alzheimer's disease (Cognex package insert, Parke-Davis 1993), increased ALT occurred as an adverse effect in 29% of tacrine-treated patients (n=634) versus 2% of placebo recipients (n=342), described as tacrine hepatotoxicity. The paper further reports that of 145 patients with serum ALT increases 3-10 times the upper limit of normal, 127 were successfully rechallenged and continued tacrine, but rechallenge is considered imprudent for patients with ALT increases 20 times or greater than normal or with signs of allergic response (rash, fever, eosinophilia), and tacrine should be stopped if jaundice occurs or serum ALT reaches three times the upper limit of normal.

raw_record.support_text: Diclofenac and other NSAIDs are known idiosyncratic hepatotoxins. The paper reports 13 cases of diclofenac hepatitis (including the present case), two with a fatal outcome, with jaundice in eleven patients, marked elevations in bilirubin, AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase, and normalization of enzymes within 4-13 weeks in most survivors. The authors conclude it seems most probable that these 13 patients had hepatitis as a result of diclofenac usage, with a reversible hepatitis related to diclofenac use in the presented patient and one survivor developing steroid-responsive chronic active hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 diclofenac hepatitis cases (12 previously reported + present case), 2 fatal fulminant hepatitis; 10 women and 3 men, average age 63 years (range 46-79); 6 on diclofenac alone, others co-medicated; presentation usually within 3 months of starting diclofenac (range 1 week to 11 months). Eleven patients jaundiced with dark urine and pale stools; pruritus, nausea, vomiting relatively infrequent. At presentation bilirubin 1-22x, AST 2-45x, ALT 7-47x, alkaline phosphatase 1.6-4.6x upper limit of normal. Normalization in 4-13 weeks in 10 survivors; one survivor developed steroid-responsive chronic active hepatitis. One patient with fatal fulminant hepatitis while taking diclofenac and glafenine was excluded due to ambiguity of cause. The patient presented here had hepatocellular necrosis with ultrastructural changes (ER vesiculation, lamellated bodies, mitochondrial pleomorphism with paracrystalline inclusions) in zone 3, without microvesicular steatosis or cholestasis; improvement after diclofenac discontinuation. Diclofenac rechallenge on two occasions reproduced hepatitis in patients 1, 6, and 11.

raw_record.support_text: The paper characterizes diclofenac hepatitis as an idiosyncratic drug reaction in humans whose mechanism remains controversial (hypersensitivity vs toxic-metabolic), describing 13 cases (12 literature cases and the present patient) of diclofenac-induced hepatitis with jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and outcomes ranging from recovery to death in 2 of 13 patients. A typically mixed cholestatic/hepatocellular biochemical profile was reported after prolonged exposure, and hepatotoxicity recurred after reintroduction of diclofenac in patients 1, 6, and 11.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 diclofenac-induced hepatitis cases compiled from 8 biopsy studies and 2 autopsies plus the present case; latency about 1-48 weeks (present case 26 weeks); outcome recovery in most, progression in 1, death in 2 (patients 5 and 6, massive/fatal hepatic necrosis; end-stage fulminant hepatitis with small, shrunken liver). Histology ranged from mild acute lobular hepatitis to massive necrosis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, ballooning degeneration, acidophil bodies, perivenular hepatocyte dropout, canalicular cholestasis and bile thrombi, and possible reactive Kupffer cell hyperplasia and noncaseating granulomas. Ultrastructurally shows lamellated bodies, bizarre mitochondria, complex phagolysosomes, and other criteria for drug-induced liver injury; eosinophilia in some patients; recurrence after reintroduction in patients 1, 6, 11; reversible after withdrawal in most, but not always (2 deaths).

raw_record.support_text: The National Halothane Study (1959-1962) evaluated ~850,000 anesthetic cases; halothane was used in 30% of cases. Among 82 fatalities with histologic confirmation of massive hepatic necrosis, nine had no obvious cause such as shock, overwhelming infection, or pre-existing hepatic disease; seven of the nine had received halothane and four had more than one exposure to halothane. Additional reported cases describe massive liver necrosis developing within three weeks of halothane anesthesia, with multiple exposures common, including a case of fulminant hepatocellular necrosis after three exposures despite corticosteroid treatment, and a series of 42 patients with hepatitis after halothane exposure in whom survival fell with repeated exposures.
raw_record.extra_details: National Halothane Study covered 1959-1962 with ~850,000 anesthetic cases; overall mortality 1.87% for halothane vs 1.93% for all agents. 82 fatalities with histologic confirmation of massive hepatic necrosis; 9 without other obvious cause (7 halothane-exposed, 4 with >1 exposure). Trey et al (1968) reported 150 cases of fulminant hepatic failure; in 35 patients massive liver necrosis developed in <3 weeks after halothane anesthesia, 77% with multiple exposures; unexplained post-surgical fever after halothane warranted investigation for hepatocellular damage. Aach and Kissane (1968) reported a patient with three halothane exposures who died of fulminant hepatocellular necrosis despite large-dose corticosteroids. Klion/Schaffner/Popper reported 42 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis, including two exposed occupationally rather than as patients; survival was 6/12 after one exposure, 7/22 (32%) after two, 0/5 after three, and 0/1 after four. Study concluded halothane was an extremely safe anesthetic relative to others used.

raw_record.extra_details: β-lactam antibiotic used to treat gram-positive bacterial infections. Associated with a high incidence of liver injury [100] with several reported deaths. The liver injury predisposes via an HLA-class I-restricted drug-specific CD8+ T-cell response; flucloxacillin binds directly to lysine residues on protein and activates T-cells via a hapten mechanism. HLA-B*57:01 screening was not introduced because greater than 13,000 individuals would need to be screened to prevent one case. Causality supported by isolation of drug-specific CD8+ T-cells and priming of naïve CD4+/CD8+ T-cells from HLA-B*57:01+ healthy donors.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatotoxicity is a well-known complication of non-steroidal anti-androgens and that fatal hepatotoxicity due to nilutamide has been described previously only twice. The reported fatal case in this paper is attributed to nilutamide therapy in a patient with metastatic prostate cancer; the only other medication taken was leuprolide, an LHRH analogue for which severe hepatotoxicity has not been noted. Nilutamide's manufacturer profile describes serum aminotransferase elevations in about 8% of patients, and the incidence of abnormal liver function tests was reported as 2-33% across various studies.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal DILI case report in a patient with metastatic prostate cancer treated with nilutamide for combined androgen blockade; the only co-medication was leuprolide (LHRH analogue), for which severe hepatotoxicity was not noted. Liver biopsy showed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, neutrophils) with cholestasis, ductular proliferation, interface injury, and spotty necrosis; lab values showed total bilirubin 30.2 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 17.7, AST 1540 U/l, ALT 977 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 138 U/l. Patient developed encephalopathy and acute-on-chronic liver failure, received plasmapheresis for 72 h without sustained improvement, developed pancytopenia, fungemia and bacteremia, was not a transplant candidate due to metastatic prostate cancer, and died 11 days after transfer. Manufacturer label reports aminotransferase elevation in ~8% of patients (vs 4% placebo); abnormal LFT incidence 2-33% in various studies; nilutamide is a nitroaromatic drug with potential nitroreductive bioactivation (oxidant stress) and mitochondrial complex I inhibition proposed as mechanisms.

The injury was characterized as 'mixed hepatocellular' hepatic injury with focal necrosis, inflammatory infiltration with eosinophilia, cholestasis, jaundice, and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic injury proved by administration of a test/challenge dose (positive rechallenge); interval from challenge dose to adverse effects ~1 day. Initial latent ('induction') period was 1-2 weeks despite several prior exposures to the drug. This is reported as the fourth case of hepatic injury associated with sulfamethoxazole and the third sulfonamide hepatotoxicity proved by a test dose. Injury described as 'mixed hepatocellular' with focal necrosis, surrounding inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophilia in liver parenchyma, cholestasis, jaundice, and elevated alkaline phosphatase.

raw_record.support_text: The authors performed a Naranjo evaluation to determine the probability that the clinical event was due to propafenone administration, obtaining a score of 7, which indicates a probable adverse drug reaction from propafenone use. A diagnosis of acute propafenone toxicity was based on temporal relationship with the drug, clinical and biochemical recovery after withdrawal, exclusion of other causes, and histology consistent with drug toxicity. This is reported as the eighth case in the world's literature of hepatotoxicity related to propafenone, with clinical presentation that can be cholestatic and/or hepatocellular, jaundice in all cases, a latency of two to six weeks, and no reported cases of fulminant liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo score 7 (probable ADR); dechallenge with withdrawal reduced alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase and normalized aminotransferases and CA19-9; latency 2-6 weeks (one case at 28 weeks); jaundice in all cases; no fulminant liver failure reported; eighth case in world literature; histology showed portal and periportal inflammatory infiltrate, macrovesicular steatosis, bile duct injury with ductular proliferation, mixed inflammatory infiltrate (eosinophils, neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells), mild periportal feathery degeneration, no fibrosis; antiarrhythmic indication.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of auxiliary partial orthotopic liver transplantation (APOLT) in a patient with isoniazid (INH)-related fulminant hepatic failure. A 10-year-old boy with INH-related fulminant hepatic failure underwent APOLT after left hepatectomy; postoperatively a graft-hepatic artery thrombosis necessitated urgent re-transplantation, while histology of the native liver showed signs of regeneration, suggesting potential for native-liver recovery after INH-related FHF.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (10-year-old boy); drug used as prophylactic treatment for latent tuberculosis that progressed to fulminant hepatic failure; single case report limiting generalization.
raw_record.extra_details: Prophylactic INH dose 300 mg/day orally (April-July 2001); presented with jaundice and abnormal LFTs (AST up to 3,640 U/l; ALT up to 2,945 U/l) and grade III encephalopathy requiring mechanical ventilation; viral, autoimmune, Wilson's disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and haemochromatosis excluded. Histology of native liver showed massive multi-acinar hepatocellular necrosis with spared portal tracts, marginal ductular proliferation, mild inflammation and no fibrosis, consistent with toxic injury. APOLT performed on day 21 after admission; on postoperative day 22 urgent re-transplantation was needed for graft hepatic artery thrombosis (HAT) and inadequate native-liver function; histology after total hepatectomy showed viable bi-nucleated hepatocytes comprising about 1/5 of the liver, suggesting regeneration potential.

Authors note the risk of INH-related liver injury increases with older age, female gender, and Oriental ethnicity, but this case occurred in a child.

raw_record.support_text: After receiving metformin 850 mg/day for 2 weeks, a 78-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 10-day history of abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and jaundice. Laboratory analysis showed severe hepatocellular and cholestatic hepatic injury, and other causes of acute liver injury were ruled out. Discontinuation of metformin led to significant subjective improvement after 1 week, and all hepatic abnormalities resolved by 2 months.

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that metformin can induce hepatic injury (hepatocellular and/or cholestatic), and notes that metformin hepatotoxicity has rarely been reported, with possible mechanisms being direct, idiosyncratic, or a drug–drug interaction leading to acute hepatocellular and/or cholestatic jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Search of PubMed yielded six published metformin hepatotoxicity reports (Table 2): two cases of acute hepatitis, two cases of cholestasis, and two cases of mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic injury; the paper's own patient is the third reported case of mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury. In all cases signs and symptoms resolved and liver enzymes normalized after metformin discontinuation, except for a persistently increased alkaline phosphatase in one case attributed to a prolonged cholestatic effect. Liver biopsy was performed in three cases and rechallenge in one; no specific treatments were given. Bilirubin normalized after 2 months in the described case.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is converted by cytochrome P-450-dependent mixed function oxidase to a reactive intermediate metabolite which binds covalently to hepatic macromolecules; after a toxic dose glutathione is depleted and the excess metabolite alkylates hepatic proteins causing cell damage and necrosis. The paper also notes paracetamol hepatotoxicity is increased in chronic alcoholics and patients taking drugs that induce microsomal enzymes.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning context; increased hepatotoxicity in chronic alcoholics and patients taking microsomal enzyme-inducing drugs; combined overdosage with CNS depressants can prolong coma.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatic necrosis with maximum liver-function abnormality delayed at least 3 days. At plasma paracetamol concentrations above 300 µg/ml 4 h after ingestion there was >90% chance of severe liver damage (AST/ALT >1000 i.u./l). Half-life prolongs from ~2 h to 4 h or more; fatal outcome likely if half-life exceeds 10-12 h. Mechanism: reactive intermediate metabolite alkylating hepatic proteins with glutathione depletion; hepatotoxicity can be modified by microsomal enzyme induction/inhibition and reduced by glutathione precursors and SH donors (L-cysteine, cysteamine). Treatment with cysteamine or N-acetylcysteine effective only if given within 10 h of ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: A 67-year-old Japanese woman with EGFR-mutation-positive lung adenocarcinoma was treated with gefitinib 250 mg once daily and after 16 weeks showed a substantial rise in transaminases (AST 112 U/L, grade 1; ALT 223 U/L, grade 3 per CTCAE v4). A liver biopsy histologically revealed drug-induced liver injury, and a drug lymphocyte stimulation test was positive for gefitinib, suggesting the hepatitis was from drug allergy rather than dose-dependent toxicity. Gefitinib was discontinued; liver function normalized within 11 weeks. The paper further states that gefitinib-induced hepatotoxicity is widely recognized, with Japanese clinical trials reporting pronounced serum hepatic-enzyme elevations that required cessation of treatment in 24-30% of patients, and a pooled trial analysis showed grade ≥3 hepatotoxicity in 18% of gefitinib-treated patients versus 5.4% for erlotinib (OR 3.71, 95% CI 2.12-6.49, P<0.0001).
raw_record.extra_details: EGFR-TKI; alkylation-independent idiosyncratic (allergic) mechanism inferred from a positive drug lymphocyte stimulation test and biopsy-confirmed drug-induced liver injury; ALT 223 U/L (grade 3) and AST 112 U/L (grade 1); resolution within 11 weeks of withdrawal; Japanese EGFR exon-19-deleted lung adenocarcinoma case in a patient with no prior liver disease; pooled phase II/III trial analysis found grade ≥3 hepatotoxicity in 18% of gefitinib-treated EGFR-mutation-positive NSCLC patients, higher in Asian than non-Asian patients, with a trial-incidence of grade 3 hepatotoxicity of 24-30%.

raw_record.support_text: Several retrospective studies reported increased risk of hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis in subjects with psoriasis or rheumatoid arthritis receiving long-term methotrexate therapy. In psoriasis the prevalence of fibrosis ranged from 6 to 30% and cirrhosis from 0% to 25%, whereas in rheumatoid arthritis rates of 3% to 31% (fibrosis) and 0% to 2% (cirrhosis) were described; under both conditions the risk of fibrosis increases with cumulative methotrexate dose exceeding 2,400 mg. The histologic features of hepatotoxicity secondary to long-term methotrexate use in inflammatory bowel disease were also described, with a 20-subject case series (cumulative dose 2,633 mg) showing normal or low-grade Roenigk I-II changes in 95% and advanced changes (Roenigk > III) in one patient with diabetes and obesity.

raw_record.support_text: Sulfasalazine caused hepatotoxic reactions in children. Two affected children were rechallenged with sulfasalazine after their hepatotoxic reaction and both experienced severe symptoms including fever, rash, and elevated liver enzyme levels within 24 hours, strongly suggesting a hypersensitivity mechanism, described as severe idiosyncratic manifestations. Hepatotoxic reactions to sulfasalazine are rare but always serious and can be fatal in children and adults, expected within the first 3 weeks of therapy; the single fatal case had a 4-day delay in discontinuing sulfasalazine, the greatest elevation in liver enzymes, and two additional potentially hepatotoxic co-medications (perphenazine, amitriptyline).

raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge with sulfasalazine reliably and quickly reproduced severe symptoms (fever, rash, elevated liver enzymes) within 24 h, supporting a hypersensitivity mechanism (probably not IgE-mediated, so desensitization not possible). Reactions were expected to occur within the first 3 weeks of therapy. The fatal case was distinguished by a 4-day delay in drug discontinuation after symptom onset, the greatest elevation in liver enzyme levels, and the presence of perphenazine and amitriptyline as additional potentially hepatotoxic drugs. Monitoring is advised after initiation of therapy; treatment with high-dose steroids recommended. Perphenazine and amitriptyline are mentioned only as potentially hepatotoxic co-medications, not independently attributed as causes.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of cholestatic hepatitis induced by the oral fungicidal drug terbinafine, characterized by a prolonged course and mild reduction in the number of interlobular bile ducts (ILBD). In the discussion they explicitly conclude terbinafine is the offending agent, noting its four-week latency to jaundice, normalization of bilirubin and aminotransferases within three months of cessation, and exclusion of other causes of liver disease, while concurrent medications (nicergoline, fenofibrate) taken for four years were considered unlikely to be responsible.

raw_record.extra_details: Oral terbinafine 250 mg/day for three weeks; onset of asthenia, anorexia, weight loss a few days after discontinuation, jaundice within ~4 weeks of start, followed by pruritus. Laboratory values ~2 weeks after discontinuation: total bilirubin 89 µmol/L (conjugated 70), ALT 277 IU/L, AST 242 IU/L, γGT 321 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 375 IU/L; normal eosinophil count and prothrombin time. Cholestyramine relieved pruritus; bilirubin normalized 10 weeks after stopping terbinafine, but anicteric cholestasis persisted, with γGT still elevated 17 months later. Percutaneous liver biopsy 6 months after withdrawal showed reduction of interlobular bile ducts (visible in 16 of 23, 70%, portal tracts; ILBD/portal tract ratio 0.7 vs 0.9-1.8 in normal liver), occasional lymphocytes between biliary cells, minimal portal/periportal fibrosis, mild mononuclear infiltration, mild centrilobular canalicular cholestasis and minimal hepatocyte necrosis; negative copper stains. The authors note terbinafine-induced hepatitis is considered uncommon (five prior self-limited cases; liver tests showed cholestatic and cytolytic features resolving within 2-6 months, with cholangitis and centrilobular cholestasis in two biopsied cases), and asymptomatic transaminase elevations occur at an estimated incidence of 1/120,000.

Initial plasma half-life 15 h rising to ~60 h in one patient, 10 to ~25 h in the other. Massive centrilobular hepatic necrosis at post-mortem. In humans, the hepatotoxicity of paracetamol is reported to be increased by previous consumption of drugs likely to cause microsomal enzyme induction, and it is stated that there is a poor correlation between the calculated dose absorbed and the severity of subsequent liver damage, with no minimum hepatotoxic or lethal dose definable due to individual variation in susceptibility.

raw_record.support_text: A case of acute severe hepatitis secondary to suloctidil (Sulocton) is presented, reported as the first such case published in Great Britain or Ireland. The authors note the importance of considering a drug aetiology in the differential diagnosis of jaundice after a number of alternate causes were excluded before the correct diagnosis was established.

raw_record.extra_details: 41-year-old Irish woman admitted mid-August 1985 with a two-week history of painless progressive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine and pale stools. Suloctidil 100 mg three times daily orally commenced mid-July. Laboratories: AST 495 U/l (normal 7-40), alkaline phosphatase 150 U/l (normal 30-100), total bilirubin 465 umol/l (normal 1-17), prothrombin time 15 s (control 12 s), 10% eosinophils, reticulocytes 5.6%, haptoglobin 0.1 g/l, positive direct Coombs, positive cold agglutinins, ANA 1/20, smooth muscle antibody 1/320. Hepatitis B surface antigen, Hepatitis A IgM, CMV IgM and Monospot negative. Liver biopsy showed acute cholestatic hepatitis with features suggesting a drug aetiology. Medications discontinued on admission. Reported as first such case published in Great Britain or Ireland.
