raw_record.support_text: Clinically evident idiosyncratic hepatitis has been observed with suloctidil, and since its introduction in France in 1981, sixty-seven cases had been reported up to July 1985; in cases where liver biopsy was performed the findings were similar to those of the reported patient. Growing concern regarding the hepatic adverse effects of suloctidil led to its withdrawal from the market in August 1985. Asymptomatic elevations of liver enzymes had also been noted in a number of trials.
raw_record.extra_details: Suloctidil is a calcium antagonist with alleged anti-platelet, antithrombotic, and vascular antispasmodic activity. In the index patient, jaundice cleared and liver tests (AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, prothrombin time) and eosinophil count returned to normal within eight weeks after drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Peripheral eosinophilia was considered compatible with an idiosyncratic drug reaction; cirrhotic cold agglutinins and haemolytic anaemia were found but not felt to account for the severe jaundice. Liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatitis with eosinophilic leucocyte infiltrate suggesting a drug aetiology, plus confluent centrilobular necrosis, acidophilic individual cell necrosis, cholestasis, and ballooned degeneration of hepatocytes; histology was not consistent with contraceptive steroid-induced liver disease. Competing causes considered and excluded included choledocholithiasis, oral contraceptive pill, autoimmune hepatitis (CRST syndrome, smooth muscle antibody positivity), viral hepatitis, and hemolysis. Sixty-seven suloctidil hepatitis cases reported in France up to July 1985; drug withdrawn from market in August 1985; extensive necrosis described in other reports.

raw_record.support_text: In this patient the relationship between Aldomet (methyldopa) and liver damage was unequivocally established. Within 1 week of starting Aldomet, gastrointestinal symptoms appeared followed by jaundice and pruritus; these remitted and recurred twice as the drug was withdrawn and readministered. After the third withdrawal, severe liver injury resolved within 7 weeks, and two further challenges each caused mild recurrences that were clinically and biochemically less severe than prior relapses. The paper notes the clinical picture of Aldomet-induced liver injury is clinically, biochemically, and histologically indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, often detected only by routine liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: gastro symptoms within 1 week of starting Aldomet, followed by jaundice and pruritus; recurred on two readministrations, then severe liver injury resolved within 7 weeks after third withdrawal; two further challenges caused mild recurrences, each less severe than the prior (dechallenge/rechallenge demonstrates causality). Onset after Aldomet start ranges from 1 week to 1 year, most severe examples within the first 3 months. Mild cases often show only elevated SGOT or serum alkaline phosphatase with normal or nonspecifically abnormal liver histology; 'obstructive' phase with alkaline phosphatase elevation, jaundice, pruritus, and hypercholesterolemia. Incidence of abnormal liver function tests varies from 0% to 35% (mean 6%) across studies using routine liver tests; among first 1,500 recipients only 11 instances of hepatic dysfunction (less than 1%). In more severe cases syndrome resembles typical viral hepatitis with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, fever, hepatomegaly. One fatal case has been described (Perret: elderly man with fulminant fatal jaundice, autopsy showing massive fatty change and perilobular liver cell necrosis) where an association was assumed but not proved; no postnecrotic cirrhosis instances reported.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 645 consecutive patients with single-dose acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning admitted from 1994 to 2000, time to intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment was the single most important independent risk factor for acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity and mortality. Mortality was 0.42% (95% CI 0.05-2.7) when time to NAC was less than 12 hours, rising to 6.1%, 13%, and 19% when time to NAC exceeded 12, 24, and 48 hours, respectively. Chronic alcohol abuse was an independent mortality risk factor (OR 3.52; 95% CI 1.78-6.97), whereas acute alcohol ingestion was protective in alcoholic patients (OR 0.08; 95% CI 0.01-0.66).

raw_record.extra_details: 645 consecutive acetaminophen poisoning patients (retrospective to 1998, prospective thereafter) at Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, 1994-2000. Major prognostic factor was time from overdose to NAC treatment. Mortality 0.42% (<12h), 6.1% (>12h), 13% (>24h), 19% (>48h). Chronic alcohol abuse OR 3.52 (95% CI 1.78-6.97); acute alcohol ingestion OR 0.08 in alcoholics (95% CI 0.01-0.66), OR 0.21 in nonalcoholics (95% CI 0.03-1.67). Acetaminophen poisoning is described as the most common cause of acute liver failure in Denmark and the UK. Proposed mechanism: CYP2E1 induction with glutathione depletion; acute alcohol inhibits microsomal acetaminophen oxidation by CYP2E1 reducing synthesis of N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).

raw_record.support_text: In a multivariate analysis of 645 cases of single-dose acetaminophen poisoning, the acetaminophen dose was a risk factor for hepatotoxicity, especially in nonalcoholic patients. Doses resulting in death ranged from 15 to 125 g, and 28 cases of severe hepatotoxicity (alanine transaminase level greater than 1,000 U/L) resulted from ingestion of a single dose of less than 12 g. Time to N-acetylcysteine was the most important risk factor for death, hepatic encephalopathy, and liver transplant, with mortality rising from 0.42% (time to NAC <12 h) to 19% (time to NAC >48 h).

raw_record.extra_details: Dose of acetaminophen was a risk factor for hepatotoxicity, most importantly in nonalcoholic patients. Doses associated with death ranged from 15 to 125 g; 28 cases of severe hepatotoxicity (ALT >1,000 U/L) followed a single dose <12 g, 21 of them in regular alcohol abusers. Time to N-acetylcysteine was the dominant risk factor: mortality was 0.42% (95% CI 0.05-2.7) when time to NAC <12 h, rising to 6.1%, 13%, and 19% at >12, >24, and >48 h, with corresponding rates of hepatic encephalopathy of 1.3%, 12%, 25%, and 38%. Chronic alcohol abuse was an independent risk factor for HE (OR 4.21; 95% CI 2.42-7.32) and mortality (OR 3.52; 95% CI 1.78-6.97); acute alcohol ingestion was protective for HE (OR 0.40) and mortality (OR 0.12), mainly in chronic abusers. Age was a risk factor for HE and death/orthotopic liver transplantation. No sex-specific differences or effect of other drugs were found.

Time to onset after dasatinib initiation was compatible, the course after dasatinib discontinuation was suggestive of drug-induced hepatitis, extensive investigations found no other cause, and zopiclone was excluded as a cause because it was continued uneventfully. This was the first reported case of acute liver injury associated with dasatinib.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, usually as a result of deliberate overdose, is described as the most common cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the United Kingdom and has also recently become so in the United States, confirming acetaminophen as a human DILI-causing agent. The study reviews outcome of orthotopic liver transplantation in 548 patients admitted with severe acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severe hepatotoxicity cohort referred to a single transplant center; injury typically followed deliberate overdose; patients selected by transfer criteria (progressive coagulopathy, INR >5, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, or renal failure).
raw_record.extra_details: 548 patients with severe acetaminophen hepatotoxicity admitted 1990-1996; 424 (77%) did not fulfill transplantation criteria (93% survived, 7% nonsurvivors); 56 of 124 not listed and 24 of 68 listed deteriorated before OLT; 44 of 124 listed underwent OLT with 33 (75%) surviving to discharge; clinical phenotype is acute liver failure (hepatic failure/necrosis) leading to consideration of liver transplantation; survival greatest with unreduced grafts; APACHE III scores used in decision making.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with metastatic renal cell carcinoma presented with new-onset nausea, decreased appetite, and jaundice, with abnormal liver profile testing (ALT 484 U/L, AST 277 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 562 U/L, total bilirubin 7.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL). He had started pazopanib six weeks prior; liver enzymes and synthetic function tests had been normal during this treatment. He denied significant acetaminophen use or herbal supplements. ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, anti-LKM-1, anti-mitochondrial antibody, ceruloplasmin, ferritin/iron profile, and viral hepatitis (A, B, C) testing were unrevealing. Liver biopsy showed a moderate portal-tract inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes with admixed eosinophils and neutrophils) and cholestasis without cirrhosis. The patient was diagnosed with pazopanib-induced hepatotoxicity and offered supportive care; he did not develop signs or symptoms of acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (indication), with metastasis to ribs, thoracic vertebrae, and pancreas.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity noted 6 weeks after starting pazopanib. Cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy with portal and lobular mixed lymphocytic and neutrophilic inflammation and mild steatosis. Labs evolution: ALT rose to 484 U/L (from 25) and improved to 183 U/L; total bilirubin rose from 7.9 to 16.1 mg/dL; INR 1.02-1.25. No acute liver failure. Discussion notes clinical-trial incidence of hepatotoxicity as high as 53%; differential consideration of Stauffer's syndrome (paraneoplastic cholestasis).

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is described as one of the most commonly ingested pharmaceuticals in overdose, and the commentary discusses risk assessment for hepatotoxicity following an acute acetaminophen overdose, using tools such as the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, Psi, and the acetaminophen aminotransferase product (APAP×AT) derived from the Canadian Acetaminophen Overdose Study (CAOS). Hepatotoxicity is defined as an aminotransferase of ≥1000 IU/L. The text explicitly attributes hepatotoxicity to acetaminophen in the supratherapeutic/overdose setting.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute acetaminophen overdose setting; injury assessed once NAC treatment is started (Psi and APAP×AT) or without treatment (Rumack-Matthew nomogram).
raw_record.extra_details: Acute overdose of the pharmaceutical. Hepatotoxicity defined as aminotransferase ≥1000 IU/L. Risk-assessment tools: Rumack-Matthew nomogram (predicts untreament risk); Psi (predicts hepatotoxicity risk once NAC started; median hepatotoxic Psi 16.5 mmol/L×h in non-alcoholics without ethanol co-ingestion); APAP×AT product >10,000 umol×IU/L² in 93 of 94 hepatotoxic acute-overdose patients (mostly late-presenting, delay to NAC ≥8 h). Ethanol co-ingestion lowered hepatotoxicity risk (Psi 27.1 mmol/L×h), whereas abstinent alcoholics had increased risk (Psi 4.79 mmol/L×h). Psi assumes a no-effect APAP threshold of 45 mg/L, hepatic glutathione reserves of ~6 h, and a 4 h elimination half-life. Acetaminophen (APAP).

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and states there is clear evidence that some individuals are at risk of significant hepatotoxicity even at paracetamol concentrations below standard treatment lines. It cites that in the largest series of paracetamol poisonings reported, 3 of 214 (1.4%) and 7 of 403 (1.7%) of individuals with concentrations below the US and UK treatment lines developed significant hepatotoxicity despite receiving acetylcysteine within 8 hours. The paracetamol nomogram indicates individuals are at risk of hepatic damage (and therefore warrant treatment) when the paracetamol concentration is above a line drawn between 200 mg/L at 4 hours and 30 mg/L at 15 hours on a log-linear graph.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity in overdose is dose-related; threshold dose in most patients is around 150 mg/kg. The treatment nomogram predicts hepatic damage risk when paracetamol concentration exceeds a line between 200 mg/L at 4 hours and 30 mg/L at 15 hours. At normal doses metabolism is largely (~95%) via sulphate and glucuronide conjugation; the remainder is oxidized by cytochrome P450 to the toxic intermediate N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which is normally reduced by glutathione; at toxic concentrations CYP metabolism increases and depleted glutathione allows the toxic metabolite to bind hepatic sulphydryl proteins and cause lipid peroxidation and cell death.

raw_record.support_text: A 40-year-old patient with pemphigus foliaceus, previously on high-dose corticosteroids, developed jaundice and pruritus three weeks after azathioprine was introduced at 100 mg daily (2 mg/kg/day). Liver tests showed marked elevations (AST 1080 IU/L, ALT 1140 IU/L, total bilirubin 415 µmol/L, ALP 301 IU/L, γGT 57 IU/L). Viral and autoimmune serologies were negative, and azathioprine-induced hepatitis was suspected; the drug was withdrawn and the icterus regressed with slow normalization of liver tests. The temporal relationship, rapid decrease after withdrawal, and exclusion of other causes were consistent with a probable azathioprine-induced hepatitis according to the Naranjo probability scale. The patient had low thiopurine methyl-transferase (TPMT) activity (4.58 nmol/h/ml RBC) and was heterozygous for the TPMT*3C mutant allele.

raw_record.support_text: Enalapril, an ACE inhibitor used for hypertension, is reported to have hepatotoxicity as one of its adverse effects, appearing from several days until 3 years after starting therapy. The authors report what they describe as the first case in the literature of Enalapril-induced ductopenia and cholestatic hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case report; abdominal ultrasonography showed cholelithiasis but no biliary ductal dilatation, so obstructive cholelithiasis was excluded as the cause.
raw_record.extra_details: 58-year-old man on Enalapril 20 mg/d for 2 years for hypertension; no prior liver disease, no transfusion/IV drug/alcohol abuse. Presented with progressive jaundice, abdominal pain, dark urine, anorexia. Elevated bilirubin (10 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase (382 UI/l), AST (286 UI/l), ALT (133 UI/l), GGT (215 UI/l). Negative viral/autoimmune serologies, normal hemochromatosis/Wilson's/α-1 antitrypsin work-up. First liver biopsy showed ductopenia, cholestasis, and centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis ('probably as a result of hepatotoxicity related to drugs'); bile duct-to-portal tract ratio 0.5 (normal 0.9-1.8). After Enalapril withdrawal symptoms and biochemistries improved in 20 days; readmitted 10 days later with severe jaundice (bilirubin up to 38.5 mg/dL, AP 540 UI/l) without aminotransferase rise, and second biopsy confirmed ductopenia.

The adverse effect occurred 2 years after starting Enalapril; a first episode of drug-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis was followed by severe prolonged cholestasis several days later. The authors regard hepatotoxicity of Enalapril as not dose-dependent and based on idiopathic late hypersensitivity.

Patient was placed on the waiting list for liver transplantation but was removed 40 days after discontinuation due to optimal resolution; jaundice disappeared within 2 months and liver function tests normalized in 6 months. Asymptomatic and biochemically normal at 2.5 years follow-up. Mechanism proposed as non-dose-dependent idiopathic late hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 20-year-old CML patient who developed recurrent hepatotoxicity with the use of imatinib, a frontline tyrosine kinase inhibitor. They note that severe hepatotoxicity, although uncommon, can occur with imatinib, tends to subside with dose reduction or cessation but can recur upon reintroduction, and recurrent severe hepatotoxicity mandates permanent discontinuation of the drug. Successful reintroduction of imatinib was achieved by adding corticosteroids.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 20-year-old woman with chronic-phase CML on oral imatinib 400 mg daily for 2 weeks at presentation. Elevated ALT 2364 IU/l, AST 1406 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 97 IU/l, total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dl; viral hepatitis profile negative. Hepatotoxicity is severe and uncommon, subsides with dose reduction or cessation, and recurs with reintroduction; recurrent severe hepatotoxicity requires permanent discontinuation. Corticosteroids (prednisone) enabled successful reintroduction of imatinib. Patient initially on hydroxyurea before imatinib.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was started on oral imatinib and developed imatinib-induced hepatitis. Because of the possibility of imatinib-induced hepatitis, imatinib was discontinued, leading to rapid resolution of clinical symptoms. On follow-up, liver function tests normalised over 3 weeks; imatinib was restarted but increased transaminases recurred after 1 week, and discontinuation again normalised liver function within 2 weeks. A rechallenge with oral imatinib 200 mg daily together with oral prednisone 25 mg daily was tolerated without liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: marked rise in transaminases (AST 1406 to 2364 IU/l during imatinib; ALT 2364 IU/l, AST 1406 IU/l), bilirubin 1.0-2.5 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase up to 131 IU/l; dechallenge resolved injury (ALT 95 IU/l at 3 weeks, ALT 83 at 2 weeks); positive rechallenge with imatinib 200 mg daily (ALT 654 IU/l, AST 332 IU/l after 1 week); tolerated upon rechallenge combined with oral prednisone 25 mg daily, then escalated to 400 mg daily with prednisone tapered over 8 weeks. Diagnosis was imatinib-induced hepatitis; histologically a drug-induced hypersensitivity/necrotic hepatitis with non-specific inflammatory infiltrate is described in the discussion.

raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), an antiviral nucleoside analogue tested against chronic hepatitis B virus infection, halted HBV in Hep G2 cells and in animals. However, in 1993, patients with chronic HBV infection treated with FIAU for 9.5 to 13 weeks developed signs of severe and, in some cases, fatal hepatotoxicity associated with lactic acidosis and multiple organ failures. Histopathology showed clear microvesicular steatosis in the liver and pancreas, now known to be due to mitochondrial DNA damage disturbing the electron transport chain; this outcome was not seen in preclinical studies in mice, rats, woodchucks, dogs, or cynomolgus monkeys.

Outcome was not seen during preclinical animal studies in mice, rats, woodchucks, dogs, and cynomolgus monkeys.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that the major drawback of INH-PZA therapy is the hepatotoxicity of PZA (pyrazinamide). Among 114 cases treated for 1–25 months, treatment was discontinued in 16 because of an asymptomatic rise in BSP retention, in one the serum alkaline phosphatase rose while BSP was normal (BSP being the more sensitive index of PZA hepatitis), three had unequivocal clinical evidence of hepatitis, one had a BSP rise with slight anorexia and nausea, and one became jaundiced after six weeks on PZA and died within 48 hours (though his liver showed only cellular infiltration and no necrosis, and this death with jaundice was considered doubtful as truly PZA-related; hepatic necrosis was noted as a uniform finding in the approximately five or six other fatal PZA hepatotoxicity cases reported). Upon withdrawal of PZA there was a rapid return to normal hepatic function tests in both the clinically involved and the abnormal-liver-function-only groups.

raw_record.extra_details: 114 cases treated 1–25 months; total hepatotoxicity 22/114 (19%). Onset ranged from ~0.5 to 10 months of treatment. BSP retention was the most sensitive index of PZA hepatitis (16 abnormal BSP only; 1 abnormal SAP only; 3 abnormal BSP with jaundice and/or hepatomegaly; 1 abnormal BSP with hepatic symptoms; 1 questionable hepatic death). Two with abnormal liver function received only 1.5 g PZA daily; liver biopsy was negative in one such case despite markedly abnormal function tests. Withdrawal of PZA led to rapid return of hepatic tests to normal. Approximately 5–6 additional fatal PZA hepatotoxicity cases were reported via personal communication, with liver cell necrosis a uniform finding. Rate data from the literature (Table VI) show cumulative totals of 39/1629 cases with jaundice and/or hepatomegaly.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of probable efavirenz-induced vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) in a patient with HIV. The Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale was used to assess drug causality and yielded a total score of 7 (probable). The VBDS was assessed as secondary to the efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (Atripla) therapy, and the cause was narrowed to efavirenz because the patient had previously tolerated emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate without hepatotoxicity. VBDS was confirmed by liver biopsy (ductopenia), ruling out other causes such as Hodgkin lymphoma, infection, autoimmune disease, and primary biliary cirrhosis.

VBDS confirmed on liver biopsy by ductopenia. Received ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol) and cholestyramine for cholestasis/pruritus management but progressed to end-stage liver disease and required liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In a 56-year-old woman taking citalopram (Cipramil) 20 mg/d for 3 weeks who presented with weakness, jaundice, and hepatomegaly, an acute hepatic injury developed while on treatment. Authors state the causal association with citalopram can be established based on a temporal relationship between drug administration and hepatic injury that was subsequently histologically confirmed, and the patient rapidly improved after the drug was stopped, with complete normalization of liver tests within 3 months. Histology showed subacute liver dystrophy and liver cell necrosis consistent with drug-induced liver injury.

Peak serum iron level (340 µg/dL) was lower than the reported hepatotoxic threshold (>1,700 µg/dL), yet rapid and significant elevations in aminotransferases (>4,000 U/L), total bilirubin (5 mg/dL), and prothrombin time (50 s) occurred within 48 hours; tests for acetaminophen, hepatatrophic viruses, and other causes of acute liver injury were negative, and the patient had a full recovery.

raw_record.support_text: Ultrastructural changes were observed in 23 consecutive patients who died from fulminant hepatic failure, including 12 due to paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose. Fatal fulminant hepatitis was characterised by massive confluent necrosis. In the paracetamol overdose (non-viral) cases the most prominent ultrastructural features were modification of the endoplasmic reticulum with enlarged attached polyribosomes, breakdown of the plasma membrane, accumulation of cytoplasmic amorphous material, and karyorrhexis and karyolysis of nuclei.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol overdose) resulting in fatal fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 12 of 23 consecutive patients who died from fulminant hepatic failure were attributed to paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose; patients died with grade IV coma/encephalopathy within 8 weeks of clinical illness. Non-viral (paracetamol overdose) cases showed prominent modification of endoplasmic reticulum with enlarged attached polyribosomes, plasma membrane breakdown, accumulation of cytoplasmic amorphous material, and karyorrhexis and karyolysis of nuclei, distinguishing them from viral fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents hepatocytes in paracetamol-overdose-induced fulminant hepatitis, describing breakdown of the plasma membrane, disarrangement of individual hepatocytes, deposits of amorphous material, and relatively intact endoplasmic reticulum. In the Discussion, all liver biopsies with fatal fulminant hepatitis showed massive confluent necrosis, and paracetamol-induced cases showed ultrastructural features (resistant endoplasmic reticulum, retained polyribosomes, karyorrhexis/karyolysis with release of nuclear contents) unlike viral cases, with most human biopsies taken ~72 h after onset of symptoms.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure resulting in fatal fulminant hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases were fatal, with massive confluent necrosis, collapse of the reticulin framework and hepatocyte drop-out on light microscopy. Ultrastructurally, paracetamol-induced necrosis differed from viral cases: the endoplasmic reticulum resisted vesiculation even at the expense of plasma-membrane fragmentation/dissolution, polyribosomes remained attached to cisternae throughout the necrotic process, and nuclei undergoing karyorrhexis/karyolysis released contents into the cytoplasm, contributing to accumulation of amorphous material. Human biopsies were mostly taken ~72 h after symptom onset, in contrast to experimental animal observations at 6-24 h. In specimens where excessive alcohol intake was suspected, considerable fatty change was also seen in addition to paracetamol-induced changes. Earlier non-specific changes and the timing of deaths are discussed.

raw_record.support_text: Plasma samples were collected from acetaminophen (APAP) overdose patients. ALT and ASS were measured in healthy volunteers (n=6), APAP overdose patients with normal liver test results (n=9), and APAP overdose patients with abnormal liver test results indicating liver injury (n=13). In the abnormal-liver-test group peak ALT was 4,382 ± 668 U/L, peak prothrombin time was 60.4 ± 12.7 seconds, and survival was 85%, establishing that APAP overdose caused clinically severe liver injury and associated mortality in these human patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: APAP overdose (supratherapeutic exposure)
raw_record.extra_details: Of 13 APAP overdose patients with abnormal liver tests indicating liver injury, survival was 85% (15% mortality), peak ALT 4,382 ± 668 U/L, and peak prothrombin time 60.4 ± 12.7 s. The paper's main focus is argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) as an early plasma biomarker of active liver injury; ASS rose in all patients and declined faster than ALT. The paper notes that therapeutic APAP use can elevate serum ALT in some people without other signs of liver injury or progression to disease. Supporting animal data from APAP-treated mice showed early increases in ASS before ALT; the rat was judged unsuitable for APAP hepatotoxicity studies.

After infusion her transaminase levels increased dramatically (ALT up to 427 U/L, AST up to 712 U/L initially), amiodarone was stopped, and hepatic injury due to intravenous administration of amiodarone was diagnosed; other causes of enzyme elevation (hepatic ultrasonography and viral serologies) were normal. Pre-amiodarone transaminases normal (ALT 3 U/L, AST 16 U/L); post-infusion peaks reached ALT 1952 U/L and AST 9912 U/L (day 3), with GGT 64 IU/mL, LDH 5913 U/L, PTZ-INR up to 2.4, total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL, and blood ammonium 142 µg/dL. raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old patient treated with doxycycline (100 mg/d) for bacterial bronchitis for one week developed malaise, jaundice, markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST 4670 U/L, ALT 5350 U/L, bilirubin 226 µmol/L) and impaired liver function (INR 1.45). After exclusion of viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease and paracetamol intoxication, the authors concluded that doxycyclin-induced liver damage seemed to be probable. Thirteen years earlier the patient had a similar jaundice episode with elevated liver enzymes after intake of doxycycline (100 mg/d), suggesting repeat doxycycline exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Doxycycline 100 mg/d for one week for bacterial bronchitis. First exposure episode 13 years earlier produced jaundice (total bilirubin 224 µmol/L) and elevated liver enzymes (AST 309 U/L, ALT 763 U/L); liver histology then showed portal lymphoplasmacellular and eosinophilic inflammation with slight bile duct epithelial lesions. Current episode progressed to acute liver failure (AST 2134 U/L, ALT 2820 U/L, INR 3.0, bilirubin up to 380 µmol/L) with renal failure and hepatic encephalopathy; liver biopsy showed severe cholestasis and 40% liver cell necrosis; patient underwent liver transplantation (MELD 40). Explanted liver revealed giant cell hepatitis with severe cholestasis and siderosis, incomplete micronodular cirrhosis with perisinusoidal and porto-central fibrosis. Extensive workup negative for viral hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, EBV, HIV, autoimmune hepatitis (ANA, SLA, LKM, SMA, AMA, pANCA), ferritin/transferrin saturation hemodromatosis (C282Y, H63D negative), Wilson's disease, alpha1-antitrypsin, and paracetamol intoxication.

raw_record.support_text: Because of uncertainty about the patient's liver disease, methyldopa rechallenge was performed as a diagnostic test, with 250 mg three times a day started on September 12, 1972. Eight days after beginning methyldopa, her SGOT rose to 325 Karmen units per ml and SGPT to 500 Karmen units per ml; the medication was stopped immediately and transaminase activity returned to pretreatment levels. Rechallenge with methyldopa 250 mg three times a day reproduced transaminase elevation (SGOT 325, SGPT 500 Karmen units/ml) after 8 days, resolving on discontinuation. raw_record.support_text: Sitaxentan (Thelin), a selective endothelin-A receptor antagonist marketed for pulmonary arterial hypertension, was withdrawn worldwide in December 2010 after severe, apparently idiosyncratic liver toxicity that included four deaths and one case of liver transplantation (the introduction cites eight deaths). Some reported cases were characterized by elevated bilirubin levels with histological evidence of lymphocytes and eosinophils, typical of idiosyncratic liver toxicity. The paper investigates whether this idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity can be rationalized by formation of a reactive ortho-quinone metabolite via P450 3A4-mediated bioactivation.
raw_record.extra_details: Marketed as Thelin in several European countries and Canada for pulmonary arterial hypertension; withdrawn worldwide by Pfizer in December 2010. The abstract reports four deaths and one case of liver transplantation from severe liver toxicity, while the introduction reports eight deaths from severe liver toxicity, both attributed to withdrawal. Some cases showed elevated bilirubin with histological evidence of lymphocytes and eosinophils. Sitaxentan has a 1,3-benzodioxole ring undergoing demethylation to an ortho-catechol metabolite that oxidizes to a reactive ortho-quinone; P450 3A4 shows time-dependent inhibition; sitaxentan appeared to have a lower incidence of liver function test abnormalities than bosentan.

raw_record.support_text: The COMT inhibitor tolcapone is an effective adjunctive agent for motor fluctuations in levodopa-treated patients. In clinical trials, elevated liver enzymes were notable in tolcapone-treated patients and regulatory agencies required frequent liver enzyme testing as a condition for drug approval. After approximately one year on the market, three cases of fatal hepatotoxicity and one case of reversible severe liver injury were attributed to tolcapone. Later reports described three additional cases of severe hepatocellular liver injury (including one with hepatocellular jaundice, one after 3 years of treatment, and one developing 17 months after starting), as well as less severe cases with SGPT/ALT or SGOT/AST elevations three times the upper limit of normal; the majority of these elevations were transient, asymptomatic, and resolved spontaneously (median time to elevation 81 days, median duration 22 days).
raw_record.extra_details: Adjunctive agent for motor fluctuations in levodopa-treated patients with Parkinson disease. Clinical trials showed elevated liver enzymes, and regulatory agencies required frequent liver enzyme monitoring as a condition of approval. After ~1 year on market, three fatal hepatotoxicity cases and one reversible severe liver injury were attributed to tolcapone. In these four cases recommended liver-monitoring guidelines were not followed, and in two cases the drug was continued despite clear clinical evidence of hepatic dysfunction. Consequence: 7-year marketing suspension in Europe and Canada and a US black box warning; tolcapone currently carries a black box warning in all countries on the risk of hepatotoxicity. Over a decade later, no further tolcapone-induced hepatic fatalities, but three additional reports of severe hepatocellular injury: one case of hepatocellular jaundice (duration unknown), one severe hepatocellular injury after 3 years, one developing hepatotoxicity 17 months after starting. Olanow and Watkins reported less severe cases with SGPT/ALT or SGOT/AST three times ULN; majority transient, asymptomatic, spontaneously resolved; median time to elevated levels 81 days, median duration 22 days.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatal case in a 16-year-old Indian girl treated with ethionamide 500 mg daily; jaundice appeared ~11 months after ethionamide started (November 1964 to November 1965), progressed to coma, death 4 days after readmission. Post mortem hepatic failure due to acute necrosis of the liver with severe centrilobular cellular necrosis, collapse of reticulin, periportal cholestasis and mononuclear/eosinophil/neutrophil infiltrate. Final admission liver tests: SGOT 700-1000 units, SGPT up to 1150 units, bilirubin 21.3-26.4 mg/100 ml, alkaline phosphatase 28 King Armstrong units, prothrombin time 35 sec vs control 12 sec. Authors note ethionamide hepatitis is clinically and pathologically indistinguishable from acute viral hepatitis; earlier reports documented hepatotoxicity that reversed on withdrawal with resumption at full dosage possible, and a few cases demonstrated a relapse after reintroduction (Pernod 1965). Only two prior published fatalities from ethionamide-associated hepatitis (Nagasawa 1964).

The clinical course supported the conclusion that hepatotoxicity should be suspected in any patient taking ethionamide who complains of persistent nausea and vomiting, even before frank jaundice and bilirubinaemia develop.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatal case report: 500 mg daily ethionamide with persistent nausea, anorexia and vomiting for about a week before admission; necropsy showed acute hepatic necrosis (H&E sections, PLATE VI). No stigmata of generalized hypersensitivity in the fatal illness. Prior literature: Conn et al. 1964 review found ~5% incidence of jaundice with ethionamide (range 0 to over 20% per other authors); two previously recorded Japanese cases of acute liver failure and death (Nagasawa et al. 1964) plus >10% jaundice incidence reported by those authors; French workers (Pernod 1965; Taquet et al. 1965; Cottin et al. 1964) found low jaundice incidence. Jaundice causation supported by rechallenge techniques and reversal on drug withdrawal (Mouldring 1962; Pernod 1965). Authors recommend withdrawing ethionamide promptly if persistent anorexia, nausea or vomiting develops.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 52-year-old woman with paranoid schizophrenia who developed hepatotoxicity on clozapine. Approximately 1 week after starting titration (clozapine 25 mg AM / 75 mg PM) she developed abdominal pain and malaise with elevated ALT (75 IU/L) and AST (198 IU/L). Clozapine was discontinued after 8 days; LFTs peaked the next day (ALT 308, AST 119, GGT 78 IU/L), then improved by day 5 and normalized by 4 weeks. On rechallenge with slower titration, LFTs remained normal for 1 month, then on clozapine 100 mg AM / 250 mg PM she had elevated AST 44, ALT 107, and GGT 37 IU/L that persisted despite a 50 mg dose reduction; she was asymptomatic. Clozapine was discontinued with subsequent normalization of LFTs.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1. First episode: abdominal pain and general malaise, ALT 75 IU/L (ref 10-40), AST 198 IU/L (ref 10-42); clozapine discontinued after 8 days; day after discontinuation ALT peaked at 308, AST 119, GGT 78 IU/L (ref 0-35); after 5 days off drug ALT 77, AST 24, GGT 53; normal at 4 weeks; abdominal ultrasound normal. Rechallenge: after ~1 month normal LFTs, on clozapine 100 mg AM/250 mg PM elevated AST 44, ALT 107, GGT 37; remained elevated despite 50 mg dose reduction; asymptomatic with normal physical exam; discontinued with normalization, ALT slightly elevated at 64. raw_record.support_text: The authors report a patient who had two episodes of severe hepatic dysfunction after two separate exposures to disulfiram, with liver biopsies showing extensive hepatocellular necrosis and no evidence of active alcoholic liver disease. Although they note that conclusive proof of a causal role would require rechallenge in a hospital setting, the extent of hepatic necrosis and the unpredictable effects of further exposure precluded rechallenge, and they describe the close temporal relation between disulfiram exposure and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Two episodes of severe hepatic dysfunction after two separate exposures to disulfiram. Re-exposure at a rehabilitation center within 4 days produced jaundice and recurrent injury, effectively a rechallenge. First admission labs: bilirubin 43.0 mg/dl, SGOT 1650 nm/ml, alkaline phosphatase 220 nm/ml, LDH 504 nm/ml, SGPT 801 nm/ml; SGOT decreased to 278 nm/ml by day 4. Second episode: bilirubin 25.0 mg/dl, SGOT 1245 nm/ml, SGPT 407 nm/ml, LDH 397 nm/ml, alkaline phosphatase 211 nm/ml. Transcostal liver biopsies showed mononuclear cellular infiltrate, hepatocellular necrosis, Councilman-like bodies, and (second biopsy) bridging necrosis; no steatosis or hyaline degeneration. HBsAg negative by radioimmunoassay; hepatitis A antibodies (immune electron microscopy) absent; G6PD activity normal; hemoglobin A on electrophoresis. Recovery occurred over ~3 months after each exposure. Authors note a similar but less severe case reported by Keeffe and Smith.

raw_record.support_text: The study examined records of patients admitted to the Freeman Liver Unit, Newcastle-upon-Tyne, UK, and patients registered in the UK for liver transplantation for paracetamol hepatotoxicity between October 1995 and December 1999. Severity data, defined by overdose characteristics and O'Grady criteria, were obtained from records of patients admitted to the Freeman. Paracetamol overdose is the causal setting of the hepatotoxicity examined.
raw_record.extra_details: 117 of 120 patients referred to the Freeman had severity data; 170 patients were listed for liver transplantation with UKTSSA for paracetamol hepatotoxicity. Median overdose dose of paracetamol was 35 g (IQR 24-50) before September 1998 and 25 g (20-54) after. Preparations taken in overdose included paracetamol alone (76% before/91% after), co-codamol (29%/18%), and co-proxamol (6%/0%). Severity was defined by O'Grady criteria; maximal severity during stay included elevated creatinine, prolonged prothrombin time, low pH, and encephalopathy (39% before/32% after). 107 (91%) patients received N-acetyl-cysteine before transfer to the Freeman. The study examined the effect of 1998 UK legislation restricting paracetamol pack sizes on referral rates.

In a retrospective study of 127 Thai patients with acute paracetamol overdose treated with the standard 21-h intravenous NAC regimen, 13 patients (10.2%) developed hepatotoxicity, and the psi toxicokinetic parameter ([APAP]₄h and time-to-NAC) was statistically significantly predictive of hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: 13 of 127 patients (10.2%) developed hepatotoxicity. Median (IQR) [APAP]₄h was 267.8 (196.0-380.0) mg/L and median (IQR) tNAC was 8.5 (6.2-12.0) h. [APAP]₄h, tNAC, and psi were significant univariate predictors of hepatotoxicity. The psi parameter (a toxicokinetic composite reflecting exposure to the hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI before NAC) was a reliable prognostic tool and possibly superior to acetaminophen level or time-to-NAC. raw_record.support_text: A phase I trial of indicine-N-oxide was carried out in 12 children with solid tumors and 16 with leukemia, using parenteral doses of 5, 6, and 7.5 g/m² as a 15-min infusion every 3 weeks. In leukemia, the maximum tolerated dose was 6.0 g/m² and hepatotoxicity was dose-limiting; half of the children with leukemia showed elevations in transaminase levels and one child died of massive hepatic necrosis. The abstract states that this hepatotoxicity limits the use of indicine-N-oxide in children with leukemia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatotoxicity was limited to children with leukemia in this study; population was pediatric patients with solid tumors or leukemia refractory to standard therapy, all of whom had prior chemotherapy and had not received chemotherapy in the 2 weeks before treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Indicine-N-oxide (NSC 132319, INO) is a naturally occurring, water-soluble pyrrolizidine alkaloid from Heliotropium indicum, given intravenously as a 10-15 min infusion every 3 weeks. Dose-limiting toxicity in solid-tumor patients was myelosuppression with MTD 7.5 g/m²; in leukemia, MTD was 6.0 g/m² with hepatotoxicity dose-limiting. Half of the children with leukemia showed transaminase elevations (graded per Pediatric Oncology Group criteria); one child died of massive hepatic necrosis, resulting in one fatality. Antineoplastic activity was limited to a transient reduction in circulating leukemic cells. This hepatotoxicity limits the use of indicine-N-oxide in children with leukemia.

raw_record.support_text: A woman with type 2 diabetes (BMI 24.2) on gliclazide 80 mg/day, troglitazone 400 mg/day, pravastatin 10 mg/day, aspirin 81 mg/day and levothyroxin 100 µg/day presented with liver dysfunction: AST 223 U/l (normal 13–33), ALT 422 U/l (normal 6–30), alkaline phosphatase 397 U/l, and γ-GTP 204 U/l. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune markers and drug allergy workups (DLST, patch tests for troglitazone, pravastatin, aspirin, gliclazide, levothyroxin) were negative. Troglitazone was withdrawn and liver tests improved (AST 36, ALT 43) by 4 weeks; a biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis around the central vein, mild lobular infiltration and portal inflammation/fibrosis compatible with protracted acute hepatitis, reported as troglitazone-induced liver dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with elevated liver chemistries (ALT 653 U/L, AST 413 U/L, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dl) that appeared 5 months after beginning troglitazone therapy, in the absence of other prescription medications, alcohol, viral hepatitis, or autoimmune markers. She was told to stop troglitazone. The paper collectively reports this as part of 'troglitazone hepatotoxicity' in two patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient continued taking troglitazone in error after initially instructed to stop; 4 weeks later aminotransferases further elevated with increased total bilirubin and prothrombin time and decreased albumin, and she appeared jaundiced/icteric. Urgent liver biopsy showed zone 3 necrosis with hemorrhage and hepatocyte dropout, occasional foci of bridging necrosis to triads, active cell injury (acidophilic bodies, cell swelling, lobular disarray), minimal macrovesicular steatosis, mild non-prominent cholestasis, enlarged Kupffer cells, diffuse mononuclear infiltrate, and early pericentral and bridging fibrosis on trichrome stain. Histology reflected severe hepatocellular injury; improvement (decreased aminotransferases and bilirubin, normal prothrombin time) occurred within 18 days after stopping troglitazone with oral vitamin K supplementation.

raw_record.support_text: A 22-year-old man treated with ciprofloxacin 2×250 mg daily for 7 days during a skin infection presented 14 days after intake with nausea and jaundice, and laboratory findings showed the typical pattern of acute liver failure (AST 907 U/l, ALT 890 U/l, AP 180 U/l, reduced PT-time 40%, bilirubin 16.9 mg/dl). Serology for viral hepatitis and autoimmune/mitochondrial antibodies was negative, there was no history of liver disease, alcohol, blood transfusion, or other medication, and liver biopsy revealed extensive hepatocellular necrosis involving zones 3 and 2 of hepatic acini with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils. A diagnosis of ciprofloxacin-associated hepatitis was rendered and the patient improved rapidly on methylprednisolone.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of ciprofloxacin-induced acute hepatitis with extensive hepatocellular necrosis (zones 3 and 2) and mixed inflammatory infiltrate with abundant eosinophils; patient improved after corticosteroid (methylprednisolone) therapy and was discharged asymptomatic 8 days after admission. Authors note up to that time 14 cases of ciprofloxacin-associated liver injury were documented in the literature, with a direct causal association proven in only 2; ciprofloxacin can reportedly produce three histological patterns (pure hepatocellular cholestasis, zone 3 hepatocellular necrosis, or mixed pattern); most cases improved on cessation, while two resulted in fulminant hepatitis and death; mean time from drug start to injury 6.3±5.9 days. One additional case of chronic cholestatic liver disease occurred ~6.5 months after treatment with ciprofloxacin and ornidazol.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a series of nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) cases (11 cases) and compares their imaging, histology, and clinical features with minocycline-induced AIH cases. Radiological changes were evident in 8 of 11 (73%) of the nitrofurantoin-induced AIH cases, showing mild atrophy, signs of cirrhosis (atrophy with portal hypertension such as ascites), coarsening of liver architecture, or confluent fibrosis/massive fibrotic bands, although cirrhosis was not confirmed histologically.
raw_record.extra_details: 11 nitrofurantoin-induced AIH cases reported. 8/11 (73%) had jaundice at presentation; all were treated with immunosuppression. AIH likelihood scores were at least 'probable' in all cases with complete data. Histology: higher inflammatory grade (Batts-Ludwig grade 3, median), interface hepatitis 3.0, lobular hepatitis 3.0, confluent necrosis 6/10, rosette formation 6/9; lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in 10/10. Imaging abnormalities in 73% of cases, including liver atrophy, cirrhosis-like appearance (not histologically confirmed), and confluent fibrosis/massive fibrotic bands seen only in nitrofurantoin patients (Figs. 1-3). One patient had a right-lobe mass considered secondary to nitrofurantoin-induced liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin can lead to a broad spectrum of liver injury with mild liver test abnormalities, acute liver failure with fatal outcome, or need for liver transplantation, and also liver cirrhosis. It was recently found to be one of the most common single agents associated with drug-induced liver injury (DILI) in a prospective study in the United States, and has been documented to induce autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH). Zone 3 necrosis was observed in the DIAIH cohort. All current-series DIAIH cases with laboratory parameters scored at least 'probable' by the new simplified AIH criteria.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Most patients had been treated for a long period with the drug (median duration 24 months in the nitrofurantoin-induced AIH cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Broad spectrum includes mild liver test abnormalities, acute liver failure with fatal outcome, need for liver transplantation, and liver cirrhosis. Zone 3 necrosis observed in DIAIH cohort. Identified as one of the most common single agents associated with DILI in a recent prospective US study. Severe imaging abnormalities (low attenuation patches, confluent fibrosis and massive fibrotic bands) seen in 8/11 (73%) nitrofurantoin DIAIH cases. Inadvertent rechallenge reported to induce chronic liver injury and severe liver injury 17 years after an initial hepatitis-like illness. Cases scored at least 'probable' by simplified AIH criteria. Favorable prognosis in current DIAIH series; no cirrhosis found at presentation or on follow-up.; qualifying_conditions_note: None

raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes most of the severe histological liver changes seen in psoriatic patients treated with methotrexate to the treatment. Nearly half of methotrexate-treated patients had hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis (46%), with mild to moderately severe fatty change in all but two of those, a combination uncommon in the U.K. except in alcoholic liver disease; no patient had a history of alcoholism and features of alcoholic hepatitis were consistently absent. These changes are said to be similar to those previously attributed to methotrexate in psoriasis and other conditions.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic treatment in patients with severe psoriasis.
raw_record.extra_details: In the methotrexate-treated group, 7 (19%) had cirrhosis and 10 (27%) had fibrosis; 46% had fibrosis or cirrhosis overall. Bromsulphthalein retention was inadequate as a diagnostic test: one patient who had discontinued methotrexate four months previously had normal bromsulphthalein retention (4%) but established cirrhosis on biopsy. Of 20 methotrexate-treated patients without cirrhosis or fibrosis, all but three showed more severe fatty change, nuclear vacuolation, and inflammation than the untreated group.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two cases of early-onset, nefazodone-induced acute liver failure presenting as early as 4 weeks after initiation of therapy, following prior reports associating nefazodone (Serzone) with the development of liver failure as soon as 6 weeks after therapy began. raw_record.support_text: Patient 2 was a 46-yr-old man who developed progressive fatigue and jaundice within 4 wk of starting nefazodone for work-related anxiety and depression, progressing to acute liver failure with marked coagulopathy and elevated enzymes/bilirubin. Transjugular biopsy showed massive centrilobular parenchymal necrosis extending to portal tracts; the patient improved upon nefazodone discontinuation, with coagulopathy correcting over 2 wk and liver enzymes normalizing over 3 months. raw_record.support_text: Marsilid (iproniazid) jaundice closely resembles viral hepatitis, with acute diffuse hepatocellular disease indicated by positive flocculation tests, hyperbilirubinemia, and considerable elevations in serum glutamic oxalacetic (SGOT) and glutamic pyruvic (SGPT) transaminases, while serum alkaline phosphatase and total cholesterol were elevated only slightly or not at all. The highest transaminase values observed in patients in whom Marsilid was reasonably suspected to cause jaundice were 357 units SGOT and 514 units SGPT (colorimetric method). The authors consider the hepatotoxicity produced by this drug a distinct problem from chlorpromazine jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Marsilid is the brand name for iproniazid. Jaundice closely resembled viral hepatitis with acute diffuse hepatocellular disease; positive flocculation tests (cephalin-cholesterol flocculation, thymol turbidity, 18-hour turbidity ratio, gamma globulin), considerably elevated SGOT and SGPT (highest 357 and 514 units, colorimetric); alkaline phosphatase and total cholesterol elevated only slightly or not at all. Mortality of jaundice from this drug reported as about 20% in over 100 cases. A fatal case treated with 100 mg daily (reduced to 50 mg daily 14 days before jaundice onset) died 12 days after jaundice onset with acute necrosis of the liver at autopsy. Histology in the authors' patient showed massive necrosis of liver cells. Summary notes the relative lack of emphasis in the literature on jaundice, and especially its possibly fatal outcome, from iproniazid administration.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with amiodarone-induced liver injury, which led to liver failure. Computed tomography revealed a gradual increase in hepatic density over a long period following initiation of amiodarone. Despite discontinuation of the drug, the patient developed hepatic encephalopathy and subsequently died, which the authors attribute to the drug's extended half-life causing persistent end-organ damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Vaughan-Williams class III antiarrhythmic used for atrial fibrillation. The molecular structure includes iodine; hepatic accumulation increases hepatic density on CT, which correlates with blood level of desethyl-amiodarone metabolite. 74-year-old woman; oral amiodarone 200 mg started perioperatively (after mitral valvuloplasty for severe mitral regurgitation) and continued after discharge; referred ~6 years later for elevated liver enzymes. Also taking atorvastatin (10 mg), vonoprazan (20 mg), diltiazem (90 mg), and warfarin (1 mg); no drinking/smoking. Patient progressed to liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy and died despite drug discontinuation, reflecting amiodarone's extended half-life; authors recommend lowest effective dose and annual liver function monitoring.

raw_record.support_text: The paper discusses the mechanism of amiodarone-related hepatic toxicity, including accumulation in hepatic macrophage lysosomes forming drug-lipid complexes that injure the hepatocyte lipid bilayer, and inhibition of mitochondrial β-oxidation with hepatocyte apoptosis leading to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). The present patient was presumed to have developed burned-out NASH. The paper also presents 11 human cases (10 prior reports plus the present case) of amiodarone-induced liver injury with increased hepatic density on CT during chronic amiodarone therapy, including deaths, and cites patients diagnosed with amiodarone-induced liver cirrhosis.

raw_record.extra_details: Total of 11 attributed human cases (10 prior reports 2005-2023 plus the present 2024 case); 3 cases had a fatal outcome (cases 6, 9, 11). Clinical phenotypes include non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)/burned-out NASH, amiodarone-induced liver injury, and amiodarone-induced liver cirrhosis (30 reported cirrhosis cases 1970-2012 reviewed). Injury manifests with elevated AST/ALT, increased hepatic CT density (iodine-rich amiodarone, 37% iodine by weight). Proposed mechanisms: lysosomal drug-lipid complex formation injuring hepatocyte lipid bilayer and inhibition of mitochondrial β-oxidation with reactive-oxygen activation and hepatocyte apoptosis. Metabolite desethyl-amiodarone also accumulates in liver and its blood concentration was measured but is not independently attributed as the injuring entity.

raw_record.support_text: Idiosyncratic drug-induced fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) is reported after clarithromycin use with exclusion of known causes of FHF. In this case the biopsy was consistent with drug-induced toxicity, other causes of FHF were absent, and the patient had no preceding liver dysfunction. Fever, eosinophilia, eosinophilic infiltration on biopsy, and a 1-week sensitization period support an immunologically mediated idiosyncratic reaction, and nonzonal panacinar necrosis is characteristic of an idiosyncratic phenomenon. The authors conclude the idiosyncratic drug reaction leading to FHF was associated with clarithromycin exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient developed FHF within 72 h; peak enzymes LDH 3529 U/L, ALP 1095 U/L, AST 2255 U/L, ALT 1974 U/L; total bilirubin rose to 33.4 mg/dl, unconjugated bilirubin 0.0 mg/dl, PT 21 s, activated PTT 51 s. Transjugular biopsy showed moderate cholestasis and microvesicular steatosis with increased eosinophilic infiltrate in portal tracts and hepatic lobules, ballooning degeneration and occasional hepatocyte dropout, no bile duct injury. Progressive encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hemodynamic instability, metabolic acidosis, and respiratory failure; terminal extubation on day 13. Same paper notes clarithromycin reported associated with cholestatic hepatitis in a patient treated for Mycobacterium chelonae lung infection, and that the manufacturer reports mild LFT elevations in <1% of patients. Acetaminophen-associated FHF was not supported (see separate record).

raw_record.support_text: In this report on the hepatotoxicity of sulphamethoxypyridazine, a 34-year-old woman developed jaundice while taking a combination of sulphamethoxypyridazine and sulphamethizole for a urinary tract infection. On oral test doses, sulphamethoxypyridazine caused a similar rise in serum aspartate and alanine aminotransferases as the combination of the two sulphonamides, confirming sulphamethoxypyridazine as the causal agent of the hepatitis, whereas sulphamethizole produced no reaction. Liver biopsy showed nonspecific changes pointing to reactive hepatitis without intrahepatic cholestasis.

raw_record.extra_details: Four cases of sulphonamide hepatitis occurred within 11 months in a single non-hepatology clinic, suggesting the condition is more common than generally thought. raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatotoxicity is a known consequence of iron overdose and that iron poisoning leads to periportal hepatic injury by free radical generation and lipid peroxidation. Two pediatric patients with intentional (suicidal) ferrous sulfate overdose rapidly developed fulminant hepatic failure severe enough to require liver transplantation despite deferoxamine treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 17-year-old female ingested 10 pills ferrous sulfate (23 mg/kg elemental iron), serum iron 1000 µg/dL at 2h and 670 µg/dL at 4h; INR rose to 6.6 by 20h and >13; AST 2000 U/L, ALT 2424 U/L, total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL; developed Grade 1-2 then Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy and lactic acidosis; treated with deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour for 24h, intravenous N-acetylcysteine, and CVVH; emergent living-donor left lobe liver transplant 4 days post-ingestion; explant histology showed diffuse parenchymal collapse, severe cholestasis and massive hepatic necrosis compatible with toxin-induced liver injury; recovered, well at 1 year. Treatment discussion includes cimetidine as a potential cytochrome P-450 inhibitor, but no human DILI claim for cimetidine.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of liver injury induced by warfarin in a 64-year-old woman taking long-term warfarin 4.5 mg/day for anticoagulation after mechanical mitral valve replacement. Stopping warfarin (with vitamin K1, artificial liver support, and antioxidant/anti-inflammatory liver therapy) improved the elevated liver enzymes and hyperbilirubinemia. The discussion refers to 'warfarin-induced liver failure' and notes that warfarin-induced acute liver injury has rarely been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 64-year-old woman after mechanical mitral valve replacement on warfarin 4.5 mg daily for about 10 years. Presented with ecchymosis and black stool; INR exceeded 10.0 and rose to 3.48; elevated ALT, AST, total/direct/indirect bilirubin, and total bile acids. Injury improved after warfarin discontinuation with vitamin K1, glutathione, polyene phosphatidylcholine, ademetionine 1,4-butanedisulfonate, ursodeoxycholic acid, and artificial liver support; patient transferred to ICU. Warfarin was restarted (2.5-3.75 mg qd) with no significant enzyme/bilirubin elevation, and the patient discharged on day 24. Authors note warfarin-induced acute liver injury is rarely reported and recommend timely warfarin discontinuation and INR adjustment to reduce warfarin-induced liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old woman with concurrent squamous cell carcinoma of the anus and renal cell carcinoma developed severe hepatotoxicity while receiving paracetamol at recommended dosage (4 g daily) under medical supervision in hospital, without enzyme-inducing agents. She was severely malnourished and had recently fasted. Four days after starting paracetamol her ALT rose to 269 IU/L and AST to 252 IU/L; the next day she had nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort and tender hepatomegaly, with ALT 5920 IU/L, AST 4875 IU/L, bilirubin 30 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 169 IU/L, prothrombin time 20 s (control 13 s) and blood glucose 2.3 mmol/L.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Severe malnutrition, weight loss and a recent ~20 h fasting period at therapeutic exposure; 53-year-old female hospitalized with concurrent anal squamous cell carcinoma and renal cell carcinoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Diagnosis of severe paracetamol-related hepatotoxicity based on highly typical enzyme pattern, with differential diagnosis of ischaemic liver injury excluded (no hypotension) and other medications considered unlikely; treated with N-acetylcysteine and glucose, normalizing over 4 weeks; hepatitis and other viral/metabolic/immune/her metastatic causes excluded. Authors attribute injury to glutathione depletion and shunting of metabolism from glucuronidation to microsomal oxidation producing N-acetyl-p-benzoquinonimine (NAPQI), and conclude the injury is dose-dependent rather than idiosyncratic; a later interval of lower-dose paracetamol (1.3-2.6 g daily up to three times weekly) after a further fasting period produced no liver injury. Patient was not encephalopathic and recovered.

The hypothesis is strongly supported by highly elevated levels of chromium in the liver biopsy (>10x the maximum normal value), and the daily chromium dose was lower than in the two previously published chromium poisoning cases (600 and 2000 µg/day over 5–6 months). Simultaneous ingestion of botanical products (E. arvense and R. purshiana, containing 0.0006% and 0.0022% Cr³⁺ respectively) was considered a possible cofactor for the elevated hepatic chromium.

raw_record.support_text: Zinc phosphide (ZnP)-containing rodenticide poisoning is recognized as a cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in India. Records of 41 patients admitted to a single centre with ZnP-induced ALF were reviewed to identify prognostic indicators (INR 9 vs 3, MELD 41 vs 24) for the requirement of liver transplantation; group I comprised patients transplanted (n=14) or who died without transplant (n=8), and group II survived without transplantation (n=19).

raw_record.extra_details: Rodenticide paste (Ratol) containing zinc phosphide; entity is the chemically defined active ingredient ZnP. ZnP poisoning presents in three phases: gastrointestinal symptoms at 2-6 h, transient abatement 12-24 h with moderate transaminase rise but normal bilirubin/INR, then ALF at 3-6 days; 14 patients underwent liver transplant and 8 died without transplant. MELD score of 36 (sensitivity 86.7%, specificity 90%) or INR of 6 plus encephalopathy (sensitivity 100%, specificity 83%) predicted mortality. Encephalopathy occurred only in group I.

Children becoming symptomatic during treatment had features of veno-occlusive disease (VOD) or acute transaminitis, while those presenting after completion of treatment showed insidious chronic hepatic parenchymal involvement in the form of nodular regenerative hyperplasia and portal venous hypertension. The paper also frames the cohort as '6-TG-induced hepatic injury' and '6-TG-induced hepatoportal complications' with 107.25 patient-years of follow-up.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children) treated for acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL); hepatoportal toxicity diagnosed during or after completion of maintenance therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort provides long-term follow-up of 6-TG-induced hepatic injury previously reported from the institute, with two additional children; total 107.25 patient-years of follow-up. During-treatment presentation featured VOD or acute transaminitis; post-treatment presentation featured nodular regenerative hyperplasia and portal venous hypertension, with 100% persistent hepatoportal involvement in the late-presentation group versus 50% in the early-presentation group. Possible explanations offered include longer maintenance duration in boys and unrecognized gender differences in 6-TG metabolism independent of TPMT (which is not sex-linked).

raw_record.support_text: Across idelalisib clinical trials, serious hepatotoxicity occurred in 109/760 (14%) patients, with one fatality (1/1192) in a patient receiving idelalisib in combination with ofatumumab in an ongoing phase 3 trial; the cause of death was determined to be acute liver failure, and the patient also had grade 4 sepsis at the time of death. Most (74%) patients with ALT/AST elevation resumed idelalisib at a lower dose without recurrence, while 26% had recurrent ALT/AST elevation despite the lower dose.
raw_record.extra_details: Serious, including fatal, hepatotoxicity reported in idelalisib-treated patients. ALT/AST elevations >5x ULN usually within first 12 weeks of treatment, mostly reversible with dose interruption. Across clinical trials serious hepatotoxicity occurred in 109/760 (14%) with 1 fatality (1/1192) attributed to acute liver failure in a patient receiving idelalisib plus ofatumumab (grade 4 sepsis present at death). In the relapsed CLL phase 3 trial (idelalisib + rituximab, n=110) any-grade ALT/AST increase was 35%/25% (placebo group 10%/14%) and grade 3-4 elevations 8%/5% (placebo 1%/0%). In iNHL patients on idelalisib 150 mg monotherapy (n=146), any-grade ALT increase was 50% (grade 3 in 14%, grade 4 in 5%) and AST in 41% (grade 3 in 8%, grade 4 in 4%); transaminase elevations were a common cause of interruption/discontinuation (10%). Residual elevations led to dose reduction; 26% recurred despite lower dose. US prescribing information advises against concomitant use with other hepatotoxic drugs and mandates ALT/AST monitoring (every 2 weeks for first 3 months, then every 4 weeks for 3 months, then every 1-3 months; weekly for ALT/AST >3x ULN; withhold idelalisib at >5-20x ULN and resume at reduced 100 mg BID once levels <=1x ULN; permanently discontinue if >20x ULN).

In patients with hepatocellular injury, postingestion APAP concentrations were not predictive of 'probable' toxicity per the Rumack-Matthews nomogram in 14% (mild) and 11% (severe) of cases. Mechanism (p10-11): APAP is bioactivated to NAPQI by hepatic cytochromes P450; NAPQI covalently binds protein thiols, disrupting enzymes/regulatory pathways and initiating an inflammatory cascade via interleukin-8, producing hepatocellular injury at the site and time of NAPQI formation.

This is the causal agent in a retrospective inception cohort of 92 patients with acute, severe, symptomatic valproate-induced hepatotoxicity drawn from the International Registry for Adverse Reactions to Valproate.

raw_record.extra_details: 92 patients with acute, severe, symptomatic valproate-induced hepatotoxicity from the International Registry for Adverse Reactions to Valproate (123 potential patients reviewed). Acute onset heralded by nonspecific symptoms such as lethargy, nausea/vomiting, or worsening seizures. Mechanism attributed to direct mitochondrial disruption and proposed drug-induced carnitine deficiency. Outcome assessed as hepatic survival, combining deceased and liver transplant patients as terminal hepatic failure; 48% of 42 L-carnitine-treated patients survived vs 10% of 50 patients on supportive care only (p<0.001); all 10 patients diagnosed in <5 days and treated with IV L-carnitine survived. L-carnitine was the treatment being evaluated, not a cause.

raw_record.support_text: The study reviewed paracetamol overdose presentations to the Austin and Repatriation Medical Centre in Australia. It reports that paracetamol overdose can cause paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure and that the annual rate of paracetamol-induced fulminant hepatic failure remained steady at about two cases per year despite an increase in overdose incidence. It concludes that serious liver injury remains uncommon but that paracetamol overdose is an established cause of fulminant hepatic failure, with the level of serious injury kept low possibly due to improved medical management and increased use of NAC.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurs in drug overdose (paracetamol poisoning); the most important predictor of significant liver damage was delay between overdose and presentation for treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: In Victoria, incidence of fulminant hepatic failure due to paracetamol poisoning estimated at <0.4 cases/million people/year with 3 deaths over 7 years (0.07 deaths/million/year), compared with up to 2.8 deaths/million/year in the UK. Fewer than 10% of local community patients presenting developed significant hepatotoxicity (ALT > 1000 IU/L) and none developed hepatic encephalopathy. Two patients developed severe liver toxicity despite early presentation and apparently adequate NAC treatment. 19% of fulminant patients had not been treated with NAC at the referring institution. Significant hepatotoxicity defined as ALT greater than 1000 IU/L.

raw_record.support_text: In patients with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (AALF), abundant CCR2⁺ and S100A9⁺ pro-inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages were found in portal tracts. These findings were obtained from AALF patients who required liver transplantation, corroborating that monocyte-derived macrophage-related pro-inflammatory responses contribute to detrimental liver injury. Increased serum CCL2 levels in ALF patients were also reported to predict an unfavorable prognosis (death or need for emergency liver transplantation) following APAP intoxication.
raw_record.extra_details: AALF patients analyzed required liver transplantation; APAP intoxication (overdose) resulted in acute liver failure with unfavorable prognosis (death or need for emergency liver transplantation) predicted by increased serum CCL2. Portal tracts showed abundant CCR2⁺/S100A9⁺ pro-inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages, in contrast to CD163⁺ and CD68⁺ resident macrophages not restricted to portal tracts. NAC administration is the only pharmacological strategy for APAP-induced liver injury, dampening initial metabolic injury but without benefit at later stages. Mechanism of action in mice and men: MoMF enhance hepatic inflammation after extravasation early after injury and contribute to resolution/repair at later times via maturation into restorative Ly-6C<sup>low</sup> MoMF; neutrophils and HMGB1-TLR4-IL23a-IL17a axis are involved in early injury.

Case 2: ALAT 5011 U/L, ASAT 9301 U/L, LDH 9376 U/L, INR 2.0; resolved with recovery by D14. The presented case is attributed to halothane: the patient developed fulminant hepatic failure after cholecystectomy with halothane anesthesia, had serum antibodies reacting with halothane-exposed rat liver microsomal proteins and CYP2A6, and died, with autopsy refused.

raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure with total bilirubin 14.3 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 8.0 mg/dl, AST 14,493 U/l, ALT 6,564 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 691 U/l, INR 5.6, blood pH 7.09, base deficit -22 mEq/l, lactate 18.6 mm; stage three hepatic encephalopathy developed and the patient died 10 days after cholecystectomy. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 46-year-old woman with advanced GISTs who developed hepatotoxicity 11 days after initiation of imatinib mesylate (400 mg daily). Before therapy her liver function tests were normal; she had no risk factors for viral or alcoholic liver disease, imatinib was her only regular medication, and she had not used acetaminophen or over-the-counter medications. One week after imatinib discontinuation her liver function tests improved significantly, and the report confirms early-onset imatinib mesylate-induced liver failure in patients treated for GISTs.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of 46-year-old woman with advanced (relapsed) c-kit-positive GIST treated with imatinib mesylate 400 mg daily; hepatotoxicity developed 11 days after starting therapy, presenting with 2 days of nausea and weakness (no jaundice, fever, or abdominal pain). Labs: ALT 2520 UI/L, AST 1845 UI/L, alkaline phosphatase 192 UI/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.3, INR 1.6. Abdominal CT showed mild diffuse fatty liver changes; ultrasound normal. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C all negative; no acetaminophen or herbal/OTC use. Liver tests began to decrease after imatinib discontinuation and were nearly normal 1 week later. Paper frames this as acute fulminant hepatitis/acute liver failure. Background context supplied: hepatotoxicity observed in ~2%–5% of patients in clinical trials (mostly mild transaminase elevation; grade 3–4 transaminase elevation in 1%–5%, grade 3–4 bilirubin elevation 0.4%–3.5%, usually resolving after dose reduction/interruption within 1–4 weeks); 5 deaths from hepatic failure reported (4 during CML treatment, 1 during polycythemia vera treatment); in the Demetri et al phase 2 trial of 147 GIST patients, abnormal liver function tests occurred in 5.4% and fatal liver disease in 0.3%. Reported histopathology varies from periportal necrosis with mixed lymphocyte/neutrophil/plasmocyte infiltration to massive hepatic necrosis or cytolytic acute hepatitis. Authors recommend early and continued surveillance of liver function tests.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic histopathology was studied in 77 patients who met clinical criteria for halothane hepatotoxicity. A spectrum of histologic patterns was identified, ranging from panlobular and multifocal spotty necrosis resembling viral hepatitis through submassive confluent zonal necrosis to massive necrosis. Progression of severity of injury from spotty to massive necrosis was more closely related to multiple exposures to halothane (especially repeated exposure within less than three months) than to the extent of the associated surgical procedures.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen is safe at therapeutic doses, but overdoses (most from suicide attempts) produce toxic blood levels and a four-stage clinical course including hepatotoxicity. Symptoms begin within 7 to 14 hours; after 24 to 48 hours SGOT, SGPT, bilirubin, and prothrombin time rise, with peak hepatotoxicity at 72 to 96 hours and SGOT levels of 20,000 I.U. not unusual. N-acetylcysteine is the treatment of choice.

raw_record.extra_details: Clinical course follows four distinct stages: nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, and anorexia within 7-14 hours; rising SGOT, SGPT, bilirubin, and prothrombin time at 24-48 hours; peak hepatotoxicity at 72-96 hours with SGOT levels of 20,000 I.U. not unusual. First described in 1966 by Davidson; UK series include Proudfoot and Wright (37 patients), Clark et al (60), James et al (54), and Crome et al (31). N-acetylcysteine reduces morbidity and mortality when given within the first 16 hours after overdose; oral N-acetylcysteine is the drug of choice in the US, intravenous used in England and Europe. Suspected mechanism involves minor metabolites formed by the P-450 mixed function oxidase pathway.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old East Indian woman treated with flutamide, 250 mg orally twice daily, for hirsutism developed severe jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools about 6 weeks after starting the drug. raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) is well-known to cause hepatotoxicity, described as its most concerning adverse effect, and has been shown to cause asymptomatic transaminase elevation and frank liver injury. In the 1970 Capitol Hill outbreak investigation, 19 of 2321 TB contacts treated with INH developed hepatotoxicity, including two deaths, with no cases in a matched control group. A subsequent USPHS surveillance study of nearly 14,000 persons taking INH identified 174 (1.3%) probable and possible cases of INH hepatotoxicity, including eight deaths; age (>35 years) and daily alcohol consumption were associated risk factors.
raw_record.extra_details: INH used to treat latent TB infection (LTBI). A meta-analysis of six studies (including the Capitol Hill investigation, the USPHS surveillance study, and the Eastern European IUAT trial) with >38,000 INH-treated persons found 0.6% overall developed hepatotoxicity (range by study 0-2.9%). More recent observational studies with routine monitoring reported lower incidence: Seattle (~11,000 patients) 0.1% and San Diego (~3,800 patients) 0.3%, with no deaths and one hospitalization. Risk factors for INH hepatotoxicity: age >35 years and daily alcohol consumption. INH also causes asymptomatic transaminase elevation and frank liver injury; peripheral neuropathy (<0.2%, preventable/treated with pyridoxine) is a separate adverse effect.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of fatal hepatitis associated with troglitazone. An 85-year-old man with type 2 diabetes developed severe hepatic dysfunction after troglitazone therapy (started 5 months prior, increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks); abdominal pain, malaise and jaundice developed and alanine aminotransferase reached 608 U/L. A diagnosis of troglitazone-induced hepatitis seemed likely, symptoms progressed to confusion, agitation, ascites and edema, and liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis; the patient died 8 weeks after presentation. The paper notes that in rare cases troglitazone use is associated with fatal hepatotoxicity and that news of six deaths and one liver transplantation led to withdrawal of the product from the British market.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 85-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes; co-medication with insulin, metoprolol, and levothyroxine during the episode.
raw_record.extra_details: Troglitazone dosed at 400 mg/day for about 5 months; initial ALT 608 U/L then 287 U/L (normal 10-45), total bilirubin 15.6 mg/dL (normal 0.1-1.1), albumin 2.5 g/dL, normal prothrombin time, glycosylated hemoglobin 5.2%; serology negative for hepatitis A, B, C; normal hepatic ultrasonogram; liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis (lobular, cholestatic hepatitis with areas of confluent necrosis); death 8 weeks after presentation; paper cites six deaths and one liver transplantation associated with troglitazone prompting British market withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in over 1000 patients in the Markers and Paracetamol Poisoning (MAPP) Study, miR-122 was a sensitive and specific biomarker of acute liver injury after acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose, which is described as the commonest cause of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) in the Western world. Testing of 192 human serum samples using a DCL assay accurately identified patients at risk of DILI after acetaminophen overdose (area under ROC curve 0.98, 95% CI 0.96–1, P<0.0001).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Attributed acute liver injury followed acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose; the paper does not specify injury outside the overdose setting.
raw_record.extra_details: miR-122 is reported as a hepatocyte-specific DILI biomarker elevated 100-1000 fold in acute liver injury compared with controls; MAPP Study cohort (>1000 patients) and 192 human serum samples evaluated with a single-molecule dynamic chemical labelling (DCL) assay (limit of detection 1.32 pM). Acetaminophen is also referred to by the alias paracetamol.
