raw_record.support_text: The paper evaluates the DCL assay for measuring miR-122 in clinical samples from the MAPP study, which prospectively recruited patients at risk of DILI due to taking an acetaminophen overdose that required treatment with the antidote acetylcysteine. In derivation and validation cohorts, the study reported that miR-122 predicted acute liver injury (pre-defined as peak ALT activity >100 U/L) at hospital presentation. In 192 sequential serum samples, patients who subsequently developed acute liver injury had higher miR-122 concentrations (median 35.8 pM) than those without injury (median 1.4 pM), indicating acetaminophen overdose as the cause of the liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol is an easily available and widely used analgesic that can cause serious hepatic injury when taken in overdose for a suicidal purpose. Five patients in whom serum paracetamol levels or the amount ingested were high enough to cause severe liver injury were treated with NAC and a molecular adsorbent recirculating system; four survived without liver transplantation and one died due to brain oedema. Paracetamol's reactive metabolite NAPQI covalently binds to liver cells causing hepatic injury and necrosis when glutathione conjugation capacity is exceeded, and hepatocyte necrosis usually develops within 3-5 days after ingestion.

raw_record.extra_details: 5 patients; NAC and MARS treatment started early; 4 survived without liver transplantation, 1 died due to brain oedema secondary to liver failure; lethal dose in Western people 15-25 g; risk estimated by Rumack-Matthew nomogram; hepatocyte necrosis develops usually within 3-5 days after ingestion; mechanism via reactive metabolite NAPQI covalently binding hepatocytes when glutathione conjugation capacity is exceeded; NAC is an antidote/source of cysteine precursor; mortality >90% without transplantation when King's College criteria met.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes five patients who took paracetamol overdoses of 17.5–45 g and developed imminent acute hepatic failure; they were treated with N-acetylcysteine and MARS albumin dialysis, four recovered without liver transplantation and one died. Paracetamol overdose is described as causing acute liver failure, with prognosis depending on the ingested amount and the time between ingestion and treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (17.5–45 g ingested). One patient also co-ingested 1800 mg codeine and was on chronic metoprolol and enalapril for hypertension.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol-overdose hepatic failure. Treatment comprised activated charcoal to reduce absorption, NAC to replenish hepatic glutathione, and supportive care; prognosis depended on the ingested amount and time to treatment. MARS albumin dialysis was used to support native-liver recovery and avoid liver transplantation. Of five overdosed patients, four recovered without transplantation and one died. Patient 1: 45 g overdose, high serum paracetamol levels (1731 µmol/l at 24 h, 922 µmol/l at 30 h, 540 µmol/l at 39 h after ingestion), grade I encephalopathy, anuria/oliguria needing haemofiltration, fulfilled high-urgent liver-transplant criteria, pH 7.22, Factor V 7%, thromboplastin time (TT) 18%.

raw_record.support_text: In all five patients studied, the ingested amount of paracetamol was high enough to cause severe liver failure and exceeded the amount considered a lethal dose. Three of the five patients fulfilled criteria for high-urgent liver transplantation (Scandiatransplant Organization, also meeting King's College criteria); of those three, two survived and one died. The two patients who did not fulfil the transplant criteria survived after MARS treatment was started before their condition deteriorated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose ingestion; case series of five patients with severe acute liver failure managed with MARS, with continuous haemodialysis also used.
raw_record.extra_details: Ingested amounts high enough to cause severe liver failure and exceeding the considered lethal dose. Three of five patients met high-urgent liver transplantation criteria (Scandiatransplant and King's College); one of these three died. Delay between paracetamol ingestion and NAC treatment was 4-100 h. Cell necrosis described as usually developing within 3-5 days after ingestion. Mechanism: NAPQI metabolite, if not conjugated by glutathione, binds to liver cell receptors causing hepatocyte damage (mechanistic only, not an independently causal entity).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in younger children, accidental paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity is described owing to error in dosage, contrasting with the common acute over-dosage seen in adolescents and adults as a suicidal gesture. The reported infant received 1565 mg paracetamol (233 mg/kg) over 36–48 hours, developed fulminant hepatic failure and hepatic encephalopathy/Reye's syndrome, had a serum paracetamol level of 91.1 mcg/ml, and was certified brain-dead 24 hours later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (infant) accidental overdose from dosing error; supratherapeutic dose of 233 mg/kg.
raw_record.extra_details: Accidental overdose: 1565 mg paracetamol over 36-48 hours (162.5 mg/5 ml suspension 5 ml every 6 hours plus 125 mg tablet every 6 hours alternating). Diagnosis of fulminant hepatic failure and hepatic encephalopathy/Reye's syndrome; treated with IV N-acetyl cysteine and intubation/ventilation. Serum paracetamol level 91.1 mcg/ml. Clinical course included recurrent seizures, refractory metabolic acidosis, hypoglycaemia and shock; certified brain-dead 24 hours later and support withdrawn. Recommended paediatric dose noted as 10-15 mg/kg/dose 4-6 hourly.

raw_record.support_text: Six technoparty participants (1 female, 5 males, ages 17-25) were admitted with severe colicky abdominal pain and subsequently developed hepatotoxicity after ingesting an alcoholic beverage spiked with a powdery substance they called MDA. All showed similar symptoms with identical time course: acute jaundice within 2 days, steadily increasing cholestasis enzymes reaching peak values of 800 U/L (AP) and 380 U/L (GGT) with only moderately elevated transaminases, and one-day fever episodes up to 40°C on days 5-7. Toxicological analysis confirmed p,p'-diaminodiphenylmethane (4,4'-methylenedianiline, CAS 101-77-9) at 130 mg/L in one of two urine extracts, and the conclusion indicates the participants had ingested the aniline derivative MDA (the cause of Epping Jaundice) rather than the amphetamine.

raw_record.support_text: In a single-center cohort of 101 patients with acute liver failure (ALF) presenting between January 2009 and December 2011, acetaminophen poisoning was identified as the cause of ALF in 54 cases (53.5%). The mean age of the cohort was 45.1 ± 15.2 years, 83 patients (82.2%) were female, and 9 of the 54 APAP-ALF patients (16.7%) had undergone prior weight loss surgery (WLS), compared with none among ALF from other causes.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen poisoning was attributed as the cause of ALF in 54 of 101 patients (53.5%). Nine of the 54 APAP-ALF patients (16.7%) had prior WLS (8 Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, 1 duodenal switch) versus none among non-APAP ALF cases. Among APAP-ALF patients, 63.0% used acetaminophen-opiate combination drugs; liver transplantation occurred in 3.7% and death in 14.8% of the APAP-ALF group. The proportion of prior WLS in the APAP-ALF group was over 25 times the estimated 0.7% prevalence of WLS in the US adult population.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase I study of ET-743 (trabectedin), pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic relationships were delineated for the main haematological and hepatic toxicities of ET-743. Both toxicities appeared to correlate with exposure to ET-743, and the risk of severe grades 3–4 hepatotoxicity increased at higher Cmax values. A referenced phase I study of ET-743 as a 24-h infusion similarly reported that the grade of transaminase elevation correlated with both the dose and AUC, and the 3-h infusion study in this report showed a similar pattern of haematological and biochemical hepatic toxicities.

raw_record.extra_details: Severe grades 3–4 hepatotoxicity risk rose with higher Cmax values; toxicity correlated with exposure to ET-743. Administered as 1650 µg/m² as a 3-h i.v. infusion (recommended phase II dose), and also studied as a 1-h and as a 24-h infusion; MTD for 1-h infusion was lower than for 3-h. Hepatic toxicity appeared to correlate with exposure and was described as biochemical hepatic toxicity with transaminase elevation.

raw_record.support_text: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was treated with oral troglitazone 200 mg daily for 10 months. He developed abdominal distention, jaundice and edema two weeks before admission and stopped troglitazone. Laboratory studies showed alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, ALT 318 U/L, AST 266 U/L, total bilirubin 36 mg/dL, and INR 2.02. He developed hepatorenal syndrome, hepatic encephalopathy and respiratory failure, and expired two weeks after admission, about 11 months after starting troglitazone. The paper attributes his fulminant hepatic injury to troglitazone.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a 58-year-old woman on atorvastatin who presented with altered liver tests and repeated epigastric abdominal pain over a year, with a mixed pattern of statin-induced liver injury. Liver biopsy revealed portal and lobular inflammation with cholangiolysis, and the patient's liver function tests normalized following cessation of atorvastatin therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In this pediatric case report, after an acute liver failure event during combined antifungal therapy, the authors judged isavuconazole to be the most probable cause of the acute liver failure, noting the well-known liver toxicity of azoles and specific reports of severe liver injury due to isavuconazole. Reintroduction of liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB) alone at 3 mg/kg was well tolerated, supporting isavuconazole as the culprit. A repeat liver biopsy one month after the event showed marked reduction of inflammatory cells, regenerative hepatocellular plates, and residual focal perivenular necrosis, consistent with progressive resolution of an acute hepatitis due to drug-related toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient with severe invasive fungal disease and cerebral involvement; isavuconazole given in combination with liposomal amphotericin B; acute liver failure occurred during the combined therapy and isavuconazole identified as the most probable culprit.
raw_record.extra_details: Isavuconazole was one component of combined antifungal therapy for invasive fungal disease (aspergillosis/mucormycosis context) in a child. Biopsy findings: marked lymphoplasmacellular inflammation in portal tracts, acinus, and around the terminal vein; follow-up biopsy showed reduced inflammatory infiltrate with reparative fibrosis around the terminal vein. Reintroduction of liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB, 3 mg/kg) was tolerated and antifungal treatment continued; treatment stopped after ~9 months with almost complete fungal infection regression. Authors note azole-mediated liver toxicity and scarce literature evidence of severe L-AMB liver toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from three patients with halothane hepatitis reacted with halothane-induced neoantigens in rat liver microsomes by immunoblotting: patient 1 recognized 100 kDa and 76 kDa neoantigens, patient 2 the 100, 76, 59 and 54 kDa neoantigens, and patient 3 the 57 kDa neoantigen. These neoantigens were shown to carry the trifluoroacetyl (TFA) hapten derived from halothane metabolism, establishing the immune response to halothane-modified liver proteins in humans.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is an immune-mediated form of DILI. Antibodies in the sera of halothane hepatitis patients recognize TFA-modified neoantigens (100, 76, 59, 54, 57 kDa) that are formed when the reactive CF3COX metabolite of halothane covalently binds liver microsomal proteins. The 59 kDa-TFA neoantigen was identified as a microsomal carboxylesterase glycoprotein (EC 3.1.1.1); antibodies reacted only negligibly with the native unmodified protein. TFA-lysine only partially inhibits antibody binding, indicating epitopes comprise the TFA hapten plus portions of the carrier protein. Similar TFA-labeled proteins were detected in the liver of a halothane-treated patient (100, 76, 59, 54 and 57 kDa forms), supporting relevance of the rat neoantigens to human halothane hepatitis. TFA labeling occurs via direct reaction of CF3COX with proteins; sodium trifluoroacetate, ethyl trifluoroacetate, and trifluoroethanol administered to rats produced no detectable protein labeling.

raw_record.support_text: After an acetaminophen overdose, the patient (Ms. A) developed hepatic failure and underwent liver transplantation 8 days after the overdose. Pathology of the excised liver showed 'subtotal central lobular hepatonecrosis with degenerative changes and severe cholestasis, compatible with acetaminophen overdose.' The authors note this is the lowest reported acetaminophen dose resulting in fulminant liver failure, with sensitivity explained by low body weight, malnutrition, and treatment with carbamazepine.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic failure developed and the patient underwent liver transplantation 8 days after overdose; explanted liver showed subtotal central lobular hepatonecrosis with degenerative changes and severe cholestasis. Reported as the lowest acetaminophen dose causing fulminant liver failure to date. Mechanism: small fraction metabolized by cytochrome P450 to toxic metabolites detoxified by glutathione; hepatonecrosis occurs when glutathione stores are depleted and toxic metabolites accumulate. Carbamazepine and fasting induce the P450 system, and low-protein diets reduce glutathione. Doses as low as 7500 mg have been shown to cause transient hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper studies patients admitted with acetaminophen poisoning who developed severe acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, some progressing to fulminant hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy and death. In a retrospective series of 220 patients with at least one galactose elimination capacity (GEC) measurement over a 10-year period, GEC was lower in patients with hepatic encephalopathy (14.5 ± 5.6 vs 23.2 ± 6.7 µmol/min/kg), higher in spontaneous survivors with encephalopathy than nonsurvivors, and independently associated with mortality. Patients with hepatic encephalopathy and GEC below 10 µmol/min/kg did not survive, establishing acetaminophen poisoning as a cause of severe human hepatotoxicity and fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Exposure was acetaminophen poisoning (overdose); patients presented with severe acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity including fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose causing fulminant hepatic failure (FHF). Study cohort of 220 patients with at least one galactose elimination capacity (GEC) measurement. GEC was associated with development of hepatic encephalopathy and with death; independent mortality association odds ratio 1.28 per 1 µmol/min/kg decrease in GEC (95% CI 1.14-1.45); GEC threshold of 16.5 µmol/min/kg for identifying nonsurvivors had sensitivity 90%, specificity 72%, PPV 49%, NPV 96%; none of 14 patients with hepatic encephalopathy and GEC < 10 µmol/min/kg survived. GEC was regarded too unspecific to be used alone for transplant candidacy selection. King's College Hospital criteria mentioned as accepted emergency transplant selection criteria.

raw_record.support_text: A 36-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes developed clinical evidence of jaundice, malaise, and crampy abdominal pain 4 months after starting troglitazone (increased from 400 to 800 mg/day); her liver function tests were normal before and 2 months after starting the drug. On presentation, total and direct bilirubin were elevated (127 and 100.8 µmol/l) and ALT was 2,040 mg/dl with normal alkaline phosphatase; viral, autoimmune, ceruloplasmin, and α1 antitrypsin work-up did not identify other causes. After troglitazone was stopped, her symptoms disappeared and liver tests normalized within several months. The authors state that the time course and improvement after withdrawal were consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity and that the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity, with no other viral or autoimmune cause identified.
raw_record.extra_details: 36-year-old woman with uncomplicated type 2 diabetes; troglitazone dosed 400 mg/day starting March 1997, increased to 800 mg/day in April 1997; jaundice developed about 4 months after initiation, 2 months after a normal 2-month liver-function check. On evaluation total and direct bilirubin 127 and 100.8 µmol/l (7.5 and 5.9 mg/dl), ALT 2,040 mg/dl, normal serum/leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, normal prothrombin time and INR, normal blood count and platelets; ANA and AMA negative, α1 antitrypsin normal, ceruloplasmin mildly elevated (61.0 mg/dl), hepatitis A/B/C panel nonreactive, iron/transferrin saturation normal. Symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized within several months of stopping troglitazone; concurrent use of insulin and later metformin; no other medications at time of hepatotoxicity, no alcohol use. Authors note a favorable dechallenge response consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Histological examination of liver tissue from 3 patients who died 6, 4, and 9 days, respectively, after an intramuscular injection of 3 ± 0.5 mg of hycanthone per kg of body weight for schistosomiasis showed features of a toxic hepatitis with massive hepatic necrosis, many acidophil bodies, minimal inflammatory response in 2 patients, and confluent necrosis with early fibrosis in 1; liver cells showed prominent fatty change. A follow-up liver biopsy in a 4th patient who had hycanthone hepatitis with liver failure 1 year before showed good recovery with chronic persistent hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: Hycanthone (trade name Etrenol) is the 4-hydroxymethyl derivative of lucanthone, given as a single intramuscular injection of 3 ± 0.5 mg/kg for mass chemotherapy of schistosomiasis (S. haematobium and S. mansoni). Three fatal cases (cases 1-3) showed toxic hepatitis with massive hepatic necrosis, acidophil bodies, minimal inflammatory response, fatty change, or confluent necrosis with early fibrosis; deaths occurred 9, 6, and 4 days after injection; two patients were jaundiced and one was comatose. A 4th patient who survived hycanthone hepatitis with liver failure showed good recovery with chronic persistent hepatitis on follow-up 1 year later. The paper also notes overt hepatitis documented by liver biopsy (1 case) and several earlier deaths attributed to severe hepatic necrosis. A transient rise in serum transaminases reported in other series is attributed by Cook et al. to damaged striated muscle at the injection site rather than liver damage.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present two patients with amiodarone-induced liver injury. In case 1, perivenular aggregates of granular cells are described as the earliest morphological manifestation of amiodarone hepatotoxicity, and on withdrawal of amiodarone the hepatic function tests became normal with complete recovery. In case 2, cirrhosis of the liver is reported as a rare complication of amiodarone treatment. The granular cells contained iodine, supporting the presence of amiodarone or a metabolite, and electron microscopy showed lamellar lysosomal inclusions consistent with known amiodarone hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Two patients: case 1 with subtle perivenular granular-cell foci and hepatic function test abnormality that normalized on amiodarone withdrawal with complete recovery; case 2 with liver cirrhosis (rare complication of amiodarone). Lysosomal inclusions (mainly lamellar) on electron microscopy; granular-cell cytoplasm contained iodine (presumptive evidence of amiodarone or a metabolite). Varma et al. described similar lysosomal bodies in two patients with mild increases in AST whose biopsies were essentially normal. Perivenular site is the main area of hepatocellular necrosis and fibrosis in amphophilic drug toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The development of hepatic toxicity in 4 individuals and the death of 3 in 1998, out of 60,000 patients treated with tolcapone, had a significant impact on its use. These patients were not monitored according to recommendations, and two were maintained on the drug after the diagnosis of hepatitis was made. These cases resulted in the withdrawal of tolcapone from the market in Europe and Canada and a black-box warning in the United States in 1998 requiring careful liver enzyme monitoring, patient consent, and use of tolcapone as a last resort.

raw_record.extra_details: 4 cases of hepatic toxicity and 3 deaths occurred among approximately 60,000 treated patients in 1998. raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose as a cause of fulminant hepatic failure, noting improved survival with intensive liver care yet persistently high mortality, and discusses liver transplantation after paracetamol overdose. In 66 patients admitted after paracetamol overdose, 6 were transplanted and 4 survived, and the authors concluded liver transplantation has a definite but limited role in fulminant hepatic failure induced by paracetamol. Earlier text states the early administration of NAC has improved the outcome of acetaminophen overdose and prevents massive hepatic necrosis probably by replenishing reduced glutathione and detoxifying the arylating metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinonimine; NAC is indicated when plasma acetaminophen exceeds the Rumack-Matthew nomogram or after single doses >150 mg/kg.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; two cases of severe paracetamol poisoning with late NAC administration and favorable outcome are reported, plus a review of acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure data.
raw_record.extra_details: Massive hepatic necrosis attributed to the arylating metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinonimine; NAC (oral or IV, 140 mg/kg loading then 70 mg/kg q4h over 72h) prevents hepatic necrosis by replenishing intracellular reduced glutathione. Nomogram risk line 200 ug/ml at 4h to 30 ug/ml at 15h. Outcome data in acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure: survival correlated with arterial blood pH <7.30, prothrombin >100s, creatinine >300 umol/l predicted poor prognosis; factor V <10% predicted adverse outcome (sensitivity 91%); 66 patients reviewed, 6 transplanted with 4 surviving. Reported as cause of fulminant hepatic failure with high mortality.

raw_record.support_text: APAP (acetaminophen), a commonly used analgesic, is known to cause acute liver injury in a dose-dependent manner. Between 1998 and 2016, DILI caused by APAP accounted for approximately 46% of all acute liver failure cases, with 28.5% of these cases resulting in death. When intake exceeds the liver's maximum metabolic capacity, excess APAP is metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes into the cytotoxic intermediate NAPQI, which is detoxified by GSH and, upon GSH depletion, forms protein adducts that drive hepatocyte oxidative stress.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose-dependent acute liver injury, commonly used analgesic. Between 1998 and 2016 APAP-induced DILI represented ~46% of all acute liver failure cases, with 28.5% resulting in death. Metabolism beyond hepatic capacity yields the cytotoxic intermediate NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) via cytochrome P450 enzymes; NAPQI is normally detoxified by GSH binding, and once GSH is consumed it covalently binds cellular proteins to form APAP protein adducts causing oxidative stress. Within safe dosage APAP is metabolized by glucuronidation and sulfation and excreted in urine. The paper also reports gender-specific susceptibility attributed to gut microbiota, considered a protective mechanistic and preclinical finding, not part of the attributed human causal claim.

raw_record.support_text: Four case reports of paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose are presented, each resulting in fatal or near-fatal acute liver failure. Case 1 was a 16 year old girl who ingested 20 paracetamol tablets (10 g), presented 4 hours after overdose with a serum paracetamol concentration of 156 mg/l, developed encephalopathy, elevated ALT (>7 500 IU/l), INR 6.3, and arterial pH 7.16, underwent total hepatectomy and liver transplant 36 hours later, but life support was withdrawn for no brain stem recovery. Cases 2-4 similarly followed paracetamol overdose (32 g, 25 g, 15 g) with acute liver failure and death on days 6, 10, and 15 after the overdose in cases 2, 3, and 4 respectively. Accompanying text notes that paracetamol overdose causes serious hepatotoxicity and rare fatal acute liver failure even when patients present within 10 hours with serum concentrations below the treatment line.

raw_record.support_text: In this cross-sectional observational multicenter study of 160 newborns from 159 pregnancies (88 exposed to nevirapine-based regimens and 71 exposed to protease inhibitor-based therapies during pregnancy), no cases of hepatotoxicity were observed according to the DAIDS Table for Grading. Two cases of ALT above normal values (2.8%; 95% CI: 0.3-9.8%) occurred in patients not exposed to nevirapine and one case (1.1%; 95% CI: 0.0-6.1%) in the nevirapine-exposed group (P = .585). The authors concluded that HAART regimens including nevirapine administered during pregnancy do not involve a higher risk of liver disease compared to other treatment combinations.

raw_record.support_text: In this comparative cohort of HIV-exposed pregnant women receiving antiretroviral therapy, no cases of hepatotoxicity were detected per the DAIDS Grading Table, and no cases of severe hepatopathy occurred in either the NVP-exposed or the non-exposed group. The identified ALT elevations (3 of 160 patients, 1.9%) were mild, self-limited, and asymptomatic, with no significant difference between groups (1 case in the NVP-exposed group, 1.1%, vs 2 cases in the non-exposed group, 2.8%, p=0.585), leading the authors to conclude that nevirapine exposure was not associated with hepatic injury.

raw_record.extra_details: Comparative cohort of HIV-exposed pregnant women (76 mothers on NVP, 48 not on NVP; 160 newborns). Mean maternal ALT 19.8 vs 20.1 UI/l (p=0.778); ALT>40 UI/l in 1.1% NVP-exposed (95% CI 0.0-6.1%) vs 2.8% non-exposed (95% CI 0.3-9.8%), p=0.585. All ALT elevations normalized spontaneously (at 4, 16, and 52 weeks of life). No grade 1-4 DILI per DAIDS Grading Table; systematic review by McKoy et al. of 3,074 exposed newborns reported only scarce grade 3-4 hepatopathy without differences by gestational NVP duration (prevalence 0.79% short vs 1.10% long).

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity, commonly due to APAP overdose (APAPo), is described as the most common identifiable cause of Acute Liver Failure (ALF) in both children and adults. The paper states that liver injury due to APAP toxicity occurs when inherent detoxification mechanisms - including conjugation with glutathione - are overwhelmed, resulting in reactive oxygen species that form destructive adducts with intracellular proteins; N-acetylcysteine (NAC) repletes glutathione stores and is the established treatment for acute APAP toxicity. The APAP overdose group is also noted as predominant within the NIH Pediatric Acute Liver Failure (PALF) Study cohort.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (PALF study population); injury occurs in the context of acetaminophen overdose (acute ingestion).
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury results when inherent detoxification (glutathione conjugation) is overwhelmed, forming reactive oxygen species that produce destructive adducts with intracellular proteins. NAC (N-acetylcysteine) repletes glutathione and is the established treatment for acute APAP toxicity. Acetaminophen overdose was the predominant etiology in the NIH Pediatric Acute Liver Failure Study cohort, including 13 survivors with APAPo who received NAC and 12 non-survivors. HMGB1 is released from necrotic cells and acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern in APAP-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-yr-old female with advanced follicular thyroid carcinoma was started on sorafenib as third-line treatment and, about six weeks later, presented with rapidly rising serum transaminases (AST 1,724 U/L), bilirubin (22 mg/dL), and INR 2.9 with beginning liver failure. Laparoscopically assisted liver biopsy showed fatty liver disease with early cirrhosis and histologically severe drug-induced necrotic hepatitis, attributed to sorafenib. Steroid therapy (prednisolone 1 mg/kg) rapidly reduced liver inflammation and normalized AST within 10 days, although the patient later died as a consequence of gastric ulcer perforation.

raw_record.support_text: Because the patient's earlier liver disease seemed possibly related to aspirin, she was admitted and challenged with aspirin beginning at 3.0 g/day, increased to 4.5 g/day on day 4. SGOT and SGPT began rising on the sixth day of aspirin therapy, continuing to rise the next day until aspirin was discontinued; peak SGOT and SGPT were 420 and 378 units/litre respectively. The transaminases dropped the day after therapy was stopped, and liver tests were normal one week later, having remained normal over 7 months. A liver biopsy taken earlier (after aspirin dose reduction) was interpreted as compatible with chronic active hepatitis.

raw_record.extra_details: 25-year-old woman (N.I.H. #09-40-57-4) with SLE. Prior to referral, while on aspirin 2-3 g/day then 4 g/day (serum level 25 mg/100 ml) she had SGOT 1690 U/litre, alkaline phosphatase 130 U/litre (normal 30-80), total bilirubin 0.2 mg/100 ml, sulfobromophthalein retention 27% at 45 min. When aspirin was reduced to 1.8 g/day transaminases and alkaline phosphatase markedly improved. On rechallenge peak morning salicylate level was 20 mg/100 ml; bilirubin remained normal; alkaline phosphatase was slightly elevated. Liver biopsy showed hepatocellular unrest, anisocytosis/anisonucleosis, ballooned hepatocytes, scattered minute foci of necrosis with lymphocytic infiltrate, periportal sinusoidal acidophilic (Councilman) bodies, periportal plasma-cell/neutrophil infiltrate, early stellate periportal fibrosis, portal inflammation with plasma cells, lymphocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils, and two portal lymphoid follicles with reactive germinal centers; interlobular bile ducts and portal vessels unchanged. Findings consistent with chronic active hepatitis. Rechallenge reproduced transaminase elevation with prompt recovery on discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that the realization that cyclophosphamide (CY) is the primary cause of sinusoidal liver injury caused by myeloablative conditioning regimens came from several observations: CY is a component of the most hepatotoxic myeloablative regimens; in vitro hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells are injured by CY metabolites generated within hepatocytes; damage to the liver microcirculation is central to post-transplant hepatic dysfunction; and there is patient-to-patient variability in CY metabolism with a relation of aberrant metabolism to toxicity. A prospective study of 147 patients receiving myeloablative CY (120 mg/kg) plus total body irradiation (12-13 Gy) found 23 (16%) developed moderate or severe sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS); exposure to the CY metabolite O-carboxyethyl-phosphoramide mustard (CEPM), whose AUC varied 16-fold, was statistically significantly related to SOS, bilirubin elevation, non-relapse mortality and survival, with the highest CEPM-exposure quartile carrying a sixfold higher risk of non-relapse mortality.

raw_record.extra_details: Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (formerly veno-occlusive disease) presents with hepatomegaly, fluid retention/weight gain, and elevated serum bilirubin in the first 20-30 days after transplant; onset before day +20. CY metabolites injure hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells in vitro; CEPM AUC varied 16-fold and highest-quartile exposure conferred a sixfold higher non-relapse mortality risk. Metabolic variability (notably CEPM) was not related to engraftment or tumour relapse. Case fatality rate of SOS reported as relatively constant at 15-20% across centres.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes cases of propylthiouracil-induced hepatic injury and notes that clinically significant hepatotoxicity is a distinctly uncommon complication of propylthiouracil therapy, despite widespread use of the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Propylthiouracil is a thionamide used since 1946 to manage hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease). Hepatotoxicity is a rare side effect compared with more common rash, urticaria, arthralgia, fever, and transient leukopenia (1%-5%) and agranulocytosis (0.2%-0.5%). The author reports a new case (32-year-old woman) and reviews previously reported cases, noting that hepatic injury is rare but must be considered whenever hepatic dysfunction develops during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Valproate-induced hepatotoxicity is described as rare, but often fatal, and is attributed to direct disruption of mitochondrial processes. It is heralded by nonspecific symptoms such as lethargy, nausea/vomiting, or worsening seizures, and occurs more frequently in at-risk populations such as mentally retarded individuals, young children, and those taking multiple drugs. One proposed mechanism is drug-induced carnitine deficiency.

raw_record.support_text: This study examined the largest series of paraquat toxicity in the literature, finding that toxic hepatitis was very common (46.5%) after paraquat exposure, but the spectrum of toxic hepatitis in these patients seemed mild and transient. None of the paraquat patients died of hepatic complications; acute respiratory failure was the most common cause of death after paraquat ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings relate to intentional (poisoning) paraquat ingestion, an overdose setting; treated with gastric lavage, activated charcoal and magnesium citrate, charcoal haemoperfusion and steroid/cyclophosphamide in many cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 187 paraquat-poisoned patients, of whom 87 (46.5%) developed toxic hepatitis. Hepatitis symptoms appeared in the first week; peaked at 9.5 ± 8.8 days after exposure (2.8 ± 5.5 days after onset), resolving within 17.3 ± 9.8 days. ALT was within 3N in 44.8%, 3N-10N in 43.7%, and >10N in 11.5% of cases; maximum ALT 1116 U/L. In 13.8% of hepatitis patients there was hyperbilirubinemia without ALT elevation; maximum total bilirubin 16.3 mg/dL. No patient died of hepatic complications; mortality did not differ between hepatitis and non-hepatitis groups (56.3% vs 53.0%), and acute respiratory failure was the most common cause of death. Toxic-hepatitis patients had longer hospitalization (16.2 ± 14.6 vs 11.2 ± 16.2 days) and more renal failure (75.9% vs 56.0%). Younger age was a borderline protective factor (OR 0.981 per year, 95% CI 0.962-1.000, P=0.051).; confidence_note: None

raw_record.support_text: A 35-year-old man from China with a two-year history of Graves' disease presented with progressive jaundice. He had taken methimazole (MMI) and was diagnosed on admission with GD overlapping with chronic hepatitis B and MMI-induced liver injury with early stage of acute-on-chronic liver failure. Liver biopsy on day 43 of hospitalization showed HBsAg on hepatocyte membranes and typical histopathological features of autoimmune hepatitis, and he was finally diagnosed with GD overlapping with chronic hepatitis B, MMI-induced liver injury, and AIH.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had underlying Graves' disease, chronic hepatitis B, and subsequent autoimmune hepatitis overlap; unresolved co-suspects for liver injury include HBV and possible AIH, and whether MMI or HBV triggered AIH is explicitly left open.
raw_record.extra_details: Case details: 35-year-old man from China; prior MMI course discontinued one year earlier due to liver toxicity and taken again for ~6 days 20 days before hospitalization, with a 10-day history of progressive jaundice. Elevated aminotransferase and bilirubin persisted despite correction of liver failure and control of HBV replication (oral entecavir) and hyperthyroidism (single oral 131-iodine). Liver biopsy on day 43 showed HBsAg on hepatocyte membranes and typical AIH histopathology. Aminotransferase and bilirubin normalized after 3-month glucocorticoid therapy plus continuous entecavir, with no recurrence at 6-month follow-up.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case of rivaroxaban-induced liver injury with a lethal outcome in a patient with COVID-19 and aortic thrombosis treated with rivaroxaban. DILI causality was assessed as highly probable to rivaroxaban based on a close and plausible temporal relationship (nausea within 3 months of therapy initiation and icterus after 4 months), liver enzyme elevation >10 ULN, and a negative differential diagnosis for alternative causes. The patient developed acute liver failure and died; percutaneous liver biopsy was contraindicated due to prolonged prothrombin time.

raw_record.extra_details: Authors report this as the first lethal outcome due to acute liver failure in a COVID-19 patient treated with rivaroxaban; only rare cases of rivaroxaban-induced liver injury described in the literature with only one prior lethal outcome. Authors advise caution and weekly liver enzyme monitoring in COVID-19-positive patients taking rivaroxaban. Rivaroxaban was used as anticoagulant for aortic thrombosis.

The patient was admitted in the fourth week after starting trimethoprim treatment for acne with fever, desquamating rash, and pruritus; on admission there was eosinophilia of 13%, a white cell count of 24.9 x 10^6/mL, and increased liver function test results, which deteriorated after transfer to a specialized liver unit.

Presentation at fourth week of treatment: fever, desquamating rash, pruritus, eosinophilia 13%; transferred to a specialized liver unit (Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham) where liver test results continued to deteriorate; blood samples obtained on referral and 3, 12, and 24 months after recovery.

raw_record.extra_details: Four case reports of paracetamol overdose causing acute liver failure (ALF). Case 1: 16-year-old girl, 10 g (20 tablets), serum paracetamol 156 mg/l, ALT >7500 IU/l, bilirubin 87 µmol/l, INR 6.3, pH 7.16, glucose 1.9 mmol/l, creatinine 146 µmol/l; underwent total hepatectomy and liver transplant, ventilatory support withdrawn after no brain stem recovery. Case 2: 24-year-old man, 32 g (64 tablets), history of alcohol misuse (~100 units/week), serum paracetamol 178 mg/l, INR 8, pH 7.3, glucose 2.1 mmol/l, creatinine 218 µmol/l; grade 3 encephalopathy; died of septicaemia and multifocal seizures on day 6 (also oliguric renal failure, lobar pneumonia, ventricular arrhythmias). Case 3: 38-year-old man, 25 g (50 tablets), serum paracetamol 178 mg/l, glucose <1 mmol/l, creatinine 435 µmol/l, INR 6, pH 7.45; died day 10 after overdose (pneumonia, fungal sepsis, intracranial pressure). Case 4: 34-year-old woman, 15 g (30 tablets), serum paracetamol 122 mg/l, INR 10, pH 7.4, glucose 2 mmol/l, creatinine 229 µmol/l; died day 15 awaiting liver transplant. Background paragraph notes that in paracetamol overdose trials no deaths occur if acetylcysteine given within 10 hours, and only 2% serious liver damage (AST >1000 IU/l) vs expected 90% when treated within 10 hours; these cases deviate from that expectation.

Three of the patients had no known additional risk factors and their overdose timing was judged accurate, yet all four progressed to acute liver failure; the authors discuss possible timing errors, a preceding overdose, or greater individual susceptibility to paracetamol's hepatotoxic effects.

raw_record.extra_details: Four cases; serum paracetamol concentration of 178 mg/l four hours after overdose in case 2; presenting concentrations considered toxic in cases 1-4 (e.g., 156 mg/l at four hours and 122 mg/l at six hours discussed with respect to timing-error effects). All four patients were medically reviewed within six hours of overdose but did not receive acetylcysteine and three were discharged without follow up. Acute liver failure developed within 48 hours of discharge; cases 1 and 3 had increasing confusion while cases 2 and 4 had abdominal pain and vomiting over the 24 hours before representation. Authors state no evidence that activated charcoal is effective four hours after overdose and no evidence supports serial testing except one reported case of a toxic concentration arising after an initial non-toxic concentration. Wide intersubject/ethnic differences in paracetamol metabolism are noted, including a 60-fold range in metabolic activation and a threefold variation in glucuronide and sulphate conjugation, though such enhanced susceptibility has not been proved in the overdose setting.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that while acetaminophen (APAP) is relatively safe at therapeutic doses, APAP in high doses can cause hepatotoxicity and is recognized as a major cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the USA and many European countries, accounting for 50% of all ALF cases in adults and 14% of cases in children in the USA. The study specifically examined children exposed to low-dose (therapeutic) and high-dose ('overdose' or toxic ingestion) APAP, and in overdose children with delayed treatment of the antidote N-acetylcysteine (>24 h) there were significant increases in serum ALT, APAP protein adducts, and acylcarnitines.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children aged 2–18 years); injury attributed to high-dose/toxic ingestion (overdose requiring hospitalization, including history of excessive dosing >150 mg/kg with elevated blood APAP).
raw_record.extra_details: APAP causes dose-related hepatotoxicity characterized by elevated ALT and is recognized as a major cause of acute liver failure, accounting for 50% of ALF cases in adults and 14% in children in the USA. In the overdose group (n=62), serum ALT (mean 554 IU/l; max 9909 IU/l) and APAP protein adducts were markedly elevated versus healthy controls; overdose children receiving delayed N-acetylcysteine treatment (>24 h) showed significant increases in ALT, APAP protein adducts, and long-chain acylcarnitines (oleoyl- and palmitoyl-carnitines). Mechanism involves oxidative metabolism and hepatic glutathione depletion, with mitochondrial injury and impaired fatty acid β-oxidation (PPARα pathway modulates mitochondrial β-oxidation). APAP protein adducts served as a biomarker of oxidative APAP metabolism; acylcarnitines were examined as proposed hepatotoxicity biomarkers.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that salicylates (aspirin) therapy in patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis caused hepatic dysfunction and, in three of their patients, hepatic encephalopathy that resolved when aspirin was discontinued. Evidence of acute hepatic failure included severely impaired mental function with striking transaminase elevations, prolonged prothrombin time, elevated blood ammonia, and an EEG consistent with metabolic encephalopathy. All three patients were subsequently rechallenged with aspirin and developed recurrent hepatotoxicity, and hepatotoxicity to aspirin was obtained even in the absence of encephalopathy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis; chronic high-dose salicylate therapy producing salicylate levels of 25-44 mg/dl; Reye syndrome considered as a differential but excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients developed hepatotoxicity with hepatic encephalopathy and signs of acute hepatic failure while on aspirin for JRA; all three recovered when aspirin was discontinued and each had recurrent hepatotoxicity upon rechallenge. In Patient 2, liver biopsy one week after onset showed ballooned hepatocytes with regeneration, focal pseudoacinar formation around dilated canaliculi, and Kupffer cell hypertrophy. Mentation recovered and liver tests normalized (e.g., SGOT) after stopping aspirin. The paper notes prior reports of hepatic dysfunction in up to 60% of JRA/SLE patients treated with salicylates, generally considered benign with mildly elevated liver enzymes.

These patients had hepatotoxicity following paracetamol overdose, some meeting criteria for liver transplantation, and N-acetyl-cysteine was used in their management.

Management included intravenous N-acetyl-cysteine (150 mg/kg for 24 h until INR below 2), norepinephrine as primary vasopressor, and continuous venovenous haemofiltration. KCH transplantation criteria: creatinine >300 µmol/L, prothrombin time >100 s (INR >6.5), and grade III/IV encephalopathy within 24 h with normal pH, or pH <7.3 after fluid replacement. Study evaluated early blood lactate as a prognostic marker for this cohort; mortality was the analysed outcome.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that after a paracetamol overdose, in untreated patients, there are two distinct phases of hepatotoxicity: an early phase with small abnormalities in plasma GST progressing to approximately 100 times the upper limit of the reference range by 40 hours, followed by a second phase of severe liver damage with plasma GST concentrations in excess of 1000 times the upper limit. Sixteen of 19 severely poisoned overdose patients had abnormal GST concentrations, while ALT was raised in only eight.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (supratherapeutic) exposure; co-exposure setting described for untreated patients; NAC treatment arrests the early phase and prevents the late phase of hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: 19 poisoned patients; GST was the most sensitive marker of acute cellular damage (16/19 abnormal versus ALT in 8). Large GST rises (>100x normal) were present on admission in all severely poisoned patients admitted more than 12 h after overdose; ALT abnormalities appeared only ~2 days later. Findings parallel those of James et al where histological abnormality was seen in 53/54 (98%) of paracetamol-overdose patients but only 24 (44%) had abnormal AST. After overdose, abnormal GST appears within 4 h; with NAC within 8 h GST peaks are lower, indicating early toxicity is clinically insignificant. Two-phase hepatotoxicity course described; proposed mechanism involves increased P450, subnormal intracellular reduced glutathione or reduced conjugating ability.

raw_record.support_text: In a single case report, cyproheptadine was implicated as the cause of a patient's acute liver failure. The patient had no history of liver or biliary disease, a negative serological work-up, and no imaging evidence of liver or hepatic vessel abnormalities; symptoms appeared 3 weeks after starting cyproheptadine and improved quickly after discontinuation. The authors note prior case reports describe patients who present with acute elevations in liver enzymes after starting cyproheptadine but resolve within weeks of discontinuing the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Cyproheptadine is an antihistamine and anti-serotonin agent sometimes used as an appetite stimulant and for pruritus relief. Latency was 3 weeks; symptoms and labs improved after drug withdrawal. Other case reports describe acute transaminase elevations resolving within weeks of stopping the drug. The mechanism of hepatotoxicity remains unproven; some postulate cholestatic or mixed-pattern acute hepatitis arising from its tricyclic ring, structurally similar to phenothiazine hepatotoxins such as chlorpromazine, imipramine, and ajmaline. This patient's presentation was more suggestive of hepatitis than cholestasis. The paper describes it as rare but life-threatening hepatotoxicity, warranting rapid drug withdrawal.

raw_record.extra_details: 15 cases reviewed (Philippine General Hospital, Aug 1991-Aug 1994); four patients (27%) died, average hospitalization 3 days; recovered patients averaged 16.5 days. Poor prognosis markers: early transaminase/alkaline phosphatase elevation, >10-fold alanine aminotransferase increase, severe prothrombin time derangement, metabolic acidosis (p<0.01) and hypoglycemia (p<0.05). Jaundice predicted length of hospital stay but not mortality (p>0.05). Intravenous N-acetylcysteine did not significantly alter outcome (p>0.05). Age range 19-45 years, mean 28.

raw_record.support_text: In a cohort of patients with severe paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity managed in intensive care, survival was 63% following a deliberate overdose and 58% after therapeutic misadventure. Acute liver failure complications were frequent: grade III–IV encephalopathy occurred in 58% and 55% of the therapeutic misadventure and deliberate overdose groups respectively, 54% (278/515) of deliberate overdose cases and 56% (21/38) of the therapeutic misadventure group required renal dialysis, and 37 patients fulfilled transplant criteria and received a transplant. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of ceftriaxone-induced acute hepatitis diagnosed in an adult patient. A RUCAM score of 6 was calculated (probable causality), and the paper states that ceftriaxone-associated acute hepatocellular severe injury is a rare occurrence. The authors note that elevated liver enzymes and cholestasis are reported in up to 6% of patients (usually mild) but ceftriaxone has rarely (<1%) been reported to cause severe DILI and acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single adult patient case; RUCAM score 6 (probable). On ceftriaxone withdrawal liver enzymes improved within 24 h (AST to 109 U/L, ALT to 323 U/L) with complete normalization by 10-day follow-up and resolution of eosinophilia; patient remained asymptomatic. CT showed fatty liver with no focal lesion. As a general claim, ceftriaxone-associated elevated liver enzymes and cholestasis occur in up to 6% of patients (mostly mild, continuation possible with monitoring), whereas severe DILI and acute hepatitis are reported in less than 1%. No rechallenge; liver biopsy not performed.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 34-year-old obese man with severe gout who developed acute liver injury with jaundice 2 months after adding febuxostat (40 mg daily) to his regimen, presenting with a cholestatic pattern of serum enzyme elevations and cholestatic hepatitis on liver biopsy. Febuxostat was temporarily continued after onset but upon discontinuation his symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized; other potentially hepatotoxic drugs were restarted without recurrence. Three Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network reviewers adjudicated the case as 'highly likely' a result of febuxostat, and the authors conclude febuxostat is a rare but convincing cause of clinically apparent liver injury presenting with a cholestatic pattern and no hypersensitivity or autoimmune features.

Historical severe psychiatric disorder or repeated suicide attempts were contraindications to transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report another case to add to the literature on isoniazid-induced hepatitis: a patient who died in hepatic failure 2 months after beginning isoniazid therapy. The patient was given isoniazid 300 mg daily (with pyridoxine 50 mg daily) following a positive PPD test, became icteric ~6 weeks later, and isoniazid was withdrawn. She deteriorated and died in hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of 53-year-old woman treated for latent tuberculosis infection; isoniazid 300 mg daily with pyridoxine 50 mg daily; latency ~2 months (isoniazid withdrawn 4 days before admission when icteric); died in hepatic failure. Antemortem labs: total bilirubin 35.4 mg/100 ml (direct 24 mg/100 ml), SGOT 1000 IU, LDH 582 IU, alkaline phosphatase 84.6 Babson units, prothrombin time 38.5 s vs control 12.5 s, BUN 23 mg/100 ml. Postmortem: shrunken soft green liver; histology showed diffuse destruction of hepatic tissue with preservation of irregular islands of hepatocytes in a pseudoacinar pattern within broad bands of fibrous tissue, bile duct proliferation, and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells; no Dane particles on EM. Concurrent exposures included earlier ablative radioiodine (5.3 mCi 131I) and propranolol 10 mg qid; causality is attributed to isoniazid.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen toxicity is described as the leading individual cause of acute liver failure in the United States, and the study evaluates events after APAP overdose in humans, including elevated circulating EV numbers observed 6 h after APAP overdose in vivo and in plasma from APAP overdose patients compared with healthy controls. Elevated APAP-protein adducts in circulation paralleled increased exosome release, though no adducts were detected inside EVs.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP toxicity stated as the leading individual cause of acute liver failure in the US. Mechanism: a small fraction is converted to toxic metabolite NAPQI via CYP2E1; at supra-therapeutic doses sulfation is saturated and glucuronidation overwhelmed, causing extensive NAPQI formation and glutathione depletion; NAPQI covalent binding to (especially mitochondrial) proteins triggers mitochondrial oxidative stress and hepatocyte necrosis. Circulating APAP-CYS adducts detected even after therapeutic doses in humans and released before ALT elevations. Study included primary mouse hepatocytes (5 mM APAP), human HepaRG cells (20 mM APAP), male C57BL/6J mice (300 mg/kg i.p.), and plasma from APAP overdose patients; APAP-protein adducts elevated in circulation/media but not detected within EVs, indicating EV release is not a significant mechanism of adduct release into circulation. Bioassay for APAP protein adducts used to identify APAP overdose in humans. Disease synonym: acetaminophen intoxication/poisoning; phenotype hepatotoxicity/acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes developed painless jaundice after 6 weeks of metformin (1,700 mg/day) with no other drugs or herbal products. Investigation ruled out viral, autoimmune, and metabolic liver disease, and the mixed-pattern liver injury (bilirubin, AST, ALT, GGT, ALP all elevated) resolved within 30 days of stopping metformin. Six weeks after discharge, a self-initiated single 850 mg dose of metformin reproduced malaise, nausea, and jaundice within 24 h with a similar elevated laboratory pattern, which normalized in 4 weeks. The authors state that exclusion of other causes, the positive unintentional rechallenge, and absence of other drugs convincingly support a diagnosis of metformin-induced liver damage.

raw_record.extra_details: First episode: metformin 1,700 mg/day for 6 weeks; labs showed total bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, AST 290 U/L, ALT 861 U/L, GGT 861 U/L, ALP 622 U/L; INR and eosinophils normal; liver biopsy refused; enzymes normalized in 30 days. Rechallenge: single 850 mg dose, symptoms within 24 h; labs total bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, AST 237 U/L, ALT 764 U/L, GGT 3,318 U/L, ALP 622 U/L; normalized in 4 weeks. Subsequent therapy with gliclazide-modified release 60 mg/day left patient asymptomatic (HbA1c 6.8%).

raw_record.support_text: Eight cases of zafirlukast-induced acute liver injury have been reported in the English literature and are summarized in a table. The nature of the liver injury clearly seems to be idiosyncratic. In all of the zafirlukast hepatotoxicity cases, the enzyme elevation was predominantly severe hepatocellular damage with aminotransferase peaks of several thousand; several patients developed acute hepatic failure, prompting orthotopic liver transplantation in two. Time to normalization of enzymes ranged from several weeks to 6 months, and biopsy findings included submassive hepatic necrosis, multilobular bridging necrosis, parenchymal collapse, and eosinophilic infiltration.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as zafirlukast-induced acute liver injury in a case series of 8 patients (references 3-8) and tabulated. Duration of drug exposure 2-18 months; time to normalization of enzymes several weeks to 6 months after discontinuation. Biopsy/explant findings: submassive hepatic necrosis (some with abundant eosinophils), multilobular bridging necrosis with parenchymal collapse and regeneration, or no biopsy. Acute hepatic failure prompted orthotopic liver transplantation in two patients; corticosteroids used in some cases. Aminotransferase peaks of several thousand with severe hepatocellular pattern. Authors speculated an immunological mechanism based on hepatic eosinophils and corticosteroid response.

raw_record.support_text: A 55-year-old male was admitted with severe liver injury after taking two capsules of artemisinin extract (containing 200 mg artemisinin extract + 10 mg alkaloid) per day for 1 month for shoulder pain. He was diagnosed with drug-induced liver injury of hepatocellular type (R ratio 9.3), acute, with a RUCAM score of 8 points (very likely) and severity level three. Other causes of liver damage (viruses, immunity, alcohol, bile ducts, blood vessels) were excluded, and he received plasma exchange with bilirubin adsorption on days 12, 14 and 18, with bilirubin returning to baseline after 40 days.

Presented with dark urine, jaundice, loss of appetite, tiredness of oil, itchy skin and tachycardia. Admission labs: ALT 908 IU/L (ref 10-55), total bilirubin 151.0 umol/L, direct bilirubin 83.4 umol/L, indirect bilirubin 83.4 umol/L, blood ammonia 40 umol/L, normal INR; HBA1c 8.70%. Negative for hepatitis A-E, Epstein-Barr virus, CMV, HIV, Treponema pallidum, AFP, CA19-9, ceruloplasmin, ANA; anti-mitochondrial M2 weakly positive. Gd-EOB-DTPA MRI cholangiopancreatography showed decreased liver uptake and bile duct excretion. RUCAM 8 (very likely), R ratio 9.3, severity level three; case described as uniquely severe cholestasis. Treated with polyene phosphatidylcholine, reduced glutathione, ursodeoxycholic acid, insulin and three sessions of plasma exchange with bilirubin adsorption (days 12, 14, 18); bilirubin decreased to baseline after 40 days (abstract states 62 days). Patient refused liver biopsy. Fever, vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain absent; no smoking or alcohol; no history of hepatitis.

Nine days later routine tests showed elevated liver enzymes (ALT 509 IU/l, AST 246 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 198 IU/l, gamma-glutamyl transferase 105 IU/l) with normal bilirubin. Hypoxaemia contributed to death in two patients. Lung-injury patients had higher median encephalopathy grades (4 vs 2) and APACHE II scores (29 vs 16); circulatory failure requiring vasoconstrictor support occurred in all patients with lung injury vs 40% without. Mortality was much higher in the lung-injury group (89% vs 13%). Paracetamol poisoning is stated to cause roughly 250 deaths per annum in the UK from fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The case report documents hepatotoxicity occurring after a massive suicidal acetaminophen (APAP) overdose. A 78-year-old man reportedly ingested approximately 96 tablets of APAP IR (each 500 mg) over one hour. IV N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was started 5 hours after ingestion, but was discontinued after 21 hours despite a residual APAP concentration of 116 µg/mL. The patient subsequently experienced hepatotoxicity, coagulopathy, and renal injury, with pharmacokinetic analysis revealing prolonged, erratic APAP absorption and a second peak APAP concentration of 228 µg/mL approximately 48 hours after ingestion.

raw_record.extra_details: APAP serum concentrations were 264 µg/mL at 2.25 h post-ingestion and 281 µg/mL at 6.25 h; a second peak of 228 µg/mL appeared approximately 48 h post-ingestion. The patient also developed coagulopathy and renal injury; re-ingestion was deemed unlikely due to direct hospital monitoring. No specific biochemical pattern (e.g., hepatocellular vs. cholestatic) was reported.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe six patients referred to their unit over 10 years who developed cholestatic liver injury after taking pyritinol 400-600 mg daily, with injury appearing within days to weeks of starting the drug (cases 3-6 detailed). The liver injury pattern was clearly cholestatic, with bilirubin above 342 µmol/l in four of six patients; transaminase peaks occurred within the first two weeks while alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase peaked two to three months later. Liver biopsy in four cases showed mild inflammatory infiltrate (polymorphonuclear cells, lymphocytes, sometimes eosinophils) with marked canalicular and parenchymal cholestasis and mild focal hepatocellular necrosis. Liver function normalized after stopping pyritinol in all cases (recovery from one month to over nine months), and one patient rechallenged inadvertently developed the same symptoms and laboratory picture.

raw_record.support_text: As indicine-N-oxide showed promising results as an anticancer agent in in vitro and in vivo assays, clinical trials were conducted for acute leukemia; however, due to severe hepatotoxicity, the compound was not further tested. One clinical trial investigated indicine-N-oxide in patients with progressive acute leukemia refractory to standard chemotherapeutics (10 patients: 6 ALL, 3 AML, 1 AMML; ages 4–67 years). A lyophilized form at 3.0 g/m2 was given intravenously for five consecutive days; two patients achieved complete remission and one partial remission. Most patients experienced side effects such as mild nausea, mild diarrhea, maculopapular rash, and jaundice, and the authors concluded that indicine-N-oxide has anticancer activity but needs modification to remove unwanted side effects.

raw_record.support_text: The characteristic morphologic features of amiodarone (AD) hepatotoxicity include changes mimicking alcoholic hepatitis ('pseudoalcoholic hepatitis') and secondary phospholipidosis. The incidence of hepatic disease in recipients of AD is approximately 1% for pseudoalcoholic liver disease, 25% for lesser parenchymal injury deduced from elevated hepatic-related serum enzymes, and an unknown but probably high incidence of phospholipidosis after chronic administration. The complete histologic spectrum of alcohol-like liver injury includes steatosis, steatonecrosis, Mallory bodies, megamitochondria, portal inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis; at least two of these features were present in most of the authors' cases.
raw_record.extra_details: 17-case series; incidence of hepatic disease ~1% for pseudoalcoholic liver disease and ~25% for lesser parenchymal injury (elevated hepatic-related serum enzymes); histologic spectrum includes steatosis, steatonecrosis, Mallory bodies, megamitochondria (42% of cases), portal inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis (2 cases); Mallory bodies located in zone I; steatosis microvesicular, macrovesicular, or both; ALT equal to or greater than AST in several cases; foam cells (PAS with diastase) in 9 of 17 cases; no cirrhosis in 9 patients who died while receiving AD; resembles pseudoalcoholic hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Of 497 hyperthyroid patients with normal baseline LFT values, symptomatic hepatic injury developed in 6 patients (1.2%) during propylthiouracil (PTU) therapy. Patients complained of jaundice and itching (5/6), fever and rash (2), and arthralgia (1). The duration of PTU administration until first symptom was 29.2±16.3 days (12–49 days) at a daily dose of 342±66 mg, and none had evidence of acute viral hepatitis A, B, or C or autoantibodies. The authors attribute the hepatic injury specifically to PTU administration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Indication-restricted: hyperthyroid patients receiving PTU; no pre-existing liver disease (normal baseline LFTs); viral hepatitis and autoantibody causes excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: PTU is propylthiouracil. Six cases (male/female 3/3, mean age 43.7±14.8 yr, range 27–61). Symptoms: jaundice/itching (5), fever and rash (2), arthralgia (1). Latency 29.2±16.3 days (12–49 days); daily dose 342±66 mg (300–450 mg). Initial labs: ALT increased 4/6 (143±111 U/L), total bilirubin increased 5/6 (293±288 µmol/L, 8.5–731 µmol/L), ALP increased 6/6 (265±81 U/L, 132–373 U/L). Injury classified per International Consensus Criteria: cholestatic (3), mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic (2), hepatocellular (1). Maximum injury persisted 17.2±7.2 days after withdrawal; ALT normalized within 29.5±19.3 days and total bilirubin within 72.8±46.4 days; cholestatic-type recovery prolonged (>2 months) vs other types. No predictors found among age, sex, hyperthyroid duration, pretreatment T3/T4, starting PTU dose, or duration. Follow-up used 131I or methimazole after LFT normalization. PTU daily dose did not differ from patients without hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: Halothane-associated liver damage includes two distinct patterns. A rare but severe form termed 'halothane hepatitis' is characterized by extremely large serum transaminase elevations, jaundice, massive hepatic necrosis, and a significant fraction of patients develop liver failure in whom mortality is common. This rare severe form caused a marked reduction in halothane usage.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is a rare but serious dose-independent adverse reaction in anesthetized patients: serum transaminase elevations, jaundice, massive hepatic necrosis, liver failure with common mortality. In this study sera came from 56 patients with a clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis defined as otherwise unexplained severe, histologically confirmed hepatitis with normal preoperative liver function. Patients are frequently female, obese, and late middle age, though the syndrome is also described in males, non-obese patients, and children. Most patients had multiple halothane exposures; median interval from anesthesia to jaundice is 7 days; findings include pyrexia, eosinophilia, circulating immune complexes, autoantibodies, and antibodies to halothane-induced liver antigens. Halothane hepatitis is considered idiosyncratic and dose-independent.

The diagnosis was established by the lack of other known causes for liver disease, the temporal relationship with the drug, and typical changes of liver histology.

Laboratory workup showed a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury (AST 3,241 U/L, ALT 2,355 U/L, ALP 170 U/L, total bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL); extensive workup for viral, autoimmune, alcoholic, ischemic, metabolic, and vascular causes was unremarkable. raw_record.support_text: The review describes halothane (1-bromo-1-chloro-2,2,2-trifluoroethane) as the best model of immune-mediated drug liver damage and the commonest drug associated with fulminant hepatic failure in the U.K. and Europe after paracetamol, with mortality approaching 90% when hepatic failure occurs. Two forms are described: a minor form after 20% of exposures with usually minor serum aminotransferase elevation (up to three times ULN), and severe 'halothane hepatitis', whose most striking feature is increased frequency after multiple exposures (incidence about 1:35,000 overall in the National Halothane Study, and 1:3,700 after multiple exposures).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Risk increased after multiple exposures and after earlier adverse halothane reactions; halothane hepatitis not observed in patients who had never had previous anaesthesia in the authors' experience; recurrence risk not avoided by a 3-month re-exposure interval (intervals ranged 17 days to 13 years, median 1 year).
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane hepatitis is presented as an immune-mediated idiosyncratic reaction, with indirect hypersensitivity features including male/female ratio 1.6:1, peripheral eosinophilia in 21% and liver-kidney microsomal auto-antibodies in 29% of cases, and an (unconfirmed) HLA-DR2 association from one Japanese study. Early reports concentrated on fulminant hepatitis with mortality up to 90%. A 3-year (1983-1985) Liver Unit series of 40 patients confirmed a wider spectrum of severe damage, with 17 of 40 developing fulminant hepatic failure and 19 cases in 1985; six children (11 months-14 years) were affected; 13 of 40 had a prior adverse halothane reaction; all survivors' liver function returned to normal. Minor form (after ~20% of exposures) consists of aminotransferase elevation up to three times ULN. Metabolism is via cytochrome P-450 oxidative and reductive pathways generating reactive metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a rare case of agranulocytosis associated with hepatic toxicity, probably related to the use of ticlopidine, a platelet inhibitor. More serious but less frequent adverse effects of ticlopidine are hematological dyscrasia and cholestatic hepatitis. In the presented patient, ticlopidine 250 mg twice daily was given after a vertebrobasilar stroke, and about four weeks later she developed agranulocytosis and hepatic toxicity; after ticlopidine was discontinued, liver tests progressively normalized.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was a 70-year-old Caucasian woman with no prior hematological or liver disease and no prior history of blood or liver disorders. Hepatic toxicity and agranulocytosis developed about 4 weeks after starting ticlopidine 250 mg twice daily; ticlopidine was discontinued and she was treated with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, with rapid rise in white blood count and progressive normalization of liver tests. Cholestatic hepatitis is described as a recognized serious, less frequent ticlopidine adverse effect. The paper recommends monitoring complete blood count and liver function tests in the first three months of ticlopidine therapy for early detection of serious and unpredictable side effects.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid treatment is a recognized cause of clinical hepatitis in the general population. Symptomatic hepatitis was first described in the early 1970s with 19 cases of clinical intolerance (0.8%) and two deaths among 2312 treated contacts. A US multicenter study of 13,838 subjects reported 1% probable hepatitis (up to 2.3% after age 50), higher with alcohol use, requiring hospitalization in 0.5%. In the UICT study, 95 of 20,840 isoniazid-treated subjects developed hepatitis, three of whom died (0.14/1000 treated). Meta-analyses found 0.36% hepatotoxicity at six months and 0.52% at 12 months of treatment, and hepatitis was seen in 6/545 subjects receiving 12 months of isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis risk increased with age (up to 2.3% after 50 years) and alcohol use. Mortality: Ferebee reported 3 deaths/20,840 treatments; two studies reported no deaths among 11,141 treatments or among 1600 elderly institution residents; a US study of 13,838 patients had 8 deaths (0.6/1000), 7 in Baltimore where liver cirrhosis prevalence was above average. A Canadian retrospective matched-cohort study (1998-2003): 9145 LTBI-treated subjects (92.8% isoniazid monotherapy), 45 (0.5%) hospitalized for acute liver disease vs 15/18,290 (0.1%) controls; risk rose per decade of age and with co-morbidities, reaching 2.6% over age 65; 7 treated subjects died (treatment attribution uncertain); 3 liver transplants but all had pre-existing liver disease. Meta-analysis of 38,257 subjects: 0.6% clinical hepatitis (0.0-2.9% by age). Transaminase surveillance: 0.3% abnormalities (3x ULN with symptoms or 5x without); in 3377 adults (5x ULN criterion) risk factors were age >50 or prior transaminase elevation; meta-analysis of 7 articles/18,610 participants: 1.8% biological+clinical toxicity, worse if age >35 (1.7% vs 0.2%), prior transaminase elevation, or alcoholism; hepatitis C and treatment duration (9 vs 6 months) not associated; 15,229 treatments hospitalized, no deaths in 15,644. Prognosis worsened by continuing treatment despite prodromal symptoms (anorexia, asthenia, malaise). Isoniazid is a first-line agent for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, which is rare but often fatal, is due to the direct disruption of mitochondrial processes, and is heralded by nonspecific symptoms such as lethargy, nausea/vomiting, or worsening seizures. It also notes that L-carnitine treatment was studied as a possible treatment for this valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, whereas valproate itself is the causative agent.

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective inception cohort from the International Registry for Adverse Reactions to Valproate of 92 patients with severe, symptomatic valproate-induced hepatotoxicity (90 epilepsy, 2 bipolar disorder); deceased and liver transplant patients were combined as terminal hepatic failure. Mechanism described as direct disruption of mitochondrial processes, with proposed drug-induced carnitine deficiency. Symptoms heralding hepatotoxicity include lethargy, nausea/vomiting, and worsening seizures. Study evaluated L-carnitine treatment (48% of 42 treated patients survived vs 10% of 50 supportive-care patients).

raw_record.support_text: The study compared L-carnitine-treated and untreated children who developed valproate-induced hepatotoxicity (92 total patients, 42 treated with L-carnitine and 50 untreated). After onset of toxicity, valproate was stopped after a median of 7 days in the L-carnitine group and 8 days in the untreated group. The children often had poor nutrition and chronic illness, and 69% were below the 25th percentile for weight.

raw_record.extra_details: Cohort of 92 children with valproate-induced hepatotoxicity collected from US, German, and other centers; valproate median dose 39 mg/kg/d (treated) and 43 mg/kg/d (untreated), duration median 81 vs 72 days. Hepatic survival was 47% (20/42) in L-carnitine-treated vs 10% (5/50) in untreated patients (p < 0.001), indicating substantial mortality from valproate-induced hepatic failure; three patients who received prophylactic L-carnitine (stopped 60-100 days before the event) had this hepatic event delayed. L-carnitine is framed as a treatment/preventive measure, not the causal agent.

raw_record.support_text: In an obese 64-year-old pre-diabetic woman taking atovaquone 1.5 g/day prophylaxis and prednisone, a probable diagnosis of drug-induced acute hepatitis due to atovaquone was made based on characteristic zone III lobular injury, negative metabolic/serologic/virologic workup, and imaging. After atovaquone was discontinued, liver function improved over days and returned to normal at 3-month follow-up. The paper states this is the first reported case of atovaquone-induced liver injury in the absence of proguanil co-therapy.

raw_record.extra_details: Atovaquone 1.5 g/day as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis. R factor 11.9 at presentation and 8.6 at peak, consistent with continued hepatocellular injury. Peak values: ALT 1252 U/L, AST 972 U/L, ALP 450 U/L, total bilirubin 9.40 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 7.0 mg/dl, INR 1.66, serum albumin 3.2 mmol/L. Liver biopsy showed zone III involvement with mild lobulitis, bile ductular reaction, central macrophage accumulation, and perivenular (spotty) necrosis without confluent necrosis; no AIH (plasma cells inconspicuous, negative serologies). Complete clinical and biochemical recovery after atovaquone discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: A 59-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia treated with nilotinib for about one year presented with elevated liver enzymes (AST 578 IU/L, ALT 499 IU/L). A percutaneous liver biopsy showed extensive centrilobular infiltration of immune cells and destruction of the lobular architecture with minimal portal inflammation; immunohistochemistry revealed many CD8+ T cells and CD56+ cells. She was diagnosed with nilotinib-induced, immune-mediated liver injury, and prednisolone 30 mg daily caused rapid normalization of liver enzyme levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: chronic myeloid leukemia; nilotinib (BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor) therapy for about one year before presentation. Laboratory: aspartate aminotransferase 578 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 499 IU/L. Histology: extensive centrilobular infiltration of immune cells and destruction of lobular architecture with minimal portal-triad inflammation. Immunohistochemistry: many CD8+ T cells and CD56+ cells; multicolor FACS showed numerous intrahepatic CD8+ T cells with an activated phenotype. Treated with prednisolone (30 mg daily), with rapid normalization of liver enzymes. The authors conclude nilotinib can cause immune-mediated liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: A 47-year-old male with hepatic hydatidosis treated with albendazole consulted after five months of uninterrupted treatment with markedly abnormal liver tests showing hepatocellular damage and was diagnosed with drug-induced liver injury due to albendazole. The diagnosis was based on the clinical record, drug consumption history, improvement of clinical and laboratory tests after discontinuation, and exclusion of other causes, and was supported by the CIOMS/RUCAM scale, which showed a 'likely' correlation between hepatocellular damage and drug toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had underlying hepatic hydatidosis (pre-existing liver infection) being treated; exposure was a prolonged five-month uninterrupted therapeutic course of albendazole.
raw_record.extra_details: 47-year-old male presenting with jaundice syndrome and marked hepatocellular damage; liver tests and clinical status improved after discontinuing the medication, with other possible causes discarded. CIOMS/RUCAM assessment gave a 'likely' correlation. Background context in the paper notes mild aminotransferase elevation in up to 15.6% of albendazole cases that resolves with temporary withdrawal without comorbidity, and only two prior published cases where transaminase elevation and symptoms obliged definite treatment suspension.

raw_record.support_text: The CIOMS/RUCAM scale was used to objectively evaluate the probability of toxic hepatitis; it showed a 'likely' correlation with a 5-point score, which confirmed the diagnosis of albendazole-induced toxic hepatitis with a pattern of hepatocellular damage. The case documents sub-acute toxicity with progressive improvement of the hepatic profile over time after discontinuing the medication as the only intervention; only two other similar human cases have been reported worldwide.
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis; CIOMS/RUCAM score 5 ('likely') supporting albendazole causality. First described case documenting sub-acute toxicity, with progressive improvement of the hepatic profile after drug discontinuation as the sole intervention; only two other human cases of albendazole-induced toxic hepatitis reported worldwide. Case ruled out ischemic liver damage, infectious causes (serology negative), and liver cystadenocarcinoma.
