raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old female on propylthiouracil (PTU) after treatment for hyperthyroidism developed grossly abnormal liver function (ALT 852 U/l, bilirubin 46 μmol/l, ALP 303 U/l, INR 0.9) and was diagnosed with acute hepatitis secondary to treatment with PTU. Ultrasound showed mild hepatic steatosis. After PTU was stopped, liver function (bilirubin 9 μmol/l, ALT 164 U/l, ALP 195 U/l) improved over 10 days and had normalized by clinic review 3 weeks later. The case highlights acute hepatitis as a potentially fatal but rare complication associated with PTU.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a previously healthy 41-year-old woman who developed liver cirrhosis as a sequela of acute hepatic injury induced by ketoconazole administration (200 mg/day for 5 months) to treat onychomycosis. The initial presentation was a typical acute hepatitis with nausea, anorexia, fatigue, and jaundice that developed during ketoconazole administration; other causes of hepatitis were excluded. The authors conclude that ketoconazole can cause liver cirrhosis through acute hepatic injury under certain circumstances.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol overdose (POD) remains the commonest cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the UK, and describes it as a defined liver insult resulting in acute liver injury (coagulopathy with INR > 1.5 and jaundice) that progresses to hepatic encephalopathy. The case of Mrs S is presented as a paracetamol-overdose ALF managed medically without meeting transplant criteria.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (paracetamol overdose, POD).
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: NAPQI, a hepatotoxic intermediate metabolite, accumulates after glutathione depletion, causing hepatonecrosis, liver dysfunction and hepatocyte enzyme release. Presentation in significant POD typically includes aminotransferases in the thousands, mildly elevated bilirubin and significant coagulopathy, with metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia and hypovolaemia. Patient Mrs S presented with ALT ~6000 U/L, INR 5.5, bilirubin 60 µmol/L, grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy and hyperammonemia (160 µmol/L at 24 h); paracetamol and salicylate levels were undetectable at presentation; treated with NAC, CVVH/CVVHDF, and supportive critical care; recovered and discharged after 3 weeks. Paracetamol levels are not reliable to exclude POD because many patients present late or with staggered overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) is described as an efficient but highly toxic solvent whose acute unintentional or intentional intoxications are potentially life-threatening. The paper discusses therapy options based on literature and clinical experience with 16 patients with acute CCl4 poisoning, and notes that only about 1% of the intoxicating CCl4 is responsible for the liver injury after conversion to toxic radicals via microsomal cytochrome P450 2E1, whereas 99% is exhaled unchanged.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute unintentional or intentional intoxication (poisoning) setting; concurrent or chronic alcohol ingestion predisposes to injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver injury in CCl4 poisoning is attributed to toxic metabolites generated via hepatic microsomal cytochrome P450 2E1 (component of the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system) rather than the parent chemical; only ~1% of the intoxicating dose mediates liver injury while ~99% is eliminated unchanged by exhalation. Historically used as an anthelmintic chemical drug (about 30,000 treatments at 1-4 mL doses without marked symptoms, as described in 1923). Cimetidine used to inhibit microsomal metabolite production. Liver enzymes monitored include GDH, ALP, ALT, and AST. Therapy discussed is CO2-induced hyperventilation (CO2 at 2-3 L/min to achieve respiratory volume of 25-30 L/min); clinical course favorable in 15/16 patients (93.8%).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports four new cases of disulfiram-related acute hepatitis of varying severity. Disulfiram was stated to be probably the agent responsible for the hepatitis because alcohol consumption had been discontinued several weeks before symptom onset and other causes of acute liver disease, particularly viral infections (hepatitis A, B and C), were excluded; in one patient symptoms and liver function tests worsened after rechallenge with the drug. An additional published case series table summarizes 23 cases of disulfiram-induced hepatitis with doses of 125-1500 mg/day, latency of 1.5-24 weeks, positive rechallenge in several cases, and outcomes including survival, orthotopic liver transplantation, and death.

raw_record.extra_details: Four new cases plus a further 19 published cases of disulfiram-induced hepatitis compiled in Table 1 (doses 125-1500 mg/day, latency 1.5-24 weeks). Of the new cases, two developed severe hepatitis with ascites, encephalopathy and low prothrombin index, two recovered completely, and two later showed cirrhosis on biopsy. One new case had a positive rechallenge (case 4: jaundice and transaminases >1000 U/l with symptoms and liver tests worsening after rechallenge). After a 5-90 day latency, jaundice and ALT/AST >1000 U/l were found. Mechanism not fully understood: some clinical/experimental data support toxic-metabolite production (disulfiram reduced to diethylthiocarbamate, partly oxidized to carbon disulphide, an industrial solvent associated with toxic hepatitis) as well as a possible allergic/hypersensitivity reaction (skin rash and pruritus in two patients). The mortality rate of disulfiram-induced fulminant hepatitis is very high and liver transplantation should be considered; one published case survived after orthotopic liver transplantation. Peak bilirubin up to 83.4 mg/dl, peak AST up to 4530 U/l, peak ALT up to 3763 U/l in compiled cases. Disulfiram should be stopped if transaminases rise >3x normal or hepatitis symptoms appear.

The incidence of hepatitis was high with isoniazid 400 mg daily, and the risk of hepatitis was appreciably higher in slow than in rapid acetylators (18% vs 2% in the spinal tuberculosis study with rifampicin and isoniazid; 21% vs 0% in a sample from the second pulmonary tuberculosis study), while incidence was low (1.3%) with isoniazid-containing regimens without rifampicin. The findings refute the hypothesis that isoniazid is more hepatotoxic for rapid rather than slow acetylators.

raw_record.support_text: A patient presented with a mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular liver injury after taking atorvastatin, with jaundice and aminotransferases greater than five times the upper limit of normal. Liver biopsy showed features compatible with autoimmune drug-induced liver injury, and the diagnosis was atorvastatin-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH). The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) score was 6 for the current admission, indicating atorvastatin was the probable causative agent, and a RUCAM score of 10 for a prior episode indicated atorvastatin was the highly probable causative agent. Symptoms improved with statin cessation alone, and the patient had a prior unexplained episode of elevated liver enzymes that resolved within three months after atorvastatin was held, with recurrence following the reintroduction of atorvastatin.

raw_record.extra_details: Case given oral suloctidil 300 mg/day in a randomized, double-blind trial for dementia; baseline liver enzymes were normal; liver enzymes rose sharply at week 7; symptoms of anorexia, fatigue, and lethargy, clay-colored stools, and dark urine began after 6-7 wk of therapy; no fever, chills, or viral syndrome; no other hepatotoxin or alcohol exposure; liver biopsy showed focal hepatocyte necrosis, mild Kupffer cell hyperplasia, and features suggestive of mild acute hepatitis; suloctidil is 1-(4-isopropyl thiophenyl)-2z-n-octylamino propanol.

raw_record.support_text: After excluding viral, toxic, alcohol-related and transfusion-related hepatitis, and noting that despite concurrent long-term ibuprofen therapy the liver enzymes returned to baseline while ibuprofen continued, while all abnormalities appeared soon after suloctidil initiation and returned to normal 2 months after discontinuing it, the authors conclude this is a case of hepatotoxicity caused by suloctidil, with no evidence of toxicity to other organ systems.
raw_record.extra_details: Index patient received suloctidil 300 mg; SGOT rose from baseline to 390 IU/L, SGPT to 565 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase to 202 IU/L, total bilirubin peaked at 1.2 mg/dl, with recovery to normal by 2 months after discontinuation; liver biopsy showed intact lobular pattern, scattered individual necrotic hepatocytes, focal Kupffer cell hyperplasia, and increased round cells in portal areas without piecemeal necrosis. Concurrent ibuprofen was excluded as cause (taken for years, enzymes returned despite continued therapy). At least 15 other reported cases: Schouten and Westerman reported 3 cases of elevated liver tests in hyperlipoproteinemia patients on 1200 mg/day suloctidil, with transaminase abnormalities between 8-10 weeks and peak elevations of 2- to 40-fold, all resolving after discontinuation; Perrin et al. reported a case progressing to cirrhosis and death after two rechallenges (early biopsy showed hepatitis with mild eosinophilic infiltrate; postmortem showed fibrosis and regenerating nodules); additional biopsy-proven cirrhosis and significant-fibrosis cases reported; Verneau et al. reported fatal fulminant hepatitis. In the Gent et al. trial of suloctidil in patients with recent thromboembolic stroke, 6 of 216 patients (2.7%) developed a twofold serum transaminase elevation that resolved after drug discontinuation; dose-relatedness and relative risk not established.

raw_record.support_text: Twenty patients with unresectable liver metastases underwent hyperthermic isolated hepatic perfusion (IHP) with melphalan. Three patients (15%) experienced grade 4 hepatic toxicity and died from liver failure and subsequent multiorgan failure; six further patients had significant (grade 3–4) but transitory hepatic toxicity. Logistic regression showed that melphalan concentration in the perfusate circuit, but not preoperative tests, significantly and independently correlated with hepatic toxicity (P = 0.028).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurred in the setting of regional hyperthermic isolated hepatic perfusion (IHP) with a locoregional delivery route, in patients with unresectable liver metastases refractory to conventional treatments and hepatic parenchyma replacement ≤50%; not ordinary systemic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Melphalan dose 1.5 mg/kg body weight. 20 patients treated; 3 (15%) grade 4 hepatic toxicity leading to death from liver failure and multiorgan failure; 6 patients with grade 3–4 transitory hepatic toxicity. Pharmacokinetic study showed a 3% mean perfusate-to-plasma drug leakage (range 1–6%). Melphalan drug concentration in the perfusate circuit independently correlated with hepatic toxicity (P = 0.028). No intraoperative mortality; systemic toxicity minimal and reversible.

raw_record.support_text: The antimetabolite methotrexate is capable of causing cirrhosis without, as a rule, giving rise to the picture of active chronic hepatitis or acute viral-type hepatitis. Given over long periods to patients with severe psoriasis and malignant disease, biopsy commonly shows a non-specific picture with fatty change, mild portal and parenchymal inflammation and increased variation in liver-cell appearances; with increasing length of treatment with frequent small oral doses, fibrosis develops as septa and cirrhosis finally ensues. Duration of treatment in patients with serious liver disease was significantly longer than in those with the milder non-specific picture, and the majority of patients treated for two years or more had severe fibrosis or cirrhosis. Methotrexate injury is described as a predictable, dose-dependent lesion; hepatotoxic effects can be greatly reduced by intermittent therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term therapy with frequent small oral doses in patients with severe psoriasis or malignant disease; liver biopsy is important since liver function tests may give a falsely optimistic picture; risk reduced by intermittent therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Common biopsy finding is a non-specific picture with fatty change, mild portal and parenchymal inflammation and increased variation in liver-cell appearances, also seen in psoriatic patients not on methotrexate; fibrosis arises as septa extending from portal tracts; duration of treatment was significantly longer in patients with serious liver disease (Dahl, Gregory, and Scheuer, 1971); majority of patients treated for two years or more had severe fibrosis or cirrhosis; intermittent therapy reduces hepatotoxicity (Dahl et al 1972; Cooperative Study 1973).

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the use of MARS albumin dialysis in treating paracetamol-induced liver failure and paracetamol-induced acute liver failure, framing paracetamol as a cause of human acute liver failure. One report notes a possible enhanced paracetamol clearance with MARS, with drug half-life decreasing from 3.4 h without albumin dialysis to 1.2 h after initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol poisoning/overdose causing acute liver failure (ALF). Helsinki study treated 113 ALF patients with MARS between 2001-2007 vs a historical 46-patient control group (1995-2001); toxic etiology in 63/113, 32 secondary to paracetamol poisoning (controls n=6). MARS group had lower baseline MELD; 6-month survival 84% vs 67% (not significant); liver recovery 81% vs 33% (p=0.031); 1 MARS patient received liver transplantation vs 2 controls, all three survived; only significant predictor of survival in the paracetamol subgroup was grade of hepatic encephalopathy at treatment start. In a separate report paracetamol half-life fell from 3.4 h to 1.2 h after MARS initiation. Paracetamol clearance associated with liver failure, encephalopathy, and hemodynamic/biochemical disturbances.

raw_record.support_text: A diagnosis of alpha-methyldopa-induced hepatitis was made in a pregnant woman treated for hypertension. After alpha-methyldopa was changed to labetolol, her symptoms and serum biochemistry gradually improved. The case was judged unique because deranged liver biochemistry was not incidental and, after excluding infective and autoimmune hepatitis, the authors concluded it was drug-induced hepatitis attributable to alpha-methyldopa.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patient treated for hypertension; therapeutic antihypertensive use; acute hepatitis with jaundice and resolution after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: acute alpha-methyldopa-induced hepatitis with jaundice (bilirubin up to 92 µmol/L) and striking ALT elevations up to 2511 U/L; prothrombin time only mildly elevated (16.4 s). Pathogenesis attributed to abnormal transformation of alpha-methyldopa by cytochrome P450 and an immune reaction to the resultant metabolite. Paper notes 5% of non-pregnant patients have minor liver-test alterations; 2.5-10% manifest hepatotoxicity; in <1%, acute liver injury resembling viral or chronic hepatitis or rarely a cholestatic reaction occurs 1-20 weeks after starting methyldopa; about 15% of methyldopa hepatotoxicity cases show moderate-to-severe chronic hepatitis with or without bridging necrosis and macronodular cirrhosis. Hepatocellular damage is reversible with discontinuation. Drug switched to labetolol with recovery over days.

raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid, an uricosuric diuretic used in hypertension, was withdrawn from the market because of cases of rare but severe hepatotoxicity. Between 0.1% and 0.7% of treated patients developed clinical hepatitis; the reaction occurred with significant delay and was dose independent. Liver damage resolved after discontinuation and recurred on rechallenge. In 60% of patients with severe hepatitis after tienilic acid, a specific anti-liver/kidney microsome type 2 (LKM-2) autoantibody targeting cytochrome P450 2C9 was detected.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic formerly used for hypertension; withdrawn from market for hepatotoxicity. Clinical hepatitis in 0.1-0.7% of treated patients; reaction delayed and dose independent; resolved on discontinuation, recurred on rechallenge. Livers infiltrated by neutrophils, eosinophils, and lymphocytes. LKM-2 autoantibody against unmodified liver/kidney microsomal proteins detected in 60% of severe cases, target cytochrome P450 2C9 (major tienilic acid metabolizing enzyme).

raw_record.support_text: After chronic treatment with the anti-hypertensive drug dihydralazine, a large number of patients with hepatitis were reported. This drug-induced hepatitis affected more female than male patients, and most patients were slow acetylators. Development of hepatitis was usually delayed by a lag period of several months, resolved after discontinuation, and was reinduced upon rechallenge. Patients had liver microsomal (LM) antibodies recognizing a single band identified as cytochrome P450 1A2.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of ticlopidine-induced prolonged cholestasis in a 60-year-old man who developed jaundice and pruritus three months after starting ticlopidine therapy. Other drugs taken by the patient were not considered probable causes; biliary obstruction and other causes of intra-hepatic cholestasis were excluded. Liver biopsy showed a cholestatic hepatitis with bile duct damage. The disease ran a severe, protracted course, with jaundice subsiding five months after drug withdrawal, though anicteric cholestasis laboratory abnormalities persisted more than a year later, fulfilling criteria for a minor form of drug-induced prolonged cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis by James et al., 41 pediatric patients who presented within 24 hours of an acetaminophen overdose with a serum acetaminophen concentration above the possible toxicity line on the nomogram were studied. Sixteen developed hepatotoxicity (9 severe, 7 mild); one patient with severe hepatotoxicity required liver transplantation and the other 15 recovered. Normal prothrombin time, aspartate aminotransferase, or alanine aminotransferase values within 48 hours of ingestion predicted low risk, whereas an abnormal value in any of these tests was a highly sensitive indicator of pending hepatotoxicity (100% sensitivity, 88% specificity). The authors concluded that all patients with acute acetaminophen overdose should be observed and treated with N-acetylcysteine for at least 48 hours.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; acute acetaminophen overdose with serum concentration above the nomogram possible-toxicity line, presenting within 24 hours of ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: 41 patients identified over a 10-year period; 16 had hepatotoxicity (9 severe, 7 mild); one severe case required liver transplantation, 15 recovered. Prothrombin time, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase within the first 24 hours failed to identify patients with (even severe) hepatotoxicity, but normal values within 48 hours predicted low risk; an abnormal value in any of these tests was 100% sensitive and 88% specific for pending hepatotoxicity. Recommendation to observe and treat with N-acetylcysteine for at least 48 hours.

raw_record.support_text: A male patient receiving azathioprine for discoid lupus erythematosus developed severe cholestatic hepatitis 14-21 days after starting treatment, with a peak bilirubin of 62.4 mg/dL. Viral hepatitis and other causes of hepatic dysfunction were clinically and serologically excluded, and liver biopsy showed cholestatic hepatocellular damage. Liver function began to improve 14 days after azathioprine was stopped, although alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase remained elevated after 4 months. The authors conclude the case argues for an idiosyncratic cholestatic hepatocellular damage caused by azathioprine.

The named hepatic phenotype is cholestatic hepatitis.

Among all the drugs the patient was receiving, metformin appears the most probably responsible agent, per the Nierenberg protocol: prior published cases of metformin-associated hepatotoxicity exist, latency from exposure onset to symptoms was a few weeks, the clinical picture improved to resolution after drug withdrawal, and other causes of hepatitis were excluded. No rechallenge was performed.

raw_record.extra_details: Metformin (dimetilbiguanida) 1700 mg/day. Presented with 2-3 weeks of dyspepsia/abdominal discomfort, then intense asthenia, anorexia, jaundice, coluria and generalized pruritus. Peak liver tests: total bilirubin 256 µmol/l, direct bilirubin 210 µmol/l, AST 1198 U/l, ALT 596 U/l, alkaline phosphatase 164 U/l, GGT 260 U/l. Injury resolved (analytical normal) within 3 months and remained normal at 9 months follow-up; no specific treatment given, insulin used to control diabetes. Viral, autoimmune, and tumor serologies, imaging (ultrasound, CT, cholangio-MRI) all negative. Liver biopsy not performed (patient refused). MEDLINE (1966-2004) search 'Metformin/adverse effects AND Hepatitis or Cholestasis' identified only 4 prior published cases; metformin hepatic toxicity described as extraordinarily rare. Comparison table of the 5 cases (Babich, Desilets, Nammour, Deutsch, present case) shows resolution in 4-12 weeks; one published case (Nammour) had rechallenge/concomitant pathology.

raw_record.support_text: A 27-year-old woman was admitted for a loculated pleural effusion secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis and received subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg for thromboembolism prevention. Elevated liver enzymes appeared four days after enoxaparin recommencement and continued to increase after discontinuation of RIPE anti-tuberculous therapy; highest values (day 16) were AST 875, ALT 489, ALP 188 IU/L with an R-factor of 6.1, consistent with a hepatocellular liver injury pattern. Liver enzymes decreased only after enoxaparin discontinuation and normalized within eight days. The RUCAM score delineated enoxaparin as the probable cause (score 8); anti-tuberculous agents scored 5 (possible) but were re-introduced after enzyme normalization with no effect on liver enzymes.

This confirms paracetamol as the cause of the liver injury in the overdose setting.

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study of 602 patients admitted with single-dose paracetamol poisoning with tobacco-use data; current daily tobacco use 70% (424/602) vs 31% in background population (P<0.0001). Mechanism mentioned: tobacco smoke induces cytochrome P450, enhancing oxidative metabolism of paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: Eight hundred patients were admitted with paracetamol (acetaminophen) intoxication; 602 with complete data were included. All received immediate N-acetylcysteine treatment. Severity of hepatotoxicity was estimated from alanine transaminase levels, international normalized ratio, and the incidence of hepatic encephalopathy and death or orthotopic liver transplant. Smoking was markedly associated with more severe hepatotoxicity, but paracetamol overdose itself was the causal toxic exposure attributed to the liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol intoxication) setting; severity of hepatotoxicity was higher among smokers than non-smokers, and smokers more often abused alcohol, were older, ingested more paracetamol, and co-overdosed with benzodiazepines.
raw_record.extra_details: Severity assessed via median alanine transaminase (1601 U/L non-smokers vs 6548 U/L smokers), INR (2.1 vs 3.1), hepatic encephalopathy (6.7% vs 19%) and death or liver transplant (2.8% vs 11%). Median paracetamol dose 400 mg/kg (non-smokers) vs 455 mg/kg (smokers); median time to N-acetylcysteine 14 h vs 20 h. In logistic regression, current daily tobacco use was an independent risk factor for hepatic encephalopathy (OR 2.68; 95% CI 1.28–5.62) and mortality (OR 3.64; 95% CI 1.23–10.75) in the overdose cohort. Proposed mechanisms (not independently established as causal): a 4-ene-VPA metabolite mediating mitochondrial/fatty-acid beta-oxidation disruption, polytherapy with microsomal P-450 inducers (e.g., phenobarbital, phenytoin) as a risk factor, carnitine deficiency, and impaired ketogenesis in malnourished or fasting children. The study measured mechanistic biomarkers of mitochondrial damage and damage-associated molecular patterns (glutamate dehydrogenase, mitochondrial DNA, and nuclear DNA fragments) in serum from 69 patients with acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure (AALF), of whom 34 did not recover and 35 did; all three biomarkers were significantly higher in those who died compared with survivors.

raw_record.extra_details: Study of 69 AALF patients (34 non-recovered/deceased vs 35 recovered). Non-survivors had higher GDH (930±145 vs 450±73 U/L), mtDNA (48±13 vs 21±6 and 43±7 vs 33±10 ng/mL for two genes), and nDNA fragments (210±13 vs 148±13 % of control). ROC AUCs at admission and at peak ALT predicted outcome comparably to peak MELD (0.77). Mechanism described: reactive metabolite depletes glutathione and binds proteins, causing mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, JNK activation, MPTP formation, nuclear DNA fragmentation, and oncotic necrosis. raw_record.support_text: Tienilic acid (TA), a uricosuric diuretic used to treat hypertension, was first marketed in Europe in 1976 and introduced in the US in 1979, then rapidly withdrawn from the US market in 1980 because of its hepatotoxic secondary effects. The incidence and clinical features of 340 reported cases supported an immune mechanism for TA-induced hepatitis, and a specific autoantibody (anti-LKM2, directed against a liver-kidney microsomal component) was detected only in patients with TA-induced hepatitis, serving as a specific marker.
raw_record.extra_details: Uricosuric diuretic used in hypertension; marketed in Europe 1976, US 1979, withdrawn from US market 1980 due to hepatotoxic effects; 340 reported cases of hepatitis supporting an immune (immunoallergic) mechanism; specific anti-LKM2 autoantibody against a liver-kidney microsomal (endoplasmic reticulum) component, a specific marker of TA-induced hepatitis; TA was devoid of direct hepatotoxic effect in laboratory animals.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase I single-agent trial, Ditercalinium (a pyridocarbazole dimer) was given as a single IV 6-hour infusion with dose escalation from 3 to 24 mg/m². The dose-limiting toxicity was hepatic, beginning at the 10 mg/m² level and characterized by increased plasma alkaline phosphatase and γgt. A liver biopsy and two post-mortem examinations showed liver microvacuolar steatosis; the hepatic toxicity was cumulative, as the three patients who received a second course showed a dramatic rise in AP and γgt, and one of these patients died 10 days later of hepatic failure. The maximal tolerated dose was 15 mg/m², and new experimental studies were required before further clinical trials.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Phase I trial in patients with histologically proven malignancy resistant to conventional therapy (advanced cancer indication); weekly single IV 6-hour infusion; hepatic toxicity cumulative with repeat (second) courses.
raw_record.extra_details: 21 patients received 24 courses. Starting dose 3 mg/m² with escalations to 6, 10, 15, 21, 24 mg/m² (at least 3 patients/level). Hepatic toxicity first appeared at the 3rd level (10 mg/m²) with elevation of alkaline phosphatase and γgt; MTD determined as 15 mg/m². Histology (liver biopsy day 28 in one patient plus two post-mortems) showed liver microvacuolar steatosis; one patient who received a second course died 10 days later of hepatic failure. Minor reversible blood-count changes; no alopecia, renal, or GI toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 48 kg female presented after a paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose; 4.5 hours post-ingestion her serum paracetamol was 885 µmol/L (134 mg/L), just below the Australian/New Zealand nomogram treatment threshold of 911 µmol/L, with ALT 23 IU/L and INR 1.4. Acetylcysteine infusion was started at 7 hours post-ingestion. By 19 hours post-overdose the paracetamol concentration was 218 µmol/L (33 mg/L) while ALT rose to 1575 IU/L, INR to 2.8 and lactate to 3.8 mmol/L, indicating drug-induced liver injury from paracetamol overdose. The patient developed transient right upper quadrant tenderness on day 2, received acetylcysteine for 132 hours until aminotransferases fell and INR was below 2.0, and was discharged well six days post-ingestion.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that fulminant hepatic failure secondary to cyproterone acetate (CPA) is rare and reports the sixth and seventh cases with a fatal outcome. All seven cases involved elderly patients with malignant disease receiving high-dose CPA, who first had nonspecific nausea, anorexia, and malaise, then progressive jaundice. Onset of liver disease from start of CPA ranged from 2 to 15 months; transaminases were 3-27 times normal, bilirubin markedly elevated at 9-30 times normal, and ALP usually under two times normal; duration from jaundice onset to death was two to seven weeks.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly patients with a malignant disease receiving high-dose CPA; both newly described cases died from liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure; postmortem in both new cases showed submassive/panlobular hepatocyte necrosis with marked cholestasis and ductular proliferation, consistent with drug-induced hepatitis; no preexisting chronic liver disease. Values across the seven reported fatal cases (Table 1): age 66-92 yr (mean 75), dose 100-300 mg (mean 257), onset 2-15 months (mean 8), duration jaundice-to-death 2-7 weeks (mean 4), AST 3-27xN, ALT 9-27xN, bilirubin 9-30xN, ALP 1-3xN. CPA discontinued at admission; progression to ascites, encephalopathy, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; death from liver failure 36 days after admission (case presented). Attribution supported by negative viral and antibody markers.

raw_record.support_text: During the study period, 1191 patients presented to hospital after paracetamol overdose; after excluding 106 without baseline urea measurement, the study population was 1085 patients (714 women, median age 33 years). N-acetylcysteine was given to 390 patients (35.9%), and the overall incidence of hepatotoxicity after paracetamol overdose was 5.4%. Hepatotoxicity was defined by prothrombin time ratio >1.3 or alanine transaminase ≥1000 U/l.
raw_record.extra_details: Prospective observational cohort of 1085 paracetamol-overdose patients (714 women, median age 33 y). Stated ingested dose 11.0 g (IQR 6.5-17.5 g), median interval ingestion-to-presentation 4.5 h (IQR 4.0-6.7 h). Hepatotoxicity defined as prothrombin time ratio >1.3 or ALT ≥1000 U/l; overall incidence 5.4%. N-acetylcysteine administered to 390 patients (35.9%). 394 patients (36.3%) were at high risk due to chronic alcohol excess (340), malnutrition (40), or enzyme-inducing drugs (14). Baseline serum urea concentration did not independently predict hepatotoxicity in multiple regression; explanatory variables were acute ethanol co-ingestion (inverse), above-normal treatment line, interval, serum paracetamol concentration, equivalent 4 h concentration, male and vomiting (R2=0.173).

Liver function tests improved after withdrawal; hepatic symptoms recurred weeks later requiring 6 months prednisolone therapy; sustained γ-GT elevation persisted. Rechallenge with low-dose etretinate for two weeks reproduced aminotransferase elevation (ASAT 2.01 µkat/l, ALAT 2.62 µkat/l, γ-GT 4.2 µkat/l) without eosinophilia or skin rash. Interval from onset of etretinate to hepatitis ranged from 2 weeks to 6 months at normal dose regimens; only 8 reported cases of biopsy-proven hepatitis in connection with etretinate (this case included).

raw_record.support_text: In the authors' patient, acute hepatitis with cholestasis appeared within a DRESS syndrome after about 3 weeks of sustained-release bupropion for smoking cessation. Other causes of acute liver injury were excluded, and the similar elevation of serum transaminases with a cholestatic pattern and weakly positive ANA supported a drug-induced reaction; because serum acetaminophen was undetectable and liver synthetic function was preserved, the acute hepatitis was attributed to an idiosyncratic reaction to bupropion. Liver enzymes normalized more than 8 weeks after bupropion was discontinued.
raw_record.extra_details: DRESS syndrome presentation with fever, rash, angioedema, eosinophilia, and low serum complement; drug-induced liver injury and cholestatic pattern with weakly positive ANA; liver enzymes normalized >8 weeks after discontinuation without liver biopsy because synthetic function (normal coagulation) was preserved and encephalopathy was absent; acetaminophen as potential co-suspect was excluded by undetectable serum levels and preserved synthetic function; also developed myositis with myocardial involvement and possible rhabdomyolysis; complex history included corticosteroid-induced hyperglycemia requiring intravenous insulin.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective study of 113 patients taking preventive isoniazid (INH) for at least 8 weeks, 19 of 101 patients with initially normal liver tests developed significant liver dysfunction, mostly hepatocellular, with three developing overt hepatitis. After excluding 12 patients who drank alcohol, 15 of 89 still developed significant liver dysfunction, 12 of whom were slow acetylators (p<0.05), and age was the only other risk factor. The paper concludes that fast acetylation is not a risk factor for INH-induced liver dysfunction.
raw_record.extra_details: Preventive INH 300 mg orally daily (or 5 mg/kg for children) in outpatients, followed prospectively; the paper cites an ~1% incidence of overt and 10-20% incidence of subclinical liver damage with INH therapy. Among 113 completing 2 months, 19/101 with normal initial tests developed significant liver dysfunction (3 overt hepatitis); excluding 12 alcohol drinkers, 15/89 remained affected, 12 being slow acetylators. Risk of INH-induced liver enzyme elevation by acetylator phenotype and age (alcohol excluded): under 35 fast acetylators 3.7%, slow 13%; over 35 fast 13.2%, slow 37% (p<0.02). Slow acetylation and older age were risk factors; fast acetylation was not a risk factor. Mitchel evidence on monoacetylhydrazine (P-450 mediated acylating agent causing liver necrosis) is discussed as a proposed mechanism, not an independent human DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: The laxative (phenolisatin) hepatitis, which runs under the mask of various liver and biliary diseases, is only reliably unmasked by the rechallenge test with phenolisatin. Glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) proved a particularly sensitive parameter, and transaminases (GOT, GPT) generally supported the proof by clear activity increases; bilirubin elevation was not obligatory. The paper reports 14 female patients with phenolisatin-induced liver diseases, whose histologic findings ranged from periportal liver fibrosis to advanced postnecrotic liver cirrhosis and scarring liver, with chronic-active hepatitis among the diagnostic forms.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All 14 reported cases were female; onset followed chronic long-term oral laxative use of 2 to 20 years; re-exposure (rechallenge) confirmed the diagnosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Rechallenge with 2 x 10 mg triacetyl-diphenolisatin on two consecutive days produced rises in GLDH (particularly sensitive), GOT and GPT; bilirubin elevation was not obligatory. Histologic spectrum included chronic-aggressive hepatitis (with transition to cirrhosis), acute recurrent and protracted hepatitis, chronic-persistent hepatitis, periportal liver fibrosis, postnecrotic scarring liver/cirrhosis, and one case of chronic-aggressive hepatitis with cholestasis (Fall 10, allegedly on oxyphenisatin-free laxatives). In six of ten examined cases low-titer antibodies against nuclei and smooth muscle were found by immunofluorescence; five of 14 were treated with immunosuppressives and/or glucocorticoids before the final diagnosis. Symptoms resembled acute/chronic liver or gallbladder disease. Before publication all 14 patients were fully investigated in hospital with entirely normal laboratory findings and histologically inactive stage. Reported hospitalizations and estimated total costs (e.g., 150,000 DM in Fall 1); some cases were reported as infectious disease or recognized as occupational disease, and some underwent cholecystectomy.

raw_record.support_text: Two pediatric patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) receiving mercaptopurine (6-MP) developed hepatotoxicity, attributed to their 6-MP treatment (case 1 with severe aminotransferase elevations, case 2 with modest aminotransferase elevations but significant hepatotoxicity out of proportion to enzyme levels). Both patients had homozygous wild-type TPMT. The hepatotoxicity resolved after the addition of allopurinol to 6-MP therapy, supporting 6-MP as the causative agent.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; hematologic malignancy (ALL); hepatotoxicity during standard 6-MP consolidation/maintenance therapy before allopurinol was added.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases. Case 1: severe elevation of aminotransferase enzyme levels. Case 2: modest aminotransferase elevations with significant hepatotoxicity. Both patients were homozygous wild-type for TPMT; metabolite testing of 6-TGN and 6-MMPN showed wide interpatient variability (about 20% of wild-type TPMT patients preferentially shunt 6-MP metabolism toward 6-MMPN). Hepatotoxicity was eliminated by adding allopurinol to reduce 6-MMPN. The mechanism of 6-MP hepatotoxicity is reported as unclear, with some evidence suggesting 6-TGN levels versus mitochondrial damage by free radicals generated by xanthine oxidase.

raw_record.support_text: This is the first report of aripiprazole-induced liver injury, in this case hepatitis. The authors conclude that despite good tolerance and few side effects, aripiprazole can also lead to severe drug-induced liver injury, and they recommend monitoring liver function before starting atypical antipsychotics and regularly thereafter.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had concurrent inhaled cocaine use for 4 years (about once per month), considered as a competing cause but deemed quite implausible due to the temporal relationship with aripiprazole and no prior signs of liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of aripiprazole-induced hepatitis. Hepatocellular mechanism judged the major cause based on ALT 22.5x upper limit of normal, AST >5x, ALP >2x, and GGT >11x upper limits. There was a temporal relationship with aripiprazole use and no previous signs or symptoms of liver injury. The change of medication to paliperidone (not CYP-metabolized, regarded safe in liver injury patients) resulted in progressive normalization of liver function tests. Authors recommend liver function monitoring before starting atypical antipsychotics.

raw_record.support_text: The paper presents 5 patients with 'isoniazid-associated hepatitis' who received prophylactic isoniazid (INH) for 3 weeks to 3 months before symptoms developed. In all 5 patients serum contained no hepatitis-associated antigen, and all drugs except INH (including indomethacin) were restarted without clinical exacerbation, supporting INH as the causal agent. INH rechallenge was not performed because a prior rechallenge of INH had been fatal.
raw_record.extra_details: 5 patients reported; duration of INH therapy before symptoms 3 weeks to 3 months; cases presented after the hospital changed to its current pharmaceutical supplier of INH. Other medications (indomethacin, phenobarbital, chloral hydrate, nitroglycerine, meprobamate, aspirin, etc.) were restarted without exacerbation; INH rechallenge avoided due to a prior fatal rechallenge report. Histology varied from classic viral hepatitis to portal inflammation, portal noncaseating granulomas, and portal/periportal eosinophil infiltration. Earlier literature: 6 cases before 1960, scattered reports including fatal cases, and 2,321 Capitol Hill INH prophylactic recipients with clinical hepatitis in 19 (2 died); Scharer and Smith prospective study found 10% asymptomatic transaminase elevations in 90 patients. The paper notes INH-associated hepatitis is apparently idiosyncratic and not dose-related, with severity ranging from transient transaminase elevations to fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The study analyzed the role of plasma exchange (PE) in acute liver failure (ALF) due to yellow phosphorus (YP) poisoning. YP is directly hepatotoxic after absorption, and YP poisoning manifests in three stages, with the third stage after 72 hours leading to resolution or death. In the study cohort, all patients had icterus and elevated liver enzymes, and 30% had grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy.

raw_record.extra_details: Ten patients with ALF due to YP poisoning treated with plasma exchange (33 sessions, mean 3.3). Recovery from ALF in 7/10 (70%); 2 patients died and 1 was referred for liver transplantation. Mean amount of YP consumed was 13.5 g (median 10 g); 85.7% recovered among those consuming <20 g vs 14.3% among those consuming >20 g. Presenting features included icterus, vomiting, nausea, abdominal pain, chills; 30% had grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy. Mechanism: phosphine gas from YP reacting with gastric acid inhibits cytochrome C oxidase and oxidative respiration. Significant post-PE improvements seen in total bilirubin (9.3 to 2.76 mg/dL), SGOT (530 to 53.5 U/L), SGPT (378 to 54.5 U/L), and INR (2.26 to 1.08).

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that drug-induced hepatitis and drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis are recognized complications of NSAIDs, and that COX-2 inhibitors have been implicated in prior case reports of AIN and hepatitis, but simultaneous presentation of both with a single therapeutic agent had previously been reported once with clometacin and never with a COX-2 inhibitor. Given the temporal sequence, clinical findings, and liver and renal biopsy histology, they believe there is good evidence to implicate rofecoxib as the causative agent of this combined drug-induced hepatitis and acute interstitial nephritis in the patient. The liver biopsy demonstrated zone 3 cholestasis, a mixed periportal infiltrate of neutrophils and eosinophils, and mild bile duct proliferation; hepatic dysfunction and cholestasis resolved over weeks and liver function tests fully recovered within months.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report. Simultaneous combined drug-induced hepatitis (zone 3 cholestasis, mixed periportal neutrophil/eosinophil infiltrate, mild bile duct proliferation on liver biopsy) and drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis attributed to rofecoxib. Hepatic dysfunction produced a coagulopathy (returned to normal within ~4 weeks, permitting renal biopsy), persistent leucocytosis with eosinophilia (1.8e9/L), and cholestasis that resolved over 4 weeks; liver function tests fully recovered over ~3 months and remained normal at 12 months. Patient also developed renal failure requiring haemodialysis, heavy proteinuria and acute tubular necrosis. Authors note this combined presentation had previously been reported once with clometacin and never with a COX-2 inhibitor.

The authors attribute these findings to acetaminophen.

raw_record.support_text: A 31-year-old man with chronic glomerulonephritis and oligozoospermia was prescribed clomiphene citrate tablets 50 mg per day. On day 3 of therapy brown urine appeared; two days later his urine turned reddish-brown and he complained of severe upper abdominal pain with icterus. He was diagnosed with liver injury and cholecystitis. As CC-induced liver injury was speculated, the drug was discontinued; jaundice resolved by day 10 after admission and laboratory values improved with uneventful recovery. In the discussion the authors note the patient had no viral hepatitis or other liver diseases, and since other causes/drugs were excluded, they speculated the liver injury was caused by CC exposure; the Naranjo algorithm score was 6 (probable ADR) after CC had been stopped for 1 week.

On day 3 of therapy brown urine appeared; later reddish-brown urine and severe upper abdominal pain, icterus on skin and sclera, no rash. Diagnosed with liver injury and cholecystitis; abdominal CT showed cholecystitis. Laboratory findings on day 1: AST 274.08 U/L, ALT 419.61 U/L, GGT 490.6 U/L, TBIL 73.53 µmol/L, DBIL 44.21 µmol/L, urobilinogen 2+. Jaundice disappeared by day 10 with normalization of several lab values; symptomatic treatment (liver protection, analgesics) and drug discontinuation; uneventful recovery. Naranjo score 6 (probable ADR). Proposed mechanisms (immune-mediated reaction, toxic metabolite accumulation, altered CYP2D6 metabolism, altered estrogen metabolism) are hypothesized, not established. Both clomiphene and tamoxifen are classified as SERMs.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old man with severe aplastic anemia was treated with cyclosporin A, steroid pulse therapy, and metenolone acetate. Marked transaminase elevation appeared after starting metenolone acetate, followed by hepatic failure and death. Autopsy findings were compatible with drug-induced liver injury, and metenolone acetate was considered the most likely causative agent. Metenolone acetate was given at 25 mg/day beginning July 18 for less than 1 month; on August 14 AST rose to 1609 IU/l, ALT to 2173 IU/l, gamma-GTP to 126 IU/l, and total bilirubin to 6.5 mg/dl. After discontinuation transaminases decreased immediately, but the patient fell into hepatic coma on August 15 and died on August 28. The authors caution that liver impairment from this drug, usually regarded as mild, reversible, and infrequent, warrants extreme caution in debilitated patients.

raw_record.support_text: Flutamide is absorbed orally and metabolized to OH-flutamide in the liver; because it is metabolized in the liver, hepatopathy has been a known side effect. In Japan, eight patients reportedly died of severe liver dysfunction including fulminant hepatitis. In the US, the FDA reported 20 deaths from hepatopathy and 26 patients with severe hepatopathy requiring hospitalization from February 1989 to December 1994. In the present cohort of 181 prostate cancer patients, hepatopathy developed in 44 (24.3%), with 36/111 (32.4%) among patients not receiving UDCA versus 8/70 (11.4%) with UDCA; hepatopathy was defined as GOT or GPT ≥1.25 times the upper limit of normal at least once.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with prostate cancer; many also received LHRH analogs or surgical castration; a subset received concurrent UDCA as a candidate preventive agent (bias risk noted for allocation).
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of flutamide hepatopathy: overall 44/181 (24.3%); 36/111 (32.4%) without UDCA vs 8/70 (11.4%) with UDCA; grade distribution without UDCA: 29 grade 1, 4 grade 2, 1 grade 3, 2 grade 4. One-year hepatopathy-free rate 59.6% without UDCA vs 88.4% with UDCA (P<0.005). Hepatopathy criterion: GOT or GPT >=1.25x ULN at least once. Japan: 8 deaths from severe liver dysfunction including fulminant hepatitis. US FDA: 20 deaths and 26 hospitalized cases (Feb 1989-Dec 1994). Phase-II study: abnormal increases in GOT 12.3% and GPT 10.8%. Comparable incidences: 35.1% (Yamamoto) and 40% (Ikemoto). Proposed mechanism: flutamide binds cytochrome P-450 and induces hepatopathy by inhibiting mitochondria and ATP synthesis; serum flutamide higher (2.76x) and OH-flutamide lower (0.76x) in patients with hepatopathy, suggesting reduced hepatic metabolism to OH-flutamide.

raw_record.support_text: Oxyphenisatin has been reported as the cause of hepatic injury in more than 100 described patients, mostly female. In about one-third the injury resembled acute hepatitis with diffuse hepatocellular necrosis, acidophilic bodies, lobular disarray, Kupffer cell prominence and portal inflammation; the other two-thirds had histologic changes of chronic active hepatitis, many with features of cirrhosis, and a few showed subacute hepatic necrosis. Withdrawal usually produced rapid improvement, while readministration of oxyphenisatin to several patients led to return or increase of abnormal values.
raw_record.extra_details: More than 100 patients with hepatic injury attributable to the drug; a few showed subacute hepatic necrosis; prognosis good with withdrawal, most patients showing rapid improvement and complete or near-complete resolution of biochemical abnormalities; readministration (rechallenge) in several patients led to return or increase of abnormal laboratory values; affected patients were predominantly female, though the paper notes the data do not permit distinguishing disproportionate female susceptibility from greater exposure.

raw_record.support_text: In a 4½-year retrospective study of hospitalized children with rheumatic fever treated with salicylates, 5 of 34 children manifested salicylate-induced hepatitis. The average serum salicylate level in those with hepatotoxicity was 30.9 mg/dL versus 19.7 mg/dL in the rest.

raw_record.extra_details: Aspirin was the administered drug; the injury is labeled both salicylate-induced and aspirin-induced hepatitis. 5 of 34 children affected. Criteria: clinical signs/symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, right upper quadrant tenderness) plus SGOT >100 IU/L. Mean age of affected group 10.8 years; mean serum salicylate 30.9 mg/dL (all five had levels >25 mg/dL, two >30 mg/dL). Liver function tests returned to normal after salicylate discontinuation. Authors recommend maintaining serum salicylate at approximately 15-25 mg/dL.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report clinically significant hepatotoxicity in 14.7% of children with rheumatic fever treated with aspirin at a dosage of 100 mg/kg/day. All affected patients showed symptomatic hepatotoxic effects in the second week of aspirin therapy; the average salicylate level in this group was 30.9 mg/dL, significantly higher than the 19.7 mg/dL average in patients not showing clinically significant hepatotoxic effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population with rheumatic fever indication; aspirin dosed at 100 mg/kg/day (high, therapeutic-dose schedule for this indication).
raw_record.extra_details: Clinically significant hepatotoxicity occurred in 14.7% of children with rheumatic fever. Symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) began in the second week of therapy. Affected group average salicylate level 30.9 mg/dL vs 19.7 mg/dL in unaffected patients. Chemical abnormalities were elevations of both SGOT and SGPT; serum bilirubin was normal and alkaline phosphatase normal or slightly increased. Liver biopsy in one patient showed preserved lobular architecture, widened sinusoidal spaces, and focal hepatocyte necrosis, degeneration, and ballooning with anisocytosis, anisonucleosis, and mitotic figures. Hepatotoxicity did not correlate with hypersensitivity (no pruritus, urticarial rash, fever, or blood eosinophilia). Salicylic acid kinetics are dose-dependent due to saturation of salicyluric acid and salicyl phenolic glucuronide formation, increasing formation of acyl glucuronide and gentisic acid. Transaminase elevations were not artifactual laboratory interference. Maximum SGOT levels 216-1,650 units with salicylate levels 26-39 mg/dL in individual patients.

raw_record.support_text: Although acetaminophen (APAP) is considered safe at therapeutic doses, overdoses can cause liver injury and acute liver failure. In the United States, 60,000–80,000 emergency department visits, 30,000–40,000 hospitalizations with more than 5,000 patients developing severe liver injury, and 300–500 deaths occur annually due to APAP overdose, and APAP overdose is the most frequent etiology of acute liver failure in the United States, the United Kingdom, and other mainly western countries.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP considered safe at therapeutic doses; injury is dose-related overdose injury. US annual estimates: 60,000–80,000 emergency department visits, 30,000–40,000 hospitalizations, >5,000 patients with severe liver injury, 300–500 deaths. APAP overdose is the most frequent etiology of acute liver failure (ALF) in the US, UK, and other western countries. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is approved as a clinical antidote and has saved many overdose patients, though with a narrow therapeutic window and limited efficacy after very high overdoses.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis developed acute hepatitis, probably due to orodispersible prednisolone (Solupred), which was started at 40 mg/d after intravenous methylprednisolone. Liver tests worsened after readministration of orodispersible prednisolone and improved after its withdrawal and replacement with oral prednisone, supporting causality. The case is titled prednisolone-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Orodispersible (Solupred) formulation; patient with ulcerative colitis receiving concurrent enoxaparine, hydroxyzine, cholecalciferol, and low-dose paracetamol.
raw_record.extra_details: At day 14 after starting prednisolone: ALT 165 U/L (3.3 N), AST 73 U/L (1.5 N), Alk Phos 369 U/L (3.2 N), GGT 706 U/L (12.8 N), bilirubin normal. Values improved on withdrawal and worsened on rechallenge (day 27: ALT 730 U/L (14.6 N), AST 313 U/L, Alk Phos 393 U/L, GGT 1097 U/L), then resolved after switch to oral prednisone (Cortancyl). Isolated antismooth muscle antibody (1/160); HBsAg, HCV, HIV, and EBV serologies negative; no alcohol. Liver function tests normal 3 months later.

raw_record.extra_details: Orodispersible prednisolone formulation (Solupred). French method causality assessment with chronobiologic and semiological scores gave 'probably related'. Recurrent hepatitis after reintroduction and rapid resolution after discontinuation; no liver biopsy performed because the accidental rechallenge was informative. Authors conclude prednisolone has joined the list of drugs known to induce hepatitis. Prednisolone is metabolized in the kidneys and liver; formulation contains polyacrylate, colloidal silica, mannitol, crospovidone, aspartam, magnesium stearate, and sodic metasulfobenzoate.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that the reappearance of liver impairment shortly after ketoconazole treatment was restarted strongly supports the evidence for ketoconazole-induced liver damage. Because no liver toxicity was found in animal experiments, they classify the hepatotoxicity as a type II (idiosyncratic) reaction per the National Institutes of Health classification: unpredictable from animal experiments, rare in humans, and dose-independent.
raw_record.extra_details: A 68-year-old woman treated for recalcitrant Trichophyton rubrum dermatophytosis; started on 200 mg ketoconazole daily for 12 weeks then increased to 400 mg daily. Two weeks later she developed pruritus, rhinorrhoea, tiredness, dizziness, dark urine, and pale faeces. LFTs (serum alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) were compatible with parenchymal liver damage. First biopsy showed enlarged portal tracts with slight bile duct proliferation, moderate mononuclear infiltration, focal parenchymal necroses, and condensed reticulin with ceroid in Kupffer's cells. Symptoms and LFTs normalized on withdrawal. On rechallenge 17 weeks later at 200 mg daily, symptoms and abnormal LFTs reappeared within two weeks; biopsy showed less prominent parenchymal changes, rare necroses, and no Kupffer cell proliferation; again resolved on stopping. Hepatitis B surface antigen and antibodies to hepatitis B and A viruses negative; eosinophilia absent; she received no other drugs. Histology resembled methyldopa-induced hepatitis (enlarged portal tracts, mononuclear infiltration, piecemeal necrosis as in chronic active hepatitis). Classified as a dose-independent, unpredictable type II idiosyncratic reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 40 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis included in the final data analysis, 4 developed fulminant hepatic failure as defined by Trey and Davidson. Of these, one died from a secondary cytomegalovirus infection 5 weeks after liver transplantation and another died before a donor organ became available; of the remaining two, one made a spontaneous recovery and the second died. All four fulminant cases developed grade 4 encephalopathy. The remaining 36 patients had no evidence of hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis; 4 developed fulminant hepatic failure (Trey and Davidson criteria), all with grade 4 encephalopathy; among them one died from secondary cytomegalovirus infection 5 weeks after liver transplantation, one died before a donor organ became available, one recovered spontaneously, and one died; remaining 36 patients had no encephalopathy. In 12 patients (30%) there was a documented hepatitis-like reaction to a previous halothane anaesthetic, and at least 27 patients (68%) had received documented previous halothane anaesthetics (median 2). Interval between final anaesthetic and most recent previous anaesthetic was 2 weeks to 20 years (median 1 year). Interval between anaesthetic exposure and onset of hepatic injury was 1-24 days (median 6 days); peak recorded AST was 61-14,500 IU/l (normal 0-45), maximal prothrombin time prolongation 68 s. Previous operations were major in 9 patients and minor in the remainder, with no recorded surgical or anaesthetic complications. Peak AST for fulminant cases was 5990 (4140-14,500) IU/l versus 1000 (61-2000) for non-fulminant; survival 25% (1/4) in fulminant versus 100% (36/36) in non-fulminant.

raw_record.support_text: The study tested serum from 40 patients with a diagnosis of halothane hepatitis for anti-TFA-RSA antibodies and assessed clinical correlates. Halothane-associated hepatitis occurred after anaesthetic exposure, with jaundice onset and fulminant course in some patients; the paper identifies halothane as the cause of the hepatitis, noting that fulminant hepatic failure secondary to halothane exposure carries ~80% mortality and is an indication for urgent liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Inhalational anaesthetic exposure; cases had a clinical diagnosis of halothane hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 40 patients with halothane hepatitis studied, 12 anti-TFA-RSA antibody positive and 28 negative. Antibody presence correlated with severity of hepatic necrosis (presence of hepatic encephalopathy) but not with transaminase rise. Median AST elevated (1240 IU/l in antibody-positive, 1000 IU/l in antibody-negative); median interval between anaesthetic and jaundice onset 6 days. Fulminant hepatic failure secondary to halothane carries ~80% mortality and is an indication for urgent liver transplantation (reference to prior series). The TFA hapten is used only as a biomarker/hapten in the anti-TFA-RSA ELISA, not independently implicated as the injuring entity.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old woman with severe atopic dermatitis and allergic contact dermatitis was started on mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 500 mg three times daily as a corticosteroid-sparing agent. After a month she developed a biochemical hepatitis with ALT rising from 22 to 418 IU/L and AST from 20 to 139 IU/L; after dose reduction to 500 mg twice daily, ALT and AST rose to 821 and 203 IU/L. Viral hepatitis serologies were negative, ANA was positive (speckled 1:160), and she denied alcohol or herbs; hydroxyzine was taken only intermittently. The hepatology consult agreed with MMF-induced hepatitis, and liver enzymes were normal 1 month after stopping MMF.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Dose 500 mg three times daily, reduced to 500 mg twice daily. ALT rose from 22 to 418 IU/L then to 821 IU/L; AST rose from 20 to 139 IU/L then to 203 IU/L. Asymptomatic (no abdominal pain, malaise, jaundice). Negative hepatitis A/B/C serologies; antinuclear antibodies positive speckled 1:160. Resolution to normal ALT/AST one month after discontinuation. Paper frames MMF-associated hepatitis as rare and as hepatitis due to drug hypersensitivity; authors conclude MMF is relatively safe but physicians should monitor for rare hepatitis. References supporting MMF-induced transaminase elevation: Balal et al (79 transplant patients, 11 with modest liver enzyme elevations, median onset 28 days, resolution 16 days after withdrawal or 50% dose reduction), Hantash and Fiorentino (2 atopic dermatitis patients), a toxic hepatitis case (AST/ALT up to 750 IU/L) in ANCA-positive vasculitis.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes 2 patients who developed hepatotoxicity on clozapine; the first had clozapine discontinued and was rechallenged at a later date with similar hepatotoxicity, while the second remained on clozapine with the abnormalities resolving spontaneously. Both intentional (self-harm) and unintentional (seeking pain relief with increased daily amounts) APAP overdoses occur, and the paper reviews cohorts of APAP-related ALF patients, including 275 APAP-related ALF patients among whom 55% had alcohol use and 53% had taken an opioid-APAP combination product.

ALFSG registry (NCT00518440) enrolled >3000 ALF subjects, 46% with severe or fatal APAP liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: In the Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) cohort, etiologic diagnoses of APAP (acetaminophen) toxicity were made by each study site's primary investigator and further adjudicated with an ALFSG causality algorithm requiring a history of APAP ingestion, detection of APAP in plasma, a biochemical pattern consistent with APAP toxicity (serum aminotransferases ≥1000 IU/L with total bilirubin <10.0 mg/dL at presentation), and, when available, presence of APAP-Cys adducts. Subjects meeting these criteria were considered highly likely/definite APAP toxicity. This establishes acetaminophen (in overdose) as a confirmed cause of acute liver failure in humans.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (infants); paracetamol given at excessive/supratherapeutic dosing (100 mg/kg/d orally for 3 days in case 1; 80 mg/kg/d rectally for 7 days in case 2) with co-administered clarithromycin and codeine, respectively; case 2 had malnutrition of unknown cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Two children (19-month and 28-month-old girls) with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure complicated by hepatic encephalopathy; paracetamol levels of 5.4 pg/ml (36 h after last intake) and 6.1 pg/ml (24 h after last intake) indicated hepatotoxicity; both treated with NAC and total plasma exchange (1200 ml / 900 ml FFP) while evaluated for orthotopic liver transplantation per King's College Hospital criteria, both recovered without transplant; case 2 had severe hypoglycemia (3 mg/dl), hyperlactemia, hyperammonemia, and signs of brain edema treated with therapeutic hypothermia. Mechanism text: ~5% of the drug is oxidized by cytochrome P450 to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, normally inactivated by glutathione; single high dose of 120-150 mg/kg or repeated supratherapeutic doses decrease intracellular glutathione, and low glutathione (e.g., malnutrition in patient 2) can lead to accumulation of toxic NAPQI with subsequent liver cell necrosis.

raw_record.support_text: Symptomatic hepatitis from ketoconazole use was documented as early as 1981. In several cases a cause-effect relationship with ketoconazole was established by rechallenge. The reaction is described as idiosyncratic rather than immunoallergic or toxic and is unrelated to daily dosage, cumulative total dose, or duration of therapy. Jaundice occurred in 63% to 100% of cases. The most serious side effect of ketoconazole is hepatitis, which has proved fatal in seven reported cases; the present report describes a 45-year-old Japanese-American woman who developed fulminant hepatic failure leading to liver transplantation after 58 days of ketoconazole 200 mg daily for candidal onychomycosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Drug-induced hepatitis that has proved fatal in seven reported cases (literature review); present index case of fulminant hepatic failure requiring liver transplant in a 45-year-old woman treated with ketoconazole 200 mg/day for 58 days for candidal onychomycosis. Cause-effect established by rechallenge in several cases. Reaction is idiosyncratic, unrelated to daily dose, cumulative dose, or therapy duration. Incidence estimated by manufacturer as 1 in 10,000 and later 1 in 15,000 exposures, with a Dutch review suggesting closer to 1 in 2000. Onset from 2 to 365 days, mean ~2 months; jaundice in 63% to 100% of cases; anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise common. Index case laboratory peak values: SGOT 2561 U/L, SGPT 3811 U/L, LDH 709 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 157 U/L, bilirubin 4.2 mg/dl. Hepatitis A/B serology and ANA negative; concurrent levothyroxine (Synthroid) not attributed as cause.

Apoptotic cell death (M30) was three times higher than normal and overall cell death (M65) was more than 30 times higher than normal, with high aminotransferase levels indicating high rates of necrosis. The case is presented as a biochemical demonstration of the osmotic gliopathy mechanism of hepatic encephalopathy in ALF.

Authors state these are the first reports of impaired hepatic synthetic function due to rifampicin monotherapy; prior tuberculosis-treatment reports were confounded by concurrent hepatotoxic antitubercular drugs.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that arsenamide has a toxic effect upon the liver. In two cases treatment was followed by jaundice (three days and four weeks after the last injection), and one patient developed fatal necrosis of the liver after receiving only three injections. This liver injury occurred during therapeutic use of arsenamide (125 mg, 1.8-2.5 mg/kg daily IV, usually 10-12 doses) in patients with bancroftian filariasis.
raw_record.extra_details: Arsenamide (p-bis-(carboxymethyl-mercapto)-arsino-benzamide) used for bancroftian filariasis; dose 125 mg (1.8-2.5 mg/kg) daily by IV injection, usually 10-12 doses. Liver injury: jaundice in two cases (3 days and 4 weeks after last injection) and fatal hepatic necrosis in one patient after only three injections. Other minor toxic effects included vomiting, dizziness, headache, and weight loss. Competitive/alternative causes (infective hepatitis, malnutrition with tocopherol/cysteine deficiency) were considered and excluded: clean syringes/needles per injection and too-short incubation period ruled out viral hepatitis. Authors concluded use is not devoid of risk and, since filariasis is not fatal, arsenamide use is not justifiable for general treatment; advised keeping dose low (preferably below 0.6 mg/kg), hospital supervision, and protein dietary supplement to fortify the liver.

raw_record.support_text: A 19-year-old female patient with Friedreich's ataxia and grand-mal epilepsy died after therapy with valproic acid (valproate) from acute liver failure with massive lactacidosis. Clinical symptoms were hyperventilation, increasing loss of consciousness and shock, leading to treatment-resistant hepatic coma. Pathoanatomy showed extensive confluent lytic necroses of the liver acini (centrolobular and intermediary accentuation) and small-to-medium droplet fatty degeneration increasing from periphery to centre. The paper states the disease picture is quite characteristic for being caused by valproic acid.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that in severe cases of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) due to paracetamol overdose there is a high mortality, the only treatment of proven benefit is orthotopic liver transplantation, and a substantial proportion of patients listed for urgent transplantation die whilst waiting because they become too ill. Patients with paracetamol-induced acute liver injury were admitted to the Scottish Liver Transplant Unit. This establishes paracetamol overdose as a definite human cause of acute liver failure/FHF with fatal outcomes.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose (POD) causing fulminant hepatic failure/acute liver failure. High mortality in severe cases; orthotopic liver transplantation is the only treatment of proven benefit, and some listed patients die awaiting a graft. King's College Hospital (KCH) prognostic criteria for transplant listing include pH <7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation or prothrombin time >100 s plus plasma creatinine >300 µmol/L plus grade III-IV coma (original positive predictive value 67%, specificity 94%, sensitivity 55%, accuracy 83%). A meta-analysis of 10 studies found available criteria not very sensitive; additional predictors evaluated include arterial blood lactate and serum phosphate. Management included N-acetyl cysteine 150 mg/kg until prothrombin time falls, volume resuscitation, norepinephrine, and continuous venovenous hemofiltration with lactate-free fluid. Clinical features of severe injury: coagulopathy (prothrombin time >50 s), metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, renal failure, and encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: Two cohorts of patients with acetaminophen (paracetamol)-induced fulminant hepatic failure admitted to the Scottish Liver Transplant Unit are described. In cohort 1 (n=97), 72 survived with medical management, 15 met KCH criteria and died, 6 met KCH criteria and were transplanted, and 4 died without meeting KCH criteria; 12 met KCHC but were not listed (alcohol abuse, IV drug abuse, psychiatric illness, or medically unfit). In cohort 2 (n=85), 50 survived medically, 23 died after meeting KCH criteria, 9 were transplanted after meeting criteria, and 3 died without meeting criteria. Table 1 reports a mean acetaminophen dose of 29.0±12.6 g in cohort 1 and 28.0±16.8 g in cohort 2, with overdose-to-treatment times and hepatic encephalopathy status.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a 47-year-old man who developed acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after consuming only four doses of troglitazone. He experienced vomiting and dehydration, and despite prompt discontinuation of troglitazone his symptoms progressed to jaundice and fatigue; he had no history of exposure to other hepatotoxins. Evaluation revealed transaminitis without underlying liver disease, and liver biopsy showed patchy cholestatic hepatitis with plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocellular giant-cell transformation, and fat accumulation, consistent with severe drug-induced hepatitis; the patient was managed supportively and liver function returned to normal. Earlier reports (Gitlin, Neuschwander-Tetri and colleagues, 1998) described severe hepatotoxicity associated with troglitazone in patients who consumed it for at least 1 month and received supportive care or liver transplantation. The authors emphasize the unpredictable nature of troglitazone hepatotoxicity and its potentially life-threatening effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Current case: acute subfulminant hepatotoxicity after only four doses, with vomiting, dehydration, jaundice, fatigue, transaminitis, no other hepatotoxins, no underlying liver disease. Biopsy: patchy cholestatic hepatitis with plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocellular giant-cell transformation, and fat accumulation; no chronic liver disease. Managed supportively with eventual normalization of liver function. Earlier 1998 reports (Gitlin and Neuschwander-Tetri, respectively) described severe troglitazone hepatotoxicity after at least 1 month of use treated with supportive care or liver transplantation. Authors highlight the unpredictable (idiosyncratic) nature and potentially life-threatening effects and call for vigilant monitoring of liver enzyme levels.

raw_record.support_text: The report describes 67 patients who developed hepatic injury after ingestion of acetaminophen (APAP) with therapeutic intent; all were regular users of alcohol. Doses were in the 'nontoxic' range (<6 g/d) in 60% of the group, within the recommended range (<4 g/d) in 40%. The characteristic feature was towering aspartate transaminase levels ranging from 3,000 to 48,000 IU in more than 90% of cases, and almost 20% of the patients died. The data were similar to 94 cases of therapeutic-intent APAP injury reported in the literature, providing further evidence of hepatic injury in regular users of alcohol, especially chronic alcoholics.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurred in regular users of alcohol (chronic alcoholics) taking acetaminophen at therapeutic (nontoxic) doses; alcohol co-exposure is the required susceptibility context.
raw_record.extra_details: Registry of 67 patients reported by hepatologists; 64% were 'alcoholic' or reported >80 g/d alcohol, 35% took 60 g/d or less. Doses were stated in 85% of cases (<6 g/d nontoxic in 60%, <4 g/d recommended in 40%, 4.1-6 g/d in 20%). AST from 3,000 to 48,000 IU in >90% of cases; almost 20% died (13/67; one transplant survivor included among fatal); 78% recovered; zone 3 necrosis in 14/16 biopsied cases. Compared with 94 literature cases (19% death). Susceptibility attributed to induction of cytochrome P-4502EI (CYP2E1) by ethanol and depletion of glutathione (GSH), malnutrition, and impaired glucuronidation from fasting. Ages 23-88, 63% male, 60% aged 30-50. Contrasted with suicidal-overdose APAP cases (usually >10 g, often >15 g), which cause dose-dependent severe hepatic necrosis and fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes APAP (acetaminophen)-induced hepatic injury in alcoholic patients as a classic, distinctive syndrome characterized by towering AST levels (usually with lower ALT), zone 3 necrosis as a classical hepatotoxic lesion, and a fatal outcome in almost one fifth of patients. Analysis of 161 regular alcohol users (67 registry, 94 literature cases) who ingested APAP with therapeutic intent showed the majority took 6 g or less per day (23% and 40% of registry/literature groups took less than 4 g/d), well below the accepted toxic range, with a presumed basis of potentiation of APAP hepatotoxicity by ethanol.

raw_record.extra_details: Analysis of 161 patients (67 from an alcohol/APAP hepatotoxicity registry and 94 from the literature) plus 91 additional literature cases; AST values of 3,000 to 48,000 U in the vast majority, with AST exceeding ALT, virtually pathognomonic compared with alcoholic hepatitis (AST rarely exceeding 250 IU) and viral hepatitis (AST 200-3,000 IU); fatal outcome in about one fifth of patients. Zone 3 necrosis seen in all but 2 of 15 patients with available histology and in 23 of 26 literature-reported cases. Mechanism: ~5% of APAP metabolized by cytochrome P-450 to a reactive electrophilic intermediate detoxified by glutathione conjugation; excessive or potentiated (ethanol-stimulated) metabolism overwhelms glutathione and causes hepatocellular necrosis via covalent binding/oxidative stress. Only 18 of the published patients took more than 10 g/d.

An adverse drug reaction due to HDMTX (high-dose methotrexate) was evaluated with the WHO Causality assessment scale, and the adverse events were rated 'Certain' since the child's haematology and liver function laboratory investigations were normal before the start of HDMTX infusion. Severity was assessed by Hartwig's severity scale as level 7, which led to the death of the patient. Earlier in the case, the child with acute lymphocytic leukaemia developed hepatic failure after HDMTX infusion (elevated SGPT to 259 IU/L, SGOT to 149-153 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.70-10.69 mg/dL) and was treated with N-acetyl cysteine, lactulose, vitamin K, and ursodeoxycholic acid for hepatic failure.

This reflects that acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose can cause hepatotoxicity, though the reported ingested dose alone is a poor predictor of that risk.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute single-event paracetamol overdose; risk of hepatotoxicity depends on plasma paracetamol concentration and time since ingestion. In 1571 acute overdose presentations to an Australian regional toxicology centre there was a positive correlation between reported ingested dose and measured plasma paracetamol concentration; based on the 150 mg/L treatment line there was a 10% chance of requiring antidote treatment after a reported dose of 13-16 g, 50% of patients were above the treatment line after 30-34 g, and 90% after 48-50 g. NAC is considered highly effective when given within 8 h of ingestion but is often given empirically when reported dose >=10 g, which would have led to unnecessary NAC administration in over 50% of early presenters (<8 h).

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of cholestatic hepatitis due to spiramycin. They note that intrahepatic cholestasis is frequent after C14 macrolide therapy with troleandomycin and erythromycin, but state that to their knowledge no case of hepatitis had been described following spiramycin (a C16 macrolide) before they observed a patient with a cholestatic hepatitis due to spiramycin treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: 52-year-old woman treated for sore throat with spiramycin 500 mg t.i.d. for 3 days. Onset of complaints (abdominal pain, pruritus, vomiting) within 5 days of start; initial labs collected 9 days after start: bilirubin 2.4 mg/dl, ASAT 5 x N, ALAT 10 x N, alkaline phosphatase 2 x N, gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase 200 mU/ml. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, CMV, EBV, HSV negative; no eosinophilia; normal liver/bile duct ultrasound. Ceased spiramycin with progressive improvement (pruritus 21 days, nausea/vomiting 29 days); heart-disease drugs (dipyridamol, lisinopril, diltiazem) continued. Intravenous cholangiography normal after bilirubin normalisation; liver biopsy 26 days after onset showed severe cholestatic hepatitis, centrilobular predominant, with mild hepatocyte necrosis and inflammatory infiltrate, reviewed as compatible with drug-induced hepatitis similar to other macrolides. Attribution based on accepted criteria: onset within 5 days of drug start, laboratory normalisation within 6 months after cessation, and exclusion of other causes.

raw_record.support_text: Liver injury is a prominent feature of the double peak (double hump) phenomenon in massive acetaminophen overdose. In the three presented cases, all treated with IV NAC within 6 h of ingestion, AST increased above 100 IU/L at 26, 42, and 59 h after ingestion and crossed 1,000 IU/L at 60, 87, and 109 h, indicating delayed onset of hepatic injury; other double hump cases in the literature also showed delayed initial AST elevation (>100 IU/L) at 41, 55, and 90 h.

raw_record.extra_details: Describes double peak/double hump acetaminophen kinetics with delayed hepatotoxicity even during prolonged continuous NAC infusion. Delayed AST elevation (>100 IU/L at ~26-59 h; crossing 1,000 IU/L at ~55-109 h). Massive ingestions >26 g correlate with double peak phenomena; ~9 L gastric fluid needed to dissolve 100 g acetaminophen. Table 4 cases report peak AST up to 8,686 IU/L. Cases in which NAC was stopped after the standard 21-h protocol while APAP remained >100 mcg/mL developed delayed liver injury. Proposed mechanisms: poor water solubility and delayed absorption, enterohepatic circulation with biliary excretion of acetaminophen/glucuronide.
