raw_record.support_text: In 102 patients with POLG-related mitochondrial disease and valproic acid (VPA) exposure from 46 articles, adverse drug reactions occurred in 91 patients (89%) and hepatotoxicity was reported in 87 patients (85%). All patients with reported genotypes (97/102) had recessive POLG variants, with compound heterozygotes having worse outcomes than homozygotes (p<0.01).

raw_record.extra_details: Synonyms: 2-propylpentanoic acid, dipropylacetic acid (Depakene, Depakine, Convulex, Epilim). raw_record.support_text: In the ENLIVEN study, pexidartinib caused two clinically distinct hepatic AE types: (1) liver enzyme abnormalities (asymptomatic, reversible, mostly grade 1-2 transaminase increases attributed to the CSF1R-inhibition class effect on Kupffer cells), and (2) unexpected mixed and cholestatic hepatotoxicity. In non-TGCT studies of pexidartinib (n=637), the two most concerning cases were one needing liver transplant (pexidartinib 1200 mg/d combined with paclitaxel) and one associated with death (pexidartinib 1000 mg/d monotherapy in a patient with advanced, loco-regionally progressing mucosal melanoma); serious hepatotoxicity emerged within the first 2 months of treatment and was associated with increased alkaline phosphatase, consistent with mixed and cholestatic hepatotoxicity and not fulfilling Hy's law criteria.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old man with surgically corrected congenital transposition of the great vessels and atrial fibrillation was restarted on dofetilide for rate and rhythm control after presenting with elevated liver enzymes (ALT 121 U/L, AST 9 U/L, total bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL, INR 3.2). After discontinuing dofetilide, all values returned to normal, and the Naranjo score estimating the probability of an adverse drug reaction was 10. raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo causality score = 10 (definite). Dofetilide is a class III antiarrhythmic (I_Kr blocker) FDA-approved for atrial fibrillation/flutter; the mechanism of dofetilide DILI requires further study.

raw_record.support_text: A 28-year-old man treated with finasteride 1 mg/day for 2 months for androgenetic alopecia presented with jaundice and acute liver dysfunction (AST 2581 IU/L, ALT 5416 IU/L, gamma-GTP 177 IU/L, total bilirubin 5.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, LDH 1055 IU/L). raw_record.support_text: In a 59-year-old woman, pyrazinamide (1500 mg/d) reintroduction during antituberculous therapy produced acute hepatitis with hypersensitivity symptoms (fever, pruritus, arthralgia, malaise) within 2 hours, marked transaminase elevation (ALT 3,240 U/l, AST 4,140 U/l) and eosinophilia; symptoms resolved after withdrawal. The authors note that acute hepatitis associated with pyrazinamide has been described as dose-related direct (intrinsic) toxicity, but conclude that in this case the liver injury was secondary to a hypersensitivity mechanism and that hypersensitivity hepatitis should be included among the causes of pyrazinamide-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 59-year-old woman with tuberculosis. Pyrazinamide 1500 mg/day was reintroduced (day 28) after ethambutol and rifampicin had been resumed and tolerated; a positive rechallenge occurred 2 hours after the pyrazinamide dose with acute malaise, fever 40°C, generalized pruritus, arthralgia, perioral paresthesia, vomiting, eosinophilia (859 x 10^6/l eosinophils) and transaminase elevation (ALT 3,240 U/l, AST 4,140 U/l); values fell after withdrawal (ALT 720 U/l, AST 120 U/l, eosinophils 280 x 10^6/l within 6 days). Initial episode had fever and hypereosinophilia. Patient remained healthy with normal laboratory data at 1-year follow-up. Authors note acute hepatitis with pyrazinamide is usually a dose-related predictable direct toxic mechanism, but attribute this case to a hypersensitivity mechanism involving antibodies and cytotoxic T-lymphocytes directed against hepatocyte proteins modified by reactive metabolites.

raw_record.support_text: In this case report, a patient on clozapine 250 mg/day developed marked liver test abnormalities (ALT 1914, AST 830, bilirubin 76, gamma-GT 99 U/L, albumin 35 g/L, WCC 21.4, Hb 107). Clozapine was stopped immediately and the patient was transferred to a gastroenterology unit for observation. The authors describe the case as illustrating the treacherous nature of a rare fulminant hepatotoxic reaction, with no pre-existing liver disease or indicator of vulnerability, and rapid progression of liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: Young male treated for a first psychotic episode; described as the youngest such case in the literature with good recovery. Peak transaminases (ALT 2282, AST 1056) occurred the day after clozapine cessation, gamma-GT peaked at 164, bilirubin peaked at 112 on day 3, INR raised to 1.3 for 5 days, albumin below normal for 2 weeks, CRP peaked at 45.5 mg/L. All enzymes returned to normal 3-4 weeks after cessation, bilirubin last to normalise; recovery so complete that liver transplant, otherwise to be considered, was not needed. Patient was subsequently restarted on amisulpride 200 mg twice daily with normal liver function tests. Clinical course included only sedation despite severe injury; no pre-existing liver disease or vulnerability indicator identified.

raw_record.support_text: In the early 1950s, a clinical cancer trial of N-methylformamide (NMF) was begun at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center. Severe, reversible hepatotoxicity was reported in all of the five patients treated on this trial, and because of the severity of the hepatotoxicity additional clinical studies were not conducted.
raw_record.extra_details: NMF (NSC 3051), a polar solvent evaluated by the NCI as an antineoplastic agent. In phase I studies dose-limiting toxicities included reversible hepatotoxicity, generalized malaise syndrome, and nausea and vomiting. Preclinical toxicology in mice, rats, and beagle dogs showed reversible hepatotoxicity as dose-limiting. Given orally and by IV; oral bioavailability 90-95%. Reports from the early-1950s trial and later phase I trials are merged for this therapeutic-use claim.

raw_record.support_text: The letter argues that the hepatotoxic potential of niacin has been understated and cites three human cases of niacin-induced hepatotoxicity: a 46-year-old man with clinical and biochemical hepatotoxicity on unmodified niacin 3 g/d for one month who, on rechallenge six weeks later, developed fulminant hepatic failure with stage 3 encephalopathy that resolved on discontinuation; a 32-year-old man taking SR niacin 500 mg/d for two months who developed acute liver failure with stage 4 encephalopathy and recovered on discontinuation; and a 44-year-old man on niacin 6 g/d who, three days after being switched to an SR formulation, developed fulminant hepatic failure and coma requiring liver transplantation. The letter concludes that severe hepatotoxicity occurs with both unmodified and sustained-release (SR) niacin.
raw_record.extra_details: Letter responding to an earlier DIAS Rounds column; argues SR niacin offers no adverse-effect profile advantage over unmodified niacin and that hepatotoxic potential is understated. Cases: (1) 46-year-old man, unmodified niacin 3 g/d for 1 month, clinical/biochemical hepatotoxicity; positive rechallenge 6 weeks later leading to fulminant hepatic failure with stage 3 encephalopathy, resolved on niacin discontinuation; (2) 32-year-old man, SR niacin 500 mg/d for 2 months, acute liver failure progressing to stage 4 encephalopathy, recovered on discontinuation; (3) 44-year-old man, niacin 6 g/d, fulminant hepatic failure and coma requiring liver transplantation, onset 3 days after switch to SR formulation. Both unmodified and SR niacin implicated.

raw_record.support_text: Benzbromarone hepatotoxicity is reported in humans. A 1994 case report from the Netherlands described a woman who developed acute hepatitis attributed to benzbromarone, confirmed when she was rechallenged with the drug two years later. In the late 1990s and early 2000s in Japan, several cases of fulminant liver failure leading to death were attributed to benzbromarone, and the drug was eventually withdrawn from the market by Sanofi-Synthélabo in 2003 after reports of severe hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: A 1994 case report from the Netherlands of acute hepatitis in a woman was confirmed on rechallenge with the drug two years later; multiple cases of fulminant liver failure leading to death in Japan (late 1990s-early 2000s); drug withdrawn from market by Sanofi-Synthélabo in 2003 after reports of severe hepatotoxicity; still marketed in some European countries, not available in the US. Used as a uricosuric for gout at standard daily doses of 100 mg, with dose increases to 150-200 mg/day.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that in this patient the time course of hepatic dysfunction and subsequent improvement after use and withdrawal of troglitazone were completely consistent with drug-induced hepatotoxicity. No other viral or autoimmune causes were identified, and the authors believe the patient experienced troglitazone-induced hepatotoxicity. On jaundice, troglitazone was stopped; tests showed total bilirubin 7.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 5.9 mg/dl, ALT 2,040 mg/dl, normal alkaline phosphatase, and negative ANA, AMA, and hepatitis A/B/C panels; symptoms disappeared and liver tests normalized within several months of stopping the drug.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient with type 2 diabetes on troglitazone. Jaundice with total bilirubin 127 µmol/l (7.5 mg/dl), direct bilirubin 100.8 µmol/l (5.9 mg/dl), ALT 2,040 mg/dl (given in text as mg/dl), normal serum and leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, normal prothrombin time/INR, negative antinuclear and anti-mitochondrial antibodies, normal α1 antitrypsin, mildly elevated ceruloplasmin 61.0 mg/dl, nonreactive hepatitis A/B/C panel, normal iron and transferrin saturation. Symptoms resolved and liver tests normalized within several months of discontinuation (dechallenge); no rechallenge with troglitazone. Metformin and escalated insulin were used around the time; the authors attributed dysfunction to troglitazone. Troglitazone is a first-generation PPAR-γ agonist (thiazolidinedione) metabolized by cytochrome P4503A4 to a quinone derivative; 3% excreted in urine.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose remains the most common aetiological factor for acute liver failure in the developed world. It attributes paracetamol hepatotoxicity to exhaustion of intrahepatic glutathione stores, collapse of the mitochondrial membrane potential, nuclear DNA damage and resultant oncotic necrosis, noting that most patients with paracetamol-induced liver injury survive with supportive care and early N-acetylcysteine, while emergency orthotopic liver transplantation remains the only cure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurs in the setting of paracetamol overdose (ingestion of >4 g/day as a single time point or staggered supratherapeutic doses) rather than ordinary therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Alias: acetaminophen. Mechanism described includes glutathione depletion, mitochondrial membrane potential collapse, and nuclear DNA damage leading to oncotic necrosis. Overdose definitions: single time-point intentional overdose (>4 g taken at one point with self-harm intent) or staggered overdose (two or more supratherapeutic doses over >8 h, cumulative >4 g/day); diagnosis required 2/3 of history of potentially toxic ingestion (>4 g/day), serum paracetamol >10 mg/l, or ALT >1000 IU/l within 7 days. Studied in the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit cohorts of 100 single time-point and 50 staggered overdoses (150 total); managed with N-acetylcysteine; death and OLT considered equivalent outcomes.

raw_record.support_text: The study included 100 single time-point and 50 staggered paracetamol overdose patients. Of the single time-point overdose patients, 49 (49%) developed hepatic encephalopathy and thus acute liver failure during their illness; of these, 22 (44.9%) met the modified King's College Criteria, three were transplanted, 14 died without liver transplantation, and five recovered spontaneously, and a further four patients died without meeting the criteria. Among the staggered overdose patients, 39/50 (78%) developed hepatic encephalopathy, with 21 (53.8%) meeting the modified King's College Criteria, of whom five were transplanted with two surviving to hospital discharge.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; patients with paracetamol overdose that progressed to acute liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy. Staggered overdose accounted for a subset, with higher rates of encephalopathy and King's College Criteria fulfillment.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causing drug-induced acute liver failure (ALF). 100 single time-point and 50 staggered overdose patients. Prognostic study evaluating the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio as a marker of outcomes in paracetamol-induced ALF. Outcomes include hepatic encephalopathy (grade III/IV prompting elective mechanical ventilation), modified King's College Criteria fulfillment, liver transplantation, death without transplantation, and spontaneous recovery.

raw_record.extra_details: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic used in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Cases reported include 2 deaths due to hepatic failure and 1 due to hepatitis secondary to clozapine. Case Report 1: a 52-year-old woman (paranoid schizophrenia) developed hepatotoxicity on clozapine, which discontinued and on later rechallenge produced similar hepatotoxicity; Case Report 2 remained on clozapine with the abnormalities resolving spontaneously.

raw_record.support_text: This autopsy-based observational study describes histopathological features of fatal yellow phosphorus (YP) poisoning cases following suicidal ingestion of rodenticide paste. Liver histopathology findings included microvesicular steatosis (68%), hepatic necrosis (62%), macrovesicular steatosis (50%), inflammatory cells (46%), sinusoidal congestion (40%), cholestasis (32%), and toxic hepatitis (18%); hepatic necrosis ranged from focal to centrilobular. The authors state that the liver histopathological features were consistent with YP poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Fatal suicidal ingestion of rodenticide paste (Ratol, 3% phosphorus) by adults (>18 years) in India; overdose/suicidal exposure setting rather than therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Largest autopsy-based study on YP poisoning to date. Liver histology: microvesicular steatosis 68%, hepatic necrosis 62% (focal to centrilobular), macrovesicular steatosis 50%, inflammatory cells 46%, sinusoidal congestion 40%, cholestasis 32%, toxic hepatitis 18%. YP (white phosphorus) is lipid-soluble and highly toxic; LD50 for acute adult exposure is ~60 mg (~1 mg/kg), with as little as 15 mg fatal. Poisoning confirmed by history, garlic odor in breath, and chemical analysis (phosphine detection by modified Monier-Williams method). Ambiguous entity 'phytophthora fungivora' (surface 'YP') in the provided entity list was not used.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that drug-induced liver injury is a common side effect of acetaminophen, and describes a follow-up human study in which participants were dosed with acetaminophen for a week followed by urine and serum collection, and urinary metabolomics after treatment distinguished individuals susceptible to mild acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity from those who were not.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Mild hepatotoxicity observed at ordinary therapeutic dosing (one week of dosing) in healthy human participants; susceptibility limited to certain individuals identifiable by post-treatment urinary metabolomics.
raw_record.extra_details: First pharmacometabolomic studies on acetaminophen aimed to identify biomarkers of drug-induced liver injury. A rat study used a single toxic dose of acetaminophen (animal evidence, not used for severity); predrug urinary taurine was associated with lower hepatotoxicity severity, whereas higher trimethylamine-N-oxide and betaine were associated with greater liver damage. In the human study, post-treatment but not predrug urinary metabolomics distinguished individuals susceptible to mild acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. Predose p-cresol is linked to lower acetaminophen sulfation, reduced N-acetylcysteinyl conjugate formation, and potentially greater susceptibility to acetaminophen toxicity. In another report, the rs8330 UGT marker showed lower risk for hepatotoxicity due to acetaminophen glucuronidation in patients with acute liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 65-year-old patient who developed jaundice, fever, and hepatocellular insufficiency that led to death at the beginning of treatment with regorafenib (3 tablets per day) for metastatic colon cancer, with no liver metastases. No concomitant treatment was given and other causes of liver damage were eliminated. Liver biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis with lymphocyte infiltration, illustrating the risk of severe hepatic involvement typically occurring within the first 2 months of treatment. Hepatotoxicity is described as a frequent side effect of regorafenib.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported case: 65-year-old female with sub- and diaphragmatic ganglionic metastases of colon adenocarcinoma; jaundice, fever, and hepatocellular insufficiency; fatal liver failure at regorafenib 3 tablets/day (subtherapeutic dosage noted in the discussion); no concomitant treatment; competing causes of liver damage eliminated; liver biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis with lymphocyte infiltration; no liver metastases. Aggregate trial data: severe drug-induced liver injury with fatal outcome occurred in 0.3% of 1,100 regorafenib-treated patients across all published clinical trials; fatal hepatic failure in 1.6% (regorafenib) vs 0.4% (placebo) in the phase III CORRECT trial, all affected patients having metastatic liver disease; 0.8% fatal hepatic failure in the GRID trial; in the CONCUR Asian trial hepatotoxicity was associated with a cytolysis syndrome (elevated ALT in 7%, elevated AST in 6%). Monitoring liver biology every 2 weeks during the first 2 months recommended.

raw_record.support_text: The TEMPO 3:4 trial illuminated a serious hepatotoxic side effect of tolvaptan, which is thought to be idiosyncratic in nature and accompanied by elevated transaminases with possible elevation of bilirubin. In most cases ALT/AST and bilirubin elevations returned to baseline after stopping the drug, but tolvaptan can cause severe liver damage in some patients; some patients required liver transplantation due to acute liver failure. Supporting trial data include the TEMPO 3:4 comparison of elevated AST (4.4% vs 3.1%), ALT (1.0% vs 0.8%) and bilirubin (0.9% vs 1.9%) in tolvaptan vs placebo (transaminases >3x ULN, bilirubin >1.5x ULN), and the REPRISE trial in which 11% of 681 tolvaptan patients versus 5% of 685 placebo patients developed hepatic side effects.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity reported in ADPKD patients on tolvaptan therapy. In most cases ALT/AST and bilirubin elevations reversed after drug discontinuation; some patients developed severe liver damage and required liver transplantation due to acute liver failure. TEMPO 3:4 trial elevations: AST 4.4% vs 3.1%, ALT 1.0% vs 0.8%, bilirubin 0.9% vs 1.9% (tolvaptan vs placebo; transaminases >3x ULN, bilirubin >1.5x ULN). REPRISE double-blinded trial: hepatic side effects in 11% of 681 tolvaptan patients vs 5% of 685 placebo patients. Tolvaptan is a vasopressin (V2) receptor antagonist.

raw_record.support_text: During Deferasirox (DFX) therapy, 56 days after the start of treatment, the patient's transaminase levels increased to 4x the upper limit of normal and the drug was discontinued. After discontinuation, AST and ALT rose progressively and bilirubin levels markedly increased; a presumable diagnosis of hepatocellular drug-induced liver injury (DILI) was made, initially classified as moderate (score 2) by Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network criteria. The patient later deteriorated with prolonged prothrombin time, encephalopathy, shock, multi-organ failure, and death. The authors report a case of probable liver failure-related death associated with Deferasirox, with a CIOMS/RUCAM score of 6 and a Naranjo score of 5, both indicating probable Deferasirox-induced hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Sickle cell anemia patient with the -17774delG polymorphism in homozygosis; the authors suggest this polymorphism may have played a role in the outcome rather than sickle cell disease itself.
raw_record.extra_details: Onset latency 56 days after start of DFX; transaminases increased 4x ULN; after drug discontinuation progressive rise in AST/ALT and marked bilirubin elevation; alkaline phosphatase and GGT increased disproportionately lower than bilirubin; initially classified as moderate (score 2) DILIN. Progressed to prolonged PT with bleeding requiring FFP, grade III/IV encephalopathy, refractory distributive shock, acute renal failure requiring dialysis, multi-organ failure, and death. CIOMS/RUCAM score 6 (time from intake to onset +2, exclusion of non-drug causes +2, previous info on hepatotoxicity +2); Naranjo score 5 (+1 previous reports, +2 appeared after drug given, +2 no other causes). Other causes of liver damage excluded; drug not referenced in FDA Liver Toxicity Knowledge Base.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol, APAP) is described as the most common cause of drug-induced liver injury in the Western world. In a study of plasma from patients treated with acetylcysteine (NAC) for a single APAP overdose (discovery cohort n=116, validation cohort n=150), patients who developed acute liver injury (ALI) had higher cytochrome P450-derived APAP metabolites (e.g., reactive N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine, NAPQI pathway conjugates) than those without ALI, and hospital-presentation CYP-metabolites predicted ALI better than ALT or APAP concentration (CYPs ROC-AUC 0.91, 95% CI 0.83-0.98).

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity attributed to reactive metabolite NAPQI formed by cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes; GSH depletion allows NAPQI protein binding leading to oxidative stress, mitochondrial injury, hepatocyte necrosis and acute liver failure. Non-toxic conjugates include APAP-glucuronide (APAP-Glu) and APAP-sulfate (APAP-Sul); GSH-derived APAP-Cys and APAP-mercapturate (APAP-Mer) conjugates measured in the non-adduct (nonprotein) plasma fraction. Background: >400,000 US ED visits for APAP overdose 2006-2010; ~100,000 UK ED presentations and 50,000 admissions annually; direct cause of ~150 UK deaths/year; leading cause of acute liver failure in the Western world. Predictive performance at presentation: CYP-metabolite ROC-AUC 0.91 (95% CI 0.83-0.98) vs ALT 0.67 (0.50-0.84) and APAP 0.50 (0.33-0.67), replicated in validation cohort.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol is described as one of the main causes of acute hepatitis and as a prototype of dose-dependent drug-induced hepatotoxicity leading to acute liver failure. The dose required to produce significant hepatic injury is generally 10 g in 24 hours or 150 mg/kg; symptoms appear within 24-48 hours as pure acute cytolytic hepatitis without inflammatory histology, and the higher the dose the more constant and severe the liver injury. A 3-year prospective US survey of more than 300 patients attributed 39% of severe hepatitis cases potentially leading to liver transplantation to paracetamol, far ahead of all other drugs (13%) and acute viral hepatitis A and B (12%). Spontaneous mortality risk in paracetamol-induced severe hepatitis is estimated at about 50%, versus 80-90% for other drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Significant injury threshold ~10 g/24 h or 150 mg/kg; onset 24-48 h; pure cytolytic acute hepatitis, histologically a 'chemical hepatectomy' with hepatocyte necrosis; hepatotoxic potential after overdose predicted by Rumack-Matthew nomogram of plasma paracetamol vs time; therapeutic plasma paracetamol 10-30 µg/mL. US 3-year prospective survey (>300 patients): paracetamol 39% of severe hepatitis possibly leading to liver transplant vs other drugs 13% and HAV/HBV 12%. Spontaneous mortality ~50% in paracetamol-induced severe hepatitis vs 80-90% with other drugs. Paracetamol is also a major suicidal agent in Anglo-Saxon countries. Mechanism: predominant CYP2E1-mediated (inducible by chronic alcohol), with CYP3A4 and CYP1A/2B families, conversion of <5% of metabolism to reactive NAPBQI normally detoxified by glutathione; excess metabolite covalently binds cell molecules causing hepatocyte necrosis; additional mechanisms include oxidative stress/ROS, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial alterations, apoptosis, and JNK involvement. Toxicity can also appear below the 10 g/24 h threshold toward the 4 g therapeutic limit when predisposed, e.g., glutathione depletion from prolonged fasting/malnutrition or CYP2E1 induction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper frames paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (ALF) as a multisystem disorder with acute renal failure, hypotension, sepsis, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and cerebral edema. The study collected serum from 12 patients (median age 36 years, median INR 3) who developed ALF due to paracetamol overdose 2–5 days after the overdose; five of the patients died, five survived, and two received orthotopic liver transplants. The aim was to study the in vitro effect of ALF serum on normal human hepatocytes, directly attributing the ALF to paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurred 2–5 days following paracetamol overdose in patients hospitalized with acute liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 12 patients (8 female, 4 male) with ALF due to paracetamol overdose, median age 36 years (range 15–60), median INR 3 (range 1.7–8.6); 5 survived, 5 died, 2 received orthotopic liver transplantation. Multisystem disorder including acute renal failure, hypotension, sepsis, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and cerebral edema. The main study objective was to test the in vitro effect of ALF serum on normal human hepatocytes (cell viability, DNA synthesis, cytochrome P-450 activity), not to characterize the liver injury phenotype.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-year-old boy with rheumatic fever was treated with aspirin 100 mg/kg/day. On day 13 of aspirin therapy, the salicylate level was 29 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) rose to 515 iu/l, peaking at 1650 iu/l with SGPT (ALT) peaking at 1010 iu/l and alkaline phosphatase rising to 320 iu/l, while serum bilirubin showed no change (anicteric). A liver biopsy showed periportal infiltration with lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils, hepatocyte ballooning and cytoplasmic vacuolization, and electron microscopy revealed proliferation of smooth ER, dilated rough ER, and mitochondrial swelling, judged consistent with a toxic hepatitis and hepatic congestion. The authors attribute this hepatotoxicity to salicylate/aspirin, and the abnormalities resolved after stopping aspirin and reinstating it at a reduced dose of 80 mg/kg/day, with normal liver function tests at three-month follow-up. The paper reports a second analogous child with rheumatic fever who also developed anicteric hepatitis on high-dose aspirin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients (children) with rheumatic fever treated with high-dose aspirin (100 mg/kg/day in case 1, reduced to 80 mg/kg/day); anicteric (bilirubin normal) injury; concurrent rheumatic fever as background disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports of anicteric hepatitis on high-dose aspirin (salicylate) therapy for rheumatic fever. Case 1: salicylate level 29 mg/dl on day 13; AST peaked at 1650 iu/l, ALT 1010 iu/l, alkaline phosphatase 320 iu/l; biopsy showed periportal lymphocytic/plasma cell/eosinophil infiltration, hepatocyte ballooning with cytoplasmic vacuolization, smooth ER proliferation, dilated rough ER, and mitochondrial swelling 'consistent with a toxic hepatitis and hepatic congestion'; dechallenge resolved abnormalities; reintroduction at 80 mg/kg/day (salicylate 19 mg/dl) gave near-normal enzymes (AST 57, ALT 148, ALP 181 iu/l); normal liver function at 3-month follow-up. Hepatitis B and Mononucleosis spot tests negative. SGOT = aspartate aminotransferase (AST); SGPT = alanine aminotransferase (ALT).; global_identifier_note: Aspirin (= 2-acetoxybenzoic acid, SMILES:1591136); salicylate treated as the active form of the same agent and merged, not a separate causal entity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors state that although salicylates have little direct toxic effect on the liver in large therapeutic doses, there are increasing reports of children and adults with rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatic fever who developed hepatotoxicity while on high-dose aspirin therapy. In Case 2, a four-year-old girl with rheumatic fever treated with aspirin (100 mg/kg/day) developed nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain on day 12 with salicylate 26.8 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 1325 iu/l; after a two-day discontinuation and re-institution at a reduced dose (80 mg/kg/day), AST fell to 109 iu/l and liver function returned to normal. The paper concludes the hepatotoxicity is dose-related and reversible and not a hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose aspirin therapy; risk appears restricted to patients with connective tissue disorders (rheumatic fever, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus).
raw_record.extra_details: Case 2: 4-year-old girl, aspirin 100 mg/kg/day; symptoms of nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain on day 12 of therapy; serum salicylate 26.8 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 1325 iu/l (79.34 nkat); Hepatitis B antigen and mononucleosis spot tests negative; aspirin discontinued two days, then reinstituted at 80 mg/kg/day; after 10 days salicylate was 18 mg/dl and SGOT (AST) 109 iu/l (6.53 nkat); liver function tests normal at three-month follow-up. Mechanism concluded dose-related (hepatotoxicity appears when salicylate concentrations exceed ~25 mg/dl) and reversible on dose reduction, not a hypersensitivity reaction; saturated formation of salicyluric acid and salicyl phenolic glucuronide at therapeutic doses increases minor metabolites, possibly hepatotoxic in uniquely sensitive connective-tissue-disorder patients. Typical features across reports: anorexia, malaise, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain; SGOT/SGPT elevation; hyperbilirubinaemia unusual; alkaline phosphatase normal or slightly increased; biopsy shows preserved lobular architecture, widened sinusoidal spaces, focal hepatocyte necrosis, degeneration and ballooning with anisocytosis and mitotic figures.

raw_record.support_text: In paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, hepatic damage defined as ALT/AST >1000 IU/L and death from hepatic failure occurred across treatment groups. Case fatality rates in patients treated within 24 h after overdose with oral methionine, oral NAC, 20·25 h NAC, and 48 h NAC were 1·5, 0·7, 2·0, and 1·5%, respectively; in more severely poisoned patients (concentrations above the 300 line) the rates were 2·7, 1·3, 3·3, and 1·4%. In a historical supportive-treated series, case fatality was 5·3% (above the 200 line) and 10·7% (300 line). Between 1.6% and 13.9% of patients treated within 10 h of overdose developed ALT/AST activities >1000 IU/L, while 26·4–63·0% of those treated 10–24 h after overdose developed severe liver damage.

raw_record.extra_details: Four non-randomised treatment studies (UK and North America, 1974–1989) comparing oral/IV NAC and oral methionine as antidotes. Hepatic damage defined as ALT/AST >1000 IU/L. Liver injury described as hepatic damage and death from hepatic failure; fulminant hepatic failure discussed for NAC treatment.

raw_record.support_text: In a report of a large population of patients who had received dantrolene for long periods, biochemical abnormalities of liver function (including moderate elevations of serum transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin) occurred in about 1.8% of patients, with symptomatic hepatitis in 0.6% and fatal hepatitis in 0.3%. The risk of hepatic injury appears about 2-fold greater in females, in patients receiving doses over 300 mg/day, and in those treated for over 60 days. The major histological pathology was subacute hepatic necrosis or chronic active hepatitis, although cholestasis has been reported; the reactions were considered unlikely to be due to hypersensitivity or autoimmune reactions. Reduced dosage recommendations for long-term use resulted in a marked decrease in severe hepatic disease reports.

raw_record.support_text: A patient being treated for psoriasis was started on acitretin 25 mg twice daily. Two days later her ALT rose to 237 U/L, ALP to 440 U/L and bilirubin to 41 µmol/L from a normal baseline. Acitretin was stopped and ALT returned to normal over 5 days; ALP peaked at 679 U/L and remained elevated at 191 U/L 6 months later. This indicates acitretin as the cause of the acute liver injury in therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient on acitretin 25 mg twice daily for pustular/erythrodermic psoriasis; ALT rose from 12 to 237 U/L, ALP from 93 to 440 U/L, bilirubin from 8 to 41 µmol/L with JAUNDICE-level bilirubin rise; ALT normalized within 5 days of discontinuation (dechallenge), ALP peaked at 679 U/L and stayed elevated at 191 U/L at 6 months. Same episode also involved drug-induced agranulocytosis (WCC 1.3 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 0.1 x 10^9/L) and subsequent total scalp alopecia. Elsewhere the paper notes hepatic toxicity is a well-recognized side-effect of acitretin, with up to 30% of patients developing raised aminotransferases and 10% ALP elevations, generally mild and transient, while genuine toxic hepatitis is rare; only isotretinoin (not acitretin) has prior retinoid-associated agranulocytosis reports.

Despite an initial acetaminophen concentration (41 mg/L at 4.5 h) below the treatment nomogram line, she developed hepatic failure (peak ALT 7009 U/L, INR 7.5) due to a delayed acetaminophen peak (85 mg/L at 38 h) caused by coingested medications slowing gastric emptying, including a combination acetaminophen product containing dextromethorphan and chlorphenamine. raw_record.support_text: Fenclozic acid (Myalex), an NSAID, was withdrawn from late stage clinical development in patients as a result of hepatotoxicity. In a clinical trial in 12 patients receiving 400 mg/day, two subjects experienced a severe adverse drug reaction and a further four subjects showed elevated liver enzymes; DILI was also observed in two subjects at other trial centres who became jaundiced. Onset on 400 mg/day was between 17 and 35 days after the first dose, with elevated circulating alkaline phosphatase, serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase, and serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase; the biochemical changes in the jaundiced subjects were interpreted as indicative of cholestasis rather than parenchymal cell damage. All patients recovered within a few days of cessation of the drug. In preclinical species fenclozic acid was not a hepatotoxin, but when administered to humans it resulted in dose-dependent DILI, and this human-specific DILI led to its withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Fenclozic acid ([2-(4-chlorophenyl)-1,3-thiazol-4-yl]acetic acid), brand name Myalex, was a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug withdrawn from clinical development due to human hepatotoxicity. Clinical trial in 12 patients at 400 mg/day: two subjects had a severe adverse drug reaction and four subjects showed elevated liver enzymes; two subjects at other trial centres became jaundiced with DILI. Onset 17-35 days after first dose; elevated alkaline phosphatase, SGOT, and SGPT; jaundiced subjects' biochemical changes interpreted as cholestasis rather than parenchymal cell damage. All patients recovered within a few days of drug cessation. Authors describe the human DILI as dose-dependent. Preclinical species (rat, mouse) did not show hepatotoxicity; repeated oral dosing of mice at 50 or 100 mg/kg/day for 7 days did not induce DILI, though acute hepatic necrosis after a single 10 mg/kg oral dose was observed in a mouse autoradiography study.

raw_record.support_text: The report notes that the most common organ affected by acetaminophen intoxication is the liver when the drug is administered in supratherapeutic doses, and that repeated therapeutic doses can also be toxic. In the presented case, a 5-year-old female was treated by her mother with different acetaminophen formulations (250 mg suppositories and 500 mg tablets) every 3 hours for three consecutive days, an approximate dose of 90 mg/kg/24h over 72 hours, and developed fulminant hepatic failure. Acetaminophen poisoning was strongly suspected and confirmed by a blood acetaminophen level of 32.9 mg/l 10 hours after the last dose; viral serologies and blood culture were negative, and the child was treated with NAC.

raw_record.support_text: In this case, hepatic failure was caused by unintentionally repeated excessive dosing of acetaminophen, given as a pediatric preparation in suppositories 250 mg combined with adult tablets of 500 mg every 3 hours for three consecutive days. The calculated dose was approximately 90 mg/kg/24h for more than 72 hours, consistent with repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (RSTI); the paper states such doses are of concern for liver injury in children younger than 6 years. The authors frame acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity as a serious pediatric condition and attribute the hepatic failure to the repeated overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Patient recovered totally within 29 days with complete resolution of clinical and laboratory abnormalities; liver function tests remained normal at 1st, 3rd, 6th and 12th month follow-up. Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity attributed to oxidative metabolism via CYP2E1, 3A4, 1A2 to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which is detoxified by glutathione; in overdose glutathione declines and toxic NAPQI produces hepatic necrosis. The child also developed acute pancreatitis (diagnosed by hyperlipasemia, hyperamylasemia, hyperglycemia and abdominal ultrasound) and renal involvement at admission. Serum acetaminophen level was assessed abroad and result was late; diagnosis based on clinical presentation and history. Treated with N-acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: A parallel Phase I trial of clofarabine in 25 pediatric patients with relapsed or refractory leukemia (17 ALL, eight AML) investigated six dose levels; the maximum tolerated dose was established at 52 mg/m2/day for five days, and the dose-limiting toxicity was identified as reversible Grade 3 hepatotoxicity and skin rash. Prior (n=9) or following (n=7) hematopoietic stem cell transplantation did not cause increased toxicity, and multiple cycles were not associated with cumulative hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity was the dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) for clofarabine in the Phase I trial and was observed in all Phase II studies, in both single-agent and combination regimens. Hepatic dysfunction was usually reversible, peaking around days 5–7 with recovery by days 15–16 (<Grade 2), but in some cases severe and potentially life-threatening hepatotoxicity occurred. In the Phase II trial based on the Phase I clofarabine-cyclophosphamide-etoposide combination study, three of the first eight patients developed veno-occlusive disease and there was one case of hyperbilirubinemia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric relapsed/refractory acute leukemia population; veno-occlusive disease cases arose in the combination regimen (clofarabine-cyclophosphamide-etoposide), where co-suspects were present.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity (elevated transaminases and/or hyperbilirubinemia) was among the most common Grade >=3 adverse events with clofarabine. Hepatic dysfunction was usually reversible, showing a peak around days 5-7 and recovery by days 15-16 (<Grade 2). In the Phase II combination trial, 3 of the first 8 patients developed veno-occlusive disease and 1 had hyperbilirubinemia; after protocol amendment, none of the further 7 patients experienced severe hepatotoxicity. Close liver-function monitoring during and after therapy is recommended, and potentially cumulative hepatotoxicity should be considered when combining with other drugs that compromise liver function.

raw_record.support_text: The authors confidently diagnosed nitrofurantoin-induced autoimmune hepatitis in their case, presenting a rapid-onset drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis occurring 18 days after a therapeutic 5-day course of nitrofurantoin (100 mg twice daily) for an uncomplicated UTI. Diagnosis was supported by elevated liver enzymes, positive smooth muscle antibodies, normal IgG levels, and a liver biopsy showing acute hepatitis with moderate necroinflammatory activity and no fibrosis after ruling out other causes.
raw_record.extra_details: Rapid-onset drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis appearing 18 days after exposure to nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days for an uncomplicated UTI; presentation included jaundice, lethargy, and elevated liver enzymes, with positive smooth muscle antibodies and normal IgG; liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with moderate necroinflammatory activity and focal portal fibrosis (no advanced fibrosis). Treated with prednisone 40 mg daily, tapered with azathioprine added as steroid-sparing agent; asymptomatic with normal liver biochemistry at 1-year follow-up. Noted as unique because of acute DIAIH after a brief 5-day course, contrasting with the widely recognized long-term prophylaxis association.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose is described as the commonest cause of acute liver failure. In England and Wales paracetamol toxicity results in 150-200 deaths and 15-20 liver transplants each year, and the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group Registry recorded 275 of 662 (42%) consecutive acute liver failure cases as due to paracetamol overdose. The abstract further states that liver failure from deliberate or accidental paracetamol overdose is an important reason for referral to liver transplant centres.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Toxicity risk is increased in susceptible groups: chronic alcoholics (threshold around 75 mg/kg), patients with malnutrition, eating disorders, HIV infection, and the elderly; concurrent drugs competing for glucuronidation (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, zidovudine) or enzyme-inducing drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, primidone, rifampicin) potentiate toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Deliberate self-harm or accidental overdose context. Toxic single doses above 10 g or 150 mg/kg are hepatotoxic in adults. Severe hepatic dysfunction typically appears 72-96 h after overdose; injury preventable by timely N-acetylcysteine (best within 8 h, beneficial at any time). Mechanism attributed to enhanced P450-mediated generation of NAPQI and reduced glutathione stores. Paracetamol accounted for 31% of 7,933 drug overdoses in Ireland in 2004 and up to 48% of poisoning admissions in the UK. Outcome includes fulminant hepatic failure, super-urgent liver transplantation, and death.

raw_record.support_text: The clinical course of acetaminophen toxicity is described in four phases after ingestion. Phase 2 (24–72 hours) is marked by right upper quadrant pain indicating beginning hepatic injury, with hepatic enzymes, bilirubin, and prothrombin time rising. Phase 3 (72–96 hours) is characterized by evidence of hepatic necrosis with jaundice, coagulation defects, renal failure, and hepatic encephalopathy, and fulminant hepatic failure is usually fatal. Phase 4 involves resolution if the patient survives.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context; the case is an individual patient (Ms. Stewart) who presented 3 hours after ingestion and was not given activated charcoal because it must be given within 2 hours of ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase-based course described: Phase 1 (30 min–24 h) nausea, vomiting, anorexia, pallor, diaphoresis, malaise, often asymptomatic; Phase 2 (24–72 h) right upper quadrant pain, rising hepatic enzymes, bilirubin and PT, possible renal deterioration (decreased consciousness, oliguria); Phase 3 (72–96 h) hepatic necrosis with jaundice, coagulation defects, renal failure, hepatic encephalopathy, with fulminant hepatic failure usually fatal; Phase 4 (4 days–2 weeks) resolution with liver returning to normal in ~3 months. In the patient, acetaminophen level was 240 mcg/mL and potassium 3.0 mEq/L; toxicity plotted on the standard nomogram.

raw_record.support_text: Eighteen days after starting valproic acid (VPA) prophylactic treatment and 11 days after discharge, the 58-year-old patient was admitted with massive elevations of liver enzymes (AST 8747 U/L, ALT 7184 U/L, GGT 153 U/L), elevated creatinine, INR 2.4 and a VPA serum level of 81 mg/L. Hepatitis serology and auto-antibodies were negative, and the diagnosis of an acute toxic liver failure most likely due to treatment with VPA and duloxetine was made. The patient developed progressive hepatic encephalopathy and underwent urgent liver transplantation, followed by a second transplant after primary graft dysfunction; she died of sepsis and multi-organ failure five months later.
raw_record.extra_details: VPA given as Ergenyl chrono prophylactic treatment (300 mg OD day 1, 300 mg three times day 2, then 300 mg 1-0-2-0). Liver function tests were normal on day 7 of VPA (serum level 73 mg/L); on admission VPA level was 81 mg/L. Histology showed massive necrosis with less than 5% of liver tissue preserved, plasma cell infiltration and slight fatty degeneration, consistent with acute drug-induced liver failure due to VPA. Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale scored the causative role of valproate as probable. Possible cytochrome P450 polymorphism was not tested. Generalized toxicity attributed to toxic metabolites such as 4-en VPA via impaired beta-oxidation. Co-suspect duloxetine was initially mentioned ('most likely due to treatment with VPA and duloxetine') but the final diagnosis and histology attributed the liver failure to VPA. Multi-organ involvement included renal failure, pancolitis and lymphadenopathy. Patient died of sepsis and multi-organ failure five months after transplantation.

In one, 11 patients treated for a median of 18 months (range 7-58) with a mean cumulative dose of 1225 mg (range 220-3400 mg) showed 5 cases of mild steatosis, one case each of granulomatous hepatitis with mild portal fibrosis, slight sinusoid dilation, and periportal fibrosis, and 3 normal biopsies. raw_record.support_text: A patient (Ms. A) developed marked hepatic injury following an acetaminophen overdose: there was a dramatic rise in SGOT, scleral icterus and mild right upper quadrant tenderness, and a liver biopsy on the third day revealed marked zonal centrolobular necrosis without architectural collapse. After protein restriction, gut cleansing and oral neomycin, the biochemical abnormalities improved, liver function tests returned to normal within two weeks, and a therapeutic abortion was performed. In the surrounding pharmacology and clinical-course text, the paper states that most patients who develop hepatic toxicity have ingested 15 g (about 46 325-mg tablets) or more of acetaminophen, and that massive doses exhaust hepatic glutathione, allowing reactive metabolites to bind tissue proteins and cause cellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy (a therapeutic abortion was performed after recovery); overdose exposure with ingestion of roughly 15 g or more (about 46 325-mg tablets).
raw_record.extra_details: Symptoms included nausea, vomiting, weakness, pallor, diaphoresis, and anorexia. Dramatic SGOT elevation, scleral icterus, and right upper quadrant tenderness were observed; arterial ammonia was elevated on day 4 but the patient remained alert. Liver biopsy on day 3 showed marked zonal centrolobular necrosis without architectural collapse. Treated with protein restriction, gut cleansing, and oral neomycin; liver function tests returned to normal about two weeks later. Proposed mechanism: after hepatic biotransformation, a reactive intermediate from a cytochrome-P450-dependent mixed-function oxidase exhausts hepatic glutathione and binds tissue proteins, causing cellular necrosis; microsomal induction (e.g., by phenobarbital or alcohol) can increase reactive metabolite formation.

raw_record.support_text: Rectal administration of acetaminophen was significantly associated with supratherapeutic dosing (mean 20.9 mg/kg, range 16.6-41.7 mg/kg). Previously reported cases of hepatotoxicity secondary to multiple supratherapeutic acetaminophen dosing per rectum included 5 children (ages 7 months to 8 years), with an overdose range of 17 to 70 mg/kg/dose or 102 to 420 mg/kg/d. Death occurred in a 2-year-old child who received 650-mg suppositories every 4 hours for a total of 17 doses. The paper also states that with greater than recommended doses the CYP450 pathway produces NAPQI, and excessive NAPQI leads to hepatic cellular necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; multiple supratherapeutic doses predominantly via the rectal route; at risk in children receiving >15 mg/kg/dose for more than 5 doses within 24 hours, children younger than 2 years who are ill and acutely malnourished, and children with chronic liver disorders or taking medications that stimulate CYP450 hepatic enzymes.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose range 17 to 70 mg/kg/dose or 102 to 420 mg/kg/d; mean rectal supratherapeutic dose 20.9 mg/kg (16.6-41.7); death in a 2-year-old given 650-mg suppositories every 4 h, 17 total doses; dosing errors attributed to parents (2), physicians (2), and pharmacists (1). Mechanism: therapeutic doses metabolized by sulfation and glucuronidation, but supratherapeutic doses saturate these pathways and activate CYP450, producing N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which is detoxified by glutathione conjugation; excessive NAPQI leads to hepatic cellular necrosis. Risk enhanced by CYP450 inducers (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, rifampin, ethanol, isoniazid) and by illness/malnutrition in young children.

The paper also refers to 11 study deaths among treated acetaminophen-overdose patients, and in another section describes hepatotoxicity in three patients with nontoxic levels of acetaminophen treated within eight hours of ingestion, attributing these unusual cases to errors in history taking.

raw_record.extra_details: In a multicenter comparative study, hepatotoxicity frequency in high-risk patients treated 16-24h was reduced 41% with 72 h oral N-acetylcysteine vs 82% with the 20 h IV protocol and 89% in historical untreated controls. Eleven study deaths were reported among treated patients; three patients with nontoxic acetaminophen levels treated within 8 h of ingestion still developed hepatotoxicity, attributed to history-taking errors. N-acetyl-p-benzoquinonimine (NAPQI) formation is discussed only as a mechanistic step in acetaminophen metabolism, not as an independently injuring entity.

raw_record.support_text: Four hours after deliberate exposure to halothane, the patient began to experience severe leg aching, a symptom previously noted at the onset of his hepatitis relapses, followed by a chill, fever to 102.8°F, tachycardia, malaise, and a rise in serum glutamic oxalacetic transaminase with a slight increase in serum bilirubin. A liver biopsy 4 days after halothane challenge showed acute hepatitis with intense mononuclear inflammation, zones of recent collapse containing acidophilic bodies, and reticuloendothelial cell proliferation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Rechallenge exposure in a patient with a history of repeated halothane hepatitis relapses over five and a half years; the patient had documented postnecrotic cirrhosis before this challenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Time course: leg aching and chill began 4 hours after halothane exposure; temperature rose to 102.2°F at 4 h and 102.8°F at 8 h, with pulse rise 80 to 108 and bilirubin/dark urine; SGOT continued to rise for 48 h after challenge then fell slowly and returned to normal about 2 weeks after exposure. Suggestive increase in eosinophils. Liver biopsy 4 days after challenge (December 11) showed acute hepatitis with small zones of recent collapse, numerous acidophilic bodies, proliferating reticuloendothelial cells, and monocytes, on top of pre-existing postnecrotic cirrhosis. Patient recovered clinically; splenomegaly noted during challenge resolved. The glutamic oxalacetic transaminase level was still elevated at discharge and took about 6 more days to return to normal.

Admission markers associated with outcome: arterial blood pH (median 7.40 survivors v 7.10 died, p=0.01), creatinine (145 v 289 µmol/l, p=0.01), factor V (11.8% v 5.1%, p=0.01), factor VIII (162% v 298%, p<=0.05), and factor VIII/V ratio (17 v 39, p<=0.001). raw_record.support_text: Fialuridine (FIAU), the 1-(2-deoxy-2-fluoro-β-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouracil nucleoside with good in vitro anti-HBV activity, caused human hepatotoxicity. Lilly's Phase II clinical trial of FIAU was halted in June 1993 because 7 of 15 subjects died after 9-13 weeks of treatment. In a previous study, 67 patients did not experience hepatotoxicity after 2-4 weeks of FIAU, but within 6 months of therapy three individuals died from liver disease and one from pancreatitis; the incident was re-evaluated as possibly due to delayed FIAU toxicity. Mechanistically, FIAU triphosphate and its metabolite inhibited DNA polymerase γ, decreasing mitochondrial DNA and causing mitochondrial structural abnormalities, and FIAU hepatotoxicity in humans was confirmed in chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Delayed FIAU hepatotoxicity emerging after prolonged dosing; deaths occurred within weeks to 6 months of therapy rather than during initial 2-4 weeks of exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism via FIAU triphosphate and metabolite inhibiting DNA polymerase γ, decreasing mitochondrial DNA levels and causing structural mitochondrial abnormalities; prior cohort of 67 patients showed no hepatotoxicity after 2-4 weeks; Lilly Phase II trial halted June 1993 with 7 of 15 subjects dying after 9-13 weeks; three individuals died from liver disease and one from pancreatitis within 6 months of therapy; human relevance supported by chimeric TK-NOG mice with humanized livers.

Nevirapine was permanently discontinued in all but one case, and all affected individuals rapidly improved after discontinuation of nevirapine. The six last cases further presented hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report four cases of niacin-induced hepatotoxicity in patients using sustained-release niacin preparations; symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after the patients stopped taking niacin. Two patients had focal fatty infiltration of the liver on imaging, and one patient had a coagulopathy despite only mildly elevated aminotransferase levels. The authors recommend periodic liver-enzyme monitoring and discontinuation if abnormalities develop.

raw_record.extra_details: Four patients; all used sustained-release niacin preparations; symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved on discontinuation (dechallenge). Focal fatty infiltration of the liver seen on imaging in two patients, presented as a not previously described presentation of niacin hepatotoxicity. One patient had a coagulopathy despite only mildly elevated aminotransferases (prothrombin time 16.6 s, AST 86 U/L, ALT 86 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 136 U/L, total bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, albumin 3.3 g/dL) and a factor VII deficiency attributed to liver disease. Niacin is a water-soluble B vitamin used for hyperlipidemia therapy.

Liver enzymes rose and continued rising over 20 days until admission with beginning liver failure (AST 1,724 U/L, bilirubin 22 mg/dL, INR 2.9). Laparoscopic liver biopsy showed fatty liver with early cirrhosis and histologically severe drug-induced necrotic hepatitis, leading to treatment with prednisolone 1 mg/kg. Within 10 days AST returned to baseline (70 U/L) and INR fell to 1.36; bilirubin decreased to 1.3 mg/dL, but the patient later died of gastric ulcer perforation.

raw_record.extra_details: INH chemoprophylaxis given at 10 mg/kg/day for 10 weeks following a positive PPD and a negative chest radiograph; exposure source was a grandmother with active pulmonary tuberculosis. Symptoms (scleral icterus, vomiting, dark urine, diffuse abdominal pain) began 10 days before admission; loss of appetite/lethargy; admission labs: prothrombin time 22%, ALT 2580 IU, AST 3200 IU, total bilirubin 17.1 mg/dl (direct 8.1); HBsAg and HAV IgM negative. Developed hepatic encephalopathy, severe coagulopathy with epistaxis, hematemesis, and occult-blood-positive stools, then irreversible hepatic failure (terminal total bilirubin 46 mg/dl) and died 22 days after admission. Previously reported fatal pediatric cases were all female and involved multiple concomitant antituberculosis medications.

raw_record.support_text: In 1993 a phase II clinical trial with 15 participants evaluated the safety and efficacy of the test compound fialuridine (FIAU) developed for hepatitis B virus infection. The trial was quickly terminated due to serious unanticipated complications: seven participants developed hepatic failure, lactic acidosis, and pancreatic failure, leading to the death of five patients and liver transplants for the two others. Post-mortem examination of liver tissue revealed steatosis and cholestasis with cytoplasmic fat droplets and swollen mitochondria, and the toxicity was thought to be due to human-specific mitochondrial toxicity caused by fialuridine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with hepatitis B virus infection receiving fialuridine in a phase II clinical trial; human-specific mitochondrial toxicity implicated.
raw_record.extra_details: 1993 phase II trial with 15 participants; 7 developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis and pancreatic failure; 5 died and 2 required liver transplants. Post-mortem liver tissue showed steatosis and cholestasis, cytoplasmic fat droplets, and swollen mitochondria with reduced cristae. A National Academy of Sciences retrospective analysis of all preclinical FIAU toxicity data concluded the animal data gave no indication of such human tragedy. In vitro studies indicated human-specific mitochondrial toxicity possibly due to expression of a nucleoside transporter in human (not mouse) mitochondria; a primary human hepatocyte model predicted fialuridine toxicity in vitro, and FIAU was more cytotoxic to human hepatocytes (IC50 ~5 µM) than rat hepatocytes (IC50 >100 µM).

raw_record.support_text: APAP (acetaminophen) is a widely used analgesic and antipyretic that is relatively safe at therapeutic doses, but in cases of acute overdose potentially fatal hepatic centrilobular necrosis occurs. The hepatotoxicity has been well correlated in animal studies with covalent binding to hepatic proteins, and no demonstration of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity in the absence of covalent binding exists.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose of acetaminophen (APAP); death of the patient occurred from the APAP overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: The paper compares selective protein arylation in the liver of a mouse killed 4 hr after 600 mg/kg APAP (oral) with that in the liver of a patient who died of an APAP overdose. In the human, covalent binding was primarily detected in the cytosolic fraction, with most prominent immunostaining of bands of approximately 58 and 130 kDa and additional arylation of 38 and 62 kDa bands; little binding was detectable in the particulate fraction. Immunohistochemistry localized bound APAP to centrilobular regions with absence of staining in periportal areas, in both the human and mouse liver after hepatotoxic APAP exposure. APAP hepatotoxicity correlated with covalent binding to hepatic proteins, and no acetaminophen hepatotoxicity has been demonstrated in the absence of covalent binding.

raw_record.support_text: The patient had evidence of tamoxifen-induced nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), as evidenced by an ALT/AST ratio greater than 1, steatosis on liver ultrasound, and normalization of these tests after discontinuing tamoxifen. The paper also states that hepatitis A, B, and C serology were negative and alcohol and other known hepatotoxin intake were excluded. Tamoxifen is N-demethylated in the liver by CYP3A4, generating reactive metabolites capable of damaging protein and DNA.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of a patient on tamoxifen. Evidence of tamoxifen-induced NASH included ALT/AST ratio greater than 1 (ALT 48 U/L, AST 42 U/L, normal 0-31), steatosis on liver ultrasound, and normalization of liver toxicity tests after stopping tamoxifen. raw_record.extra_details: Case report of terbinafine-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity prescribed for its usual indication. Latency (exposure-jaundice/icterus) ranges from 2 to 6 weeks; maximum bilirubin peak typically occurs 3-5 weeks after drug discontinuation. Resolution after withdrawal is usually the rule. raw_record.support_text: The paper attributes clinically meaningful human liver injury to isoniazid. In a Capitol Hill cohort, 19 of 2,321 employees given isoniazid developed hepatitis (attack rate 8.2 per 1,000), 13 were jaundiced, and 2 died, versus attack rates of 0.5 per 1,000 in matched non-isoniazid controls and 0 per 1,000 in tuberculin reactors who refused treatment. A subsequent prospective Public Health Service surveillance of 13,838 patients, including 3,196 in Baltimore, recorded 41 isoniazid-associated cases of liver dysfunction with 7 deaths (rate 12.83 per 1,000) and 133 probable/possible hepatitis cases with 1 fatality in the other 20 health departments (rate 12.50 per 1,000). He notes this clinical condition was first reported in 1963 by Schultz and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine, describing six young women who died late in pregnancy of rapidly progressive liver disease and azotemia following intravenous administration of large doses of tetracycline for acute pyelonephritis. raw_record.support_text: The paper presents a case series titled 'Amiodarone Hepatotoxicity' describing five patients who developed drug-induced liver injury while on therapeutic amiodarone. raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is reported among amiodarone's adverse reactions, with mild aminotransferase elevations seen in 15% to 20% of patients in most studies. Among four recently published cases of amiodarone hepatotoxicity, one simulated active alcoholic hepatitis histologically and the other three showed fibrosis, cholangitis, mixed inflammatory infiltrate, and hepatocyte cytoplasmic granularity; Mallory bodies were found in three of the four patients. Electron microscopy in all four patients showed numerous membranous or lamellar cytoplasmic inclusions identical to those of phospholipidosis, which the authors consider possibly integral to the toxic reaction to amiodarone.

Electron microscopy showed lamellated/membranous cytoplasmic inclusions identical to those of phospholipidosis in all four cases, considered a possible key diagnostic feature or marker of drug effect rather than a direct cause of toxicity. The authors note the histologic picture can differ substantially (toxic or hypersensitivity pattern) and that treatment duration and dosage do not appear directly correlated with the degree of injury.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of acute liver failure attributed to chlorzoxazone (CZ), requiring orthotopic liver transplantation. Histopathologic findings were consistent with drug-induced injury (necrosis, ballooning degeneration, mixed inflammatory infiltrate). The paper states hepatic toxicity of CZ appears idiosyncratic, that there is no clear dose- or time-dependent relationship, that hepatotoxicity is sustained with rechallenge, and reviews a 1986 series in which CZ hepatotoxicity varied from mild reversible jaundice to fulminant liver failure and death. It also notes the FDA strengthened its hepatotoxicity warning for CZ in 1995 and that this is the first reported CZ-induced ALF requiring transplantation.

Histology (pre-transplant and explant) showed massive hepatic necrosis, ballooning degeneration, and mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Literature review: clinical liver injury recognized since 1967, ranging from mild reversible jaundice to fulminant liver failure and death; 1986 series with age range 25-74 years and therapy duration 2 days to years, with short-latency (mean 15 days) and long-latency (mean 10.4 months) groups, the latter older with more co-medications and higher death frequency. Hepatotoxicity sustained with rechallenge; FDA strengthened hepatotoxicity warning in 1995; no identified risk factors for CZ-induced hepatotoxicity; no routine liver chemistry monitoring recommended. CZ metabolized by CYP2E1 to 6-hydroxychlorzoxazone, used as a probe of CYP2E1 activity.

Poisoning from ingestion of YP is reported to be associated with severe hepatotoxicity, a lethal (more than 10-fold) increase in ALT, and severe derangement in prothrombin time. In the authors' series of 11 children who ingested fireworks, there was a subclinical hepatic injury rate of 66.6% and an ALF rate of 9%; all recovered with supportive therapy except for 2, one of whom required liver transplantation and the other died.

raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatitis with or without acute liver failure is the most common presentation; severe hepatotoxicity with >10-fold ALT increase and severe prothrombin-time derangement reported. In the 11-child series, subclinical hepatic injury rate 66.6% and ALF rate 9%; one case required cadaveric liver transplantation (explanted liver showed submassive necrosis) and another died. Dose-related zone 1/periportal hepatic injury, in contrast to the centrilobular (zone 3) pattern of hepatotoxic drugs such as isoniazid and metronidazole; acute liver necrosis, large vacuoles, and fatty degenerative changes observed within 6 hours of ingestion. raw_record.support_text: Twenty-five cases of acute hepatitis, probably related to the use of niperotidine, were reported in Italy between March and August 1995. The diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury was supported by the chronological correlation (onset after therapy, dramatic improvement on withdrawal) and by exclusion of viral hepatitis, other drugs, alcohol, biliary obstruction, and travel-related causes. One patient had a positive rechallenge that confirmed the reaction was most probably niperotidine-related. The paper concludes the liver injury is idiosyncratic, with no dose-relationship, rarity and unpredictability, and variable latency, possibly related to a toxic metabolite.
raw_record.extra_details: 25 patients treated with niperotidine (daily doses 23-920 mg, treatment duration 15-210 days) had acute hepatitis; causal assessment followed International Consensus Meeting criteria (reference 3), with a positive rechallenge in one patient (115 mg/day; ALT, AST, bilirubin rose to 1000 UI/l, 1200 UI/l, 15 mg/dl and normalized 7 days after withdrawal). Liver injury patterns in the 25 cases were hepatocellular (3), cholestatic (9), or mixed (13). One 54-year-old woman on 230 mg/d for 2 months developed fulminant hepatitis (bilirubin 30 mg/dl, grade 2 encephalopathy, ascites, prothrombin time 18%) and died following an acute episode of digestive haemorrhage. Pathogenesis proposed as idiosyncratic, possibly via a toxic metabolite; niperotidine is an H2-receptor antagonist structurally related to ranitidine (furan ring) with a piperonyl side chain.

raw_record.support_text: Of the patients using thioguanine (TG), 14 (25%) had to discontinue therapy within 1 year, mostly due to adverse events or ineffectiveness. Of these, 2 were asymptomatic, 2 had thrombocytopenia (platelet counts 46 and 67 x 10⁹/L after 15 and 28 months of TG), and 1 had symptoms of noncirrhotic portal hypertension (esophageal varices grade III-IV, splenomegaly) after 44 months. raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH), discovered in 1952, remains a mainstay of mycobacterial therapy, given orally at 5-8 mg/kg up to 300 mg/day, or 600 mg twice weekly in intermittent regimens. Its mass-administration use was limited by the subsequent demonstration of severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose-related hepatotoxicity. Usual therapeutic dose 5-8 mg/kg/day to a 300 mg maximum, plus intermittent 600 mg twice-weekly short-course regimens. Onset typically occurs within the first weeks to months of therapy but can occur at any time. Heralding signs include nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite; stopping the drug at that point almost always prevents progression. Established hepatitis has a 10% mortality. Minor transaminase increases (up to 3x) are common early in therapy and need not prompt discontinuation unless liver function tests progress or signs of hepatitis appear. Reported hepatitis rates per 1000 patients by age group (25/35/45/55/65): definite and probable 1.3/5.9/10.9/17.5/10.5; including possible cases 6.3/12.7/20.4/31.4/25.5. Mechanism is not conclusively known; attention has centered on differences in drug metabolism producing toxic metabolites, with somewhat contradictory recent studies.

raw_record.support_text: A six-month fialuridine course began in March 1993 and was terminated on an emergency basis 13 weeks later when hepatic failure and lactic acidosis occurred in one of 15 patients; three patients had already discontinued therapy between weeks 10 and 12. raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 15 trial patients developed hepatic failure with lactic acidosis. Two patients with rapidly progressive hepatic failure died 22 and 36 hours after emergency liver transplantation; two others died of hemodynamic collapse due to pancreatitis and lactic acidosis before transplantation; one died of pancreatitis complications after transplantation; the remaining two underwent successful liver transplantation and survived with only little residual toxicity over 24 months follow-up. The seven patients with severe hepatotoxicity had biochemical evidence of pancreatitis, and all five who died showed pancreatitis at autopsy. Earlier-reported side effects included crampy abdominal pain, foot paresthesia, fatigue, nausea, numbness/tingling of feet or hands, lower abdominal pain, constipation, and mild thrombocytopenia.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a previously well 20-year-old woman who developed liver dysfunction with jaundice and malaise following a 1-year course of minocycline (100 mg daily) for acne vulgaris. raw_record.support_text: In a case report, a 79-year-old man treated for prostate adenocarcinoma with flutamide 750 mg/d orally developed cholestatic hepatitis 5 weeks after starting therapy, with jaundice, elevated bilirubin and a predominantly cholestatic biochemical pattern. After flutamide was discontinued, liver-enzyme and bilirubin levels rapidly declined and returned to normal within 3 weeks. The authors concluded flutamide was the most likely cause of the cholestatic hepatitis in this patient, although they were unsure of the mechanism; repeated eosinophilia (10%-16%) was considered compatible with an immunoallergic type of reaction. The paper also notes that jaundice after 1-3 months of flutamide therapy during clinical trials and fatal liver failure in the setting of flutamide treatment have been reported, but with no details given.

Hepatitis A, hepatitis B, cytomegalovirus and infectious mononucleosis excluded by serology; no transfusions. Dechallenge led to rapid decline in enzymes/bilirubin with complete recovery within 3 weeks; follow-up to 18 months unremarkable. raw_record.support_text: An adolescent patient with Cushing's syndrome was re-treated with ketoconazole (restarted at 200 mg daily, increased after one week to 200 mg twice daily). One month after restarting, she presented with jaundice, generalized itching, fever, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, and biochemistry confirmed hepatitis. As ketoconazole was thought to be the most likely cause, it was stopped. Tests excluded alternative aetiologies (hepatitis A, B, C, CMV and HIV antibodies negative, EBNA IgG positive). Within 6 days she developed frank hepatorenal failure with disseminated intravascular coagulation, was transferred to intensive care, deteriorated rapidly and died before a suitable donor liver became available.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old man with ALK-positive, EML4-ALK fusion lung adenocarcinoma (stage IVB) treated with alectinib 600 mg/day as first-line therapy developed serum AST and ALT elevation to CTCAE grade 3 on day 79. The injury was determined to be alectinib-induced hepatotoxicity of the cholestatic type (Digestive Disease Week Japan 2004 scale and R value), with hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, and EBV excluded. After recovery with UDCA and glycyrrhizin, rechallenge with reduced alectinib (150 then 300 mg/day) caused recurrent grade 2 and then grade 3 elevations, requiring discontinuation and a switch to lorlatinib on day 235.

Paper notes approximately 1-5% of patients experience alectinib-induced liver damage.

APAP is available in prescription and over-the-counter preparations, including APAP-opioid combinations used more often by unintentional overdose patients. Diagnostic criteria for APAP hepatotoxicity: history of ingestion of APAP compounds and a biochemical pattern of very high aminotransferases with low bilirubin, with or without detectable serum acetaminophen at admission; ALI defined as INR >=2.0 and ALT >=10x elevated; ALF defined as INR >=1.5 with any degree of hepatic encephalopathy. raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of acute hepatitis probably caused by terfenadine, an H1-receptor antagonist used as an antiallergic agent. A 43-year-old woman taking terfenadine 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria developed asthenia and jaundice, with elevated serum bilirubin (160 µmol/L), ALT (920 U), and alkaline phosphatase (188 U); HBsAg was absent and ultrasonography was normal. After jaundice resolved and liver tests normalized, she again took terfenadine intermittently and developed a second episode of jaundice with elevated bilirubin (70 µmol/L), ALT (512 U), and alkaline phosphatase (484 U), with viral serologies negative; this also resolved.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 60 mg/d for recurrent urticaria. First episode: latency about 5 months (started 15 Sep 1983; jaundice Feb 1984) with bilirubin 160 µmol/L, ALT 920 U (normal 5-40), alkaline phosphatase 188 U (normal 50-100), 3% eosinophils, HBsAg absent, normal liver/biliary ultrasound. Resolved by July 1984. On intermittent rechallenge, second episode (jaundice 5 Sep 1984) with bilirubin 70 µmol/L, ALT 512 U, alkaline phosphatase 484 U, negative viral serology (HBV, HAV IgM, mononucleosis); resolved by October 1984. Jaundice (icterus) and asthenia were the presenting features. Causality attributed as 'probably caused.'

Injury documented by inadvertent rechallenge. raw_record.support_text: The study identified extensive hepatotoxicity with sustained-release (SR) niacin, an effect widely reported through patient case reports. Most cases of hepatotoxicity occurred in patients taking SR niacin dosages of 2000 mg/d or more, with duration of therapy before hepatotoxicity ranging from 1 week to as much as 48 months. Symptoms included malaise, fatigue, somnolence, weakness, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, and dark urine, and resolved within weeks of discontinuing niacin. Several cases of severe liver dysfunction and fulminant hepatitis were reported, some progressing to stage 3 and 4 encephalopathy and one requiring liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Sustained-release (SR) dosage form used therapeutically for hypercholesterolemia; hepatotoxicity occurred predominantly at SR niacin dosages of 2000 mg/d or more.
raw_record.extra_details: In this controlled trial, hepatotoxic effects occurred in 52% of SR niacin-treated patients vs 0% of immediate-release (IR) niacin-treated patients. Symptoms accompanying elevated liver function tests included malaise, fatigue, somnolence, weakness, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, and dark urine; hepatotoxicity resolved within weeks of discontinuing niacin. Case reports describe severe liver dysfunction and fulminant hepatitis, some progressing to stage 3-4 encephalopathy and one requiring liver transplantation; duration of therapy before hepatotoxicity ranged from 1 week to 48 months. Multiple SR products with various release mechanisms were implicated in niacin-induced hepatitis, including Nicobid, Slo-Niacin, Nature's Plus, Niatrol, Endur-Acin, and generic products from Goldline, Rugby Laboratories, and Major Pharmaceutical.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 4 patients with liver injury secondary to cocaine use, 1 of whom died. Biopsies from two patients showed well-demarcated zone-3 necrosis identical to that seen with acetaminophen toxicity; the patient who died had necrosis of almost all hepatocytes at biopsy and autopsy; another patient biopsied after resolution had hyperplastic endoplasmic reticulum but no necrosis. All patients had mild large- and small-droplet steatosis in surviving hepatocytes, mild inflammation, early marked increase and rapid decrease of serum aminotransferases, mild-to-moderate increase in prothrombin time, myoglobinuria, and moderate azotemia. Drug screenings showed the presence of a cocaine metabolite and absence of acetaminophen, alcohol, and other potential toxins.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a new case of fatal hepatic toxicity due to dacarbazine (DTIC), a drug used for 20 years in melanoma treatment, noting only few published cases of this complication. In the presented 50-year-old woman on her second course of DTIC (250 mg/m² daily for 5 days), acute vascular hepatic toxicity from DTIC was suspected; post-mortem histology confirmed fulminant hepatitis with medio-lobular extensive necrosis and dilated hepatic veins, and the patient died 5 days later.
raw_record.extra_details: 50-year-old woman with malignant melanoma; second course of dacarbazine (DTIC) 250 mg/m² daily for 5 days; pre-course basal labs were normal except eosinophilia (1.4x10⁹/L). On day 2 of second course developed abdominal pain, nausea, fever, then shock and respiratory failure/anuria. Peak labs: ALT 2348 IU/l, AST 5160 IU/l, LDH 20430 IU/l, INR 3.95, serum protein 2.8 g/100 ml. Treated with high-dose dexamethasone (250 mg/6 hourly) and recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (100 mg) without benefit. Patient died 5 days later; post-mortem showed fulminant hepatitis with medio-lobular extensive necrosis, poor inflammatory infiltration, and dilated hepatic veins without thrombi or vessel-wall inflammatory infiltrate. Complications previously reported as Budd-Chiari syndrome, veno-occlusive disease, or small hepatic vessel thrombosis; allergic pathogenesis discussed given occurrence during second course and eosinophilia. Doppler sonography confirmed patent main hepatic and portal veins. Indication: melanoma treatment.
