raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of recurrent severe acute hepatitis induced by omeprazole. A 30-year-old man with advanced renal failure secondary to diabetic nephropathy, on ranitidine, calcium carbonate, furosemide, and nifedipine, was started on omeprazole 20 mg once daily for erosive gastritis and duodenal ulcer after ranitidine was stopped; nine days later he developed acute liver injury (AST 1788 U/L, ALT 1294 U/L) with hepatomegaly, which resolved within four weeks of discontinuing omeprazole. Six months later, rechallenge with omeprazole produced acute liver injury again (AST 954 U/L, ALT 762 U/L) within one week, which resolved after stopping the drug. Hepatitis and immunologic serologies were negative, supporting omeprazole as the cause of the recurrent hepatitis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient had advanced renal failure (diabetic nephropathy); concurrent furosemide, nifedipine, and calcium carbonate; ranitidine was stopped before omeprazole initiation.
raw_record.extra_details: Omeprazole 20 mg once daily for acid-related disorders (erosive gastritis and duodenal ulcer). raw_record.support_text: The paper states that liver toxicity is a potentially serious effect of treatment with niacin (nicotinic acid), first reported by Rivin, and that liver toxicity of time-release niacin preparations has also been recognized for many years. Additional cases of adverse hepatic effects of unmodified and time-release niacin have been reported, with severe cases resulting in fulminant hepatic failure and hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Also called niacin/NA. Compiles multiple reported patient cases of hepatic toxicity for unmodified and time-release preparations. Doses mostly 3-4.5 g/day for hyperlipidemia with toxicity latency 1-18 months; patients typically experienced nausea and vomiting, sometimes jaundice, with more severe cases showing elevated bilirubin, ammonia and prolonged prothrombin time. Table II cases: 3.0 g/day JA/AST/alk phos/bilirubin elevation normalizing in 20 days; 3.0 g/day peripheral edema, increased SBP retention; 0.75 g/day with cholestatic hepatitis on biopsy (in a man who had attempted suicide by carbon monoxide inhalation 3 days earlier); 0.9-4.5 g/day nausea/vomiting/jaundice; 3.0 g/day; 3.0 g/day case with jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy resolving in <10 days; time-release cases include aluminum nicotinate 3 g/day for 48 months with intrahepatic cholestasis and chronic portal inflammation/fibrosis, and 0.5 g/day for 2 months with fulminant liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy (taken as 'super timed-release' tablets for health effects). Most severe cases (refs 10,11,13) led to fulminant hepatic failure and hepatic encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a patient who developed hepatitis with systemic symptoms, fever, eosinophilia, prompt recurrence on rechallenge with ranitidine (150 mg twice daily, onset about 36 hours), and a variable latency, consistent with a hypersensitivity-type, dose-unrelated drug reaction. raw_record.support_text: The authors report two adult patients who developed fulminant hepatitis after 17 and 103 days of ketoconazole administration, with histologic evidence of massive, predominantly centrilobular necrosis. Clinical manifestations of hypersensitivity and eosinophilia were absent, which the authors interpret as suggesting ketoconazole hepatotoxicity is not mediated through an immunoallergic mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two patients who developed fulminant hepatitis with massive hepatic necrosis, which they state 'can be reasonably ascribed to ketoconazole.' Patient 1 received only ketoconazole; patient 2 received other drugs (cytarabine, zorubicin, colistin, amikacin, amphotericin B) none of which was judged likely responsible, as cytarabine and zorubicin were stopped 26 days before jaundice and amikacin/amphotericin B are not considered hepatotoxic.

Patient 1 received only ketoconazole; patient 2's co-medications (cytarabine, zorubicin, colistin, amikacin, amphotericin B) considered unlikely responsible. Mechanism considered direct or reactive-metabolite-mediated rather than immunoallergic, consistent with relatively high prevalence of asymptomatic serum ALT increase. Liver function continued deteriorating despite cessation; patient 2 died of fulminant hepatitis less than a month after starting the drug. Authors recommend bimonthly/weekly serum ALT monitoring and immediate interruption on ALT increase. Increased wedged-to-free hepatic venous pressure gradient (portal hypertension) and ascites also observed.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was concurrently on glibenclamide for non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus; hepatotoxicity was attributed to the newly added acarbose.
raw_record.extra_details: 65-year-old woman; acarbose 100 mg three times daily added to glibenclamide in mid-1993; symptoms of malaise and anorexia presented 2 months later with jaundice. Labs: aspartate aminotransferase 638 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL (direct 7.84 mg/dL), gamma-glutamyltransferase 156 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L. Viral hepatitis ruled out by serology; no antinuclear or anti-smooth-muscle antibodies; ultrasonography showed normal liver and no dilated bile ducts. After acarbose was stopped, total bilirubin fell to 1.8 mg/dL, AST to 159 U/L, ALT to 155 U/L within 4 weeks; laboratory results were normal within 9 months. Patient refused hospitalization and was managed as outpatient.

The strength of association was graded 'highly probable' using the RUCAM causality assessment method (score of 9), and 'probable' by the Danan-Benichou (score 8) and Maria-Victorino (score 14) scales.

raw_record.support_text: A 27-year-old woman with SLE developed severe and progressive jaundice a few days after starting cyclophosphamide, with normal liver function before therapy. Viral hepatitis, cholelithiasis/biliary disease, and lupus hepatitis were excluded, while other signs of cyclophosphamide toxicity (leukopenia, severe monomorphic haematuria) were present. Liver abnormalities resolved only months after cyclophosphamide withdrawal, and the authors concluded the patient suffered from severe hepatic toxicity caused by cyclophosphamide.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: severe cholestasis with minimal hepatocellular injury on biopsy, severe monomorphic haematuria and leukopenia (bladder toxicity). Literature aggregate of 13 total cases: severe hepatotoxicity became clinically evident after 2-40 weeks of oral or IV cyclophosphamide; two patients died of hepatic failure (Aubrey 1970, massive hepatic necrosis; Arai 1992), the rest recovered after drug withdrawal. Biopsy patterns varied: perivascular/perivenous hepatocyte necrosis, diffuse hepatocellular destruction with mild fatty infiltration, massive hepatic necrosis, small hepatic vein damage and fibrosis, drug-induced hepatitis, and (in index case) severe cholestasis. Indications included breast carcinoma, Still's disease, SLE, polymyositis, Sjögren's, Wegener's syndrome, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, minimal-change glomerulonephritis. Mechanism hypothesized to involve abnormal hepatic conjugation of acrolein metabolite. Authors advise monitoring of liver enzymes/bilirubin and prompt discontinuation on liver dysfunction.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 5 published patients plus one new patient (6 total) with amitriptyline-induced jaundice. Hepatitis occurred 24-430 days after starting amitriptyline at 30-150 mg daily. Hypersensitivity manifestations (fever, rash, hypereosinophilia) were seen in 3 patients. Serum ALAT was markedly increased in 4 patients; alkaline phosphatase was usually increased. Liver histology showed necrosis, cholestasis, or both. The jaundice induced by amitriptyline is classified as 'mixed' with the hepatocellular component usually predominating. Two of the 3 patients with fulminant hepatitis died; our patient survived; patients without hepatic encephalopathy recovered in 53-128 days.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician with fingernail onychomycosis was treated with ketoconazole as a single oral dose of 200 mg daily. He had no history of liver disease, no excessive ethanol intake, and took no other medications. After 81 days of therapy he developed fatigue and nausea, with markedly elevated ALT and later the appearance of icterus and marked malaise; serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase were all markedly elevated. Viral hepatitis A and B were excluded serologically, and imaging of the liver and pancreas was normal. He refused biopsy, and laboratory findings returned to normal within 2 months after the episode.
raw_record.extra_details: Second reported case from the authors' institution; the earlier communication described a case of biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis in a ketoconazole-treated patient. The paper states hepatic damage associated with ketoconazole is 'probably an idiosyncratic reaction' with estimated incidence between 0.1% and 1%, many cases subclinical. In this case a single 200 mg ketoconazole dose on day 86 appeared to further accelerate the ALT rise. Case details: ALT peaked near 1900 U/L (normal 10-40), total bilirubin peaked at 111 µmol/L (normal 2-17), alkaline phosphatase peaked at 480 U/L (normal 50-275). Abnormal findings resolved within normal limits 2 months after the episode. Also notes a manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reporting death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy, with an estimated 300,000 prescriptions since 1981 licensing.

raw_record.support_text: The described hepatic injury is attributed to amineptine: an anicteric acute hepatitis developed 15 days after the onset of amineptine (300 mg daily for depression) and improved rapidly after its cessation, with no other cause of liver disease. Multiple cases of amineptine-induced hepatitis with similar features (abdominal pain, fever) had been reported, and at therapeutic dose amineptine hepatotoxicity is described as likely immuno(activating) — a hypersensitivity pattern.

raw_record.support_text: Case report of a 25-year-old woman with hepatic failure admitted to Loghman-Hakim Poison Centre 24 hours after an attempted suicide with 100 tablets of acetaminophen (325 mg each). She was treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and discharged 12 days after admission. The authors conclude that acetaminophen poisoning should be considered in the differential diagnoses of hepatic failure and that NAC administration must always be considered in acetaminophen-induced hepatic damage even after 24 hours of overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-agent intentional overdose (attempted suicide with 100 tablets of 325 mg, total 32.5 g) leading to hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Poisoning reported as frequent in Iran; of 7000 poison-centre admissions in 6 months, 758 (11%) were analgesic poisonings, especially acetaminophen; 0.3% of 349 fatalities among 35,580 poisoned patients (1997-1998) were due to acetaminophen. Patient presented with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, icterus, elevated SGOT, SGPT, total and direct bilirubin, hypoglycaemia, prolonged PT (30 s, activity 24%), and later hepatic failure; treated with N-acetylcysteine (300 mg/kg over 20 hours), ranitidine, vitamin K1, PRBC and FFP; discharged on day 12 with resolution of abnormalities by days 9 and 30. Mechanism: CYP2E1-generated toxic metabolite N-acetyl-para-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) binds covalently to hepatic cells causing centrilobular necrosis when hepatic glutathione stores fall below 30% of normal.

He developed progressive hepatic and renal failure during a 2-week hospitalization. Viral hepatitis and ischemic hepatitis were ruled out, ultrasounds showed no focal abnormality. Gastroenterology and nephrology consults concurred that his liver failure was most likely due to his trabectedin treatment. The patient died on Day 54 from irreversible hepatic and renal insufficiency, with causes of death ruled as fulminant hepatic failure and acute renal failure.

raw_record.support_text: The diagnosis of pantoprazole-induced acute hepatitis was made in a 46-year-old woman who had taken pantoprazole for 8 days for reflux symptoms. Because clinical and laboratory findings showed gradual improvement after discontinuing the drug under symptomatic measures, and infectious, autoimmune, and metabolic causes were largely excluded (with duplex sonography showing no biliary obstruction or Budd-Chiari syndrome), the authors concluded it was a pantoprazole-induced acute hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report; 46-year-old woman presented with colic-like upper abdominal pain and markedly impaired general condition after taking pantoprazole for 8 days for gastroesophageal reflux; elevated liver values consistent with hepatitis; serology largely excluded infectious, autoimmune, and metabolic causes; duplex sonography showed no biliary obstruction or Budd-Chiari syndrome; gradual clinical and laboratory improvement after dechallenge under symptomatic treatment. The authors note that liver damage under proton pump inhibitor therapy is considered rare but should be considered in the differential diagnosis of unclear hepatitis.

The discussion describes mechanisms for liver necrosis after cocaine intoxication including direct effects of cocaine metabolism, hyperthermia, hypoxia, and shock, with periportal and midzonal necrosis of hepatocytes sparing the centrilobular zone.

Histology described in human cocaine-induced hepatotoxicity shows periportal and midzonal hepatocyte necrosis sparing centrilobular cells, distinct from hyperthermia/hypoxia/shock-induced centrilobular necrosis. Hepatitis A, B, C and EBV tests were negative, with no alcoholism or prior hepatic illness; last laboratory values showed prothrombin time 13%, total bilirubin 447 µmol/L and ALT 2169 U/L, and the hepatic biopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis. This hepatic necrosis case with fatal outcome was reported to the manufacturer, and two further fatal tolrestat hepatic-necrosis cases (Canada, Italy) plus poor efficacy in trials led to worldwide market suspension.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity resulting from methotrexate therapy for psoriasis is described as the most significant long-term problem. Liver chemistry studies and liver scans have not been uniformly predictive of fibrosis and cirrhosis in psoriasis patients before or during methotrexate therapy, strengthening the need for liver biopsy. Abnormal liver histologic findings (fibrosis and cirrhosis) are reported to be more common in psoriasis patients than in rheumatoid arthritis patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term methotrexate therapy for psoriasis; cumulative-dose- and duration-dependent risk; patients with preexisting liver disease relevant to biopsy decisions in rheumatoid arthritis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity is the most significant long-term problem of methotrexate therapy. Liver biopsy findings of fibrosis and cirrhosis were compiled across multiple studies (e.g., Weinstein 1973, international cooperative study of 550 patients with 81 paired premethotrexate/postmethotrexate biopsies; with cumulative doses >2.2 gm there was no significant increase in cirrhosis but a small increase in fibrosis; single posttreatment biopsies showed 3% cirrhosis). Higher cumulative doses (e.g., 4 gm in Nyfors 1977 and Zachariae 1980 cohorts) were associated with higher cirrhosis incidence (up to ~21-25.6%), while cirrhosis incidence was low at total methotrexate doses <1.5 gm. The clinical course of methotrexate-induced cirrhosis is often nonaggressive, and many patients were continued on methotrexate without worsening. Deaths resulting from hepatic damage after long-term treatment have occurred but appear very uncommon, mainly during the era before routine assessment of renal and liver function. Several studies conflict on cirrhosis incidence at high cumulative doses.

raw_record.extra_details: Three adolescents in whom autoimmune hepatitis developed related to oral minocycline use for acne (one received 100 mg once daily). Features included hypergammaglobulinemia, elevated ANA, positive anti-smooth muscle antibody, elevated serum IgG, elevated AST/ALT (e.g., patient 1: AST 363 U/L, ALT 459 U/L). Two patients underwent liver biopsy showing severe chronic lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, necrosis, and fibrosis. All other causes of liver disease were excluded. One patient resolved on drug withdrawal; 2 required immunosuppression therapy. A literature review identified only 18 similar cases, none pediatric, most with incomplete data. The authors note the potential severity of the hepatitis warrants immediate attention and drug discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a patient who developed acute hepatitis of probable drug origin attributed to valsartan. Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with irregular inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils and polymorphonuclears with focal hepatocellular necrosis, hepatocytes with feathery degeneration and some bile canalicular thrombi. On admission, with suspicion of valsartan-induced pharmacological hepatitis, the drug was withdrawn and evolution was favorable with progressive normalization of liver tests; at one month bilirubin was 4 mg/dl and transaminases had normalized, with enzymatic normalization confirmed at two months. The case was reported to the National Pharmacovigilance Service.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case reported as the first described valsartan hepatotoxicity in the reviewed literature (MEDLINE 1998-2001). Biopsy reported acute hepatitis of probable drug origin with lymphocytic/eosinophilic/polymorphonuclear infiltrate, focal hepatocellular necrosis, feathery degeneration and bile canalicular thrombi. PCR for hepatotropic viruses and serology for CMV, EBV and HSV were negative; abdominal ultrasound, CT and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (CPRE) were normal; bilirubin 4 mg/dl at discharge one month later with normalized transaminases; normal enzymes at two months. Causality supported by chronological relationship, absence of other causes, and rapid improvement after drug withdrawal; reported to national pharmacovigilance system.

raw_record.support_text: 95 patients had acute hepatitis with features of veno-occlusive disease during the trial, and all instances were related to 6-thioguanine exposure: 82 had been assigned that drug, one was taking non-randomised 6-thioguanine, and 12 were patients assigned 6-mercaptopurine who developed veno-occlusive disease whilst taking 6-thioguanine during intensification. Diagnosis was centrally validated and required at least two of: tender hepatomegaly, ascites, hyperbilirubinaemia (>17 µmol/L), or persistent thrombocytopenia out of proportion to neutropenia for more than 4 weeks. In the 82 assigned 6-thioguanine, 85% of veno-occlusive disease episodes occurred during continuing treatment or interim maintenance. Most patients had transient tender hepatomegaly with mild to moderate hyperbilirubinaemia and raised aminotransferases; one patient died of biopsy-proven adenovirus infection.

raw_record.extra_details: 95 cases of acute hepatitis with veno-occlusive disease features; 82 patients assigned 6-thioguanine, 1 on non-randomised 6-thioguanine, 12 assigned 6-mercaptopurine who developed VOD while taking 6-thioguanine in intensification. Diagnosis required at least two of: tender hepatomegaly, ascites, hyperbilirubinaemia (>17 µmol/L), persistent thrombocytopenia out of proportion to neutropenia for >4 weeks. Among patients assigned 6-thioguanine, 85% of VOD episodes occurred during continuing treatment (75%) or interim maintenance (10%), 15% during intensification. >90% had transient tender hepatomegaly, mild-moderate hyperbilirubinaemia with raised aminotransferases, and moderate-severe thrombocytopenia. One patient died of biopsy-proven adenovirus infection after presenting with VOD features; two admitted to intensive care for pulmonary complications; ~20% needed platelet/RBC transfusions. All switched to 6-mercaptopurine after VOD. Liver tests normalised after mean 4 weeks (range 1-52). 24 patients (25% of affected) developed splenomegaly with persistent mild-moderate thrombocytopenia; a further 19 patients had splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia without antecedent acute VOD, all in 6-thioguanine recipients.

raw_record.extra_details: Ketoconazole given as a single oral daily dose of 200 mg; therapy stopped after 81 days when fatigue and nausea occurred. ALT (aspartate transaminase) rose to 1030-1900 U/L (normal 10-40), with markedly elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (450-480 U/L), and lactic dehydrogenase; icterus and malaise present. A single 200 mg ketoconazole dose 48 h before day 86 accelerated the rise. Viral hepatitis A and B excluded by serology; liver ultrasound and CT showed no abnormalities; liver biopsy refused. Abnormal findings subsided and returned to normal within 2 months. Hepatic damage is stated to be probably an idiosyncratic reaction; incidence estimated between 0.1% and 1%, with many cases subclinical and detected only by routine liver function tests. A manufacturer advisory reported the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy. Recommendation to check liver function tests before and monthly or more frequently during ketoconazole therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In a population-based study of 14,662 Victorian hospital admissions for paracetamol overdose between July 1, 2000 and June 30, 2007, complications were uncommon, with acute liver failure reported in 137 cases (0.9%) and acute renal failure in 163 (1.1%). Overall 30-day mortality was 1.1% (n=154), dropping to 0.2% (n=26) when death was attributed to paracetamol or liver failure on the death certificate; nine of these 26 deaths (34%) were in patients with accidental overdose and none in children under 15. The discussion refers to 'life-threatening paracetamol-induced acute liver failure.'

raw_record.extra_details: 14,662 hospital admissions for paracetamol overdose over 7 years (mean 2095/year), 71% in women, most aged 15-50. Of overdoses, 9157 (62.5%) intentional, 2149 (15%, 307/year) accidental, remainder unknown. Acute liver failure n=137 (0.9%) and acute renal failure n=163 (1.1%); 0.8% of pediatric (<15 y) overdoses had a complication vs 3.5% in adults. 30-day mortality 1.1% (n=154), but 0.2% (n=26) when death attributed to paracetamol/liver failure. 26% of patients referred to the Victorian Liver Transplant Unit had accidental overdose (P=0.01). Overdose admissions decreased from 46/100,000 (2001) to 39/100,000 (2006), with no reduction in liver transplant unit referrals or mortality.

raw_record.support_text: A percutaneous liver biopsy showed features of a severe acute cholestatic hepatitis with bridging necrosis involving 30%–40% of the parenchyma, cholestasis, bile ductular proliferation, and injury to native bile ducts. The pathologist's overall impression was that the patient's liver injury was acute and most likely due to nilotinib-induced, acute liver toxicity, with the possibility of autoimmune hepatitis considered but thought to be less likely. The patient recovered after stopping nilotinib, with liver tests near normal at follow-up.

raw_record.extra_details: Liver biopsy showed severe acute cholestatic hepatitis with bridging necrosis (30%–40% of parenchyma), mixed inflammatory portal infiltrate with plasma cells and PAS-positive foamy macrophages, cholestasis, bile ductular proliferation, injury to native bile ducts, periportal hepatocyte injury with acidophil bodies and ballooning degeneration; copper and iron stains negative and no abnormal fibrosis. The patient did not develop hepatic encephalopathy; coagulopathy resolved after stopping nilotinib, transaminases and bilirubin peaked in late November and gradually normalized, and liver tests were near normal at the April 2018 visit (total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, ALT 47 U/L, AST 54 U/L, ALP 175 U/L, albumin 3.5 g/dL). Patient's UGT1A1 genotype was *36/*36 and a NAT2 slow acetylator allele was present. The authors found no prior reports of clinically apparent liver injury for nilotinib in the literature, while trial data reported transaminase elevations >5x ULN in 4%–9% of patients and hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice in a small percentage, with hyperbilirubinemia linked to the UGT1A1 (TA)7/(TA)7 polymorphism.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen, one of the most widely consumed OTC analgesics, is one of the most common medications toxicologists encounter in overdose, and toxicity can result in severe liver damage culminating in acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure. This retrospective cohort study of patients aged ≥14 with a discharge diagnosis of acetaminophen-induced hepatic failure (confirmed by a documented toxic serum acetaminophen concentration or a history consistent with ingestion) compared hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and lactic acidosis with the King's College criteria for predicting a composite endpoint of death or transplant.

raw_record.support_text: Osimertinib (80 mg/day) was started as sixth-line therapy in a 62-year-old woman with EGFR T790M-mutated NSCLC. On day 15 she developed general malaise; after reduction to 40 mg/day she was admitted with high fever and elevated serum AST (284 IU/L) and ALT (183 IU/L). No other cause was found, and fever and transaminase elevations improved immediately after discontinuation, leading to the diagnosis of drug-induced fever and hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case in a 62-year-old woman with relapsed stage IV NSCLC harboring EGFR L858R and acquired T790M, receiving osimertinib as sixth-line therapy. Initial dose 80 mg/day; reduced to 40 mg/day after day-15 general malaise; hepatotoxicity (AST 284 IU/L, ALT 183 IU/L) with high fever noted three days after the reduced dose, prompting emergency ward admission. No other cause identified; fever and transaminase elevations resolved after osimertinib discontinuation (dechallenge). Oral desensitization with milled osimertinib tablets mixed in lactose was performed over ~2 weeks (0.1 mg/day up to 40 mg/day on day 17) with no recurrence of hepatotoxicity or fever for the following 6 months on 40 mg/day. The paper notes osimertinib treatment is permanently stopped in 7–13% of patients due to drug-induced toxicities and that severe hepatotoxicity was the most common drug-induced side effect in clinical trials.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, on glibenclamide, had acarbose (100 mg three times daily) added in mid-1993. Two months later she presented with malaise, anorexia, and jaundice; AST was 638 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL (direct 7.84), γ-glutamyltransferase 156 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 221 U/L. Viral hepatitis and autoimmune antibodies were excluded, and ultrasonography was normal. After acarbose was stopped, bilirubin decreased to 1.8 mg/dL within 4 weeks and laboratory values normalized within 9 months. The authors conclude that acarbose caused the hepatic injury.

Injury classified as 'hepatocellular' per international consensus criteria; mechanism unknown, compatible with metabolic idiosyncrasy given long latency and absent hypersensitivity; dechallenge led to resolution (bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL at 4 weeks, laboratory values normal within 9 months). raw_record.support_text: Patient number 9, a 58-year-old woman with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia who had been taking a maintenance oral dose of 300 mg amiodarone (AMD) for over 3 years, was found to have abnormal liver tests compatible with cholestatic liver injury. Alcohol consumption and injection drug abuse were excluded; hepatitis A, B and C tests were negative, and antinuclear, anti-LKM and anti-mitochondrial antibodies were not detected. The serum amiodarone concentration was 1012 ng/mL (therapeutic range 500-1000 ng/mL). The patient was diagnosed with AMD-induced hepatotoxicity, the drug was discontinued, and a liver biopsy two weeks later showed moderate fibrosis and steatosis with periportal Mallory bodies. Liver enzymes gradually returned to normal after about three months, and amiodarone was not resumed.

raw_record.support_text: In this clinical cohort treated with arsenic trioxide (ATO) for acute promyelocytic leukemia, overall hepatotoxicity was seen in 24 patients (33.3%), was grade 1/2 in the majority, occurred mainly during induction, and was mainly associated with elevated levels of liver enzymes. raw_record.support_text: The paper reviews cases of low-dose cyclophosphamide-induced hepatotoxicity in humans. The first confirmed case (1982) was a female with SLE who developed hepatitis during initial treatment at 1.5 mg/kg CY and again on rechallenge at 50 mg/day. Additional cases include a male on 100 mg CY for scleroderma with a hepatocellular injury pattern after six weeks; a female with acute liver injury and hypereosinophilia eight weeks after 100 mg CY daily for SLE; a female with hepatotoxicity five weeks after 100 mg CY daily for granulomatosis with polyangiitis; and a patient developing acute hepatitis within 24 hours on two occasions two weeks apart after 200 mg CY (ALT 568 after the first dose, rising to 1253 after the second). All cases resolved with LFT normalization weeks after discontinuation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Low-dose oral cyclophosphamide for autoimmune diseases (SLE, scleroderma, granulomatosis with polyangiitis); reversible injury with LFT normalization weeks after discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: First case confirmed by rechallenge (hepatitis during both initial treatment and second challenge). Akay case: hepatocellular injury pattern after 6 weeks of 100 mg/day, LFTs normalized 11 weeks after stopping. Cleland/Pokorny: acute liver injury with hypereosinophilia. Snyder: hepatotoxicity within 5 weeks. Subramaniam: ALT 568 four days after first 200 mg dose, improving to 104, then 1253 after second dose. Paper notes this is the first reported combined low-dose cyclophosphamide-induced hyponatremia and hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports the first case of carbamazepine-induced vanishing bile duct syndrome (VBDS) in the English literature. The patient presented with jaundice, cholestasis (bilirubin 212 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 1030 IU/L, AST 99 IU/L), a liver biopsy showing an activated T-lymphocyte portal infiltrate with damaged and destroyed interlobular bile ducts, and had no large-duct obstruction, PBC, PSC, or sarcoidosis. Ductal loss and portal fibrosis progressed after CBZ withdrawal, and the immunoallergic/hypersensitivity mechanism (eosinophilia, rash, fever) is invoked for CBZ hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported CBZ-induced VBDS case. Patient had fever, rash, pruritus, eosinophilia (20% of WBC), elevated bilirubin 212 micromol/L, alkaline phosphatase 1030 IU/L, AST 99 IU/L, prolonged PT corrected by vitamin K. Biopsy showed activated T-lymphocyte portal infiltration with damaged/destroyed interlobular bile ducts; loss of bile ducts and portal fibrosis progressed on follow-up biopsies. PBC, PSC, sarcoidosis, large-duct obstruction, CMV and HIV excluded. Hypersensitivity/immunoallergic mechanism proposed. Treated with prednisolone and ursodeoxycholic acid; recovered clinically with persistent abnormal liver biochemistry.

With a 200 mg/day lead-in dose for the first 2 weeks followed by 400 mg/day, liver toxicity was detected in 1% of the tested population. Postmarketing reports gathered by Boehringer-Ingelheim indicated the incidence of liver toxicity was greater than before approval, increasing from 1% to 3%.

Abstract reports rare life-threatening liver failure associated with nevirapine therapy; first 6 weeks of therapy are most critical for adverse drug reactions with close clinical/laboratory monitoring urged during the first 12 weeks.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (APAP) is a widely used over-the-counter analgesic. At higher doses APAP causes acute liver failure characterized by centrilobular hepatic necrosis, and APAP-induced hepatotoxicity is the leading cause of acute liver failure, accounting for nearly 50% of all cases. The spectrum ranges from intentional overdose (42%) to accidental overdose (49%). In the US, APAP overdose causes over 56,000 emergency room visits, 2,600 hospitalizations, and over 450 deaths from acute liver failure annually.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure, including both intentional (42%) and accidental (49%) overdose; stated as a dose-dependent hepatotoxin active at supratherapeutic doses.
raw_record.extra_details: APAP overdose is the most frequent cause of acute liver failure in the US, accounting for ~50% of all acute liver failure cases. Annual burden: >56,000 ER visits, 2,600 hospitalizations, >450 deaths from acute liver failure. Pattern described as centrilobular hepatic necrosis. Mechanism (toxic metabolite NAPQI, glutathione depletion, reactive oxygen species, innate-immune 'two-hit' participation) described but the mouse DC-depletion/Flt3L findings are animal-only and not part of this human DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: In clinical trials anastrozole has shown a good liver safety profile, but the reported patient developed acute liver damage during treatment with this aromatase inhibitor and recovered fully after drug discontinuation. Considering the time lapse between drug exposure and onset of hepatitis, patient age, exclusion of other non-drug-related causes, improvement after withdrawal and other reported anastrozole-related hepatitis cases, the case achieved a score of 7 on the Roussel-Uclaf Causality Method, suggesting a probable correlation between anastrozole and liver damage.
raw_record.extra_details: 70-year-old woman on anastrozole 1 mg/day for ER-positive breast carcinoma; liver injury appeared ~4 months (January 2009) after start (August 2008). Baseline liver tests were normal. At onset: AST 640 U/l, ALT 1344 U/l, ALP 355 U/l, total bilirubin 3.54 mg/dl, conjugated bilirubin 2.29 mg/dl, GGT 234 U/l. Hepatitis A/B/C, EBV, CMV serologies and autoimmune Abs negative (ANA 1:80 speckled). Liver biopsy showed mild steatosis (10%), moderate inflammatory activity and moderate-to-severe fibrosis (Ishak 5-6). Prompt normalization of liver parameters within one month and ANA became undetectable after 12 months after anastrozole withdrawal; switched to tamoxifen without side effects. RUCAM score 7. Two prior reported cases of anastrozole-related hepatitis (patients aged 58 and 89 years, acute mainly cholestatic injury improving after withdrawal, anastrozole considered most probable cause); in the de la Cruz case biopsy showed diffuse zone-3 liver cell necrosis without inflammation, considered metabolically-mediated hepatocellular injury. Anastrozole is extensively metabolized by N-dealkylation, hydroxylation and glucuronidation; potential and mechanisms of hepatotoxicity remain uncertain.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial discusses halothane hepatitis as a form of human drug-induced liver injury occurring after halothane anesthesia, encompassing both severe or fulminant cases and more frequent mild, often asymptomatic cases. It notes that features of hypersensitivity are present in no more than approximately 25 per cent of cases and occur equally in severe and mild halothane-induced liver injury.
raw_record.extra_details: Cases include fulminant hepatic failure after halothane anesthesia (11 patients, 14 serum samples); centrilobular necrosis seen in many cases is characteristic of true hepatotoxicity; the paper concludes that 'idiosyncrasy' is a more appropriate designation than 'hypersensitivity', accommodating both idiosyncratic allergic reactions and metabolic idiosyncrasy with enhanced toxic-metabolite production; halothane is also described as toxic to cultured hepatocyte membranes and hepatotoxic in several animal models.

raw_record.support_text: Zou et al reported 2 cases of cholestatic hepatitis caused by methimazole (Tapazole). Case 1: a 50-year-old female who initiated methimazole 10 mg daily and propranolol for newly diagnosed hyperthyroidism developed cholestatic hepatitis with severe icterus; after methimazole was stopped (propranolol continued), her liver tests were nearly normal in 4 weeks. Case 2: a 42-year-old female on methimazole 30 mg daily (reduced to 15 mg daily) had severe pruritus and icterus after 27 days of therapy; methimazole was discontinued and she recovered following methylprednisolone treatment.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatobiliary toxicity, first manifested by cholestatic patterns of enzyme elevation, is the principal and nearly universal toxicity of IA FUDR (floxuridine) given as a 14-day course every 28 days. All reported liver biopsies in patients receiving single-agent IA FUDR showed cholestatic abnormalities rather than hepatocellular changes. At an initial dose of 0.3 mg/kg/day x 14, severe biliary sclerosis occurred and this dose is advised against; after reduction to 0.2 mg/kg/day, treatment-limiting alkaline phosphatase elevations still occurred in essentially all patients. One patient died of biliary cirrhosis with liver failure after only three cycles of IA FUDR at 0.2 mg/kg/day despite appropriate liver enzyme monitoring.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intra-arterial hepatic artery infusion of single-agent FUDR, 14-day course every 28 days; hepatobiliary toxicity described as principal and nearly universal in this setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Also known as floxuridine (5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine). Dose escalation: 0.3 mg/kg/day x14 produced severe biliary sclerosis and is considered no longer acceptable; 0.2 mg/kg/day still caused treatment-limiting alkaline phosphatase elevations in essentially all patients. Toxicity spectrum ranges from minor enzyme elevations to advanced biliary sclerosis, bile duct strictures, and biliary cirrhosis with liver failure. One patient died of biliary cirrhosis with liver failure after three cycles at 0.2 mg/kg/day despite careful monitoring. IA doses of 0.3 mg/kg/day and IV doses of 0.15 mg/kg/day (measured pump flow) predictably caused severe, potentially irreversible toxicity. Liver biopsy reports describe cholestatic abnormalities, not hepatocellular changes. Biliary toxicity requires close enzyme monitoring and low threshold for dose reduction/interruption.

raw_record.support_text: In a fatal human case, a man with mild chronic renal failure but no prior hepatic dysfunction developed fulminating hepatic failure after sevoflurane administration. He had no previous general anesthesia, viral hepatitis, known allergies, or other hepatotoxic drugs, and operative hepatic hypoperfusion, hypotension, or ischemia were excluded. Microscopic liver examination showed extensive and confluent hepatic necrosis with large calcium deposition in hepatocyte cytoplasm, and the findings were interpreted as sevoflurane-induced hepatotoxicity consistent with earlier reports that cytoplasmic calcium elevation underlies it.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal case; exitus preceded by symptoms of fulminating hepatic failure. Patient had mild chronic renal failure but no hepatic dysfunction before sevoflurane administration; no previous general anesthesia, viral hepatitis, allergies, or other hepatotoxic drugs; operative hepatic hypoperfusion, hypotension, and ischemia excluded. Microscopy revealed extensive confluent hepatic necrosis with large calcium deposition in hepatocyte cytoplasm, confirmed by confocal laser microscopy and 3-D visualization. Mechanism previously reported as elevation of cytoplasmic calcium underlying sevoflurane-induced hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old man with hepatocellular carcinoma and Child-Pugh class A cirrhosis started sorafenib at 800 mg/day. After 32 days grade 4 liver injury developed and sorafenib was discontinued; the liver injury then progressed (ALT rose from 874 to 1,665 U/L and total bilirubin to 10.1 mg/dL) before fully resolving after intravenous methylprednisolone followed by tapering oral prednisolone. raw_record.support_text: A 51-year-old white man developed cephalexin-induced cholestatic hepatitis. He started a 10-day course of cephalexin (500 mg orally three times daily) for a postoperative wound infection and was taking no other medications at the start of therapy; previously he had tolerated penicillin and had received 1 g of cefazolin preoperatively. About 3 days after starting cephalexin he noted dark urine and pale stool, and within 24 hours of completing therapy developed fever, hives, pruritus and jaundice. A diagnosis of cephalosporin-induced (cephalexin) cholestatic hepatitis was made based on the temporal, clinical and biochemical course.

raw_record.support_text: Yellow phosphorus (YP) poisoning from ingestion of firecrackers caused death in 16 children aged 2-15 years from 1997 to 2012 in Turkey. Autopsies (15 of 16 cases) showed macroscopically yellowish-discolored livers with petechial bleeding, and histopathologic examination revealed acute toxic hepatitis. YP is described as an extremely toxic protoplasmic poison that is easily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with an estimated lethal dose of 1 mg/kg, and produces serious pathologic effects particularly in the liver.

Red phosphorus is noted as nonvolatile, unabsorbable, and nontoxic when ingested.

raw_record.support_text: Atorvastatin-induced autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is described as a rare but well-documented life-threatening adverse event. In this report, a 57-year-old female prescribed atorvastatin 20 mg daily for dyslipidemia three months prior presented with worsening fatigue, jaundice, and deranged liver function tests; a liver biopsy confirmed a drug-induced autoimmune picture, and she was diagnosed with atorvastatin-induced AIH after ruling out all other possible causes, with improvement after prolonged treatment with prednisone.
raw_record.extra_details: Atorvastatin 20 mg daily for 3 months before presentation, used for dyslipidemia (patient also had type 2 diabetes mellitus). ANA titer 1:180; IgG within normal range; smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial, and liver-kidney microsomal antibodies negative; negative hepatitis A/B/C, HIV, CMV, and EBV serology; normal MRCP. Liver biopsy confirmed a drug-induced autoimmune picture; other causes ruled out. Atorvastatin was discontinued and the patient improved after prolonged treatment with prednisone. Paper notes drug-induced AIH is a rare but documented cause of liver failure/transplantation, with a hepatocellular pattern of enzyme elevations.

raw_record.support_text: Mr. A, a 57-year-old man taking fluoxetine 20 mg/day (started ~10 weeks prior) together with clonazepam and long-term chlorpropamide, presented with clinical hepatitis and an enlarged nontender liver. Liver tests showed AST 410 IU/L, ALT 829 IU/L, and gamma-glutamyltransferase 860 IU/L with normal bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, and prothrombin time. Because drug-induced hepatotoxicity was suspected, fluoxetine was discontinued; liver enzymes were nearly normal 9 days later and completely normal at 1 year. No rechallenge or biopsy was performed. raw_record.support_text: The reported cases of etretinate-induced hepatotoxicity are summarized; the cause of the hepatic disease appears to be drug hypersensitivity, supported by lack of correlation between dose, appearance of liver disease, clinical/pathologic severity, and usually rapid recovery. The pathologic process can be fulminant, and four patients have died of etretinate-induced hypersensitivity hepatitis. In reported studies the dosage of etretinate ranged from 0.3 to 1.5 mg/kg/day, and in most cases liver disease onset appeared 3 to 6 months after initiation of therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 0.3-1.5 mg/kg/day; onset of liver disease mostly 3-6 months after starting therapy; four deaths from fulminant etretinate-induced hypersensitivity hepatitis; according to histologic descriptions, reactions classified as 10 nonspecific reactive hepatitis, 4 acute hepatitis, 6 chronic active hepatitis, and 3 each fibrosis and cirrhosis; central lobular inflammation and necrosis seen in some reactions; two patients implicated in etretinate hypersensitivity with fever and peripheral eosinophilia (Weiss et al., Khouri et al.); no correlation between overall severity of liver disease and cumulative dose in 18 severe-psoriasis patients; Ito cells (lipocytes) decreased in etretinate hepatotoxicity in contrast to increased in vitamin A intoxication, suggesting unrelated mechanisms.

raw_record.support_text: In this serial liver biopsy study of 24 patients with psoriasis on chronic methotrexate therapy, 21 of 24 patients showed progressive liver injury when biopsies were scored by a modified Brunt grading/staging method, with progression deemed when fibrosis, steatosis, or necroinflammation increased by a score of one or more. The mean cumulative methotrexate dose in the progressing group was 5813 mg (vs 3330 mg in the three patients without progression), and progression was caused by an increase in fibrosis in 16 of 21 patients. Methotrexate was stopped in one obese diabetic patient after 6 months (cumulative dose 378 mg) because the risk of further liver injury outweighed therapeutic benefit.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic methotrexate for psoriasis followed with serial liver biopsies; patients selected had baseline steatosis, hepatitis, and/or zone 3 fibrosis scoring at least 1; many had clinical risk factors of obesity, diabetes, and/or alcohol.
raw_record.extra_details: 24 patients (ages 28-65 y, mean 52 y); total MTX dose range 378-22750 mg (mean 5502 mg); mean therapy duration about 5 y 7 mo (range 6 mo to 17.5 y); 17 of 24 showed a NASH-like histologic pattern, 15 of whom progressed; 21/24 progressed (16 by fibrosis increase, 5 by steatosis or necroinflammation increase); progression graded by Roenigk classification and a semiquantitative score modified from Brunt et al.; bridging fibrosis (Roenigk IIIB) seen without cirrhosis; one patient (case 16) had bridging fibrosis in both biopsies that did not reach cirrhosis; MTX stopped in case 3 due to liver-injury risk outweighing benefit.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first case of fulminant hepatitis in a patient with sulfasalazine-induced DRESS syndrome (drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms) who survived without liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: A 45-year-old woman with seronegative rheumatoid polyarthritis; oral corticosteroid was given before sulfasalazine (day 1). Sulfasalazine was stopped on day 15 due to generalized maculopapulous rash. On admission (day 22) she had abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, hepatic cytolysis (aminotransferases at 5 N); DRESS with hypereosinophilia (12.10%/l), major cytolysis (transaminases >2,000 IU/l), cholestasis (total bilirubin at 5 N) and liver failure (factor V 45%). Hepatic biopsy showed massive centrolobular necrosis with lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates, consistent with immunoallergic drug-induced hepatitis. Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy with cerebral edema, factor V fell to 17%; emergency liver transplantation proposed on day 33 but postponed after improvement. Patient came out of coma on day 40 and was discharged on day 74. Treated with intensive methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days then corticosteroids 2 mg/kg/day. The authors attribute establishment of DRESS syndrome to sulfasalazine; rare immunoallergic reactions including the 3-week sulfasalazine syndrome with some fulminant hepatitis cases are noted.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose is described as a leading cause of acute liver failure (ALF), and when patients fulfill the King's College criteria for acetaminophen-induced ALF (AALF) they have a poor prognosis for survival without liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a 41-year-old female with no documented history of liver disease who presented with acute acetaminophen toxicity and developed hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy and lactic acidosis; she met King's College criteria for liver transplantation based on pH and INR but was deemed not suitable due to psychosocial comorbidities. Treated with single-pass albumin dialysis (SPAD) starting day 3 of ICU admission for five consecutive daily runs (~77 hours) as a bridge to recovery; course complicated by cerebral edema requiring mannitol. Native liver function recovered by hospital discharge (day 46), with bilirubin <100 mmol/L; no long-term neurological sequelae.

raw_record.support_text: A 64-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia treated with imatinib mesylate (400 mg/day, later reduced to 200 mg/day) presented with acute hepatitis. Liver transaminases rose (ASAT up to 20xN, ALAT up to 28xN) with later GGT 8.5xN, alkaline phosphatase 3xN, bilirubin 98 µmol/L, and prothrombin 68%. Evaluations for viral, autoimmune, and other causes were negative, and liver biopsy showed severe centrolobular necrosis with a polymorphic portal and lobular inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils), evoking acute drug-induced hepatitis with an immune mechanism. Transaminases decreased within weeks after imatinib was stopped, and rechallenge at 400 mg/day again reproduced transaminase, GGT, and alkaline phosphatase elevation, resolving after permanent discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: This case illustrates the development of acute hepatitis as a likely adverse event of leflunomide therapy. Liver biopsy 44 days after starting leflunomide was diagnostic of acute hepatitis consistent with primary liver-cell damage, with preserved architecture, no fibrosis, mild portal mononuclear inflammation, scattered apoptotic bodies, and focal zone 3 lymphocytic infiltrate without confluent necrosis. The RUCAM-CIOMS score of seven established the causal relation of leflunomide with the liver disease as probable, considered against previous (methotrexate, acetaminophen, omeprazole, alendronate) and simultaneous (sodium aurothiomalate) use of other potentially hepatotoxic drugs and unavailable serologic tests for EBV, CMV and HIV. The patient was homozygous for the mutated CYP2C9*3 allele and recovered with cholestyramine treatment, with liver enzymes normal at 3 months.

raw_record.extra_details: 44-day-old single case. RUCAM-CIOMS causality score 7 ('probable'). Biopsy showed acute hepatitis with primary liver-cell damage: preserved structure, no fibrosis, mild portal mononuclear infiltrate, preserved bile ductules, acidophilic change, scattered apoptotic bodies, focal zone 3 lymphocytic infiltrate, no confluent necrosis, Kupffer cells with PAS-positive material, condensed reticulin near terminal venules. Injury was preceded by diarrhoea; clinically mild but more severe biochemically and histologically. Treated with cholestyramine (which interferes with leflunomide's enterohepatic cycle) and recovered; liver enzymes normal at Day 28 after admission and at 3 months. Authors recommend monthly serum aminotransferase monitoring during the first 6 months of leflunomide therapy.

raw_record.support_text: Three percent (3%) of yellow phosphorus is the active component of the rodenticide Ratol®. It is a potent hepatotoxin that leads to acute liver failure (ALF) with high mortality. The paper reports a 19-year-old male with an alleged history of Ratol® ingestion who developed ALF with acute kidney injury; a diagnosis of fulminant hepatic failure with AKI secondary to yellow phosphorus toxicity was made after four days post-ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate (suicidal) ingestion of about 35 g of Rodenticide Ratol® paste, 3% yellow phosphorus, in a 19-year-old male; acute kidney injury also present.
raw_record.extra_details: Active component is yellow phosphorus (3%) in the rodenticide Ratol®. Latency ~4 days before symptoms and presentation. Presented with grade 2 hepatic encephalopathy (GCS E3V4M5), icterus, cerebral edema on NCCT head, coagulopathy (INR 4.2, aPTT 47.8 s), acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.8 mg/dL), severe LFT derangement (total bilirubin 17.2 mg/dL, direct 9.3 mg/dL, AST 112 U/L, ALT 114 U/L). No antidote available; definitive management is liver transplantation. Patient underwent five cycles of plasmapheresis with clinical and laboratory improvement and complete reversal. Paper notes minimal fatal dose of yellow phosphorus is 8 mg and LD50 ~1 mg/kg, with >50% fatality in Indian suicidal poisonings.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic injury during isoniazid (INH) therapy had an overall incidence of about 1% in the general population, was more common in older age groups and moderately enhanced by excessive alcohol consumption, reaching up to 2.5% in some groups aged 35-65 years who drank excessively. Laboratory investigations were consistent with acute, often severe, hepatocellular injury; histopathology ranged from mild acute hepatocellular inflammation to extensive necrosis and collapse (massive hepatic necrosis), with marked lobular collapse; the authors concluded chronic irreversible damage rarely results from INH-induced hepatic disease.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chemoprophylaxis use; risk much higher in those aged 35-65 years and moderately enhanced by excessive alcohol consumption; no evidence that chronic liver disease predisposed patients.
raw_record.extra_details: In the Public Health Service comparative study (Garibaldi 1971), 19 of 2,321 persons given INH for chemoprophylaxis developed acute hepatocellular injury (2 died) over a 9-month period versus 1 hepatitis-like case among 2,414 non-treated persons at the same location. A surveillance program admitted 13,838 patients in 21 US health departments (July 1971-November 1972), giving ~1% overall incidence. Presentation peaked at 4-8 weeks after starting; symptoms included anorexia, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, and weight loss; in at least one third of patients gastrointestinal symptoms were minor/absent, with a systemic/viral-like illness or asymptomatic jaundice. Peripheral eosinophilia (expected in a true hypersensitivity reaction) was distinctly unusual; hepatitis B antigen testing was negative. Histology ranged from mild acute hepatocellular inflammation to extensive necrosis and collapse (massive hepatic necrosis); marked lobular collapse with substantial scarring was noted. The 1967 statement of 'virtually no side effects' was rendered inoperative by accumulating case reports.

raw_record.support_text: An 82-year-old man with essential hypertension presented with jaundice, pruritus, and anorexia of 2 days' duration, having received candesartan cilexetil 16 mg/day for 3 weeks. On admission he had elevated AST (111 U/l), ALT (272 U/l), GGT (456 U/l), alkaline phosphatase (1045 U/l), and total/direct bilirubin (141/117 µg/dl). Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, CMV, EBV, and autoantibodies were negative, as were iron/copper studies and abdominal imaging. Medication was stopped; AST/ALT fell over the following 2 weeks while bilirubin continued rising. Prednisone was started, later increased to 60 mg/day for one week, after which bilirubin fell; prednisone was stopped at week 8 when liver function tests were normal. The patient remained asymptomatic 7 months later.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (82-year-old male) patient with essential hypertension; prednisone used to treat the hepatitis was not implicated as a cause.
raw_record.extra_details: The authors judged the case a definitive diagnosis on the CIOMS scale (10 points) or probable on the María y Victorino index (14 points) of candesartan hepatitis; case was one of the first described (year 2000) plus 2 other reported cases. Dose was 16 mg/day with a 3-week latency; dechallenge led to initial improvement in transaminases but transiently rising bilirubin (up to 379 µg/dl) before recovery with prednisone. A metabolic idiosyncrasy mechanism was proposed, noting candesartan cilexetil is converted to the active metabolite candesartan, with possible intrahepatic accumulation of candesartan or potentially toxic acyl glucuronides generated via UGT1A3-catalyzed O-glucuronidation during biliary excretion; CYP2C9-mediated hepatic transformation is minor.

This differed from most previously reported cases in the literature, which resulted in transplantation or death.

Peak LFTs: ALT 1964-2236 IU/L, AST 2068-1648 IU/L, ALP 96 IU/L, GGT 179 IU/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, ammonia 38 µmol/L. CT abdomen showed fatty liver infiltrate, small pelvic ascites, and cholestasis. Concomitant medications quetiapine and clonazepam discontinued and mirtazapine reduced; only nefazodone is attributed as cause. raw_record.support_text: A 27-year-old female treated with chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) for cholesterol gallstones developed jaundice with increasing pruritus; liver biopsy demonstrated feathery degeneration and vacuolated nuclei of hepatocytes, intrahepatic cholestasis, focal liver cell necrosis and bile thrombi with little portal inflammation, findings the authors state are compatible with toxic liver injury. After CDCA was discontinued and taurine (TS-201) was prescribed, T-Bil, TBA and Al-P normalized and itching improved; a scratched patch test with CDCA was fairly positive. The paper attributes the intrahepatic cholestatic liver injury to CDCA.

Values normalized after CDCA discontinuation plus taurine (TS-201, Taisho). Positive scratched patch test with CDCA on September 25. raw_record.support_text: A 53-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections developed hepatic injury after sulfamethoxazole therapy. Two episodes occurred: after 10 days of sulfamethoxazole 2 g/day (August 1978) and again after 7 days of the sulfamethoxazole-phenazopyridine combination Uro-Gantanol (October 1979), each causing fever, malaise, abdominal pain and scleral icterus. raw_record.support_text: This case is the third report of sulfamethoxazole-induced liver injury in which the causal role of the sulfonamide was proven by readministration of a test dose, along with biochemical abnormalities associated with two courses of treatment and a challenge dose of 1 g sulfamethoxazole. The patient developed fever, malaise, nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, and arthralgias that were followed after a few days by jaundice. Liver biopsy showed a 'pure' cholestatic picture with canalicular bile plugs and accumulation of bile pigment in hepatocytes, with no hepatocellular necrosis evident.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality proven by rechallenge with a 1 g test dose of sulfamethoxazole and by readministration across two treatment courses. Clinical features: fever, malaise, nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, arthralgias, and jaundice that appeared a few days later. Biopsy showed pure cholestasis with canalicular bile plugs and bile pigment accumulation without hepatocellular necrosis. The pattern of response to challenge was interpreted as characteristic of an immunologically-mediated hypersensitivity reaction; the patient's lymphocytes did not undergo blast transformation to sulfamethoxazole, sulfisoxazole, or plasma from volunteers after ingestion. All sulfonamide drugs were subsequently proscribed due to reported cross-sensitization.

raw_record.support_text: This is reported as the first documented case of daptomycin-induced acute liver failure, characterized by significant LFT elevations, impaired synthetic function, and encephalopathy. After exclusion of other potential causes of acute liver failure, daptomycin was identified as the likely instigator; the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale assigned a score of 5 (probable range 5-8), indicating daptomycin as the probable cause of the liver injury. Concurrent acute-on-chronic renal failure was observed, but rhabdomyolysis was absent. Prior case reports (Janda, Bohn, Abraham) had attributed elevated transaminases/liver injury to daptomycin without synthetic dysfunction or encephalopathy.

Case #2: pemoline over ~5 years at 37.5-56.25 mg/day until age 10, resumed at 37.5 mg/day for 7 months; initial AST 2,448 U/L with total bilirubin 3.7 mg/100 ml, then AST 3,205 U/L/ALT 2,344 U/L with total bilirubin 15.1 mg/100 ml; deep jaundice (total bilirubin up to 19.2, direct 10.0 mg/100 ml); hepatitis panel (HBsAg, HBsAb, HBcAb, anti-HAV IgM), ANA, CMV, and EBV negative; prothrombin time 18.1 s (control 11.0 s), PTT 45.9 s (control 34.4 s); became comatose with hypoglycemia; open liver biopsy showed shrunken liver (~20-25% of normal), submassive hepatic necrosis with bridging fibrosis and bile ductule proliferation; patient referred for possible hepatic transplantation before improving; HIDA scan 3 years later normal (extraction fraction 88.9%). Prior published reports describe milder disease in a 10-year-old and four adults over 60 (asymptomatic AST/ALT elevations to about 10x normal; histology of fatty metamorphosis, scattered cellular necrosis, nuclear vacuolization, portal inflammation). Both hypersensitive immunologically mediated and direct chemical hepatotoxic mechanisms have been postulated. Spectrum from mild asymptomatic aminotransferase elevation to severe fulminant hepatitis considered.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old female with unremarkable history except for minocycline 50 mg/day for 18 months for acne presented with elevated serum transaminases (ALT 392 units/liter, AST 357 units/liter) and ANA 1/1280. Liver biopsy showed chronic portal inflammation with lymphocytes, plasmocytes, eosinophils, and piecemeal necrosis with intralobular inflammation. Autoimmune hepatitis was suspected. After cessation of minocycline, arthralgias disappeared and serum transaminases normalized and remained normal during two-year follow-up.

raw_record.extra_details: ANA of homogenous type titer 1/1280 with no hypergammaglobulinemia. Liver biopsy: chronic portal inflammation with lymphocytes, plasmocytes, eosinophils, minimal piecemeal necrosis, intralobular inflammation and councilman bodies. No coagulopathy or cholestasis. Transaminases decreased at biopsy to ALT 136, AST 156 units/liter and normalized after drug cessation, remaining normal over two-year follow-up; arthralgias resolved. This case supports previously described eight ANA-positive cases of chronic active hepatitis secondary to minocycline.

raw_record.support_text: A 50-year-old man treated for a urinary tract infection with oral ciprofloxacin 250 mg twice a day for 5 days developed asthenia, abdominal discomfort, anorexia, diarrhea, mild fever and jaundice on the last day of therapy, with ALT 202 IU/l, AST 111 IU/l, AP 314 IU/l, γGT 135 IU/l and bilirubin 82 µmol/l. Viral hepatitis, autoimmune antibodies and bile duct obstruction were excluded, and a liver biopsy showed pronounced centrolobular cholestasis with minimal portal lympho-eosinophilic infiltration. The patient recovered completely after jaundice lasting 9 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1 of cholestatic hepatitis. No rechallenge performed; authors concluded the time course, exclusion of other causes and histology support cholestasis being induced by ciprofloxacin. Fever and eosinophilia argued for an idiosyncratic (immunoallergic) reaction. Bilirubin peaked at 159 µmol/l; severe pruritus; full recovery. Background literature noted: icteric cholestatic injury after ciprofloxacin (refs 5,6) and a reported case of fulminant hepatitis possibly related to ciprofloxacin (ref 9).

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity due to papaverine was observed in four patients, and a cause and effect relation was demonstrated by repeated rechallenge with the drug. The patients had abdominal discomfort but jaundice was not prominent; serum alkaline phosphatase and transaminases were elevated. Liver biopsies in Cases 2 and 3 showed numerous eosinophils in the periportal spaces, and symptoms and signs appeared to be fully reversible. The most likely mechanism is a hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Four cases of a hepatic disorder arising during oral treatment with papaverine; hepatotoxicity had not previously been described for papaverine, which is generally considered of very low toxicity. Patients had abdominal discomfort with jaundice not prominent; serum alkaline phosphatase and transaminases were elevated. Liver biopsies in Cases 2 and 3 showed numerous eosinophils in the periportal spaces. Symptoms and signs fully reversible. Cause and effect demonstrated by repeated rechallenge; most likely mechanism is a hypersensitivity reaction. Papaverine belongs to the benzylisoquinoline group and is used for disturbances of cardiac and cerebral circulation and for acute pulmonary and peripheral embolism.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes Phenprocoumon-induced hepatopathy in a patient who developed clinically significant liver injury and (sub)acute liver failure after therapeutic oral anticoagulation with Phenprocoumon. The paper cites that latency to liver injury is 6-9 months, that rechallenge (reexposure) in all cases led to faster and more severe liver damage including one death from liver failure within 4 weeks and one case requiring liver transplantation, and that histology shows predominantly liver cell (perivenous) necrosis, supporting an immunologic idiosyncratic genesis with eosinophilia. The case conclusion states the patient's icterus was the expression of drug-induced liver failure (medikamentös-induziertes Leberversagen) attributable to Phenprocoumon, with improvement after conservative treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: postoperative worsening of liver function, patient declined liver transplantation, treated conservatively with lactulose, vitamin K, diuretic; discharged after 2-month hospital stay; final Quick 65% (INR 1.41); at follow-up asymptomatic with normal transaminases, bilirubin and liver function tests; mildly inhomogeneous liver echotexture on ultrasound. Literature: latency 6-9 months (occasionally much later, mimicking post-transfusion, viral or autoimmune genesis); rechallenge produced faster and more severe injury in all cases, with one reported death from liver failure within 4 weeks and one case needing liver transplantation; frequent blood eosinophilia; immunologic/molecular pathomechanism proposed (coumarin metabolite as hapten/neoantigen presented in Kupffer cells, genetic individual predisposition); histology predominantly perivenous liver cell necrosis with variable or minimal inflammation; lymphocyte stimulation tests can support the suspicion; steroids sometimes given with improvement; cross-reactivity with warfarin reported, though complication-free warfarin continuation also documented.

raw_record.support_text: In humans, cocaine hepatotoxicity was first reported in 1967, when chronic abusers of both heroin and cocaine had high serum transaminase levels, some with jaundice. One human case report describes fulminant hepatic failure and rhabdomyolysis from regular cocaine use, with histologic features of coagulative-type perivenular and midzonal necrosis and periportal microvesicular fatty changes. Another report of four patients described similar zone-III morphological changes as those seen in mice given cocaine.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure that resulted in the need for a liver transplant. A 9-year-old boy diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and treated with pemoline developed signs and symptoms consistent with liver failure; pemoline therapy was discontinued but hepatic function continued to deteriorate, and the patient ultimately required a liver transplant. Pemoline was associated with the development of hepatotoxicity, mostly in pediatric patients, and this is reported as the second case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure resulting in liver transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (9-year-old boy)
raw_record.extra_details: Indication: attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Hepatic function continued to deteriorate after pemoline discontinuation. Reported as the second known case of pemoline-induced hepatic failure resulting in liver transplant; most reported cases occurred in pediatric patients. Mechanism of the adverse effect is unknown; hypotheses proposed include hypersensitivity reactions, dose-related phenomena, and autoimmune reactions. Authors advise against pemoline as first-line ADHD treatment and recommend liver function testing before and during therapy.

raw_record.support_text: In this case, according to the CIOMS scale, the causality relationship between simvastatin (simvastatina) and the described clinical picture is probable (8 points); after discontinuation of the drug the problem resolved within one month, as reflected in the medical literature. The distinction between autoimmune-like hepatitis and other forms of drug-induced liver injury is made on the basis of the presence of autoantibodies.
raw_record.extra_details: Causality scored as probable (8 points) on the CIOMS scale; liver injury resolved within one month after discontinuation. Described as autoimmune-like hepatitis distinguished by presence of autoantibodies. Pathogenic basis described as loss of immune tolerance initiated by a reactive drug metabolite that covalently binds a hepatocyte surface protein to form a neoantigen that activates the immune system, with injury persisting only while the drug is administered. Treatment consists of stopping the causal agent, adding corticosteroids if the damage is significant; continued administration would produce chronic progressive liver injury, and long-term surveillance for autoimmune diseases is recommended.

raw_record.support_text: A case of acute liver injury associated with therapeutic dosing of IV acetaminophen in a patient with spinal muscular atrophy type 3 is reported. Dosing was documented with no evidence of overdose. Other common etiologies such as shock liver, heart failure, biliary obstruction, and viral hepatitis were excluded, and no evidence of ischemic hepatitis was found. Causality was assessed using the CIOMS/RUCAM scale, yielding a probable relationship between liver injury and acetaminophen intake (score 7). Elevated serum acetaminophen (22 mg/L) at 38 hours after the last dose indicated prolonged clearance possibly due to impaired metabolism from hepatic injury.

raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS/RUCAM causality score 7 (probable); biopsy showed high-grade acute liver cell damage with disseminated hepatocellular necrosis compatible with acute drug-induced toxic liver cell damage with acute liver dystrophy; peak ALT >1000 U/L, INR >5, bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, serum cholinesterase 0.74 kU/L; no hepatic encephalopathy; serum acetaminophen 22 mg/L measured 38 h after last dose (levels first measured late); treated with acetylcysteine 21-hour protocol starting 11 h after last acetaminophen dose; recovered completely and discharged. Proposed mechanism in muscle-wasting patients: reduced glutathione stores and reduced volume of distribution raising acetaminophen/NAPQI levels. Table 1 lists prior reports of acute liver failure after therapeutic acetaminophen in two adult and three pediatric patients with other myopathies (limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, Duchenne, SMA type 2, congenital muscular dystrophy).

raw_record.support_text: Among the 19 cases of INH-hepatitis in HIV-infected adults receiving isoniazid preventive therapy, 9 patients had probable attributions to isoniazid and 10 had possible attributions. Seven of the 19 were receiving antiretroviral therapy when diagnosed with hepatitis, and 8 of 19 reported alcohol use meeting at least one CAGE criterion.

raw_record.extra_details: 19 total INH-hepatitis events in a cohort of 1,762 participants (rate 1.1%), with 9 of 19 rated probable and 10 of 19 possible attributions to INH; 74% occurred within the first 3 months. Severe hepatitis defined as grade 3 or higher elevations of AST, ALT, or total bilirubin. One 41-year-old female died from hepatic encephalopathy (grade 5) in Month 6 after jaundice and dark urine, reportedly without alcohol, traditional, or other medications. Attribution reflects an available causality assessment (possible/probable) in this study.

raw_record.support_text: In the Botswana clinical trial of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) in HIV-infected adults (n = 1,995), isoniazid-associated biochemical hepatitis (AST/ALT > 5× ULN, with or without symptoms) occurred in 19 participants (0.95%), clinical hepatitis (symptoms plus AST/ALT > 5× ULN) in 6 (0.30%), and one hepatitis death (50 per 100,000). These rates were compared with published INH studies and trials.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: HIV-infected adults (people living with HIV) receiving isoniazid preventive therapy in Botswana; isoniazid given as 6 months of preventive monotherapy rather than combination anti-TB therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Biochemical hepatitis (AST/ALT > 5x ULN) 19/1,995 (0.95%); clinical hepatitis (symptoms + AST/ALT > 5x ULN) 6/1,995 (0.30%); 1 hepatitis death (50 per 100,000) with 89% completion. For participants not on ART with at least 4 months of IPT (n=1,288): clinical 0.93%, biochemical 0.23%, deaths 78/100,000. Three-fourths of INH-hepatitis cases occurred in the first 3 months. Risk factors: CD4 < 200 cells/mm3 associated with increased risk (RR 2.80, 95% CI 1.14-6.84); age >35 yr RR 1.56, ART RR 1.56, NVP RR 2.09, co-trimoxazole RR 1.65, alcohol RR 1.42, CAGE>=1 RR 2.37; no evidence that efavirenz increased risk (RR 0.96). None of the INH-hepatitis cases had chronic HBV infection. Patient education about hepatitis symptoms (nausea, vomiting, yellow eyes, dark urine, fatigue, abdominal pain) and monthly monitoring were recommended.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that tolvaptan causing potential liver injury is well established in patients with ADPKD, including elevations in bilirubin levels. Supporting trial data: the TEMPO trial (961 patients) showed 1.5% discontinued the drug due to liver damage, 4.5% had a significant increase in aminotransferases, and 0.9% had an increase in bilirubin; the REPRISE trial found ~10.9% of ADPKD patients treated with tolvaptan had adverse hepatic events versus 5.3% of untreated patients, the most common being AST elevation >3x ULN with resolution after cessation. In most cases patients exhibit a hepatocellular or mixed pattern of liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings in patients with ADPKD treated with tolvaptan; FDA-approved April 2018 for ADPKD with recommendation not to prescribe to patients with preexisting moderate to severe liver disease.
raw_record.extra_details: TEMPO trial: 961 patients, 1.5% discontinued due to liver damage, 4.5% significant aminotransferase increase, 0.9% bilirubin increase. REPRISE trial: 10.9% adverse hepatic events vs 5.3% in untreated ADPKD patients; most common adverse effect is AST elevation >3x ULN with resolution upon cessation. Most cases show a hepatocellular or mixed pattern of liver injury. Standard monitoring recommendation: AST, ALT, bilirubin at 2 and 4 weeks, then monthly for 18 months, then every 3 months.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a new case of acute cholestatic hepatic injury in a 54-year-old man, probably secondary to glimepiride, a sulfonylurea antidiabetic; DILI with glimepiride is rare, with only 2 published cases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: History of chronic alcoholism (abstinent for 1 year); concurrent losartan therapy excluded as cause; on glimepiride 4 mg/day for recently diagnosed non-insulin-dependent diabetes.
raw_record.extra_details: Third reported case of glimepiride-induced acute hepatitis. Jaundice appeared 8 days after starting glimepiride (18/01/2003), earlier than the two prior cases (onset after ~3 months); the first prior case was cytolytic acute hepatitis at month 4 and the second was acute cholestatic hepatitis at 3 months. At admission: ALP 9N, GGT 66N, ALAT 12N, ASAT 7N, total bilirubin 288 µmol/L (conjugated 201 µmol/L), prothrombin 100%. Causality assessed using the international consensus meeting criteria (onset 8 days after start, >50% ALAT decrease 7 days after withdrawal, no other cause, cholestatic pattern); losartan not reintroduced. No liver biopsy; rapid recovery with normalization of liver tests within about one month; mechanism of glimepiride hepatotoxicity unknown.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a single case of fulminant hepatic failure in a 36-year-old pregnant woman that occurred at 17 weeks gestation following propylthiouracil (PTU) treatment for Graves' disease. The liver failure was managed by liver transplantation and thyroidectomy, and the pregnancy continued to term with unfavorable early childhood sequelae. The case is framed throughout as 'PTU-induced severe hepatotoxicity' and a rare complication of PTU treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnancy (fulminant hepatic failure occurred at 17 weeks gestation in the second trimester); PTU treatment for Graves' disease.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a previous 36-year-old gravida 2 woman of African descent. PTU dosed at 100 mg thrice daily started at 10 weeks gestation, led to significant improvement in thyroid function; scleral icterus developed at 17 weeks, with diagnosis of fulminant hepatitis progressing to stage IV liver failure despite plasmapheresis and intravenous steroids, requiring ICU ventilation; liver transplant at 18 weeks gestation followed by thyroidectomy two weeks later. A one in 10,000 incidence of liver failure following PTU treatment has been reported in the USA. Neonatal sequelae noted.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that propylthiouracil (PTU) induces hepatotoxicity, with a frequency ranging from 0.1% to 0.2%, occurring at any time during treatment with sudden, rapidly progressive onset. The described patient had been on PTU for eight weeks when the diagnosis was made.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Onset during pregnancy in a patient with prior liver transplantation on concurrent immunosuppressive therapy (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, prednisolone) and levothyroxine replacement.
raw_record.extra_details: PTU-induced hepatotoxicity frequency 0.1%-0.2%. Patient was treated for 8 weeks before diagnosis; onset sudden and rapidly progressive. Hepatotoxicity associated with marked elevation in aminotransferases and massive hepatic necrosis on biopsy, with jaundice as the presenting complaint; findings confirmed histopathologically. Mother's liver function tests returned to normal after delivery. PTU also causes agranulocytosis (0.37%). FDA and American Thyroid Association do not recommend routine liver-function monitoring in asymptomatic patients because of rapid onset.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old man was admitted with acute severe jaundice and itching after self-administering high doses of stanozolol (Winstrol) by intramuscular injection three times a week for three weeks. Biochemistry showed bilirubin of 19.16 mg/dL (direct 15.84 mg/dL), AST 45 U/L, ALT 58 U/L, AP 152 U/L and GGT 19 U/L; viral and autoimmune causes were excluded and an ultrasound showed no biliary dilation. A toxic hepatitis was suspected and the CIOMS scale gave 9 points, supporting this impression; with supportive treatment the patient improved, and eight weeks after stopping stanozolol tests gradually normalized and he was completely asymptomatic within three months.
