raw_record.extra_details: Case title: 'Colestasis canalicular inducida por estanozolol' (canalicular cholestasis induced by stanozolol). The paper notes stanozolol hepatotoxic effects include cholestasis and that its effect is dose-dependent though influenced by individual susceptibility and other toxic habits such as alcohol abuse. CIOMS causality score 9/9. On admission: bilirubin 19.16 mg/dL (direct 15.84 mg/dL), AST 45 U/L, ALT 58 U/L, AP 152 U/L, GGT 19 U/L; severe jaundice and itching, dark urine, no fever/abdominal pain/nausea/vomiting. Dechallenge led to gradual biochemical improvement over 8 weeks, with complete recovery to normal tests within 3 months. Liver biopsy not performed.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that since 1966 paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose has been recognised as potentially fatal and can cause centrilobular hepatic necrosis and, in severe cases, hepatic failure, and that it is now one of the commonest causes of hepatic failure in Britain. The study then prospectively assessed 54 patients admitted after paracetamol overdose with daily liver-function tests, fasting serum bile-acids, and blind-reviewed liver biopsies, finding a histological abnormality in 53 of 54 patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdose (deliberate/accidental self-poisoning); patients excluded if history of other potentially hepatotoxic drug ingestion, excess alcohol in 24h before admission, prior liver disease within 2 years, or HBAg positivity.
raw_record.extra_details: 54 patients (aged 15-50) studied; plasma-paracetamol measured at admission; liver biopsy done on day 4; 53 of 54 had histological abnormality (23 minor, 24 moderate, rest...); grades defined as Grade I (centrilobular lipofuscin, Kupffer-cell hyperplasia, up to 2 foci of hepatocytolytic necrosis), Grade II (multiple foci of necrosis, focal reticulin collapse, inflammation), Grade III (severe centrilobular necrosis, liver-cell loss, inflammation, reticulin collapse, regeneration); serum-AST >400 units/l always associated with severe histological damage; fasting serum bile-acids raised in 51 patients and a more sensitive indicator of mild liver-cell damage than transaminase; fatalities reported (liver tissue obtained just after death in 3 patients); empirically determined plasma-paracetamol levels drawn as a guide to likelihood of liver damage after overdose.

raw_record.support_text: The study concerned patients admitted after paracetamol overdose, some given cysteamine as part of a controlled trial of this treatment for paracetamol overdose. Liver histology showed 23 patients with grade I (minor) changes, 16 with grade II (moderate) abnormality, and 14 with severe grade III changes; 24 patients (44%) had no abnormally high AST in the four days after admission, yet 2 patients who reached grade-IV hepatic coma died despite charcoal haemoperfusion. These liver injury findings are attributed to paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver injury occurred in the setting of paracetamol overdose (supratherapeutic exposure).
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of paracetamol-overdose patients admitted for acute liver failure management. 14/54 patients had severe (grade III) histologic changes; 2 patients with grade-IV hepatic coma treated with charcoal column haemoperfusion both died. 24/54 (44%) showed no abnormally high AST; 2 patients had serum bilirubin above 12 µmol/l (22 and 32 µmol/l) with normal AST. Cysteamine was given to 11 patients with high initial plasma-paracetamol levels within a controlled trial of that treatment, and is a protective/management agent rather than a suspected causative agent. Supportive treatment included 5% dextrose infusion, phytomenadione, folic acid, Parentrovite, potassium, and lactulose for moderate/severe liver-function abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: A 67-yr-old teetotaler woman treated with prednisolone (25 mg t.i.d. i.v.) for primary dermatomyositis developed, 8 days after initiation of therapy, painless icteric hepatitis with progressive liver biochemistry deterioration (day 19: total bilirubin 10.80 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 8.56 mg/dl, ALT 545 IU/L, AST 1229 IU/L, ALP 467 IU/L, GGT 2902 IU/L) and fatty infiltration on ultrasound/CT. She took no other hepatotoxic drug and viral and autoimmune serologies were negative. The authors describe a patient who developed fatal acute liver failure induced by prednisolone therapy; despite tapering with falling aminotransferases, she died of pneumonia on hospital day 26.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatty liver/steatosis is described as a rarely severe side effect of long-term prednisolone therapy; here it progressed to acute severe steatohepatitis and fatal acute liver failure. raw_record.support_text: A 41-year-old man with chronic heavy alcohol use and known peptic ulcer disease increased his acetaminophen consumption from his usual 4-5 gm/day to 10 gm/day due to worsening back pain. At admission he was jaundiced with markedly elevated SGOT (6500) and SGPT (1930), elevated bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time. A serum acetaminophen level of 15 mg/dl was found, and acetaminophen hepatotoxicity was diagnosed. The severe hepatic abnormalities were judged too far advanced for specific therapy, so only supportive treatment was attempted, and his symptoms and liver function studies improved dramatically within two days.

Specific (N-acetylcysteine) therapy was withheld because injury was judged too advanced; supportive care with dextrose, thiamine, folic acid, and 4 units fresh frozen plasma led to dramatic improvement by hospital day 5.

raw_record.support_text: Sera from 39 patients who developed hepatitis following halothane anaesthesia between January 1983 and December 1985 were tested for antibodies to halothane-induced liver antigens using an ELISA; 22 had hepatitis without encephalopathy. All patients had undergone previous anaesthesia 17 days to 13 yr (median 3 yr) earlier. Twelve of the patients died. In all patients, evidence of hepatic damage had appeared within 28 days of a documented halothane anaesthetic and no other cause for the liver damage was identified (hepatitis A and B, cytomegalovirus and toxoplasma excluded serologically, no history of alcohol excess), forming a case series of halothane-associated hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: 39 patients with halothane-associated hepatitis after halothane anaesthesia; spectrum ranges from minor rises in serum aminotransferase to fulminant hepatic failure; 9 of 11 Liver Unit patients had fulminant hepatic failure overall (7 of 28 referred sera) and 12 of 39 patients died; hepatic damage appeared within 28 days of a documented halothane anaesthetic; all had prior halothane exposure 17 days to 13 yr (median 3 yr) earlier. Halothane antibodies detected in 12/16 (75%) patients with hepatic encephalopathy and 16/23 (70%) without. The study focused on diagnostic value of halothane antibodies, which are absent in other liver diseases and in patients with fulminant hepatic failure from other causes.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of fatal hepatitis associated with troglitazone in an 85-year-old man with type 2 diabetes. Troglitazone therapy had been started 5 months before presentation and increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks; abdominal pain, malaise, and jaundice developed. A diagnosis of troglitazone-induced hepatitis was made, liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis, and the patient died 8 weeks after presentation. The paper notes that troglitazone use is in rare cases associated with fatal hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Elderly (85-year-old) male patient with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin; troglitazone added for glycemic control.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose increased to 400 mg/day after 15 weeks of therapy; fatal case. Symptoms included abdominal pain, malaise, and jaundice; ALT 608 U/L initially then 287 U/L at presentation, total bilirubin 15.6 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL, normal prothrombin time, glycosylated hemoglobin 5.2%; serology negative for hepatitis A, B, and C; normal hepatic ultrasonogram. Liver biopsy showed lobular cholestatic hepatitis with areas of confluent necrosis (submassive hepatic necrosis); patient died 8 weeks after presentation despite aggressive therapy. Concomitant medications included metoprolol (50 mg) and levothyroxine (0.05 mg daily). Author note that postmarketing reports of troglitazone-related death and transplantation led to withdrawal from the British market.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of fatal hepatitis associated with troglitazone. They note that troglitazone-related hepatotoxicity is usually asymptomatic, mild, and reversible in clinical trials, but that postmarketing use is associated with six deaths and one liver transplantation leading to withdrawal of the product from the British market. The prior report context concerns troglitazone-associated hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Dosage increased to 400 mg/d after 15 weeks of therapy; onset of symptoms about 5 months after starting troglitazone. Symptoms included abdominal pain, malaise, jaundice, confusion, agitation, ascites, and edema; ALT 608 U/L initially and 287 U/L at referral (normal 10-45); total bilirubin 15.6 mg/dL (normal 0.1-1.1); albumin 2.5 g/dL; prothrombin time normal; negative serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C; normal hepatic ultrasonogram. Liver biopsy showed submassive hepatic necrosis; the patient deteriorated despite medical therapy and died 8 weeks after presentation. Authors noted that the six known deaths and one liver transplantation associated with troglitazone prompted its withdrawal from the British market.

raw_record.support_text: The coronary dilator coragil was recalled in Japan after causing more than a hundred instances of severe liver injury. Hypertensive, arteriosclerotic and heart failure patients developed liver toxicity and hepatic necrosis after several months of treatment with coragil, and also developed pronounced phospholipidosis of the liver, spleen, muscle and lymph nodes. BMP levels were increased in the phospholipidosis-affected tissues and urinary sediment of coragil-treated patients compared with healthy subjects.
raw_record.extra_details: Coronary dilator; recalled in Japan after >100 instances of severe liver injury; patients developed liver toxicity and hepatic necrosis after several months of treatment. Reported in hypertensive, arteriosclerotic and heart failure patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old woman presented 4 hours after ingesting around 90 ferrous sulfate pills (9.45 g of elemental iron, 172 mg/kg body weight) in what was later described as an adult iron overdose, typically a suicide attempt. She developed acute liver failure with a marked elevation of aminotransferases (AST 8674 IU/L, ALT 7877 IU/L), INR 9.3, and metabolic acidosis, and eventually required an orthotopic liver transplant. The paper frames iron as causing dose-dependent direct (intrinsic) toxicity with a stage described as hepatotoxicity and signs of acute liver failure, progressing to fulminant liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose is described as a significant cause of hospital admission that occasionally produces severe liver injury and acute liver failure. In a Western Australian study of 306 paracetamol overdose admissions, severe liver injury (ALT >45 IU/l, PT >18 s, and encephalopathy) occurred in 6.9%, all of whom recovered without transplant. In a UK specialist liver failure unit cohort of acute liver failure due to paracetamol poisoning, only 30% fulfilled transplant criteria, and in a prospective trial of 80 overdose patients, 25 had acute liver dysfunction (INR >1.2 with or without abnormal LFTs) after taking more than 25 tablets (12.5 g) of paracetamol. Separately, deaths attributed to paracetamol and paracetamol-containing drugs in England and Wales rose from 144 in 1977 to about 500 per year in 1993-1997, indicating fatal outcomes from paracetamol-induced liver injury in overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury arises in the setting of deliberate or accidental supratherapeutic (overdose) ingestion; US data indicate 53% of pediatric (<18 y) overdose presentations were unintentional and 3% due to dosage error, while about 30% of excess-ingestion hospitalizations were considered accidental; some patients presented more than 24 h after ingestion, with those presenting late having a higher incidence of hepatic coma and death.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe liver injury defined as ALT >45 IU/l, prothrombin time >18 s and encephalopathy, occurring in 6.9% of 306 admissions (1985-1990, Western Australia) with full recovery and no transplants. In a UK specialist liver failure unit cohort (1987-1993) of paracetamol-poisoning acute liver failure, only 30% fulfilled clinically defined transplant criteria. In a prospective trial of 80 patients (1992-1993), 25 had acute liver dysfunction (INR >1.2 with or without abnormal LFTs) after consuming >25 tablets (12.5 g); patients with poorer outcomes and listing for transplant tended to present later and to have taken a larger overdose. Deaths attributed to paracetamol: 144 in England and Wales in 1977, about 500 per year in 1993-1997; only 0.1% of all US paracetamol overdoses resulted in death; the drug is the most frequently used agent in intentional overdose in the UK.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective cohort of 279 critically ill patients with severe burn injury, a dose- and time-dependent relationship was observed between ketamine exposure and cholestatic liver injury. Ketamine restriction was associated with a reduced risk of cholestatic liver injury (adjusted OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.04–0.50; p=0.003). The revised electronic causality assessment method indicated that ketamine was probably the cause of cholestatic liver injury for 14 patients and possibly the cause for 10 patients. Ketamine exposure ≥10,000 mg with cholestatic liver injury was associated with higher 3-month mortality (adjusted OR 9.92, 95% CI 2.76–39.05).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Critically ill patients with severe burn injury receiving ketamine for analgesia/sedation; required co-exposure to other sedative drugs (which were themselves not associated with liver injury or outcome); dose exposure varied by unrestricted versus capped (ketamine-restricted) prescription periods.
raw_record.extra_details: 279 patients (median age 51 [IQR 31–67] years; 63.1% men; burned surface area 28.5% [IQR 20–45%]); 155 in ketamine-liberal group (median cumulative dose 265.0 [IQR 0–8,021] mg) and 124 in ketamine-restricted group (median 20 [IQR 0–105] mg), p<0.001. Revised electronic causality assessment method (rEICA) graded causality as probable in 14 and possible in 10 patients. Cholangitis was observed and was not present in the ketamine-restricted group. Cholestatic liver injury with ketamine exposure ≥10,000 mg associated with higher 3-month mortality (adjusted OR 9.92, 95% CI 2.76–39.05; p=0.001); ketamine restriction associated with greater probability of 3-month survival (p=0.035). Primary endpoint cholestatic liver injury, secondary endpoint 3-month mortality.

raw_record.support_text: In this ICU study of 279 severe burn patients, 34 (12%) patients developed cholestatic liver injury attributed to ketamine. A post hoc RECAM analysis of all cholestatic liver injury cases indicated ketamine was most likely the cause for 3 patients, probably the cause for 11, and possibly the cause for 10 cases. Among these patients, 19 (54%) progressed to overt cholangitis (grade ≥3 ALP elevation in 16, unexplained prolonged cholestasis in 11, biliary sepsis in 3, and one multiple liver abscess), four had progressive bile duct strictures, and one showed biliary casts and features of sclerosing cholangitis on MRCP; all but one cholangitis case were in the ketamine-liberal group. The multivariate analysis associated the ketamine-restricted period with a lower risk of cholestatic liver injury (AOR 0.11, 95% CI 0.02–0.44).

Cholestatic liver injury with total ketamine ≥10,000 mg was associated with 3-month mortality (AOR 9.92, 95% CI 2.76–39.05) in propensity-matched analysis.

Brusilow and Cooper report a case of acetaminophen overdose in a 22-yr-old woman who ingested 15 g of acetaminophen and 36 hrs later demonstrated biomarkers of toxicity (ammonia, glutamine, aspartate aminotransferase) and encephalopathy, reported as a biochemical demonstration of the osmotic gliopathy theory, a proposed final common pathway to encephalopathy in acute liver failure (ALF).

raw_record.extra_details: Ingested 15 g acetaminophen; at 36 hrs demonstrated interrelationships between serum biomarkers (ammonia, glutamine, aspartate aminotransferase) and the Glasgow Coma Score as a surrogate for depth of encephalopathy in ALF. Acetaminophen is the most widely used over-the-counter medication, most commonly recommended analgesic/antipyretic in pregnancy, used in more drug-combination products than any other drug, and the most common drug in suicide overdoses, now responsible for the majority of ALF cases in the United States (surpassing acute viral hepatitis). Increasing therapeutic doses, alcohol use, advancing age, and concomitant NSAID use increase susceptibility to acetaminophen hepatotoxicity; n-acetylcysteine is a safe and effective antidote, and neonates/young children are metabolically resistant to acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Ms. A developed hepatic failure and, 8 days after her acetaminophen overdose, underwent liver transplantation. Pathology of the excised liver showed subtotal central lobular hepatonecrosis with degenerative changes and severe cholestasis, compatible with acetaminophen overdose. The paper reports this as the lowest acetaminophen dose causing fulminant liver failure to date, and attributes her sensitivity to low body weight, malnutrition, and concurrent carbamazepine treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the lowest acetaminophen dose causing fulminant liver failure to date; hepatic failure developed and liver transplant performed 8 days after overdose. Pathology: subtotal central lobular hepatonecrosis with degenerative changes and severe cholestasis. Mechanism described: acetaminophen is metabolized via cytochrome P450 to toxic metabolites detoxified by glutathione; hepatonecrosis occurs when glutathione stores are depleted; carbamazepine and fasting induce P450, and low-protein diets lower glutathione, increasing toxicity. Creatinine/cholestasis values not provided.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 30-year-old woman with thyrotoxicosis treated with carbimazole 60 mg daily presented with one week of scleral and urine discoloration and pruritus. Investigations showed hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 208 µmol/L, conjugated 124 µmol/L) and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 224 U/L, AST 163 U/L, ALP 347 U/L). A probable diagnosis of carbimazole-induced cholestatic hepatitis was made; the drug was discontinued, other causes of hepatitis and cholestasis were excluded, and LFTs normalized within four weeks. The authors conclude that carbimazole-induced hepatitis, although rare, should be considered in jaundiced thyrotoxic patients.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose carbimazole 60 mg daily; onset of symptoms (icterus, pruritus) approximately one month after starting treatment. Admission labs: total bilirubin 208 µmol/L, conjugated 124 µmol/L, ALT 224 U/L, AST 163 U/L, ALP 347 U/L; bilirubin peaked by day 6 (445 µmol/L) before declining; LFTs normalized within 4 weeks and remained normal at 6 months. Described as carbimazole-induced hepatitis with severe cholestasis. Other causes of hepatitis and cholestasis excluded. Radioiodine or surgery considered but not arranged; substitution of carbimazole with propylthiouracil reported without increased hepatotoxicity as the liver-injury mechanism is said to differ between the two thionamides.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of sheltered homeless men, the frequency of hepatotoxic reactions (2.1%) requiring cessation of isoniazid (INH) preventive therapy was similar to that reported by Stead and coworkers in nursing home residents (hepatotoxicity 4.4%, other drug intolerance 6.0% among nearly 2,000 residents). Isoniazid was not considered to have contributed to deaths among those elderly persons. By contrast, Moulding and colleagues controversially implicated INH in 20 deaths from hepatitis in California residents over a 14-yr period.
raw_record.extra_details: Study of directly observed INH preventive therapy in sheltered homeless men. Hepatotoxic reactions caused cessation of therapy in 2.1% of all men who began therapy; the one incident occurred in a reportedly alcoholic man, representing hepatotoxic effects in 3.7% of the 27 men with reported alcoholism. The paper concludes directly observed INH preventive therapy largely removes the threat of fatal INH hepatotoxicity even in high-risk populations (alcoholic homeless men, elderly nursing home residents, methadone-treated addicts). Stead and coworkers reported 4.4% hepatotoxicity among nursing home residents. Moulding and colleagues controversially implicated INH in 20 deaths from hepatitis in California over 14 years, noting infrequent medical follow-up in fatal cases.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report what they believe to be the first definitive case of doxycycline-induced autoimmune hepatitis, occurring in the setting of chronic systemic tetracycline therapy for acne vulgaris. They note that while this rare serious adverse event is well described with minocycline, there have been no prior cases linking doxycycline to drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: A 22-year-old female with acne vulgaris had taken doxycycline 100 mg daily for 4 months before presentation with 2 weeks of jaundice, diffuse pruritus, and fatigue. ALT 1,559 IU/L, AST 938 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 101 IU/L. ANA positive >1:640, anti-smooth muscle antibody positive 1:80; soluble liver antibody 1.1U, anti-LKM negative, IgG 1210 mg/dL. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C) and CMV/EBV PCR negative. Liver biopsy compatible with chronic, Batts-Ludwig grade 3 autoimmune hepatitis without fibrosis. After doxycycline discontinuation and methylprednisolone 60 mg IV for two doses followed by an 8-week prednisone taper, AST normalized within 14 days and complete liver chemistry normalization within 20 days; chemistries normal 6 months after steroid discontinuation. Concurrent only blueberry extract and a daily probiotic; ~1.2 oz alcohol weekly. Authors note drug-induced AIH can be difficult to differentiate from idiosyncratic DILI.

raw_record.support_text: An adult female developed persistent fevers, abdominal and flank pain, malaise, and generalized muscle weakness without any cutaneous reaction after 20 days of atorvastatin therapy. Peak labs showed ALP 792 U/L, ALT 265 U/L, GGT 236 U/L, total bilirubin 21 mg/dL, eosinophils 3100 cells/µL, and leukocytes 20.2 K/µL; serologies for hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, and autoimmune markers were negative. After being initially treated as pyelonephritis without improvement, a diagnosis of atorvastatin-induced DRESS syndrome was considered probable and atorvastatin was discontinued, after which the patient's clinical status improved and her liver enzymes and eosinophils normalized over about a month.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of probable atorvastatin-induced DRESS syndrome without cutaneous findings; regarded as a hypersensitivity reaction (RegiSCAR probable). Liver involvement shown by elevated ALP 792 U/L, ALT 265 U/L, GGT 236 U/L, total bilirubin 21 mg/dL with eosinophilia and fever; no rash throughout the course. Injury resolved after drug discontinuation (dechallenge) with normalization of liver enzymes and eosinophils over about one month without further therapy; hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, ANA, RF, ANCA, mitochondrial and smooth muscle antibodies negative. Prior review reportedly found only 4 case reports of statin-associated DRESS.

raw_record.extra_details: 20 cases total (5 newly reported plus 15 published). Duration of continuous drug exposure ranged from 30 days to 3 years; most cases exceeded 6 months. Histology showed chronic active hepatitis with multilobular/massive hepatic necrosis (one patient with extensive hepatic necrosis at autopsy without identifiable chronicity features). Autoimmune features prominent: antinuclear antibodies (71%), antismooth muscle antibodies (91%), plasma-cell portal infiltrate, hyperglobulinemia (82%), hypoalbuminemia (87%). After nitrofurantoin withdrawal, clinical and biochemical improvement occurred in 18 of 20 patients; three still had chronic active hepatitis on follow-up biopsy 2 to 6 months later. Two patients had drug rechallenge; some patients received prednisone/methylprednisolone/azathioprine; two patients died. Associated lung disease and a lupus-erythematosus-like syndrome were noted in some patients.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose in children causes hepatotoxicity. A British study of 417 children aged 5 years or younger who had taken an overdose of paracetamol found only three had significantly raised plasma concentrations of liver enzymes. A subsequent American study of 322 paediatric patients found that among 140 adolescents who deliberately ingested paracetamol, 26 developed liver toxicity, while only one of 172 young children with accidental ingestion developed elevated liver enzymes only, and one of ten patients with dosing errors developed liver toxicity. The reduced hepatotoxicity in young children is attributed to their greater capacity for sulphation.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman with hypertension was started on methyldopa (Aldomet), 250 mg every 8 hours, and 41 days later developed conjunctival icterus, nausea, fatigue, and malaise, with elevated SGOT (up to 2,070 units) and bilirubin (15.0 mg/100 ml) about 53 days after starting therapy. The authors conclude 'There seems little doubt that methyldopa can cause hepatitis,' noting a nonspecific syndrome resembling viral hepatitis, with liver biopsy showing mononuclear infiltrates and focal liver cell necrosis, similar to drug-induced hepatitis, an immunologic basis, rechallenge recurrences in several reported patients, and no permanent hepatic changes or fatalities.

raw_record.support_text: Studies evaluating MTX-related hepatotoxicity in pediatric patients receiving MTX for ALL are limited. Antifolate-induced liver injury was first reported in 1955 in a series of five children who developed clinical and laboratory evidence of hepatitis while receiving aminopterin, an agent similar to MTX; autopsies on three of the patients showed hepatic fibrosis, though interpretation is complicated by lack of effective antileukemia therapy and extensive leukemic involvement of the liver. Later, several small series reported fibrosis and/or cirrhosis in variable numbers of children treated with MTX for ALL, also documenting aminotransferase elevation in the majority of patients, though the extent of elevation was not predictive of abnormal liver histology.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Five children receiving aminopterin; interpretation complicated by the lack of effective antileukemia therapy and resulting extensive leukemic involvement of the liver during treatment and at autopsy in this 1955 series.
raw_record.extra_details: Clinical and laboratory evidence of hepatitis reported in the five children; autopsies on three patients showed hepatic fibrosis. Aminopterin is an antifolate agent similar to MTX.

raw_record.support_text: Our patient presented approximately four weeks after beginning phenytoin therapy with physical signs and laboratory findings consistent with an acute inflammatory reaction and severe liver dysfunction, typical of the phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by fever, exanthems, hepatosplenomegaly, hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, lymphadenopathy, and leukocytosis with eosinophilia, and usually begins within six weeks of the onset of phenytoin therapy if there has been no prior exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome with an acute inflammatory reaction and severe liver dysfunction; syndrome usually begins within six weeks of therapy onset, has no sex or age predilection, and at increased risk in blacks, patients with prior reactions who are reexposed, and those who continue drug after unrecognized hypersensitivity. Mechanism attributed to allergic hypersensitivity (no dose linearity, induction period, recurrence on rechallenge) via direct antigen/hapten action, altered lymphocyte function, or toxic arene-oxide metabolites from reduced epoxide hydrolase detoxification; some patients have circulating IgG antibodies without proven causation. Reported morphologic types of hepatic injury include active and chronic hepatitis, granulomatous hepatitis, mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic hepatitis, submassive and massive necrosis, with fatty infiltration, monocyte/eosinophil infiltration, necrotizing vasculitis; mortality estimated at 30-40%, mostly from massive or submassive necrosis. Our patient's liver function tests peaked on days 3-5 and then decreased; rash and hepatosplenomegaly resolved after drug discontinuation with supportive prednisone tapering; intradermal phenytoin skin test weakly positive and phenytoin stimulation test negative; patient later placed on mexiletine. This is the phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome rather than the false phenytoin labeling in the entity list.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a fatal case of liver injury with both hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern attributable to apixaban in an 87-year-old woman with non-valvular atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily. Five weeks after starting, she developed fatigue, jaundice and itching; liver tests showed AST 50x UNL, ALT 36x UNL, total bilirubin 36 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase 2x UNL and GGT 8x UNL. Viral, autoimmune and obstructive causes were excluded, apixaban was discontinued, and RUCAM score was 9 (apixaban-induced DILI highly probable) while the Naranjo score was 7 (probable). The patient died after 21 days due to liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: 87-year-old female (elderly) with non-valvular atrial fibrillation; concurrent long-term bisoprolol, furosemide and ramipril continued without being implicated; alternative causes (viral, autoimmune, biliary obstruction) excluded.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 2.5 mg bid; latency 5 weeks; presenting symptoms fatigue, jaundice and itching; liver enzymes AST >50x UNL, ALT >36x UNL, total bilirubin 36 mg/dl, ALP 2x UNL, GGT 8x UNL; RUCAM score 9, Naranjo score 7; apixaban stopped on admission and low-molecular-weight heparin started; patient died after 21 days from liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that liver damage from disulfiram has been clearly accepted since the report of Keeffe and Smith, and 27 cases of acceptable disulfiram liver reaction were identified from the reported cases with clinical information. Onset of hepatitis occurred in as little as 10 days after starting treatment, with the majority manifesting within 3 months; nearly all patients had nausea, malaise, fatigue, and many had fever. The AST was prominently elevated, usually above 800 units, with less prominent elevations of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Nine deaths have been recorded in all, and at least five patients manifested hepatotoxicity on rechallenge; ten nonalcoholic patients have developed hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: 27 acceptable disulfiram liver reactions identified; onset 10 days to within 3 months; symptoms nausea, malaise, fatigue, fever (sometimes fever preceding jaundice by 3-7 days), occasional arthralgias, rash, pruritus; prominent AST elevation usually exceeding 800 units; bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase elevations less prominent; prompt improvement within about 2 weeks after withdrawal; 9 deaths recorded and no deaths when withdrawal occurred shortly after jaundice; at least 5 patients with hepatotoxicity on rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: Imatinib-induced acute liver failure is reported as a rare and serious complication of imatinib therapy; the case shares features with 13 other reported cases (three in male patients) from eight case reports, with patient ages 22-79 years and imatinib treatment durations before toxicity recognition of 8 weeks to 1 year. Coagulopathy or encephalopathy was associated with poor outcome: of five patients with coagulopathy, only one survived without liver transplantation, and that survivor's presentation was associated with an alcohol binge and paracetamol consumption. Successful liver transplantation for imatinib-induced hepatic failure in CML is described, and the paper reports the first use of dasatinib for CML after liver transplantation for imatinib-induced liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of imatinib-induced acute liver failure/fulminant hepatic failure in a CML patient who required liver transplantation within 24 hours of developing fulminant hepatic failure; the report aggregates 13 other reported cases (three male) in eight case reports. Coagulopathy or encephalopathy associated with poor outcome; of five patients with coagulopathy, only one survived without liver transplant (that survivor's presentation was associated with an alcohol binge and paracetamol consumption, but this is a separate patient, not the index case). Six cases without coagulopathy received steroids and recovered; three other non-coagulopathic cases recovered without steroids. Duration of imatinib before recognition of toxicity 8 weeks to 1 year; age range 22-79 years. Dasatinib was subsequently used for CML after liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The study describes 150 consecutive patients with paracetamol induced fulminant hepatic failure admitted between October 1986 and February 1989, assessing death as the main outcome. The paper explicitly frames paracetamol as the cause of fulminant hepatic failure in these overdose patients, with results showing 72 (48%) died and that a continued rise in prothrombin time on day 4 after overdose and a peak prothrombin time ≥180 s identify patients with a poor prognosis.

raw_record.extra_details: 150 consecutive patients admitted October 1986-February 1989 with paracetamol induced fulminant hepatic failure; 72 (48%) died. Mortality by peak prothrombin time: 34/37 (92%) for ≥180 s, 20/41 (49%) for 130-179 s, 9/25 (36%) for 90-129 s, 9/47 (19%) for <90 s. Continuing rise in prothrombin time between days 3 and 4 after overdose: 39/42 (93%) died versus 21/96 (22%) when it fell. Liver transplantation was recommended for patients with these prognostic criteria.

raw_record.support_text: In the exposure-response analysis of hepatic safety (increased ALT, AST), there was a probable relationship between increased pexidartinib exposure and the risk of hepatic events, with the relationship most apparent in the first 2 weeks of treatment. The risk of liver transaminase elevations was lower in men versus women, in non-TGCT disease versus TGCT, and in placebo crossover patients versus patients originally assigned to pexidartinib. The paper further notes an unpredictable risk of serious mixed or cholestatic hepatic injury seen in the clinical trials, which requires weekly liver test monitoring for the first 8 weeks and biweekly for the third month.
raw_record.extra_details: Population exposure-response analysis of pexidartinib clinical-trial data in adult patients with tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) with locally advanced disease; hepatic risk (ALT/AST elevations) was most apparent in the first 2 weeks; a 1000-mg initial dose during the first 2 weeks increased aminotransferase risk; model-predicted ALT>3xULN event rates ranged from 0.18 (95% CrI 0.12-0.24) at 400 mg/day to 0.22 (0.15-0.29) at 800 mg/day and 0.22 (0.15-0.30) at 1000/800 mg/day, with similar AST>3xULN rates; recommended dose 800 mg/day (400 mg b.i.d.); liver tests monitored weekly for first 8 weeks and biweekly for third month, with dose modifications (withholding, 200-mg dose reductions, discontinuation); lower transaminase-elevation risk in men vs women, non-TGCT vs TGCT, and placebo crossover vs pexidartinib-assigned patients.

raw_record.support_text: Following discontinuation of carbamazepine, the authors concluded a diagnosis of carbamazepine-induced cholestatic hepatitis. The patient, who developed fever, jaundice, dark urine, hepatomegaly, a maculopapular rash, eosinophilia (27%) and elevated bilirubin and liver enzymes about five weeks after starting carbamazepine for dysesthetic pain, recovered within three weeks of stopping the drug, with normalization of liver function tests and blood cell counts and resolution of the rash.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient treated for dysesthetic pain following spinal cord lesion; dose given as carbamazepine 100 mg three times daily, increased to 200 mg three times daily (600 mg/day). Onset of symptoms about 5 weeks after starting the drug. Findings included fever, jaundice, enlarged nontender liver 4 cm below the right costal margin, generalized nonpruritic maculopapular rash, leukocyte count 15,400 with 27% eosinophilia, total bilirubin 150 µmol/L (normal 3–24), alkaline phosphatase 413 U/L (normal 32–103), alanine transferase 166 U/L (normal 7–36), aspartate transferase 70 U/L (normal 15–33). Serology negative for hepatitis A, B, C; three blood cultures negative; ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly with decreased liver echogenicity and normal biliary tract. Initially treated for suspected biliary sepsis with parenteral antibiotics, which were stopped after 3 days; fever settled within 3 days of stopping carbamazepine. Complete recovery by third week of cessation; carbamazepine replaced by amitriptyline.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatitis developing from carbamazepine use is distinctly uncommon and can take the form of hepatocellular jaundice, cholestatic jaundice (as in the patient), or a mixture of both. Six previous cases of carbamazepine-caused hepatitis had a sensitization period of about 4 weeks before fever and jaundice, with liver biopsies showing granulomas with or without eosinophilic infiltrates; one patient rechallenged with the drug had recurrence of fever and abdominal pain that resolved on discontinuation. The index patient had been on carbamazepine for 5 weeks (total dose 18.9 g) before fever and jaundice, with skin rash and eosinophilia supporting drug hypersensitivity.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis from carbamazepine is uncommon (references 2-4). Liver injury presented as hepatocellular jaundice, cholestatic jaundice (index patient), or a mixture. Mechanism attributed to immunologic hypersensitivity supported by ~4-week sensitization period, fever, and granulomas on liver histology; index patient had skin rash and eosinophilia. Six prior literature cases; one rechallenge reproduced fever and abdominal pain that resolved on drug stoppage. One fatal hepatitis case reported (reference 6). Prognosis good if drug discontinued, with reversal of biochemical and histological abnormalities. Baseline liver function tests and blood counts recommended; about 5-10% of patients develop transient liver enzyme elevation resolving within first months; monthly LFT monitoring for the first year recommended. Index patient was treated for 5 weeks (total carbamazepine dose 18.9 g) before fever and jaundice.

Developed hepatic encephalopathy and anuria requiring hemodialysis; complete normalization of liver and renal function within 2 months. Liver biopsy showed focal necrosis, macrovesicular steatosis with mononuclear infiltrates, and diffuse canalicular cholestasis; ultrasound showed moderate steatosis without cirrhosis. HCV-RNA was positive at admission and became undetectable during recovery; histology did not show features of HCV reactivation. No CYP3A4 poor-metabolizer variants found among six genotyped SNPs; authors hypothesized possible direct mitochondrial toxicity and speculated enhanced susceptibility from HCV and small acetaminophen doses.

raw_record.support_text: Among patients admitted for inadvertent paracetamol overdose secondary to dental pain, one case (2%) of new onset acute hepatic failure required an extended inpatient stay of six days. The paper describes paracetamol overdose causing liver injury: in overdosage the hepatically conjugated paracetamol is shifted to an alternative pathway producing the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which, once glutathione is depleted to below approximately 30%, reacts with hepatic cells causing hepatic necrosis.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury occurred in the setting of unintentional paracetamol overdose (126 unintentional overdose cases; 116 analysed, 48 secondary to dental pain); one case (2%) of new onset acute hepatic failure within this dental-pain subgroup.
raw_record.extra_details: All cases had no malicious intent or deliberate self-harm. 96% of unintentional paracetamol overdose cases secondary to dental pain underwent serum paracetamol toxicity monitoring; 79% required active medical management with N-acetylcysteine (Parvolex, a treatment/protectant). Mechanism described: overdose overwhelms liver conjugation, paracetamol is metabolized by an alternative pathway to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which is inactivated by glutathione; when glutathione stores fall below ~30%, NAPQI reacts with nucleophilic hepatic cell components causing necrosis. Hepatic toxicity is increased by cytochrome P450 induction via drugs such as rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine and alcohol, and in patients with low glutathione reserves due to genetic variation, malnutrition, alcohol intake or other liver diseases.

raw_record.support_text: Among 25 patients with hematological malignancies and invasive aspergillosis receiving voriconazole, abnormal liver function tests occurred in 48% (12/25). Voriconazole-related serious adverse events (SAEs) included hepatotoxicities in 5 patients, with patterns of abnormal liver function tests being cholestatic (n=3), hepatic (n=1), or mixed (n=1). One patient (patient 7) required discontinuation of voriconazole because of severe hepatotoxicity deemed to be probably related, but finally died from hepatic failure 11 days after discontinuation.

raw_record.extra_details: Abnormal liver function tests in 48% (12/25); voriconazole-related SAEs in 8/25 including hepatotoxicity in 5. Patterns of abnormal LFTs: cholestatic (n=3), hepatic (n=1), mixed (n=1). Two patients discontinued voriconazole due to SAEs; patient 7 had severe hepatotoxicity deemed probably related and died from hepatic failure 11 days after discontinuation. Median duration of IV voriconazole therapy 8 days (IQR 7-14); loading dose 12.0 mg/kg/day, maintenance 7.7 mg/kg/day. A trough plasma concentration of >=5.83 mg/l was the only independent risk factor independently associated with an SAE (adjusted OR 7.745, 95% CI 1.064-93.570; p=0.043). raw_record.support_text: Prospective data were gathered on 662 consecutive US patients with acute liver failure (ALF) from 22 tertiary care centers over 6 years. In 275 patients (42%), ALF was determined to have resulted from acetaminophen-induced (AI) liver injury. Unintentional overdoses accounted for 48% of cases, 38% involved taking ≥2 acetaminophen-containing preparations, and 63% involved narcotic compounds. 65% of patients survived, with 8% undergoing liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury arose in overdose (both intentional/suicidal and unintentional ingestion without suicidal intent); unintentional cases often involved ≥2 acetaminophen-containing products (38%) and narcotic acetaminophen compounds (63%), mainly for chronic pain; 19 patients who took <4 g/d had ALF and about 80% used or abused alcohol.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen-induced ALF accounted for 275/662 cases (42%); annual share of ALF cases rose from 28% (1998) to 51% (2003). Intentional overdose accounted for about half of cases; unintentional overdosers took as little as 1 g/d up to 78 g/d (total dose as low as 2.5 g); 19 patients took <4 g/d (upper safety limit). Diagnostic criteria included potentially toxic ingestion >4 g/d within 7 days, any detectable serum acetaminophen level, or ALT >1,000 IU/L with history of ingestion. Outcomes: 65% survived without transplantation to 3 weeks, ~70% of both groups survived with/without transplant; 72 listed, 23 transplanted, 20 died, 29 survived without transplant. Substance abuse history positive in 28% tested (marijuana, cocaine, amphetamines); ~one third of overdosers on antidepressants. Clinical phenotype is acute liver failure with coagulopathy (INR >1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy; prognosis assessed by APACHE II, MELD, and King's College Criteria.; confidence: 0.9

raw_record.support_text: An 18-year-old Hispanic male with POLG mutations developed pulmonary tuberculosis and complex partial seizures for which he was placed on valproic acid (VPA) after failing oxcarbazepine. Within 2 months of VPA exposure he developed foot drop, pes cavus, and ophthalmoplegia, then pancreatitis that progressed to multiple organ failure including the liver; VPA was stopped but liver function impairment progressed and he died of sepsis and ARDS 27 days after muscle biopsy. A companion table lists four POLG-deficient patients (Patients 1-4) who developed hepatotoxicity 2-3 months after VPA was added, with outcomes including liver failure, liver transplantation, encephalopathy, psychomotor regression, and three deaths.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All four patients carried biallelic POLG mutations (DNA polymerase gamma deficiency), representing a genotype-restricted susceptible population. Hepatotoxicity occurred with therapeutic add-on VPA for seizure control (2-3 months latency) and was not attributable to overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Add-on VPA used as an anticonvulsant after other agents failed or alongside other antiepileptics (OXC, PHT, CBZ, LTG, TOP, CLON, PB). Latency to hepatotoxicity was ~2-3 months (2, 2.5, 3, 3 months across the four patients). Outcomes: Patient 1 liver failure with renal failure and pancreatitis, died at 18.5 years; Patient 2 liver failure leading to liver transplantation, died 2 days post-transplant, pre-transplant biopsy showing extensive necrosis, bile stasis, bile ductular proliferation, moderate lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, and bridging fibrosis; Patient 3 admitted with liver failure 3 months after starting VPA, expired within 3 weeks on hospice; Patient 4 psychomotor regression and vegetative state, survived. Patient 2 also showed complex III activity <15% of normal and COX-negative fibers on biopsy. VPA hepatotoxicity attributed to impaired mitochondrial function in the setting of POLG deficiency.

raw_record.support_text: 17 cases of amiodarone induced liver injury (AILI) confirmed by transmission electron microscopy from 1990-2020 were identified, with a mean amiodarone usage of 20.4 months and a mean dose of 300 mg. AILI histologically mimics alcoholic steatohepatitis and can be definitely diagnosed by identifying characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy.
raw_record.extra_details: 17 EM-confirmed AILI cases (1990-2020); mean usage 20.4 months at mean dose 300 mg. Histology: steatohepatitis with ballooning degeneration, periportally located Mallory hyalines, satellitosis, periportal pericellular fibrosis, sinusoidal Kupffer cell lipidosis (1 case); less frequently ductular reaction, macrovesicular steatosis, hepatocellular and canalicular cholestasis than ASH. A histologic scoring system (score <10 suggestive of AILI) correctly classified 100% of cases, with all AILI cases scoring <8. Diagnosis confirmed by characteristic lamellar lysosomal inclusions on transmission electron microscopy.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old woman with undifferentiated connective tissue disease developed cholestatic hepatitis after 4 weeks of quinacrine 100 mg/day. The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) scale was 6, indicating a probable causal relationship between the offending drug and liver damage. raw_record.support_text: The patient ingested a concentrated solution of chloroform, which caused rapid loss of consciousness and respiratory depression; her major problems were delayed hepatotoxicity without liver impairment and severe gastrointestinal effects. Chloroform is metabolized by cytochrome P450 to phosgene and free radicals, which cause mitochondrial damage and cell death in the liver; hepatotoxicity associated with chloroform is well documented and manifests clinically as delayed elevation of transaminases, with the ALT rising about 36 h after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Oral overdose of a concentrated chloroform solution; hepatotoxicity was delayed and occurred without evidence of liver impairment or acute liver failure in this single case.
raw_record.extra_details: Initial plasma chloroform concentration 0.1667 µg/mL at 74 min post-ingestion, peak 2.00 µg/mL at 4 h 20 min; 1-compartment elimination half-life 6.5 h. ALT rise delayed to ~36 h (longer than paracetamol's 12–24 h, which delayed commencement of acetylcysteine). Mechanism via CYP-mediated formation of phosgene and free radicals causing mitochondrial damage and liver cell death. Prior cases have used oral and IV acetylcysteine to prevent chloroform-induced liver injury, though evidence is limited. Chloroform also causes proximal tubular necrosis in the kidney; gastrointestinal findings (severe erosive gastritis, extensive bowel oedema/thickening, contact dermatitis) were also present. Hepatotoxicity first reported in 1923, often seen after inhalation and skin exposure.

raw_record.support_text: A patient developed hepatitis after treatment with trovafloxacin; trovalfloxacin use was discontinued while use of other medications was continued, and the patient was treated with prednisone. Hepatic and renal function returned to normal and eosinophilia resolved. The authors describe this as a biopsy-proved case of hepatic toxicity associated with the use of trovafloxacin and thank Dr. Peter B. Kelsey for permitting study of the patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Biopsy-proved hepatic toxicity: liver biopsy (H&E) showed centrilobular necrosis with a mixed cellular infiltrate of eosinophils, polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and mononuclear cells, and marked hepatic necrosis out of proportion to the extent of inflammation, a finding suggesting toxic injury. The patient was concurrently treated for Clostridium difficile infection (metronidazole) and had eosinophilia; trovafloxacin was discontinued while other medications were continued, and hepatic and renal function returned to normal.

No toxins other than VPA were present in blood or urine, and serologic and metabolic evaluations for hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, Wilson disease, and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency were negative, implicating VPA as the cause of the hepatic failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic failure developed after 9 weeks of VPA therapy, with trough plasma valproic acid concentration 52 µg/ml at 1 month. A mild aspartate aminotransferase elevation was noted after halothane anesthesia for fundoplication before hepatic failure. Other toxins were excluded and hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, Wilson disease, and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency evaluations were negative.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old male farmer developed fulminant hepatic failure after ingesting about 10–15 mL of 1,2,3-trichloropropane (TCP) on a wager. Based on blood toxicology screening, patient history, and rapid deterioration, the cause of the fulminant hepatic failure was determined to be acute intoxication of 1,2,3-trichloropropane by unintentional toxicity. The abstract states TCP has histopathological toxic effects on many organs within a short period after ingestion, with the liver as the major affected organ.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Unintentional ingestion of ~10-15 mL unknown liquid on a wager leading to acute poisoning; patient had a past history of untreated chronic hepatitis C and >10 years of alcohol consumption (pre-existing liver disease).
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure developed within about 24 hr after inadvertent oral intake. Presenting symptoms included nausea, vomiting, consciousness disturbance, petechiae on hands and limbs, and fever; laboratory tests at a local hospital showed alanine aminotransferase 57 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 88 U/L with normal coagulation and routine blood counts. Treatment with reduced glutathione, vitamin K, pantoprazole, and transfusions of plasma/platelets/red blood cells was given; the family stopped treatment ~20 hr after admission because of low chance of recovery. Abstract notes TCP-induced hepatotoxicity has rarely been reported.

raw_record.support_text: Research development of fialuridine (FIAU, 1-(2-deoxy-2-fluoro-beta-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouracil) suffered a setback with reports of unanticipated lethal toxicity in an NIH phase II study using 0.1-0.25 mg/kg/day. The trial, stopped in June 1993 after 15 patients were enrolled, saw 7 of the 15 develop severe liver toxicity, including hepatic failure with lactic acidosis, pancreatitis, myopathy, and neuropathy. Of those seven, five died and two survived after liver transplantation. Liver histology showed marked microvesicular and macrovesicular fat accumulation with minimal hepatocyte necrosis or architectural changes.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II NIH study of fialuridine (FIAU) for hepatitis B; doses 0.1 mg/kg/day and 0.25 mg/kg/day; trial stopped June 1993 after 15 patients enrolled; 7 of 15 developed severe liver toxicity including hepatic failure with lactic acidosis, pancreatitis, myopathy, and neuropathy; 5 died and 2 survived after liver transplantation; liver histology showed marked microvesicular and macrovesicular fat accumulation with minimal hepatocyte necrosis or architectural changes; possible mechanism: incorporation into mitochondrial DNA (McKenzie et al, 1995); clinical course described in McKenzie et al 1995 and Stevenson et al 1995.

raw_record.support_text: Tolcapone is a potent, blood-brain-barrier-permeable COMT inhibitor, but its clinical use is currently very restricted because of the risk of drug-induced liver injury (DILI). It was associated with three fatal cases of fulminant hepatitis and was briefly withdrawn from the market, only to be later reintroduced because of a lack of equally effective drugs.
raw_record.extra_details: Associated with three fatal cases of fulminant hepatitis; briefly withdrawn from the market and later reintroduced due to a lack of equally effective drugs; clinical use currently very restricted because of DILI risk. Mechanistically, a lipophilic p-tolyl moiety (cLogP=3.17) facilitates mitochondrial uncoupling and possible bioactivation to reactive quinone-imines, though most evidence points to mitochondrial toxicity via uncoupling as the cause of hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A 72-year-old man with a 2-year history of type 2 diabetes developed itching and jaundice after taking repaglinide (1 mg/day for 1 month, then increased to 2 mg/day) for a total of about 2 months. Laboratory tests showed elevated transaminases (AST 83 U/l, ALT 183 U/l), alkaline phosphatase (307 U/l), γ-GT (303 U/l), and total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl with direct bilirubin 9.4 mg/dl; viral serology, autoantibody screening, and MR cholangiography were negative. A liver biopsy showed expanded portal areas with bile duct proliferation, a moderate lymphocytic/eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate, and hepatocyte ballooning. After repaglinide was discontinued, laboratory findings normalized within a month. The authors report this as the first published case of cholestatic hepatitis related to repaglinide, with the drug's role strongly supported by temporal eligibility, exclusion of alternative causes, histological features, and rapid improvement after withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (diet-controlled initially) with normal prior liver function. Repaglinide dosing: 1 mg/day initially, increased to 2 mg/day one month before presentation; 2-week history of itching and jaundice before admission. No other drugs or herbal remedies, no toxic habits. Labs: AST 83 U/l (<37), ALT 183 U/l (<40), ALP 307 U/l (<136), γ-GT 303 U/l (<85), total bilirubin 12.2 mg/dl (direct 9.4 mg/dl), serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dl. Viral causes and autoantibodies ruled out; MR cholangiography normal. Biopsy: expanded portal areas, mild bile duct proliferation, moderate lymphocytic infiltrate with some eosinophils, hepatocyte ballooning. Recovery (normal labs) within a month after discontinuation. Authors note presence of eosinophils suggesting a possible immune mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports isoniazid (INH)-associated hepatitis observed in a Philadelphia tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis and treatment program. A table of annual surveillance data (1969-1973) shows 7-9 annual cases of INH-associated hepatitis among the INH-treated population (rates of 0.12%-0.22% of the total INH population), including cases arising during both treatment and prophylaxis. The paper states that with proper surveillance isoniazid-associated hepatitis is readily reversible and shows no permanent defect on follow-up, and that the relatively low incidence of isoniazid-associated hepatitis does not preclude prophylactic use when there is a significant community problem.

raw_record.extra_details: Annual Philadelphia surveillance data 1969-1973: total INH-associated hepatitis cases 7 (1969), 5 (1970), 7 (1971), 5 (1972), 9 (1973); rates of 0.15%-0.22% of the total INH population, including cases in both treatment and prophylaxis groups. The paper concludes the low incidence does not preclude prophylactic use given a significant community problem.

raw_record.support_text: Guidelines for isoniazid administration aim to identify hepatotoxicity as early as possible; at the first suggestion of hepatitis-like symptoms isoniazid should be discontinued and liver function tests performed. A reported series of 14 cases of isoniazid-associated hepatitis showed prodromal fatigue, weakness, and anorexia, and the severity of subsequent hepatitis was related to the duration of continued isoniazid consumption: patients with histologic patchy hepatitis continued isoniazid an average of 2.2 weeks, while those with multilobular or bridging necrosis continued it an average of 4.6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 cases of isoniazid-associated hepatitis (Maddry and Boitnott report); prodromal symptoms fatigue, weakness, anorexia; severity proportional to duration of continued isoniazid intake despite symptoms; histologic patchy hepatitis observed after ~2.2 weeks continued use versus multilobular or bridging necrosis after ~4.6 weeks; severity of isoniazid-induced hepatitis judged best by onset of hepatitis-like symptoms; routine LFT monitoring considered impractical.

Dexamethasone added to HAI FUDR decreases hepatic toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The commentary reports 33 published cases of severe propylthiouracil (PTU)-related liver failure in adults and 14 in children, plus 16 liver transplants in adults and seven in children due to PTU-induced liver failure reported by UNOS between 1990 and 2007. FDA AERS data detail severe liver injury in 22 adults over 20 yr, nine of whom died and five received liver transplants, and 12 pediatric patients who sustained severe liver injury resulting in three deaths and six liver transplants. The average daily dose of PTU associated with liver failure was approximately 300 mg in both children and adults, with liver failure occurring after 6 to 450 d (median 120 d) of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism/Graves' disease; also inhibits T4 to T3 conversion. Published reports: 33 severe liver failure cases in adults, 14 in children. UNOS reported 16 liver transplants in adults and seven in children (1990-2007) due to PTU-induced liver failure; one to three PTU-related liver transplants per year over 17 yr. AERS: severe liver injury in 22 adults (9 died, 5 transplanted) and 12 pediatric cases (3 deaths, 6 transplants) over 20 yr. Two reports of serious maternal liver injury during pregnancy and two reports of liver injury in fetuses whose mothers took PTU. Average daily dose associated with liver failure ~300 mg in children and adults; latency 6-450 d (median 120 d). Estimated incidence of severe hepatic damage ~0.1% in adults; projected liver-failure (transplant or death) incidence ~1:10,000, giving 1-2 deaths/transplants per year in U.S. adults. Children: ~1 in 1000 incidence of liver failure. US PTU prescriptions: 101,000 patients in 2008, >340,000 prescriptions.

raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity is reported as the most common long-term adverse effect of methotrexate therapy. Zachariae, Kragballe, and Sogaard series: >700 liver biopsy specimens in >300 psoriasis patients; cirrhosis in >1/4 of 39 patients treated >5 years; cirrhosis first detected at a mean cumulative dose of 2200 mg; repeat biopsy sometimes failed to show progression, suggesting induced cirrhosis is not always progressive. 1996 reexamination of 25 patients: one died of liver toxicity, and 5/5 autopsies showed cirrhosis. Roenigk guidelines monitor with liver biopsies, with timing based on cumulative methotrexate dose and hepatic risk factors.

Of 29 patients with a very poor prognosis considered for urgent liver transplantation, 14 were registered: six received liver transplants (four survived, one survived without transplant, seven died). Three of 15 poor-prognosis patients not selected for transplantation survived. Prognostic criteria for identifying fatal cases include arterial pH <7.30 on day 2+ after overdose, or later coexisting prothrombin time >100 s, serum creatinine >300 µmol/l, and grade III or IV encephalopathy. Clinical phenotype is fulminant hepatic failure (acute liver failure with encephalopathy).

raw_record.support_text: In paracetamol overdose, the reactive intermediate formed by microsomal oxidation conjugates with hepatic reduced glutathione; once glutathione is depleted, the intermediate covalently binds to liver cell proteins and the extent of ensuing hepatic cell necrosis is commensurate with the degree of binding. Paragraph 37 adds that among 16 patients given a toxic paracetamol overdose, six had biochemical evidence of moderate or severe hepatic damage before mercaptamine was started, two developed acute renal failure and one grade III hepatic encephalopathy, with no deaths from hepatic failure, and the mercaptamine treatment was considered in the context of the hepatotoxic effects of paracetamol.

raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: paracetamol is oxidized by cytochrome P-450 mixed function oxidase to a reactive intermediate (not independently named in text) that is normally conjugated with hepatic reduced glutathione; once 70-80% of glutathione is consumed the intermediate covalently binds liver cell proteins and the extent of hepatic cell necrosis parallels binding. In a 16-patient series of paracetamol overdose treated with mercaptamine >10 h post-ingestion, six had moderate or severe hepatic damage on admission, two developed acute renal failure, one developed grade III hepatic encephalopathy, and there were no deaths from hepatic failure; 13 of 16 later had normal liver function. Chemically defined active metabolite is treated as mechanism only, not a separate causal entity.

raw_record.extra_details: Case presented a systemic immunoallergic reaction including rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, low-grade DIC, disseminated non-caseating granulomas with eosinophilia in GI and bone marrow biopsies. Both severe hepatitis and acute liver failure have been attributed to SSZ; symptoms recur promptly on rechallenge with SSZ or sulfonamide. Proposed mechanism is idiosyncratic hypersensitivity involving interaction of N-acetylation and detoxification pathways; it remains unclear whether genetic differences in drug-metabolizing enzyme expression increase risk.

raw_record.support_text: The case report attributes cholestatic hepatitis to penicillamine. A 53-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis treated with penicillamine (escalated from 250 mg/day to 500 mg/day after a week and 750 mg/day in the third week) developed jaundice, hepatomegaly, nausea, weakness, anorexia, and dark urine; liver biopsy and transhepatic cholangiography showed cholestatic hepatitis without obstruction. Jaundice cleared within two weeks after penicillamine was discontinued, and other abnormal liver tests gradually normalized, supporting a causal relationship. The authors note that penicillamine is another agent capable of provoking cholestatic hepatitis and that a literature search revealed six prior reports of penicillamine-caused hepatic abnormalities.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: 53-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis (7 years, severe exacerbation). Penicillamine dose escalated 250 -> 500 mg/day after 1 week -> 750 mg/day in week 3; nausea, weakness, anorexia, dark urine, and jaundice followed about a week after reaching the higher dose, with simultaneous marked amelioration of rheumatoid disease. Liver edge 3 cm below right costal margin. Liver biopsy and transhepatic cholangiogram showed cholestatic hepatitis without obstruction. Labs: bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 820 IU, LDH 413 mU/mL, SGOT 390 IU/mL; normal 2 days before starting penicillamine. No eosinophilia; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; HLA A1, A26, B8, Bw37. Dechallenge: jaundice cleared within 2 weeks; other abnormal tests returned to normal; RA remained quiescent ~2 months then relapsed. Concurrent medications: prednisone 10 mg qam, aspirin 900 mg qid, ferrous sulfate (Feosol Spansules), ergocalciferol+calcium (Os-Cal), hydrochlorothiazide, propoxyphene, rarely acetaminophen with codeine. Comment notes six prior literature reports of penicillamine-caused hepatic abnormalities.

Fulminating hepatic necrosis on the 13th day with decreasing hepatic enzymes (SGOT 562, SGPT 712), increasing bilirubin/prothrombin time, then fourth-stage hepatic coma on the 28th day. Treated with hemodialysis and exchange transfusion (10 units of heparinized whole blood); consciousness improved about 24 h after exchange, with complete recovery. The authors state halothane hepatitis is a well established clinical entity and that the role of halothane as the pathogenetic agent was assumed after excluding other etiological factors; obesity and middle age are regarded as favorable factors for halothane hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Regorafenib, an oral multi-kinase inhibitor approved for unresectable GIST and previously treated metastatic colorectal cancer, caused severe drug-induced liver injury seen only in the regorafenib group in a phase 3 trial (Grothey et al.), described as potentially life-threatening, with elevated bilirubin, AST and ALT in 2% vs 1% of patients compared to placebo. In a separate phase 3 trial for advanced GIST (Demetri et al.), one death due to hepatic failure was described. Regorafenib carries an FDA black box warning for hepatotoxicity, with recommended dose reduction from 160 mg to 120 mg for grade 3 AST/ALT elevations and defined discontinuation criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Approved for unresectable GIST progressed on imatinib/sunitinib and for metastatic colorectal cancer previously treated with fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, anti-VEGF and (if KRAS wild-type) anti-EGFR therapy. Inhibits VEGFR 2 and 3, Ret, Kit, PDGFR and Raf kinases. In Grothey et al. phase 3 mCRC trial, elevated bilirubin, AST and ALT in 2% vs 1% vs placebo; severe DILI seen only in regorafenib group and can be life-threatening. In Demetri et al. phase 3 GIST trial, one death due to hepatic failure. FDA black box warning for hepatotoxicity. Dose reduced from 160 to 120 mg for grade 3 AST/ALT; discontinue if AST/ALT >20x ULN, AST/ALT >3x ULN with bilirubin >2x ULN, recurrence of AST/ALT >5x ULN with bilirubin >2x ULN, recurrence of AST/ALT >5x ULN at 120 mg, or grade 4 adverse reaction.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report their own autopsy case of severe steatohepatitis related to chronic valproic acid (VPA) administration. The patient, a 22-year-old man with an approximately 14-year medical history of VPA therapy under a diagnosis of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, died of fatal aspiration pneumonia. Autopsy revealed a markedly fatty liver (955 g), incomplete septal cirrhosis, and steatohepatitis. Because the patient was nonobese, a nondrinker, and negative for hepatitis viruses, it was concluded that VPA was the most likely cause of steatohepatitis in this case; the liver disorder had been subclinical, with serum aminotransferases almost normal until just before death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic therapeutic VPA administration over approximately 14 years for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome; autopsy-detected injury that was subclinical during life; nonobese nondrinker with no viral hepatitis; incomplete septal cirrhosis accompanying steatohepatitis; death was due to aspiration pneumonia rather than liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Steatohepatitis attributed to chronic VPA use; associated with a peculiar nodular cut surface and severe fatty liver weighing 955 g; liver disorder subclinical with serum aminotransferases almost normal until death; the case supports that VPA can induce even liver fibrosis via undetectable persistent inflammation and steatosis. The authors also note reports warning of VPA hepatotoxicity including microvesicular steatosis, steatohepatitis, hepatocellular carcinomas, and fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Analysis of Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) data (as of August 25, 2009) covering pediatric patients (<18 years) transplanted between October 1987 and June 2008 found 98 children underwent liver transplantation (LT) for drug-induced acute liver failure (DIALF), of whom 17 were transplanted specifically for valproic acid (VPA)-induced acute liver failure (VPA-ALF). Among the 42 children younger than 8 years transplanted for DIALF, 15 (36%) underwent LT for VPA-ALF and 27 (64%) for nonVPA-DIALF, establishing valproic acid as a human cause of acute liver failure requiring transplantation in children.

raw_record.extra_details: OPTN STAR dataset analysis; 17 of 98 pediatric LT recipients for DIALF were VPA-ALF, 15 of whom were under 8 years. Median ALT was markedly lower in VPA-ALF versus nonVPA-DIALF (45, IQR 36 versus 1179, IQR 2243 IU/L, P=0.004). VPA-ALF transplant recipients had significantly worse survival than nonVPA-DIALF (P<0.0001); 1-year survival probabilities 20% vs 69%; median survival after LT 2.8 months; no long-term survivors; 14 of 17 died within the first year after LT. Phenotype is acute liver failure (ALF) requiring liver transplantation.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (poisoning) setting; cohort of patients with established acute liver injury admitted to a tertiary liver transplant unit, treated with N-acetylcysteine and coded for eligibility for liver transplantation per King's College Criteria.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-center retrospective cohort of APAP overdose patients with APAP-ALI (acute liver injury). Primary endpoint was death or liver transplantation (LT). Day 1 plasma KIM-1 was a significant independent predictor of outcome in multivariable logistic regression (P=0.039) and outperformed serum creatinine (AUC-ROC, sensitivity 0.56 vs 0.08 at 0.95 specificity) and other markers (ALT, PT, bilirubin, encephalopathy grade, SOFA). Authors note APAP exposure did not elevate plasma KIM-1 above healthy-volunteer values in patients not developing organ injury. Findings described as hypothesis generating.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose (AOD) has emerged as the leading cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in the United States. The authors describe a pilot program of subtotal hepatectomy and auxiliary orthotopic liver transplantation for 13 patients with AOD ALF fulfilling King's College criteria for super-urgent transplantation, compared with 13 AOD ALF patients receiving standard orthotopic liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen overdose described as the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States. From December 1994 to April 2005 the transplant unit admitted 427 acetaminophen overdose patients, of whom 47 were transplanted. Between January 1998 and April 2005, 26 AOD ALF patients were transplanted: 13 received subtotal hepatectomy plus auxiliary orthotopic liver transplant and 13 received standard orthotopic transplant. The 13 ALT patients had median survival 68 months, with 9 of 13 alive (69%) versus 7 of 13 OLT (54%); 8 surviving ALT patients are off immunosuppression with normal liver function. Patients fulfilled King's College criteria for super-urgent transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: The present case report presents a case of hepatotoxicity associated with mirtazapine consumption with a cholestatic pattern of liver damage that resolved upon drug discontinuation. Per the Spanish Pharmacovigilance causality algorithm (modified from Karch-Lasagna), the adverse reaction was defined as 'probable' because there was a clear temporal sequence, the reaction is previously published, no alternative cause explains it, and the hepatic profile abnormality improved after drug withdrawal; the drug was not re-challenged. The authors note that an interaction between mirtazapine and duloxetine cannot be excluded because the patient was also taking duloxetine.

raw_record.support_text: Elevation in ALT and AST levels can occur during treatment with idelalisib, and hepatotoxicity was one of the most common reasons for discontinuation of the drug in clinical trials. It typically manifests 4–12 weeks after treatment initiation in asymptomatic patients, is reversible in most cases after dose interruption, and grade 3–4 ALT/AST elevation (>5x ULN) was reported in 14% of patients, leading to death in one case. In the phase I trial 28% of patients experienced liver enzyme elevation of any grade, and in the phase III study transaminase elevations were more common in the idelalisib plus rituximab arm, with grade ≥3 elevations in 5–8% and any-grade increases in 25–35%.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was a common reason for idelalisib discontinuation in clinical trials. ALT/AST elevation typically manifests 4–12 weeks after treatment initiation in asymptomatic patients and is reversible after dose interruption; about 75% of patients do not experience recurrence upon resumption at a lower dose. Grade 3–4 ALT/AST elevation (>5x ULN) reported in 14% of patients, with one associated death. Phase I trial: 28% any-grade liver enzyme elevation, one grade 3. Phase III (idelalisib plus rituximab): grade ≥3 elevations in 5–8% and any-grade increase in 25–35%; drug withheld and successfully reinitiated in two thirds of patients. Prescribing information recommends against concomitant hepatotoxic drugs and close ALT/AST monitoring (3–5x ULN maintain with monitoring; 5–20x ULN interrupt until resolution; >20x ULN permanently discontinue). In frontline trials grade ≥3 elevations occurred in 67% (O'Brien) and 57% (Lampson); liver biopsies in the Lampson study showed increased activated cytotoxic T cells within the liver parenchyma.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the first biopsy-proven case of efavirenz-induced hepatitis. Hepatitis and hepatic laboratory abnormalities resolved after the entire antiretroviral regimen was stopped, and although dechallenge was not with efavirenz alone, the authors state that the causal role of efavirenz is obvious because zidovudine and lamivudine had been taken for 2 years without problems and efavirenz was the only new drug. They concluded that HCV infection played a limited role because HCV RNA remained negative throughout the course of hepatitis and no HCV-related abnormalities were found on liver biopsy.

Symptoms: nausea, right upper quadrant pain, rash, fever (38°C). Laboratory: ALT 718 IU/l (normal <38), AST 336 IU/l, GGT 1180 IU/l rising to 1611, ALP 684 IU/l rising to 928, eosinophilia (460 to 1110/mm3), bilirubin 18 µmol/l (no jaundice). Biopsy showed dense portal infiltrate of histiocytes, lymphocytes and eosinophilic polymorphonuclears with some apoptotic bodies; no interlobular bile duct damage and no microvesicular steatosis. Liver tests and eosinophilia returned to normal within 1 month after stopping antiretroviral treatment. Autoantibodies (antimitochondrial, anti-smooth muscle, anti-endoplasmic reticulum, anti-LKM, anti-nuclear) negative; HCV RNA negative throughout. No rechallenge attempted because of possible immuno-allergic mechanism. Efavirenz is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (1,4-dihydro-2H-3,1-benzoxazin-2-one), extensively metabolized by P450 cytochromes to 8-hydroxylated metabolites then conjugated as glucuronides.

raw_record.support_text: A 45-year-old female with severe hyperthyroidism was treated with Carbimazole 30 mg/day. Within six weeks of starting therapy, she developed potentially life-threatening acute cholestatic hepatitis and agranulocytosis as adverse effects to carbimazole; her symptoms and laboratory abnormalities resolved after the offending drug was withdrawn. The report describes carbimazole-induced acute cholestatic hepatitis together with agranulocytosis as an extremely rare idiosyncratic side effect of carbimazole treatment that is considered dose- and age-related.

Authors describe the cholestatic hepatitis plus agranulocytosis combination as extremely rare, idiosyncratic, and dose- and age-related.

raw_record.support_text: The paper notes that TAK-875 (fasiglifam), an example of a GPR40/FFA1 agonist, had its development terminated during phase III of clinical trials due to hepatotoxicity, underscoring that the safety profile should be examined early in structure optimization. In paragraph 70, the authors discuss proposed mechanisms of TAK-875 hepatotoxicity after multiple administrations in humans, including its long half-life and accumulation in the liver at high doses, and note the half-life is longer in patients with type 2 diabetes compared with healthy volunteers (51.6 hours vs. 36.6 hours for a 50-mg dose).
raw_record.extra_details: TAK-875 (fasiglifam), a GPR40/FFA1 agonist, had its development terminated during phase III clinical trials due to hepatotoxicity. Proposed mechanism of hepatotoxicity after multiple administrations in humans includes a long half-life and accumulation in the liver at high doses (Wolenski et al., 2017). Half-life was longer in type 2 diabetes patients than in healthy volunteers (51.6 h vs. 36.6 h for a 50-mg dose) (Leifke et al., 2012; Naik et al., 2012). Plasma-protein binding is high (99.8% in rats) (Otieno et al., 2018). Preclinical data showed TAK-875 reduced viability of rat and mouse insulinoma cells at higher concentrations, suggesting a narrow safety window.
