raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old woman with EGFR exon 19 deletion non-small-cell lung cancer received oral gefitinib 250 mg once daily. After 13 weeks transaminases rose (AST 84 U/L, ALT 181 U/L), and at 36-37 weeks they reached a pronounced peak (AST 599 U/L, ALT 1,011 U/L) despite ursodeoxycholic acid and ammonium glycyrrhizate. Gefitinib was discontinued, and a drug lymphocyte stimulation test was strongly positive, suggesting the hepatitis was attributable to drug allergy rather than dose-dependent toxicity; the authors concluded gefitinib should not be given again at any schedule. Liver function normalized within 7 weeks of withdrawal.

This is reported as the first documented case of chloroform ingestion with both diagnostic radiopacity and hepatotoxicity. Hepatotoxicity occurred on post-ingestion day 3, and liver enzyme elevation reached peak levels on post-ingestion day 5; the patient was treated with haemoperfusion, activated charcoal, laxatives, and N-acetylcysteine, improved from hepatic dysfunction, and was discharged on post-ingestion day 11.

raw_record.support_text: The overall incidence of hepatic cytolysis on antiretroviral therapy is low (4.5–6.3%), but the risk is particularly marked during the first 12 weeks of treatment with nevirapine (NVP), especially with pre-existing hepatopathy and hepatitis B or C coinfection (15.6% under NVP, 8% under efavirenz). In the 2NN study, grade 3–4 cytolysis (AST >5N) was reported in 8.3% of patients on NVP (13.6% on once-daily NVP), with one fatal fulminant hepatitis case in 587 NVP-treated patients. In another study, grade 3–4 hepatotoxicity under NVP had an incidence of 17%, with female sex (RR=3.9) and BMI <18.5 (RR=4.7) as risk factors; of 385 NVP-treated patients, 2 died of fulminant hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: During the observation period up to 2004, 55 patients underwent liver transplantation (LT) for fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) secondary to paracetamol overdose (POD), with a median age of 32 years (range, 12-57). These POD patients were compared with matched cohorts who underwent LT for non-POD FHF or for chronic liver disease in the same period.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate overdose of paracetamol causing fulminant hepatic failure; outcomes assessed in patients who underwent liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol overdose (POD) was the attributed cause of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) in this cohort. 55 patients underwent LT for FHF secondary to POD (median age 32, range 12-57; 17 male; median follow-up 53 months for those surviving ≥30 days). 30-day mortality was 14/55 (25%), significantly greater than for non-POD FHF (3/57, 5%) and chronic liver disease (1/56, 2%) (P<0.0001); for those surviving 30 days there was no significant between-group difference in later survival (P=0.1). Pre-LT renal support was required in 30 POD patients vs 5 non-POD FHF patients (P<0.0001); POD patients had greater grade of encephalopathy (P=0.041). Overdose context: 30 of 42 identified recent stressors (relationship difficulties 22, financial 5, bereavement 3); all but 2 admitted deliberate overdose. Post-LT, adherence with outpatient appointments and immunosuppression was worse in POD patients; 1 POD patient with bipolar disorder committed suicide within 2 months of LT and 1 POD patient with bulimia and alcohol misuse died 5 years post-LT from alcoholic liver disease.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old woman developed a severe toxic hepatitis 8 weeks after starting escitalopram 10 mg/day for depression, with jaundice, pruritus, elevated bilirubin and transaminases, and 2 spontaneous reactivation flares despite drug withdrawal; liver biopsy showed perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis and eosinophilic necrosis. The biochemical pattern was initially cytolytic and later mixed. The patient improved and normalized fully by week 20.
raw_record.extra_details: Escitalopram is the pure S enantiomer of citalopram, ~300x more selective for serotonin reuptake than noradrenaline, in the SSRI class. Dose 10 mg/day; symptoms began ~8 weeks after start. Labs: total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dl rising to 10.8 mg/dl and 6.3 mg/dl at flares; initial ALT 2,400 U/dl, AST 1,065 U/dl, GGT 224 U/dl, ALP 116 U/dl; later mixed pattern ALT 1,624-2,714 U/dl, GGT 703-1,145 U/dl. Biopsy: perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis, eosinophilic necrosis, moderate periportal round-cell/eosinophil infiltrate with lobular sparing, no bile duct lesion or cholestasis. CIOMS causality score 7 = 'probable'. Negative viral and autoimmune serology; no prior liver disease, alcohol, or herbal use. Dechallenge with subjective improvement but 2 icteric reactivation flares; full normalization at week 20. Reported as the first described case of escitalopram-induced toxic hepatitis, supporting that even severe hepatotoxicity can occur during escitalopram treatment. Underlying case: female, 49 years old.

raw_record.support_text: In a prospective randomized trial of hepatic arterial (I.A.) versus intravenous (I.V.) FUDR (floxuridine) for colorectal liver metastases, I.A. FUDR was associated with major hepatobiliary toxicity, described as chemical injury to normal hepatocytes and ductal structures. Chemical hepatitis occurred in 79% (19/24) of I.A. patients versus 7% (2/29) on I.V. therapy, and biliary sclerosis occurred in 21% (5/24) of I.A. patients. The biliary sclerosis led to a treatment-related death from liver failure, and the authors attribute the complication specifically to FUDR, noting no other reports of this complication with other drugs delivered through the hepatic artery.

raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma started osimertinib 80 mg once daily. One month later she developed grade 2 hepatotoxicity (AST 106 U/L, ALT 63 U/L); after discontinuation her liver function improved to near normal within 10 days. Rechallenge at a reduced dose (40 mg) produced grade 2 deterioration within a week and, after a second discontinuation, worsened to grade 4 (AST 1302 U/L, ALT 551 U/L). The hepatotoxicity was considered osimertinib related because she had no history of liver disease, viral hepatitis, or habitual alcohol intake, and her liver metastases were improving on osimertinib. Osimertinib was later successfully readministered using a desensitization method.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 66-year-old woman with EGFR L858R/T790M metastatic lung adenocarcinoma treated for pleural-effusion and liver progression after erlotinib. Osimertinib started at 80 mg once daily; grade 2 hepatotoxicity (AST 106 U/L, ALT 63 U/L) after 1 month; improved to near normal in 10 days after discontinuation. Rechallenge at reduced 40 mg dose caused grade 2 deterioration within 1 week; after second discontinuation enzymes worsened to grade 4 (AST 1302 U/L, ALT 551 U/L). No viral hepatitis, liver disease, or alcohol intake; liver metastases were improving, supporting causality. Osimertinib withheld 5 weeks until enzymes normalized, then successfully restarted via a desensitization method; at 5 months after rechallenge brain metastases, pulmonary tumor, and pleural effusion had decreased.

raw_record.support_text: A seven-year King's College London study examined 560 patients admitted for severe acetaminophen (paracetamol)-induced hepatotoxicity, mostly after deliberate suicidal overdose. Acute admissions rose from 58 in 1987 to 123 in 1993 while overall survival improved from <50% to 78%. The threshold dose for relevant hepatotoxicity is placed near 8-12 g, but 45 patients (8%) had taken <12 g (down to 5 g), attributed to wide individual susceptibility.

raw_record.support_text: Sudoxicam, an enolcarboxamide COX inhibitor carrying a 2-aminothiazole group, manifested a pronounced difference in toxicological profile during clinical trials, and it was withdrawn from clinical development as a consequence of the observed hepatotoxicity. Its major metabolic route is CYP-mediated thiazole ring cleavage (bioactivation) via epoxide formation and hydrolysis, yielding an acylthiourea prone to S-oxidation to electrophilic sulfenic and sulfinic acid derivatives.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from clinical development during clinical trials due to observed hepatotoxicity. Mechanistic discussion attributes injury to CYP-mediated thiazole ring cleavage (epoxidation and hydrolysis) yielding an acylthiourea that undergoes further S-oxidation to electrophilic sulfenic and sulfinic acid derivatives. Contrasted with the close structural analog meloxicam, which differs only by a methyl group at the C5-position of the 2-carboxamidothiazole motif.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of 1376 paracetamol overdose admissions from the toxicology service database (1987-2013), 63 patients (4.6%) developed hepatotoxicity with a peak ALT>1000 U/L. The median paracetamol dose ingested was 12 g (IQR 7.5-20 g), and 564/1376 (41%) received acetylcysteine to prevent or treat hepatotoxicity; there were no deaths.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; all presentations with co-ingestants including alcohol excluded; acetylcysteine administered to prevent/treat toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: 1376 admissions (929 paracetamol alone, 346 paracetamol-codeine, 101 paracetamol-codeine-doxylamine); median age 23 years, 73% female; hepatotoxicity defined as peak ALT>1000 U/L; peak ALT>1000 in 63/1376 (4.6%); median LOS 16 h; no deaths; more patients with paracetamol alone developed hepatotoxicity but not statistically significant (p=0.32).

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen overdose caused human liver injury in several reported cases. A 15-year-old female admitted 55 h after ingesting an unknown quantity of acetaminophen (plasma acetaminophen 41 µg/mL) developed transaminitis (ALT 790 U/L, AST 1075 U/L), elevated bilirubin (56 µmol/L) and prothrombin time (65 s), with autopsy liver histology revealing significant hepatocyte necrosis. Additional overdose cases in the same report describe hepatic damage without encephalopathy (29-year-old woman, acetaminophen 115 µg/mL, AST >14,000 U/L, ALT >8,000 U/L), hepatic failure in a pregnant 19-year-old after ingesting 30–50 tablets (AST 24–1350 IU/L), and peak AST 3795 U/L / ALT 6080 U/L in a 29-year-old man after a 50 g overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acetaminophen overdose. Includes one case in a pregnant 19-year-old woman. In the Wakeel case the immediate cause of death was cardiac failure (with hepatocyte necrosis on autopsy), not liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Overdose cases (not including the Contractor case, in which liver and renal function tests were normal): 15-yo female, dose unknown, plasma APAP 41 µg/mL, ALT 790 U/L, AST 1075 U/L, bilirubin 56 µmol/L, prothrombin time 65 s, hepatocyte necrosis, died of cardiac failure; 29-yo woman, APAP 115 µg/mL, AST >14,000 U/L, ALT >8,000 U/L, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, hepatic damage without encephalopathy; 19-yo pregnant woman, ~30–50 tablets, APAP 184 µg/mL at 10 h, AST 24–1350 IU/L, bilirubin 0.1–1.6 mg/100 ml, hepatic failure (potassium not reported; inappropriate fluid management noted); 29-yo man, 50 g overdose, APAP 31.7 µg/mL at ~23 h, peak AST 3795 U/L and ALT 6080 U/L on day 3.

raw_record.support_text: Multiple case reports in this paper attribute acute hepatotoxicity to acetaminophen overdose. A 15-year-old female died 40 h after an acetaminophen overdose, having taken 36 tablets of Lobak (each tablet containing 450 mg paracetamol and 100 mg chlormezanone); autopsy revealed centrilobular liver necrosis and fatty degeneration of the hepatocytes. In additional cases, a 40-year-old woman ingesting 30 g acetaminophen became jaundiced and comatose 5 days later and died; a 41-year-old patient taking acetaminophen 12.5 g (plus phentermine and barbiturate) developed hepatic encephalopathy with biopsy-confirmed centrilobular necrosis that resolved after 6 months; and a 26-year-old woman after an acetaminophen overdose (60–80 tablets) developed hepatic encephalopathy on hospital day 4, then jaundice and coma, and died on hospital day 8.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting (36 tablets of Lobak with chlormezanone in one case; 30 g ingestion; 12.5 g plus phentermine and a small quantity of barbiturate; 60–80 tablets). Reported cases include a 15-year-old female, a 40-year-old woman, a 41-year-old patient, and a 26-year-old woman.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: death 40 h after overdose; autopsy showed centrilobular liver necrosis, hepatocyte fatty degeneration, renal tubule fatty degeneration, hyperemic zones, myocardial necrosis and fatty degeneration. Case 3 resolved spontaneously with centrilobular necrosis seen on liver biopsy resolving after 6 months. Case 4: AST 2320, alkaline phosphatase (KA units) 8, hepatic encephalopathy on hospital day 4, jaundice and coma on day 5, death on day 8; autopsy showed sub-endocardial hemorrhage, diffuse myocardial fibrosis, and focal left ventricular necrosis. Non-hepatic manifestations (sinus tachycardia, hypotension, ECG ST changes) reported in several cases.

raw_record.support_text: The paper summarizes a series of acute liver failure (ALF) cases caused by acetaminophen, distinguishing intentional and unintentional overdosers. Doses ranged from ~1 g/d to 78 g/d, with a minimal total ingestion of 2.5 g; in patients taking <4 g/d acetaminophen, about 80% used or abused alcohol. Overall 65% of ALF patients survived without transplantation up to 3 weeks, just over 70% of intentional and unintentional acetaminophen-induced ALF (AI-ALF) patients survived with or without transplantation; 72 patients were listed, 23 transplanted, 20 died, and 29 survived without an organ.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes hypersensitivity hepatitis attributed to minocycline, described since 1989. It typically occurs in a febrile general setting, sometimes with exfoliative maculopapular rash and adenopathies; biologically there is leukocytosis with often eosinophilia, markedly elevated transaminases, a more inconstant cholestasis, and sometimes signs of hepatocellular insufficiency. Evolution is usually favorable after stopping minocycline with regression of hepatic biological abnormalities over about one month (spontaneously or with corticosteroids); however there are reported cases of severe hepatitis with fulminant necrosis requiring transplantation, and at least one fatal case.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hypersensitivity-mediated hepatitis; usually favorable course upon minocycline discontinuation, with fatal cases and cases requiring transplantation reported from the literature.
raw_record.extra_details: Hypersensitivity hepatitis described since 1989 (refs 32-35); occurs in febrile general setting with possible exfoliative maculopapular rash and adenopathies; leukocytosis with often eosinophilia; transaminases clearly elevated with more inconstant cholestasis; possible signs of hepatocellular insufficiency; transaminase abnormalities regress over about one month after drug withdrawal, spontaneously or with corticosteroids; severe forms with fulminant necrosis requiring transplantation (ref 36) and at least one fatal case (ref 33).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of a maternal paracetamol overdose in pregnancy, discusses the mechanism of toxicity of paracetamol, and notes that few cases of hepatotoxicity from paracetamol overdose have been reported in the very young. It discusses 'paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity' and resistance to it in neonates, and states that the peak excretion of toxic conjugates seen in the case is a pattern that occurs in adults only when paracetamol poisoning has resulted in severe liver damage. The production of cysteine and mercapturic acid conjugates is described as of major toxicological significance, derived from the glutathione conjugate of the hepatotoxic metabolite of paracetamol.

raw_record.extra_details: Present case: maternal plasma paracetamol level 280 mg/l at 3-4 h after overdose with plasma half-life 4.5 h (treatment level by Prescott criteria), while h.p.l.c. free paracetamol was 205 mg/l with half-life 2.5 h (level at which N-acetylcysteine would not be needed). Exchange transfusion had no significant effect on plasma paracetamol half-life and is not effective. Cysteine and mercapturic acid conjugates reflect the hepatotoxic glutathione-derived metabolite; their peak excretion was delayed 20-30 h, a pattern seen in adults only with severe liver damage. N-acetylcysteine treatment considered for children with paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose (POD) is described as a major cause of acute liver failure (ALF) requiring liver transplantation in the United Kingdom. Of 127 liver transplants performed for ALF in the Scottish Liver Transplant Unit over 1992–2006, 44 were for POD; post-transplant mortality during the index admission was 30% (13 patients) with five further deaths during follow-up, and actuarial 5-year patient survival was 54.5%.

raw_record.extra_details: The paper states paracetamol is one of the most widely used analgesics with a lack of adverse effects at therapeutic doses, but overdosage can lead to acute liver failure requiring liver transplantation. 44 liver transplants for POD over 14 years (out of 608 POD patients managed; 436 did not meet King's College criteria; 172 assessed; 68 suitable; 44 transplanted). Post-transplant index-admission mortality 30% (13 patients) plus 5 late deaths; 5-year patient survival 54.5%, graft survival 49.5%; 23% re-transplanted (primary nonfunction 1, hepatic artery thrombosis 3, chronic rejection 2). Median age 30 (18–51); median follow-up 7 years; 19 (43.2%) had prior overdose/psychiatric illness.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report three epileptic children (aged 2 years 8 months to 5 years 1 month) who developed hepatotoxicity induced by valproic acid, with onset of hepatic complications within 6 months of valproate therapy in two patients and 12 months in one. All patients were receiving polytherapy (carbamazepine in two and phenobarbital in one). All developed clinical signs of hepatotoxicity with mild transaminase elevation (maximum SGOT 194 IU) and bilirubin 5.5-19.8 mg%. Two recovered with normalization of laboratory abnormalities and one had a fatal course. The authors frame hepatic insufficiency as a possible severe, potentially fatal and reversible side effect of valproic acid.

raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatic failure/insufficiency associated with valproic acid. Onset of hepatic complications within 6 months in two patients and 12 months in one. Initial signs: vomiting, edema, jaundice; fever in two patients. Laboratory findings: transaminases mildly elevated (<194 U/l), bilirubin 5.5-19.8 mg% (one case 19.8 mg% total with direct 9.08 mg%), thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenemia in the fatal case. Two patients recovered after drug withdrawal; one fatal case (died 30 days after onset). Authors note the condition can be reversible with drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that valproic acid (AVP), a widely used antiepileptic, can cause liver insufficiency as its most serious side effect, ranging from isolated elevation of hepatic enzymes to death, with an incidence of fatal hepatic insufficiency of 1:49,000 among AVP users. It describes both reversible, dose-related hepatic dysfunction (normalizing upon dose reduction or drug withdrawal) and a non-dose-related form that causes irreversible, sometimes fatal liver injury. The highest-risk group is children under 2 years of age with mental deficiency using the drug in polytherapy for less than 6 months, in whom the incidence of fatal cases is 1:800.

raw_record.extra_details: Therapeutic doses 37-45 mg/kg/day. Case 2 (2y8m, male, West syndrome) on valproic acid 37 mg/kg/d for 6 months plus carbamazepine 20 mg/kg/d for 1 month developed jaundice, pallor, vomiting, fever, choluria, acholic stools, ankle edema and hepatosplenomegaly; liver biopsy showed bridging hepatic necrosis and cholestasis compatible with drug intoxication; viral hepatitis markers negative; recovered 4 days after drug withdrawal. Case 3 (5y1m, male) on valproic acid 45 mg/kg/d plus carbamazepine 25 mg/kg/d for 12 months developed respiratory insufficiency, chest pain, vomiting, fever, choluria, jaundice; recovered 8 days after withdrawal of antiepileptic drugs (retrospectively considered probably dose-dependent). Case 1 (fatal) was considered an idiosyncratic, non-dose-dependent reaction; patients 2 and 3 on relatively low polytherapy doses regressed after drug discontinuation (probably dose-dependent). Fatal hepatic insufficiency incidence 1:49,000 overall and 1:800 in the high-risk group.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes halothane hepatic necrosis as a human liver-injury entity with age-related morbidity and mortality similar to viral hepatitis. In the authors' small series of five patients with halothane hepatic necrosis, there was one death, in an adolescent female. Related text notes that unexplained postoperative fever is one of the most constant features indicating liver damage from halothane, and that jaundice is typically delayed unless there have been multiple exposures to halothane anesthesia.

raw_record.support_text: A 30-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma was treated with fotemustine (176 mg (100 mg/m²) i.v. infusion weekly for 3 weeks) and developed serious hepatotoxicity after the third dose, with marked elevation of liver transaminase levels and jaundice. Viral, metabolic and immune-mediated causes of acute liver injury were excluded and liver imaging showed no metastases or vascular occlusion. Hepatotoxicity was attributed to fotemustine and further treatment was suspended; liver enzyme and bilirubin levels normalized over the following 3 months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult melanoma patient with brain and visceral metastases; injury resolved and chemotherapy was resumed under antioxidant cover.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose was 176 mg (100 mg/m²) by i.v. infusion weekly for 3 weeks; hepatotoxicity (marked transaminase elevation with jaundice) appeared after the third dose; viral, metabolic and immune-mediated causes were excluded; enzyme and bilirubin normalized over about 3 months. On rechallenge 3 months later at 176 mg every 3 weeks under an N-acetylcysteine-based antioxidant regimen, three cycles were completed without liver enzyme disturbance; in a subsequent course when the N-acetylcysteine infusion was interrupted (blocked central line) the patient had a lesser increase in transaminases that normalized over 28 days, attributed to the cytoprotective effect of N-acetylcysteine and incomplete efficacy of vitamin E and methionine. The paper also cites rat hepatocyte studies implicating the metabolite diethylphosphonate isocyanate via glutathione conjugation and depletion leading to lipid peroxidation, and protection by N-acetylcysteine.

raw_record.support_text: Acute hepatic necrosis developed in 23 of 41 patients studied after paracetamol overdosage, and two patients died in hepatic failure; renal failure also occurred in three cases. The paper also notes that paracetamol overdosage often results in hepatic necrosis and that hepatotoxicity is increased by prior exposure to enzyme-inducing drugs.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Paracetamol overdosage; hepatotoxicity increased by previous exposure to drugs likely to cause enzyme induction.
raw_record.extra_details: 23 of 41 patients studied after overdosage developed acute hepatic necrosis; two died in hepatic failure; renal failure occurred in three cases. Drug metabolism (probed with antipyrine) was greatly delayed during paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis, returning to normal within 7-21 days (Forrest et al., 1974). No close correlation between paracetamol dosage and degree of liver damage (Prescott and Wright, 1973). Lesion attributed to binding of intermediate metabolites to liver cell proteins (Mitchell et al., 1973; Jollow et al., 1973).

raw_record.support_text: Cases of usnic acid toxicity in humans are described, mainly associated with the dietary supplement LipoKinetix (Syntrax), a weight-loss product containing 100 mg of sodium usnate (the salt form of usnic acid) per capsule. Favreau et al. (2002) reported 7 previously healthy patients who developed severe hepatotoxicity while consuming LipoKinetix, with nausea, vomiting, fatigue, abdominal pain, increased transaminases, jaundice, and one case of fulminant hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy requiring intubation and mannitol; all recovered after discontinuation and liver tests normalized in five patients within 4 months. A 2005 National Toxicology Program/FDA document reported at least 21 adverse-event reports for LipoKinetix, including one death, one liver transplant, seven hepatic failure cases, ten chemical hepatitis cases, and four acute hepatotoxicity cases, and the product was withdrawn from the market in November 2001 after an FDA public warning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatotoxicity attributed to usnic acid (as sodium usnate) delivered via the defined dietary supplement LipoKinetix, a weight-loss product with a fixed composition; causal relationship is tied to this supplement exposure context.
raw_record.extra_details: Recommended LipoKinetix dosing was 1-2 capsules three times daily, exceeding the roughly 60-120 mg/day Traditional Chinese Medicine dose for usnic acid. Of the 7 Favreau patients, 5 took the product ≤1 month and 2 for 2-3 months; symptoms included nausea, vomiting, fatigue, abdominal pain, transaminase elevation, and jaundice, with one fulminant hepatic failure requiring intubation/mannitol; all recovered after discontinuation. The 2005 NTP/FDA compilation reported 21 LipoKinetix adverse reports: 1 death, 1 liver transplant, 7 hepatic failure, 10 chemical hepatitis, and 4 acute hepatotoxicity; withdrawn from market November 2001 after FDA public warning. Proposed mechanism is mitochondrial uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation (proton leakage dissipating the inner-membrane proton gradient, inhibiting electron transport and ATP synthesis). Supporting animal/cell findings (not human evidence): usnic acid caused hepatic necrosis and transaminase increases in mice, hepatic mitochondrial/ER swelling with mild hepatic damage in rats, and reduced hepatocyte viability/ATP in vitro.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that while paracetamol is normally a very safe drug, in overdosage it can cause acute centrilobular hepatic necrosis, and notes a prior report in which twelve of sixty self-poisoning patients died in hepatic failure. The summary describes five patients with severe paracetamol overdosage and eleven untreated control patients with 4-hour plasma paracetamol concentrations above 300 µg per ml who all developed severe hepatic necrosis (mean maximum aspartate aminotransferase 5180 IU per litre), with two deaths in hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/supratherapeutic exposure (self-poisoning); therapeutic use explicitly reported not to cause liver damage. Five patients received intravenous cysteamine 4.25-10 h after ingestion as treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute centrilobular hepatic necrosis in paracetamol overdose. Treated-case 4-hour plasma paracetamol concentrations 258-542 µg/ml with urinary recovery of paracetamol 7.58-31.09 g; five of seven episodes showed no clinical/biochemical hepatic necrosis and two showed only mild transient liver damage (max AST 160-180 IU/L). Eleven untreated control patients with 4-h plasma paracetamol >300 µg/ml developed severe hepatic necrosis (mean max AST 5180 IU/L), two dying in hepatic failure. Mechanism: microsomal-enzyme-dependent metabolism of paracetamol to a highly reactive intermediate metabolite that covalently binds to liver-cell macromolecules; toxic doses deplete hepatic glutathione to below about 30% of normal, allowing the excess metabolite to alkylate vital cell constituents and cause necrosis. Therapeutic doses do not cause liver damage because the small amount of active metabolite is rapidly inactivated by conjugation with glutathione and excreted as cysteine and mercapturic-acid conjugates. Methylprednisolone/corticosteroids, mepyramine, activated charcoal, haemodialysis, forced diuresis, and charcoal-column haemoperfusion have been advocated as treatment but none shown to prevent liver damage.

raw_record.extra_details: Case of fatal fulminant acute liver failure due to liver cell necrosis in a Caucasian patient with ALK-positive stage IV NSCLC, described as the first such reported case. Dose 250 mg twice daily; onset of fulminant failure ~24 days after start. Peak ALT 6194 IU/L, AST 2053 IU/L, total bilirubin up to 443 µmol/L, PT-INR 5.33; coagulation factor V 11%; ferritin 10756 µg/L; hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome; MELD 36; met King's College criteria for poor prognosis but not a transplant candidate due to poor cancer prognosis; died on day 40. Other causes excluded (biliary obstruction, viral hepatitis A/B/C, alcohol, concomitant medication). Plasma crizotinib levels within expected range after discontinuation; estimated t1/2 ~50 h. No autopsy/biopsy. Authors note crizotinib-induced fatal hepatotoxicity occurs in 0.2% of patients and grade 3-4 ALT elevations in ~15% in pivotal phase III trials.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdoses cause liver injury, with hospital admissions for paracetamol poisoning and liver injury increasing at twice the rate of all paracetamol-related admissions (7.7% v 3.3% per year). Fatal paracetamol overdoses were recorded in the National Coronial Information System (median age 53 years), and the NSWPIC database showed median overdose age of 18 years (IQR 16–28). The authors attribute the liver injury to paracetamol poisoning, although they note in the limitations that other causes cannot be excluded. Modified-release (MR) paracetamol overdoses involve higher total doses and can cause hepatotoxicity despite early acetylcysteine administration.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Poisoning/overdose setting; liver injury attributed to paracetamol poisoning, but the authors note in the limitations that other causes cannot be excluded in the linked admission/death coding.
raw_record.extra_details: An observational analysis of the Australian National Hospital Morbidity Database, National Coronial Information System and NSWPIC. Admissions for paracetamol poisoning with liver injury rose 7.7% per year versus 3.3% for all paracetamol-related admissions. ~70% of overdoses involved women; median age 18 y (IQR 16–28) in NSWPIC. Fatal overdoses in NCIS had median age 53 y. Deaths attributed to paracetamol with toxic liver disease; overall number of deaths fairly consistent across the study period, with an apparent drop in case fatality rate attributed to improved treatment guidelines. MR (modified-release) paracetamol (96 x 665 mg pack) overdoses involved more tablets and higher total dose (median 12.6 g v 8 g), unpredictable pharmacokinetics, are harder to treat, and can cause hepatotoxicity despite early acetylcysteine. MR paracetamol was implicated in 9.5% of overdoses 2009–2017 but 33% of fatal overdoses with documented formulation. Pack-size/availability differences across countries discussed (Australia 10 g and 50 g packs; pack-size restriction reduced in Sept 2013 from 25 to 20 x 500 mg with little impact). European Medicines Agency suspended MR paracetamol marketing in 2018; Australian TGA planned up-scheduling from Schedule 2 to 3.

raw_record.extra_details: 1,543 patients hospitalized for acetaminophen overdose in the Calgary Health Region (population ~1.1 million) between 1995 and 2004 identified via administrative data. Age/sex-adjusted hospitalization rate fell 41% from 19.6 to 12.1 per 100,000 (1995 to 2004). Intentional overdoses fell (RR 0.49); accidental overdoses rose above baseline by 2004 (RR 1.24). Risk factors included female sex (RR 2.19), Aboriginal status (RR 4.04), and social assistance (RR 5.15). Background notes toxic quantity ~150 mg/kg, <5% develop acute liver toxicity, and roughly one-third of those developing encephalopathy die and 8% require transplantation. US ALF Study Group data identified acetaminophen as etiology in ~50% of acute liver failure cases.

raw_record.support_text: In this retrospective study, 20 patients with metastatic melanoma were treated with dacarbazine (DTIC); 5 developed hypersensitivity manifestations, all after DTIC administered over 4 days. Two patients had major life-threatening involvement with fever, hypereosinophilia, hepatic injury (cytolysis and cholestasis), and delayed bone marrow aplasia, appearing at the first cure in one patient and at the second in the other. A myelogram in one patient showed a promyelocyte-stage block favoring an iatrogenic etiology; DTIC was stopped and all manifestations regressed under symptomatic treatment.

raw_record.extra_details: Hypersensitivity was observed in 5 of 20 patients (20%) treated for metastatic melanoma; 3 had fever and hypereosinophilia only, with normal liver tests, appearing on day 3 of the second cure; 2 of the 5 had major life-threatening involvement with hepatic cytolysis and cholestasis plus delayed bone marrow aplasia, at the first and second cure respectively. Myelogram in one patient showed a medullary block at the promyelocyte stage supporting an iatrogenic etiology. DTIC was stopped and manifestations regressed with symptomatic treatment. Onset was early (within the first two cures) and appeared independent of daily dose. DTIC was first-line in 19 of 20 patients; given over 4 days in 10 patients and over 1 day in 10.

raw_record.support_text: The summary of a series of sixty patients admitted after paracetamol overdose states that forty-nine developed liver damage, seventeen progressed to hepatic encephalopathy, and twelve of these died from fulminant hepatic failure. All but two of the patients with bilirubin levels above 4 mg/100 ml by the 3rd-5th day developed encephalopathy, and histology of liver-biopsy specimens from those who recovered showed severe centrilobular necrosis and collapse, with no progression to cirrhosis. Liver damage is considered preventable only in the first 24 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate suicidal overdose (supratherapeutic ingestion).
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen, N-acetyl-p-aminophenol). Of sixty patients admitted after paracetamol overdose, forty-nine developed liver damage; seventeen progressed to hepatic encephalopathy; twelve died from fulminant hepatic failure. Severe centrilobular necrosis and collapse on liver biopsy in survivors; no progression to cirrhosis. Prognosis in first days assessed by serum bilirubin (>4 mg/100 ml by 3rd-5th day) and prothrombin time. Paper also notes first British hepatotoxicity cases from suicidal overdose published in 1966, that studies in rats showed paracetamol was a predictable hepatotoxin in large doses, and that fatal hepatic necrosis in man after overdose has been reported from several countries. Data also drawn from King's College Hospital Liver Unit admissions (March 1971-June 1972) plus three earlier cases (1967-1970); nine of the period cases died from fulminant hepatic failure.

raw_record.support_text: A 75-year-old male with recurrent retroperitoneal undifferentiated/unclassified soft tissue sarcoma was started on oral pazopanib 800 mg/day. Two weeks later he showed signs of liver dysfunction (elevated serum liver enzyme levels) and pazopanib was stopped; after 1 week he was restarted at 400 mg/day and 6 days later presented with fever, malaise, fatigue, and appetite loss together with severe liver dysfunction (elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin). He was admitted, pazopanib was stopped, and liver biopsy confirmed drug-induced hepatitis; after treatment with hepatoprotectors and prednisolone he recovered from drug-induced hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of severe pazopanib-associated liver dysfunction in a 75-year-old male with recurrent retroperitoneal undifferentiated/unclassified soft tissue sarcoma. Initial dose 800 mg/day produced liver enzyme elevation within 2 weeks (treatment stopped); rechallenge at reduced dose 400 mg/day led 6 days later to fever, malaise, fatigue, appetite loss, and severe liver dysfunction with elevated transaminases and bilirubin. Liver biopsy confirmed drug-induced hepatitis. Treated with hepatoprotectors and prednisolone; recovered and discharged. Tumor showed complete response but regrew 4 months after cessation. Pazopanib is an orally bioavailable VEGFR-1/2/3, c-kit, and PDGFR-alpha/beta tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

Authors state that large doses of acetaminophen taken alone (without additional drugs or alcohol) trigger multiorgan insults after acute liver injury, including remote colon ischemia/infarction. Patient 1 underwent liver transplantation but developed colon infarction without vascular obstruction, recovered after segmental colon resections. Patient 2 was withdrawn from the transplant list as liver tests stopped worsening, survived after segmental colon removal but with multiple organ failure. raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a case of severe acetaminophen overdose hepatotoxicity: the patient ingested 208 mg/kg of acetaminophen (nearly twice expected) and presented with markedly elevated transaminases (AST 3294 U/L, ALT 5107 U/L) and coagulopathy before dialysis, progressing to hepatic failure. The discussion states that 'Acetaminophen after overdose is primarily regarded as a hepatotoxin and is the most commonly implicated drug in cases of acute liver failure,' with a single acute threshold dose of 150-250 mg/kg in adults, and that fatalities from acetaminophen poisoning due to hepatic failure generally occur 3-5 days after acute overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single acute overdose (208 mg/kg) in a young adult female; injury attributed specifically to the overdose setting rather than therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose: 208 mg/kg (approx. 4 g/day context of intentional overdose). Initial acetaminophen level 73.9 mcg/mL (<100 mcg/mL). On admission AST 56 U/L, ALT 76 U/L; prior to dialysis AST 3294 U/L, ALT 5107 U/L, INR 1.765, ammonia 95 µmol/L. Treated with N-acetylcysteine (loading 140 mg/kg, then 70 mg/kg every 4 h) and Prometheus FPSA (fractionated plasma separation and adsorption) dialysis at 30th hour of admission and again at 80th hour. Mechanism described: P450-mediated metabolism to reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which depletes glutathione after overdose and binds to hepatocyte constituents causing cell death. Recovery by ~1 week after discharge with normalization of transaminases and coagulation tests. Reported population risk: serum acetaminophen 200 mg/L at 4 h / 30 mg/L at 15 h carries ~60% chance of severe often-fatal liver damage (transaminases >1000 IU/L); 300 mg/L at 4 h / 50 mg/L at 15 h raises probability to ~90%.

In the PETIT and PETIT2 pediatric trials, ALT and bilirubin increases were mild with no clinical consequence and fully corrected after cessation, with 4.7% of patients developing ALT ≥3 × ULN and 3% withdrawing due to hepatobiliary laboratory abnormalities.

raw_record.support_text: Kelsey and associates observed three types of pathologic liver conditions associated with chlorpromazine: a diffuse inflammatory change with biliary stasis producing obstructive jaundice with moderate alkaline phosphatase elevation, a type resembling acute hepatitis with parenchymal liver damage, and an uncommon early-cirrhosis type. Dreyfuss reported that the incidence of chlorpromazine jaundice was 4.4% in 362 patients given no extra fluids but dropped to 0.34% in 588 patients given about 2.3 L of additional fluids, supporting an inspissation-of-bile mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Kelsey's three liver types: (1) diffuse inflammatory change with biliary stasis, obstructive jaundice with moderate alkaline phosphatase elevation and no abnormal parenchymal liver-function tests; (2) acute-hepatitis-like with elevated thymol turbidity and prothrombin deficiency; (3) uncommon early cirrhosis with marked azotemia and severe prolonged chronic liver disease. Dreyfuss fluid study: jaundice incidence 4.4% (362 patients, no extra fluids) vs 0.34% (588 patients, ~2.3 L extra fluids). Read/Harrison/Sherlock: 4 women developed obstructive jaundice after 1-4 weeks on 75 mg/day chlorpromazine, with very high serum cholesterol and xanthomas; clinical recovery in all, but serum cholesterol and phosphatase levels not normalized even 7-18 months later.

raw_record.support_text: The lower dose of lapaquistat (50 mg/day) had relatively few commonly reported side effects such as headache and back pain. Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Ltd. discontinued clinical development of lapaquistat because of hepatotoxicity. Although almost every known antihyperlipidemic drug, including all statins, is hepatotoxic at high doses, the dose-dependent hepatotoxicity of lapaquistat was a major reason that terminated its clinical development, and the major threat was that hepatotoxicity was observed at low doses, 50 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: Squalene synthase inhibitor tested in Phase II and Phase III clinical trials in Europe and the United States; hepatotoxicity was dose-dependent and, importantly, observed at the low therapeutic dose of 50 mg/day, prompting discontinuation of clinical development by Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Ltd.; the compound is no longer pursued as a statin complement. Lower-dose side effects included headache and back pain.

Twenty-four hours after ingestion SGOT and SGPT were 850 and 622 IU/dl, and jaundice subsequently developed (total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dl). Autopsy showed a large liver with extensive hemorrhagic necrosis, most marked in the periportal areas, and the patient died after cardiac arrest. The case is interpreted as acute hepatic failure, the clinical syndrome of severe hepatic dysfunction or massive hepatic necrosis, occurring as a component of iron poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: The study of paracetamol overdose patients treated with cysteamine or dimercaprol reports that cysteamine affords greater protection than dimercaprol against hepatocellular necrosis after paracetamol overdose. One patient treated with dimercaprol 12 hours after overdose died after developing fulminant hepatic failure, and peak serum bilirubin concentration and prothrombin time abnormalities and the severity of hepatic necrosis on liver biopsy were greater in the dimercaprol group. The paracetamol overdose itself is thus the attributed cause of the hepatic necrosis and fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Patients presented with paracetamol overdose (mean initial plasma paracetamol ~2.0 mmol/l in cysteamine group, ~1.8 mmol/l in dimercaprol group; mean interval between ingestion and admission ~4.8-6.0 h). Randomised comparison of cysteamine vs dimercaprol as antidotes. One patient who received dimercaprol 12 h after overdose died of fulminant hepatic failure; no other patient developed hepatic encephalopathy. Hepatic necrosis severity on biopsy, peak serum bilirubin and prothrombin time were greater in the dimercaprol group. Mean erythrocyte sulphydryl group concentration was significantly reduced in the dimercaprol group (P<0.01). Authors also saw two other patients who died in fulminant hepatic failure when cysteamine was given at 15-16 h post-overdose.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) is preferred over other analgesic-antipyretics due to its low toxicity, but the most serious adverse effect of an acute overdose is hepatic necrosis. A 19-year-old woman who ingested an acetaminophen overdose developed hepatotoxicity (along with reactive plasmacytosis with thrombocytosis and agranulocytosis followed by a leukemoid reaction), and the findings reversed spontaneously with symptomatic therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute oral overdose in a 19-year-old woman; hepatotoxicity resolved spontaneously with symptomatic therapy rather than progressing to liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the most serious adverse effect of acute acetaminophen overdose. The same case also exhibited agranulocytosis, reactive plasmacytosis with thrombocytosis, and a subsequent leukemoid reaction, all of which reversed spontaneously. Amphotericin B in the same article is discussed only as a cause of hypertension/hypotension, which is not liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The authors, responding to a critique, discuss the incidence of isoniazid-induced hepatitis and isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity in persons receiving isoniazid preventive therapy for tuberculosis. They explain that their previously reported age-specific incidence rates were computed by excluding from the denominator persons not known to be taking isoniazid as prescribed, which tends to overestimate incidence. If excluded persons were included, the calculated incidence of hepatotoxicity would have been 0.2% for ages 20-34, 0.7% for ages 35-49, 1.6% for ages 50-64, and 0.6% for ages >64, and they conclude the true age-specific incidence lies between the high and low figures.
raw_record.extra_details: Letters/correspondence discussing incidence of isoniazid-induced hepatitis during preventive therapy for tuberculosis. Age-specific incidence of hepatotoxicity: 0.2% for persons 20-34 years, 0.7% for 35-49, 1.6% for 50-64, 0.6% for >64 years (when excluded, probably still-medicated persons are included in the denominator); true incidence considered to lie between the high and low figures. Standard adult dosing of 300 mg daily is mentioned. The authors note that about half of patients discontinued isoniazid during the year of therapy. A separate paragraph mentions future consideration of high-dose isoniazid given twice weekly, without making an additional DILI claim.

raw_record.support_text: Troglitazone, the first glitazone approved by the US FDA, proved to be hepatotoxic and was withdrawn from the market after reports of several dozen deaths and cases of severe hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation. An observational retrospective inception cohort using US claims data confirmed that troglitazone use was associated with a marked increase in the risk of acute idiopathic liver injury and acute liver failure leading to hospitalisation. In controlled clinical trials, troglitazone was associated with a ~3-fold greater incidence of significant (>3x ULN) ALT elevations than placebo.
raw_record.extra_details: Withdrawn from market after reports of several dozen deaths and severe hepatic failure requiring liver transplantation. Retrospective inception cohort assembled from claims data of a large multistate US healthcare organisation showed marked increase in risk of acute idiopathic liver injury and acute liver failure leading to hospitalisation. In controlled trials, troglitazone showed a ~3-fold greater incidence of ALT elevations >3x ULN than placebo. In a troglitazone-insulin combination study, 3 patients on troglitazone 600mg had ALT >3x ULN during the 26-week treatment period; one patient discontinued permanently due to jaundice and hyperbilirubinaemia. Hepatotoxicity is not a glitazone class effect.

raw_record.support_text: In India, an unusual but not uncommon cause of acute liver failure (ALF) is the ingestion of rodenticides containing zinc phosphide (Ratol®), and overall survival following Ratol® poisoning is poor without liver transplantation. This is supported by a retrospective analysis of 30 patients admitted after Ratol ingestion, of whom 9 underwent living donor liver transplant and 6 died without transplant, with the average interval between consumption and ALF being 6.5 days.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute rodenticide poisoning by ingestion of the commercial product Ratol®; all 30 patients poisoned by deliberate/accidental ingestion rather than therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective single-center series (Jan 2006–Apr 2011, 30 patients): 9 underwent living donor liver transplant (LDLT), 6 died without transplant (Group I), and 15 with very minimal exposure recovered without transplant (Group II). Average time between ingestion and ALF was 6.5 days. Group I mean MELD 38 vs 18 in Group II; median INR 8 vs 3; median total bilirubin 13 vs 5 mg/dL. All patients who developed encephalopathy either died or required LT. MELD >31 on day 6 and onset of encephalopathy at any time predicted need for LT / mortality without LT.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatic injury is described as the principal toxic effect of acetaminophen overdose. Substantial overdose can markedly increase reactive metabolite production via the cytochrome P-450-dependent oxidative pathway, and if glutathione depletion exceeds repletion, the reactive intermediate is not adequately detoxified. Several large case series have been reported, and mortality from fulminant hepatic failure in untreated cases ranges from 2 to 4 per cent, substantially reduced by prompt N-acetylcysteine therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholics may be predisposed to hepatotoxicity following significant acute acetaminophen overdosage; acute alcohol ingestion may decrease toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism involves glucuronidation, sulfation, and cytochrome P-450-dependent mixed-function oxidative metabolism to a reactive metabolite; glutathione depletion beyond repletion in overdose. Mortality from fulminant hepatic failure in untreated cases 2-4%; prompt N-acetylcysteine therapy substantially reduces mortality.

raw_record.support_text: The paper's section on acute iron overload hepatotoxicity states that children relatively commonly ingest large numbers of ferrous sulfate tablets prescribed for their mothers, and adults sometimes take ferrous sulfate in a suicide attempt. It cites Luongo and Bjornson, who described periportal hepatic necrosis in three fatal cases in children, relating the dose to liver damage; this represents human liver injury (hepatic necrosis) from ferrous sulfate overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting: children ingesting ferrous sulfate tablets prescribed for their mothers, and adult suicide attempts with ferrous sulfate.
raw_record.extra_details: Luongo and Bjornson reported three fatal pediatric cases with periportal hepatic necrosis. In rabbits given ferrous sulfate by gastric intubation, 0.75 g/kg produced congestion without necrosis whereas 1.0 g/kg produced severe hemorrhagic periportal necrosis involving about one-third of the liver within 24-48 hr; Brown and Gray showed similar changes with intravenous doses of 35-47 mg/kg, and Witzleben documented mitochondrial swelling in periportal hepatocytes by electron microscopy (animal findings accompanying the human cases).

raw_record.support_text: The editorial states that daily isoniazid for 6-9 months for latent tuberculosis is one of the most commonly prescribed regimens, that its most common adverse effect is drug-induced abnormal aminotransferases, and that its most worrisome toxicity, though extremely rare (less than 0.01%), is fatal hepatitis, noting that mortality rates in patients with acute liver failure due to idiosyncratic drug reactions such as those from isoniazid approach 80-90%. Reported cofactors for hepatotoxicity include older age, concurrent alcohol, acetaminophen or injection drug use, hepatitis B infection, lower body mass index, and lower albumin levels.
raw_record.extra_details: Used daily for 6-9 months for latent tuberculosis. Drug-induced abnormal aminotransferases is the most common adverse effect; fatal hepatitis is extremely rare (<0.01%). Mortality in acute liver failure from idiosyncratic drug reactions such as isoniazid approaches 80-90%. Reported cofactors for hepatotoxicity: older age, concurrent alcohol, acetaminophen or injection drug use, hepatitis B infection, lower BMI, lower albumin. Patel & Voigt case cohort study (327 of 743 Vietnamese immigrants, 9 yr): isoniazid hepatotoxicity defined as jaundice with transaminases >5x ULN resolving after withdrawal, per gastroenterologist evaluation excluding other causes; hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation rates were 3% (HBsAg-negative), 6% (HBsAg-positive/HBeAg-negative), and 48% (HBsAg-positive/HBeAg-positive). Another study in Southeast Asian immigrants in Philadelphia found no significant difference in isoniazid hepatotoxicity rates between HBV carriers and controls.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that during the first year tolcapone was marketed, a fulminant and fatal hepatopathy was documented in 3 patients, with an estimated 60,000 patients having received tolcapone by the time of the third fatal hepatopathy. Because of this hepatotoxicity, tolcapone was relegated to a secondary-choice adjunctive therapy, with pharmaceutical-company directives requiring monitoring of serum aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase values at baseline and at regular intervals during treatment.

Pharma directives mandate monitoring of serum aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase at baseline, every 2 weeks for the first year, every 4 weeks for the next 6 months, and every 2 months thereafter. Context: adjunctive treatment of levodopa-related fluctuations in Parkinson's disease.

raw_record.support_text: Side effects such as liver toxicity and serious gastrointestinal reactions occurred when gram quantities of nicotinic acid were taken to lower serum lipids. Liver toxicity is most commonly manifested by increases in serum transaminase enzymes released as a result of damage to liver cells, and high doses have produced jaundice, fatigue, and, in at least one case, fulminant liver failure. This is corroborated by clinical trial data showing mild liver toxicity beginning at 1000 mg/d with slow-release nicotinic acid and occurring typically with intakes of 2-6 g/d.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose therapeutic use as an antihyperlipidemic; severe reactions, especially liver toxicity, often involved switching to slow-release formulations; no adverse effects at 500 mg/d for either form and significant effects beginning at 1000 mg/d (gastrointestinal effects with unmodified nicotinic acid; mild liver toxicity with slow-release nicotinic acid).
raw_record.extra_details: Liver toxicity manifested by increases in serum transaminase enzymes from damage to liver cells; high doses produced jaundice, fatigue, and fulminant liver failure in at least one case. Most reported adverse reactions occurred with intakes of 2-6 g/d; only two anecdotal cases occurred at <1000 mg (slow-release at 500 mg/d and unmodified at 750 mg/d). Dose-response clinical trial tested immediate-release and slow-release forms at 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, and 3000 mg/d (initial then 6 weeks per level). Uncertainties in case reports include accuracy of reported intake and preexisting/confounding conditions such as alcoholism; clinical trial data considered useful for safety/risk evaluation, concluding 1000 mg/d carries significant risk and 500 mg/d carries no identifiable risk.

raw_record.support_text: Nicotinic acid is associated with flushing and pruritus, and liver toxicity is a well-recognized adverse effect of treatment at pharmacologic doses (1.5 to 6 g/day), reported as more common with slow-release than immediate-release (crystalline) nicotinic acid. In the current report, 3 cases of hepatic toxicity induced by treatment of dyslipidemia with crystalline nicotinic acid are described, characterized by signs of generalized synthetic dysfunction of the liver out of proportion to transaminase elevation, manifesting as a striking decrease in apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins and plasma LCAT, and in some cases increased prothrombin time and decreased serum albumin. In 2 of the 3 patients these changes occurred without hyperbilirubinemia and with normal or only mildly elevated transaminases.
raw_record.extra_details: Treatment for dyslipidemia with crystalline (immediate-release) nicotinic acid. Novel presentation of generalized hepatic synthetic dysfunction out of proportion to transaminase elevation: decreased plasma apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins and LCAT activity, increased prothrombin time and decreased serum albumin; in 2 of 3 patients without hyperbilirubinemia and with normal/mildly elevated transaminases. At 3.0 g/d, LCAT activity fell (Patient 1: 320 to 147; Patient 2: 355 to 151; Patient 3: 394 to 133 nmol/h/ml), AST/ALT rose mildly, and recovery of LCAT/transaminases followed dose reduction (1.5 g/d) or cessation. Liver toxicity noted as more common with slow-release than immediate-release nicotinic acid.

raw_record.support_text: A 17-year-old, previously healthy female ingested 16,000 mg iron sulphate (96.15 mg of iron ions per kg b.wt.) with suicidal intent. In the course of the intoxication, hemorrhagic gastritis, renal insufficiency and increasing signs of fulminant hepatic failure complicated with coagulopathy and encephalopathy were observed. Despite deferoxamine treatment and albumin dialysis (Prometheus system) bridging to liver transplant, the patient died 80 hours after iron ingestion. The authors state that ingestion of a very high dose of iron and late introduction of deferoxamine treatment contributed to fulminant liver failure and the fatal outcome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Suicidal overdose (16,000 mg iron sulphate; 96.15 mg iron ions/kg b.wt.); concurrent ingestion of naproxen (Apo-Naproxen 15 x 500 mg) and ibuprofen (Ibum 5 x 200 mg) with suicidal intent; adolescent female (17 years old).
raw_record.extra_details: Also referred to as iron ions and iron(II) sulfate. Serum iron on admission (10 h post-ingestion) was 2351 µg% (421.0 µmol/L), falling to 145 µg% (25.9 µmol/L) after deferoxamine (15 mg/kg/h for 15 h). Fulminant hepatic failure with coagulopathy and encephalopathy; progressive transaminase elevation (AspAT up to 8289 U/L, AIAT up to 12538 U/L), hyperbilirubinemia, rising INR, ammonia elevation; hemorrhagic gastritis and renal insufficiency also present. Patient qualified for liver transplant; two albumin dialysis (Prometheus) procedures performed but deep coma, shock and respiratory insufficiency developed; death 80 hours after ingestion. Late deferoxamine initiation considered contributory to fatal outcome. Keywords: iron poisoning, hepatotoxicity, albumin dialysis.

Patient died two days after admission from multiple organ failure; blood and urine analysis confirmed tramadol intoxication at medico-legal autopsy. raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a 1993 phase II clinical trial (Eli Lilly Trial H3X-MC-PPPC, NIH protocol #93-DK-0031) evaluating fialuridine as an anti-HBV antiviral drug. Although the preliminary results reduced HBV DNA in patients, the study was terminated on an emergency basis by week 13 because of serious hepatotoxicity in seven patients, of whom five died and two required emergency liver transplantation. The paper attributes the human-specific toxicity to mitochondrial toxicity through a nucleoside transporter expressed in human mitochondria, and notes fialuridine toxicity was recapitulated in human liver organoids but not in HepG2 cells.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II trial (Eli Lilly Trial H3X-MC-PPPC, NIH protocol #93-DK-0031) terminated emergently at week 13; serious hepatotoxicity in 7 patients, 5 deaths and 2 emergency liver transplants. Mechanism attributed to human-specific mitochondrial toxicity via a nucleoside transporter expressed in human mitochondria. Fialuridine passed preclinical toxicity studies; its toxicity was significant and quantifiable in primary human liver organoids but not observed in HepG2 hepatoma cells.

raw_record.support_text: Case reports of chronic active hepatitis with prolonged use of nitrofurantoin have included biochemical and liver biopsy evidence for direct hepatocellular toxicity, as well as immunologic reactions including hyperglobulinemia and antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies in some patients. Some patients also had evidence of pulmonary damage. The role of immune phenomena in the hepatic damage is unclear; antinuclear antibodies have persisted in some patients after drug discontinuation despite improved hepatic function. The paper frames this within an increasing recognition of nitrofurantoin's potential for hepatic injury in an idiosyncratic drug reaction context.
raw_record.extra_details: Chronic active hepatitis reported with prolonged therapeutic use of nitrofurantoin. Immunologic features included hyperglobulinemia and antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies in some patients; antinuclear antibodies persisted in some patients after discontinuation despite improvement in hepatic function. Some patients also had pulmonary damage. Proposed mechanisms: metabolism to a reactive electrophilic intermediate capable of covalent binding to cell macromolecules, possibly via nitroreduction of the furan ring, and/or superoxide formation from redox cycling.

raw_record.support_text: The letter responds to a study describing an association between high serum phosphate and death in patients with acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity, and presents the authors' own experience managing 29 patients with acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure, of whom 18 survived spontaneously, one died following transplantation, and 6 died without transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Fulminant hepatic failure occurred in the setting of acetaminophen overdose; case series of 29 patients managed at a tertiary transplant center.
raw_record.extra_details: Of 25 patients with available measurements, 18 survived spontaneously, one died following transplantation, and 6 died without transplantation. Serum phosphate >/= day 2 was specific (94%) but insensitive (57%) for death; of 5 hyperphosphatemic patients, 3 were moribund at presentation and died within hours, one was listed for transplant but died before organ availability, and one recovered. The authors caution against using hyperphosphatemia or King's College criteria as sole determinants for transplantation, recommending that transplantation be reserved for patients with severe and progressive coagulopathy or cerebral edema.

raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity computed from Public Health Service study using criteria established by a panel of hepatic-disease experts. Reported rates: 2.3% per year for persons 50-64 years, 0.8% for persons >64 years, and 1.7% per year for all persons ≥50 years. The paper corrects claims that figures underestimate incidence, noting half the patients discontinued the year of therapy and that excluding persons not known to be taking isoniazid as prescribed tends to overestimate incidence; if not excluded, calculated incidence would be 0.2% for ages 20-34, 0.7% for 35-49, 1.6% for 50-64, and 0.6% for >64, so the true age-specific incidence likely lies between the high and low figures. Also discusses that it is not known whether high-dose isoniazid given twice weekly for preventive therapy of tuberculosis would reduce isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity risk; standard 300 mg daily adult dosing recommended.

raw_record.support_text: After one month of treatment with the CDK4/6 inhibitor ribociclib, the patient developed grade 2 liver toxicity with alanine and aspartate aminotransferases four times the upper limit of normal (ULN). Liver enzyme values returned to baseline after stopping the drug, but the patient again developed grade 2 liver toxicity upon re-administration, prompting a first ribociclib dose reduction (200 mg twice daily orally). After four months on 400 mg ribociclib daily the patient developed grade 3 liver toxicity (transaminases 12x ULN), and subsequently grade 4 liver toxicity (transaminases >27x ULN) in February 2022, requiring complete discontinuation of ribociclib. Other probable causes of hypertransaminasemia were excluded (no infectious disease, no liver metastases, no concomitant hepatotoxic medications, negative viral serology for hepatitis A, B, and C). Total bilirubin remained within normal limits, and it took about 5 months for AST and ALT to return to baseline, with corticosteroid therapy required after the grade 4 episode.

Recovery to baseline took ~5 months; corticosteroid therapy required after grade 4 hypertransaminasemia. No hepatic DLT occurred at 40 mg/m².

raw_record.support_text: In Table 5, listing the main adverse effects of azathioprine (AZA) in 35 ulcerative colitis patients, hepatotoxicity was reported in 8 patients (23%). All 5 patients with AZA hepatotoxicity who were shifted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) were 6-MP-tolerant, indicating the hepatotoxicity was attributed to AZA rather than 6-MP. A separate patient case noted that AZA was discontinued due to hepatotoxicity after which the patient tolerated 6-MP.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity was a main adverse effect of AZA in 8 of 35 (23%) ulcerative colitis patients (Table 5). Five of the 8 were shifted to 6-MP and all tolerated it (5 6-MP-tolerant). In one illustrative case, a patient discontinued AZA due to hepatotoxicity and was successfully treated with 6-MP with improved endoscopic findings. No biochemical pattern, histology, or severity grade beyond hepatotoxicity requiring drug discontinuation is reported.

raw_record.support_text: In 30 colorectal cancer patients undergoing isolated hepatic perfusion with 200 mg melphalan via hepatic artery infusion, veno-occlusive disease (VOD) occurred in 4 patients and portal hypertension (possibly a result of VOD) in 2 others. Grade 4 biliary toxicity occurred in 5 of 30 patients and 1 patient died of progressive liver failure. Toxic hepatitis was reported as a major complication in 1 patient. The discussion attributes these liver toxicities to the melphalan perfusion exposure.

raw_record.extra_details: 200 mg melphalan given as 20-min hepatic artery infusion followed by 40-min perfusion; peak perfusate concentration 93.2 µg/mL, AUC 2841.6 µg·min/mL. Reported liver events: toxic hepatitis in 1 patient, veno-occlusive disease in 4 patients, portal hypertension in 2, grade 4 biliary toxicity in 5 of 30 patients, and 1 death from progressive liver failure. GGT, ALAT, ASAT and bilirubin elevations were graded per NCI CTC across 30 patients. VOD was noted as possibly resulting from accumulative exposure to chemotherapeutic agents; toxicity had a steep concentration-toxicity relationship independent of total melphalan dose (supported by a rat cholangiofibrosis model).

raw_record.support_text: In a PGx genome-wide association study, the HLA-B*57:01 allele was identified as a major risk factor for flucloxacillin-induced liver injury, described as a severe but quite rare adverse drug reaction (~8.5 in every 100,000). Despite the strong association, only one in every 500 to 1,000 flucloxacillin-treated individuals carrying this allele develops liver injury, an example of incomplete penetrance that limits clinical utility.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen taken in moderate doses (≤ 4 gm/d) is a safe and effective analgesic and antipyretic, but ingestion of excessive amounts can result in fulminant hepatic failure. Acetaminophen overdoses remain a leading cause of fulminant hepatic failure in the US, Great Britain, and most of Europe; epidemiologic data from the Acute Liver Failure Study Group indicate ~50% of US fulminant hepatic failure cases are due to excessive acetaminophen ingestion, nearly half being intentional overdoses/suicide attempts.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/self-harm exposure (excessive ingestion); includes both intentional suicide attempts and accidental overdose; hepatotoxicity described only at supratherapeutic (excessive) doses, with therapeutic use (≤4 gm/d) noted as safe.
raw_record.extra_details: About 30-40,000 US adolescents and adults ingest acetaminophen annually with intent of self-harm; found in hundreds of OTC and prescription products, over 24 billion doses sold annually. ~50% of fulminant hepatic failure cases in the US attributed to excessive acetaminophen ingestion, nearly half intentional; 30% mortality rate and 7-9% require liver transplantation; while a majority recover. Paper focuses on psychosocial assessment and candidacy of acetaminophen overdose patients requiring liver transplantation, including suicide risk factors and post-LT outcomes (repeat suicide attempts and graft failure due to non-adherence).

raw_record.support_text: Six weeks after initiating temozolomide and radiation therapy for glioblastoma, the patient developed rapidly increasing transaminitis, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and hyperbilirubinemia; liver biopsy showed a cholestatic pattern of injury with mild ductopenia and portal eosinophilia consistent with a drug-induced liver injury. Temozolomide was held, and repeat biopsy three weeks later revealed progression to severe biliary ductopenia consistent with vanishing bile duct syndrome. She was treated with ursodeoxycholic acid and zinc with gradual improvement over several months, and the paper concludes that biliary ductopenia is a rare manifestation of temozolomide-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Concurrent radiation therapy at time of injury; indication glioblastoma; single case at therapeutic exposure; no other hepatotoxic medications at admission.
raw_record.extra_details: Latency six weeks after temozolomide start; labs aspartate transaminase 425 IU/L, alanine transaminase 1028 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 291 U/L, total bilirubin 7.9 mg/dl at admission rising to peak 36.8 mg/dl. Initial biopsy: cholestatic pattern, mild ductopenia, portal eosinophilia; subsequent biopsy: severe biliary ductopenia (vanishing bile duct syndrome). Dechallenge: on holding temozolomide transaminases improved while bilirubin continued to rise. Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid and zinc; gradual normalization over months; followed 2 years without disease. Cites Mason et al. case of a 62-year-old woman who developed liver failure 17 days after temozolomide initiation with peak bilirubin 289 mg/dl and biopsy-confirmed vanishing bile duct syndrome. Mechanism of temozolomide-induced hepatotoxicity is unclear; drug does not require hepatic metabolism for activation.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that adverse side effects of isoniazid are many and varied, but the most serious is isoniazid-induced hepatitis. The incidences of hepatic toxicity and intolerance both increase somewhat with advancing age; there was no significant difference between men and women in the incidence of hepatitis, though other types of intolerance were greater in women than men (7.3% compared with 3.8%, p < 0.05).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings from an elderly nursing home population (Arkansas) receiving isoniazid as preventive therapy for tuberculosis infection; hepatic toxicity incidence increased with advancing age.
raw_record.extra_details: Incidence of other types of intolerance was greater in women than men (7.3% vs 3.8%, p<0.05), but no significant sex difference for hepatitis. A benefit-risk analysis weighed nonfatal hepatitis risk against the benefit of avoiding clinical tuberculosis (Table 3), most favorable for converters. In a separate safety assessment of 135 deaths while on isoniazid, public health nurses, nursing home directors, death certificates (liver mentioned on only four), and the private physicians of those four found no indication that isoniazid contributed to any death. Survival comparison of treated versus untreated converters favored treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Paracetamol overdose is described as the commonest cause of acute liver failure in the UK, prompting measures to restrict its sale. Data from patients admitted to the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit in 1992-98 compared with 1998-2001 showed that the incidence of paracetamol-induced liver failure, severity of illness, and outcome did not differ between groups, but patients with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure had higher Carstairs scores (1.99, 95% CI 1.33-2.65; n=190) than patients with non-paracetamol acute liver failure (0.02, -0.79 to 0.84; n=68), establishing an association between paracetamol-induced acute liver failure and social deprivation.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure specifically; paracetamol is commonly taken in overdose. The paper notes acute liver failure has a high mortality rate and that N-acetyl-cysteine is a highly effective antidote only if given within ~15 h to be most effective. Patients were admitted to the Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit; comparison covered 1992-98 versus 1998-2001, and the key finding was an association between paracetamol-induced acute liver failure and social deprivation (Carstairs score).

raw_record.support_text: The letter corrects previous statements about Public Health Service data on isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity. Using criteria established by a panel of experts in hepatic disease, the Public Health Service study showed that the incidence of hepatotoxicity was 2.3% per year for persons 50 to 64 years of age and 0.8% for persons over 64 years of age, with a rate of 1.7% per year for all persons 50 or more years of age. The letter also disputes the claim that these figures underestimate the incidence of isoniazid hepatitis, explaining that the reported rates were computed by excluding from the denominator persons not known to be taking isoniazid as prescribed, which tends to overestimate rather than underestimate incidence.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Findings apply to isoniazid preventive therapy for tuberculosis in a general adult population; incidence is age-specific. Standard regimen is 300 mg daily in adults.
raw_record.extra_details: Public Health Service study using criteria established by a panel of hepatic-disease experts. Reported (high) age-specific annual incidence of hepatotoxicity: 2.3% for ages 50-64, 0.8% for >64, 1.7% for all ages >=50. Recalculated (low) incidence excluding persons not clearly at risk of isoniazid-induced hepatitis: 0.2% for ages 20-34, 0.7% for 35-49, 1.6% for 50-64, 0.6% for >64. The authors state the true age-specific incidence likely lies between these high and low figures. The letter also notes that the safety/efficacy of high-dose twice-weekly isoniazid preventive therapy is not yet established, and recommends continuing the standard 300 mg daily regimen.

raw_record.support_text: Busulfan is an alkylating agent used in conditioning for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant, and its dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) is liver toxicity, often presenting as sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/veno-occlusive disease (SOS/VOD). Increased busulfan systemic exposure (AUC) is associated with an increased risk for SOS/VOD, though risk is also influenced by other medications, particularly cyclophosphamide, and by transplant procedures.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intravenous busulfan given as conditioning for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant in patients with advanced hematologic malignancies; exposure escalated above the standard starting AUC of 4800 µmol-min/L, with SOS/VOD occurring at higher AUC levels.
raw_record.extra_details: In this phase I dose-escalation study (NCT00943319), severe late-occurring sinusodial obstruction syndrome/veno-occlusive disease (SOS/VOD) was the dose-limiting toxicity observed in 5/8 patients at an AUC level of 6800 µmol-min/L; the risk for SOS/VOD correlated with the highest observed AUC (AUCmax) rather than average cumulative AUC (AUCavg). Maximum tolerated busulfan AUC was 5800 µmol-min/L. Busulfan is [1,4-bis-(methanesolfonoxyl)butane]. Regimen included fludarabine/alemtuzumab; SOS/VOD risk is also influenced by cyclophosphamide and transplant procedures.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective analysis of 50 consecutive patients with fulminant hepatic failure due to a paracetamol overdose, the paper describes the clinical course, noting that deterioration in neurological status was more frequent when patients were transferred during grade III or IV coma than when moved earlier in grade I or II. This explicitly attributes fulminant hepatic failure to paracetamol overdose in a human cohort.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective analysis of 50 consecutive patients with fulminant hepatic failure due to paracetamol overdose. Transfer during grade III or IV coma (22 patients) was followed by deterioration of conscious level in 14 patients, versus only 4 of 28 patients transferred earlier in grade I or II. Median time from grade III encephalopathy to brainstem coning was 96 h for early transfer vs 48 h for late transfer (p=0.001). Paper focuses on prevention of cerebral oedema in fulminant hepatic failure; overdose is the exposure setting.

raw_record.support_text: A 70-year-old white woman developed metformin-induced liver injury 5 weeks after starting metformin 500 mg twice daily for type 2 diabetes, and she was not on any other hepatotoxic agent. The case is reported to draw attention to this rare but important metformin side effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 70-year-old white woman with type 2 diabetes and hypothyroidism on only metformin 500 mg twice daily and levothyroxine, denying OTC medications, alcohol, or illicit drugs; injury developed 5 weeks after starting metformin, with no other hepatotoxic agent. Initial labs showed hepatocellular pattern: total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, ALT 1093 U/L, AST 1152 U/L, ALP 176 U/L, ALT/ALP ratio >5; normal INR and eosinophil counts. Metformin was discontinued with supportive care only; AST fell to 358 (day 2) and 71 (day 4), ALT to 747 (day 2) and 432 (day 4), bilirubin to 0.8 (day 3); labs normal 10 days after discharge. Viral hepatitis A/B/C, autoimmune and metabolic liver disease testing (iron, antimitochondrial/antinuclear/antismooth-muscle antibodies, ceruloplasmin, copper), abdominal ultrasound and MRCP were unremarkable. No rechallenge, causality instrument, or formal assessment reported.

raw_record.support_text: AstraZeneca decided to withdraw its anticoagulant Exanta (ximelagatran) following safety concerns related to liver toxicity. Phase III trials had raised questions about liver toxicity, and AstraZeneca pulled the drug after discovering a new case of serious liver injury in an ongoing trial examining use over 35 days. All clinical trials were ended and regulatory applications withdrawn.
raw_record.extra_details: Sold as Exanta; anticoagulant positioned as an alternative to warfarin. Phase III trials showed efficacy comparable to warfarin and low-molecular-weight heparin for deep vein thrombosis and stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, but raised liver toxicity questions. Withdrawal triggered by a new case of serious liver injury in an ongoing trial examining treatment over 35 days; all clinical trials were ended and all regulatory applications withdrawn.
