raw_record.support_text: In two presented cases, terfenadine administration was followed within a few weeks by acute cholestatic hepatitis. Rechallenge was not performed because of severity, but the temporal relation between drug administration and jaundice, absence of other identifiable causes of hepatitis, and liver histology compatible with drug-induced disease argued in favour of a causal relation between terfenadine and the observed liver abnormalities. The authors state that cholestatic hepatitis is a rare and probably idiosyncratic reaction to terfenadine.
raw_record.extra_details: Two case reports; rechallenge not performed in either case; no previous personal or family history of liver disease and no hepatitis risk factors; initial liver tests AST 232 IU/L, ALT 665 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 146 IU/L, total bilirubin 185 µmol/L; liver biopsy showed preservation of architecture, intracellular and intracanalicular cholestasis in a centrilobular pattern, mild portal tract fibrosis, and inflammation with neutrophilic and eosinophilic leucocytes, compatible with drug-induced hepatotoxicity; total bilirubin rose to a maximum of 909 µmol/L over 6 weeks after stopping; liver tests returned to normal within 3 months; product monograph (Seldane) notes isolated reports of jaundice, cholestatic hepatitis and hepatitis from marketing experience but without clear causal relationship; only one previous possible terfenadine hepatitis report found on MEDLINE.

The paracetamol overdose of 50 g caused acute liver failure in this patient.

The case is reported primarily to describe acute pulmonary oedema occurring after intermittent haemodialysis about 9 days after the paracetamol overdose, attributed to neurogenic pulmonary oedema.

raw_record.support_text: Cerebral oedema is described as a well-recognized feature of acute liver failure, particularly following paracetamol (acetaminophen) self-poisoning, with liver damage typically greatest 3-4 days after the overdose and resolving in survivors. The patient in this case ingested a potentially lethal amount of paracetamol and developed acute hepatic necrosis/liver failure. The metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone is separately described as toxic to renal tubules causing acute kidney injury, not liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (self-poisoning) context rather than therapeutic use; single-agent attribution with no competing co-suspect described in this context.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of acute hepatic necrosis with acute liver failure; cerebral oedema and possible brain stem swelling/herniation are recognized complications of paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (cerebellar herniation is a recognized cause of death in acute liver failure). Liver damage peaks ~3-4 days after overdose and resolves in survivors without liver transplantation. Patient treated promptly with n-acetylcysteine, which reduces severity of acute liver injury and improves spontaneous recovery. N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone, a paracetamol metabolite, is toxic to renal tubules and can cause acute kidney injury typically 7-10 days after overdose (kidney, not liver).

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes indications for emergency liver transplantation after a paracetamol overdose, based on King's College Hospital criteria (arterial pH < 7.30 more than 24 h after ingestion, or prothrombin time > 100 s with serum creatinine > 300 µmol/L and encephalopathy of at least Grade 3). Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose is thereby presented as a recognized cause of acute liver failure. Fig. 4 shows the survival curve for acetaminophen acute liver failure patients managed without transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver failure arises specifically after deliberate paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose; applies to ALF patients with Grade 3-4 encephalopathy considered for transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported survival rates of 39-67% for paracetamol patients with Grade 3-4 encephalopathy managed without transplantation (Fig. 4). Acute liver failure transplantation criteria for paracetamol overdose: arterial pH < 7.30 (>24 h after ingestion) or prothrombin time > 100 s plus serum creatinine > 300 µmol/L plus Grade 3+ encephalopathy; these criteria identified 77% of fatal cases while 88.6% of the remaining cases survived. Overdose often an impulsive parasuicidal gesture in a young person with good psychiatric prognosis.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of 449 cadaveric renal transplant recipients (mycophenolate mofetil 2 g/day, n=167; 3 g/day, n=166; or azathioprine 1–2 mg/kg/day, n=166), no hepatotoxicity was reported in the mycophenolate mofetil groups. In a separate randomized trial of 49 renal allograft patients given mycophenolate mofetil (100–3500 mg/day), bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, and nephrotoxicity were not observed.
raw_record.extra_details: Mycophenolate mofetil evaluated for prevention of acute rejection after renal transplantation, given with antithymocyte globulin or Minnesota antilymphocyte globulin, cyclosporine, and prednisone. The 449-patient US Renal Transplant Mycophenolate Mofetil Study Group trial reported no hepatotoxicity; the 49-patient dose-ranging trial explicitly stated hepatotoxicity was not observed. Reported adverse effects were GI (diarrhea, esophagitis, gastritis, GI hemorrhage), anemia, hypertension, and opportunistic infections; neutropenia and thrombocytopenia occurred infrequently. Mycophenolate mofetil is primarily eliminated renally as the glucuronide metabolite mycophenolic acid glucuronide (MPAG).

raw_record.support_text: In pooled analyses of the ENLIVEN trial and phase 1 extension (N=130, median follow-up 39 months), 92% of pexidartinib-treated patients experienced aminotransferase elevations (dose-dependent, resolved with treatment interruption), and 4 (3%) cases of mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity occurred within the first 8 weeks of treatment, all recovering within 1-7 months after discontinuation. A further pooled analysis of the clinical program (N=140) found 91% with dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations (66% of ALT/AST increases were 1 to <3x ULN) and 5 (4%) cases of mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity, all recovering after discontinuation. The US prescribing information includes a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity, and a retrospective analysis of 3-year hepatic safety data from the tREMS program (N=451) found 21 (4.7%) patients met criteria for a hepatic AE or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of a serious and potentially fatal liver injury, with event onset within 2 months of starting pexidartinib.
raw_record.extra_details: Pooled analyses of ENLIVEN (phase 3 trial) + phase 1 extension (N=130; median follow-up 39 mo): 92% aminotransferase elevations, 4 (3%) mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity within first 8 weeks, recovered within 1-7 months after discontinuation. Clinical program pooled analysis (N=140): 91% dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations resolved with interruption, 66% of ALT/AST increases were 1 to <3x ULN, 5 (4%) mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity recovered after discontinuation. Final ENLIVEN analysis (median follow-up 31 mo, cutoff April 2021): no new safety signals, no additional mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity cases. Indication: diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor. USPI carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity; drug available only through the TURALIO REMS (tREMS) program. tREMS retrospective hepatic safety analysis (N=451): 21 (4.7%) met criteria for hepatic AE or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of serious and potentially fatal liver injury; onset within 2 months; treatment interrupted in 1, permanently discontinued in 20. Both ALT (UMLS:C0151905) and AST (UMLS:C0151904) elevations reported.

raw_record.support_text: A liver biopsy showed hepatitis with a dense predominantly mononuclear portal infiltrate containing scattered eosinophils, a mild sinusoidal lobular mononuclear infiltrate, and piecemeal necrosis without bridging necrosis or evidence of underlying chronic liver disease. Treatment with aspirin, vitamin E, glucotrol, pravastatin, and troglitazone was discontinued and insulin was given for blood sugar control. The accompanying title frames the case as 'Troglitazone Hepatitis.' The patient's pruritus and diarrhea improved and liver chemistry tests (total bilirubin 36.9 mg/dl then 13.9 mg/dl, AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase) gradually improved and returned to normal by June 1998, with a normal prothrombin time.

Patient reported fatigue, diarrhea, anorexia, pruritus, and 10-pound weight loss. Labs improved by February 1998 (bilirubin 13.9 mg/dl, ALT 218 U/L) and returned to normal by June 1998.

raw_record.support_text: A 37-year-old man developed drug-induced hepatitis after a course of 0.5% chloramphenicol eye drops for conjunctivitis, presenting seven days after completing the drops with lethargy, pruritus, dark urine, and icteric sclera. Liver function tests showed predominant transaminitis (AST 868 IU/l, bilirubin 32 µmol/l, alkaline phosphatase 224 IU/l), and a liver biopsy six weeks later showed interface hepatitis with an inflammatory infiltrate carrying a high eosinophil load, highly suggestive of drug-induced hepatitis. Causality scores for topical chloramphenicol were 7 on the Naranjo scale (probable) and 6 on the RUCAM scale (probable), indicating that topical chloramphenicol was the probable cause of this hepatitis; liver function normalized within 10 months after stopping treatment.

Liver screen negative (hepatitis A/B/C, CMV, EBV, toxoplasmosis, ECHO viruses, autoantibodies, copper/ferritin). raw_record.support_text: In a clinical case, the causal relationship between intravenous amiodarone exposure and acute hepatitis was established based on: sudden hepatic test abnormalities within 24 h after starting amiodarone, a hepatocellular injury pattern with peak aminotransferase levels more than 50 times the upper limit of normal, rapid improvement after amiodarone withdrawal, and exclusion of other causes. The paper describes acute intravenous amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity as a rare but potentially lethal side effect warranting serial liver-test monitoring.

raw_record.extra_details: Peak aminotransferases >50x upper limit of normal within 24 h of starting intravenous amiodarone; rapid improvement upon withdrawal; competing etiologies excluded. Possible mechanisms discussed include immunologic mediation, free radical/peroxidative membrane injury, increased PPARα expression, and polysorbate 80 (the IV solvent, absent in oral amiodarone) possibly contributing via hypotensive effect. Treatment supportive; N-acetylcysteine considered for acute liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: The letter presenting Public Health Service data on isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity states that, using criteria established by a panel of experts in hepatic disease, the incidence of hepatotoxicity was 2.3% per year for persons 50 to 64 years of age and 0.8% for persons over 64 years of age, and 1.7% per year for all persons 50 or more years of age. The discussion refers to 'isoniazid hepatitis' and reports age-specific incidence of 'isoniazid-induced hepatitis' for adults taking isoniazid.
raw_record.extra_details: Data from the Public Health Service isoniazid hepatitis surveillance study adjudicated by a panel of hepatic-disease experts. Reported incidence of hepatotoxicity, computed excluding from the denominator persons not clearly at risk, was per year: about 0.2% for ages 20-34, about 0.7% for ages 35-49, about 2.3% (high) / 1.6% (low) for ages 50-64, about 0.8% (high) / 0.6% (low) for ages >64, and 1.7% per year for all persons 50 or more years of age. The author argues the method tends to overestimate incidence because some excluded persons were probably taking the drug; the 'true' age-specific incidence likely lies between the high and low figures. Context is isoniazid preventive therapy for tuberculosis; the standard method discussed is 300 mg daily in adults. Whether high-dose twice-weekly isoniazid would reduce the incidence of isoniazid-related hepatotoxicity is stated as not known.

raw_record.support_text: A patient treated with captopril developed persisting jaundice after a presumptive diagnosis of cholangitis; a liver biopsy showed cholestatic changes compatible with captopril-induced hepatitis, and bilirubin rose to 358 µmol/L with elevated aminotransferases. Captopril was discontinued and jaundice and pruritus resolved within 6 months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Presented with a small stone extracted from the common bile duct and classic cholangitis signs, an unresolved competing cause considered but judged most probably not responsible for the symptoms.
raw_record.extra_details: Captopril dosages in all patients were within the recommended range; lag period from therapy initiation to jaundice was 1 week to 10 months (mostly 1-8 weeks). Bilirubin levels ranged from 4.0 to 34.2 mg/dL in reported cases. Injury pattern was cholestatic or mixed cholestatic and hepatocellular in all but one of the reported cases; 7 of 9 biopsy specimens showed cholestatic changes. In this patient bilirubin reached 358 µmol/L, AST 462 U/L, ALT 192 U/L, with alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyltransferase back to normal; biopsy showed portal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with eosinophils, Kupffer cell hyperplasia, and hepatic cell degeneration. Dechallenge led to gradual improvement, with jaundice and pruritus resolving within 6 months.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a randomized comparison of intravenous acetylcysteine versus control in patients with fulminant hepatic failure resulting from paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose. Paracetamol overdose is attributed as the cause of the fulminant hepatic failure, with 48% (12/25) survival in the acetylcysteine-treated group versus 20% (5/25) in controls.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; patients presenting with fulminant hepatic failure after paracetamol overdose (median 28-32 hours from overdose to presentation at referring hospital).
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure following paracetamol overdose. Randomized controlled trial of intravenous acetylcysteine (25 patients) versus control (25 patients); survival 48% vs 20% (p=0.037; 95% CI 3% to 53%). Acetylcysteine treated patients showed fewer clinical signs of cerebral oedema (40% vs 68%, p=0.047) and less hypotension requiring inotropic support (48% vs 80%, p=0.018). Poor-prognosis criteria included admission pH <7.30, prothrombin time >100 s with serum creatinine >300 µmol/l and grade 3 or 4 coma, and rise in prothrombin time on day 4. Acetylcysteine was well tolerated with no hypersensitivity reactions. Paracetamol is also listed in the entities as the injuring agent (acetaminophen/paracetamol).

raw_record.support_text: The paper concludes that captopril is a cause of drug-induced liver injury in humans, reporting 14 cases of jaundice associated with captopril. Of these, 9 showed 'pure' cholestatic injury, 4 mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular injury, and only 1 'pure' hepatocellular injury. The authors describe the index case as a clear instance of captopril-induced cholestatic jaundice, with the mechanism appearing to be a hypersensitivity reaction, as jaundice and fever appeared within 2 weeks of starting the drug and subsided promptly upon withdrawal.
raw_record.extra_details: 14 icteric patients reviewed (including the authors' case; 3 previously reported). Jaundice was the most striking feature; 9 cases considered cholestatic with prominent pruritus; ERCP done in 4 and ultrasound in 7 to exclude extrahepatic obstruction. 5 patients had fever and rash, 3 had eosinophilia. Bilirubin ranged 4-35 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase >3x ULN in all but two patients. Per the pattern categorization, 9 cholestatic (hepatocanalicular), 1 'pure' hepatocellular, 4 mixed. Biopsy reports: two consistent with drug reaction, two cholestasis without inflammation, one intrahepatic cholestasis with mild parenchymal injury and portal eosinophilic infiltrate, one submassive necrosis (the pure hepatocellular patient), one ballooning degeneration and acidophilic bodies without cholestasis. Jaundice lasted 1 week to 6 months; 8 recovered, 3 died of other medical problems, 3 lost to follow-up. Index case: deep jaundice, pruritus, bilirubin >20 mg/dL, slight aminotransferase elevation, 11-fold alkaline phosphatase elevation; fever, chills, marked eosinophilia; jaundice and fever subsided on drug withdrawal (dechallenge). Dose of captopril at onset mean 225-800 mg/d; time to onset mean 46-150 d across subgroups. Mechanism proposed as hypersensitivity to captopril.

raw_record.support_text: A 58-year-old woman developed an atorvastatin-induced severe autoimmune hepatitis with a concomitant systemic lupus-like syndrome. Although atorvastatin was immediately withdrawn, the disease persisted and deteriorated to a fulminant course with evidence of acute hepatic failure; the patient recovered only after intense immunosuppressive therapy as used in solid organ transplantation. She was HLA DR3- and HLA DR4-positive.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was HLA DR3- and HLA DR4-positive (genetic susceptibility); concomitant systemic lupus-like syndrome; disease persisted and progressed despite drug withdrawal; required intense immunosuppressive therapy as used in solid organ transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: 58-year-old woman took atorvastatin for 7 months for primary hypercholesterolaemia before presentation with abdominal pain, jaundice and elevated liver function tests. Liver biopsy showed highly active chronic hepatitis with marked fibrosis; positive antinuclear antibodies. On admission: bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl (normal <1.14), AST 95 IU/l (2-18), ALT 263 IU/l (2-22), alkaline phosphatase 270 IU/l (50-155), prothrombin time 99%, IgG 2692 mg/dl. Failed conventional immunosuppression with corticosteroids and azathioprine; recovered fully after intense immunosuppression. Presented as the first report of drug-induced lupus-like syndrome concomitant with severe autoimmune hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The letter reports a case of acute liver toxicity induced by sildenafil citrate (Viagra). While therapeutic dosages (25–100 mg/day) are usually well tolerated, the authors describe a case of acute liver toxicity attributed to sildenafil.
raw_record.extra_details: A 49-year-old man with diabetes (treated with glibenclamide) and no liver disease risk factors took Viagra 50 mg/day for erectile dysfunction; routine blood tests were normal when sildenafil was started. Four weeks later he developed right hypochondriac pain without fever, jaundice, or encephalopathy, with palpable hepatomegaly and an increase in serum aminotransferases (AST 7.4x normal, ALT 1.2x) while GGT, ALP, and total bilirubin remained normal. Prothrombin time, hematocrit, leukocyte and eosinophil counts were normal; tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B core antibody, IgM and total anti-hepatitis A, anti-hepatitis C, and IgM anti-cytomegalovirus were negative, and anti-mitochondrial, anti-nuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies were absent. Liver tests normalized after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: The report is framed as 'Features of cloxacillin-induced cholestasis', attributing cholestatic liver injury to cloxacillin. The accompanying case table records multiple patients given cloxacillin, including one receiving cloxacillin alone (the present report), with time to onset of symptoms ranging from 3 to 27 days, jaundice duration from 15 to 100 days, and time to recovery from 23 to 180 days. The paper states the hepatotoxic effect of cloxacillin does not appear to be dose related and is reversible, and that rechallenge is not recommended because of the severity and duration of the toxic reaction.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism of hepatic injury is presumably hypersensitivity, though the exact mechanism is not clear; in the present report fever, rash, and eosinophilia were not present. Hepatotoxic effect is not dose-related and is reversible; rechallenge is not recommended due to severity and duration. Case table (refs 1-5 plus present report) details patients with cloxacillin alone or with concomitant drugs (nitrofurantoin, ampicillin, penicillin G, triamterene/Dyazide, digoxin/furosemide, isosorbide, azathioprine/prednisone); onset of symptoms 3-27 days, jaundice duration 15-100 days, recovery 23-180 days. Cloxacillin is a penicillin antibacterial agent.

raw_record.support_text: A 12-year-old girl with hyperthyroidism who had started treatment with propylthiouracil (PTU) 100 mg tid developed hepatitis. The drug was stopped and the clinical and laboratory findings of hepatitis disappeared within a week; she received no other hepatotoxic drugs and viral investigations were negative. The authors report this as the ninth reported case of PTU-induced hepatitis, with a clinical picture similar to viral hepatitis, noting that recovery usually follows drug withdrawal but that two fatal cases of PTU-induced hepatitis have been reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (12-year-old girl); indication of hyperthyroidism; prior urticarial rash with initial PTU exposure that resolved and recurred on rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose PTU 100 mg tid. Onset of urticarial rash on day 3 after first administration; symptoms (diarrhea, fever, headache, nausea, vomiting) developed within days of the second administration. Dechallenge led to resolution of hepatitis within one week. Mild jaundice appeared two days after admission; enlarged liver and spleen. No other drugs used and viral investigations negative. Ninth reported case of PTU-induced hepatitis; two fatal cases previously reported; recovery usually follows withdrawal of the drug. Clinical picture similar to viral hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: An 87-year-old man presented with severe acute liver injury <24 hours after a single 20 mg dose of rivaroxaban. The patient's R-value at initial elevation and peak was consistent with hepatocellular injury (R > 5), and a thorough workup to rule out other causes of severe hepatocellular injury was unrevealing. The diagnosis of DILI secondary to rivaroxaban was established; Hy's Law was fulfilled and the CIOMS/RUCAM score of 8 made the diagnosis probable. The paper states this rapid progression to acute liver failure after single-dose rivaroxaban had not been previously reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single-dose administration (one 20 mg rivaroxaban tablet) in an 87-year-old man, with liver injury presenting less than one day after the dose; patient also had pneumonia/sepsis treated with antibiotics and was otherwise described as healthy.
raw_record.extra_details: R-value > 5 at initial elevation and peak, consistent with hepatocellular injury; Hy's Law fulfilled; CIOMS/RUCAM score of 8 indicating probable causality; liver enzymes peaked about 47 hours after rivaroxaban administration; abdominal ultrasound showed diffuse hepatic echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis; N-acetylcysteine infusion initiated; patient stabilized and was discharged after 9 days. Authors note ~2.3% of rivaroxaban use is associated with ALT elevation <3x ULN and that only 17 reports of severe rivaroxaban-induced liver injury existed since 2008, typically presenting 1-8 weeks after multidose administration.

raw_record.support_text: In a clearly documented case, a patient being treated with sulfamethoxazole was admitted with arthralgia and hepatitis; symptoms subsided when the drug was discontinued and liver function tests returned to normal. Rechallenge with the congener drug sulfisoxazole resulted in recurrence of hepatitis with jaundice and an elevated serum transaminase level within one day, which again subsided on withdrawal. The temporal association between the second drug and the reappearance of hepatitis, together with rapid resolution on withdrawal, made it almost certain that sulfamethoxazole was a cause of hepatitis in this patient.
raw_record.extra_details: Presented as Gantanol. Case with rechallenge evidence: recurrence of hepatitis with jaundice and elevated serum transaminase within one day of sulfisoxazole (congener) re-exposure, resolving rapidly on withdrawal; initial presentation with arthralgia. Soluble sulfonamide implicated with four other temporally associated patients.

raw_record.support_text: In phase I clinical trials of the investigational anticancer agent N-MF (N-methylformamide), hepatic damage was seen in all patients at total doses between 80-870 mg/kg, and one autopsy showed irregular lobular disorganization, large hepatocytes, and areas of liver regeneration. In a second phase I study the authors reported liver function abnormalities and hepatomegaly and concluded that hepatic toxicity was dose dependent and readily reversible.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with solid tumors in investigational (phase I) anticancer trials; drug given orally or intravenously; degree of toxicity did not correlate well with the patient's general condition.
raw_record.extra_details: Laird Myers trial (started 1956): 5 patients, oral doses 0.1-4 g/day for 2-36 days, cumulative 4-34 g (highest 0.87 g/kg); hepatic damage in all patients at total doses 80-870 mg/kg; one patient received drug both IV and orally with toxicity at approximately the same total dose; autopsy in one patient showed irregular lobular disorganization, large hepatocytes, and liver regeneration. McVie trial: 20 patients, 50 cycles, oral or IV on a daily x5 schedule, highest dose 1,200 mg/m2/day; toxicities included nausea, vomiting, anorexia, sleepiness, phlebitis, alcohol flush, hepatomegaly, peripheral neuropathy; liver function abnormalities, with rises in bilirubin not correlating well with dose; conclusions: oral bioavailability 95%, urinary excretion <5%, MTD 1,000 mg/m2, hepatic toxicity dose dependent and reversible, recommended phase II dose 800 mg/m2.

raw_record.support_text: The authors formally assessed causality of the alosetron-associated acute hepatitis case using Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences criteria and the case was scored as 'probable.'
raw_record.extra_details: Reported as the first case of acute hepatitis associated with alosetron in clinical practice (female patient with diarrhea-predominant IBS). Causality scored 'probable' using CIOMS criteria. Per the package insert, mild serum ALT elevation incidence was similar in alosetron vs placebo clinical trials (1.0% vs 1.2%), with 1 case of hepatitis without jaundice of uncertain etiology in a 12-week study; no alosetron-associated hepatitis cases were found in postmarketing surveillance/literature or via manufacturer consultation. Mechanism unknown; alosetron is extensively metabolized in the liver by cytochrome P-450 enzymes. Absence of immunoallergic features raised the possibility of metabolic idiosyncrasy, but toxic metabolites of the parent compound have not been identified. No concomitant ischemic colitis, making ischemic hepatitis less likely.

raw_record.support_text: The patient ingested approximately 65 g of acetaminophen in an overdose. Follow-up acetaminophen level at approximately twelve hours post-ingestion was 322 mcg/mL and the patient remained on NAC until the level became undetectable on day 3. Peak AST/ALT were 1791/743 U/L with an INR of 1.44 on day 2; the patient was discharged after 4 days with no hepatic function abnormalities. The authors also note acetaminophen is the leading cause of liver transplantation in the United States and that toxic ingestions lead to depletion of hepatic glutathione, covalent binding to hepatocyte proteins, and centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis and hepatic failure if untreated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose ingestion of approximately 65 g of acetaminophen with concurrent ingestion of an undisclosed amount of melatonin; treated with NAC (increased to 18.75 mg/kg/hr) and hemodialysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient presented with severe acetaminophen ingestion; acetaminophen level 322 mcg/mL about 12 h post-ingestion, undetectable by day 3; peak AST/ALT 1791/743 U/L and INR 1.44 on day 2; NAC discontinued before full AST/ALT normalization with downward trend; extubated day 2; discharged to psychiatric facility after 4 days. Mechanism: therapeutic doses metabolized by CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which binds glutathione; in overdose NAPQI depletes glutathione and covalently binds hepatocyte proteins causing centrilobular necrosis and hepatic failure. Paper notes acetaminophen is the leading cause of liver transplantation in the US with ~450 acetaminophen-related deaths/year and ~50-70 thousand ED visits/year; toxic alcohol screen negative for ethylene glycol/methanol.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report two women who developed reversible hepatic dysfunction with sulindac. Sulindac had been started one month before admission for back pain and was stopped one week after developing jaundice. Case 1 was similar to previous reports in biochemical presentation, while Case 2 demonstrated a predominantly cholestatic picture. The authors note three prior cases of hepatitis associated with sulindac use.
raw_record.extra_details: Two female patients; sulindac started one month before admission for back pain, stopped one week after jaundice developed (dechallenge). Clinical jaundice without chronic liver disease stigmata; liver enzymes took seven months to return to normal (recovery). Case 2 showed a predominantly cholestatic picture; Case 1 similar to previous reports. Labs (case presented): SGOT 65 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 278 IU/l, bilirubin 213 µmol/l (12.6 mg/dl), normal albumin and thyroid indices, negative hepatitis markers, normal ultrasound/ERCP. Liver biopsy showed zone III (centrilobular) hepatocellular damage with acidophil bodies, focal hepatocyte drop-out with mononuclear infiltrates, mild small and large droplet steatosis, pigmented Kupffer cells, and dilated bile canaliculi with bile plugs. NSAID therapeutic indication.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a young child who developed severe hepatotoxicity, renal failure, and pancytopenia after repeated acetaminophen overdosing and who survived after supportive treatment and late N-acetylcysteine therapy. They note that previously reported cases of repeated acetaminophen overdosing in children either had a fatal outcome or presented with severe hepatotoxicity and/or renal failure.

raw_record.extra_details: Child developed severe hepatotoxicity together with renal failure and pancytopenia after repeated acetaminophen overdosing and survived with supportive treatment and late N-acetylcysteine therapy. Presenting signs included fever, vomiting, cough, lethargy, diffuse abdominal tenderness, soft tender liver extending 3-4 cm below costal margin, and anicteric skin. raw_record.support_text: APAP (acetaminophen) is primarily metabolized by glucuronide/sulfate conjugation to nontoxic mercaptate conjugates that are excreted. Above the toxic threshold, APAP administration produces NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine), a toxic compound that binds proteins resulting in hepatocyte necrosis, occurring when liver glutathione concentration decreases to <30% of normal levels. The paper frames this hepatotoxicity in the context of APAP overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (supratherapeutic) exposure; the reported patient ingested a toxic APAP amount, developed hepatocyte necrosis, and expired approximately 12 hours after intensive management.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: NAPQI protein binding and hepatocyte necrosis occurs once liver glutathione falls below 30% of normal levels. Patient case: managed with NAC, bicarbonate, pressors (vasopressin, epinephrine, neosynephrine), and CRRT consideration, but progressed to cardiopulmonary arrest and death. Clinical course also included a chest radiograph showing mild bilateral perihilar airspace opacities. Treatment guidance: activated charcoal if within 2 hours of ingestion; IV NAC regimen described (150 mg/kg over 30 min, 50 mg/kg over 4 h, 100 mg/kg over 16 h); discontinue NAC if serum APAP <10 micrograms/mL with normal transaminases.

Liver dysfunction developed about five months after initial troglitazone treatment, and the patient died despite hepatic auxiliary treatments such as plasmapheresis. Autopsy revealed focal liver cell necrosis, cholestasis and steatosis with lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltration and lack of regenerative activity. The authors state the fatal subacute hepatic failure was 'due unequivocally to troglitazone' and proposed metabolite aberration with accumulation of hepatotoxic metabolite(s), categorized as idiosyncratic liver injury.

Latency about 5 months before liver dysfunction; presented with jaundice and hepatic failure and died despite plasmapheresis, FFP, and methylprednisolone pulse. An etiological role for the drug was proved when the patient underwent a provocative challenge and developed evidence of hepatocellular damage, reversible on withdrawal of the drug. raw_record.extra_details: A 53-year-old male was treated with disulfiram 500 mg daily for 5 days followed by 250 mg daily for chronic alcoholism. On day 21 he developed jaundice, light stools, dark urine, scleral icterus, tender hepatomegaly; peak values were SGOT 1400 mU/ml, alkaline phosphatase 440 mU/ml, and serum bilirubin 9.8 mg/100 ml. HBsAg was negative. Percutaneous liver biopsy on day 28 showed portal inflammation, hepatocellular necrosis, and a moderate mostly mononuclear infiltrate. Initial liver chemistries (SGOT 30, SGPT 15, alkaline phosphatase 80 mU/ml, bilirubin 0.5 mg/100 ml) were normal. The paper recommends screening liver chemistries before and during disulfiram therapy.

raw_record.support_text: A case report describes a patient who developed isolated acute hepatitis after propofol administration and had spontaneous resolution of the hepatitis. The liver biopsy results and rapid normalization of the transaminases were consistent with hepatitis from drug or toxin injury, and the validated Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method gave a drug causality score of +6 (scale -9 to +15), indicating a probable relationship between propofol and the acute hepatitis.

Two prior literature cases of isolated acute hepatitis after propofol (a 66-year-old male after therapeutic ERCP and a 17-year-old female one day after femoral hernia repair) also resolved spontaneously; neither had liver biopsy confirmation. A liver biopsy showed severe inflammatory changes with centrilobular and bridging necrosis, focal liver cell necrosis with steatosis and cholestasis, and portal fibrosis with bile-duct proliferation. Biopsy showed centrilobular and bridging necrosis, focal necrosis with histiocytic accumulation, slight steatosis and cholestasis, portal fibrosis, bile-duct proliferation and inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, polymorphs and eosinophils; no Mallory bodies. raw_record.support_text: This letter to the editor reports a case of methyldopa-induced granulomatous hepatitis with positive rechallenge. Methyldopa, a widely used antihypertensive agent, is stated to cause chronic or acute hepatitis in about six percent of patients, and much more infrequently granulomatous hepatitis.

Improved on withdrawal, then relapsed with jaundice one week after rechallenge (bilirubin 4651.2 umol/L, ALP 696 IU/L, GGT 252 IU/L, normal transaminases), resolving after permanent withdrawal. The paper notes methyldopa hepatitis is generally thought to be a delayed hypersensitivity manifestation (auto-antibodies against endoplasmic reticulum), spanning acute forms indistinguishable from viral hepatitis, and less common forms such as bridging necrosis, cholestasis with necrosis, submassive periportal fibrosis, regenerative nodules, and cirrhosis; a 1982 Bezahler case of fatal granulomatous hepatitis and myocarditis is also referenced.

raw_record.support_text: The survey reports that etifoxine can be associated with acute hepatitis showing a cytolytic or mixed biological pattern of liver injury, based on 18 previously reported cases plus 11 additional cases. Evidence supporting a causative role includes uniform liver damage (64% cytolytic hepatitis among acute liver injury cases), time to onset after starting etifoxine of ≤2 months in 92% of cases, lack of association with known hepatotoxicants in 68%, exclusion of non-drug causes of hepatitis in most patients, and favorable outcome after etifoxine discontinuation in all patients with available follow-up. The causal relationship was considered plausible in 64% of patients who developed acute liver injury; the mechanism is unknown, and the lack of clear clinical or biological signs of hypersensitivity supports an idiosyncratic rather than immune-allergic mechanism.
raw_record.extra_details: Total of 29 acute hepatitis cases (18 previously reported in detail plus 11 additional). Time to onset ≤2 months in 92% of cases; 64% cytolytic pattern on acute liver injury; no known hepatotoxic co-medication in 68% of cases; other common causes (viral hepatitis, biliary tract abnormalities) excluded in most patients; favorable outcome after etifoxine discontinuation in all patients with available follow-up. Causal relationship judged plausible in 64% of acute liver injury patients. Mechanism unknown; classified as idiosyncratic (non-immune-allergic). Setting is ordinary therapeutic use of etifoxine as anxiolytic.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 51-year-old Korean woman treated for onychomycosis with oral itraconazole 100 mg daily who, after 116 days of therapy, developed nausea and jaundice. A diagnosis of drug-induced hepatitis was made based on absent infectious aetiology (negative HAV/HBV/HCV, ANA, and anti-DNA serologies); liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis and laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 13.1 mg/dl, ALP 214 IU/l, AST 721 IU/l, and ALT 844 IU/l. Symptoms and liver tests improved after itraconazole was discontinued, and the authors state they consider the patient's reaction to be an adverse reaction to itraconazole.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Long-term oral itraconazole treatment extending beyond the usual 30-day treatment limit (116 days); unresolved possibility of hepatitis C infection was noted by the authors as a potential competing cause despite negative serologies.
raw_record.extra_details: Standard 100 mg daily dose for onychomycosis; onset of nausea and jaundice after 116 days of therapy; laboratory values at presentation total bilirubin 13.1 mg/dl, ALP 214 IU/l, AST 721 IU/l, ALT 844 IU/l; abdominal ultrasound showed gallbladder wall thickening attributed to acute hepatitis; liver biopsy showed changes of acute hepatitis; negative hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B core antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, anti-HCV, ANA, and anti-DNA antibody; improvement and hospital discharge with bilirubin 5.2 mg/dl, ALP 100 IU/l, AST 53 IU/l, ALT 72 IU/l after discontinuation and conservative treatment; authors cite Tucker et al. assessment of 189 long-term itraconazole patients and a Lavrijsen et al. case with definite hepatic injury. The paper also notes that in the introduction itraconazole is described as better tolerated and less hepatotoxic than ketoconazole.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a case report of acute cholestatic hepatitis caused by flutamide, an oral antiandrogen used for advanced prostate cancer. They note that flutamide is described as capable of producing severe hepatotoxicity in a very low percentage of cases, and report a case that resolved favorably after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of an 82-year-old man with advanced prostate adenocarcinoma treated with flutamide 250 mg every 8 hours (started October 2001, jaundice noted early January 2002). Labs: GPT 1369 U/l, GOT 1102 U/l, bilirubin 13.6 mg/dl, GGT 586 U/l, LDH 400 U/l, platelets 97,000, prothrombin time 51.5%. Negative HAV/HBV/HCV/EBV serologies, normal abdominal ultrasound. Comedications: amiloride, hydrochlorothiazide, acetylsalicylic acid, lovastatin, atenolol, and leuprorelin (analog of GnRH). Jaundice with coluria clinically; recovered and discharged at 2 weeks with improving labs, flutamide treatment prohibited thereafter. Flutamide marketed since 1989; also mentioned as sometimes used in benign prostatic hyperplasia and hirsutism, with debatable use given risk of severe hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Deltenre et al. reported the first case of mesalazine-induced autoimmune hepatitis. Laboratory changes indicative of hepatocellular inflammation were observed in a 65-year-old man during 8 months of treatment with mesalazine, 3 grams daily. High titer smooth muscle antibodies (SMA) and ANA, abnormal serum immunoglobulin G concentration, and histologic features of interface hepatitis and fibrosis of the portal, periportal, and perisinusoidal areas supported the diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis, and laboratory abnormalities fully resolved within 2 months after drug discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of mesalazine-induced autoimmune hepatitis; 65-year-old man, 8 months treatment at 3 grams daily; high titer SMA and ANA, abnormal serum IgG, histologic interface hepatitis with portal/periportal/perisinusoidal fibrosis; laboratory abnormalities fully resolved within 2 months after discontinuation. Mesalazine (5-aminosalicylic acid) was developed to deliver 5-ASA to inflamed GI mucosa and avoid sulphasalazine toxicity, but the report and others indicate 5-aminosalicylic acid has its own potential for liver injury and should be discontinued in patients with liver dysfunction.

raw_record.extra_details: Single-patient case report (PMID 10206223). The patient (treated with niacin for hyperlipidemia) presented with acute hepatitis showing a 'starry sky liver' sonographic pattern; admission labs included AST 168 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 97 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, PT 22.1 s, INR 1.95; hepatitis A, B, C serology negative. Niacin (nicotinic acid) frequently used to treat hyperlipidemia; side effects include flushing, nausea, vomiting, decreased appetite, abdominal discomfort, diaphoresis, hypotension, hyperglycemia, and hepatic dysfunction. Starry sky liver not previously reported with niacin-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: A 31-year-old primigravida was treated with nitrofurantoin 100 mg/day in the 36th week of gestation for dysuria with enterococcus in urine culture. After induced delivery, repeated labs showed elevated AST and ALT with negative hepatitis C and B markers, and the patient was subicteric. Nitrofurantoin was discontinued, and discontinuation plus methylprednisolone therapy significantly lowered liver enzyme levels. The authors concluded this was probably toxic liver damage caused by nitrofurantoin. The case is described as a rare case of acute toxic hepatitis in pregnancy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pregnant patient (31-year-old primigravida, 36th week of gestation); delivery was induced near term because of hypertension, which coexists with the exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 100 mg/day for treatment of dysuria from enterococcus urinary tract infection. Elevated aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase, negative hepatitis C and B markers, patient subicteric, normal coagulation and complete blood count, slight hepatomegaly on ultrasound without focal or diffuse lesions. Nitrofurantoin was discontinued and methylprednisolone therapy was introduced; liver enzymes significantly decreased to near normal. Authors described the injury as 'acute toxic hepatitis' (toxic drug-induced hepatitis).

raw_record.support_text: A 60-year-old male with left renal cell carcinoma and suspected lung metastases was started on pazopanib 800 mg/day. On day 29 AST/ALT rose to 102/205 U/L, then on day 37 AST 184 U/L and ALT 305 U/L (both grade 3), at which point the patient was diagnosed with pazopanib-associated liver injury. Pazopanib was withdrawn and later resumed at 400 mg/day with UDCA, but on day 92 AST/ALT again increased to 117/233 U/L, after which pazopanib was permanently discontinued. Plasma pazopanib concentrations ranged 39.6-56.7 µg/mL.

raw_record.support_text: The most important side effect of isoniazid administration is hepatitis, which can be fatal. By 1969 it had been established that isoniazid frequently caused asymptomatic hepatocellular injury, and fatal isoniazid hepatitis during preventive therapy was recognized in 1970. In a US Public Health Service surveillance study of isoniazid preventive therapy, the risk of isoniazid-associated hepatitis was age-related, being rare in persons aged <20 years and increasing to over 2% in those aged >50 years, with deaths recognized; an estimated mortality rate of 14 per 100,000 persons starting IPT and 23.2 per 100,000 completing a full course was reported.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Preventive therapy for latent tuberculosis infection; hepatitis risk varies directly with age and is potentiated by alcohol and possibly concomitant acetaminophen; hepatitis deaths clustered with possible cofactor potentiation; increased hepatitis-mortality risk suggested in women especially post-partum.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis most frequent during the initial 3 months of treatment. Less important side effects include polyneuropathy, sedation, gastrointestinal symptoms and rash. Isoniazid-associated hepatitis mortality estimated at 14 per 100,000 persons starting IPT and 23.2 per 100,000 completing a full course. Similar age relationship found in the Eastern Europe trial but with lower incidence than the US study.

raw_record.support_text: At least 10 cases of hepatitis due to troglitazone, a thiazolidinedione used to treat diabetes mellitus, were reported in 2000, contributing to its removal from the marketplace. Most studies showed severe lesions with zone 3 necrosis, bridging and confluent necrosis, or submassive necrosis with reactive bile ductules; portal infiltrates were mononuclear or mixed lymphocytic-plasmacytic with eosinophils, and hepatocyte ballooning, apoptosis, and cholestasis were frequent; portal and lobular granulomas were present in one case.

It further states that APAP overdose is often associated with acute liver failure and renal damage in humans.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Human injury is attributed to APAP overdose, not therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: US Poison Control Center statistics: >56,000 emergency room visits, 2,600 hospitalizations, and an estimated 458 deaths yearly due to APAP overdose; APAP overdose also associated with renal damage. Implicated toxic mechanism described elsewhere: CYP-450-mediated reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) reacts with GSH, and at overdose GSH depletion allows NAPQI to bind cellular proteins and initiate lipid peroxidation leading to hepatic injury.

raw_record.support_text: A 65-year-old woman taking quinine sulphate for nocturnal leg cramps presented with episodes of malaise, fever, nausea, vomiting, and polyarthralgia, and granulomatous hepatitis was diagnosed with no common cause found. Upon rechallenge with quinine sulphate her temperature rose and symptoms returned within hours, transaminase activities rose within 48 hours along with erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and after withdrawal symptoms abated and transaminase activities returned to normal. The paper concludes that the biochemical response to quinine challenge implicates the drug as the cause of the liver disturbances and that quinine should be added to the list of drugs known to cause granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of quinine-induced granulomatous hepatitis (case report of a 65-year-old woman). Administered as quinine sulphate for nocturnal leg cramps; four episodes of malaise, fever, nausea, vomiting, and polyarthralgia over five months, each spontaneously subsiding after 3-28 days. No common cause for granulomatous hepatitis found. Rechallenge with quinine sulphate reproduced fever within hours and returned symptoms; transaminases and ESR rose within 48 hours; dechallenge led to symptom resolution and normalization of transaminases. Concurrent daily medications (pindolol, methyclothiazide) and rare alcohol use were noted but not implicated. Granulomatous hepatitis is the attributed specific phenotype, recorded under other_specific_phenotype. Related optical isomer quinidine was noted as a previously reported cause of granulomatous hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes chronic active hepatitis caused by benzarone, a benzofuran derivative used in Europe for peripheral venous disorders. The patient developed jaundice with elevated serum ALT while on the drug, which decreased upon discontinuation, and liver lesions were those of chronic active hepatitis with anti-smooth muscle antibodies present.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the clinical syndrome and lesion of hepatic injury induced by valproate (VPA), noting that it is readily distinguishable from phenytoin hepatic injury. VPA injury involves microvesicular steatosis and/or zonal necrosis, with a syndrome including jaundice, ascites, coma, terminal renal failure, hemorrhagic phenomena, and hypoglycemia in ~1/3 of patients, sometimes presenting as overt liver failure. The authors conclude that the large variety of other drugs employed cannot be held accountable, attributing the injury to VPA.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Young individuals appear disproportionately vulnerable; over 80% of patients with severe VPA toxicity are less than 20 years old, though only ~40% of VPA users are in this group.
raw_record.extra_details: Lesion characterized by microvesicular steatosis (seen in ~80% of patients) and/or zonal necrosis, centrilobular necrosis, and massive hepatocellular necrosis; syndrome includes jaundice, with or without ascites, progressing to coma and terminal renal failure, hemorrhagic phenomena, nausea, vomiting, lassitude, generalized edema, and hypoglycemia recorded in 1/3 of patients. Idiosyncrasy attributed to metabolic aberration producing toxic metabolites (e.g., 4-en-VPA) rather than hypersensitivity, since the syndrome lacks rash/eosinophilia and steatosis is not characteristic of hypersensitivity; onset after >1 month exposure in over 80% of patients. VPA metabolized via glucuronide conjugation, beta-oxidation, omega-oxidation (giving 2-n-propylglutaric acid, 4-en-VPA, 5-hydroxy-VPA), and omega1-oxidation (4-hydroxy-VPA via 3-en-VPA). Observed metabolic abnormalities include inhibited glycolysis/citric acid cycle, depleted hepatic glycogen, depressed plasma hydroxybutyrate and ketones, hyperglycinemia/glycinuria, propionic acidemia, and hyperammonemia from suppressed urea cycle. Lesion resembles Jamaican vomiting sickness and Reye's syndrome and is reproducible by 4-pentanoic acid; structural similarity noted to hypoglycin A metabolite and 4-pentanoic acid.

raw_record.support_text: The authors concluded that this patient was likely to have ticlopidine-induced cholestatic hepatitis because of the temporal relationship with commencement of the medication and resolution with its withdrawal; the liver biopsy was consistent with a drug-induced phenomenon, and there was an absence of other possible aetiologies on laboratory testing and imaging. They recommended that ticlopidine be considered as a cause of intrahepatic cholestasis in patients presenting with jaundice.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of cholestatic hepatitis attributed to ticlopidine in a patient presenting with jaundice. Causality was based on temporal relationship to drug start, resolution (dechallenge) on withdrawal, a liver biopsy consistent with a drug-induced phenomenon (portal tract fibrosis, inflammation, and florid bile ductule proliferation highlighted by cytokeratin 7, with mixed inflammation including eosinophils and neutrophils), and exclusion of other aetiologies. The paper notes hepatotoxicity has been reported in up to 4.4% of cases, mainly as asymptomatic elevations of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, and that cholestatic hepatitis is a rare side-effect; typically jaundice appears after a latent period of about 6 weeks and lasts approximately 4 months, and the condition is generally benign with resolution after drug withdrawal. Pathogenesis is unknown, with both direct intrinsic hepatotoxicity and immuno-allergic mechanisms proposed.

raw_record.support_text: A non-alcoholic, previously healthy 49-year-old man was put on tienilic acid 250 mg daily for mild hypertension. raw_record.support_text: The paper documents for the first time a marked increase in malformed compacted mitochondria in the liver in a case of hepatic toxicity due to the antiretroviral drug Stavudine. The patient had hepatic toxicity manifesting as lactic acidosis, and the liver biopsy showed features of mitochondrial cytopathy except for the expected steatosis; liver function and lactic acidosis reversed when the drug was withdrawn (dechallenge).
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of antiretroviral (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor) hepatic toxicity featuring lactic acidosis and mitochondrial cytopathy on liver biopsy. Electron microscopy showed mitochondrial proliferation with oncocytic changes, reduced and occasionally abnormal cristae, and dividing mitochondria with a median partition of two parallel inner membranes within a single outer membrane; steatosis was notably absent. Dechallenge: liver functions returned toward normal and lactic acidosis resolved upon drug withdrawal. Mechanism discussed as mitochondrial biogenesis/dysfunction with decreased electron transport, reduced ATP and NAD, and inhibition of fatty acid beta-oxidation.

raw_record.support_text: Nimesulide-associated hepatitis was diagnosed, and the patient was treated with methylprednisolone. Liver function tests and aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels improved rapidly and were within normal limits 3 weeks after admission; the patient was discharged asymptomatic. The paper reports this as the 12th case of nimesulide-associated liver injury published, with unclear frequency and mechanism, and notes nimesulide causes two characteristic histologic patterns: centrilobular hepatocellular necrosis and pure cholestasis resembling ethinyl estradiol- or androgen-induced cholestasis. This patient showed extensive centrilobular necrosis with a mixed eosinophil-rich infiltrate and a severe vasculitis of hepatic veins.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a patient admitted with nausea, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, pleural effusions, and icteric sclerae. Symptoms recurred 5 days after nimesulide was restarted and the patient was readmitted after 12 days of repeated intake (positive rechallenge). Laboratory findings showed the typical pattern of acute liver failure (AST 1006 U/l, ALT 1115 U/l, prothrombin time 39%, bilirubin 2.2 mg/dl) with marked eosinophilia (35%). Cavography/duplex sonography excluded large-vein thrombotic outflow block (Budd-Chiari) but showed drop-out of hepatic vein branches and decreased portal flow; biopsy showed centrilobular necrosis in zones 3 and 2, mixed eosinophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate, and severe vasculitis of hepatic vein branches. Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic causes excluded. Concurrent medication was oral contraceptives (cyproterone acetate 2 mg/day and ethinyl estradiol 0.035 mg/day for 5 months). Treated with methylprednisolone (100 mg/day, tapering to 4 mg) and diuretics; recovered within 3 weeks. Reported as the 12th published case of nimesulide-associated liver injury.

A follow-up report states that after 10 to 12 weeks of fialuridine (1.5 mg/kg/day orally), virus-carrier and uninfected woodchucks had levels of lactic acidosis and hepatic failure much like those seen in humans, with the dose only slightly higher than the 0.1 and 0.25 mg/kg/day used in the 1993 trial.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with chronic hepatitis B infection treated in an experimental clinical trial; outcomes include hepatic failure with lactic acidosis leading to five deaths.
raw_record.extra_details: Nucleoside analogue used as experimental treatment for chronic hepatitis B. Delayed mitochondrial toxicity was considered the probable cause; in vitro, the inhibition constant (Ki) of fialuridine triphosphate against DNA polymerase gamma was lower than that found with other eukaryotic DNA polymerases. 1993 trial used 0.1 and 0.25 mg/kg/day orally; woodchuck studies at 1.5 mg/kg/day orally produced similar lactic acidosis and hepatic failure after 10 to 12 weeks. Subtext: patients' hepatitis was examined as a possible exacerbating factor but viral infection was not considered to produce or exacerbate the toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The patient was admitted with probable sulfasalazine induced hepatitis 3 weeks after commencing the drug, consistent with the 3-week syndrome, characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, and widespread erythematous rash followed by rising liver enzymes and bilirubin, with rarely reported fatal fulminant hepatic failure. raw_record.support_text: A 46-year-old man developed acute severe hepatic injury (malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly) while taking losartan, 50 mg/d, for hypertension. Laboratory evaluation showed markedly elevated aminotransferases (AST 2042 U/L, ALT 2574 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 738 U/L, and total bilirubin 164 µmol/L; serologic, viral, autoimmune, iron, and copper studies were negative. Injury resolved after losartan was discontinued and atenolol substituted. On rechallenge with losartan 25 mg/d, hepatotoxicity recurred within 3 weeks (mild jaundice, tender hepatomegaly; AST 206 U/L, ALT 254 U/L, total bilirubin 72 µmol/L), and liver tests normalized after losartan was again stopped. The case is presented under the heading 'Losartan-Induced Hepatotoxicity.'
raw_record.extra_details: Losartan 50 mg/d given for moderate essential hypertension after enalapril was stopped for cough. Initial episode: about 1 month of losartan exposure preceding admission, with 2-week symptom history; AST 2042 U/L, ALT 2574 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 738 U/L, GGT 266 U/L, total bilirubin 164 µmol/L (conjugated 152 µmol/L), moderately prolonged prothrombin time, normal eosinophil count; negative hepatitis A/B/C and other viral serologies, normal/negative iron, copper, and autoantibody tests. Dechallenge with atenolol substitution led to improvement (one month later AST 154 U/L, ALT 218 U/L, bilirubin 39 µmol/L) and full normalization 4 months after admission. Positive rechallenge with losartan 25 mg/d after atenolol was stopped produced recurrence within 3 weeks; losartan was then definitively discontinued and the liver profile normalized 1.5 months later.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes the well-known clinical picture of acute acetaminophen poisoning: after a single massive dose (usually 10 g or more), patients develop nausea, vomiting, and then biochemical evidence of severe hepatocellular injury with dramatic increases in serum transaminase levels, severe hypoprothrombinemia, and hypoglycemia. Liver biopsy usually shows acute centrilobular necrosis, and death, when it occurs, is usually secondary to hepatic failure. All three presented patients had ingested excessive amounts and showed severe hepatocellular injury with markedly elevated transaminases and prothrombin times; enhancetoxicity in alcohol and other drug abusers is attributed to a reactive toxic metabolite generated through the mixed function oxidase system, with glutathione depletion on overdose.

Additional features included renal failure (two patients) and hemolysis (one). Mechanism: highly reactive toxic metabolite (via mixed function oxidase minor pathway) detoxified by glutathione conjugation; in massive overdose glutathione is depleted and the metabolite binds to macromolecules causing cell death.; extra_field_unused: None

raw_record.support_text: Stricker et al. described 50 cases of nitrofurantoin-associated and 2 cases of hydroxymethyl nitrofurantoin-associated hepatic injury reported to The Netherlands Center for Adverse Reaction Monitoring; nitrofurantoin was likely responsible for the hepatic injury in 38 of these cases. Acute reactions (25 of 38 cases) were reported twice as frequently as chronic reactions (13 of 38 cases).
raw_record.extra_details: Stricker et al. Netherlands pharmacovigilance series: nitrofurantoin likely responsible in 38 of 50 cases; acute (25) twice as common as chronic (13). Acute reactions occurred within 1 week of starting therapy in 52% and between 1-6 weeks in 28%. Some patients developed rash and eosinophilia; chronic injury associated with positive antinuclear and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies. Injury usually reversible but fatal in 5 reported instances: two in Stricker's series (one acute, one chronic, massive hepatic necrosis), one cirrhosis death among 5 Iwarson cases despite discontinuation, and two of five Sharp cases died of severe hepatic necrosis after continuing therapy after jaundice onset. Affected patients ranged in age (61-80 years most frequent; the described patient was 40), and women more frequently affected, possibly reflecting prescribing predominance to women. Case described: female, acute hepatocellular reaction, symptoms 2 weeks after starting therapy (jaundice, malaise, abdominal discomfort, nausea/vomiting, no fever, no rash/eosinophilia), massive hepatic necrosis on liver explant, successful liver transplantation.

Of these, 14 were paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and 5 were listed as drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Among the paracetamol overdose cases, 7 survived without liver transplantation (LT), 1 had LT and survived, 4 had LT and died, and 2 died without LT. This explicitly attributes paracetamol overdose as a cause of fulminant hepatic failure in children.

raw_record.support_text: A 14-year-old girl presenting with jaundice, ascites, and coagulation failure was found to have been on multiple Ayurvedic herbal medications for seizures since age 9. Chemical and toxicology analyses revealed extremely high arsenic levels in several herbal formulations (up to 1982.4 mg/kg). Nail (2.8 mg/kg) and hair (4.3 mg/kg) arsenic were elevated in the patient while family members were below detection. After excluding genetic causes by clinical exome analysis (insignificant NPHP4, PEX12, HNF1B variants), a final diagnosis of Ayurvedic medicine-related severe alcoholic hepatitis with background non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (hepatoportal sclerosis variant with incomplete septal cirrhosis) due to chronic arsenic exposure was made. Injury resolved after stopping the medicines.

The paper describes liver biopsies performed between 1974 and 1978 on psoriatics to assess their value in managing the psoriatic and monitoring liver damage due to methotrexate.

raw_record.extra_details: 31 liver biopsies performed on 22 severe psoriasis patients (12 men, 10 women; ages 22-75, mean 53). Of 21 attempted pre-methotrexate biopsies, 4 were abnormal and 1 failed; 5 of 10 post-methotrexate biopsies were abnormal. Histological abnormalities were mild and cirrhosis was not seen. Three patients developed serious morbidity after biopsy (post-biopsy complication, not drug-related). Liver function tests were not found to be a reliable indicator of hepatic damage.

raw_record.support_text: In the ENLIVEN trial, 8 of 61 (13.11%) pexidartinib-treated patients experienced a serious adverse event that led to discontinuation, 7 of which were liver-related: four patients with increased liver enzymes, one each with hepatitis A and E infection, one unspecified liver disorder, and one due to hepatotoxicity. In rare cases, pexidartinib can cause more serious, potentially irreversible and/or fatal liver injury, with persistent elevations of total bilirubin and ALP in the background of elevated transaminases; liver biopsies showed significant ductopenia and cholestasis. Because of the risk of serious or potentially fatal liver injury, the FDA placed a black box warning for hepatotoxicity requiring frequent monitoring of liver function tests, and pexidartinib should be avoided in patients with preexisting liver or biliary tract disease or elevated baseline bilirubin/transaminases.

raw_record.extra_details: ENLIVEN randomized trial (61 pexidartinib vs 59 placebo). Eight (13.11%) pexidartinib patients had a serious AE leading to discontinuation, seven liver-related: four increased liver enzymes (4.92%), one hepatitis A and E infection (1.64%), one unspecified liver disorder (1.64%), one hepatotoxicity (1.64%). Laboratory findings showed persistent elevations of total bilirubin and ALP on a background of elevated transaminases; liver biopsies showed significant ductopenia and cholestasis. FDA issued a black box warning for hepatotoxicity with a monitoring schedule (LFTs prior to initiation, weekly for 8 weeks, then every 2 weeks for a month, then every 3 months). Common, reversible liver-related AEs in ENLIVEN were increased AST (39%) and ALT (28%), attributed to pexidartinib-mediated inhibition of Kupffer cells (CSF-1R-expressing resident liver macrophages), which also raises creatinine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase and commonly returns to baseline on discontinuation. Usual dose is 400 mg twice daily.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports acute hepatotoxicity after paracetamol overdose in nine patients. GST and F protein concentrations in plasma were more sensitive than ALT activity for detecting this hepatotoxicity: all nine patients had abnormal GST concentrations and eight had abnormal F protein concentrations at some time after the paracetamol overdose, whereas ALT became abnormal in only six. Five of the patients developed moderate or severe liver damage with maximal ALT activities 9.4 to 390 times the upper reference limit, and abnormal hepatocellular damage markers were measurable as early as 4 h after overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol poisoning) exposure; series of nine patients who took a paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.extra_details: Five of nine patients developed moderate or severe liver damage with maximal ALT activities ranging from 9.4 to 390 times the upper reference limit; GST maxima ranged from about 300 to 3000 times the upper reference limit. Hepatocellular damage was measurable as early as 4 h after overdose. GST, ALT, and F protein concentrations continued to increase after treatment with N-acetylcysteine was begun. Admission GST >10 µg/L distinguished the five patients who developed severe or moderate liver damage from the four who did not. The paper's focus is on comparing GST and F protein (more sensitive) with ALT for detecting acute hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In Case 2, a 78-year-old woman being treated for peptic ulcer was placed on chlorpromazine 40 mg daily on December 7, 1954. Severe pruritus developed about December 14, and on December 20 chlorpromazine was discontinued. Dark urine and gray stools were noted on December 25, and by December 30 slight icterus was present with the liver extended below the costal margin and slightly tender. Liver tests on December 30 showed total bilirubin 2.9 mg/100cc (direct 2.1), alkaline phosphatase 9.5 Bodansky units (normal <4.5), and 21% eosinophils. The patient recovered rapidly after discontinuation, with no icterus or pruritus by January 12, 1955, indicating dechallenge-associated resolution of the chlorpromazine-attributed liver injury.

raw_record.support_text: Two patients developed obstructive jaundice during chlorpromazine therapy. For the first, jaundice appeared after 16 days of chlorpromazine at 100 mg/day and lasted 27 days, with fever and a flu-like onset followed by severe pruritus, mild eosinophilia, and a laboratory picture suggesting obstructive jaundice; recovery occurred with symptomatic management and drug withdrawal. The second received chlorpromazine 40 mg daily for 13 days and developed generalized pruritus, dark urine, light stools, and mild jaundice with obstructive liver-function findings and 21% blood eosinophils, recovering uneventfully 19 days after discontinuation. The authors state the jaundice in these cases is thought to be secondary to chlorpromazine therapy, and that jaundice from stone, other obstructive phenomena, or infectious hepatitis appears remote.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient 1: chlorpromazine 100 mg/day, jaundice after 16 days persisting 27 days, fever and flu-like onset, severe pruritus, mild eosinophilia, obstructive laboratory picture, active marginal ulcer and marked duodenal deformity; recovered after withdrawal and symptomatic management. Patient 2: chlorpromazine 40 mg daily for 13 days, generalized pruritus within a week, dark urine, light stools, mild jaundice at two weeks, obstructive liver-function tests, 21% eosinophils, duodenal spasm; icterus lasted about two weeks, uneventful recovery 19 days after stopping. Liver biopsy in the case reported by Zatuchni and Miller showed acute periportal inflammation, bile plugs in canaliculi, and numerous eosinophils, suggesting hypersensitivity as the principal mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes drug-induced mitochondrial toxicity as the fatal lactic acidosis and liver failure that developed in seven adults with chronic hepatitis B treated with the experimental antiviral nucleoside analogue fialuridine (FIAU). Liver tissue from the explants of five patients who underwent liver transplantation showed marked microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis and cholestasis and swollen dysmorphic mitochondria, and the episode was fatal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adults with chronic hepatitis B infection receiving the agent as an experimental antiviral.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven affected patients presented with fatigue, nausea, constipation, abdominal pain, coagulopathy, hyperammonemia, and profound lactic acidosis, with only mild jaundice and minimal increases in serum aminotransferase values; several also developed pancreatitis, peripheral neuropathy, and myopathy. Five patients underwent liver transplantation; explants showed marked microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis, cholestasis, and swollen dysmorphic mitochondria. Mechanism: FIAU is incorporated into mtDNA, producing dysfunctional transcription and impaired mtDNA gene expression.

One month later he presented with apathy, lethargy, dark urine, pruritus and subictericia, with symptoms starting one week after treatment initiation; laboratory tests showed GOT 68 U/l, GPT 222 U/l, GGT 1,371 U/l, FA 291 U/l, bilirubin 2.8 mg/dl and normal liver ultrasound, without eosinophilia. raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of fatal hepatotoxicity without overt marrow suppression from mercaptopurine in the maintenance treatment of adult acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. A 68-year-old man on maintenance therapy (daily mercaptopurine 75 mg/m2, weekly methotrexate 20 mg/m2, monthly IV vincristine, oral prednisolone) with normal baseline liver function developed marked elevation of serum bilirubin (to 155 then 600 µmol/l), aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase and alkaline phosphatase, progressed to hepatic encephalopathy with renal failure and death. Autopsy showed marked intrahepatic cholestasis, focal bile infarcts, mild intercellular fibrosis and scattered hepatocyte necrosis, with no biliary obstruction and negative hepatitis serology. The paper states the hepatotoxic effects of mercaptopurine are well documented and that the characteristic features are a combination of intrahepatic cholestasis and parenchymal cell necrosis, usually reversible on discontinuation although deaths have been reported.

Liver function normal on starting maintenance; mild AST/ALT elevation with normal bilirubin before a marked rise after the fifth monthly cycle: bilirubin 155 then 600 µmol/l (normal 1-24), AST 182 to 132 IU/l (normal 5-40), ALT 149 IU/l (normal 7-56), ALP 143 to 152 IU/l (normal 36-125). raw_record.support_text: Tolcapone (Tasmar) was associated with severe hepatotoxicity leading to the EMEA recommendation to suspend its marketing authorization. Three cases of acute, unpredictable hepatitis with fatal outcome had been reported, including a fulminant hepatitis in a 74-year-old woman 9 weeks after starting tolcapone as add-on therapy for Parkinson's disease (liver biopsy showed severe centrolobular necrosis and a lobular inflammatory infiltrate mostly of plasma cells and eosinophils) and a US patient who died from hepatic necrosis. A third case of fulminant hepatitis related to tolcapone occurred in a patient already under close liver-enzyme monitoring. The underlying mechanism was considered possibly a severe idiosyncratic reaction, similar to that seen with isoniazid or diclofenac.

raw_record.extra_details: Three fatal human cases of acute unpredictable hepatitis reported after tolcapone marketing (approximately 100,000 patients worldwide treated). Index case: 74-year-old woman, fulminant hepatitis 9 weeks after starting tolcapone, biopsy showing severe centrolobular necrosis with lobular inflammatory infiltrate of plasma cells and eosinophils; a US patient died from hepatic necrosis. Possible immune-mediated/mixed mechanism and role of hepatic COMT inhibition/catabolism (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, CYP oxidation) considered unknown.

In patients with self-poisoning by acetaminophen, the half-life of the ingested poison is related to the extent of liver injury: the mean half-life of unchanged drug was twice as long in patients with hepatic necrosis (7.6 ± 0.8 hr) than in those without (2.9 ± 0.3 hr). The paper attributes an acute centrilobular hepatic necrosis to acetaminophen overdose in humans.

raw_record.extra_details: Acute centrilobular necrosis described (ref 68). Mean half-life of unchanged drug 7.6 ± 0.8 hr in patients with hepatic necrosis vs 2.9 ± 0.3 hr without and 2.0 ± 0.1 hr after high therapeutic doses. In patients with liver damage, plasma unchanged-acetaminophen concentration 12 hr after overdose was about two-fold greater than that of conjugated metabolites, the inverse of individuals without necrosis. Acetaminophen-induced injury also impaired elimination of other drugs: antipyrine half-life measured within 48 hr of self-poisoning was 20.6 hr, falling to 13.3 hr (normal range) in eight patients after 7-63 days; case reports indicate impaired elimination of amylobarbital, phenobarbital, and diphenylhydantoin with this hepatic damage.

The patient had jaundice and markedly elevated cholestatic enzymes about 4 weeks after starting carbamazepine, and a biopsy showed severely damaged bile ductules with only a few identifiable ductules.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral carbamazepine 200 mg t.i.d.; liver enzymes normal at start except pre-existing elevated GGT (155 U/ml). Four weeks later admitted with fever, jaundice, AST 166, ALT 122, ALP 2906, GGT 4026 U/ml, total/direct bilirubin 4.2/4.0 mg/dl, PT 20 s (INR 1.9), peripheral eosinophils 14%; serum CBZ 11 mg/dl. Biopsy: portal expansion with lymphocytes/eosinophils, mild piecemeal necrosis, severely damaged bile ductules with only a few identifiable, canalicular bile plugging, mild lobular inflammation, focal severe hepatocyte ballooning. Enzymes gradually improved after discontinuation; aminotransferases returned to normal. Patient later died of a massive stroke (unrelated to liver injury). Concurrent long-term (>6 months) aspirin, gliburide, and nifedipine; prior phenytoin for seizures.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports 230 cases of hepatitis associated with iproniazid therapy, with 51 deaths among them, and states that a cause-and-effect relationship has been well established and accepted. The estimated incidence is one per 3,000 to 4,000 patients treated with iproniazid, with death occurring in 20 to 25 per cent of the afflicted. The hepatotoxicity has an insidious onset and a particularly fulminant course, is not readily differentiated pathologically from infectious hepatitis, and no relationship of dose to incidence appears to exist.
raw_record.extra_details: 230 reported cases of hepatitis with 51 deaths. Estimated incidence 1 per 3,000-4,000 patients treated; fatality in 20-25% of the afflicted. Insidious onset and particularly fulminant course; not readily differentiated pathologically from infectious hepatitis other than by severity. No dose-incidence relationship evident; hepatotoxic effects occurred only rarely within the first few weeks of therapy. Predictive susceptibility factors not identified; routine liver-function testing did not predict impending disease; course not immediately reversible after drug discontinuation. Iproniazid (Marsilid) was used in selected patients with mental depression and as adjunctive therapy in terminal malignancies and advanced collagen diseases.

raw_record.support_text: This paper reports patients with severe paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning, treated with supportive care, cysteamine and methionine, or acetylcysteine. Acetylcysteine given within 10 hours reduced severe liver damage to 1/62 (2%), whereas given 10-24 hours after ingestion it did not prevent it (20/38, 53%). Deaths from hepatic failure occurred in the supportive-treatment group (3/57) and in late-treatment groups. The liver damage is attributed to paracetamol poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes phenprocoumon-induced liver damage (phenprocoumoninduzierter Leberschaden), first described in 1963. According to a BfArM analysis based on spontaneous reports it constitutes ~2% of all phenprocoumon side effects and ~1% of all hepatopathies are phenprocoumon-induced. The clinical picture is extremely variable, ranging from simple hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure with fatal outcome, as in the presented case. Hepatopathy typically occurs 3-9 months after starting phenprocoumon, with latencies up to 7 years reported; in the presented case the patient had taken Marcumar (phenprocoumon) for 6 years.
raw_record.extra_details: Sold as Marcumar; anticoagulation indication. Latency typically 3-9 months, up to 7 years; present patient used phenprocoumon for 6 years. Clinical spectrum from simple hepatitis to (sub)acute liver failure with death. BfArM spontaneous-report analysis: ~2% of phenprocoumon side effects and ~1% of hepatopathies attributed to phenprocoumon. Four cases of this complication occurred in the authors' patient population during 2006-2008, two fatal; a Mainz case series illustrates the broad clinical spectrum. An immunologic genesis is considered likely (borderline ANA titer, exacerbation upon re-exposure, 'drug-allergic' course); cross-sensitization with other coumarins noted. Steroid therapy attempted without influence on outcome. Histology showed portal inflammatory infiltrate, group necrosis with cholestasis, collapse zone with clearing, and focal fiber increase; the course evolved into rapidly developing liver cirrhosis with subacute liver failure.
