raw_record.extra_details: Fatal case report: child given approximately 45 mg/kg/dose of acetaminophen for several days, death with centrilobular hepatocellular necrosis. Untreated acute overdose exceeding 140 mg/kg as a single dose produces the same centrilobular necrosis histology. Phenacetin, though largely metabolized to acetaminophen, does not cause the same hepatic injury because it competitively inhibits the microsomal oxidative pathway that activates acetaminophen to its toxic reactive intermediate; cimetidine showed similar interference in mice.

raw_record.support_text: Valproic acid (VPA) has been incriminated as the cause of a series of irreversible and fatal liver injuries; up to 1982 there were 62 cases of fatal liver disease associated with VPA treatment. The paper reports one such fatal case: a 7-year-old boy who died from hepatic failure resembling Reye syndrome after VPA was added to phenobarbital therapy, with elevated VPA unsaturated metabolites (4-en-VPA and 4,4'-dien-VPA) and suppressed beta-oxidation in plasma and urine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (7-year-old boy); VPA co-administered with phenobarbital (PB 4 mg/kg, VPA 36 mg/kg); hepatic failure resembled Reye syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatic failure developed ~3 months after VPA addition, while seizure-free; treated with peritoneal dialysis. VPA metabolism showed abnormally increased 3-mono and 4-double unsaturated metabolites (58%-71% of VPA+metabolites in plasma, 34%-61% in urine; controls max 15%/10%); 4-en-VPA (5%-21% plasma) and 4,4'-dien-VPA (4%-7%) were not detectable in controls; beta-oxidation suppressed (lack of 3-keto-VPA), omega-oxidation enhanced with high urinary excretion of adipic acid, suberic acid, and 4-octen-1,8-dicarboxylic acid.

raw_record.support_text: The authors present a 49-year-old woman who developed severe toxic hepatitis 8 weeks after starting escitalopram 10 mg/day for depression, with initially cytolytic and then mixed biochemical pattern, two spontaneous cholestatic/jaundice reactivation flares despite drug withdrawal, and biopsy showing perivenular ballooned hepatocytes, microvacuolar steatosis, and eosinophilic necrosis consistent with hepatotoxicity. CIOMS causality assessment scored 7, corresponding to 'probable'. The authors state this is the first described case of toxic hepatitis due to escitalopram and caution that hepatotoxicity, even severe, should be considered during escitalopram treatment.

Author reports this as the first described case of toxic hepatitis from escitalopram.

raw_record.support_text: All 38 Japanese patients had been diagnosed from clinical and biological evidence as having halothane hepatitis, with onset of jaundice or abnormal liver function within less than 3 weeks of anesthesia; none abused alcohol or took other known hepatotoxic drugs at illness onset. Five cases were fulminant hepatitis; two who received large fresh blood transfusions for fulminant hepatic failure developed secondary chronic active hepatitis and liver cirrhosis.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatitis developed within <3 weeks of halothane anesthesia in all 38 cases. Jaundice group (24 cases) had female:male ratio 2:1 (4:1 among fulminant cases), pyrexia (>38°C) in all jaundice patients, eosinophilia (>=6%) in 64–68%, and 42% had prior halothane anesthesia; 5 cases of fulminant hepatitis were included. Two patients had secondary chronic active hepatitis and liver cirrhosis attributed to large fresh-blood transfusion for fulminant hepatic failure. HLA-Bw44 was increased in non-jaundice patients (RR 6.86, P<0.001) and HLA-Bw52 and DR2 in jaundice patients; Aw24-Bw52-DR2 haplotype frequency was high in jaundice patients (Hf=0.2362). All patients recuperated with complete recovery of liver function except the two with transfusion-related complications.

raw_record.support_text: The most important factor limiting the tolerated dose of tacrine was liver toxicity. Raised liver enzyme concentrations have often been reported, with reported incidences ranging from 13% to 42%; in this trial 14 of 53 patients (26%) given tacrine during the dose-finding phase had liver enzyme concentrations three times the upper limit of normal. Although no permanent damage was reported and all subjects had normal concentrations within a month of withdrawing the drug, biopsies from patients with raised liver function test results showed damage ranging from focal inflammatory infiltration to extensive hepatocellular necrosis, and the authors consequently restricted doses to 100 mg daily.

Biopsies showed damage ranging from focal inflammatory infiltration to extensive hepatocellular necrosis. Doses were restricted to 100 mg daily because of this liver toxicity; mean best dose was 72.6 (SD 28.94) mg daily.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen toxicity accounted for 14% of 348 pediatric ALF cases enrolled December 1999-December 2004. Nonacetaminophen drug toxicity accounted for 5% of cases without specific agents named; cause was indeterminate in 49% of the whole cohort and 54% of children under 3 years.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report the case of a thrombophilic patient with activated protein C resistance who was repeatedly treated with oral anticoagulants for recurrent venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism and who twice developed a hepatitis-like clinical presentation following exposure to phenprocoumon. The patient improved and laboratory findings normalized within 3 to 4 months after withdrawal of the drug, and the authors note there are only few well-documented cases of liver toxicity due to coumarin derivatives such as phenprocoumon.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 38-year-old woman with APC resistance (heterozygous factor V R506Q/Leiden) and thrombophilia on phenprocoumon for venous thromboembolism. Episode 1: ~4 months after starting phenprocoumon developed jaundice and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 3,330 U/L, AST 2,090 U/L, AP 272 U/L, γ-GT 357 U/L, bilirubin 526 μmol/L); anticoagulation stopped (liver biopsy refused) and enzymes normalized within 3 months. Episode 2 (age 43): ~5 weeks after restarting phenprocoumon developed nausea, fatigue, jaundice (ALT 1,724 U/L, AST 1,219 U/L, AP 200 U/L, γ-GT 326 U/L, bilirubin 128 μmol/L); phenprocoumon stopped, switched to acenocoumarol, and the patient improved with decreasing liver values, indicating positive dechallenge and rechallenge. Viral hepatitis, CMV, and EBV serologies were negative; remote HBV infection (anti-HBc/anti-HBs) without active infection. Acenocoumarol was continued without new injury.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of hypersensitivity reaction to diltiazem manifested by thrombocytopenia, spiking fever, hepatotoxicity, and rash, stated to be the first report of thrombocytopenia due to diltiazem. In the 61-year-old patient, diltiazem 60 mg three times daily had been started 7 days before hospitalization; on admission he had tender hepatomegaly, AST 236 IU/L, ALT 200 IU/L, elevated gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase (66.4 IU/L) and 5'-nucleotidase (14.1 IU/L) with normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Within 6 days of discontinuing only diltiazem (other medications continued), fever and rash resolved, and liver-function tests returned to normal within 8 days; an MIF and MCDT test in the presence of diltiazem were positive while controls with his other medications were negative. No rechallenge was attempted.

Tender hepatomegaly with 16 cm liver span. Liver function tests returned to normal 2 days after fever/rash resolved (about 8 days after diltiazem discontinuation). Macrophage inhibitory factor (MIF) and mast cell degranulation (MCDT) tests positive in presence of diltiazem, negative with other medications and normal plasma. Hypersensitivity reaction profile including thrombocytopenia (platelets down to 44,000/mm3), spiking fever, and maculopapular rash; one month later fully well with platelet count 350,000/mm3.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that liver toxicity from methotrexate is felt to be related to the cumulative dosage, though the relationship is not linear or predictable. This is supported by the study of 63 psoriasis patients (23 with paired biopsies and scans while receiving methotrexate, mean cumulative dose 1.5 g over a mean 32 months), where six patients receiving methotrexate had liver biopsies showing grade 2-3 fibrosis and several progressed to cirrhosis.

raw_record.extra_details: Among 87 paired liver biopsies and dynamic hepatic scintigraphy (DHS) studies on 63 patients (41 M, 22 F; mean age 52 y, range 21-84), 38 scans were performed during methotrexate therapy; 6 patients had grade 2-3 fibrosis on biopsy (5/6 detected by DHS, sensitivity 83.3%, specificity 81.5%). A 66-year-old male developed grade 2 fibrosis after 0.5 g methotrexate over 12 months (DHS fell from 77% to 51%), which resolved to grade 1 (DHS 74%) a year after discontinuation (rechallenge-style dechallenge). An 84-year-old woman received 3.4 g over 9 years and had cirrhosis at post-mortem 5 months after an abnormal DHS. Mean DHS for grade 2-3 fibrosis was 46±5% vs 65±18% for grade 0-1. Liver toxicity was felt related to cumulative methotrexate dose.

Cumulative methotrexate doses were 1.0 g (case 1), 0.5 g (case 6) and 3.4 g (case 7). Liver enzyme monitoring was unhelpful in detecting fibrosis; frequent false elevations occurred with normal biopsies and one grade-3 fibrosis/cirrhosis patient had entirely normal enzymes. Dynamic hepatic scintigraphy had 83.3% sensitivity and 81.5% specificity for detecting fibrosis of grade 2 or worse, with 98.5% predictive value of a normal scan.

It notes that continued paracetamol conversion to metabolites damages the liver for days after overdose, and that in patients vulnerable by virtue of hepatic glutathione deficiency as little as 4 g paracetamol can precipitate hepatic failure. The text also describes hepatic necrosis measured on liver biopsy as correlating with clinical grade of hepatic encephalopathy, indicating paracetamol overdose produces liver injury.

raw_record.extra_details: Severe paracetamol overdose treated with charcoal haemoperfusion and/or high-flux dialysis. Continued conversion of paracetamol to metabolites damages the liver for several days after overdose; a blood level of ~100 mg/l in a 70 kg patient represents roughly 5 g body load (assumed volume of distribution 0.7 g/l). Extent of hepatic necrosis on liver biopsy correlated with clinical grade of hepatic encephalopathy. Prognostic markers included venous bicarbonate and serial factor V and VII levels; patients with later arrival had significantly higher prothrombin times on days 2-5. Plasma selenium was lower in the treated group than the good-prognosis group (42.9 vs 54.8 µg/l).

raw_record.support_text: Prognostic indicators were assessed retrospectively in 121 patients admitted to a Liver Failure Unit after an acetaminophen overdose in 1986-1987, who had acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure with a mortality rate of 35.5%. Poor prognostic indicators included arterial pH <7.30 (95% of such patients died), peak prothrombin time >100 s (72% died), and serum creatinine >300 µmol/L; the best predictor of death in nonacidotic patients was prothrombin time >100 s combined with serum creatinine >300 µmol/L with grade III encephalopathy (67% died).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose context (therapeutic-use DILI not separately addressed).
raw_record.extra_details: Final cohort of 121 patients admitted after acetaminophen overdose in 1986-1987 with fulminant hepatic failure; overall mortality 35.5% (43 deaths). Prognostic indicators: arterial pH <7.30 (PPV 0.95, mortality 95%), peak prothrombin time >100 s (72% died, accounting for 79% of 43 deaths), serum creatinine >300 µmol/L (least discriminating); best predictor in nonacidotic patients was prothrombin time >100 s plus creatinine >300 µmol/L plus grade III-IV encephalopathy (67% died). Admission serum bilirubin did not correlate with survival, only peak value. Presence of metabolic acidosis or the combined indicators predicted 77% of total deaths. Once liver failure developed, blood paracetamol levels and prior administration of N-acetylcysteine or methionine were not of prognostic significance. These indicators are applied to a larger 1986-1987 cohort (n=121) as part of a single-unit prognostic study; not a primary hepatotoxicity trial.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was female, obese, with a tendency to develop organ-specific autoimmune disease; attribution made only after exclusion of other causes of postoperative jaundice and by presumption in the absence of a specific diagnostic test.
raw_record.extra_details: Multiple exposures, particularly within four weeks, increased the incidence of hepatitis and shortened the interval between exposure and jaundice. The patient had prominent hypersensitivity-type features (rash, fever, arthralgia), and circulating immune complexes with complement activation via the classical pathway were found in serum and synovial fluid. The proposed antigen (substance X), found bound to serum proteins via non-covalent forces, was thought to be derived from halothane.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports six nonpregnant women who died unexpectedly after hospitalization and each had received substantial quantities of intravenous tetracycline. The terminal clinical and laboratory features of the patients were similar, and autopsy study disclosed that the liver showed the peculiar foamy type of fatty change characteristic of tetracycline toxicity. The authors note that the hepatotoxic effect of tetracycline given intravenously had previously been described, and the report underscores intravenous tetracycline as a cause of severe, fatal liver injury.

References prior reports of hepatotoxic effect of tetracycline given intravenously to pregnant women [1-4].

raw_record.support_text: In an isoniazid-treated patient, an open liver biopsy showed thick fibrous capsule, dense connective tissue septa, periportal necrosis with ballooning and condensed liver cells and spotty focal necrosis, judged most consistent with a chronic progressive, precirrhotic drug-related form of hepatitis. Three months after cessation of isoniazid, splenomegaly and varices resolved and serum values returned to normal, supporting isoniazid as the cause.

raw_record.support_text: A case of massive Acetaminophen (APAP; N-acetyl-p-aminophenol) overdose presented with altered mental status and lactic acidosis and was refractory to intermittent hemodialysis, continuous renal replacement therapy, high-dose N-acetylcysteine, and fomepizole. Despite these interventions, fulminant liver failure progressed with cerebral edema, coagulopathy, and death. The authors describe this as the first description of a fatal acetaminophen ingestion refractory to both IHD and prolonged CRRT.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Massive overdose ingestion (above 0.5 g/kg) with refractory lactic acidosis, altered mental status; case refractory to multiple IHD sessions, prolonged CRRT, high-dose N-acetylcysteine and fomepizole.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant liver failure progressed with cerebral edema, coagulopathy and death. Early lactic acidosis attributed to hepatic glutathione depletion leading to 5-oxoprolinemia, NAPQI-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, and APAP binding to mitochondrial enzymes; late acidosis hypothesized to reflect reduced hepatic lactate clearance. NAPQI production also hypothesized as culprit of acute kidney injury causing renal tubular damage. Treated with NAC, IHD, CRRT, and fomepizole. EXTRIP guidelines recommend ECTR alongside NAC for altered mental status, metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, and APAP level greater than 5960 μM.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with seizures was changed to phenytoin 300 mg daily, with liver function tests normal prior to commencement. Six weeks after starting phenytoin she developed a generalised pruritic rash, dark urine, fever and malaise. On admission she was icteric and febrile with a confluent maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy and 8% eosinophilia; liver biopsy showed granulomatous hepatitis with numerous well-formed granulomas, portal/periportal and focal lobular inflammation, and minimal hepatocytic degeneration with individual cellular necrosis. Phenytoin was ceased on admission and the patient made a slow clinical and biochemical recovery, with temperature and liver function tests returning to normal, implicating phenytoin as the cause of the granulomatous hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Anticonvulsant given at 300 mg/day for seizures; latency of about 6 weeks. Admission labs: bilirubin 41 µmol/l (<17), ALP 639 u/l (100-350), AST 212 u/l (6-42); 8% eosinophilia; transient atypical lymphocytosis (14%, 1792 x 10^6/l). Liver biopsy showed granulomatous hepatitis (granulomata with giant/epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, few eosinophils, no necrosis or caseation), portal/periportal and focal lobular inflammation. Dechallenge: phenytoin ceased on admission with gradual clinical and biochemical recovery (temperature normal by day 8, liver function tests by day 25); no recurrence at 12-week follow-up after restarting methylphenobarbitone. Serology negative for hepatitis A/B, toxoplasma, CMV and streptococcus; negative antimitochondrial antibodies. Reported phenotype: granulomatous hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Idelalisib is reported to induce hepatotoxicity. Fatal and/or serious hepatotoxicity occurred in 18% of patients treated with idelalisib monotherapy and 16% treated in combination with rituximab or unapproved combination therapies. ALT or AST elevations greater than 5x ULN occurred, generally within the first 12 weeks of treatment, were reversible with dose interruption, and recurred in 26% of patients after resumption at a lower dose. The FDA-approved label includes a black box warning on its potential for hepatotoxicity, and discontinuation is advised for recurrent hepatic injury.

raw_record.extra_details: Sulfone syndrome (dapsone hypersensitivity) developed 4 weeks after dapsone was started. Naranjo probability scale rated the association as probable. Sulfone syndrome is described as not dose-related, resolving within 1-14 days (time course) after stopping dapsone; fatal reactions have been reported in the literature. raw_record.support_text: The paper describes hepatotoxicity as one of the most common toxicological effects of antiviral nucleoside drugs and then presents a Phase II clinical trial in which 15 patients with chronic hepatitis B were treated with the antiviral nucleoside fialuridine (FIAU). After 12 weeks of treatment, seven patients developed severe hepatotoxicity: five died and two survived only after liver transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with chronic hepatitis B enrolled in a Phase II clinical trial; mitochondrial-toxicity-based injury attributed to phosphorylated metabolites accumulating in mitochondria.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase II clinical trial: 15 patients treated with FIAU for 12 weeks; 7 developed severe hepatotoxicity, of whom 5 died and 2 survived following liver transplantation. Mechanism attributed to inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma and mitochondrial DNA depletion by triphosphate metabolites, causing mitochondrial toxicity. FIAU entry into mitochondria is facilitated by hENT1 on mitochondrial membranes.

raw_record.support_text: Our adolescent patient ingested a large amount of acetaminophen and diphenhydramine and developed acute hepatic failure despite early and complete treatment with acetylcysteine. The authors attribute the course to a very large acetaminophen dose (1742 mg/kg) and co-ingested diphenhydramine delaying acetaminophen absorption, resulting in a very high serum acetaminophen concentration (>470 µg/mL) >20 hours after ingestion.

raw_record.extra_details: Case report of an adolescent who developed acute hepatic failure despite early and complete acetylcysteine treatment started 5 hours after ingestion. Persistently elevated serum acetaminophen (653 µg/mL at 4 h; 470 µg/mL at 45 h); rising transaminases; mild hepatic encephalopathy; INR peaked at 4.8 on hospital day 4; placed on the liver-transplant list but removed as transaminases fell and encephalopathy resolved on hospital day 6. Received a second acetylcysteine bolus; treated with fresh-frozen plasma, vitamin K, and factor VII for coffee-ground emesis; also received cefotaxime for Haemophilus influenzae bacteremia.

raw_record.support_text: In the ODIXa-DVT trial there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity with long-term (3 months) rivaroxaban administration for deep venous thrombosis; in the first 3 weeks patients on rivaroxaban had a lower incidence of ALT > 3x ULN (1.9–4.3%) than enoxaparin recipients (21.6%), and after 3 weeks the incidences were similar (1.9% CI 0.8–3.6 vs 0.9% CI 0.0–4.8). A pooled analysis of 1343 Phase II patients found no difference in ALT > 3x ULN between rivaroxaban and enoxaparin (3.8–6.0 vs 7.7%). Rivaroxaban was stopped in three patients for abnormal liver tests, two of whom died (one from acute fulminant hepatitis B, one from carcinoma with hepatic metastasis). The authors conclude there is no evidence of increased hepatotoxicity with rivaroxaban.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: No hepatotoxicity demonstrated for rivaroxaban; abnormal liver tests in three patients are attributed to competing causes (acute fulminant hepatitis B and carcinoma with hepatic metastasis) rather than to rivaroxaban.
raw_record.extra_details: Evidence from the ODIXa-DVT trial (3 months treatment for DVT) and a pooled analysis of 1343 patients from Phase II studies for postoperative VTE prophylaxis. ALT > 3x ULN incidences: first 3 weeks 1.9–4.3% (rivaroxaban) vs 21.6% (enoxaparin); after 3 weeks 1.9% (95% CI 0.8–3.6) vs 0.9% (95% CI 0.0–4.8); pooled 3.8–6.0% vs 7.7%. Authors state more long-term data are needed.

raw_record.support_text: In January 2011, in response to numerous reports of liver damage attributable to high doses of acetaminophen, the FDA required that prescription acetaminophen products be limited to 325 mg per single dosage unit and carry a boxed warning by 2014, to reduce liver failure, the need for liver transplantation, and death due to acetaminophen toxicity from unintentional overdose (defined as multiple-timepoint ingestion to relieve pain or other somatic symptoms). In a population-based surveillance study of acute liver failure, acetaminophen was the most common cause of ALF in adults (41%), and among these unintentional acetaminophen overdose was the most common cause (61% of patients). The paper also states that acetaminophen is generally safe at recommended doses, that ALF occurs with daily doses exceeding 4 g (both long-term and short-term ingestion of >4 g/day within seven days), and that the minimal dosage shown to result in liver injury is 4–10 g.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury is attributed to high-dose exposure (intentional and unintentional overdose of >4 g/day); the paper notes the drug is generally safe at recommended doses.
raw_record.extra_details: FDA January 2011 decision limited prescription acetaminophen to 325 mg per single dosage unit and required a boxed warning by 2014 to reduce ALF, liver transplantation, and death from unintentional overdose. Minimal dose shown to cause liver injury is 4–10 g; ALF occurs with daily doses exceeding 4 g. Reported clinical injury phenotype is acute liver failure (ALF). Availability of the i.v. formulation (FDA-approved Nov 2, 2010, labeled for patients ≥2 years) was noted to raise the risk of exceeding the 4 g/day maximum in hospital settings (postoperative patients with multiple acetaminophen-containing products).; confidence_note: None

The reason for the hepatotoxicity remained undetermined, and it did not appear to be associated with the APL dose or mechanism of action.

raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist developed for treatment of HIV-1 infection. In the human phase IIb study CCR100136, 191 ART-naive subjects received 400/100 mg lopinavir-ritonavir BID plus either 200 mg APL BID, 400 mg APL BID, 800 mg APL QD, or 150/300 mg lamivudine-zidovudine (Combivir) BID. Study was prematurely terminated because of the treatment-emergent idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity; hepatotoxicity did not appear dose-related or mechanism-related. Reasons for the hepatotoxicity remain to be determined.

raw_record.support_text: An infant presented with hepatomegaly and markedly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 455 U/L, AST 1907 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 603 U/L), total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, ammonia 135 µmol/L, PT 53.5 s, and INR 2.5. The child had received an inadvertent acetaminophen overdose: the mother gave 200 mg/dose every 4 hours (~162 mg/kg/day for several days) because a language barrier led her to misuse the acetaminophen and amoxicillin doses. Plasma acetaminophen was 78.5 µg/mL approximately 96 hours after the first dose. The patient was treated with N-acetylcysteine (loading dose plus 18 doses), transferred to a regional transplant center, and made a complete recovery over 3 weeks. The paper states acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is well described in acute overdosage and results from formation of N-acetyl-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI) via the cytochrome P-450 pathway.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric infant; chronic supratherapeutic dosing (~162 mg/kg/day for several days) due to a caregiver medication-dose error (acetaminophen switched with amoxicillin) related to a language barrier; plasma level was from chronic supratherapeutic dosing, not a single acute ingestion, so the Rumack-Matthew nomogram did not apply.
raw_record.extra_details: Plasma acetaminophen 78.5 µg/mL measured ~96 h after the last/first dose; 2 mL of 80 mg/0.8 mL (200 mg/dose) every 4 h. Initial labs: hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, WBC 29,700/mm3, PT 53.5 s, PTT 75 s, INR 2.5, ammonia 135 µmol/L, total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL (conjugated 1.9), ALT 455 U/L, AST 1907 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 603 U/L. Transferred to regional transplant center; treated with NAC (oral loading 140 mg/kg plus 18 doses) and recovered completely over ~3 weeks with near-normal liver enzymes by hospital day 5. Mechanism attributed to NAPQI formation via cytochrome P-450. The paper notes acute adult ingestions >140 mg/kg (≥7.5 g) or >150 mg/kg in a child are potentially toxic, and prognostic factors for severe liver damage/transplant include PT >37 s, pH <7.3, creatinine >3 mg/dL, and grade 3-4 encephalopathy.

raw_record.support_text: A 9½-year-old girl with hyperthyroidism was treated with propylthiouracil (PTU) 150 mg po q6h and propranolol. About four months after PTU was started she became confused with yellow sclerae; PTU was discontinued and she was admitted with hepatic failure. Laboratory results included total bilirubin 239 µmol/L, prothrombin time 27.5 sec, ammonia 140 µmol/L, and aspartate aminotransferase 1215 IU/L. She had complications of hepatic failure and was treated with mannitol, intubation, hyperventilation, and fresh frozen plasma, then recovered. Serologies were negative for hepatitis A and B. The report calls this the fifth reported case of PTU-induced hepatotoxicity in a child.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (9½-year-old girl) patient with hyperthyroidism; therapeutic maintenance dosing (100 mg po q8h at time of injury); propranolol was a co-medication but was discontinued and was not attributed as cause.
raw_record.extra_details: Fifth reported pediatric case of severe PTU-induced hepatic injury; onset about 4 months after PTU initiation; peak labs total bilirubin 239 µmol/L, prothrombin time 27.5 sec, aspartate aminotransferase 1215 IU/L, ammonia 140 µmol/L; CT showed cerebral edema; complications included coagulopathy, hyperammonemia, hypocalcemia, hypoproteinemia, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia; negative hepatitis A/B serology; patient recovered and later developed hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. Causal link supported by negative serologies and rapid deterioration; the paper states mechanisms of the hepatic injury are unknown.

raw_record.support_text: Dietary supplement sustained-release (SR) niacin formulations exhibit increased hepatotoxicity compared with immediate-release (IR) formulations. In a randomized, double-blind parallel comparison of IR vs SR niacin in 46 patients with LDL-C >4.14 mmol/L at doses of 500–3000 mg/day, none of the 23 patients on IR niacin developed hepatotoxicity, whereas 52% of patients taking SR niacin developed aminotransferase levels >3× ULN, half of whom had symptoms of fatigue, nausea and anorexia; most hepatotoxicity occurred above doses of 1500 mg. Prescription ER niacin (Niaspan) had a better hepatic safety profile, with <1% showing ALT/AST >2× ULN.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatotoxicity attributed specifically to the sustained-release (SR) formulation of niacin; most cases occurred at doses above 1500 mg/day; OTC SR formulations recommended to be avoided.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized double-blind parallel trial, 46 patients with LDL-C >4.14 mmol/L (160 mg/dl), doses 500–3000 mg/day; 0/23 IR niacin patients developed hepatotoxicity vs 52% of SR niacin patients with aminotransferase >3× ULN, half with fatigue, nausea and anorexia; IR niacin has no such effect; prescription ER niacin (Niaspan) showed <1% ALT/AST >2× ULN at 2000 mg over up to 96 weeks in an open-label study of 723 patients.

The team made a collective decision to stop lamotrigine within 24 hours of arrival, and clinical improvement followed drug discontinuation. The patient displayed a cholestatic liver injury, which the authors note is a rarer presentation in DRESS syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: Conditioning regimens containing busulfan are described as well known to induce hepatotoxicity in human HPCT recipients, ranging from elevated liver enzyme levels to hepatitis and hepatic veno-occlusive disease (HVOD). In paediatric patients most autologous and allogeneic recipients had regimen-related grade 1–2 elevations of AST/ALT, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, or bilirubin with none of grade 4. In adult patients 15% of serious adverse events involved hepatotoxicity, and HVOD occurred in 8.2% of 61 adult allogeneic recipients (fatal in two patients) and in 2.5% of 42 autologous recipients.

raw_record.extra_details: In paediatric patients (n=55, aged 0.3–17.2 y) most regimen-related elevations of AST/ALT, GGT or bilirubin were grade 1–2, none grade 4. In adults, 15% of serious adverse events involved hepatotoxicity; HVOD in 8.2% of 61 adult allogeneic HPCT recipients (fatal in two) and 2.5% of 42 adult autologous recipients; serious bilirubin elevations in three patients and AST elevations in one patient, two of these among those with HVOD. In a separate report, HVOD occurred in 4 of 31 autologous and 3 of 36 allogeneic paediatric recipients receiving bodyweight-based IV busulfan, all mild-to-moderate and resolving with symptomatic treatment within 18 days.

raw_record.support_text: The most serious toxic effect of pyrazinamide is upon the liver. The U.S. Public Health Service Tuberculosis Therapy Trial (1959) reported, in a series of 780 patients, an incidence of hepatic toxicity of 2-6%, depending upon the dosage employed. A summary by the Committee on Therapy of the American Trudeau Society covering 13 published clinic reports on 1,070 patients showed 33 (3.1%) instances of jaundice and 43 (4%) instances of increased bromsulphthalein excretion without clinical jaundice.

The authors conclude that these studies provide direct evidence that sensitisation to halothane-altered liver-cell components is present in those occasional patients in whom severe liver damage develops after halothane anaesthesia.

raw_record.extra_details: 12 patients (4 male, 8 female) with fulminant hepatic failure after halothane anaesthesia; 7 died, survivors showed complete recovery of liver function. Interval between anaesthesia and jaundice 3-14 days; postoperative pyrexia in 10; liver-kidney microsomal antibodies in 5, smooth-muscle antibodies in 3; all negative for HB3Ag. In-vitro leucocyte sensitisation to halothane-pretreated rabbit liver homogenate in 8/12 hepatitis patients; such sensitisation absent with ether-pretreated homogenates, and normal in 11 halothane-exposed patients without liver dysfunction and in 30 patients with other liver diseases. Rarity of association and evidence of sensitisation support an immunologic mechanism.

Seven of the 12 patients died and the remainder survived. Postoperative pyrexia and autoantibodies (liver-kidney microsomal and smooth-muscle antibodies) were variable across cases.

The discussion notes that in colchicine intoxication the severity generally depends on the dose ingested (<0.5 mg/kg associated with good prognosis; >0.8 mg/kg with higher mortality), although point-of-time non-consensus exists; the clinical picture of intoxication included multiorgan failure with hypotension, cardiogenic shock, respiratory distress, renal insufficiency, hepatic damage, CNS involvement, hypocalcemia and bone marrow suppression. raw_record.support_text: The paper states that halothane causes two types of hepatotoxicity in humans: a milder form (minor serum transaminase increases, ~20% of patients, attributed to cytotoxic effects of halothane metabolites) and the severe halothane hepatitis (1 in 10,000) that can lead to massive hepatic necrosis and death, possibly via an immune response to halothane-modified (trifluoroacetylated) liver proteins. Among 20 patients with clinically defined halothane hepatitis (otherwise unexplained hepatitis within 28 days of halothane anaesthesia), 13 had liver failure and 12 died; 17 (85%) had autoantibodies to human liver microsomal carboxylesterase (CES1), which the authors report as a target antigen localized to the centrilobular region, consistent with the pattern of halothane hepatitis damage.

raw_record.support_text: Soon after valproic acid was marketed in 1978, case reports of serious events in children began to emerge. Dreifuss and colleagues reviewed all U.S. reports of fatal hepatic dysfunction received by the manufacturer in the first six years of marketing; 86.5% of these reports involved use of another anticonvulsant in addition to valproate. Age and combination use were the greatest risk factors for fatal hepatotoxicity: children under age 2 receiving valproate as polytherapy had a 20-fold greater risk compared to older ages, and a world-literature review found more than 90% of approximately 100 fatalities occurred in patients under 20 years of age.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that acetaminophen dose-dependent hepatotoxicity is the most frequent cause of acute liver failure (ALF), accounting for about 50% of cases in the United States. It further describes that with doses above 4 g/d the metabolism shifts to the cytochrome P450 pathway producing NAPQI, a reactive metabolite leading to irreversible hepatocellular damage.

raw_record.extra_details: Chronic high-dose acetaminophen consumption in a 24-year-old woman led to hepatorenal syndrome, a rare life-threatening complication, with nausea, vomiting, lethargy, oliguria, severe metabolic acidosis, and progressive decline in renal function secondary to liver failure, requiring emergent liver transplantation. At doses above 4 g/d, metabolism shifts from glucuronidation/sulfation to the cytochrome P450 pathway producing the reactive metabolite NAPQI (SMILES:1230119) which causes irreversible hepatocellular damage. Acetaminophen (paracetamol, APAP) is used as an antipyretic/analgesic and is widely available over the counter as single or combination products.

raw_record.support_text: A 69-year-old man on ticlopidine for a cerebral infarction developed malaise, anorexia, jaundice and pruritus with marked liver dysfunction and hyperbilirubinemia (ALT 455 IU/L, AST 190 IU/L, total bilirubin 8.2 mg/dL, γ-GTP 806 IU/L). raw_record.support_text: The paper describes 247 patients treated at King's College Hospital in 1982 and 1983 after a paracetamol overdose. Survival in local patients was 100%, whereas in patients referred because of severe liver damage it was 49% and 63% (1982 and 1983). Delay in presentation (median 30 h in referred, 8 h in local patients) precluded antidote administration to most referred patients, and patients dying from liver failure included those with serum paracetamol concentrations in the 'non-toxic' range. One patient with a chronic alcohol history (>200 g/day) who received N-acetylcysteine at 12 h died from liver failure, yet in the complete series prior or concomitant alcohol consumption had no significant effect on outcome.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure; concurrent alcohol use did not significantly worsen prognosis in the series.
raw_record.extra_details: 247 patients, 147 referred from other centres due to severe liver damage and 100 local; deaths from liver failure including fulminant hepatic failure. Delay to presentation median 30 h (referred) vs 8 h (local); lack of antidote in 11 treatable cases led to death in all 11. Mechanism described: paracetamol is metabolized to an electrophilic metabolite that initiates hepatocyte damage and liver necrosis (Mitchell et al., 1973). Antidote N-acetylcysteine and methionine are considered effective only within <15 h after overdose.

In the liver-failure populations, patients with toxic-range serum paracetamol concentrations, especially those presenting more than 16 h after the overdose, frequently developed progressive liver failure (grade III–IV encephalopathy) and died, including a chronic alcoholic who died despite N-acetylcysteine given at 12 h.

raw_record.support_text: In referred overdose patients who also took dextropropoxyphene/paracetamol tablets together with 25 g of paracetamol, both patients became unconscious within 24 h and later developed signs of hepatic failure from which they died. The paper as a whole attributes hepatic failure and its mortality to paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose: patients with serum paracetamol levels above the treatment line had substantial mortality (e.g., 16/36 (44%) survival in referred 1982), and the most significant prognostic factor was delay between ingestion and presentation precluding antidote administration.
raw_record.extra_details: Series of local (1982) and referred (1982, 1983) paracetamol overdose patients; referred median presentation 30 h vs 8 h local; overall referred survival 56% (147 patients) with 60% having prothrombin time >50 s and 36% AST >1000 i.u. In local patients taking paracetamol/dextropropoxyphene tablets serum paracetamol never reached toxic levels and PT/AST remained normal. Antidote (N-acetylcysteine, methionine) prevented toxicity when given early; failure of timely antidote was a feature in 11 adverse cases. Concomitant alcohol (>80 g/day) did not significantly alter course or outcome.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatic toxicity secondary to quinidine is an uncommonly reported event. In the author's series, serial liver function tests were available in 5 of 11 patients with fever, and in one of these patients granulomatous hepatitis was demonstrated after biopsy (case 6). The authors also cite four previously reported cases of quinidine-related hepatic abnormality, including one with chemical evidence of both cholestatic and hepatocellular injury, and two cases with biopsy evidence of reversible noncaseating hepatic granulomas. The current case had similar histology during fever with resolution of granulomas one year later. The paper supports routine hepatic function testing in all patients with quinidine fever to clarify the frequency of quinidine-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: DRESS syndrome was suspected in the patient because of the close temporal relationship of symptom onset within 2-6 weeks of initiation of sulthiame, typical clinical features of DRESS syndrome (persistent fever >38 °C, classical rash, hepatitis, pneumonitis, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia with atypical lymphocytes of 4%), ruling out of autoimmune disorders and connective tissue disease, and clinical improvement with corticosteroid treatment. Using the Naranjo ADR probability scale the patient scored 6, indicating a probable ADR relationship between sulthiame and the development of DRESS syndrome, which included hepatitis with liver transaminases ≥2 times normal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient treated in a Paediatric Intensive Care Unit; hepatitis occurred as a systemic manifestation of DRESS syndrome together with pneumonitis, rash, and hematologic abnormalities.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo ADR probability scale score of 6 (probable ADR). Case fulfilled Bocquet et al. criteria (all 3), RegiSCAR scoring (score 6 of 7 criteria, classed definite DRESS), and J-SCAR criteria (5 of 7, atypical DRESS). Serial ALT rose up to 238 u/L and AST to 391 u/L; hepatosplenomegaly present. Latency within 2-6 weeks of sulthiame initiation; treated with IV immunoglobulin and corticosteroids with recovery.

raw_record.support_text: The product labeling warns that cases of hepatotoxicity, including granulomatous hepatitis, due to quinidine hypersensitivity have been reported. Unexplained fever and/or elevation of hepatic enzymes, particularly early in therapy, warrant consideration of possible hepatotoxicity, and monitoring of liver function during the first 4-8 weeks should be considered. Cessation of quinidine in these cases usually results in the disappearance of toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported liver injury is described as hepatotoxicity including granulomatous hepatitis, attributed to quinidine hypersensitivity. Presenting features include unexplained fever and/or elevation of hepatic enzymes, especially in the early stages of therapy; liver function monitoring is recommended during the first 4-8 weeks, and discontinuation of quinidine usually leads to resolution of toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In 28 patients with grade 3 or 4 hepatic coma, liver damage in 13 patients was attributed to an overdose of paracetamol, in eight patients to viral hepatitis, and in the remainder to other drugs and hepatotoxins; 12 patients recovered overall. The paracetamol overdose was explicitly reported as the cause of the liver damage that led to fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: An overdose/supratherapeutic exposure caused liver damage progressing to fulminant hepatic failure (grade 3 or 4 hepatic coma) in 13 of 28 patients; the disease context is established fulminant hepatic failure.
raw_record.extra_details: 13 patients were affected. Metabolic acidosis occurred in only three of all 28 patients, all of whom had taken a paracetamol overdose; in those three the acidosis was severe, present before onset of clinical hepatic failure, associated with hypoglycaemia and mild hypotension, and shown in two to be due to lactic acid accumulation. Twelve of the 28 patients recovered overall. Blood lactate, pyruvate, and acetoacetate were significantly raised, with elevated citrate, succinate, and fumarate in individual cases; blood citrate rose progressively as clinical condition worsened. Plasma free fatty acid concentrations were elevated out of proportion to the degree of ketosis.

raw_record.support_text: Acute hepatic necrosis, whether due to fulminant hepatitis or drug toxicity, carries an appalling mortality. In the latest account from the Fulminant Hepatic Surveillance Study (Trey et al., 1970) the mortality of the 284 patients who went into coma was 82%, with a figure of 96% for those with a halothane-induced hepatic necrosis. The text explicitly attributes hepatic necrosis to halothane using an induced-injury construction.
raw_record.extra_details: From the Fulminant Hepatic Failure Surveillance Study (Trey et al., 1970); among the 284 patients who went into coma the overall mortality was 82%, and it was 96% among those with halothane-induced hepatic necrosis. The 96% figure applies to halothane-induced hepatic necrosis cases who had progressed to coma.

raw_record.support_text: An iron-loaded liver from a 40-year-old man with occult haemochromatosis was transplanted into a 19-year-old woman with acute liver failure secondary to a paracetamol overdose. A liver biopsy taken 30 days after transplantation for mild rejection showed increased parenchymal hepatic iron, and the hepatic iron concentration fell from 161 µmol/g on day 30 to 26.5 µmol/g (normal <40) on day 210 after transplant. The same case is described in the commentary as fulminant liver failure caused by acetaminophen.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case (case report/commentary): a 19-year-old woman with acute liver failure secondary to paracetamol overdose (described as fulminant liver failure caused by acetaminophen) who received an orthotopic liver transplant from a donor with occult haemochromatosis. The case is reported in the context of a discussion of iron metabolism and inherited haemochromatosis rather than as the primary focus. Liver allograft showed increased parenchymal hepatic iron by Perls' stain at day 30; hepatic iron fell from 161 µmol/g (day 30) to 26.5 µmol/g (day 210, normal <40); serum ferritin 2,940 µg/L initially falling to 243 µg/L by day 570; two biopsy-confirmed rejection episodes.

raw_record.support_text: Among people receiving tuberculosis preventive therapy in Tibetan schools in Himachal Pradesh, India, 11 schoolchildren (1.4%) and 1 staff member (1.0%) experienced hepatotoxicity attributed to isoniazid, with elevated liver enzymes and symptoms that regressed after the drug was discontinued. Preventive therapy was permanently stopped for 2 people with hepatotoxicity; 10 others completed treatment. Separately, 1 of 20 individuals with latent TB and HBV coinfection who received preventive therapy with isoniazid and rifampicin developed hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation of treatment.
raw_record.extra_details: Recipients were schoolchildren and staff with latent TB infection receiving TB preventive therapy in Tibetan boarding/day schools in Himachal Pradesh, India, 2017. Of those treated, 227 (25%) people developed at least 1 treatment side effect, almost all attributed to isoniazid; fatigue, drowsiness, and gastrointestinal complaints were reported by 8%-10% of schoolchildren and 5%-13% of staff. Isoniazid-attributed hepatotoxicity occurred in 11/799 (1.4%) schoolchildren and 1/101 (1.0%) staff, with elevated liver enzymes and symptoms regressing after drug discontinuation; preventive therapy was permanently stopped in 2 people. One of 20 (44%) HBV-coinfected latent TB individuals receiving isoniazid + rifampicin developed hepatotoxicity requiring discontinuation. Isoniazid was used both as part of a regimen with rifampicin (isoniazid-rifampicin) and alone for 4-6 months in some individuals.

raw_record.support_text: Acute hepatic failure has been reported in 18 patients in the United States on felbamate. Nine of these cases had confounding factors (six due to status epilepticus, and one each to acetaminophen overdose, infectious hepatitis, septicemia, and diffuse intravascular coagulation), and several others had insufficient information to determine causality. The estimated incidence of death due to felbamate-associated hepatic failure is 1 in 26,000 to 34,000 exposures.

raw_record.support_text: The drug amodiaquine, a 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial, became of importance when some P. falciparum strains resistant to chloroquine retained sensitivity to amodiaquine. In 1986 it was shown that 1 in 2000 subjects taking amodiaquine for prophylaxis of malaria developed neutropenia or hepatotoxicity, or both, illustrating idiosyncratic (Type B) drug toxicity.
raw_record.extra_details: Used for prophylaxis of malaria; 1 in 2000 subjects developed neutropenia or hepatotoxicity, or both. Mechanism attributed to an unstable reactive quinoneimine metabolite formed in liver and white cells that acts as a hapten, and high titres of specific antibodies to the reactive metabolite were found in the blood of patients who developed myelotoxicity or hepatotoxicity, giving evidence for an immunological basis. Whereas chloroquine retained sensitivity in resistant strains, amodiaquine was toxic.

raw_record.support_text: The first recipient was a 26-yr-old woman suffering from fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) due to acetaminophen poisoning, with markedly abnormal liver tests (bilirubin 77.2 µmol/L, AST 14786 U/L, ALT 8453 U/L, INR > 10, lactic acid 20.6 mmol/L, pH 7.24). She progressed from stage II to stage IV hepatic encephalopathy and was accepted for liver transplantation. After transplantation the graft functioned well, but the patient developed cerebral herniation and brain death; the paper explicitly frames both this case and three previously reported cases as liver graft reuse in the context of previous OLT for acetaminophen-induced FHF.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (acetaminophen poisoning) leading to fulminant hepatic failure; original transplant recipient of a reused liver graft who died from cerebral herniation after otherwise successful transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 26-yr-old woman with acetaminophen-induced FHF (fulminant hepatic failure). Admission labs: bilirubin 77.2 µmol/L (n≤24), AST 14786 U/L (n≤40), ALT 8453 U/L (n≤44), INR>10 (0.9–1.1), albumin 38 g/L, BUN 2.7 mmol/L, creatinine 113 µmol/L, lactic acid 20.6 mmol/L (n≤2.4), pH 7.24, bicarbonates 8.6 mmol/L. Progressed from stage II to stage IV hepatic encephalopathy; intubated. After OLT, liver graft function recovered (ALT 5600→150 U/L, AST 9905→156 U/L across days) but the first recipient died from cerebral herniation/brain death within 24 h; graft was successfully reused in a second recipient (normal LFTs, no rejection after 30 months). Three other reported cases (Rubay, Pruvot, Ortiz) involved reuse of liver grafts from acetaminophen-induced FHF recipients, all in stage IV encephalopathy at OLT.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old male was admitted with fatigue, a history of bipolar disorder, and recent acetaminophen use (four grams per day for 2 weeks for rib pain) at the upper limit of the maximum recommended dosage. Laboratory findings showed acute kidney injury (creatinine 296 µmol/l, urea 68 mg/dl) and acute hepatitis with markedly elevated AST (16427 IU/l), ALT (6200 IU/l), and INR of 3.07. The primary working diagnosis was acute hepatic injury secondary to acetaminophen intoxication, consistent with the recent medical history and unremarkable viral serological and autoimmune panels. The patient subsequently developed Grade IV hepatic encephalopathy, cerebral oedema, severe metabolic acidosis, refractory shock, and ultimately cardiac arrest. Additionally, the paper states acetaminophen intoxication is one of the most common causes leading to cerebral oedema and hepatic encephalopathy in patients with acute liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Prolonged dosing at the upper limit of the maximum recommended dose (4 g/day for 2 weeks); diagnosis supported by recent drug history with unremarkable viral serology and autoimmune panels.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 56-year-old male with acute liver failure and multiple organ failure after acetaminophen use for rib pain. Labs: AST 16427 IU/l, ALT 6200 IU/l, INR 3.07, creatinine 296 µmol/l, urea 68 mg/dl; acute kidney injury also present. Course included Grade I then Grade IV hepatic encephalopathy, ammonium rise from 132 to 1574 mcg/dl within 48 h, cerebral oedema (no brain oedema on CT), vasoplegic shock, refractory to norepinephrine, hyperlactatemia, myoclonic status epilepticus, and cardiac arrest/death. Urgent liver transplantation was prioritized but not performed. NAC (100 mg/kg/day IV) given on admission; multiple supportive treatments administered. Paper further notes acetaminophen intoxication is one of the most common causes of cerebral oedema and hepatic encephalopathy in ALF patients.

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes a patient with APAP (acetaminophen) overdose at high risk of progression to fulminant hepatic failure (FHF), who was treated with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and avoided liver transplant, making a full recovery. Serum labs following APAP ingestion showed markedly elevated AST (peak 10,927 U/L) and ALT (peak 5,671 U/L) with elevated INR (peak 3.6), and the presenting serum APAP level was inconsistent with her history, indicating significant acetaminophen-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; clinical scenario of acetaminophen overdose with high risk of progression to fulminant hepatic failure; patient treated with NAC (treatment, not a causal agent).
raw_record.extra_details: 12-year-old (female) patient with risk factors for severe anaphylactoid reaction to NAC including female sex, late presentation, and undetectable serum APAP concentration at the time of the event. Serum APAP peaked at 149 mcg/mL at 11 h post-ingestion, undetectable by 33 h. Peak AST 10,927 U/L, ALT 5,671 U/L, INR 3.6 at 44 h post-ingestion. Patient avoided liver transplant and made a full recovery. Anaphylactoid reaction to IV NAC occurred ~24 h after NAC initiation.

raw_record.support_text: The authors diagnosed toxic hepatitis due to paroxetine in a 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes who had taken paroxetine 20 mg/day for 4 months. The causal link was supported by the temporal relationship between drug intake and the reaction, an excellent response to withdrawal, and reasonable exclusion of other causes of acute hepatopathy; the Naranjo adverse-event probability scale gave a 'probable' result (6 points). Rechallenge was not performed for ethical reasons and a biopsy was not needed.

raw_record.extra_details: Paroxetine (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) 20 mg/day for about 4 months for anxious-depressive syndrome. On admission: AST 259 U/l (normal <37), ALT 224 U/l (normal <41), GGT 65 U/l (normal <50); alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin normal. Serologies negative for hepatitis A/B/C/E, HIV, and antinuclear, anticentromere, antimitochondrial, hepatic microsomal, and anti-smooth-muscle antibodies. Liver tests normalized and symptoms resolved after paroxetine withdrawal; no rechallenge for ethical reasons. Switching to citalopram 20 mg/day was well tolerated with no cross-reaction; patient asymptomatic with normal liver function 4 months later.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized controlled trial, 39 patients receiving repeated general anaesthetics for radium treatment for carcinoma of the uterine cervix were allocated to anaesthetics with or without halothane, and SGPT was monitored before each anaesthetic. Four of 18 patients in the halothane group had SGPT levels above 100 IU/l before the third radium treatment, whereas no patient in the 21-patient control group did (one-tailed test, P < 0.025). One halothane patient reached a maximum SGPT of 1800 IU/l and another 900 IU/l; neither had symptomatic illness or altered other liver function tests, but liver biopsies showed changes characteristic of hepatitis. Seven halothane patients showed an SGPT rise greater than 20 IU/l versus one control (P < 0.02).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with carcinoma of the uterine cervix undergoing repeated radium-treatment anaesthetics; repeated anaesthetic exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized controlled trial in 39 patients. 4/18 halothane patients had SGPT >100 IU/l before the third radium treatment vs 0/21 controls (P<0.025). One patient max SGPT 1800 IU/l, another 900 IU/l; both asymptomatic with normal other liver function tests but liver biopsies showed changes characteristic of hepatitis. 7 halothane patients had SGPT rise >20 IU/l vs 1 control (P<0.02).

raw_record.support_text: Histological examination of the liver showed a marked periportal acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrate with increased eosinophils and lobular hepatocyte necrosis, consistent with a severe drug-induced hepatitis. Skin biopsy showed toxic epidermal necrolysis and lymph node features were consistent with phenytoin-induced pseudolymphoma, all attributed to the phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Case presented with fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, leucocytosis, eosinophilia, toxic epidermal necrolysis and hypersensitivity myocarditis. Phenytoin hypersensitivity syndrome typically onsets 3 weeks to 3 months after initiation of therapy and is more common in blacks. Drug-induced hepatitis with or without hepatocyte necrosis is a potentially fatal complication carrying a mortality of up to 50%. Liver histology showed periportal acute and chronic inflammation with eosinophils and lobular hepatocyte necrosis. The patient died and autopsy revealed Alzheimer's disease, amyloid angiopathy, extracellular amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles and Hirano bodies. Cross-reactivity with other aromatic anticonvulsants (phenobarbital, carbamazepine) has been reported in patients with a history of phenytoin hypersensitivity.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 15 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) studied, 12 had taken a paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose; the remaining etiologies were acute type B viral hepatitis, non-A, non-B viral hepatitis, and acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Ten patients were in grade III and five in grade IV encephalopathy on admission, and 11 received liver support (charcoal or resin hemoperfusion) for 4-6 hr each day. Seven patients regained consciousness and made a full recovery, while eight died after being in coma for 2-14 days.

The paper's focus was on plasma fibronectin levels, opsonic activity, and Kupffer cell (reticuloendothelial) function in FHF, not a specific pharmacovigilance or causality assessment of paracetamol.

raw_record.support_text: A 66-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer was treated with bilateral orchiectomy and 750 mg flutamide per day. Near fatal liver dysfunction developed 10 weeks later; flutamide was discontinued and liver enzymes returned to normal by 8 weeks. The discussion concludes that hepatotoxicity associated with flutamide therapy can be severe but appears completely reversible, and notes that other patients were found to have asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations on flutamide that resolved on discontinuation.

raw_record.extra_details: Nonsteroidal antiandrogen for metastatic prostate cancer. Hepatotoxicity developed about 10 weeks after flutamide initiation (started July 12, hospitalized late September) with jaundice, marked enzyme elevation (SGOT up to 1005, SGPT up to 1323 units/l, total bilirubin up to 17.4-18.5 mg/dl), and nausea/anorexia/weight loss/dehydration. Marked transaminase improvement within 6 days of discontinuation, full recovery by November 13; patient refused further antiandrogen treatment. Authors cite known serious, even fatal, flutamide hepatotoxicity and recommend structured liver enzyme monitoring. The paper describes this index case, plus additional asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations on routine testing that normalized after flutamide discontinuation.

raw_record.support_text: Six women were diagnosed with halothane-induced hepatitis based on criteria of no pre-existing liver disease, hepatitis onset within two weeks of halothane exposure, and no alternative explanations. All had jaundice and high transaminase levels, all were female, and most were obese; the interval between anesthesia and hepatitis was two days in the one previously exposed patient and six to ten days in the others. Three patients died with autopsy findings consistent with post-halothane hepatitis, and no other causes such as prior hepatotoxin exposure, shock, or hepatitis B infection were found.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: All affected patients were women, markedly obese or at upper limits of normal weight, and from closely related families of common ethnic origin; only the patient with prior halothane exposure had a short (two-day) latency.
raw_record.extra_details: Halothane anesthesia exposure; all six cases satisfied the diagnostic criteria for hepatitis induced by halothane. Clinical features included jaundice, high transaminase levels, fever rising to 40°C (104°F) in five of six, peripheral eosinophil counts above 500/mm3 in three, and two-to-ten day interval from anesthesia to hepatitis. Three patients died; autopsy findings were consistent with post-halothane hepatitis, and alternative causes (prior hepatotoxin exposure, shock, hepatitis B virus) were excluded. Survivors remained healthy with no recurrence. Anti-HBs testing was performed on three surviving patients; a four-to-five-generation survey of 154 blood relatives revealed no additional cases of postoperative hepatic injury.

raw_record.extra_details: Aplaviroc is a chirally pure 2,5-diketopiperazine CCR5 antagonist (ONO-4128, GW873140). Grade 4 hepatotoxicity with drug-induced hepatitis occurred in ~1% of patients; no deaths; resolved on discontinuation. In phase IIb, 600 mg twice daily for 10 days gave ~1.6 log10 mean viral load decrease. Rapamycin reduces the anti-HIV effective dose of aplaviroc by up to 25-fold, potentially minimizing toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A comprehensive retrospective analysis of fatal hepatic dysfunction cases reported with valproate in the United States from 1978 to 1984 provided definitive information on primary risk factors for fatal liver failure. Patients at primary risk are children two years old or younger receiving valproate as part of anticonvulsant polypharmacy who also have other medical problems besides severe epilepsy (hepatic fatality rate birth to two years: one of 500 with anticonvulsant polypharmacy). The overall risk of fatal hepatic dysfunction is higher among patients receiving multiple anticonvulsants (more than two years: one of 12,000 with polypharmacy versus one of 45,000 with valproate monotherapy), and no hepatic failure cases were identified over age 10 on valproate monotherapy.

Mechanism per the paper: depletion of intracellular reduced glutathione, detoxification of the arylating metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinonimine produced by 2-electron oxidation through cytochrome P450; neutrophil accumulation within the liver exacerbates paracetamol-induced damage. Two young women without chronic alcohol abuse or enzyme-inducing drugs developed fulminant hepatic failure despite antidote given within 10 h of overdose, and both survived. Liver damage was measured by median peak prothrombin time; late acetylcysteine reduced progression to grade III/IV encephalopathy and improved survival even in patients with poor prognostic criteria.

raw_record.support_text: Tanespimycin (17-AAG) was evaluated in Phase I clinical trials. The dose-limiting toxicity of the daily × 5 schedule was hepatotoxicity with elevations in transaminases and bilirubin, which led to abandonment of this schedule. The weekly schedule was better tolerated without significant hepatotoxicity, and the commonest toxicities of the weekly and twice-weekly schedules included mild hepatotoxicity reflected as reversible transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia.
raw_record.extra_details: Tanespimycin is 17-AAG (17-allyl-aminodemethoxygeldanamycin), an HSP90 inhibitor used as an antitumor agent. In the daily × 5 schedule (every 3 weeks), hepatotoxicity with transaminase and bilirubin elevations was the dose-limiting toxicity and led to abandonment of this schedule; weekly and twice-weekly schedules showed only mild reversible hepatotoxicity (transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia). Other common toxicities were diarrhea, fatigue, nausea, and myalgia. Reported recommended Phase II doses were 220 mg/m² (twice weekly), 295 mg/m² (weekly × 3), 308 mg/m², 450 mg/m² (weekly), 40 mg/m² (daily × 5), and 112 mg/m² (daily × 3). In a combination study with docetaxel, the 17-AAG dose was 300 mg/m².

raw_record.extra_details: FIAU (fialuridine) was evaluated as a treatment for chronic HBV infection. raw_record.support_text: In 1963 McAlister and co-workers reported deaths of three children from acute hepatic necrosis after administration of enemas containing 0.75% tannic acid. A Canadian report followed of five cases of fulminating liver failure; in four of these tannic acid was the sole potential hepatotoxin and in the fifth halothane anaesthesia had also been given. Symptoms of vomiting and abdominal pain appeared the same day or next morning after the enema, progressing to jaundice and coma, with survival of one to five days. Necropsy in four cases showed generalized liver haemorrhages with centrilobular degeneration and necrosis; the picture resembled acute chemical poisoning rather than acute virus hepatitis. Paragraph 4 additionally notes that the FDA stopped the use of tannic acid in barium enemas after liver damage was reported, and that tannic acid treatment for burns was abandoned after liver necrosis was traced to absorption of tannic acid through burned skin.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Administered as a barium enema (colonic route) for radiological examination of the colon; in one of the five Canadian cases halothane anaesthesia was a co-administered competing exposure; three fatal pediatric cases followed enemas containing 0.75% tannic acid.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal acute hepatic necrosis in three children after 0.75% tannic-acid enemas and five Canadian cases of fulminating liver failure; symptoms of vomiting and abdominal pain appeared late the same day or early next morning, progressing through irritability, drowsiness, jaundice, and coma; survival one to five days; necropsy in four cases showed generalized haemorrhages and centrilobular degeneration/necrosis with minimal cellular reaction, unlike acute virus hepatitis but resembling acute chemical poisoning; background also from tannic acid burn treatment (1942, Wells) where liver necrosis at necropsy was attributed to absorption of tannic acid through burned skin; U.S. FDA discontinued its use in barium enemas.

One transplanted patient died of cerebral oedema 24 h later; the other 13 recovered fully under conservative management. raw_record.support_text: A 30-year-old woman developed fulminant hepatic failure after an acetaminophen overdose of 15 g. Presenting with nausea and abdominal discomfort, laboratory results showed serum bilirubin 67 µM/L, alanine aminotransferase 2598 U/L, and a prothrombin time of 59.3 s. She progressed to severe hepatic encephalopathy and coma; Ro 15-1788 (flumazenil) was administered repeatedly without clinical benefit, and the patient died from status epilepticus, hypotension, and anuria.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (supratherapeutic) as the causal setting; no clinical relationship attributed to concurrently administered Ro 15-1788 or mannitol.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report: 30-year-old woman, acetaminophen overdose of 15 g; bilirubin 67 µM/L (normal 3-20), ALT 2598 U/L (normal 0-36), prothrombin time 59.3 s (control 11-13), plasma ammonia 220 µM/L (normal 11-35); progressed to fulminant hepatic failure with severe encephalopathy and coma; no improvement with repeated Ro 15-1788 (0.5 mg, repeat bolus, 2 x 1.0 mg) or mannitol; patient died (status epilepticus, hypotension, anuria).

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid (INH) is the mainstay treatment for active and latent tuberculosis, and its main adverse effect is hepatotoxicity, with a spectrum ranging from mild transient aminotransferase elevations to severe hepatitis that can lead to liver transplantation. Reported incidences of INH hepatotoxicity range from 0.1% to 4-8% in different studies; data on INH hepatotoxicity in children are limited.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population (children with tuberculosis or latent tuberculosis infection); study-specific evaluation of INH hepatotoxicity in childhood.
raw_record.extra_details: Among 695 children treated with INH (2002 to January 2009), overall hepatotoxicity was observed in 12 patients (1.7%), and 4 patients (0.57%) had moderate-to-severe (grade III-IV) hepatotoxicity. No statistically significant differences were found between TB and latent TB cases or across age groups (<5, 5-10, ≥10 years) for overall, grade I-II, or grade III-IV hepatotoxicity (P>0.05). Grade breakdown (TB n=78 vs latent TB n=617): grade I-II 2 (2.5%) vs 6 (0.9%); grade III 0 vs 2 (0.33%); grade IV 1 (1.3%) vs 1 (0.16%); total 3 (3.8%) vs 9 (1.5%). Assessment used World Health Organization Toxicity Classification Standards. The paper also notes the broader spectrum of INH hepatotoxicity can include severe hepatitis leading to liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: A 20-year-old female consumed multiple ferrous sulfate (iron) tablets with suicidal intention. She developed fulminant hepatic failure with marked elevation of liver enzymes (ALT 1982 IU/L), high bilirubin, and INR 5.7, and died of multiorgan failure within 48 h of admission despite chelation with desferrioxamine. The cause of death was attributed to multiorgan failure due to iron poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose: suicidal ingestion of multiple ferrous sulfate tablets in an adult; treatment delay due to initial misdiagnosis as aluminum phosphide poisoning.
raw_record.extra_details: 20-year-old female; ferrous sulfate tablets consumed with suicidal intent; liver enzymes AST 404 IU/L and ALT 1982 IU/L; total bilirubin 6.37 mg/dL; INR 5.7; serum iron 185 μg/dl, ferritin 692 ng/dl, transferrin saturation 2%; severe metabolic acidosis; chelation with desferrioxamine; died of multiorgan failure within 48 h of admission; autopsy showed enlarged liver with periportal necrosis and bile cholestasis, and Perl's stain iron deposits in liver, lungs and spleen (iron overload); iron described as an intracellular poison toxic to mitochondria via uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity is described as a known sequela of iron poisoning, associated with 50% mortality and found to be dose dependent. In the presented case of suicidal iron tablet overdose, hepatic toxicity was manifested by periportal necrosis and cholestasis, with Perl's-stained iron deposits found in hepatocytes in a noncirrhotic, nonalcoholic patient.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Suicidal overdose of multiple iron tablets; delayed presentation ~48 h after ingestion; hepatotoxicity known to be dose dependent; patient was noncirrhotic and nonalcoholic.
raw_record.extra_details: Liver histology showed periportal necrosis, cholestasis in bile canaliculi, granular iron deposits in and outside hepatocytes and in splenic parenchyma; coagulative degeneration, shrinkage of hepatocytes, intense cytoplasmic eosinophilia, and karyorrhexis also reported. Patient had deranged liver function tests, coagulopathy and shock; serum iron level 185 IU/L after 48 h; AST and ALT raised. Initial history misled to aluminum phosphide poisoning, which was ruled out by negative toxicology. Hepatotoxicity-associated mortality ~50%.

raw_record.support_text: In a study of 273 Caucasian rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with methotrexate (MTX), adverse reactions occurred in 53% during at least one visit and led to discontinuation of MTX in 17%. The report specifically states that alopecia and hepatotoxicity during MTX therapy were more frequent in patients with the RFC-1 80AA genotype (OR = 3.5, p = 0.01 and OR = 2.4, p = 0.04, respectively), and that the MTHFR 677T allele was associated with increased transaminase activity (OR = 3.4, p = 0.02).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate; hepatotoxicity occurrence was genotype-dependent, being more frequent in RFC-1 (SLC19A1) 80AA carriers.
raw_record.extra_details: 273 Caucasian RA patients treated with MTX for at least 6 months or with MTX discontinued due to adverse reactions. Adverse reactions in 53% during at least one visit; 17% caused MTX discontinuation. Hepatotoxicity more frequent with RFC-1 80AA genotype (OR = 2.4, p = 0.04); alopecia OR = 3.5, p = 0.01. MTHFR 677T allele associated with increased transaminases (OR = 3.4, p = 0.02). Genetic associations studied included RFC-1 c.80G>A, GGH c.-401C>T, MTHFR c.1298A>C and c.677C>T, TYMS 2R/3R, TYMS 6-bp deletion, TCII c.593T>C.

raw_record.support_text: Patient 1: a 73-year-old woman with suspected drug overdose had a serum paracetamol concentration of 2713 µmol/L at 6 hours after ingestion (above the 150 mg/L treatment level). Intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was ordered but only 10% of the recommended doses were given; the error was not detected until 40 hours after presentation, by which time serum ALT was 4940 IU/L and INR was 2.2. raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl presented 19 hours after ingesting two handfuls of Tylenol Extended Relief, an extended-release acetaminophen formulation containing 650 mg per caplet. She developed vomiting, abdominal pain, elevated alanine aminotransferase (peaking at 7459 U/L) and international normalized ratio (peaking at 4.2) consistent with acetaminophen-induced liver injury following overdose; she was treated with acetylcysteine and sent home on day 4 with resolving liver-function values. Serial acetaminophen levels showed a linear decline with an elimination half-life of 11.08 hours.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (13-year-old) patient; overdose by ingestion of two handfuls of the extended-release formulation Tylenol Extended Relief (650 mg per caplet).
raw_record.extra_details: Ingestion occurred 19 hours before presentation; vomiting and abdominal pain began six hours after ingestion. Serum acetaminophen 89 µg/mL, ALT 180 U/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, INR 1.5 at presentation; ALT peaked at 7459 U/L and INR at 4.2 at 59 hours. Treated with acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg oral load then 6 x 70 mg/kg and 11 x 100 mg/kg). Patient remained clinically well and was discharged on day 4 with resolving liver function. Apparent elimination half-life 11.08 hours, linear decline (Fig. 1).; extra_details_note: Severity not explicitly labeled as acute liver failure; patient remained clinically well.

raw_record.support_text: In a phase 1 clinical trial of spisulosine in patients with advanced solid tumors, drug-related adverse reactions included nausea, pyrexia, injection site reactions, vomiting, and one case of death of the patient due to neuro- and hepatotoxicity. This observation led to halting clinical trials for spisulosine. The adverse events were attributed to the drug's poor physicochemical properties, including high lipophilicity and intramolecular hydrogen-bond formation, which caused gel formation and prolonged infusion times up to 24 and 72 h.

raw_record.extra_details: Dose level VIII (200 mg/m2) was the MTD and dose level IX (160 mg/m2) the RD (recommended dose); limited antitumor activity noted. Infusion time increased up to 24 and up to 72 h due to gel formation from aggregation of the lipophilic portion of the molecule in plasma. The hepatotoxicity/neurotoxicity event prompted halting clinical development of spisulosine.

raw_record.support_text: A two-week old girl with cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis was started on chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) supplementation at the advised dosage of 15 mg/kg/day. Within 6 weeks she developed jaundice with hepatomegaly. CDCA was stopped, after which liver size and function rapidly normalised; CDCA was then restarted at 5 mg/kg/day, and cholestanol, liver enzymes and total bilirubin have remained within normal range up to age 2.8 years. The authors conclude that CDCA supplementation at 15 mg/kg/day seems hepatotoxic in infants and should not be used, while 5 mg/kg/day was well tolerated.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (two-week-old infant) patient with cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis; hepatotoxicity attributed to the advised 15 mg/kg/day dosage, whereas 5 mg/kg/day was tolerated.
raw_record.extra_details: Developed jaundice with hepatomegaly within 6 weeks of starting CDCA at 15 mg/kg/day; liver size and function rapidly normalised after discontinuation; tolerated and maintained on 5 mg/kg/day with cholestanol, liver enzymes and total bilirubin remaining within normal range; patient now 2.8 years old with normal psychomotor development. Authors describe the injury as 'toxic hepatitis' and state that 15 mg/kg/day seems hepatotoxic in infants.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective single-centre analysis of 118 deaths among 503 patients with fulminant liver failure admitted between 1996 and 2001, paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose was the most common aetiology (n = 57, 48.3%). Among paracetamol overdose patients who died, multiorgan failure was the cause of death in 33 (57.9%) and cerebral oedema in 20 (35.1%; P < 0.05), establishing that paracetamol overdose caused fulminant hepatic failure leading to death in these patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose (paracetamol overdose) exposure in patients admitted to a liver unit with fulminant hepatic failure and grade III/IV hepatic encephalopathy.
raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (paracetomol) overdose was the most common cause of FHF (n = 57; 48.3%) in this cohort of fatal cases. Aetiology listed before non-A-non-B hepatitis (n = 37; 31.3%). Of the 118 deaths studied (62 males; median age 44 years, range 19-73; 24 were liver transplant recipients), MOF caused 80 (67.7%) and cerebral oedema 29 (24.5%) deaths. Among POD patients, death was more often due to MOF than cerebral oedema (P < 0.05). N-acetylcysteine is noted as a treatment for paracetamol-induced FHF that is associated with improved outcome.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc, a GlaxoSmithKline CCR5 antagonist compound, demonstrated antiviral activity with minimal toxicities in short-term monotherapy studies. In phase 2b trials, four out of roughly 300 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity that, on liver biopsy, was consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, leading to cessation of the trial. Similarly, one out of 26 patients in a phase 3 trial had alanine aminotransferase elevated to 24 times normal; no deaths occurred, the hepatitis resolved with aplaviroc discontinuation, the trial was stopped, and clinical development of aplaviroc was terminated.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist (GlaxoSmithKline). Phase 2b: 4 of ~300 patients developed severe hepatotoxicity with liver biopsy consistent with drug-induced hepatitis, leading to trial cessation. Phase 3: 1 of 26 patients showed ALT elevation to 24 times normal; no deaths, hepatitis resolved on aplaviroc discontinuation; trial stopped and clinical development terminated. Aplaviroc produced 1.0-1.6 log10 viral load reduction in 10-day monotherapy.
