raw_record.support_text: A case report describes an industrial worker who developed severe intoxication after inhaling methylene bis(thiocyanate) (MBT) powder during occupational exposure. Within minutes the patient developed methemoglobinemia and respiratory failure, and subsequently progressed to multi-organ failure involving the liver, kidneys, and lungs, with liver failure leading. The paper characterizes this as acute liver failure secondary to intoxication with MBT, with liver failure attributed to MBT toxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occupational inhalation of escaped MBT powder (acute intoxication/supratherapeutic exposure) without personal protective equipment; multi-organ failure (liver, kidney, lung) developed. Liver failure was the leading organ failure in the course of this intoxication.
raw_record.extra_details: 39-year-old male industrial worker, no prior medical history; swept several kilograms of powder. Rapid onset: nausea, dizziness, respiratory tract irritation, dyspnea, profound cyanosis, severe methemoglobinemia (peak 51%). Progressive hepatic failure with prominent hyperbilirubinemia (TBIL 16.5 mg/dl, DBIL 13.0 mg/dl), mild transaminase elevation (ALAT 50 U/l, ASAT 49 U/l), and impaired synthetic function (CHE 2820 U/l, prothrombine time 51%, INR 1.83). Extrahepatic cholestasis excluded by ultrasound; no sepsis. Patient survived following three MARS (molecular adsorbent recirculating system) albumin dialysis sessions and hemodialysis, with gradual hepatic recovery. Also developed anuric acute renal failure, ARDS, massive hemolysis, and peripheral neuropathy (possibly MBT-mediated).

raw_record.support_text: This is a case report of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS). Dapsone is described as one of the commonly implicated drugs in drug-induced systemic hypersensitivity syndrome, and DHS is a rare dose-independent adverse effect reported with dapsone use. Manifestations include hepatitis with mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic features, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and shock. In the presented patient, the diagnosis of DHS with hepatitis was made after typical clinical manifestations following 3 weeks of dapsone intake, after excluding other drug exposures and close differential diagnoses, and was supported by prompt response to systemic steroids.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS syndrome). DHS is a rare dose-independent adverse effect; latency several weeks to up to 6 months after treatment initiation; reported incidence 0.5%-3%. The patient had severe systemic manifestations including hepatitis with mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic features, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, shock and exfoliative dermatitis. Diagnosis followed 3 weeks of dapsone intake after excluding viral hepatitis, rickettsial infection, CMV, EBV, complicated malaria and leptospirosis; supported by prompt response to systemic steroids (prednisolone or methylprednisolone). Rechallenge not recommended. Mortality as high as 12%-23% reported in severe DHS. Pathogenesis proposed to involve dapsone metabolites (hydroxylamines via hepatic microsomal cytochrome P-450). Dapsone used for leprosy, Pneumocystis jirovecii infection, toxoplasmosis, malaria, dermatological conditions and immune thrombocytopenic purpura.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with bone mycetoma being treated with oral voriconazole developed cholestasis after the first month (alkaline phosphatase 616 IU/l; γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 1126 IU/l) with mild cytolysis (AST up to ~3N, ALT 2–3N). After 18 months of treatment she presented right hypochondrium tenderness and significant cytolysis (ALT 17N, AST 8N) with normal prothrombin time; infectious and autoimmune causes were excluded, and a liver biopsy showed lesions compatible with toxic hepatitis. Voriconazole was stopped on 25 September; hepatic enzymes returned to normal within one week and cholestasis markedly diminished within four weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Oral dosing was 400 mg twice daily for 2 days then 200 mg twice daily (Pfizer, Paris, France). Cholestasis appeared after the first month and remained stable (alkaline phosphatase 616 IU/l [100–280]; γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 1126 IU/l [7–38]); significant cytolysis appeared at month 18 (ALT 17N, AST 8N) with right hypochondrium tenderness and normal prothrombin time. Infectious and autoimmune causes were negative; liver biopsy showed lesions compatible with toxic hepatitis. After stopping voriconazole (25 September), enzymes normalized within one week and cholestasis declined (alkaline phosphatase 50 IU/l, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 480 IU/l) at four weeks. The drug had been well tolerated for 18 months without visual disturbances.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 13-year-old girl presented 19 hours after ingesting two handfuls of Tylenol Extended Relief (extended-release acetaminophen, 650 mg per caplet) with vomiting, abdominal pain, and epigastric and right-upper-quadrant tenderness. Serum acetaminophen was 89 µg/mL with ALT 180 IU/L, bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL, and INR 1.5; ALT (7459 IU/L) and INR (4.2) peaked 59 hours after ingestion. She was treated with acetylcysteine, remained clinically well, and was sent home on day 4 with resolving liver-function values. The author notes that unless acetaminophen levels after such an overdose are in the potentially toxic range, the nomogram is of doubtful value, and even elevated nontoxic levels do not exclude subsequent hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric (13-year-old) patient; overdose of the extended-release formulation Tylenol Extended Relief; delayed presentation 19 hours after ingestion.
raw_record.extra_details: Vomiting and abdominal pain began 6 hours after ingestion; serum acetaminophen 89 µg/mL on arrival; ALT peaked at 7459 IU/L and INR at 4.2 at 59 hours post-ingestion; bilirubin 1.7 mg/dL initially; apparent elimination half-life 11.08 hours with linear decline in drug concentrations; treated with oral acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg loading, then 6 doses of 70 mg/kg and 11 doses of 100 mg/kg); patient remained clinically well and was discharged on day 4 with resolving liver-function values. Authors discuss uncertainty over whether slowed elimination reflected prolonged absorption or hepatic dysfunction and question the value of the immediate-release acetaminophen nomogram for sustained-release overdoses.

Hepatitis B surface antigen, anti-HBV and anti-HAV antibodies negative; normal haematology, no eosinophilia; patient received no other drugs. Animal experiments found no liver toxicity.

These data led the FDA in January 2011 to recommend capping acetaminophen at 325 mg in prescribed combination products and to run public awareness campaigns focused on the risk of acetaminophen-related liver injury.

Only one adverse reaction (myalgia). Biochemical safety monitoring showed no change between Day 0 and Day 4 or Day 7 except lower cholesterol at Day 4 (Table 3). raw_record.support_text: The paper states that to date the principal late problem with azathioprine has been hepatotoxicity. In dogs the drug is a significant liver poison causing hepatic injury within days, though this toxicity is species-specific for the dog; however, four adults in the authors' experience suffered severe liver injury after months or years of azathioprine therapy, and one of these patients died of a combination of liver failure and bacterial sepsis. This hepatotoxicity had not been observed in patients of 18 years or less, and the authors recommend periodic liver chemistry studies on all patients receiving the agent.

raw_record.support_text: The editorial reports an analysis of hepatotoxicity from the PREVENT TB study in patients treated for latent tuberculous infection (LTBI). Among 6862 patients who took at least one dose, hepatotoxicity was lower in the once-weekly rifapentine-plus-isoniazid (3HP1) group than in the daily isoniazid for 9 months (9H) group (0.4% vs 1.9%, P<0.001), for both symptomatic and asymptomatic cases. The editorial also states generally that hepatotoxicity limits completion of daily isoniazid LTBI therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Daily isoniazid monotherapy for 9 months (9H) for LTBI preventive chemotherapy. In the PREVENT TB study (6862 patients taking at least one dose), hepatotoxicity was 1.9% in the 9H group vs 0.4% in the 3HP1 (weekly rifapentine+isoniazid) group, P<0.001, seen in both symptomatic and asymptomatic patients; monitoring of liver enzymes varied by site (baseline AST measured for 76% of participants; repeat AST for 40% on 9H and 35% on 3HP1). Multivariable risk factors: abnormal baseline AST (relative risk 5.57, 95% CI 3.31–9.37), increased age, female sex, white race, non-Hispanic ethnicity, history of chronic liver disease; nested case-control identified hepatitis C as a risk factor (OR 3.24, 95% CI 1.12–9.34). Editorial notes hepatotoxicity limits completion rates of daily 6–9 month isoniazid LTBI therapy.

raw_record.support_text: The authors compiled 47 pediatric cases (age range, 5 weeks to 10 years) of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity following multiple overdoses (60-420 mg/kg/day for 1-42 days), from published cases, FDA reports, and Children's Hospital Medical Center, Cincinnati. Mean peak serum AST was 10,225 IU/L and ALT was 7,355 IU/L, significantly higher than in children with non-acetaminophen-associated hepatic failure. Twenty-four of 43 patients (55%) died and 3 survived after orthotopic liver transplantation. Parents are advised about the potential hepatotoxicity of acetaminophen when given to ill children in doses exceeding weight-based recommendations.

raw_record.extra_details: 47 children treated with 60-420 mg/kg/day for 1-42 days. Mean peak serum AST 10,225 IU/L (n=45) and ALT 7,355 IU/L (n=31), both p<0.001 versus non-acetaminophen hepatic failure (mean AST 3,500 IU/L, ALT 3,098 IU/L; n=12). Serum acetaminophen levels above the acute-ingestion toxic range in 22 of 30 patients with estimable time-from-last-dose. 24 of 43 (55%) died; 3 survived after orthotopic liver transplantation. raw_record.support_text: Dacarbazine has been associated with allergy-induced hepatic toxicity which has been fatal. Autopsy findings in reported cases revealed massive hepatic necrosis, thrombus in small hepatic veins, and frequently vasculitis with lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration. This allergic-induced Budd-Chiari syndrome usually occurred during the second cycle of dacarbazine and was associated with peripheral eosinophilia. The toxicity, although rare, indicates the drug should only be used where it has shown activity, such as in palliating metastatic melanoma.
raw_record.extra_details: Allergy-induced hepatotoxicity; autopsy findings of massive hepatic necrosis, thrombus in small hepatic veins, and vasculitis with lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltration; allergic-induced Budd-Chiari syndrome usually occurring during the second cycle of dacarbazine; associated with peripheral eosinophilia; described as rare; used in palliating metastatic melanoma.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity, previously reported in animal toxicology and open-label studies, remained a significant problem in the double-blind trial of frentizole in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus. Sixty percent of frentizole-exposed patients exhibited signs of hepatotoxicity, defined as a greater than 2-fold elevation over the upper limit of normal for SGOT, SGPT, or gamma-GT and a greater than 1.5-fold upper-limit-of-normal increase in alkaline phosphatase. Twenty-two percent experienced hepatotoxicity severe enough to warrant withdrawal from the study, and two patients developed mild jaundice; liver function tests returned to normal within 2-8 weeks after discontinuing frentizole.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Attributions in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus treated with frentizole in a double-blind trial; placebo-comparison context.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity in 60% of 23 frentizole-treated patients, defined as >2-fold ULN elevation of SGOT, SGPT, or gamma-GT and >1.5-fold ULN increase in alkaline phosphatase; 22% had hepatotoxicity severe enough to warrant withdrawal; 2 patients developed mild jaundice; liver function tests returned to normal within 2-8 weeks after discontinuation. Among patients who had one less severe episode of hepatotoxicity, 38% did not develop abnormal liver function tests upon reexposure and continued treatment without side effects. In the placebo group (n=20), 29% developed hepatic dysfunction, none attributable to drugs. Hepatotoxicity was previously seen in animal toxicology and in the open-label studies of Kay et al and Sabharwal et al. No hematologic or thyroid toxicity was encountered during the double-blind trials.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that isoniazid (INH) hepatotoxicity is defined as an increase in serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) more than three times the upper limit of normal with symptoms of hepatitis and/or jaundice, or ALT more than five times normal without symptoms. In children receiving INH as prophylaxis, liver impairment is considered rare with an incidence below 1%. A retrospective study by Chang et al. enrolling 1,582 children under INH treatment for latent TB found 13/1,582 children (0.8%) developed INH hepatotoxicity, with abdominal pain, anorexia, vomiting and nausea as the most common symptoms; a study by Leeb et al. reported elevated serum transaminases in 113/277 children (41%).

raw_record.extra_details: Definition: ALT >3x ULN with symptoms of hepatitis and/or jaundice, or ALT >5x ULN without symptoms. Chang et al.: 13/1582 children (0.8%) developed INH hepatotoxicity; 13/1235 (1.1%) among those who completed the nine-month course; symptoms included abdominal pain, anorexia, vomiting, nausea. Leeb et al.: 113/277 (41%) had elevated serum transaminases, of which 34% mild, 8% moderate and 8% severe. Peripheral neuropathy occurs in <0.2% of children at conventional INH dose.

The toxic threshold for hepatic injury is generally considered above 7.5-10 g in adults within 24 hours (approximately >150 mg/kg body weight) and above 200 mg/kg in children as a single dose.

raw_record.support_text: In a 4-month placebo-controlled clinical trial of calcium carbimide (CC) in chronic alcoholics, with high treatment compliance and little drinking during the study, patients reported no more symptoms or medical problems during CC than placebo, and there was no evidence of hepatotoxicity or behavioural toxicity. Mean white blood cell count rose slightly during CC and returned to baseline on stopping; one patient with pre-existing reduced thyroid function became hypothyroid after CC. The authors conclude CC is safe for alcoholics with normal thyroid function.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic alcoholic patients; concurrent report that one patient with pre-existing reduced thyroid function became hypothyroid after CC, with recommendation for systematic thyroid monitoring.
raw_record.extra_details: 4-month double-blind placebo-controlled outpatient trial of calcium carbimide (calcium cyanamide; Temposil) in citrated form; 85% of study medications taken and little drinking occurred; no difference in drinking or compliance variables between CC and placebo; no evidence of hepatotoxicity or behavioural toxicity; slightly increased mean white blood cell count that returned to baseline when CC was stopped; no thyroid effect in patients with normal pretreatment function.

raw_record.support_text: A 27 year old unemployed woman was admitted with jaundice after confessing to have taken an overdose of paracetamol five days previously. Investigations showed deranged liver function and abnormal clotting with a raised international normalised ratio. She received full medical treatment to prevent hepatic encephalopathy but developed acute liver failure and renal failure over the next two days, and died a week after admission. The answer key confirms this death resulted from an overdose of drugs (possible accident or suicide), i.e., not a natural cause.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure (five days before admission), consistent with deliberate/accidental overdose; concurrent renal failure also developed over the following two days.
raw_record.extra_details: 27 year old woman; presented with jaundice and deranged liver function and abnormal clotting (raised INR); treated to prevent hepatic encephalopathy but developed acute liver failure and renal failure over two days; died one week after admission. Presented as a case exercise on reportable deaths, with acute liver failure attributed to the paracetamol overdose.

raw_record.support_text: A 57-year-old patient died 24 hours after ingesting an abortifacient/laxative preparation containing 1,2-dichloroethane, from therapy-resistant cardiovascular failure. Along with the typical gastroenterocolitis and acute yellow liver dystrophy (acute liver failure), a severe hemorrhagic diathesis was observed. The complex coagulation disorder with thrombocytopenia and decreased activity of factors I, II, V, VII and XIII was interpreted as consumptive coagulopathy with secondary hyperfibrinolysis. Treatment recommendations, including immediate gastric lavage with paraffin oil and intensive liver protection, were given for acute liver failure from oral 1,2-dichloroethane poisoning.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Oral poisoning after ingestion of a preparation (an 'Ereibemittel') containing 1,2-dichloroethane; overdose setting.
raw_record.extra_details: 57-year-old patient died 24 h after ingestion from therapy-resistant cardiovascular failure. Along with acute yellow liver dystrophy (acute liver failure) there was gastroenterocolitis and a severe hemorrhagic diathesis; the coagulation disorder (thrombocytopenia, reduced activity of factors I, II, V, VII, XIII) was interpreted as consumptive coagulopathy with secondary hyperfibrinolysis. The paper states the tolerated single human dose should not exceed 1 ml of dichloroethane, with a daily maximum of 3 ml, and that no specific antidote exists. Mechanisms discussed include possible cardiogenic-shock-driven or cor pulmonale-related intravascular coagulation, with small thrombi in the pulmonary circulation noted histologically.

raw_record.support_text: The paper identifies hepatitis as the risk of greatest concern from isoniazid chemoprophylaxis. A CDC cooperative surveillance study following 13,838 people in 21 health departments found 82 possible and 92 probable isoniazid hepatitis cases, with the authors judging the true incidence best approximated by the probable cases. Age-specific rates (per 1000 persons) were used: one possible and no probable for those under age 20 years; seven possible and three probable for ages 20-34; 11 possible and 12 probable for ages 35-49; 18 possible and 23 probable for ages 50-64; and 18 possible and eight probable for those over 64 years. The probability of terminating chemoprophylaxis because of hepatitis used combined possible and probable rates.
raw_record.extra_details: Isoniazid given as tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis, assumed 70% effective in preventing activation (varied 30%-90% in sensitivity analysis). Hepatitis led to termination of prophylaxis in the analysis. In a CDC cooperative surveillance study of 13,838 people in 21 health departments there were 82 possible and 92 probable isoniazid hepatitis cases; incidence rates per 1000 persons by age (possible/probable): under 20 y: 1/0; 20-34 y: 7/3; 35-49 y: 11/12; 50-64 y: 18/23; over 64 y: 18/8. Rates varied by 75%-125% in sensitivity analysis.

raw_record.support_text: A 67-year-old man developed aplastic anaemia 11 weeks after a carbamazepine-induced DRESS. Among the systemic manifestations of the DRESS he had liver involvement with a pattern of cholestatic hepatitis. Carbamazepine was stopped at onset of the eruption, prednisone was started, the skin eruption resolved, and his liver function tests returned to normal values.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Occurred within a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) hypersensitivity syndrome in a 67-year-old man; liver involvement was one of the systemic manifestations of carbamazepine-induced DRESS.
raw_record.extra_details: Carbamazepine was taken for facial post-herpetic neuralgia; rash and fever began about 2 months after starting therapy. Cholestatic hepatitis was documented by elevated alkaline phosphatase (855 U/L), gamma-glutamyl transferase (1267 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (161 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (51 U/L); bilirubin remained near normal (0.7 mg/dL). Liver tests returned to normal after carbamazepine withdrawal and prednisone. The patient later died of haemoptysis in the setting of probable pneumonia and severe thrombocytopenia during aplastic anaemia, not of liver failure.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that although aplastic anaemia can occur as an idiosyncratic reaction to carbamazepine, in this patient carbamazepine triggered a DRESS syndrome with liver involvement (hepatitis). They state there was an obvious relationship of the drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction with the subsequent development of bone marrow aplasia, reporting this as the first case of aplastic anaemia associated with carbamazepine-induced DRESS syndrome. Laboratory monitoring (from DRESS diagnosis onward) showed peak alkaline phosphatase 855 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 1267 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 161 U/L, and aspartate aminotransferase 51 U/L, with bilirubin remaining ≤1.2 mg/dL and subsequently resolving.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver injury occurred as hepatitis within a carbamazepine-induced DRESS (drug hypersensitivity) syndrome in a single patient, later complicated by aplastic anaemia.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported case of aplastic anaemia associated with carbamazepine-induced DRESS. Laboratory timeline from DRESS diagnosis: peak ALP 855 U/L (range 120–450), GGT 1267 U/L (range 2–40), ALT 161 U/L (range 13–40), AST 51 U/L (range 19–48), bilirubin 0.5–1.2 mg/dL; elevated liver enzymes resolved over subsequent weeks. Sero-negative for hepatotropic viruses; proposed immune-mediated mechanism with activated CD8+ T cells and inverted CD4:CD8 ratio in bone marrow.

raw_record.support_text: In the pivotal phase III trials of rimegepant (75 mg) for acute migraine treatment, no serious adverse events related to treatment occurred and no hepatotoxicity was described; nausea and urinary tract infections were the most common adverse events. A companion open-label study (NCT03266588) with up to 75 mg rimegepant taken as needed for up to 52 weeks likewise reported that hepatotoxicity was not observed with long-term and high-frequency dosing.
raw_record.extra_details: NURTEC ODT 75 mg; approved by the US FDA for acute migraine treatment in February 2020. In phase III trials (NCT03235479, NCT03237845, NCT03461757) no hepatotoxicity was described; in the long-term open-label study (NCT03266588) hepatotoxicity was not observed with high-frequency dosing up to one tablet per day for 52 weeks. Use should be avoided in severe hepatic impairment due to higher plasma rimegepant concentrations, but no DILI-related injury is attributed.

raw_record.support_text: At a BCNU (carmustine) dose of 1,200 mg/m², severe hepatotoxicity developed in four patients with malignant glioma: two had reversible hepatocellular dysfunction and two had fatal centrilobular hepatic necrosis. In the 1,200 mg/m² group (21 patients), severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 11% of all patients (4 cases, 2 fatal), contributing to an overall severe toxicity rate of 33% and fatal rate of 15%.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: High-dose BCNU (carmustine) chemotherapy at 1,200 mg/m² in patients with malignant glioma.
raw_record.extra_details: Severe hepatotoxicity followed a single 1,200 mg/m² BCNU course (21 patients: 4 hepatotoxicity, 2 fatal); no severe hepatotoxicity in 2 patients receiving two courses totaling 1,350 mg/m², and none in the 1,050 mg/m² group (13 patients). Overall, severe hepatotoxicity affected 11% of all 36 patients. Two patients had reversible hepatocellular dysfunction; two had fatal centrilobular hepatic necrosis. No causality scoring instrument reported. Lung (interstitial pneumonitis) and CNS toxicities also reported separately.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity, defined as a 1.5 times rise in pre-treatment alanine transaminase (ALT) levels, was assessed among MDR-TB patients on a DOTS-Plus regimen. Pyrazinamide-induced hepatotoxicity had a probable causal relationship by Naranjo causality assessment, belonged to the not-avoidable category by the Hallas scale, and was assigned severity level 4 by the Hartwig scale. The authors noted that anti-TB drug-induced hepatotoxicity typically results from the formation or reduced clearance of toxic metabolites, with derangement of laboratory parameters within two to three months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: MDR-TB patients receiving a multi-drug DOTS-Plus regimen; hepatotoxicity attributed to pyrazinamide as part of a combination anti-TB exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity defined as 1.5x rise in pre-treatment ALT. Causality assessed with Naranjo questionnaire (probable); Hallas avoidability = not avoidable; Hartwig severity = level 4. Authors note anti-TB hepatotoxicity typically occurs via toxic metabolite formation or reduced clearance with laboratory derangement within two to three months.

raw_record.support_text: In a series of 17 patients with fulminant hepatic failure, 13 had fibronectin concentrations below the normal range on admission. The four patients with concentrations within the normal range had fulminant hepatic failure due to viral hepatitis, and the mean concentration in that group was higher than in patients with fulminant hepatic failure due to paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose (214.0±15.0 v 80.5±17.0 µg/ml; p<0.001). Paracetamol overdose is thus attributed as the cause of fulminant hepatic failure in several patients in this series.
raw_record.extra_details: Fulminant hepatic failure caused by paracetamol overdose, in patients admitted to a liver unit (17 patients total). Paracetamol-overdose group mean plasma fibronectin 80.5±17.0 µg/ml. Two surviving paracetamol-overdose patients had very low initial fibronectin that slowly returned to normal; one patient who died received fresh-frozen plasma. Fibronectin correlated negatively with aspartate aminotransferase (r=-0.766) and positively with total bilirubin (r=0.654).

raw_record.support_text: The therapeutic use of chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) for gallstone dissolution has been associated with liver injury. In the National Cooperative Gallstone Study of 916 patients given 375 mg/day or 750 mg/day CDCA for over 2 years, increased plasma AST occurred in 31% of patients on 750 mg/day and 18% on 375 mg/day, and 3% of patients presented clinically significant hepatotoxicity that required termination of CDCA. The final product label carries a boxed warning for potential liver toxicity, and CDCA is recommended only for radiolucent gallstones when surgery is too risky, with regular monitoring of serum aminotransferases.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapy limited to radiolucent gallstones, preferably small or floatable stones, when cholecystectomy is too risky; safety beyond 24 months not established.
raw_record.extra_details: National Cooperative Gallstone Study, 916 patients, doses 375 mg/day and 750 mg/day for over 2 years; increased plasma AST in 31% (750 mg/day) and 18% (375 mg/day); clinically significant hepatotoxicity in about 3% (also noted in the 1993 meta-analysis as occurring in 3% of patients on 750 mg/day, always biochemically reversible) requiring termination of CDCA; diarrhea in 41% (750 mg/day, P<0.05 vs placebo) and 20% (375 mg/day); elevation of >=10% serum cholesterol, mostly LDL, in 85.2% of patients on the higher dose; boxed warning for liver toxicity in the final product label; regular monitoring of serum aminotransferases recommended.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old boy ingested an unknown quantity of potassium dichromate in a suicide attempt and developed vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and acute renal and liver failure in January 1996. Supportive treatment and dimercaprol did not prevent deterioration of renal and liver function within two days. On day 6 orthotopic cadaveric liver transplantation was performed; histopathological examination of the explanted liver showed diffuse hepatocellular necrosis. The patient recovered after transplantation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adolescent (16-year-old boy); intentional suicide ingestion of an unknown quantity, i.e., overdose exposure; poison obtained from a school chemical laboratory.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute liver failure progressed over six days leading to orthotopic cadaveric liver transplantation. Histopathology of the explanted liver showed diffuse hepatocellular necrosis. Serum chromium levels decreased over time, suggesting chromium accumulation in the liver. Plasmapheresis and hemodialysis did not remove substantial chromium from circulation as documented by filtrate measurements. Dimercaprol (250 mg IV twice daily) was administered as chelation treatment. Patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 14 with normal laboratory findings; normal liver and kidney function at two-year follow-up. Authors recommend delaying liver transplantation to allow the native liver to extract chromium.

raw_record.support_text: Pazopanib is reported to cause hepatotoxicity as a severe adverse effect in treated cancer patients, resulting in an enhanced, significant risk of severe hepatotoxicity, which was among the most common reasons for pazopanib discontinuation. Grade 3 hepatotoxicity occurred in 12% of patients, whereas fatal adverse events (FAE) of hepatotoxicity were rare (0.05% of cases). Hepatotoxicity was identified by increased serum ALT, AST, and bilirubin; in a large Phase II study of metastatic RCC, ALT and AST were increased in 54% and 53% of patients, respectively, and in Phase II/III RCC trials 84% of patients had hyperbilirubinemia, linked to genetic polymorphism consistent with Gilbert's syndrome.

raw_record.support_text: Significant hepatotoxicity has been reported with the use of tacrine. All patients receiving tacrine should have baseline liver function tests performed, and liver function tests should be followed during weeks 4 through 16. Patients should be alert for symptoms of liver failure, and dosing guidelines are adjusted in response to liver function testing.
raw_record.extra_details: Tacrine (Cognex) is an acridine-derivative cholinesterase inhibitor FDA-approved in 1995 for Alzheimer's disease. In double-blind placebo-controlled trials, a significant percentage of patients, especially those at higher doses, withdrew because of intolerable hepatotoxicity and cholinergic side effects. Liver function test monitoring is recommended from weeks 4 through 16 with baseline testing; dosing is adjusted based on LFT results, and tacrine should be used with caution in hepatic insufficiency. Oral dosing divided into initial (10 mg four times daily for 4 weeks), titration up to maximum 160 mg total per day.

raw_record.support_text: For flutamide, the major adverse effects include gastrointestinal disorders, hematological disorders, muscle cramps, and gynecomastia, with acute liver failure highlighted as the most relevant adverse effect due to high mortality and frequent need for liver transplantation. A 14-year retrospective observational study observed 10 cases of acute and fulminant hepatitis induced by flutamide; two of these patients were treated for acne vulgaris and developed fulminant flutamide-induced hepatitis that responded well after discontinuation. A separate retrospective study of 230 patients on flutamide for acne and seborrhea initiated at 250 mg daily (annually halved to a minimum of 62.5 mg daily) found that only 5% discontinued due to increased liver enzymes at 250 mg daily, with no enzyme elevation at 125 mg and 62.5 mg.
raw_record.extra_details: In a 14-year retrospective observational study, 10 cases of flutamide-induced acute and fulminant hepatitis were observed; 2 of the 10 cases were patients treated with flutamide for acne vulgaris, both developing fulminant hepatitis with good response after discontinuation. In another retrospective study of flutamide tolerability in 230 patients with acne and seborrhea (started at 250 mg daily, annually reduced by half to a minimum of 62.5 mg daily), only 5% discontinued at 250 mg daily due to increased liver enzymes, and no enzyme elevation was seen at 125 mg and 62.5 mg daily. Acute liver failure from flutamide is associated with high mortality and necessity of liver transplantation.

raw_record.support_text: In the pivotal phase III trial of idelalisib plus rituximab in patients with heavily pre-treated CLL, transaminitis (8% grade ≥3) occurred more frequently in patients on idelalisib therapy. A trial in treatment-naïve younger patients (median age 67 years) was complicated by frequent immune-mediated hepatotoxicity, which was less common in older patients (median age 71 years). Data from a series of idelalisib combination trials demonstrate increased toxicity, including hepatotoxicity, in patients receiving idelalisib. The toxicities of hepatitis, colitis, and pneumonitis are considered autoimmune-mediated and responsive to glucocorticoids, with T cell infiltration into inflamed organs; the paper notes this immune-mediated injury as a recognized adverse effect of idelalisib treatment.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatotoxicity reported in patients with CLL treated with idelalisib, including single-agent and idelalisib-containing combination regimens (with rituximab or ofatumumab); described as immune-mediated, more frequent in a trial of younger treatment-naïve patients and less common in older patients.
raw_record.extra_details: Pivotal phase III trial (idelalisib + rituximab vs placebo + rituximab) reported transaminitis 8% grade ≥3. In treatment-naïve younger patients (median age 67, range 58–85) given single-agent idelalisib then + ofatumumab, immune-mediated hepatotoxicity was frequent; less common in a separate trial of older patients (median age 71, range 65–90) on idelalisib + rituximab. Hepatitis (with colitis and pneumonitis) considered autoimmune-mediated, responsive to glucocorticoids, with T cell infiltration; supported by preclinical evidence that PI3Kδ inactivation in regulatory T cells unleashes CD8+ cytotoxic T cell responses. Idelalisib is an oral reversible inhibitor of PI3Kδ (previously GS-1101, CAL-101), approved with rituximab for relapsed/refractory CLL.

raw_record.support_text: During a developmental study of the fluorinated thymidine analog fialuridine for HBV infection, 7 of 15 treated patients developed severe hepatotoxicity and lactic acidosis, with 3 patients showing milder changes. Treatment with intravenous thymidine or uridine was of no benefit. Subsequently, 5 participants died, and 2 patients survived after liver transplantation. Pancreatitis, neuropathy, and myopathy often accompanied the syndrome, and liver histologic findings showed macrovesicular and microvesicular steatosis and abnormal mitochondria.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Developmental-phase clinical study for HBV infection; not predicted by animal studies; IV thymidine/uridine rescue ineffective.
raw_record.extra_details: 7 of 15 treated patients developed severe hepatotoxicity and lactic acidosis, 3 with milder changes; 5 died, 2 survived after liver transplantation; pancreatitis, neuropathy and myopathy often accompanied the syndrome; histology showed macrovesicular and microvesicular steatosis and abnormal mitochondria.

raw_record.support_text: In a pediatric phase I trial of dexrazoxane given as a single agent (a 2-hour infusion daily for 3 days) to children with refractory solid tumors, hepatic toxicity was reported as the dose-limiting toxicity and the maximum-tolerated dose was 3,500 mg/m² per day. By contrast, myelosuppression was the dose-limiting toxicity in the adult dose-finding study, with a maximum-tolerated dose of 1,000–1,250 mg/m² per day for 3 days as a short infusion. The single-agent maximum-tolerated dose of dexrazoxane in children is significantly higher than the dosage range used in the protocols studying its use as a cardioprotective agent.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients with refractory solid tumors; investigational single-agent high-dose setting (3,500 mg/m² per day, 2-hour infusion daily for 3 days), substantially above the dosage range used for cardioprotection.
raw_record.extra_details: Phase I dose-finding; hepatic toxicity identified as dose-limiting toxicity. In adults, myelosuppression was the dose-limiting toxicity with an MTD of 1,000–1,250 mg/m² per day for 3 days as a short infusion.

Drug-related chemical hepatitis, gastroduodenal ulcerations and biliary toxicity are the most common reported complications resulting in cessation of therapy in many patients. In Johnson's study, 50% of patients had to discontinue therapy because of therapy-related chemical hepatitis, three patients died of perforation and bleeding from peptic ulcers, and two patients died from severe sclerosing cholangitis.

raw_record.support_text: In a randomized double-blind trial, 44 patients with radiolucent gallstones were randomly allotted to ursodeoxycholic acid (600 mg/day), ursodeoxycholic acid (150 mg/day), or placebo. After six months, gallstone dissolution occurred in 8 (26%) of the 31 patients treated with ursodeoxycholic acid but not in the placebo group. The paper explicitly states that ursodeoxycholic acid had no hepatotoxicity as assessed by standard liver-function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in patients with radiolucent gallstones and radiologically visible gallbladders; ursodeoxycholic acid given at 600 mg/day or 150 mg/day for six months; gallstone dissolution in 8 of 31 treated patients (26%), none in placebo group; no hepatotoxicity found on standard liver-function tests. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the 7beta-epimer of chenodeoxycholic acid, synthesized by Tokyo Tanabe Company (>99% pure); patients excluded those with obstructive hepatic dysfunction or drug allergy.

raw_record.support_text: Moon and Chun reported 52 patients hospitalized with acute poisoning after oral ingestion of endosulfan. Hepatic toxicity occurred in 36.5% of these patients as a complication. Liver function tests returned to normal within 18 days of ingestion in surviving patients, while non-surviving patients continued to have ALT levels above 100 U/L until death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute oral poisoning, most often via suicide attempt or contaminated food.
raw_record.extra_details: 52 hospitalized patients in the Moon and Chun series; hepatic toxicity in 36.5% of patients; rhabdomyolysis 59.6%, hypotension 34.6%; LFTs normalized within 18 days in survivors while non-survivors maintained ALT >100 U/L until death; overall mortality 30.7% with deaths attributed to refractory status epilepticus (12 patients), multiple organ failure (2), and acute renal failure with metabolic acidosis (2), not directly to hepatic toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: A case of hepatitis attributed to moxifloxacin is presented, with the diagnosis supported by known hepatotoxic potential of the drug, a compatible temporal sequence, reasonable exclusion of alternative causes, and rapid improvement after drug withdrawal. Re-exposure was not performed.
raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS/RUCAM causality score of 8 points (probable). Of 16 Spanish notifications of moxifloxacin hepatitis, 2 were fatal (12.5%); symptoms appear in most cases between 3 and 10 days of treatment, with late hepatotoxic effects also described. The European Medicines Agency published a July 2008 press release concluding moxifloxacin should only be used in its authorized indications when no other antibiotic can be used, and recommending caution regarding certain adverse effects including fatal hepatic reactions. Probable genetic determinants of some idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity reactions are noted. The case diagnosis was based on known hepatotoxic potential, compatible temporal sequence, exclusion of alternative causes, and rapid improvement on withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: A 44-year-old man with a history of alcoholism, after three months of sobriety, began disulfiram therapy (0.5 gm daily for five days then 0.25 gm daily). Ten days into therapy he rapidly developed fatigue, malaise, and jaundice without fever. Disulfiram, chlordiazepoxide hydrochloride, and methylphenidate hydrochloride (the latter two taken for months) were stopped; bilirubin peaked at 6.9 mg/100 ml and SGOT at 2,040 units with only slight serum alkaline phosphatase elevation, and hepatitis resolved in six weeks. After rechallenge with disulfiram 0.25 gm daily, the same biochemical and clinical sequelae recurred in ten days (with urticaria and no other medication), again improving after drug discontinuation, supporting disulfiram as the cause of the hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Single patient case report. Two episodes reproducible on rechallenge. Standard dosage 0.5 gm daily for five days then 0.25 gm daily; rechallenge at 0.25 gm daily reproduced sequelae within ten days. Peak bilirubin 6.9 mg/100 ml and SGOT 2,040 units with only slight alkaline phosphatase elevation; no fever or eosinophilia on the first episode, urticaria present on rechallenge. Rapid resolution of hepatitis after withdrawal; liver tests normal in six weeks. HAA negative on two occasions. Patient had a prior episode of hepatitis after halothane anesthesia in 1968. First episode occurred with co-medications chlordiazepoxide and methylphenidate; rechallenge episode occurred without other medication, supporting disulfiram attribution.

raw_record.support_text: Acute hepatic failure, leading to coagulopathy or hepatic encephalopathy, was noted in all patients in this study of yellow phosphorus ingestion. The paper describes ingestion of yellow phosphorus as producing multi-organ toxicity including the liver, with acute hepatic failure a consistent consequence. Additional context notes delayed presentation (mean 5 days to a tertiary care hospital) and that liver transplantation is the only modality for irreversible liver failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Deliberate ingestion (intentional poisoning/consumption) in a case series of 9 patients; delayed presentation to hospital averaging 5 days; some patients received N-acetylcysteine and/or gastric decontamination, and liver transplantation for irreversible liver failure.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatic failure with coagulopathy or hepatic encephalopathy occurred in all 9 studied patients. Clinical phases described: immediate perioral burns, vomiting and diarrhoea with phosphorescence of faeces/vomitus; a latent period of 2-4 weeks; then multi-organ involvement including acute renal failure, altered mentation (confusion to coma), and cardiac toxicity (hypotension, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock). Proposed toxicity mechanisms include altered ribosomal function/protein synthesis, glucose regulation failure, and altered lipoprotein synthesis/triglyceride secretion leading to fatty degeneration of liver, kidney, heart and brain. Outcome comparison (improved n=4 vs adverse n=5) shows higher renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and metabolic acidosis in the adverse group. No specific antidote exists; NAC benefit is contradictory.

Of 30 selected pharmacovigilance cases, 18 were retained, with cytolytic hepatitis in 15 and mixed-type hepatitis in 3; one patient also exposed to lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide developed fulminant hepatitis requiring liver transplantation, and outcome after etifoxine withdrawal was recovery in 15 patients and improvement in 2.

raw_record.extra_details: Etifoxine chlorhydrate (Stresam, Laboratoire Biocodex, France), a benzoxazine derivative approved for psychosomatic manifestations of anxiety at daily dose of 150-200 mg, marketed since 1979, mostly used in France. Of 30 selected French pharmacovigilance database cases reported since November 1995, 18 retained. Median treatment duration before symptom onset 18 days (range 11-61 days). Cytolytic hepatitis in 15 cases, mixed-type hepatitis in 3. One fulminant hepatitis requiring liver transplantation; six other patients had biological signs of severity. Except the transplanted patient, 15 recovered within 3 months and 2 clearly improved (further outcome unknown) after etifoxine withdrawal. Only one case of acute hepatitis previously published. Adverse effect not mentioned in the summary of product characteristics.

raw_record.support_text: A previously healthy 58-year-old man developed jaundice, pruritus, and malaise about 1 month after taking sildenafil 50 mg; no other medications, including NSAIDs, were used and tests for viral hepatitis, autoantibodies, and bile duct obstruction were negative. A liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis with marked bile stasis. On the basis of criteria for drug-induced liver disorders and the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, the authors diagnosed probable sildenafil-induced cholestatic hepatotoxicity, and laboratory values returned to normal 4 months after symptom onset.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of severe cholestatic hepatotoxicity attributed to sildenafil in a 58-year-old man treated for erectile dysfunction. Dose 50 mg; onset about 1 month before symptoms. Labs: ALP 476 IU/l, ALT 64 IU/l, AST 42 IU/l, total bilirubin 8.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 6.3 mg/dl, albumin 3.6 g/dl, eosinophils 2.8%, prothrombin time 95%. Laparoscopy showed a green, enlarged, non-nodular liver. Liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis with marked pericentral canalicular bile stasis and minimal portal necroinflammation. Diagnosis supported by drug-induced liver disorder criteria and the Naranjo scale. No rechallenge; liver tests normalized without treatment by 4 months. The authors note a prior literature case (Daghfous et al.) of acute hepatotoxicity attributed to sildenafil with an uncertain causal relation and no recurrence on rechallenge.

raw_record.support_text: Of the 13 patients who discontinued bosentan because of safety concerns, 12 were due to hepatotoxicity and 1 due to rash. Six of the 12 patients with hepatotoxicity had been re-challenged with bosentan with documented recurrence of acute hepatotoxicity before enrollment, and 8 of the 12 had discontinued bosentan within the first 3 months of therapy. Elevated hepatic transaminases (5 to 8 times ULN in some) resolved after bosentan discontinuation.

Reported in a PAH clinical-trial safety subset recruiting patients switched from bosentan with prior hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: Tacrine (Cognex) is described as causing clinically evident liver toxicity: of more than 8000 patients exposed in clinical studies and the treatment IND program, one documented patient had elevated bilirubin (5.3 × ULN), jaundice, and transaminase levels (AST/SGOT) nearly 20 × ULN. In the 30-week clinical study and all trials (2446 patients), approximately 50% had at least one ALT/SGPT elevation above ULN, about 25% developed elevations >3 × ULN, ~7% (>10 × ULN in trials) and 3% of 5665 treatment IND patients had ALT >10 × ULN; all transaminase levels returned to normal after discontinuation or dose reduction, usually within 4-6 weeks.
raw_record.extra_details: Brand: Cognex. Intended for Alzheimer's disease. One case of jaundice with bilirubin 5.3 × ULN and AST/SGOT ~20 × ULN among >8000 exposed in clinical studies and the treatment IND program. In the 30-week study (N=479), ALT elevations: >ULN 54%, >2×ULN 38%, >3×ULN 29%, >10×ULN 6%, >20×ULN 2%; median time to first ALT elevation ~6 weeks, maximum ~1 week later; 95% of >3×ULN elevations within first 18 weeks under forced slow dose titration; 99% of 10-fold elevations by 12th week at ≤80 mg. All transaminases returned to normal on discontinuation or dose reduction, usually within 4-6 weeks. Transaminase monitoring and discontinuation criteria recommended (label WARNINGS: Liver Injury).

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude that, in their 48-year-old female patient who presented with pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, hypocholia, nausea, vomiting and epigastric pain one week after taking 3 tablets of zolmitriptan for a severe migraine episode, the liver disease was very probably related to zolmitriptan use, based on the temporal relationship of symptoms to intake, resolution with conservative measures while avoiding re-exposure, and the exclusion of other causes of acute hepatitis (negative viral and autoimmune serology, normal abdominal ultrasound).
raw_record.extra_details: 48-year-old woman with no other risk factors for liver disease, no alcohol, drugs or other potentially hepatotoxic agents, no transfusions. Took 3 tablets of zolmitriptan one week before onset for severe migraine. Presentation: intense pruritus, jaundice, dark urine, hypocholia, nausea, vomiting, moderate epigastric pain. Elevated AST (355 U/l, normal <31), ALT (331 U/l, normal <31), alkaline phosphatase (530 U/l, normal <270), GGT (206 U/l, normal <32) and bilirubin (4.31, normal <1). Negative HCV/RNA, HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, HAV IgM, EBV IgM, CMV, HEV IgM, HSV-1/2 IgM, Toxoplasma IgM; negative ANA, AMA, ASMA, p-ANCA and LKM-1. Normal albumin, prothrombin and abdominal ultrasound. Complete recovery with conservative measures; liver biopsy avoided. Paper notes the predominant presentation of drug-related liver disease is usually acute hepatitis or cholestatic liver disease and that the mechanism of acute toxic hepatitis is believed to be immunoallergic, tending to occur in immunologically susceptible individuals.

raw_record.support_text: This case report attributes the initial hepatic injury to trifluperazine use. On the Naranjo ADR probability scale the likelihood of an ADR due to trifluperazine in this case was probable (score 6), based on elevation of liver enzymes after initiation of trifluoperazine, deterioration of liver function under continued treatment, and a considerable decrease in enzymes after stopping the drug. Other causes of cholestatic jaundice were ruled out, and the authors recognized trifluperazine as a cause; they note only a few cases of cholestatic jaundice induced by trifluperazine have been reported since its introduction in 1958.
raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo ADR probability scale score 6 (probable). Liver enzymes rose after therapy initiation, deteriorated on continued treatment, and decreased substantially after drug discontinuation (dechallenge). Other causes of cholestatic jaundice ruled out. A prior 1968 case (Margulies et al.) reported jaundice in a 26-year-old woman with psychosis after 15 days of trifluoperazine. The drug has been marketed since 1958 with only a few reported DILI cases; small numbers of spontaneous reports are not necessarily a reliable risk indicator.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that of the more widely used anticonvulsant drugs, phenacemide is the only one proved to have caused severe toxic effects on the normal liver, and that the clinician must continuously look for evidence of impending liver damage during therapy. It also cites earlier reports of nonfatal hepatitis: Lloyd-Smith described acute hepatitis with jaundice developing after 70 gm of phenacemide given for two months (serum bilirubin 4.4 mg/100 cc), with jaundice resolving one week after stopping the drug; Livingston and Kajdi noted nonfatal hepatitis in one of 104 patients; and Carter described two cases of acute hepatitis with recovery among 63 patients taking phenacemide.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenacemide therapy (anticonvulsant) caused fatal and nonfatal toxic liver injury. Eight fatalities were attributed to phenacemide therapy with pathological findings of acute yellow atrophy or massive necrosis of liver parenchyma (cases 4, 6, 8: acute yellow atrophy; case 7: massive necrosis; case 3: hepatorenal syndrome; case 5: acute severe parenchymal liver damage superimposed on mild portal cirrhosis). Deaths followed phenacemide doses of 42-669 gm over 25-210 days. Nonfatal hepatitis reports: jaundice after 70 gm over two months; 1/104 patients; 2 cases among 63 patients, all with recovery.

raw_record.support_text: Fosinopril induced severe cholestasis with high bilirubin levels (maximum 40 mg/dl) and a minor anicteric cholestasis persisting for 4 and 18 months, respectively. raw_record.extra_details: Case report of fosinopril-induced cholestasis. Maximum serum bilirubin 40 mg/dl; minor anicteric cholestasis persisted 4 and 18 months (chronic cholestasis). The authors conclude fosinopril, as a widely used ACE inhibitor, should be included in the list of potential causes of chronic liver disease; a MEDLINE search of important adverse reactions to fosinopril retrieved no other case.

raw_record.support_text: Liver injury caused by tolvaptan is well established in patients with ADPKD, demonstrated by RCTs: Torres et al. reported that out of 961 patients, 1.5% discontinued the drug due to liver dysfunction, 4.5% had a clinically significant aminotransferase increase, and 0.9% had increased bilirubin; that study and its open-label extension indicated three cases of severe liver injury attributed to this drug that led to liver failure. In the TEMPO 2:3 trial, approximately 10.9% of tolvaptan-treated patients had adverse hepatic events versus 5.3% in placebo, most often ALT elevation three times the upper limit of normal, with resolution of LFTs after stopping tolvaptan.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Population restricted to patients with ADPKD.
raw_record.extra_details: Tolvaptan-induced liver injury is an idiosyncratic drug reaction; major risk factor ADPKD. Liver injury typically occurs after 3-18 months of use. Torres et al. RCT (n=961): 1.5% discontinued for liver dysfunction, 4.5% clinically significant aminotransferase increase, 0.9% bilirubin increase; 3 cases of severe liver injury progressing to liver failure (study plus open-label extension). TEMPO 2:3 trial: 10.9% vs 5.3% adverse hepatic events, most commonly ALT >3x ULN; all cases resolved after drug discontinuation. Mechanism studies (Mosedale et al., mice) implicated genetic susceptibility (epoxide hydrolase, IRF3, mitochondrial fission factor loci, chromosome 14) with oxidative stress, innate immune response, and bile acid homeostasis alterations.

raw_record.support_text: Minocycline is recognized to cause an autoimmune hepatitis, generally appearing after a long period of exposure, with average onset within 2 years but possibly within a few months. Features include fever, polyarthralgia, rash, anorexia, fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, and jaundice; serology resembles idiopathic autoimmune hepatitis with ANA, ASMA, and anti-LKM positivity, elevated IgG, and typical histology of chronic active hepatitis with periportal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and piecemeal necrosis. A higher frequency of HLA-B*35:02 is found in patients with minocycline-induced autoimmune hepatitis than in the general population, while HLA-DRB1*03:01 and *04:01 are not risk factors. Hepatitis occurs twice as often in women, who also develop symptoms after shorter therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported case: transaminitis persisted after minocycline discontinuation, peaking at ALT 3,422 U/L, AST 3,909 U/L and direct bilirubin 17.54 µg/dL about two weeks after stopping; improved with prednisone and lab values normalized within 12 weeks; hepatitis did not recur after prednisone. Minocycline hepatotoxicity risk is higher than other tetracyclines; symptoms/lab abnormalities typically resolve within 3 months of discontinuation; recurrence does not typically occur unless rechallenged. Serology: ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM, p-ANCA possible, IgG >1.5x ULN; eosinophils rare; bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis uncommon. Mechanism unknown but possibly immune-mediated via HLA-B*35:02 antigen presentation; onset average within 2 years of exposure.

raw_record.support_text: A 48-year-old physician developed sudden fatigue and nausea during daily oral ketoconazole 200 mg for fingernail onychomycosis, with cessation of therapy after 81 days. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated ALT (aspartate transaminase up to 1900 U/L), icterus, and markedly elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lactic dehydrogenase; viral hepatitis A and B were excluded and recovery occurred within 2 months. The authors note a previously reported biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis in a ketoconazole-treated patient and conclude that hepatic damage associated with ketoconazole therapy is probably an idiosyncratic reaction, with estimated incidence of 0.1% to 1% and many subclinical cases. The paper also cites a manufacturer advisory reporting the death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Second reported case of ketoconazole hepatotoxicity in a 48-year-old physician treated for fingernail onychomycosis (a prior biopsy-proven toxic hepatitis case was reported from the same institution). Dose 200 mg/day for 81 days; onset of fatigue and nausea after ~8 weeks with an ALT increase still within normal limits, then marked elevation (aspartate transaminase 1900 U/L, bilirubin 107-111 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 450-480 U/L, LDH 600-800 U/L); a single rechallenge dose (200 mg, 48 h before day 86 studies) appeared to accelerate the ALT rise. Icterus and marked malaise present; viral hepatitis A and B excluded by serology; ultrasonography and CT of liver and pancreas normal; liver biopsy refused; findings returned to normal within 2 months. Estimated incidence of hepatic damage 0.1% to 1%, many cases subclinical. Manufacturer (Janssen) advisory reported death of a patient who developed hepatitis during ketoconazole therapy. Authors recommend liver function tests before and during ketoconazole treatment. Prior griseofulvin treatment was discontinued due to diarrhea; no other medications, no history of liver disease or excessive ethanol.

The paper presents this as the first reported case of cytolytic hepatic injury imputable to nomégestrol, since prior reports of nomégestrol hepatotoxicity were rare, generally moderate, and cholestatic (p[2]); recovery after drug discontinuation was rapid.
raw_record.extra_details: 43-year-old female treated with Lutényl® (nomégestrol) 1 tablet/day days 10–25 of cycle for 5 months for premenstrual disorders; jaundice appeared ~7 days after symptom onset (24 h after last dose). Viral serologies (Hep A/B/C, EBV, CMV) and autoantibodies negative; liver biopsy refused. Rapid clinical and biologic recovery with disappearance of jaundice and normalization of aminotransferases, bilirubin, and prothrombin within 3 weeks after discontinuation (favorable dechallenge). Concomitant paracetamol (0.5–1.5 g/day ×4 days) was excluded as causative by later uneventful paracetamol use (0.5–2 g/day) after recovery. First reported cytolytic hepatic injury attributed to nomégestrol (previously only rare, moderate, cholestatic injury); physiopathologic mechanism not established.

raw_record.support_text: A retrospective analysis of inpatients who received tigecycline treatment from January 2018 to January 2020 assessed Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) using biochemical criteria and the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM), retaining cases with a probable or highly probable causality grading. The author found that tigecycline was associated with liver injury, with a slightly higher incidence (5.7%) than the frequency of "frequent" (5%) defined by the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities. Tigecycline-associated DILI was related to a high maintenance dose, prolonged treatment duration, and a number of concomitant medications with known hepatotoxicity.

One month after tamoxifen discontinuation bilirubin normalized, and aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase returned to baseline in about 6 weeks; rechallenge was not attempted.

raw_record.support_text: Acetaminophen toxicity was the most common etiology of acute fulminant hepatic failure (9 of 25 AFHF cases in the NeuroICU). Twelve patients had cerebral edema on CT, including 8 of the 9 with acetaminophen toxicity, and fourteen patients died, including all 12 with cerebral edema. The conclusion states that acetaminophen toxicity is a common cause of AFHF, and that early cerebral edema occurs in almost all AFHF cases with acetaminophen overdose.

raw_record.extra_details: Acetaminophen toxicity accounted for 9 of 25 AFHF cases; 8 of the 9 had cerebral edema on CT. Fourteen patients died, including all 12 with cerebral edema; no hematological or biochemical variables (INR, bilirubin, creatinine, albumin) correlated significantly with mortality. AFHF patients developed brain parenchyma changes within 24 hours of symptom onset during Grade I-II encephalopathy, most strikingly with acetaminophen overdose.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a case of mixed cholestatic-hepatocellular liver injury in a patient on trazodone at the recommended starting dose. They state: 'We believe our patient also had an idiosyncratic drug reaction to trazodone, characterized by both a cholestatic and hepatocellular resemblance and profound hyperbilirubinemia.' The reaction peaked 2 weeks after drug discontinuation and resolved over 8 weeks, and they advise monitoring liver enzymes and bilirubin during the first 4 weeks in patients starting trazodone, regardless of dosage.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a patient presenting with what appeared to be obstructive jaundice with hepatocellular inflammation; extensive evaluation was negative. Liver biopsy showed intrahepatic cholestasis and inflammatory response consistent with a drug reaction. Bilirubin peaked at 29 mg/dL two weeks after drug discontinuation; aspartate transaminase and alkaline phosphatase decreased to 235 IU/L and 152 IU/L, respectively, and all liver enzymes and bilirubin returned to normal eight weeks after trazodone was discontinued. The reaction occurred at the recommended starting dose. A prior published case (Chu et al., reference 1) of a mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic reaction at trazodone 500 mg/d was the first published case of liver toxicity. Trazodone is a triazolopyridine derivative (nontricyclic antidepressant); its primary side effects are drowsiness and dizziness. Authors recommend monitoring liver enzymes and bilirubin for the first 4 weeks in patients starting trazodone.

raw_record.support_text: Sixteen cases of symptomatic hepatobiliary reactions to terbinafine are summarized, all prescribed 250 mg/day for onychomycosis or fungal skin infections, with a median time to onset of 27 days. All cases showed a mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic picture of liver function test disturbance, no other cause of liver disease was found after thorough investigation, and biopsy findings were consistent with a drug reaction in all cases. One patient developed fulminant hepatic failure and required a liver transplant. The paper describes the reactions as idiosyncratic, without fever or rash typical of a generalized hypersensitivity reaction.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Three of the 16 patients had a history of hepatobiliary disease (cholecystectomy, cholecystitis, hepatitis A); two were taking steroids simultaneously; one had a history of drug allergy (griseofulvin-related skin reaction).
raw_record.extra_details: 16 symptomatic hepatobiliary reaction cases (8 men, median age 54, range 24-75; 11 European, 1 Pakistani, 3 Canadian, 1 American, 1 Israeli); terbinafine 250 mg/day for onychomycosis or fungal skin infections; average time to onset 27 days; prodrome of lassitude, asthenia, anorexia, abdominal pain ~1 week before jaundice with pale stools and dark urine; mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic LFT picture; no other cause found. One biopsy at 6 months showed discrete portal fibrosis, centrilobular cholestasis and reduced interlobular bile ducts. LFTs normalized at a median of 5 months (range 1-12 months) where available. One patient required liver transplantation for fulminant hepatic failure; a second was transplanted after 5 days of therapy and died. No patient had raised eosinophil count; one patient stopped after 8 days, restarted, and developed symptoms 4 days later suggesting sensitization. The author's own case showed canalicular cholestasis and eosinophils in sinusoids and portal tract, longest recovery (LFTs normal at 15 months) and highest bilirubin rise; patient had diabetes and was not given steroids for cholestasis.

raw_record.support_text: The incidence of flutamide-related liver toxicity was studied in 1,091 consecutive patients treated for stage C or D prostate cancer with the antiandrogen flutamide plus the LHRH agonist [D-Trp6,des-Gly-NH2 10] LHRH ethylamide. Liver tests (AST, ALT, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-GT, prothrombin/thromboplastin times) were monitored. An increase in AST and ALT to 4-fold or more above upper normal limits occurred in only 4 patients (0.36%); only 2 developed clinical manifestations of liver disease (0.18%), one biopsy showing a mixed pattern of cytotoxic and cholestatic changes. raw_record.support_text: Two 38-year-old women developed elevated transaminases with fever and gastrointestinal symptoms after receiving carbamazepine (CBZ) for eye pain (Case 1, trigeminal neuralgia) and for epilepsy (Case 2). In Case 1, a small rechallenge dose of CBZ reproduced a multi-peaked rise in transaminases that took about 2 months to normalize. Case 2 developed progressive jaundice and impaired consciousness and died of fulminant hepatic failure on day 63. The authors add 17 reported Japanese and Western cases and characterize CBZ liver injury: onset typically 3-4 weeks after starting the drug with fever, jaundice, and GI symptoms; mechanisms proposed include direct action of CBZ or its metabolites and a delayed-type allergic reaction; granulomatous hepatitis has been reported; after drug withdrawal most resolve within 1 week, but 4 deaths have been reported.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 1: 38yo woman with trigeminal neuralgia; initial CBZ 400 mg/day led to elevated GOT 363 U/l, GPT 309 U/l, ALP 504 U/l, γ-GTP 396 U/l, T-bil 0.7 mg/dl, normalizing ~2 weeks after discontinuation; rechallenge with CBZ 600 mg produced chills, fever (39.5°C), and recurrent hepatic dysfunction with a bimodal transaminase peak normalizing in ~1 month. Case 2: 38yo woman with epilepsy; progressive jaundice and impaired consciousness, fulminant hepatic failure, died on day 63. Literature review adds 17 reported cases (Japan and Western): typical onset 3-4 weeks after start with fever, jaundice, GI symptoms; proposed mechanisms include direct action of CBZ or its metabolites and delayed-type hypersensitivity; granulomatous hepatitis reported; 4 deaths reported, some cases protracted. CBZ is a dibenzoazepine used for epilepsy and trigeminal neuralgia; liver injury is rare (17 published cases before this report).

raw_record.support_text: Three female patients were hospitalized for acute hepatitis related to repeated therapeutic use of ketoconazole prescribed for leucorrhea. The first patient had received 10 courses over 7 years and developed jaundice and anaphylactic shock within 24 hours of a 200 mg ketoconazole tablet; the second and third developed acute hepatitis within 1-3 days of ketoconazole rechallenge. The first two had prolonged prothrombin time (INR >1.2), and injury responded to corticosteroids. The authors describe this as consistent with the previously described idiosyncratic liver reaction to ketoconazole (dose-independent, hepatocellular damage with ballooning degeneration) yet with features more suggestive of an immunoallergic response.
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatotoxicity reported to appear within 1.5 to 24 weeks after drug administration; postulated mechanisms include glutathione chelation with active metabolites and formation of drug-protein adducts. Injury required repeated ketoconazole treatments and appeared within 1-3 days of rechallenge. First patient had jaundice and anaphylactic shock within 24 h of one 200 mg tablet after 10 courses over 7 years; first two patients had prolonged prothrombin time (INR >1.2) and 2-3-fold eosinophilia; ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes in the first patient; response to corticosteroids; absence of antinuclear antibodies did not support autoimmune hepatitis. Controlled cohort study (Chien et al) reported ~20% of patients had asymptomatic liver enzyme increases and 5% developed overt hepatitis, with biochemical alterations returning to normal after discontinuation; authors recommended continuing therapy with caution in the absence of symptoms/hyperbilirubinemia but discontinuing if overt hepatitis occurs.

raw_record.support_text: In three patients, symptoms of severe malaise and abdominal pain began within 24 hours after rechallenge with a low dose of dextropropoxyphene hydrochloride (32.5 mg). In patients 1 and 2, liver function tests became abnormal within 24 hours and were predominantly hepatitic initially, followed by a more prolonged cholestatic phase; abnormalities returned completely to normal. The authors state that hepatic toxicity reliably attributable to dextropropoxyphene is rare, and that incrimination of the drug was proven by rechallenge.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 3 new patients (plus 12 previously reported literature cases) presenting with epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, fever/rigors, jaundice, pale stools and dark urine, commonly leading to a misdiagnosis of biliary tract disease (two patients underwent laparotomy/cholecystectomy). Hepatic injury proven by rechallenge: symptoms within 24 hours of a single 32.5 mg oral dose of dextropropoxyphene hydrochloride; LFTs predominantly hepatitic initially then a prolonged cholestatic phase, all returning to normal. Liver histology (postchallenge) showed centrilobular/intrahepatic cholestasis with bile thrombi, oedematous portal tracts infiltrated by eosinophils and lymphocytes, and dilated bile canaliculae with granular material, suggestive of a drug hypersensitivity reaction; ultrastructural changes compared to chlorpromazine jaundice. Clinical diagnosis was cholestatic hepatitis with mixed LFTs.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old male developed jaundice and severe hyperbilirubinemia beginning about 1 year after starting carbimazole (40 mg with levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily as block-and-replace) for Graves' disease. He had no prior history of liver disease and had taken no other prescribed, over-the-counter, or illicit substances. Carbimazole was stopped; liver biopsy showed a mixed cholestatic-hepatitic injury (cholestatic more prominent), and it was considered most likely to represent a drug-related liver injury. Liver function slowly improved and the jaundice resolved completely.
raw_record.extra_details: Case: 38-year-old male with Graves' disease/hyperthyroidism; block-and-replace carbimazole 40 mg + levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily; late onset about 1 year after commencement (jaundice for 6 weeks, mild abdominal pain, malaise); bilirubin rose from 129 to 459 with prothrombin time 15 then 18.6; normal US liver structure and normal MRCP biliary tree; liver biopsy showed mixed cholestatic-hepatitic injury with cholestatic component more prominent; no evidence of hepatic necrosis on biopsy mentioned in case; recovered completely; propylthiouracil avoided due to hepatotoxicity risk, total thyroidectomy performed.

raw_record.support_text: In the trial, 27 (44%) and 7 (12%) patients receiving pexidartinib or placebo, respectively, had Grade 3 or 4 adverse events. Elevations in alanine transaminase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alkaline phosphatase occurred more frequently with pexidartinib (7%–10% vs. 0%). Seven patients discontinued pexidartinib due to mixed and cholestatic liver toxicity, most of which was reversible within 1–2 months of stopping. Serious hepatotoxicity emerges within the first 2 months of treatment, and pexidartinib carries a black box warning regarding the risk of potentially fatal liver injury, is prescribed only through a REMS program, and should be avoided in patients with pre-existing liver or biliary tract diseases or elevated bilirubin/transaminases at baseline.

raw_record.support_text: The paper lists transaminitis and hepatotoxicity among the major toxicities of idelalisib. In relapsed/refractory CLL patients, grade 3 or higher transaminitis occurred in approximately 14% of patients. When idelalisib was used as upfront therapy for CLL, it caused early, severe grade 3 or higher hepatotoxicity in 54% of patients, with steroids usually effective at treating the transaminitis once it develops.

Front-line safety concerns (serious adverse events including deaths mainly due to infections) led to premature closure of phase 3 trials and EMA/FDA reviews warning against initiating this drug in treatment-naive patients with del(17p) or TP53 mutation.

raw_record.support_text: Nitrofurantoin, used since 1953 for prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection, is associated with a wide range of adverse drug reactions; chronic active hepatitis has increasingly been observed with many case fatalities reported. The authors present a case of nitrofurantoin-induced chronic active hepatitis and review the serological and clinicopathological features of 57 similar cases reported in English literature, noting consistent antinuclear antibody, anti-smooth-muscle antibody, and elevated immunoglobulin suggestive of an immunologic mechanism, with complete recovery possible in most cases if the drug is discontinued.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic/prolonged therapeutic use (e.g., 200 mg daily for recurrent UTI prophylaxis), predominantly female patients (55 of 57), frequently prolonged exposure; index case had concomitant hydrochlorothiazide and bronchodilator inhalers.
raw_record.extra_details: Index case: 62-year-old woman, nitrofurantoin 200 mg/day for 3 years; AST 1173 IU/L, ALT 504 IU/L, total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dL (direct 3.2), ALP 245 IU/L; anti-SMA positive 1:160, polyclonal gammaglobulins elevated (1.81 g/dL), ANA negative; liver biopsy showed chronic active interface hepatitis with plasma cells, portal fibrosis and bridging fibrosis; simplified AIH score 7; improvement after drug cessation and short steroid course, enzymes normal by 2 months. Among 57 literature cases: daily dose 50-400 mg, exposure duration 2 months to 12 years, most (93%) symptomatic after 6 months; ANA positive 78%, anti-SMA positive 72%, either test positive 88%, hypergammaglobulinemia 79%; cirrhosis in 8 cases; 8/57 (14%) died despite drug withdrawal; one patient underwent orthotopic liver transplant after fulminant liver failure; estimated frequency of nitrofurantoin hepatotoxic reactions 0.3 to 35 per 100,000 treated patients.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old woman presented with jaundice, pruritus, anorexia and vomiting, with elevated liver enzymes (AST 676 U/L, ALT 425 U/L, ALP 384 U/L, GGT 406 U/L, total bilirubin 19.87 mg/dL). Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C and autoantibodies were negative. A liver biopsy obtained during the eighth week after terbinafine discontinuation revealed cholestatic hepatitis, and use of the Naranjo probability scale indicated a probable relationship between terbinafine and cholestatic hepatitis.

UDCA (1000 mg/day) was given for elevated liver enzymes and intractable pruritus; liver tests normalized by 15 weeks after terbinafine cessation (AST 30, ALT 32 U/L, total bilirubin 1.17 mg/dL). Competing viral/autoimmune causes ruled out.

raw_record.support_text: A 63-year-old man developed granulomatous hepatitis probably due to the administration of aprindine (200 mg/day for paroxysmal supraventricular arrhythmia). Evidence of hepatitis appeared within 6 weeks of initiating aprindine therapy and resolved rapidly when the drug was withdrawn; six months later, fibrosis but no granulomata were found in the expanded portal tracts. The authors conclude that granulomatous hepatitis can occur during aprindine therapy. Biopsy 5 days after withdrawal showed granulomata in portal tracts and lobules with an infiltrate of eosinophils, plasma cells and lymphocytes and no caseous necrosis; HBsAg, PPD, CMV and EBV tests were negative, and serum aprindine concentration was not determined.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis presented within 6 weeks of aprindine at 200 mg/day; symptoms included abdominal discomfort, right hypochondrium pain, rigor, fever (38°C), nausea, vomiting, fatigue, headache, pruritus and jaundice; marked elevation of serum bilirubin and moderate aminotransferase abnormalities; liver resolved on withdrawal; second biopsy at 6 months showed portal tract fibrosis without granulomata.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case of granulomatous hepatitis probably due to the administration of aprindine. Although drug rechallenge was not done, the hepatic damage appeared within 6 weeks of initiating aprindine therapy and resolved rapidly after drug withdrawal, which the authors state is suggestive of aprindine-induced liver toxicity. The patient had received no other medication during the past year, had no history of liver disease or sarcoidosis/tuberculosis, and was negative for HBV/HCV/HAV markers.
raw_record.extra_details: Granulomatous hepatitis is the named phenotype. Drug rechallenge was not performed. Hepatic damage appeared within 6 weeks of initiating aprindine therapy and resolved after withdrawal. A liver biopsy 5 days after withdrawal showed moderate inflammatory infiltration consisting predominantly of eosinophils and granulomata in most portal tracts and lobules, without caseous necrosis or fibrosis; 6 months later granulomata had disappeared and fibrosis was present in expanded portal tracts. No competing medications, liver disease history, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, hypotension, blood transfusion, or HBV/HCV/HAV markers were present. The paper also cites at least eight previously published cases of aprindine-induced hepatitis with mild to moderate clinical illness occurring within 12 days to 6 weeks of starting therapy and resolving after drug withdrawal, with rechallenge reproducing hepatitis in all four rechallenged patients; no granulomatous hepatitis was identified in the four prior biopsied cases.

raw_record.support_text: The temporal relationship between rofecoxib administration and onset of symptoms is highly suggestive of rofecoxib-induced hepatotoxicity. Clinical, biochemical and histological findings were consistent with a hypersensitivity-like liver injury. Although the patient had also taken phenprocoumon and estrogens, these drugs had been used for several years with repeatedly normal previous liver tests, so they were excluded as causes. The WHO database of adverse drug reactions contains several reports of hepatitis under rofecoxib, hinting to a causal relationship between serious liver injury and rofecoxib.
