raw_record.extra_details: Admission labs: total bilirubin 420 µmol/l (<26), total bile acids 120 µmol/l (<5), AST 240 U/l (<19), ALT 228 U/l (<24), ALP 1314 U/l (60-190). Liver biopsy showed severe hepatocellular, focal intracanalicular cholestasis and an inflammatory reaction including eosinophils involving portal tracts. Severe cholestasis with pruritus was treated with three sessions of extracorporal albumin dialysis (MARS, 8 h each, mean flow 80 ml/min) with marked improvement; symptoms and labs resolved ~10 weeks after ceasing MARS. Viral/autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease and obstructive cholestasis excluded. No prior case of rofecoxib-induced cholestatic hepatitis published; WHO pharmacovigilance database contains several reports of hepatitis under rofecoxib.

raw_record.support_text: In a 10-year study of 322 pediatric patients presenting for acetaminophen overdose, hepatocellular injury developed in 27 patients (8.4%) and hepatic failure in 4 of these; 4 had severe hepatocellular injury and 1 died of multisystem organ failure, none required liver transplantation though 2 were accepted but recovered. At Memorial Sloan-Kettering, doses ≥250 mg/m² produced nausea, hyperglycemia, and hepatic toxicity, and 350 mg/m² caused irreversible hepatic toxicity in 2 patients with a drug-related death from liver toxicity. Hepatic toxicity was also reported at M.D. Anderson, at the Mayo Clinic, at Wayne State University (described as reversible), and at Brown University.

raw_record.support_text: This case series reports three patients with halothane hepatitis followed for 10 to 14 months. Despite initially severe clinical and biochemical presentations with extensive bridging hepatic necrosis on liver biopsy, all three patients resolved completely and had minimally abnormal liver biopsy appearances at follow-up. The authors conclude that hepatic necrosis associated with halothane hypersensitivity is self-limited and that postnecrotic cirrhosis does not develop, provided reexposure to halothane is avoided.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients diagnosed with halothane hepatitis after halothane anesthesia, all initially severe with extensive bridging hepatic necrosis; all recovered fully and no postnecrotic cirrhosis developed within 10-14 months of follow-up, as long as reexposure to halothane was avoided. Patient 2: similar course with icterus and abnormal liver function; biopsy showed acute hepatitis with bridging necrosis. The necrosis is attributed to halothane hypersensitivity and described as self-limited.

The authors conclude that the evidence supports the diagnosis of a halothane-induced sensitization reaction with hepatitis, based on the characteristic temporal relation between halothane exposure and fever/jaundice, onset with chills and high fever, significant eosinophilia, antecedent atopy and drug-hypersensitivity reactions, occurrence of the hepatitis after a second halothane exposure in two of the three cases, and histologic features consistent with drug-induced hepatitis. raw_record.support_text: The authors report that a patient's death was caused in part by valproate-induced hepatotoxicity, attributing the mechanism to an idiosyncratic response to a toxic metabolite of valproic acid. Clinical deterioration began 6 days after starting valproic acid, with prodromal anorexia, lethargy, and new seizure activity; liver function tests showed no clear-cut injury until late in the course. Liver histology showed microvesicular steatosis and centrilobular necrosis, and although liver failure was not the sole cause of death it was a contributing factor. The authors conclude valproic acid should be used with caution in treating epilepsy in renal transplant recipients receiving cyclosporine.

raw_record.support_text: In a case series of 35 patients with drug-induced hepatitis at Shinko Hospital, Kobe, Japan, nine had a severe hepatic lesion with bridging necrosis as determined in liver biopsy during the acute episode (two males, seven females). Causative drugs were identified by cautious rechallenge in eight patients and by an in-vitro test in one. N-Methyl carbamate was the causative drug in four patients and mefenamic acid, kanamycin, pyrazinamide, difenamizole, and pyrithioxin hydrochloride in one each. All nine recovered fully within 6 months after drug withdrawal.

raw_record.support_text: Three deaths due to fulminant hepatitis were reported in 1998 among tolcapone-treated patients. The deaths prompted a black box warning in the United States along with stricter liver monitoring guidelines. A postmarketing surveillance analysis later found no deaths among 1725 patients treated with tolcapone for up to 2 years or longer, and transaminase elevations were rare and transient, which led the FDA to relax hepatic enzyme monitoring guidelines in February 2006.
raw_record.extra_details: Three deaths due to fulminant hepatitis reported in 1998 among tolcapone-treated patients; prompted a black box warning in the US and stricter liver monitoring guidelines (Olanow and Tasmar Advisory Panel 2000). A postmarketing surveillance analysis reported no deaths among 1725 patients treated for up to 2 years or longer, with rare and transient transaminase elevations (Lew and Kricorian 2007). FDA relaxed hepatic enzyme monitoring in February 2006: ALT/AST every 2-4 weeks for first 6 months then at clinically relevant intervals, discontinue if AST/ALT exceeds 2x ULN (prior label was stricter); EU monitoring requirements unchanged. Proposed mechanism involves uncoupling of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation reducing ATP generation at concentrations higher than those needed to inhibit COMT (Borges 2005). Used as adjunctive therapy with levodopa/carbidopa for Parkinson's disease.

Postmortem biopsy showed micronodular cirrhosis with portal-tract and pericellular fibrosis, ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes with abundant Mallory hyaline, small foci of steatosis, and nodularity, findings the authors considered consistent with amiodarone hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Death from severe hepatic failure occurred during the 3 weeks after amiodarone was discontinued. Postmortem findings included micronodular cirrhosis with moderate-to-severe portal-tract fibrosis suggesting bridging, marked pericellular fibrosis, nodularity with absence of central veins, marked ballooning degeneration, abundant Mallory hyaline, small steatosis foci, and slight inflammatory activity. The enzymatic picture (glutamic oxalacetic transaminases > glutamic pyruvic transaminases, more than two-fold) supported amiodarone liver injury. Discussion notes amiodarone's variable hepatic effects including acute hepatitis after parenteral administration, asymptomatic aminotransferase increase resolving after oral withdrawal, granulomas, cirrhosis with long-term use, and rare fatalities such as a Reye-syndrome-like case in an 8-year-old child.

raw_record.support_text: Early clinical trials reported increased serum alkaline phosphatase, and in 1979 the first report of sulindac hepatitis appeared, followed by eleven further published cases of acute sulindac hepatitis plus the three cases in the present report. In five published cases sulindac was definitely implicated on the basis of rechallenge; in the others it was implicated by association of drug administration with symptom onset, resolution on cessation, and exclusion of other causes. The present cases were implicated on the same grounds, with rechallenge considered unjustifiable due to a report of a potentially life-threatening reaction on inadvertent re-exposure.
raw_record.extra_details: Sulindac (Clinoril, Charles E. Frosst) is a substituted indene structurally related to indomethacin; the parent drug is metabolised in the liver to the sulphide analogue, the major pharmacologically active anti-inflammatory agent. Reacts at recommended dosages of 200-400 mg/day; two reports described intermittent non-usual dosing for four to six months with reaction only after recommended dosing, indicating some degree of dose dependency. Initial symptoms occurred within one week to one month of commencement: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, then fever and jaundice; some cases had diffuse pharyngitis or stomatitis, facial swelling, or generalised rash; tender hepatomegaly occasionally present. 14 published cases plus 3 present cases are tabulated; one published case (Park et al. 1982) died. Histology showed focal lobular hepatitis with lipofuscin-laden macrophages in centrilobular regions, canalicular bile plugging in a predominantly cholestatic case, and hepatocyte regeneration (thickened plates, binucleated hepatocytes) in a late-resolution biopsy; sulindac hepatitis did not progress to irreversible structural injury. Reaction independent of age, sex, and underlying rheumatic disorder, and independent of prior adverse reactions to other NSAIDs including aspirin; lack of reactions to other NSAIDs (naproxen, aspirin, indomethacin) did not preclude sulindac hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a single patient who developed hepatic granulomatosis (granulomatous hepatitis) as an idiosyncratic adverse reaction to allopurinol, tel with no other cause identified despite physical, skin, microbiological, biochemical, and radiological investigation. After re-exposure to the drug the patient showed a prompt exacerbation of previous symptoms and abnormal liver function values; the reappearance of a dose-independent reaction when medication was resumed after a drug-free interval was considered consistent with a 'definitive' adverse allergic reaction, and the authors conclude the hepatic adverse effect of allopurinol in susceptible hosts is probably immunologically mediated.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report. Hepatic granulomas consisted of multinucleated giant cells (up to 50 nuclei) surrounded by epithelioid cells and mononuclear infiltrate, located in portal tracts and throughout the three zones of Rappaport's acinus, with readily shown eosinophils; mild large-droplet fatty change but no focal necrosis; special stains for acid-fast bacteria and fungi negative. Latency of 6 years before allergic symptoms (fever, malaise, eosinophilia, granulomas) became manifest. On re-exposure there was prompt exacerbation of symptoms and abnormal liver function values, interpreted as a 'definitive' allergic reaction. Liver function and eosinophilia returned to normal 16 days after allopurinol discontinuation; follow-up liver biopsy at 6 months showed no granulomas or inflammatory infiltrate; patient well at 10 months. Hypothesis of oxypurine (hypoxanthine/xanthine) crystal deposition considered unlikely since no crystalline material seen.

raw_record.support_text: Chronic active hepatitis resulting from prolonged nitrofurantoin therapy was first reported in 1975. Four patients treated with nitrofurantoin for 9 weeks to 9 months showed rises in serum transaminase values with various degrees of hypergammaglobulinemia on routine laboratory screening, and liver biopsy showed typical changes of a chronic aggressive hepatitis; withdrawal of nitrofurantoin returned transaminase values to normal within 2 to 6 weeks. Additional cases brought the total to 10 patients, most treated for chronic urinary tract problems, with therapy duration ranging from 2 months to 2 years, all with marked transaminase rises, variable hyperbilirubinemia, and polyclonal gammopathy. The necroinflammatory liver disease resolved rapidly after drug discontinuation, indicating continued drug presence is essential for perpetuation of the inflammation.

raw_record.extra_details: First reported in 1975; combined literature and authors' patients total 10, plus another reported patient in the addendum (ref 23). Histological examination of the explanted liver showed massive necrosis with no evidence of regenerative activity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion resulted in acute liver failure complicated by cerebral edema, decerebration, and raised intracranial pressure requiring liver removal and liver support followed by transplantation; low plasma acetaminophen level at the time of neurological deterioration.
raw_record.extra_details: Patient was a woman (case report) with acetaminophen overdosage culminating in fulminant liver failure. Glasgow Coma Score fell from 8 to 4; cerebral perfusion pressure dropped from 89 to 46 mm Hg; unilateral pupillary dilatation and unreactive pupils occurred. Explanted liver showed massive necrosis without regenerative activity. Liver support reduced intracranial pressure and normalized ICP during the anhepatic phase. Discussion notes a porcine anhepatic model (20 pigs maintained anhepatic for 40 ± 3 h) became comatose without increased ICP.

raw_record.support_text: A 49-year-old male was treated with ketoprofen (200 mg/day) along with noramidopyrine and tiemonium for renal colic. On day two he developed fever, weakness, right hypochondrium pain, mild elevation of serum aminotransferases and significantly high alkaline phosphatases, with subsequent jaundice. Viral hepatitis and other causes of hepatopathy were excluded. Ketoprofen was withdrawn on day four, jaundice disappeared three days later, and biological abnormalities normalized within five weeks. The paper concludes this cholestatic hepatitis is probably due to treatment with ketoprofen.
raw_record.extra_details: Acute hepatitis due to ketoprofen, an NSAID; only one other similar case report found in the literature. 49-year-old male admitted March 1988 for renal colic with moderate renal insufficiency (creatinine 115 µmol/l). Ketoprofen 200 mg/day; fever (38.2°C) and weakness on day two. No hypereosinophilia; viral hepatitis serologies negative (A, B, non-A non-B); abdominal echography normal; liver histology not obtained. Jaundice resolved three days after drug withdrawal; laboratory values returned to normal within 5 weeks. No alcoholism, no anti-tissue antibody. Concomitant drugs noramidopyrine and tiemonium were not considered causative. Named cholestatic hepatitis phenotype recorded under other_specific_phenotype.

He had hypercholesterolaemia and also received chondroitin sulphate 500 mg thrice daily, with no history of self-medication or alcohol abuse. Six and a half months after starting beclobrate 100 mg daily he became anorexic and jaundiced; total bilirubin was 304 µmol/l (normal <17) with greatly raised transaminases. He was admitted 3 weeks later with a diagnosis of acute hepatitis and died 7 days later. Investigations showed no infectious (viral or toxoplasmosis) or obstructive cause.

After initial withdrawal, re-exposition to oral phenprocoumon for a recurrent DVT produced a fourfold increase in liver transaminases (ALT 360 U/L, AST 347 U/L, GGT 158 U/L) two weeks later, at which point the diagnosis of phenprocoumon-induced allergic hepatitis was made.

Re-exposure caused fourfold increase in transaminases (ALT 360 U/L, AST 347 U/L, GGT 158 U/L); the paper describes the reaction as allergic hepatitis and demonstrates in vitro CD69-based activation of the patient's CD4+CD45RO+ memory T-helper cells with phenprocoumon and cross-reactivity with acenocoumarol and warfarin sodium; patient was CYP2C9 wildtype (CYP2C9*2/*3 absent).

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate, a folic acid antagonist most heavily used in psoriasis, is described as 'well established' as hepatotoxic and a cause of cirrhosis. A recent study in England performed liver biopsies on 28 psoriasis patients on methotrexate for substantial periods (not because of clinical evidence of liver disease): 3 had cirrhosis, 9 had portal fibrosis, 14 had reactive hepatitis (mononuclear inflammation with nuclear vacuolation of parenchymal cells), and 2 were normal. Duration of treatment correlated with hepatic disease severity (mean 18 months for normal/reactive-hepatitis group, 33 months for fibrotic patients, 49 months for cirrhotic patients); in the unselected series, 7 of 9 patients treated for 3 years had either fibrosis or cirrhosis.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report that rosiglitazone was the only medication the patient used regularly, and state that the temporal association between rosiglitazone use, the presence of eosinophils in the granulomas, and resolution of both symptoms and elevated liver enzymes after drug withdrawal make it the most likely cause of the patient's granulomatous hepatitis. A liver biopsy showed a periportal mixed cellular infiltrate with granulomas in portal triads and hepatic parenchyma, inflammation crossing the limiting plate with focal hepatocyte degeneration, and fibrous portal expansion; symptoms resolved within 2 weeks and liver enzymes neared normal 2 months after rosiglitazone discontinuation.
raw_record.extra_details: Single case report of granulomatous hepatitis attributed to rosiglitazone. Histology: periportal mixed infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, neutrophils, multinucleated giant cells), noncaseating granulomas in portal triads and parenchyma, lobular extension across the limiting plate with focal hepatocyte degeneration, fibrous portal expansion; stains for polarizing material, Giemsa, Gomori methenamine-silver, mucin and acid-fast negative. Presented with elevated bilirubin (total 5.0-5.9 mg/dL, direct 4.1-5.0 mg/dL), AST 49 U/L, ALT 82-84 U/L, ALP 125-162 U/L; ALT 33 U/L and AST 21 U/L near normal 2 months after cessation. Symptoms resolved within 2 weeks after discontinuation (dechallenge). Sarcoidosis excluded by normal chest radiograph and serum ACE; infectious causes considered less likely. Authors note uncertainty whether the high dose of 8 mg was a contributing factor, and recommend monitoring liver enzymes before and periodically during rosiglitazone therapy. Granulomas framed mechanistically as a delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction.

raw_record.support_text: Autoimmune hepatitis induced by minocycline has been described in 30 patients who used minocycline for acne (mean dose, 100 mg/day). In 13 patients the syndrome remitted after drug discontinuation, transaminases returning to normal within 3 months in most; three patients needed corticosteroids and another was treated with azathioprine.

raw_record.support_text: A female patient developed toxic hepatitis attributed to paroxetine. Although no biopsy was performed and rechallenge was not done for ethical reasons, the temporal relationship between drug intake and the reaction, the excellent response to drug withdrawal, and reasonable exclusion of other causes of acute liver disease led to a diagnosis of toxic hepatitis due to paroxetine. This was confirmed using the Naranjo adverse-event probability scale, which gave a 'probable' rating (6 points). Switching to citalopram produced no cross-reaction and subsequent evolution was satisfactory.

raw_record.extra_details: Naranjo adverse-effect probability score 6 = probable. Authors note toxic hepatitis due to paroxetine is rare; previous reported cases involved patients with pre-existing liver disease, concurrent potentially hepatotoxic drugs, or octogenarians, though cases without risk factors are also described. Paroxetine hepatotoxicity is described as an unpredictable, potentially serious but extremely infrequent phenomenon; physicians should anticipate possible mild toxic hepatitis and consider drug withdrawal and substitution with another SSRI.

raw_record.support_text: Déticène (dacarbazine, DTIC), an alkylating agent used for over 15 years in palliative treatment of malignant melanoma, is generally considered low toxicity with minor side effects (nausea, vomiting, moderate marrow suppression, influenza-like syndrome). Since 1979, a rare but often fatal complication has been recognized: acute hepatic failure from extensive hepatic necrosis caused by acute occlusion of the hepatic veins, either at the suprahepatic level (Budd-Chiari syndrome) or at the intrahepatic level, classified as hepatic veno-occlusive disease (MVO). The mechanism of these events remains debated.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report: a 53-year-old woman on sequential dacarbazine monotherapy for malignant melanoma of the right leg (tumor resected 4 months earlier; untreated moderate arterial hypertension in history) developed acute hypovolaemic shock a few hours after the second chemotherapy infusion, with absent peripheral pulses, right hypochondrial pain/guarding, and slight flank dullness. Right-heart catheterization hemodynamic studies confirmed hypovolaemic shock. Diagnosis of hepatic veno-occlusive disease (MVO) was established; after massive fluid resuscitation (4 L macromolecules over 2 hours) plus dopamine (10 µg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) and corticosteroid therapy, outcome was favorable. Liver injury was acute hepatic failure by extensive necrosis from acute hepatic vein occlusion (Budd-Chiari or MVO). Second course began 48 h prior. Paper notes such veno-occlusive complications are rare but often fatal.

raw_record.support_text: The abstract reports a 53-year-old female undergoing a second course of intravenous chemotherapy with DTIC (dacarbazine) for malignant melanoma, who developed severe hypovolaemic shock a few hours after injection, with right hypochondrial pain, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hepatic cytolysis and hepatic failure. Fluid replacement, dopamine, heparin, and hydrocortisone were given, but the patient developed massive exudative ascites and bilateral pleural effusions, became anuric requiring haemodialysis, then slowly improved with liver function tests returning to normal after the third week. The abstract states physicians should be aware of this rare, often fatal side-effect, probably of immuno-allergic origin. The discussion identifies this as hepatic veno-occlusive disease (MVO) caused by DTIC ('la MVO au DTIC'), frequently associated with peripheral eosinophilia and, at histology in early deaths, hepatic necrosis with marked eosinophilic infiltration of intrahepatic veins.
raw_record.extra_details: Individual case of hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD) in a 53-year-old female given a second course of intravenous DTIC for malignant melanoma; shock onset a few hours after injection. Associated features: lactic acidosis, hepatic cytolysis, hepatic failure, hepatomegaly, hypovolaemic shock, right hypochondrial pain/pain and guarding, reduced portal venous flow and abnormally small hepatic veins on NMR, massive exudative ascites, bilateral pleural effusions, anuria requiring haemodialysis. Index patient recovered (liver tests normal by week 3, ICU discharge at day 24). Peripheral eosinophilia and, at histology in early deaths, hepatic necrosis with prominent eosinophilic infiltration of intrahepatic veins; mechanism considered immuno-allergic with proposed early corticosteroid therapy. Notes VOD usually occurs at the start of the second course; in a 1988 randomized study by Ceci et al. two fatal accidents were observed among 68 treated patients; exact frequency thought very low but possibly underestimated.

raw_record.support_text: A 64-year-old woman with stage IIIA multiple myeloma and a chronic hepatitis B carrier state developed fatal fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) with encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome 12 days after starting single-agent thalidomide (100 mg/d). Transaminases and bilirubin rose while alkaline phosphatase stayed normal; after thalidomide discontinuation transaminases transiently improved, but the patient died on hospital day 14. Exhaustive investigations found no other cause, and the authors report a Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability score of 6, indicating a probable association between thalidomide and FHF; they state thalidomide-induced fatal FHF had not been described previously.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patient was a chronic hepatitis B carrier (HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative, HBeAb positive) with normal baseline liver function, which was evaluated and excluded as the cause; thalidomide treatment was continued after admission and only discontinued later.
raw_record.extra_details: Thalidomide (Thalomid, Celgene Corp) dosed at 100 mg/d for multiple myeloma (stage IIIA). Latency 12 days. Peak aspartate aminotransferase 510 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 598 U/L; total bilirubin 16.7 mg/dL, direct 10.2 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase normal (101 U/L); albumin fell from 3.7 to 1.2 g/dL; INR rose from 1.1 to 4.1. Clinical picture: confusion, abdominal pain, jaundice, asterixis, anasarca, hepatomegaly without biliary ductal dilatation, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome requiring hemodialysis. Hepatitis A/C/delta, CMV, HSV, EBV, autoimmune hepatitis, and PBC serologies negative; hepatitis B DNA undetectable, pattern not consistent with reactivation. Transient transaminase improvement after discontinuation before death from worsening coagulopathy, acidosis, and renal failure. Naranjo score 6 (probable). Mechanism unknown; thalidomide has little hepatic metabolism, possible interference with NAD-adenoribosylation.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion describes a case of fatal fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) with encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome attributed to thalidomide. Thalidomide-induced fatal FHF had not been described previously. The authors state that the lack of any obvious cause of hepatic failure despite exhaustive investigations, combined with the temporal relationship of hepatic dysfunction with initiation of thalidomide therapy, indicates severe drug-induced hepatic injury. The Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score was 6, indicating a probable association between thalidomide and FHF. The paper notes that rare cases of transient hepatitis associated with thalidomide have been reported and that the mechanism of injury is not known, possibly involving interference with hepatic metabolism of NAD-adenoribosylation.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatic failure of unclear etiology in a patient on therapeutic thalidomide, despite exhaustive investigations; presented with encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome; Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale score of 6 (probable association). Thalidomide is FDA-approved for multiple myeloma and erythema nodosum leprosum. Rare cases of transient thalidomide-associated hepatitis previously reported. Mechanism unknown, possibly interference with hepatic metabolism of NAD-adenoribosylation; thalidomide does not undergo major hepatic metabolism.

raw_record.support_text: Diltiazem is associated with a relatively low incidence of side effects. The paper reports a case of hypersensitivity reaction to diltiazem manifested by thrombocytopenia, spiking fever, hepatotoxicity, and rash, described as the first report of thrombocytopenia due to diltiazem.
raw_record.extra_details: 61-year-old man treated with diltiazem 60 mg three times a day started 7 days before hospitalization; developed fever, tender hepatomegaly, liver span 16 cm, aspartate aminotransferase 236 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 200 IU/L, lactic dehydrogenase 600 IU/L, gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase 66.4 IU/L (normal 6-28), 5'-nucleotidase 14.1 IU/L (normal 2-10), with normal bilirubin (0.4 mg/dL) and normal alkaline phosphatase; a maculopapular rash appeared and platelet count fell to 44,000/mm^3 without consumption coagulopathy; liver function tests returned to normal within days after diltiazem discontinuation. Macrophage inhibitory factor (MIF) and mast cell degranulation (MCDT) tests were positive in the presence of diltiazem and negative with the patient's other medications (nifedipine, isosorbide dinitrate, dipyridamole) and normal plasma. No rechallenge was attempted. The paper cites prior reports of diltiazem causing mild liver enzyme abnormalities in three patients and a severe hypersensitivity reaction in another. Attribution is part of the drug-hypersensitivity syndrome; infectious, viral, typhoid, syphilis, Leptospira, Brucella, and Rickettsia work-up was negative.

raw_record.support_text: In a consecutive series of 68 patients with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF) progressing to grade IV encephalopathy, the etiology was listed as paracetamol overdose in 44 patients, among non-A/non-B hepatitis (16), hepatitis B (3), hepatitis A (3), halothane-induced hepatic necrosis (1), and acute fatty liver of pregnancy (1). The paper therefore attributes paracetamol overdose as a cause of the human fulminant hepatic failure seen in these patients.

raw_record.extra_details: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose was the most frequent etiology, accounting for 44 of 68 consecutive FHF patients in this series; median time from onset of grade IV encephalopathy to ICP monitor insertion was 10 h (range 1-40). Clinical phenotype is fulminant hepatic failure per Trey and Davidson definition.

raw_record.support_text: Serum samples were referred for patients clinically diagnosed with halothane hepatitis, who typically developed jaundice, increased serum liver enzymes, and other signs of hepatitis after halothane anaesthesia. Three samples were from male patients (one a 22-month-old infant), and two of the patients died of hepatitis. In most cases other potential causes of hepatitis (hepatitis A, hepatitis B, CMV, EBV) were reported excluded.

Article evaluates laboratory immunoassay methods (TFA-RSA based) for diagnosing halothane hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that isoniazid-induced hepatitis is rare in children and that there are reported cases of fatal and near-fatal hepatotoxicity of isoniazid, with two reported childhood deaths caused by confirmed single-drug isoniazid-induced hepatitis. Possible predisposing factors in children include malnutrition and underlying illness, including tuberculosis. The paper also states that anemia and hepatotoxic effects are known side effects of isoniazid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric population; hepatitis stated to be rare in children, with malnutrition and underlying illness (including tuberculosis) as possible predisposing factors.
raw_record.extra_details: Two reported childhood deaths caused by confirmed single-drug isoniazid-induced hepatitis; subclinical cases usually resolve without sequelae. Separately, transient serum aminotransferase elevations are a common side effect of antituberculosis therapy (incidence 0.5%-82%, rarely rising 100 U or more, generally returning to normal within 14-120 days without stopping therapy, not dose related) and are explicitly distinguished from clinically significant hepatitis, and liver dysfunction is reported more often in patients on combination isoniazid plus rifampin regimens.

raw_record.support_text: A patient with severe paraquat poisoning (admission blood paraquat 15.8 µg/ml) after oral ingestion received combined hemoperfusion-hemodialysis (HP-HD). raw_record.support_text: In a 24-week randomized trial, 15 patients with chronic hepatitis B received fialuridine (FIAU) at 0.1 or 0.25 mg/kg/day. The trial was abruptly terminated when 2 patients developed severe liver disease. Of 10 patients treated for more than 4 weeks, 7 developed severe toxicity and 3 mild toxicity; toxicities included liver failure, lactic acidosis, pancreatitis, myopathy and neuropathy. Five of the 7 severely toxic patients died (3 despite liver transplant), and 2 survived after liver transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients with chronic hepatitis B; therapeutic dosing at 0.1 or 0.25 mg/kg/day for 24 weeks (planned).
raw_record.extra_details: FIAU is a fluorinated nucleoside analog of 5-iodouracil (metabolite of FIAC) that inhibits HBV polymerase by incorporating into the viral nucleotide chain as a thymidine analog. In the prior 28-day non-HIV immunocompetent study, serum HBV DNA decreased markedly and ALT levels generally rose at end of treatment without HBeAg loss. In this 24-week study, 6 of 10 patients treated >4 weeks became HBV DNA-negative. Of 10 treated >4 weeks, 7 had severe and 3 mild toxicity; toxicities were liver failure, lactic acidosis, pancreatitis, myopathy and neuropathy; 5 of 7 severely toxic patients died, 3 despite liver transplant, 2 survived after transplant. It was postulated FIAU irreversibly damaged cellular mitochondrial DNA causing severe multiorgan failure, with potentially cumulative, progressive damage explaining delayed toxicity.

After the 25th day of treatment he presented with fever, fatigue, cough and sore throat, widespread skin lesions, mucosal involvement, and also developed acute liver failure and bronchitis. Laboratory findings showed elevated liver enzymes and eosinophilia. He was positive for HLA-B*15:02 and negative for HLA-B*57:01, HLA-B*58:01, HLA-A*31:01 and various CYP/other pharmacogenetic markers.

raw_record.support_text: The authors conclude erythromycin sensitivity is the likely cause of acute liver failure in this patient. They note that cholestatic jaundice due to erythromycin estolate is well known and that the patient had simple erythromycin BP, suggesting the erythromycin molecule itself, as well as the ester, is hepatotoxic.
raw_record.extra_details: Single-case report of acute liver failure with an unusually selective factor X deficiency (1% of normal), a less marked factor VII deficiency (24%), and a prolonged prothrombin time that increased despite 11 units of fresh frozen plasma and 8 units of factor IX concentrate (also containing factors II and X). The patient improved and at 1-month follow-up factor X activity was 136%, prothrombin time 31 s, AST 48 iu/litre, alkaline phosphatase 399 iu/litre. Liver biopsy was declined. Erythromycin sensitivity proposed as likely cause; the paper argues the erythromycin molecule itself, in addition to its esters, is hepatotoxic.

raw_record.support_text: A 38-year-old female was treated with methimazole for hyperthyroidism, then switched to propylthiouracil after methimazole caused elevated liver transaminase. After propylthiouracil was started, she developed nausea, rash, high fever, acute toxic hepatitis and multiple organ dysfunction (liver, lung, heart) lasting 1 month. She was diagnosed with DRESS/DiHS syndrome induced by propylthiouracil, which resolved after drug withdrawal and treatment with adalimumab, corticosteroids and plasmapheresis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case report of a 38-year-old female with hyperthyroidism; DRESS/DiHS developed after propylthiouracil taken for 4 weeks, manifesting as acute toxic hepatitis with multiple organ dysfunction (liver, lung, heart); treated with adalimumab, systematic corticosteroids and plasmapheresis with symptom resolution 4 weeks later; propylthiouracil withdrawn. Literature context: only 3 prior cases of propylthiouracil-induced DRESS/DiHS reported. The patient first used methimazole (stopped for elevated liver transaminase that improved in 2 weeks) before switching to propylthiouracil.

raw_record.support_text: In the randomized TARGET study, six of nine cases adjudicated as probable or possible drug-induced clinical hepatitis arose in patients randomised to lumiracoxib (6/9117, 0.07%). The incidence of serious liver abnormalities on lumiracoxib was 0.07% (six events), and 2.57% (230 patients) had transaminase concentrations greater than three times the upper limit of normal, versus 0.63% (56) with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (3.97 [2.96–5.32], p<0.0001). Abnormalities resolved on cessation of treatment, with no liver failure, transplantation, or death attributable to drug-induced hepatitis.

raw_record.support_text: Lactophenin, a chemical cousin of aspirin used as an anti-rheumatic agent in Scandinavia, had remarkable side-effects: more than half of the patients who took the drug experienced an illness surprisingly like acute infectious hepatitis, starting some 9 to 12 days after therapy began, with epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, jaundice, and abnormal urinary excretion of urobilinogen and bilirubin. Complete recovery was the rule. Lactophenin itself was not directly hepatotoxic for experimental animals, leading the authors to speculate whether the drug activates a latent virus to produce symptoms of hepatitis.

Complete recovery was the rule. Lactophenin was not directly hepatotoxic to monkeys and rats; authors speculated on possible activation of a latent virus as the mechanism.

raw_record.support_text: In this acute/fulminant liver failure trial of hemoperfusion, patients with an acetaminophen overdose were an etiologic subgroup; 51.7% of 29 patients in the 5-h hemoperfusion group survived versus 58.3% of 24 in the 10-h group (overall 54.7% for 53 acetaminophen-overdose patients). Cerebral edema was observed in 77.3% of acetaminophen-overdose patients, and median survival among those who died was 7 days (range 3-56 days) from tablet ingestion.

raw_record.extra_details: Overall survival for acetaminophen-overdose subgroup combined across both trials was 52.9%; cerebral edema in 77.3-80.6% of acetaminophen patients; survival across trial arms 51.7-58.3% (5-h/10-h hemoperfusion) and 42.9-55.6% (trial B no perfusion/10-h).

raw_record.support_text: This case report describes an 11-year-old girl who developed anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS), a potentially fatal multisystem disorder, after receiving oral phenobarbital for 10 days following a focal seizure. During the course, she developed jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, raised serum transaminases (AST 179 IU/dL, ALT 475 IU/dL), elevated bilirubin (total 6.5 mg/dL, direct 4 mg/dL), and reduced serum protein and albumin. Other etiologies (hepatitis A, hepatitis B, infectious mononucleosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Kawasaki disease) were ruled out. Using Naranjo's causality method, the event was assessed to be probably caused by phenobarbital. The patient recovered, with normalization of hepatic and renal parameters, after withdrawal of phenobarbital and treatment with methylprednisolone.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patient (11-year-old girl); hepatic involvement occurred as part of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome.
raw_record.extra_details: Phenobarbital given orally for 10 days after a focal seizure; fever on day 6, rash on day 9, drug withdrawn on day 13. On day 20 developed facial puffiness, jaundice, and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory values: AST 179 IU/dL, ALT 475 IU/dL, total bilirubin 6.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 4 mg/dL, creatinine 2.12 mg/dL, serum protein 5.36 g/dL, albumin 2.29 g/dL. Serum phenobarbital 14.2 µg/mL (within therapeutic range) on day 12. Naranjo causality assessment scored the event as probably caused by phenobarbital. Managed with methylprednisolone 0.5 mg/kg every 8 hours for 5 days; recovered by day 21 with normalization of hepatic and renal parameters; well at 2-year follow-up and switched to valproic acid.

raw_record.support_text: The 60-year-old male patient presented after a drug overdose involving cyclosporine (CsA), imipramine, prednisone, azathioprine, fluoxetine, alprazolam, oxazepam, and whisky. Despite toxic whole-blood levels of total cyclosporine (1,800 ng/ml) and specific cyclosporine (714 ng/ml), the authors explicitly state that no alteration in renal, liver, or neurological function appeared. No drug-induced liver injury was therefore reported in this overdose case.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose in a renal-transplant patient taking CsA 200 mg/day (Sp-CsA therapeutic levels 117-320 ng/ml) and imipramine; overdose also included prednisone, azathioprine, fluoxetine, alprazolam, oxazepam and ~100 ml whisky in a suicide attempt.
raw_record.extra_details: Post-transplant immunosuppression of CsA, prednisone, azathioprine; therapeutic CsA blood level monitoring. On admission after overdose, laboratory hematology and chemistry profiles were normal; urine toxicology positive for imipramine/desipramine and benzodiazepine metabolites; alcohol test negative due to elapsed time. TCA imipramine level 2,260 ng/ml caused QTc prolongation from 430 to 500 ms without arrhythmias or hemodynamic deterioration. Calculated elimination half-lives after overdose: Sp-CsA 70.1 h, T-CsA 90.6 h (vs reported therapeutic-dose means of 10.0 and 16.1 h, respectively); prolonged imipramine half-life 43.4 h.

raw_record.support_text: A 26-year-old man with spinal muscular atrophy type 3 who had received IV acetaminophen 1 g three times daily developed severe liver injury with INR >5, peak alanine transaminase >1000 U/L, bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, and serum cholinesterase 0.74 kU/L. Transjugular liver biopsy showed high-grade acute liver cell damage with disseminated hepatocellular necrosis compatible with acute drug-induced toxic liver cell damage with acute liver dystrophy. Acetaminophen was discontinued, acetylcysteine was administered, and hepatic function recovered completely. The risk was attributed to acetaminophen at therapeutic dosing without evidence of overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Therapeutic IV dosing (1 g three times daily) with no overdose in a patient with spinal muscular atrophy type 3; sepsis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) and Clostridium difficile infection were present and received multiple co-medications.
raw_record.extra_details: CIOMS/RUCAM causality score 7 (probable relationship). Serum acetaminophen was 22 mg/L measured 38 h after the last dose. Initial findings included coagulopathy (INR 2.64, factor V 29.0%, antithrombin III 29.1%) and moderately elevated transaminases (ALT 68 U/L, AST 111 U/L). Acetylcysteine given per standard protocol 11 h after last acetaminophen dose. Contrast CT showed ascites, pleural and pericardial effusions, and hypodense liver parenchyma compatible with liver edema; no compromised liver perfusion or hepatic encephalopathy. Shock liver, heart failure, biliary obstruction, and viral hepatitis were excluded. Other medications present: lenograstim, meropenem, aciclovir, metronidazole, vancomycin.

raw_record.support_text: In the largest retrospective study to date (FReSKO), 200 patients with Cushing's disease received ketoconazole at 200-1200 mg daily. Generally reversible upon drug withdrawal, up to 5-fold increases in liver enzymes were found in 13.5% of patients while severe hepatotoxicity (>5-fold elevation) was observed in 2.5%. The authors recommend close liver function monitoring and advise dose reduction or discontinuation when liver enzymes are 3-fold elevated. The drug treatment table also lists hepatitis among ketoconazole's possible adverse events.
raw_record.extra_details: Adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitor used for Cushing's disease; FReSKO retrospective cohort of 200 patients, oral 200-1200 mg/day; up to 5-fold liver enzyme increases in 13.5% and severe hepatotoxicity (>5-fold elevation) in 2.5%, generally reversible on withdrawal; liver monitoring advised and dose reduction/discontinuation when enzymes 3-fold elevated; listed under 'Hepatitis' in adverse-event treatment table.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a case of toxic hepatitis caused by ingestion of firework crackers containing yellow phosphorus in an uncontrolled paranoid patient with schizophrenia who was sent for liver transplantation. They note that yellow phosphorus is a highly toxic cellular poison with a mortality ranging from 23% to 73% and a fatal oral dose of approximately 1 mg/kg, and that most reported deaths were attributable to hepatic complications.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Ingestion of firework crackers containing yellow phosphorus; patient was an uncontrolled paranoid schizophrenic; injury unrelated to therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: A 38-year-old man ingested firework crackers containing yellow phosphorus and developed toxic hepatitis with fulminant liver failure, referred for probable urgent liver transplantation. On admission he was found to be psychotic (paranoid schizophrenia) and amisulpride (Solian) was initiated. Laboratory profile showed aspartate aminotransferase 2128 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 1304 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 123 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 2354 U/L, total bilirubin 6.51 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.26 mg/dL, prothrombin time 51 s, international normalized ratio 4.28, and platelet count 110 x 10^3/uL; hemoglobin, WBC, alkaline phosphatase, urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose and electrolytes were normal. Yellow phosphorus used in fireworks production; fatal oral dose approximately 1 mg/kg; mortality 23%-73%, most deaths attributable to hepatic complications.

raw_record.support_text: A 23-year-old female being treated for porphyria cutanea tarda was mistakenly given a single 1250 mg dose of chloroquine instead of the intended 125 mg. In contrast to typical chloroquine toxicity (mainly cardiac arrhythmias), she died 13 days after ingestion in a coma caused by irreversible, acute decompensation of the liver. Forensic autopsy and histological and toxicological investigations confirmed the findings, and the authors explain the severe hepatotoxic effect of chloroquine in this case from its pharmacological mechanism of action in p.c.t. The authors warn against exceeding the recommended p.c.t. dose of 125-250 mg twice weekly and consider clinically manifest p.c.t. a contraindication to chloroquine.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Accidental overdose of 1250 mg instead of intended 125 mg; patient had porphyria cutanea tarda (chronic porphyria hepatica), which the authors consider a contraindication to chloroquine use.
raw_record.extra_details: Single oral dose of 1250 mg chloroquine (Resochin) instead of 125 mg; death occurred 13 days post-ingestion in a coma due to irreversible acute liver decompensation; confirmed by forensic autopsy and histological and toxicological investigations; the severe hepatotoxic effect is explained by chloroquine's pharmacological mechanism in p.c.t.; authors recommend p.c.t. dosing of 125-250 mg twice weekly and warn against exceeding it. Typical chloroquine overdose toxicity (cardiac arrhythmia) was not the course in this patient.

raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Attribution described in the context of an HLA-B*5701-restricted genetic association; only about 1 of 13,000 HLA-B*5701 carriers exposed to flucloxacillin develop the liver injury, consistent with a multiple-hit model requiring both genetic variation and unidentified environmental factors.
raw_record.extra_details: Antibiotic (antibacterial agent). GWAS in 51 cases of flucloxacillin hepatotoxicity and 282 drug-exposed controls without ADRs found a very strong association with HLA-B*5701 (P=10⁻³³; odds ratio ≈80). Context notes rare adverse drug reactions such as this are generally not detected before drug marketing and labels the injury as idiosyncratic in framing.

Clinical evidence has stressed female sex, pregnancy, hormonal status and/or abnormal renal function as predisposing aggravating factors, while experimental studies indicate the development of liver failure is directly related to the dose and mode of administration of tetracyclines.

raw_record.support_text: The authors describe a retrospective study of acetaminophen (APAP) poisonings with aminotransferase (AT) concentrations >1000 IU/L, in which six cases had initial AT concentrations within normal laboratory reference ranges up to 14 h post-ingestion yet subsequently developed hepatotoxicity (AST/ALT >1000 IU/L) 48-72 h post-ingestion. All exposures were acute APAP ingestions (with and without co-ingestants), all had potentially toxic initial serum APAP concentrations on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, and all were successfully treated with n-acetylcysteine with no deaths or liver transplantation. The letter also reports that Doyon and Klein-Schwartz described four patients with initially normal ATs (three with potentially toxic APAP concentrations) in which, despite NAC treatment, one patient died and one underwent liver transplantation, and that the authors' dataset contained 10 APAP-associated deaths.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute acetaminophen overdose (with and without co-ingestants); some patients presented with initially normal aminotransferase concentrations before hepatotoxicity developed.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective APAP poisoning dataset with AT concentrations >1000 IU/L; six cases showed normal initial ATs up to 14 h post-ingestion but developed AST/ALT >1000 IU/L 48-72 h post-ingestion; potentially toxic serum APAP concentrations on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram; all treated with n-acetylcysteine with no deaths or transplant in these six. In the authors' dataset there were 10 APAP-associated deaths in which ATs declined while other hepatic biomarkers (bilirubin, coagulation) rose. Doyon and Klein-Schwartz reported four patients with initially normal ATs (three with potentially toxic APAP concentrations) treated with NAC, one of whom died and one underwent liver transplantation. Authors conclude initial AT concentrations are neither sensitive nor specific enough to reliably predict risk of severe hepatotoxicity in acute APAP poisoning.

raw_record.support_text: A 56-year-old HIV-positive woman developed subclinical jaundice and fatigue 5 days before admission, about 8 weeks after atazanavir replaced lopinavir–ritonavir. Transaminase activity rose up to 10 times normal (AST 236 IU/L, ALT 405 IU/L) with discrete cholestasis, and liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with intralobular macrophagic infiltrates and moderate macrovacuolar steatosis. Viral, autoimmune, and toxic causes were excluded, and the causality of atazanavir in the onset of hepatic cytolysis was classified as 'probable'. After atazanavir was discontinued, transaminases nearly normalized within 8 weeks, and rechallenge with the other nucleoside inhibitors did not cause re-elevation.

Liver biopsy showed acute hepatitis with intralobular macrophage infiltrates and moderate macrovacuolar steatosis, no fibrosis or cholestasis. raw_record.support_text: In the case of VPA (valproic acid) overdose, VPA binds to carnitine within hepatocytes to form the VPA–carnitine complex, leading to carnitine deficiency, which impairs fatty acid oxidation and causes steatosis and liver failure. Mitochondrial VPA–carnitine oxidation also produces 2-propyl-4-pentenoic acid (4-EN-VPA), which interferes with the urea cycle and causes hyperammonemia.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional massive overdose of approximately 60 g of VPA ingested for suicidal purposes; patient had used VPA as a mood stabilizer for the preceding year for bipolar affective disorder.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of a middle-aged woman who intentionally ingested ~60 g VPA. Course required ICU admission and intubation for CNS depression. Managed with multiple doses of activated charcoal (AC), L-carnitine, hemodialysis (HD), intensive ventilation, and supportive/ICU bundle measures. She improved after 12 days, was extubated, and was discharged from ICU two days later. Mechanism involves VPA–carnitine complex formation causing carnitine deficiency, impaired fatty acid oxidation, steatosis and liver failure, and 4-EN-VPA (2-propyl-4-pentenoic acid) interference with the urea cycle causing hyperammonemia. Management guidelines (2008) based on AAPCC data of over 9,000 ingestions; C and D recommendations highest available grade of evidence.

raw_record.support_text: Hepatotoxicity of valproic acid (VPA) is reported in a psychomotor retarded boy. After a four-month antiepileptic VPA therapy followed by combined VPA/phenytoin treatment, the patient died in hepatic coma two months later due to VPA-induced liver damage. In the final state, the VPA metabolic pattern was within the normal range except for the abnormal metabolites 4-en-VPA (2-propyl-4-pentenoic acid) and 4,4'-dien-VPA (2-(2-propenyl-4-pentenoic acid) detected at low concentration; plasma branched-chain amino acids were decreased by 50% and aromatic amino acids increased, with methionine normal.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric male patient with psychomotor retardation; concurrent phenytoin (combined VPA/phenytoin) therapy at the time of fatal hepatic coma.
raw_record.extra_details: Antiepileptic therapy for 4 months in monotherapy, then combined VPA/phenytoin for 2 months before death in hepatic coma. Terminal VPA metabolite pattern normal except for abnormal unsaturated 4-en-VPA and 4,4'-dien-VPA detected at low concentration; plasma branched-chain amino acids reduced 50%, aromatic amino acids increased, methionine normal. Paper also notes reversible hyperammonemia as an expression of reversible hepatic dysfunction in VPA therapy, with or without transaminase elevation and an ammonia increase up to 140 µmol/L tolerated; authors recommend stopping VPA when abnormal unsaturated metabolites are detected or dien-VPA/3 excretion is increased, and propose L-carnitine as prophylactic treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity with fatal outcome was observed in 0.1% of patients. Grade 3 or 4 transaminase elevations were observed in 11% and 6% of patients, respectively. Concurrent elevation in ALT and/or AST ≥ 3 × ULN and total bilirubin ≥ 2 × ULN without significant ALP elevation occurred in < 1% of patients. Transaminase elevations generally occurred within the first 2 months of treatment, were manageable by dose interruption/modifications, and crizotinib should be discontinued with grade 2 or higher AST/ALT plus bilirubin elevation in the absence of cholestasis or hemolysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Fatal hepatotoxicity in 0.1% of patients; grade 3 transaminase elevations in 11% and grade 4 in 6%; concurrent ALT/AST ≥ 3x ULN plus total bilirubin ≥ 2x ULN without significant ALP elevation in <1%; elevations generally began within the first 2 months of treatment, manageable by dose interruption/modification; recommendation to discontinue on grade ≥2 AST/ALT plus bilirubin elevation without cholestasis or hemolysis; liver function test monitoring recommended weekly for first 2 months.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is the most severe side effect associated with antituberculosis medications such as isoniazid, and describes a study by Lee et al. (2019) in which 38 patients with tuberculosis who had experienced DILI (16 attributed to pyrazinamide, 14 to rifampin, 8 to isoniazid) were compared with 38 sex- and age-matched non-DILI TB-positive controls. Patients presenting with isoniazid-induced hepatotoxicity were explicitly identified, making isoniazid the attributed liver-injuring agent.
raw_record.extra_details: Lee et al. (2019) case-control study (38 TB patients with DILI, including 8 isoniazid-attributed cases, vs 38 matched non-DILI controls) using PacBio SMRT sequencing of the mitochondrial genome. The paper's focus was mtDNA variant associations: patients with isoniazid-induced DILI had more mtDNA variants in complex I ND1 (p=0.025) and ND5 (p=0.028), more non-synonymous ND5 mutations (1.5±1.6 vs 0.7±0.8; p=0.033), and a higher ratio of non-synonymous to total substitutions than non-DILI controls. The authors hypothesized variation in complex I subunits predisposes to isoniazid-induced DILI via the primary metabolite hydrazine, a complex II inhibitor.

raw_record.support_text: A 16-year-old female with osteosarcoma treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy including high-dose methotrexate (12 g/m² over 4 hours plus leucovorin rescue) developed transient chemical hepatitis with marked elevation of serum transaminases (aspartate aminotransferase 755 U/l, alanine aminotransferase 1353 U/l, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dl, direct 0.5 mg/dl) during the first cycle of high-dose methotrexate, while renal function remained normal. The dose of leucovorin was escalated as a result of this hepatotoxicity, and chemical hepatitis was observed again (AST 239 U/l, ALT 858 U/l, total bilirubin 3.6 mg/dl, direct 2.8 mg/dl) after the second high-dose methotrexate infusion, resolving within 3 weeks.

raw_record.extra_details: Transient chemical hepatitis with marked transaminase elevation (cycle 1: AST 755 U/l, ALT 1353 U/l, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dl direct 0.5 mg/dl; cycle 2: AST 239 U/l, ALT 858 U/l, total bilirubin 3.6 mg/dl direct 2.8 mg/dl). Hepatitis resolved within 3 weeks. Leucovorin dose escalated (150 mg every 6 h then 150 mg every 3 h then 1000 mg/m² every 6 h) in response to hepatotoxicity. Same cycle complicated by high-dose methotrexate acute renal dysfunction (serum creatinine peaking 5.2 mg/dl) and delayed methotrexate elimination (plasma 300-500 µM by FPIA), requiring CPDG₂ (carboxypeptidase-G₂) and thymidine rescue.

raw_record.support_text: In 2002, the authors isolated and identified N-nitrosofenfluramine as the causative substance (原因物質) for the liver injury (肝障害) that occurred in users of a Chinese-manufactured health food product marketed for slimming. This was reported as the first instance of a compound with a slightly modified structure of an approved drug ingredient. The N-nitrosofenfluramine-containing formulation also incorporated other natural products/extracts (probably tea extract), including nicotinic acid, epigallocatechin, gallocatechin, caffeine, epicatechin, vitamin B2, catechin, gallocatechin gallate, and epicatechin gallate; N-nitrosofenfluramine eluted at roughly twice the retention time of fenfluramine on reversed-phase HPLC.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Consumed via a Chinese-manufactured health food supplement marketed for slimming (not an approved medicine); the product also contained tea-derived constituents alongside N-nitrosofenfluramine, which is a structural modification of the approved drug fenfluramine.
raw_record.extra_details: First reported appearance of a compound with a modified structure of an approved drug ingredient; because the nitroso form is absent from natural products and has lower polarity, identification was difficult and it was detected by reversed-phase HPLC after fenfluramine at nearly double the retention time.

raw_record.support_text: The paper opens by noting renewed interest in paracetamol since Mitchell, Thorgeirsson and others (1974) described the mechanisms of hepatic necrosis induced by this drug, and it discusses a hepatotoxic intermediate metabolite formation. The study then examines 10 patients (5 males, 5 females) admitted following severe paracetamol poisoning, with a mean plasma paracetamol concentration of 371 µg/ml at 4 h and mean total urinary recovery ranging from 11.8-24.2 g. Severe liver damage (aminotransferases > 1000 i.u. litre-1) occurred in 3 patients given L-methionine and in the two receiving supportive therapy, one of whom died in hepatic failure.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury is attributed to paracetamol overdosage (poisoning), with the hepatotoxic injury dependent on dose/overdose; patients were treated within 10 h of ingestion with L-methionine, cysteamine, L-cysteine, or supportive therapy.
raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 10 patients (5 male, 5 female; age 19-54 years, mean 30.4) admitted to the Regional Poisoning Treatment Centre, Edinburgh, after severe paracetamol poisoning; mean plasma paracetamol 371 µg/ml 4 h after ingestion; mean total urinary recovery of paracetamol 11.8-24.2 g (mean 18.3 g). One patient died in hepatic failure; severe liver damage (aminotransferases > 1000 i.u. litre-1) occurred in 5 patients. Cysteine and mercapturic acid conjugates are linked to a hepatotoxic intermediate metabolite; no patient developed renal failure. Sulphydryl donors (cysteamine, L-methionine) were given as protective agents against severe liver damage following overdosage.

raw_record.support_text: In this cohort of patients with colorectal liver metastases receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy, oxaliplatin therapy was attributed to chemotherapy-associated liver injury, specifically sinusoidal injury seen to a moderate degree. Rubbia-Brandt et al reported sinusoidal dilatation and congestion with fibrosis in 78% of oxaliplatin-treated patients versus none in the control group. Patients with sinusoidal dilatation after oxaliplatin therapy had a significantly increased postoperative complication rate, and long-term therapy (>6 cycles of oxaliplatin-based therapy) was associated with a significantly enhanced complication rate.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for colorectal cancer liver metastases before hepatic resection; long-term therapy (>6 cycles) associated with enhanced postoperative complication rate.
raw_record.extra_details: Sinusoidal injury (sinusoidal dilatation and congestion with fibrosis) reported in 78% of oxaliplatin-treated patients per Rubbia-Brandt et al vs none in control; moderate sinusoidal injury in this cohort; sinusoidal dilatation linked to significantly higher postoperative morbidity; duration of treatment (>6 cycles) relevant. Part of chemotherapy-associated liver injury morbidity risk score.

FDA denied the New Drug Application in 2004 due to hepatotoxicity concerns (other issues also raised, including coronary events after discontinuation); the European-approved regimen of ximelagatran plus subcutaneous melagatran for short-term DVT prophylaxis was removed from the market in 2006.

raw_record.support_text: This case series describes seven psoriasis patients with acute methotrexate toxicity resulting from overdosing of methotrexate. The acute cumulative dose of methotrexate ranged from 35 mg to 150 mg taken over 3–7 days and was responsible for acute toxicity, which included deranged liver function (hepatotoxicity). All cases presented with ulceration, bleeding and pain in skin lesions; five had oral mucosal ulceration and two had genital mucosal involvement. Five cases recovered and two expired after receiving injectable folinic acid.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose exposure in psoriasis patients: acute cumulative methotrexate dose 35–150 mg taken over 3–7 days. Case 1 co-ingested paracetamol and diclofenac with methotrexate for joint pain; cases 5 and 6 were alcoholic, and both expired.
raw_record.extra_details: Seven cases (6 male, 1 female; ages 35–57 years). Deranged liver function tests included SGOT up to 510 U/L and SGPT up to 420 U/L (normal 0–37 and 0–40 U/L). Two cases died due to grossly deranged liver function tests, renal function tests and pancytopenia leading to septicaemia; the other five recovered. Serum methotrexate levels (available in cases 2,3,4,5,7) ranged 0.21–97 μmol/L. Acute methotrexate toxicity is attributed to inhibition of DNA synthesis in rapidly proliferating cells, with higher doses causing deranged liver function, lowered blood counts and skin/mucosal necrosis. All patients treated with intravenous folinic acid (leucovorin) 20 mg 6-hourly then 10 mg 6-hourly until counts normalized. No patients had pre-existing renal or hepatic disease.

raw_record.support_text: In a National Institute of Health phase 2 clinical trial, the thymidine analog Fialuridine, an antiviral against Hepatitis B virus, caused adverse reactions leading to death of five human volunteers due to severe hepatic toxicity and lactic acidosis; seven other patients showed signs of severe hepatic toxicity, five of whom died and two survived only after liver transplantation. The trial was stopped after one patient developed hepatic toxicity and lactic acidosis in the 13th week. A pilot study of 43 patients treated for 2 and 4 weeks revealed no hepatic toxicity on initial examination. The authors attribute Fialuridine's toxic effects to its accumulation in genomic DNA in the liver, producing defective mitochondrial DNA, high lactic acid, and fat deposition in mitochondrial microvesicles.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were being treated for Hepatitis B virus infection (therapeutic indication for the antiviral).
raw_record.extra_details: Thymidine analog with antiviral activity against Hepatitis B virus. Phase 2 trial (NIH): 5 of 7 patients with severe hepatic toxicity died, 2 survived only after liver transplantation; trial stopped after one patient developed hepatic toxicity and lactic acidosis in week 13 after a pilot study of 43 patients treated for 2 and 4 weeks showed no hepatic toxicity. Injury associated with lactic acidosis and microvesicular fat deposition. Mechanism attributed to Fialuridine accumulation in genomic and mitochondrial DNA in the liver, inhibiting or producing abnormal DNA synthesis (mitochondrial injury). Preclinical animal studies (mice, rats, dogs, monkeys, woodchucks) at doses ~100x higher than human doses showed no such toxicity.

raw_record.support_text: The authors report a 57-year-old man who underwent two operations (femoral hernia repair followed by ligation of a saphenous varix three days later), with anesthesia maintained by halothane during both procedures. Six days after the second operation he developed spiking fevers up to 105°F, jaundice, and markedly deranged liver chemistries, which returned to normal or near-normal forty-five days after the second operation. A liver biopsy on day 21 showed fatty metamorphosis, liver-cell necrosis, and round-cell infiltration of the portal tracts. The authors add this as a case of hepatitis apparently due to halothane, having reasonably excluded hypoxia, hypotension, pre-existing liver disease, and exposure to other toxins as causes.

raw_record.support_text: In India, an unusual but not uncommon cause of acute liver failure (ALF) is the ingestion of rodenticides containing zinc phosphide (Ratol®). Overall survival following Ratol® poisoning is poor without liver transplantation, which is the only salvage therapy for patients unable to recover from ALF. Retrospective analysis of 30 patients admitted after Ratol ingestion found 9 who underwent living donor liver transplant, 6 who died without transplant, and 15 with minimal exposure who recovered without transplant.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional ingestion of the rodenticide Ratol® (zinc phosphide) at toxic/poisoning doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective series of 30 patients (Jan 2006–Apr 2011). 9 underwent living donor liver transplant (LDLT), 6 died without transplant, 15 with minimal poison exposure recovered without transplant. Average interval between poison consumption and ALF was 6.5 days. Mean MELD score 38 (Group I) vs 18 (Group II); median INR 8 vs 3; median total bilirubin 13 vs 5 mg/dL. MELD >31 on day 6 and onset of encephalopathy at any time were reliable predictors of need for LT. Liver transplantation is indicated because overall survival following Ratol® poisoning is poor without LT.

One participant had a transient elevation of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to 111 IU/L (greater than twice the upper limit of reference range) four days after DMAU 100 mg while fasting, but it normalized to 33 IU/L on repeat testing and no DILI or clinically meaningful drug-related liver injury was attributed.
raw_record.extra_details: No serious adverse events; DMAU capsules well tolerated. One transient isolated AST elevation to 111 IU/L (>2x ULN) in one participant 4 days after oral DMAU 100 mg fasting, which normalized to 33 IU/L on repeat testing and was not considered a clinically meaningful liver injury; liver enzymes otherwise stayed within reference range. Early-stage clinical study (19 men, mean age 31.7 years); single oral doses of DMAU 50-800 mg fasting and after high-fat meal.

raw_record.support_text: Within 3 weeks of treatment with dapsone 1 mg/kg/day and prednisolone for linear IgA bullous dermatosis, liver enzymes and cholestasis parameters rose up to 10-fold above normal in a 15-year-old girl, and dapsone was discontinued. After withdrawal the liver parameters normalized; upon reintroduction of dapsone at 0.5 mg/kg/day the liver enzymes markedly increased again, requiring withdrawal. The rechallenge confirmed dapsone's causative role in the hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.extra_details: Liver enzymes and cholestasis parameters rose up to 10-fold above normal within ~3 weeks; normalized within 1 week after withdrawal; rebound on rechallenge with dapsone 0.5 mg/kg/day. The paper notes hepatotoxicity is a very rare dapsone side-effect, possibly part of a hypersensitivity reaction ('dapsone syndrome'), mostly when combined with antimalarial or antileprosial agents. Dapsone was treating LABD.

raw_record.support_text: Serious hepatotoxicity developed in 7 of 15 patients given the nucleoside analogue fialuridine for 8 to 12 weeks; five of these patients died. Cell-culture studies showed fialuridine is incorporated into nuclear and mitochondrial DNA, causing marked mitochondrial dysfunction, and it contains a free 3'-hydroxyl group. These findings are presented as contrast to lamivudine, for which no serious hepatotoxicity and no mitochondrial effects were observed.

raw_record.support_text: The systematic review used Richardus and Smith criteria for Dapsone Hypersensitivity Syndrome (DHS/DRESS), which require at least two of fever, skin eruption, lymphadenopathy, and liver abnormalities (hepatomegaly, hepatitis, jaundice, and/or deranged liver function tests), appearing between the second and eighth week of dapsone administration and resolving upon drug discontinuation, with symptoms not attributed to other drugs, lepra reactions, or other diseases. Across 84 articles (60 Chinese case reports, 21 non-Chinese articles, and 3 epidemiological studies) a total of 877 patients were included. Among the Chinese case-report patients, hepatic involvement was observed in 93.4% of cases, the average latent period for DHS was 30 days (range 3-90 days), and a majority (77/91, 84.6%) received 50-100 mg dapsone daily; outcome was classified as full recovery versus death.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Liver injury occurs as hepatic involvement within Dapsone Hypersensitivity Syndrome / DRESS; subjects had underlying diseases including leprosy (50.5% of Chinese cases) and other conditions, with DHS being a hypersensitivity reaction to therapeutic dapsone use.
raw_record.extra_details: DHS is dapsone-induced DRESS/hypersensitivity syndrome and its hepatic involvement (hepatomegaly, hepatitis, jaundice, deranged LFTs) is one diagnostic criterion. Chinese cohort: 44 male/47 female, mean age 32.3 years (range 8-74); average latency 30 days (3-90); complete DHS in 63.7%; hepatic involvement 93.4%; mucosal involvement 14.3%, pyrexia 100%, maculopapular rash 100%, lymphadenopathy 73.6%; complications included disseminated intravascular coagulation, coagulopathy, complete AV block (1.1%), myocarditis (2.2%), pneumonia (18.7%). Doses of 50-100 mg daily in majority; resolution upon drug discontinuation; outcome full recovery versus death.

raw_record.support_text: The fialuridine case illustrates imperfection of drug toxicity screening: a phase 2 clinical trial of fialuridine in chronic hepatitis B patients was halted after 13 weeks because liver failure occurred in 7 of 15 treated patients. Five patients died and 2 survived after liver transplantation. This outcome was not predicted by preclinical toxicity tests.

raw_record.extra_details: Trial halted after 13 weeks; liver failure in 7 of 15 treated patients, with 5 deaths and 2 survivors after liver transplantation. Outcome not predicted by preclinical toxicity testing in rodents, dogs, and rhesus monkeys; later, mitochondrial toxicity was demonstrated in various organs of long-term treated woodchucks independent of their woodchuck hepatitis virus infection.

The paper also notes CDCA is a more potent FXR agonist than CA but was avoided due to better tolerance and less hepatotoxicity of CA.

Authors note prothionamide has been reported as the most likely factor responsible for fatal events and is more commonly associated with hepatitis than ethionamide or para-aminosalicylic acid.

raw_record.support_text: The letter argues that haemodialysis is of conjectural value in paracetamol overdose and reiterates the mechanism of paracetamol hepatotoxicity: the lesion is caused by covalent binding of active intermediate metabolites of paracetamol to liver-cell proteins; these metabolites are normally inactivated by conjugation with glutathione and excreted as mercapturic-acid derivatives, and liver necrosis does not occur until hepatic glutathione stores are depleted. Because the plasma-paracetamol half-life is prolonged from the outset in patients who develop liver damage and the lesion occurs very early, paracetamol is described as a 'hit-and-run' hepatotoxin. The accompanying text refers to paracetamol-overdose patients (patients 3, 4, and 6 in Farid et al.) treated with haemodialysis who developed liver damage.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Injury attributed in the setting of paracetamol overdose with dangerously high plasma concentrations, in patients who underwent haemodialysis.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: hepatic necrosis caused by covalent binding of active intermediate metabolites of paracetamol to liver-cell proteins; metabolites normally inactivated by conjugation with glutathione and excreted in urine as mercapturic-acid derivatives; liver necrosis occurs only after hepatic glutathione stores are depleted; lesion occurs early ('hit-and-run' hepatotoxin) since plasma half-life is prolonged from the outset in patients developing liver damage. Prevention of paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis by inhibition of hepatic microsomal mixed-function oxidase and maintenance of glutathione is shown in animals. The letter critiques haemodialysis as not preventing liver damage and questions its value; it requests serial liver-function test and prothrombin-time data which were not provided.

raw_record.support_text: The paper describes a case report of a 12-year-old (64-kg) girl with a total estimated ingestion of 1742 mg/kg acetaminophen (paracetamol) and 19 mg/kg diphenhydramine. Despite early treatment with n-acetylcysteine (NAC), she developed hepatic failure with plasma ALT activity peaking at approximately 8000 IU/L around 90 hours after ingestion. This human case attributes hepatic failure/DILI to a massive paracetamol overdose.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric case (12-year-old, 64-kg girl) of massive overdose (total estimated ingestion 1742 mg/kg acetaminophen) with co-ingestion of 19 mg/kg diphenhydramine; treated with n-acetylcysteine (NAC).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic failure developed despite early NAC treatment, with plasma ALT peaking at approximately 8000 IU/L around 90 hours after ingestion; 22 ALT concentration values from 0 to 250 hours were extracted for model fitting. The paper presents the case to demonstrate/validate a mathematical model of ALT biomarker release after paracetamol overdose, and assumed a linear relationship between parent drug concentration and the toxic metabolite NAPQI and that diphenhydramine had no effect on the ALT release profile.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports on ICU-admitted patients with paracetamol-induced liver injury and severe acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT). It describes paracetamol-induced acute liver injury and POD-induced liver failure as the cause of ICU admission, with high mortality among affected patients and lower mortality in those who received a liver transplant. It also notes that bilirubin, pH, and INR have prognostic value in patients with paracetamol-induced liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Critically ill patients admitted to ICU with severe AKI requiring RRT; includes both survivors and non-survivors, with a subgroup receiving liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective single-center analysis of ICU patients with paracetamol (POD)-induced liver injury and severe AKI requiring RRT. High mortality; lower mortality in liver transplant recipients. Acute liver failure requiring ICU management; MELD score and KCH transplant-listing criteria predicted mortality. ALT at ICU admission was higher in the transplant group (p = 0.01). Bilirubin, pH, and INR had prognostic value in paracetamol-induced liver injury. RRT dependence, dialysis, chronic liver disease assessment (MELD), APACHE II.

raw_record.support_text: In this phase 1 trial of the investigational agent REM127 in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, adverse events in the hepatobiliary dysfunction system organ class were observed only in participants on active REM127 treatment and not in placebo recipients. One serious adverse event in the 350 mg dose group was considered related to study treatment and reported as toxic hepatitis. Drug-induced liver injury was reported in six participants leading to study discontinuation, and one case fulfilled Hy's Law criteria, led to hospitalization, and was reported as a suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction (SUSAR), prompting termination of the trial. Increased serum transaminases occurred in all 1400 mg (2/2) and 350 mg (2/2) participants and 1/5 in the 88 mg group versus none in placebo; increases typically started around the fourth week, peaked days to weeks after study discontinuation, and returned to normal in all participants over several weeks to months.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Investgational agent evaluated in a phase 1 clinical trial in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease at daily oral doses of 88, 350, and 1400 mg/day.
raw_record.extra_details: AE terms reported included drug-induced liver injury, toxic hepatitis, hepatitis toxic, hepatic enzyme increased, alanine aminotransferase increased, blood lactate dehydrogenase increased, and transaminases increased. Six participants had hepatobiliary dysfunction leading to study discontinuation; trial was terminated early for safety. One case fulfilled Hy's Law, required hospitalization, and was reported as SUSAR. Transaminase elevations typically began around the fourth week (at last study-drug day or follow-up), peaked days to weeks after discontinuation, and resolved over several weeks to months; an associated decrease in total cholesterol was noted. No deaths or liver transplantations occurred. REM127 is a septin 6 (SEPT6) modulator; one participant received the co-medication quetiapine from Day 21 to Day 23.

raw_record.support_text: Six months after starting imatinib 100 mg/day for FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive chronic eosinophilic leukemia, the patient developed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (417 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase (770 U/L). Other possible causes of liver dysfunction (drug or alcohol abuse, hepatitis virus infection) were excluded, and a liver biopsy showed hepatocyte necrosis with infiltration of lymphocytes, findings compatible with previously reported cases of biopsy-proven imatinib-induced hepatotoxicity. The liver injury was diagnosed as grade 4 imatinib-induced liver dysfunction, and imatinib was discontinued; liver function tests normalized within 4 weeks, but the CEL relapsed 6 months later. Upon rechallenge with imatinib 100 mg/day plus 25 mg/day prednisolone, ALT transiently rose to a grade 1 level and normalized within a month.
