raw_record.support_text: A 68-year-old male with adenocarcinoma of unknown primary treated once daily with 8 mg oral gemcitabine was considered to have a toxic death. Nine days after starting the second cycle he developed fever, grade 4 liver and kidney failure with steep rises in ALT (2,424 U/L), AST (2,781 U/L), γ-GT (237 U/L) and LDH (3,360 U/L), and died 5 days later. Obduction revealed severe toxic-induced liver necrosis which was likely related to the study drug. Other possible causes (viral hepatitis B and C, liver metastasis, alcohol abuse) were excluded and an interaction with comedication (simvastatin, irbesartan/hydrochlorothiazide, oxazepam, omeprazol) was deemed unlikely.
raw_record.extra_details: Single fatal case from a phase I trial of oral gemcitabine (30 patients; dose levels 1-8 mg part A, 8-20 mg part B). Autopsy showed severe toxic-induced liver necrosis. Viral hepatitis (B, C), liver metastasis, and alcohol abuse excluded; interaction with comedication judged unlikely.

raw_record.support_text: The antemortem serum venlafaxine level was 18.6 mg/L, nearly 70 times above the therapeutic upper limit (therapeutic range 0.07–0.27 mg/L); the liver contained 46 mg/kg of venlafaxine. The liver showed macrovesicular steatosis, a scattered inflammatory infiltrate indicating acute hepatitis, and an acinar zone 3 pattern of hepatic necrosis. Only therapeutic levels of chlorpromazine and risperidone and a low level of ethanol were detected as co-exposures.

raw_record.extra_details: Fatal case report (individual case). Antemortem serum venlafaxine 18.6 mg/L (~70x the therapeutic upper limit); postmortem liver venlafaxine 46 mg/kg, stomach content 0.006 mg/L; therapeutic steady-state range 0.07–0.27 mg/L. Liver histology showed macrovesicular steatosis, acute hepatitis with scattered inflammatory infiltrate, and acinar zone 3 hepatic necrosis. Death certified as multiple organ failure secondary to venlafaxine overdose; features of serotonin syndrome (altered consciousness, fever, tachycardia), seizures, rhabdomyolysis, and renal failure also present. 8 previously reported fatal venlafaxine overdoses had postmortem blood levels of 6.6–84 mg/L (mean ~45 mg/L).

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that potential hepatotoxicity is the most serious safety issue associated with COMT inhibitors and that liver toxicity has been observed with tolcapone. In clinical trials elevations of liver enzyme levels were reported for 1-3% of tolcapone-treated patients, and soon after tolcapone's market introduction four cases of fulminant liver failure were reported, three of which resulted in death, in patients who had received tolcapone for 2-4 months. These reports led to a temporary withdrawal of tolcapone from the market in Europe and Canada and a black box warning in the USA; tolcapone was later reintroduced in the EU and now requires prior failure of other COMT inhibitors and regular liver enzyme monitoring.
raw_record.extra_details: COMT inhibitor used to treat Parkinson disease. Liver enzyme elevations in 1-3% of treated patients in clinical trials; four cases of fulminant liver failure reported soon after market introduction, three fatal, after 2-4 months of treatment. Led to temporary European/Canadian market withdrawal and US black box warning; reintroduced in EU with requirement to try other COMT inhibitors first and regular liver enzyme monitoring. Mechanism open, possibly uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation or toxic metabolite accumulation in genetically prone patients; less likely COMT inhibition per se since not seen with entacapone.

raw_record.support_text: Chloroform is metabolized to phosgene, primarily in the liver and kidneys; phosgene depletes hepatocellular glutathione and results in liver injury in the form of hepatocellular steatosis and necrosis. In the case report, a patient who ingested about 50 mL of chloroform developed significant liver injury with markedly elevated transaminases, peaking around the fifth day after exposure and recovering to near-normal by the tenth day.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Intentional ingestion (poisoning) of approximately 50 mL chloroform; overdose/poisoning context rather than medicinal use.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanism: oxidative dehydrochlorination of the C-H bond to phosgene, which depletes hepatic GSH and causes hepatocellular steatosis and necrosis; primary metabolism sites are liver and kidneys. Case laboratory values: ALT peaked at 3560 IU/L, AST 1160 IU/L, total/conjugated bilirubin 17/10 mg/dL; injury peaked ~72-96 h after ingestion and returned to normal within 6-8 weeks, with near-normal return by day 10 in this patient. Managed with NAC (150 mg/kg over 1 h, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 6.25 mg/kg/h drip), GI decontamination, ventilator support, and dialysis; both recovery and fatality have been described in the literature. Patient also had nonoliguric renal failure; rhabdomyolysis excluded by normal CPK.

raw_record.support_text: Crizotinib-induced hepatotoxicity, as measured by alanine aminotransferase increases, has been observed in 13% of patients, with grade 3 and 4 alanine aminotransferase increases occurring in 5% of patients. Fatal hepatotoxicity was rare, occurring in less than 1% of patients in clinical trials. Concurrent elevations in ALT >3x ULN and total bilirubin >2x ULN with normal alkaline phosphatase occurred in less than 1% of patients. ALT >5x ULN occurred in 7% (study A) and 4% (study B) of patients; these findings were generally asymptomatic and reversible upon treatment interruption, and crizotinib should be permanently discontinued for more severe hepatotoxicity, with routine monthly monitoring of liver function tests.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported in clinical trials leading to FDA approval (NSCLC indication); hepatotoxicity measured as ALT increases in 13% of patients, grade 3-4 ALT increases in 5%; fatal hepatotoxicity <1% of patients; concurrent ALT >3x ULN with total bilirubin >2x ULN and normal alkaline phosphatase (Hy's Law-like) in <1%; ALT >5x ULN in 7% (study A) and 4% (study B); generally asymptomatic and reversible upon treatment interruption; most resumed lower dose without recurrence; permanent discontinuation required in 2% (study A) and <1% (study B); monitoring with ALT and total bilirubin monthly recommended; symptoms counseled include weakness, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain (especially right upper quadrant), jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, and bleeding diathesis.

raw_record.support_text: Among 6 pediatric patients treated with the MARS liver support device as a bridging procedure to liver transplantation, 1 child who had experienced paracetamol overdose was transplanted (patient A, alive at 14 months), and another child with paracetamol overdose resolved clinically without liver transplantation (patient D). Paracetamol overdose is thereby attributed as the cause of the acute liver failure that necessitated MARS bridging therapy in these two patients.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric patients; paracetamol overdose causing acute liver failure treated with MARS as a bridge to liver transplantation.
raw_record.extra_details: Two cases of paracetamol overdose were reported: patient A required liver transplantation and was alive at 14 months follow-up; patient D resolved clinically without transplantation. Patient A's pre-MARS AST was 444 IU/L and ALT 568 IU/L; patient D's AST was 6621 IU/L and ALT 4322 IU/L.

raw_record.support_text: Acute paraquat poisoning was evaluated in eight Thai autopsy cases, with survival periods from 26 h to 59 days; the main causes of death included hepatic necrosis among other findings. A separate case report of a Thai male farmer showed that dermal exposure to paraquat solution caused serious systemic toxicity including renal failure, respiratory failure, and hepatic damage. This indicates that paraquat poisoning causes human liver injury.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Self-poisoning by ingestion and an additional dermal exposure case; all liver injury occurred in a poisoning context (paraquat is a herbicide and not a therapeutic drug), so this is an overdose/supratherapeutic harmful exposure rather than ordinary therapeutic use.
raw_record.extra_details: Paraquat (1,1'-dimethyl, 4,4'-bipyridinium dichloride; PQ) poisoning mortality ranges from 33.0% to 91.7%, primarily from multiple organ failure and pulmonary fibrosis. Systemic toxicity includes liver insufficiency, acute kidney injury, respiratory failure, and convulsions. Moderate-to-severe poisoning often leads to acute hepatitis as well as acute renal failure, acute lung injury, and progressive pulmonary fibrosis; fulminant poisoning results in multiple organ failure and death within days. Eight autopsy cases showed hepatic necrosis among causes of death; a dermal-exposure case showed hepatic damage. Paraquat bioavailability 0.3-10%, volume of distribution 1.2-1.6 l/kg, mean elimination half-life 84 h; cellular toxicity attributed to ROS generation via redox cycling and mitochondrial electron transport chain disruption.

raw_record.support_text: In a letter on sulphasalazine in rheumatoid arthritis, the authors describe that among 158 rheumatoid patients treated in Glasgow with sulphasalazine, one patient had a biopsy picture of drug-induced hepatitis and another had raised hepatic transaminases; neither had evidence of viral infection, and in both cases laboratory tests returned to normal when treatment was stopped. They conclude these potentially serious toxic effects mean careful monitoring is important early in therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Single case in a cohort of 158 rheumatoid arthritis patients treated therapeutically with sulphasalazine; viral infection excluded as competing cause.
raw_record.extra_details: One patient had a biopsy picture of drug-induced hepatitis; another had raised hepatic transaminases; laboratory tests returned to normal when treatment was stopped. Authors also report leukopenia (2 cases with total polymorph count below 0.1x10^9/l after 5 and 9 weeks, and 5 more with total white-blood-cell counts 2.0-3.5x10^9/l within 10 weeks); blood counts returned to pretreatment levels on stopping the drug. Monitoring recommended (fortnightly blood counts for 12 weeks then 6-weekly, liver function at weeks 6 and 12 then 12-weekly).

raw_record.support_text: From TESS data covering acetaminophen (APAP) overdoses from 1993 through 2004, including 44,579 overdoses without co-ingestants and 53,381 with co-ingestants that received N-acetylcysteine (NAC) therapy, the analysis recorded outcome measures and measures of hepatic and renal injury, with a significant difference in these measures between patients who received both activated charcoal (AC) and NAC versus NAC alone. The paper frames acute APAP overdose as causing hepatic injury, with transaminase elevation and prolonged prothrombin time used as markers, and reports deaths in these overdoses.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Acute overdose setting (supratherapeutic exposure); hepatic injury markers evaluated after overdose treated with NAC (with or without activated charcoal).
raw_record.extra_details: TESS (Toxic Exposure Surveillance System) data, 1993-2004; 97,960 acute APAP overdoses reviewed. Markers recorded included AST/ALT >100 and >1000 U/L, prolonged PT, hypoglycemia, increased creatinine, renal failure, oliguria/anuria, major effect, and death. Out of 39,873 without co-ingestants with known outcomes, 156 deaths were reported in the NAC-alone group versus 37 in the AC+NAC group (p<0.005, OR 0.33 for death). NAC is a DILI treatment/protectant and is not itself attributed as a causal agent.

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports a 37-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis treated with pyrazinamide (25-30 mg/kg daily), who developed rising serum ALAT, jaundice, confusion and asterixis; transjugular liver biopsy showed massive hepatic necrosis with no fibrosis, and the patient died. raw_record.support_text: A 32-year-old woman with CML-CP developed histology-confirmed imatinib-induced liver toxicity after 6 months of treatment with standard-dose imatinib (400 mg/day). She presented with jaundice, nausea, and epigastric pain; lab tests showed acute liver dysfunction (ALT 1638 U/l, AST 1182 U/l, GGT 69 U/l, ALP 94 U/l, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dl, INR 1.33). Viral and autoimmune hepatitis and a vascular event were ruled out. Early corticosteroid therapy led to rapid and complete hepatic recovery, and treatment was resumed safely with dasatinib.

raw_record.extra_details: 32-year-old woman; standard-dose imatinib 400 mg/day; histology-confirmed induced liver toxicity appearing after 6 months of treatment; jaundice, nausea, epigastric pain; ALT 1638 U/l, AST 1182 U/l, GGT 69 U/l, ALP 94 U/l, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dl, INR 1.33; viral/autoimmune hepatitis and vascular event ruled out.

raw_record.support_text: In the randomized phase III study of pexidartinib for tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), eight patients in the treatment arm discontinued pexidartinib due to hepatic adverse events (hyperbilirubinemia and increased transaminase), which were serious in four cases and lasted about 7 months in one patient; three patients had alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase at least 3x ULN with total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase at least 2x ULN, and one patient had biopsy-confirmed ductopenia with prolonged bilirubin increase lasting about 7 months. Mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity was also observed in non-TGCT studies of pexidartinib (n=637), the most concerning cases being an individual needing liver transplant (pexidartinib 1200 mg/day combined with paclitaxel) and the death of one individual (pexidartinib 1000 mg/day monotherapy in a patient with advanced melanoma). The pexidartinib prescribing information carries a boxed warning about the risk of serious and potentially fatal liver injury, with monitoring requirements and a REMS program.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: One fatal case occurred with pexidartinib 1000 mg/day monotherapy in a patient with advanced melanoma; one liver-transplant case occurred with pexidartinib 1200 mg/day combined with paclitaxel (unresolved co-suspect). Additional hepatotoxicity was reported in non-TGCT studies (indication-restricted).
raw_record.extra_details: FDA boxed warning and Pexidartinib REMS Program for serious and potentially fatal liver injury; liver-test monitoring required at baseline and periodically (weekly for first 8 weeks, then every 2 weeks for 1 month, then every 3 months). In the phase III TGCT trial, 8 of the treatment arm discontinued for hepatic AEs (hyperbilirubinemia and increased transaminase), 4 serious, lasting ~7 months in one; 3 patients had ALT/AST >=3x ULN with total bilirubin and ALP >=2x ULN; one biopsy-confirmed ductopenia with prolonged bilirubin increase. The final diagnosis was colchicine poisoning, confirmed by characteristic mitotic arrests found at post-mortem examination of the esophagus, small bowel, and bone marrow.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Chronic kidney disease/dialysis patient with kidney transplant and chronic allograft nephropathy; colchicine dose escalated from 0.5 mg to 1 mg o.d.; on cyclosporin, prednisolone, and rosuvastatin (possible drug-drug interactions).
raw_record.extra_details: Laboratory worsening: AST rose to 5330 IU/l, ALT to 1361 IU/l, LDH to 7260 IU/l, INR to 3.52 24 h after ICU admission. Colchicine poisoning staging described: initial GI symptoms (day 1), multiple-organ failure with bone-marrow suppression and myopathy (days 2–7), possible recovery. Mechanism: binds tubulin, disrupts microtubules. Diagnosis based on toxidrome; no correlation between plasma level and severity. Post-mortem mitotic arrests in esophagus, small bowel, bone marrow. Patient died 36 h after ICU admission from refractory shock.

raw_record.support_text: In Lister's time, the most important cause of liver failure was the toxic effect of chloroform, then the major anaesthetic. The 'delayed chloroform poisoning' became a dreaded and usually fatal complication of operation, typically presenting within the first few days after operation with vomiting, jaundice, and coma; central necrosis of the liver was the usual autopsy finding. Cases were still being reported as late as 1935, when about 10 cases were reviewed by Gibberd.
raw_record.extra_details: Delayed chloroform poisoning after operative anaesthesia; presented within first few days after operation with vomiting, jaundice, and coma; central necrosis of the liver at autopsy; usually fatal; reports still appearing as late as 1935 when about 10 cases were reviewed by Gibberd.

raw_record.support_text: A 73-year-old African-American woman with Alzheimer's disease was prescribed phenytoin 100 mg three times daily after two seizures. Four weeks after starting the drug she was hospitalized with high fever, confusion, altered mental status, and a diffuse maculopapular pruritic rash. Laboratory values showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (peak 96 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase (peak 77 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase (peak 521 IU/L), and eosinophilia, consistent with an anticonvulsant hypersensitivity reaction with hepatitis.
raw_record.extra_details: Case of anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) in a 73-year-old woman; onset ~4 weeks after starting phenytoin 100 mg 3 times/day. AHS features included fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, and laboratory abnormalities with eosinophilia (eosinophils up to 19%). Selected laboratory values: AST up to 96 IU/L, ALT up to 77 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase up to 521 IU/L, total bilirubin <1 mg/dl, phenytoin level 11.7 µg/ml on admission. Phenytoin was discontinued on hospital day 3 as the rash persisted and elevated eosinophils indicated an allergic drug reaction.

raw_record.support_text: A 26-year-old man was criminally intoxicated over the two weeks preceding admission by surreptitious oral administration of probably 10 g of arsenic trioxide (As₂O₃). The patient developed severe manifestations of toxic hepatitis and pancreatitis, followed by neurological disorders, respiratory distress, acute renal failure, and cardiovascular disturbances. Despite chelation (dimercaprol and dimercaptosuccinic acid) and extrarenal elimination, the patient died on day 26 from multiple organ failure with subarachnoid hemorrhage and Aspergillus fumigatus infection.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Criminal surreptitious oral administration of approximately 10 g arsenic trioxide over the two weeks before admission (deliberate intoxication/overdose).
raw_record.extra_details: Toxic hepatitis and pancreatitis were diagnosed; symptoms began five days before admission; hepatic failure progressed and liver enzymes peaked on hospital day 7 (ASAT 291 IU/l, alkaline phosphatase 75 IU/l, bilirubin 8.0 mg/dl); on admission ASAT 129 IU/l (<25), ALAT 130 IU/l (<32), alkaline phosphatase 31 IU/l (<60), bilirubin 5.2 mg/dl (<1). Patient died on day 26 from multiple organ failure with subarachnoid hemorrhage and generalized Aspergillus fumigatus infection. Chelating agents dimercaprol (BAL) and dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA/succimer) were used therapeutically and are not implicated as causes.

raw_record.support_text: A 33-year-old pregnant woman (35 weeks) presented 3 days after intentional ingestion of 30 grams of acetaminophen, with elevated ALT (785 IU/L) and AST (630 IU/L), a detectable acetaminophen level of 14 mg/dL, and INR of 1.7, consistent with delayed acetaminophen toxicity. She was treated with n-acetylcysteine, but developed worsening coagulopathy, fulminant hepatic failure with peak AST 6693 IU/L and peak ALT 5566 IU/L, acute renal injury, congestive heart failure, and acute lung injury requiring ventilation. She recovered and was discharged on day 14; the fetus delivered stillborn 72 hours after ingestion.

raw_record.extra_details: Delayed acetaminophen toxicity; fulminant hepatic failure attributed to acetaminophen-induced liver injury; presenting ALT 785 IU/L and AST 630 IU/L, INR 1.7 rising to 3.0; peak AST 6693 IU/L and peak ALT 5566 IU/L; acetaminophen level 14 mg/dL; acute renal injury, congestive heart failure, acute lung injury; n-acetylcysteine continued until hepatic improvement; discharged day 14 after complete recovery. NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) toxic byproduct forms in fetal liver at a lower rate than adults due to immature P450 system; acetaminophen crosses the placenta with fetal levels approximating maternal levels.

The study was terminated as an emergency at week 13 when seven of 15 patients were discovered to have developed severe hepatotoxicity and progressive lactic acidosis that progressed despite the drug being stopped. Three other patients showed mild hepatotoxicity; of the seven worst affected, only two survived following orthotopic liver transplantation, three died despite receiving a transplant, and two succumbed before transplantation.

raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective analysis of 454 patients referred with paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity during 1992-2002, of whom 117 with available phosphate measurements at 48-96 h postoverdose were analysed. Median time from ingestion to admission was 24 h (range 5-96 h). 58 (49.6%) spontaneous survivors did not meet KCH criteria; 50.4% met KCH criteria, of whom 11 were transplanted and 48 died without transplant. Serum phosphate was significantly higher in nonsurvivors/transplanted patients than survivors on day 2 (1.32 ± 1.06 vs 0.66 ± 0.26 mmol/L, P<0.001) but not day 3 (P=0.16). Related risk prediction literature (Schmidt and Dalhoff) referenced.

raw_record.support_text: Aplaviroc (GSK873140, ONO-4128, AK-602), a small-molecule CCR5 antagonist licensed from Ono Pharmaceuticals, appeared well tolerated on short-term administration apart from mild/moderate gastrointestinal effects. However, chronic administration produced cases of severe liver toxicity, leading to early termination of Phase IIb studies in treatment-naive patients in September 2005. A further case of elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin in a treatment-experienced patient from the Phase III trial ended all development activities on aplaviroc. The authors note the absence of reported human hepatotoxicity with the other advanced CCR5 antagonists supports the idea that these findings are compound specific rather than due to CCR5 blockade.
raw_record.extra_details: CCR5 antagonist for HIV-1 therapy. Chronic administration produced severe liver toxicity, leading to early termination of Phase IIb studies in treatment-naive patients in September 2005; a further case of elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin in a treatment-experienced patient in the Phase III trial ended all development. In a Phase IIa study, 600 mg b.i.d. for 10 days gave mean viral load reduction of 1.66 log10 copies/ml; short-term administration showed only mild/moderate GI side effects (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain). No hepatotoxicity attributed to CCR5 blockade itself; absence of hepatotoxicity with other advanced CCR5 antagonists supports compound specificity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that excessive intake of APAP (acetaminophen/paracetamol) can lead to serious complications, including acute liver injury, liver failure, and even death (Yoon et al., 2016), primarily as liver failure caused by centrilobular necrosis. Doses greater than 12 g or serum APAP concentrations above the therapeutic threshold on the APAP nomogram increase the risk of hepatotoxicity, and N-acetylcysteine is the standard antidote. In the reported case, a previously healthy 15-year-old female ingested 108 Compound paracetamol and Amantadine hydrochloride tablets (each containing 250 mg APAP, about 27 g total APAP) and developed liver injury, coagulation abnormalities, electrolyte imbalances, and psychiatric symptoms, recovering on the seventh day after overdosing.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; the patient ingested 108 combination tablets in a single-acting suicide-type event (adolescent). Liver injury occurred in combination-tablet overdose in which paracetamol is identified as the hepatotoxic constituent.
raw_record.extra_details: Ingested total APAP dose about 27 g (108 tablets x 250 mg). Excessive APAP intake associated with risk of acute liver injury, liver failure, and death; hepatotoxicity risk increased at doses >12 g or serum APAP above the nomogram therapeutic threshold. Injury characterized as centrilobular necrosis (liver failure). Approximately 300 deaths from APAP poisoning in the US in 2020 (Gummin et al.). N-Acetylcysteine used as antidote; hemodialysis considered for large ingestions. Case patient also developed coagulation abnormalities, electrolyte imbalances, psychiatric symptoms, diffuse subcutaneous pneumatosis, and recovered by day 7.

raw_record.support_text: When FIAU (1-(2'-deoxy-2'-fluoro-1-β-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-iodouracil) was orally applied to 15 patients with chronic hepatitis B, unanticipated liver toxicity was observed weeks later in 10 patients, of whom seven suffered severe toxicity and five died. Paragraph 2 states the clinical symptoms indicated mitochondrial toxicity, i.e., interference with mitochondrial DNA synthesis and function, as a result of FIAU treatment, involving incorporation of FIAU triphosphate into mtDNA.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients had underlying chronic hepatitis B; FIAU was administered orally as antiviral treatment. Liver toxicity was attributed to mitochondrial toxicity (interference with mtDNA synthesis/function) rather than a defined clinical hepatitis phenotype.
raw_record.extra_details: Adverse event data: of 15 treated patients, 10 developed liver toxicity, 7 had severe toxicity, and 5 died. Proposed mechanism: FIAU-TP is incorporated into mtDNA by mtDNA polymerase (low selectivity), leading to mtDNA synthesis dysfunction with no efficient repair of incorporated FIAU monophosphate. FIAU and its in vivo metabolite FMAU are more efficient substrates for TK2 (~30% of deoxythymidine Vmax/Km) than TK1 (2-5%), providing a basis for mitochondrial toxicity. FMAU (1-(2'-deoxy-2'-fluoro-β-D-arabinofuranosyl)-5-methyluracil) noted only as an in vivo metabolite, not independently attributed as the injuring entity.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that hepatic effects of copper sulfate poisoning occur 2 to 3 days after ingestion and present clinically as hepatomegaly and jaundice. When the copper content of the liver exceeds 45 mg/g dry weight, necrosis of hepatocytes occurs, and histologic findings include centrilobular necrosis and centrilobular biliary stasis. A pediatric case in the accompanying table (Salmon, 15 months, CuSO4-containing hot water system) was reported with pink disease and hepatotoxicity treated with D-penicillamine and corticosteroids, with full recovery.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose/poisoning context (copper sulfate ingestion or systemic absorption); includes a pediatric case (15-month-old, hepatotoxicity from a CuSO4-containing hot water system).
raw_record.extra_details: Hepatic effects appear 2-3 days after ingestion; hepatocyte necrosis occurs when liver copper exceeds 45 mg/g dry weight; histology showed centrilobular necrosis and centrilobular biliary stasis. Pediatric hepatotoxicity case (Salmon): treated with D-penicillamine and corticosteroids, outcome full recovery. General manifestations of copper sulfate poisoning also include jaundice and hepatomegaly.

She died shortly afterwards, and gross hepatic and renal damage were found at necropsy.

Affected liver cells showed coagulative degeneration with shrinkage, intense cytoplasmic eosinophilia, and nuclear lysis or karyorrhexis, with variable dropout of cells. Iron stains showed mild to moderate staining of necrotic hepatocytes and some staining of sinusoids in affected areas, with liver tissue iron levels ranging from 1600 to 4182 microg of dry tissue (reference value 21-450 microg).

raw_record.extra_details: Case series of 11 pediatric patients (autopsy material) with liver involvement in several cases (patients 1, 4, 6, 7). Liver tissue iron levels 1600-4182 microg/g dry tissue (reference 21-450 microg/g). Stated liver-cell damage is likely direct toxicity by absorbed metal reaching cells via the portal vein; main mechanism of death was gastrointestinal hemorrhage with shock and neurologic symptoms.

The donor had undergone liver transplantation for the acute liver failure; the acute kidney injury was attributed to acute hepatorenal syndrome because no interstitial nephritis or vasculitis was present on renal biopsy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Adult patient treated with PTU for hyperthyroidism; injury described in a kidney donor. Kidneys were transplanted from this donor and functioned, indicating the PTU-related liver failure did not preclude kidney use.
raw_record.extra_details: The donor was a 19-year-old African American woman. She presented with acute hepatic and renal failure after PTU treatment and underwent liver transplantation 5 days after presentation, but was declared brain dead 1 day after that transplant. No PTU-associated renal disease (interstitial nephritis or ANCA-positive vasculitis) was seen on donor kidney biopsy; the acute kidney injury was attributed to hepatorenal syndrome. The paper reports no adverse PTU hepatotoxicity in the kidney recipients.
